title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.1 Our data, a payment register
An auditor rarely does just one thing to the data. Take the payment register of a Public Works division. We may want to keep the vouchers of one office, then keep those above a limit, then sort them by amount, and then look at the top ten. That is four steps, one after the other. Each step works on the result of the step before it.
Written the usual way, such a chain of steps is hard to read. Either the functions sit one inside another, and must be read from the inside out. Or we create a new object after every step, and the workspace fills with objects we do not need. Pipes solve this problem. They let us write the steps in the order in which we think of them, one step per line. The code then reads like the audit programme itself.
In this chapter we learn the two pipes of R, how to send the result into an argument other than the first, and which pipe to use. We practise on a small payment register. At the end we use a short chain of pipes to find bills kept just below a sanction limit.
There are two pipes in R.
Let us create a small payment register of a Public Works division for the financial year 2024-25. Each row is one payment voucher, made by one of four sub-division offices. All names are made up. The code is folded. New readers need not worry about it now.
Code to create the payment registerset.seed(2024)
offices <- c("Pune", "Nashik", "Nagpur", "Kolhapur")
vendors <- c("Shree Ganesh Builders", "Patil Constructions", "Deshmukh Traders",
             "Sai Krupa Enterprises", "Jadhav Electricals", "Mahalaxmi Suppliers",
             "Gawande Infra", "Om Stationers")
n <- 54
payments <- data.frame(
  office       = sample(offices, n, replace = TRUE),
  vendor       = sample(vendors, n, replace = TRUE),
  voucher_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:364, n, replace = TRUE),
  amount       = round(exp(runif(n, log(5000), log(450000))), -2)
)

# Planted. Six bills of one vendor at Nashik, each just below Rs 1 lakh,
# paid within a fortnight
split_bills <- data.frame(
  office       = "Nashik",
  vendor       = "Sai Krupa Enterprises",
  voucher_date = as.Date("2025-01-06") + c(0, 2, 3, 7, 9, 12),
  amount       = c(99500, 98000, 99900, 97800, 99000, 98600)
)

payments <- rbind(payments, split_bills)
payments <- payments[order(payments$voucher_date), ]
payments$voucher_no <- sprintf("PV/24-25/%03d", seq_len(nrow(payments)))
payments <- payments[, c("voucher_no", "voucher_date", "office", "vendor", "amount")]
rownames(payments) <- NULL
head(payments)

    voucher_no voucher_date   office                vendor amount
1 PV/24-25/001   2024-05-01   Nashik      Deshmukh Traders   7200
2 PV/24-25/002   2024-05-01     Pune         Om Stationers 329700
3 PV/24-25/003   2024-05-04   Nagpur   Mahalaxmi Suppliers 277300
4 PV/24-25/004   2024-05-07 Kolhapur Sai Krupa Enterprises  46700
5 PV/24-25/005   2024-05-26   Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  43300
6 PV/24-25/006   2024-06-03   Nagpur         Om Stationers 396000
The register has 60 vouchers, worth ₹63.71 lakh in all.

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.2 What a pipe does
Suppose we have to apply three functions, FIRST, SECOND and THIRD, to an object OBJ, in that order. We could write
THIRD(SECOND(FIRST(OBJ)))
which has to be read from the inside out. Or we could create intermediate objects which we do not really need.
OBJ1 <- FIRST(OBJ)
OBJ2 <- SECOND(OBJ1)
OBJ3 <- THIRD(OBJ2)
So we either give up readability, or clutter the workspace with objects like OBJ1 and OBJ2. Pipes solve both problems at once. The pipe passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right. With pipes we can write the above as either of these.
OBJ |> FIRST() |> SECOND() |> THIRD()
OBJ %>% FIRST() %>% SECOND() %>% THIRD()
Read |> as “and then”. Take OBJ, and then apply FIRST(), and then SECOND(), and then THIRD().
Let us find the three largest payments in our register, in ₹ lakh. First the usual way, and then with pipes.

# the three largest amounts, in lakh, the usual way
round(head(sort(payments$amount, decreasing = TRUE), 3) / 1e5, 2)

[1] 4.38 4.23 3.96

# the same with pipes
payments$amount |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |>
  head(3) |>
  (\(x) round(x / 1e5, 2))()

[1] 4.38 4.23 3.96


The second form reads from top to bottom. Take the amounts, and then sort them in decreasing order, and then keep the first three, and then convert them to lakh. (The last line uses a small anonymous function. We explain it later in this chapter.)






WarningCaution



A pipe does not change the object it starts from. After the chain above, payments still holds all 60 vouchers in the original order. The result is only printed. To keep it, assign it to a new name, like top3 <- payments$amount |> .... Otherwise a later step may use the old object by mistake.


The real power of pipes shows with the tidyverse, where a whole analysis, filtering, grouping and summarising, reads as one sentence. We will use them in every chapter from Chapter 15 onward. A diagrammatic representation is given in Figure 5.2.







Figure 5.2: A diagrammatic illustration of the pipe in base R and tidyverse




Two questions may arise here.

What if the result on the left is needed in some argument other than the first?
Is there any difference between the two pipes, and which is better?

To answer these, we discuss the two pipes separately.







Figure 5.3: Using pipes in R

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.3 Magrittr/Dplyr pipe %>%

The pipe passes the result on its left into the first argument of the function on its right. So data %>% filter(col == 'A') means filter(data, col == 'A'). But sometimes the result is needed in another argument.
A good example is the base R function aggregate(). It totals a column by groups. We write the formula first, like amount ~ office, which means “amount by office”. The data comes second, in the argument data. For such cases, %>% has the placeholder ., which stands for the result on the left. The filter example could be written as data %>% filter(., col == 'A'). With the placeholder, we can put the result wherever we want. Let us total the payments of each office.

payments %>% aggregate(amount ~ office, data = ., FUN = sum)

    office  amount
1 Kolhapur 1297100
2   Nagpur 1310500
3   Nashik 1574200
4     Pune 2189400


Thus x %>% f(y) is equivalent to f(x, y) but x %>% f(y, .) is equivalent to f(y, x).

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.4 Base R pipe |>

R version 4.2.0 gave the native pipe a placeholder too, _, similar to the . of magrittr, but with a few differences.

The argument where _ is used must be named. So f(y, z = x) can be written as x |> f(y, z = _).

_ can be used only once on the right side.


payments |>
  aggregate(amount ~ office, data = _, FUN = sum)

    office  amount
1 Kolhapur 1297100
2   Nagpur 1310500
3   Nashik 1574200
4     Pune 2189400


The magrittr pipe does not need the argument to be named. So payments %>% aggregate(amount ~ office, ., sum) works. But payments |> aggregate(amount ~ office, _, sum) gives an error. In such cases, we can use an anonymous function, \(x), which we learnt in Chapter 3. See these.
# placeholder without named argument
payments |> aggregate(amount ~ office, _, sum)

# Correct way to use unnamed argument
payments |>
  (\(d) aggregate(amount ~ office, d, sum))()

    office  amount
1 Kolhapur 1297100
2   Nagpur 1310500
3   Nashik 1574200
4     Pune 2189400


The anonymous function is wrapped in parentheses and followed by (), so that the pipe sees a function call.
Since R 4.3, _ can also start a chain of extractions, like payments |> _$amount, or x |> _[[1]]. This is handy when we want one column out of a table in the middle of a chain.

payments |> _$amount |> sum()

[1] 6371200


Type ?`|>` in the console and see the help page for more details.

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.5 Which pipe to use?
For most work, the two pipes are interchangeable. The differences are small.


Table 5.1: The two pipes compared









|>
%>%



Needs a package
No, built into R 4.1 and later
Yes, magrittr (loaded with tidyverse)


Placeholder

_, only with a named argument

., anywhere


Function without ()

Not allowed, x |> head()

Allowed, x %>% head



Speed
Slightly faster
Slightly slower






We use |> in this book, because it needs no package and is now the standard. In RStudio, the shortcut Ctrl + Shift + M types a pipe. To make it type |>, tick Use native pipe operator under Tools > Global Options > Code.






TipAudit tip



A pipe reads as a sequence of audit steps. Take the payments, and then keep those of 2024-25, and then group by vendor, and then total them. Write each step on its own line, with a comment where the reason is not obvious. Your reviewer can then check the logic line by line, just like a working paper.

title: 5  Pipes
section: 5.6 Audit use case, bills kept just below a sanction limit
text:
5.6 Audit use case, bills kept just below a sanction limit
Suppose the head of a sub-division office may sanction a bill of up to ₹1 lakh. A larger purchase needs the sanction of a higher authority. An office which wants to avoid that sanction may split one purchase into several bills, each just below ₹1 lakh. Auditors call this splitting of bills.
Let us look for it with a short chain of pipes. We keep the vouchers between ₹95,000 and ₹1 lakh, take out the office column, and count the vouchers of each office. The base R function subset() keeps the rows of a data frame which meet a condition. table() counts each value (Chapter 4).

payments |>
  subset(amount >= 95000 & amount < 100000) |>
  _$office |>
  table()


Nashik 
     6 


Only one office has any. Nashik has 6 such vouchers. Let us see them.

payments |>
  subset(office == "Nashik" & amount >= 95000 & amount < 100000)

     voucher_no voucher_date office                vendor amount
43 PV/24-25/043   2025-01-06 Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  99500
45 PV/24-25/045   2025-01-08 Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  98000
46 PV/24-25/046   2025-01-09 Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  99900
47 PV/24-25/047   2025-01-13 Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  97800
48 PV/24-25/048   2025-01-15 Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  99000
50 PV/24-25/050   2025-01-18 Nashik Sai Krupa Enterprises  98600


All 6 bills are from one vendor, Sai Krupa Enterprises. They were paid between 06 January 2025 and 18 January 2025. Together they come to ₹5.93 lakh, well above the limit of ₹1 lakh.
This is not yet proof of splitting. The bills may be for different works, each genuinely small. The auditor would next call for the files of these vouchers. Were they for the same item or the same work? Was there one demand, broken up into several bills? Was the higher sanction needed? The answers, and copies of the bills, go into the working papers.
Note how the chain reads. Take the payments, and then keep those just below the limit, and then take the office column, and then count by office. Each line is one audit step.

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.7 A suggested workflow
Here is a simple routine for writing a chain of steps with pipes.


Plan the steps in words. Write the audit steps as one sentence joined by “and then”. Each “and then” becomes one pipe.

Start with the data. Begin the chain with the object, like the payments, and not with a function wrapped around it.

Use the native pipe. Use |> in your own code. Tick Use native pipe operator under Tools > Global Options > Code, so that Ctrl + Shift + M types it.

Write one step per line. End each line with the pipe. Add a comment where the reason for a step is not obvious.

Build the chain bit by bit. Run the chain after adding each step, and check the result before adding the next one.

Handle other arguments. When the result must go into an argument other than the first, use _ with a named argument. If the argument has no name, use an anonymous function \(x). Use _$column to take out one column in the middle of a chain.

Recognise both pipes. Read %>% in code from books and the internet as the same “and then”. Its placeholder is ..







ImportantRemember



A pipe passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then”. A chain written one step per line reads like a working paper, so a reviewer can check it line by line.

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.8 Where next
Pipes are used in almost every later chapter. In Chapter 15 we join them with the verbs of dplyr, which select, filter, sort and summarise data in one readable chain.

title: 5  Pipes
text:
5.9 Try it yourself
These exercises use the payment register payments of this chapter. Write each answer as a chain of pipes, and try it before opening the solution.


The five largest payments. Change the chain of this chapter to show the five largest payments, in ₹ lakh, instead of three.






TipSolution






payments$amount |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |>
  head(5) |>
  (\(x) round(x / 1e5, 2))()

[1] 4.38 4.23 3.96 3.75 3.30


Only head(3) changes to head(5). The largest payment is ₹4.38 lakh.





Bills above ₹1 lakh in each office. Count the vouchers of more than ₹1 lakh in each office. Which office has the most?






TipSolution






payments |>
  subset(amount > 100000) |>
  _$office |>
  table() |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)


    Pune Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik 
       8        4        4        4 


Pune has the most, with 8 such vouchers. The chain is the same as in the audit use case. Only the condition changes, and sort() puts the largest count first.





Total paid to each vendor. Total the payments of each vendor with aggregate() and the native pipe. Then write the same chain with %>%.






TipSolution






payments |>
  aggregate(amount ~ vendor, data = _, FUN = sum)

                 vendor  amount
1      Deshmukh Traders  320700
2         Gawande Infra  307900
3    Jadhav Electricals  952100
4   Mahalaxmi Suppliers  927200
5         Om Stationers  839400
6   Patil Constructions  391000
7 Sai Krupa Enterprises 1238500
8 Shree Ganesh Builders 1394400

payments %>%
  aggregate(amount ~ vendor, data = ., FUN = sum)

                 vendor  amount
1      Deshmukh Traders  320700
2         Gawande Infra  307900
3    Jadhav Electricals  952100
4   Mahalaxmi Suppliers  927200
5         Om Stationers  839400
6   Patil Constructions  391000
7 Sai Krupa Enterprises 1238500
8 Shree Ganesh Builders 1394400


Both give the same table. The native pipe needs _ in the named argument data. The magrittr pipe uses .. The largest total, ₹13.94 lakh, went to Shree Ganesh Builders.





A wider band below the limit. The audit use case looked at bills between ₹95,000 and ₹1 lakh. Widen the band to ₹90,000 and count the vouchers of each office again. Does any other office now appear?






TipSolution






payments |>
  subset(amount >= 90000 & amount < 100000) |>
  _$office |>
  table()


Nagpur Nashik 
     1      6 


Now Nagpur also appears, with 1 voucher. One or two bills near a limit are common. What marked Nashik was many bills of one vendor in a short time. A wider band catches more cases, but each extra case needs time to check. Choose the band with the delegation order in mind.

title: 5  Pipes
text: Stefan Milton Bache and Hadley Wickham, Magrittr: A Forward-Pipe Operator for r, 2025, https://magrittr.tidyverse.org.↩︎

title: 6  Conditions and Loops
text:
6.1 Control flow and loops
Audit rules are full of conditions. If the bill is above ₹50,000, it needs the sanction of a higher authority. If the work is not completed by the due date, liquidated damages are to be recovered. If a pensioner has not submitted a life certificate, the pension is to be stopped. And audit work is full of repetition. The same checks are run on the accounts of every district, and the same file is read for every month. In R, conditions are written with if and else, and repetition with loops.
So far our code has run line by line, from top to bottom. Control statements change this flow. if and else run some code only when a condition holds, and loops (for, while and repeat) run some code again and again. Together with functions (Chapter 3), they let us automate any task.
In data analysis we need them less than in other programming, because R’s functions work on whole vectors at once, and the tidyverse handles most repetition for us. Still, they are core concepts of any programming language, and are needed often enough, for example to process a folder of files one by one, or inside our own functions.

title: 6  Conditions and Loops
text:
if else
The basic forms of the if else statement in R are these.
if (test) do_this_if_true
if (test) do_this_if_true else else_do_this
So, if test is TRUE, do_this_if_true is run, and, optionally, if it is FALSE, else_do_this is run. See this example.

x <- 50
if(x < 10){
  'Smaller than 10'
} else {
  '10 or more'
}

[1] "10 or more"


The same pattern answers a simple audit question about one bill.

bill_amount <- 62000
if (bill_amount > 50000) {
  'Check the sanction of the higher authority'
} else {
  'Within the powers of the drawing officer'
}

[1] "Check the sanction of the higher authority"


Several conditions can be chained with else if. They are checked in order, and the first one which is TRUE decides. Let us write a function which tells the authority competent to sanction an expenditure, under some made-up financial powers.

sanctioning_authority <- function(amount) {
  if (amount <= 50000) {
    "Section Officer"
  } else if (amount <= 500000) {
    "Deputy Secretary"
  } else if (amount <= 2500000) {
    "Joint Secretary"
  } else {
    "Secretary"
  }
}
sanctioning_authority(42000)

[1] "Section Officer"

sanctioning_authority(1800000)

[1] "Joint Secretary"








TipAudit tip



Look hard at the limits. The function uses <=, so an amount of exactly ₹50,000 goes to the Section Officer. Read the actual delegation order. If it says “below ₹50,000”, the test must be < instead. Test the function with amounts exactly on each limit, and one rupee on either side.








WarningCaution



if checks a single TRUE or FALSE. Unlike the function ifelse(), it is not vectorised. Given a vector of conditions, it stops with an error (since R 4.2). And given NA, it stops too, since it cannot decide which way to go.



if (c(10, 60) > 50) "large"

Error in `if (c(10, 60) > 50) ...`:
! the condition has length > 1

if (NA > 50) "large"

Error in `if (NA > 50) ...`:
! missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed


To combine conditions in if, use && and ||, which work on single values. To guard against NA, wrap the condition in isTRUE(), which is TRUE only for a single TRUE. And to apply the function above to a whole vector of amounts, use sapply() or purrr::map_chr(), which we will learn in Section 7.5, or better, the vectorised dplyr::case_when().
switch()
When the choice depends on a single value, switch() is neater than a long chain of else if.

fund_name <- function(code) {
  switch(code,
         CFI = "Consolidated Fund of India",
         CON = "Contingency Fund",
         PA  = "Public Account",
         "Unknown code")   # the last, unnamed value is the default
}
fund_name("PA")

[1] "Public Account"

fund_name("XYZ")

[1] "Unknown code"



for loop
A for loop runs some code once for each item of a vector. The basic structure is this.
for(item in vector) perform_some_action

# OR

for(item in vector) {
  perform_some_action
}
For each item in vector, perform_some_action is run once, with item taking the next value each time. See this simple example.

for(i in 1:3){
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3


By convention, i is used for the item, but any name may be used.

for(item in 1:3){
  print(item)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3


The for loop creates the item in the current environment, overwriting any existing object with the same name. See this example.

x <- 500
for(x in 1:3){
  # do nothing
}
x

[1] 3






A Diagrammatic representation of For Loop



We can loop over positions, to work with as many elements as we want. See these two examples. The first loops over the first four offices only.

my_offices <- c('DTO Ajmer', 'DTO Alwar', 'DTO Bikaner', 'DTO Jaipur', 'DTO Kota')
# If we want first 4 elements
for(i in 1:4){
  print(my_offices[i])
}

[1] "DTO Ajmer"
[1] "DTO Alwar"
[1] "DTO Bikaner"
[1] "DTO Jaipur"


The second loops over all of them.

# if we want all elements
for(i in seq_along(my_offices)){
  print(my_offices[i])
}

[1] "DTO Ajmer"
[1] "DTO Alwar"
[1] "DTO Bikaner"
[1] "DTO Jaipur"
[1] "DTO Kota"


Storing the results. A loop which only prints is of limited use. Usually we store each result. Create an empty vector of the right length before the loop, and fill it in. Growing a vector inside a loop, with c(), works but becomes very slow for long loops.

amounts <- c(42000, 1800000, 260000, 9000000)
authority <- character(length(amounts))   # empty vector, filled in below
for (i in seq_along(amounts)) {
  authority[i] <- sanctioning_authority(amounts[i])
}
authority

[1] "Section Officer"  "Joint Secretary"  "Deputy Secretary" "Secretary"       


There are two ways to end an iteration, or the loop, early.


next skips the rest of the current iteration, and moves to the next item.

break ends the entire loop.

See these examples. With next, the loop skips the fourth item and carries on.

for(i in 1:5){
  if (i == 4){
    next
  }
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 5


With break, the loop stops at the fourth item.

for(i in 1:5){
  if (i == 4){
    break
  }
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3


In audit, next is handy to skip records that should not be checked, like cancelled vouchers.

voucher <- c("V-101", "V-102", "V-103", "V-104")
status  <- c("Paid", "Cancelled", "Paid", "Paid")
for (i in seq_along(voucher)) {
  if (status[i] == "Cancelled") next
  print(paste("Checking", voucher[i]))
}

[1] "Checking V-101"
[1] "Checking V-103"
[1] "Checking V-104"



while loop
A for loop runs over known values, a known number of times. To repeat something an unknown number of times, we use a while loop, which repeats as long as a condition is TRUE. Another option is the repeat loop, which repeats until it meets a break.
The basic syntax of the while loop is this.
while (condition) action
See these examples. The first counts up.

i <- 1
while(i <=4){
  print(LETTERS[i])
  i <- i+1
}

[1] "A"
[1] "B"
[1] "C"
[1] "D"


We may check the value of i after the loop has run.

i

[1] 5


The second counts down.

i <- 4
while(i >= 1){
  print(LETTERS[i])
  i <- i-1
}

[1] "D"
[1] "C"
[1] "B"
[1] "A"


The code inside the loop must change something in the condition, so that sooner or later it is no longer TRUE. Otherwise the loop never ends. If that happens, press Esc in RStudio to stop it.
Here is a while loop with a real use. How many years will a deposit of ₹10 lakh at 7% compound interest take to double? An auditor may ask this when checking the maturity value claimed for a fixed deposit of idle scheme funds.

balance <- 1000000
years <- 0
while (balance < 2000000) {
  balance <- balance * 1.07
  years <- years + 1
}
years

[1] 11


The same can be written with repeat and break.

balance <- 1000000
years <- 0
repeat {
  balance <- balance * 1.07
  years <- years + 1
  if (balance >= 2000000) break
}
years

[1] 11






Author’s illustration of While Loop









NoteLoops or vectors?



Before writing a loop over the rows of a table, check whether a vectorised function can do the job, as it usually can. amounts * 1.18 adds GST to every amount at once, and ifelse() or dplyr::case_when() classify every row at once. Such code is shorter, clearer, and much faster on large data. Where repetition is really needed, like reading many files, the functions of the apply family and of purrr, discussed in Chapter 7, are usually neater than a loop. Loops are not wrong, though. A clear loop is better than clever code you cannot check.

title: 6  Conditions and Loops
text:
6.2 A suggested workflow


Look for a vectorised way first. Before writing a loop over rows, check whether ifelse() or dplyr::case_when() can do the job on the whole column at once.

Write the rule for one value. Express the decision with if, else if and else, or with switch() when the choice depends on a single code.

Guard against NA. Use &&, || and isTRUE() so that a missing value does not stop the code.

Test the rule on a few known values. Try amounts just below and just above each limit. Check that the answer is what the rules say.

Prepare storage before looping. Create an empty vector of the right length with character() or numeric(), and loop over seq_along().

Use next and break with care. Skip items that should not be processed, and stop early only when the job is truly done.

Make sure a while loop can end. The code inside must change the condition. If it runs forever, press Esc in RStudio.







ImportantRemember



if checks a single TRUE or FALSE, not a whole column. For a column of amounts, use a vectorised function. A clear loop is still better than clever code you cannot check.

title: 6  Conditions and Loops
text:
6.3 Try it yourself
These exercises use the function sanctioning_authority() and the small vectors of this chapter. Try each before opening the solution.


Test the first limit. Check sanctioning_authority() with ₹50,000 and ₹50,001. Who sanctions each?






TipSolution






sanctioning_authority(50000)

[1] "Section Officer"

sanctioning_authority(50001)

[1] "Deputy Secretary"


₹50,000 goes to the Section Officer, and one rupee more goes to the Deputy Secretary. This is the test with amounts on a limit that the Audit tip asks for. Compare the answers with the delegation order.





Name the voucher type. Write a function voucher_type() with switch(). It should give “Payment voucher” for the code PV, “Transfer voucher” for TV, “Journal voucher” for JV, and “Check the code” for anything else. Test it with JV and XV.






TipSolution






voucher_type <- function(code) {
  switch(code,
         PV = "Payment voucher",
         TV = "Transfer voucher",
         JV = "Journal voucher",
         "Check the code")
}
voucher_type("JV")

[1] "Journal voucher"

voucher_type("XV")

[1] "Check the code"


The last, unnamed value is the default. A code that is not in the list gets “Check the code”, so a wrong code in the auditee’s data does not pass unnoticed.





A missing amount. A bill has no amount recorded, so bill <- NA. Write an if statement that says “Amount missing” for such a bill, “Check the higher sanction” above ₹50,000, and “Within powers” otherwise.






TipSolution






bill <- NA
if (is.na(bill)) {
  "Amount missing"
} else if (bill > 50000) {
  "Check the higher sanction"
} else {
  "Within powers"
}

[1] "Amount missing"


The test for NA must come first. Otherwise if (NA > 50000) stops with an error, as we saw in this chapter. A missing amount is itself a point for audit, so it should not be quietly put under “Within powers”.





Skip the cancelled vouchers. Five vouchers have these amounts and status. Loop over them, skip the cancelled ones, and store the sanctioning authority of each paid voucher. Leave the cancelled ones empty.
v_no     <- c("V-201", "V-202", "V-203", "V-204", "V-205")
v_amount <- c(48000, 650000, 3200000, 75000, 51000)
v_status <- c("Paid", "Paid", "Cancelled", "Paid", "Paid")






TipSolution






v_no     <- c("V-201", "V-202", "V-203", "V-204", "V-205")
v_amount <- c(48000, 650000, 3200000, 75000, 51000)
v_status <- c("Paid", "Paid", "Cancelled", "Paid", "Paid")

v_authority <- character(length(v_no))   # empty, filled in below
for (i in seq_along(v_no)) {
  if (v_status[i] == "Cancelled") next
  v_authority[i] <- sanctioning_authority(v_amount[i])
}
data.frame(v_no, v_amount, v_status, v_authority)

   v_no v_amount  v_status      v_authority
1 V-201    48000      Paid  Section Officer
2 V-202   650000      Paid  Joint Secretary
3 V-203  3200000 Cancelled                 
4 V-204    75000      Paid Deputy Secretary
5 V-205    51000      Paid Deputy Secretary


The cancelled voucher V-203 is skipped, so its authority stays empty. Of the paid vouchers, 2 needed the Deputy Secretary. The auditor would check that each file carries the sanction of that authority.





Doubling at a lower rate. A bank offered 6.5% compound interest on ₹10 lakh of idle scheme funds. With a while loop, find how many years the deposit takes to double.






TipSolution






deposit <- 1000000
n_years <- 0
while (deposit < 2000000) {
  deposit <- deposit * 1.065
  n_years <- n_years + 1
}
n_years

[1] 12

round(deposit / 1e5, 2)   # the balance in lakh at that time

[1] 21.29


It takes 12 years, against 11 years at 7%. By then the deposit is ₹21.29 lakh. The same loop, with the actual rate and period, checks the maturity value that the bank has claimed.

title: 7  Functional Programming
text:
7.1 What is functional programming?
A Public Works department has dozens of divisions. Each sends its voucher file every month. The auditor wants to run the same checks on every file. What did the division spend? How much of it was spent in March? Which vouchers are above the limit? Doing this by hand, file by file, is slow. Copying the code for each file and editing it is quicker, but risky. One forgotten edit, and one division is checked against the wrong limit, without anyone noticing.
The better way is to write the check once, as a function, and then tell R to apply it to every file. This idea, applying a function to each element of a collection, is the heart of functional programming. R is very good at it.
In this chapter we learn the base R tools for this, the apply family, and then the more consistent tools of the package purrr. We practise on the voucher register of four sub-division offices, and on its quarter-wise expenditure. At the end, we check every office for a rush of expenditure in March, with one function applied to all four.
Conceptually functional programming philosophy is based on lambda calculus. Lambda calculus is a framework developed by Alonzo Church1 to study computations with functions.
Functional programming is a style of programming built around functions, in the mathematical sense. It is declarative. Its focus is on what to solve, in contrast to the imperative style, like a for loop, whose focus is on how to solve. For a fuller definition, readers may see this Wikipedia link. Put simply, instead of writing a loop which says “take the first element, do this, store the result, take the next element…”, we say “apply this function to every element”, and let R do the rest.
Functional programming uses higher-order functions, functions which take another function as an argument, or return a function. We have already seen one, perhaps without noticing. args() takes a function as its argument, and returns its arguments.
Let us learn a bit more here.

title: 7  Functional Programming
section: 7.2 Our data, vouchers of four offices
text:
7.2 Our data, vouchers of four offices
Our data is the voucher register of a Public Works division for the financial year 2024-25. It has four sub-division offices, at Pune, Nashik, Nagpur and Kolhapur. Each row is one voucher, with its office, date, amount and the GST in it. One office has a rush of large payments in the last fortnight of March, which we find at the end of the chapter. From the vouchers we also make a small matrix, qexp, of the expenditure of each office in each quarter, in lakh. All names are made up, and the code is folded.

Code to create the vouchers and the quarter-wise expenditureset.seed(7)
offices <- c("Pune", "Nashik", "Nagpur", "Kolhapur")
n <- 160
vouchers <- data.frame(
  office       = sample(offices, n, replace = TRUE),
  voucher_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:364, n, replace = TRUE),
  amount       = round(runif(n, 20000, 200000), -2)
)

# Planted. A rush of large payments at Nagpur in the second half of March 2025
march_rush <- data.frame(
  office       = "Nagpur",
  voucher_date = as.Date("2025-03-17") + c(0, 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 13),
  amount       = c(480000, 520000, 450000, 610000, 395000, 560000, 470000)
)

vouchers <- rbind(vouchers, march_rush)
vouchers <- vouchers[order(vouchers$voucher_date), ]
vouchers$voucher_no <- sprintf("TV/24-25/%03d", seq_len(nrow(vouchers)))
vouchers$gst <- round(vouchers$amount * 18 / 118)
vouchers <- vouchers[, c("voucher_no", "office", "voucher_date", "amount", "gst")]
rownames(vouchers) <- NULL

# Quarter of the financial year. April to June is Q1, January to March is Q4
quarter <- paste0("Q", (as.integer(format(vouchers$voucher_date, "%m")) - 4) %% 12 %/% 3 + 1)
# Expenditure of each office in each quarter, in lakh
qexp <- round(tapply(vouchers$amount, list(vouchers$office, quarter), sum) / 1e5, 2)



head(vouchers)

    voucher_no   office voucher_date amount   gst
1 TV/24-25/001     Pune   2024-04-01  53000  8085
2 TV/24-25/002   Nagpur   2024-04-02 163500 24941
3 TV/24-25/003     Pune   2024-04-03 170200 25963
4 TV/24-25/004   Nashik   2024-04-05  36200  5522
5 TV/24-25/005   Nagpur   2024-04-08  65100  9931
6 TV/24-25/006 Kolhapur   2024-04-14 187800 28647

qexp

            Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4
Kolhapur  8.19 19.80 15.51 14.02
Nagpur   10.91 10.86 11.92 40.51
Nashik    6.76 10.54 12.62  8.24
Pune      5.94  7.16  8.86  8.39


The register has 167 vouchers, worth ₹200.25 lakh in all.

7.2.1 Usage of functional programming in R
Strictly speaking, R is not a pure functional programming language, but it supports the style well. We have seen that most functions work on whole vectors at once. But what about lists? Many functions do not work on them. Suppose three amounts have been kept in a list. Check this example.

list1 <- list(50000, 5000, 56)
sum(list1)

Error in `sum()`:
! invalid 'type' (list) of argument


Of course, we can solve the above problem with a for loop. See

list1 <- list(50000, 5000, 56)
# for loop strategy
x <- c()
for(i in seq_along(list1)){
  x[i] <- list1[[i]]
}
sum(x)

[1] 55056


Consider another list, the bills passed by three offices in one week, where we want the average bill of each office.

office_bills <- list(
  Pune   = c(42000, 18500, 61000, 27500),
  Nashik = c(99500, 98000, 99900),
  Nagpur = c(12500, 230000, 45000, 8800, 76000)
)

We may use a for loop again, but in R such operations are done more simply with the apply family of functions, one of the best known features of R. We will come back to office_bills shortly.

title: 7  Functional Programming
text:
7.3 apply family of functions
The first of these functions is apply(), which works on matrices and data frames.

7.3.1 Function apply()

The basic syntax of apply is
apply(m, MARGIN, FUN, f_args)
where


m is the matrix

MARGIN is the dimension. To apply the function to each row, use 1, and to each column, 2


FUN is the function to apply

f_args are any further arguments to be passed to FUN.

An illustrative construction of apply function can be seen in Figure 7.1.







Figure 7.1: Illustration of function apply




Let us find the average quarterly expenditure of each office, from our matrix qexp. Each row is an office, so MARGIN is 1.

apply(qexp, 1, mean)

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
 14.3800  18.5500   9.5400   7.5875 


Note: rowMeans(qexp) would have given the same result. We use a simple example to show the idea.
We may also pass our own function. Government instructions discourage a rush of expenditure at the end of the year. A common yardstick is that not more than a third, 33%, of the year’s spending should fall in the last quarter. Let us write a function which gives the share of the last quarter, Q4, in a row, and then apply it to every office.

q4_share <- function(x){
  round(x[4] / sum(x) * 100, 1)
}
apply(qexp, 1, q4_share)

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
    24.4     54.6     21.6     27.6 


Nagpur spent 54.6% of its year’s money in the last quarter. The other offices are within the yardstick.
If the function is not needed elsewhere, there is no need to define it beforehand. We may write an anonymous function directly inside apply().

apply(qexp, 1, FUN = function(x) round(x[4] / sum(x) * 100, 1))

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
    24.4     54.6     21.6     27.6 








Note



Since R 4.1, a function can be written with a backslash \ in place of the word function (see Chapter 3). We could have written the above as

apply(qexp, 1, FUN = \(x) round(x[4] / sum(x) * 100, 1))
## Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
##     24.4     54.6     21.6     27.6




apply() need not necessarily output vectors only
If FUN returns more than one value for each row or column, the output is a matrix. The thing to note is that the result for each row or column is always placed in a column of the output, whether MARGIN is 1 or 2. (A function like sqrt would not show this well, since apply(m, 1, sqrt) gives the same values as sqrt(m).)
Suppose we want the progressive expenditure of each office, that is, its running total at the end of each quarter. The running total is given by cumsum(). First, let us do it on each column, with MARGIN = 2.

apply(qexp, 2, cumsum)

            Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4
Kolhapur  8.19 19.80 15.51 14.02
Nagpur   19.10 30.66 27.43 54.53
Nashik   25.86 41.20 40.05 62.77
Pune     31.80 48.36 48.91 71.16


The layout is the same as that of qexp. But a running total down a column adds up the offices, which means nothing to us. We want the running total along each row, over the quarters.

apply(qexp, 1, cumsum)

   Kolhapur Nagpur Nashik  Pune
Q1     8.19  10.91   6.76  5.94
Q2    27.99  21.77  17.30 13.10
Q3    43.50  33.69  29.92 21.96
Q4    57.52  74.20  38.16 30.35


The numbers are right, but the output is the transpose of what we expected. The offices are now columns, because the result for each row has gone into a column. Wrap it in t() to get the expected layout.

t(apply(qexp, 1, cumsum))

            Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4
Kolhapur  8.19 27.99 43.50 57.52
Nagpur   10.91 21.77 33.69 74.20
Nashik    6.76 17.30 29.92 38.16
Pune      5.94 13.10 21.96 30.35


Let us check our understanding with one more example, using a function whose output length does not depend on the input. range() always gives two values, the smallest and the largest.

apply(qexp, 1, range)

     Kolhapur Nagpur Nashik Pune
[1,]     8.19  10.86   6.76 5.94
[2,]    19.80  40.51  12.62 8.86


Thus we may conclude that

if FUN returns a single value, the output of apply is a vector whose length is

the number of rows of the input, if MARGIN is 1,
the number of columns of the input, if MARGIN is 2;


if FUN returns a vector of length more than 1, the output is a matrix whose number of columns is

the number of rows of the input, if MARGIN is 1,
the number of columns of the input, if MARGIN is 2.



These have been tabulated in Table 7.1.


Table 7.1: Relation between input and output data structure in apply



Input matrix \(m*n\)

MARGIN = 1
MARGIN = 2



FUN gives scalar
Vector size \(m\)

Vector size \(n\)



FUN gives vector size \(p\)

Matrix \(p*m\)

Matrix \(p*n\)







So we have to be careful with the output of apply(), or it may introduce a bug in our code.

apply() on data frames
Data frames, though a kind of list, also behave like matrices, so we may use apply() on them too. Let us turn qexp into a data frame, and total each quarter.

(qexp_df <- as.data.frame(qexp))

            Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4
Kolhapur  8.19 19.80 15.51 14.02
Nagpur   10.91 10.86 11.92 40.51
Nashik    6.76 10.54 12.62  8.24
Pune      5.94  7.16  8.86  8.39

apply(qexp_df, 2, sum)

   Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4 
31.80 48.36 48.91 71.16 








WarningCaution



apply() first converts a data frame into a matrix. If the data frame has even one text column, every value becomes text, and numeric functions fail or give wrong results. See what happens when we try to add GST to each amount, row by row, while the voucher number is also in the data.

small <- vouchers[1:4, c("voucher_no", "amount")]
apply(small, 1, \(r) r["amount"] * 1.18)

Error in `r["amount"] * 1.18`:
! non-numeric argument to binary operator


The amounts had become text, and text cannot be multiplied. Use apply() only on all-numeric data, and prefer lapply(), sapply() or, in the tidyverse, across() (Section 15.15) for data frames.



7.3.2 Function lapply()

lapply() is the cousin of apply() for lists, as its name suggests. Since a data frame is also a list, lapply() works on data frames too, column by column. The basic syntax of lapply() is
lapply(l, FUN, f_args)
where


l is the list

FUN is the function to apply

f_args are any further arguments to be passed to FUN.

Note that there is no MARGIN argument here. Let us total each quarter again, this time with lapply().

lapply(qexp_df, sum)

$Q1
[1] 31.8

$Q2
[1] 48.36

$Q3
[1] 48.91

$Q4
[1] 71.16


You may have noticed two things here.

The output is a list.

FUN is applied to every element of the list. Each column of a data frame is an element, so lapply() works column by column, never row by row.

Thus lapply()

loops over a list, iterating over each element in that list
then applies the function FUN to each element
and then returns a list.

The first thing to check in any file received from an auditee is the type of each column. Is the date really a date? Is the amount a number, or text? lapply() with class() tells us at once.

lapply(vouchers, class)

$voucher_no
[1] "character"

$office
[1] "character"

$voucher_date
[1] "Date"

$amount
[1] "numeric"

$gst
[1] "numeric"


As with apply(), we can write FUN inline (anonymously). This gives the share of each office in each quarter’s expenditure, in per cent.

lapply(qexp_df, \(a) round(a / sum(a) * 100, 1))

$Q1
[1] 25.8 34.3 21.3 18.7

$Q2
[1] 40.9 22.5 21.8 14.8

$Q3
[1] 31.7 24.4 25.8 18.1

$Q4
[1] 19.7 56.9 11.6 11.8


The element of the list goes to the first argument of FUN which is not already named. Suppose we want to pick 3, 2 and 4 voucher numbers at random from the range 1001 to 1050, for three audit teams. sample() takes the values to pick from as x, and the number to pick as size. Since we have named x, each number goes to size.

set.seed(1)
lapply(c(3, 2, 4), sample, x = 1001:1050)

[[1]]
[1] 1004 1039 1001

[[2]]
[1] 1034 1023

[[3]]
[1] 1043 1014 1018 1033


Note that even when lapply() is applied to a vector, it returns a list.
And now office_bills, from the beginning of the chapter. The average bill of each office is simply

lapply(office_bills, mean)

$Pune
[1] 37250

$Nashik
[1] 99133.33

$Nagpur
[1] 74460



7.3.3 Function sapply()

sapply() is a simplified lapply(). It works the same way, but simplifies the result as much as possible, usually into a vector or a matrix.

sapply(qexp_df, sum)

   Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4 
31.80 48.36 48.91 71.16 

sapply(office_bills, mean)

    Pune   Nashik   Nagpur 
37250.00 99133.33 74460.00 








WarningCaution



The convenience has a cost. What sapply() returns depends on the data, a vector one day and a list another, which can break code silently. For code that will be reused, prefer vapply(), described below, or the purrr functions.

title: 7  Functional Programming
text:
7.4 Other loop functions

7.4.1 Function replicate()

replicate() evaluates an expression repeatedly. It is mostly used in simulations. The syntax is
replicate(n, expr, simplify = "array")
where


n is the number of replications

expr is the expression to evaluate repeatedly

simplify says whether the results should be simplified into a vector, matrix or array.

Suppose we draw a random sample of 10 vouchers, and work out their average amount. How much would that average change from one sample to another? replicate() draws five such samples, and gives the five averages. Then, with simplify = FALSE, it draws three samples of four voucher numbers each, and keeps each sample as an element of a list.

set.seed(123)
# Default value of simplify will simplify the results as much possible
replicate(5, mean(sample(vouchers$amount, 10)))

[1] 128070 104530  95220 196320 108110

# Notice the difference with simplify=FALSE
replicate(3, sample(vouchers$voucher_no, 4), simplify = FALSE)

[[1]]
[1] "TV/24-25/016" "TV/24-25/116" "TV/24-25/094" "TV/24-25/006"

[[2]]
[1] "TV/24-25/086" "TV/24-25/167" "TV/24-25/039" "TV/24-25/159"

[[3]]
[1] "TV/24-25/118" "TV/24-25/050" "TV/24-25/034" "TV/24-25/004"


Audit sampling itself is the subject of Chapter 29.

7.4.2 Function split()

split() divides an object (a vector, list or data frame) into groups, given by a factor. The result is a list, with one element for each group. The basic syntax is
split(x, f, drop=FALSE, ...)
where


x is the object to split, a vector, list or data.frame


f is a factor, or a list of factors. Anything else is converted to a factor.

drop says whether groups with no data should be dropped.

For example, to share the first ten vouchers between two audit teams, alternately,

split(vouchers$voucher_no[1:10], rep(c("Team A", "Team B"), 5))

$`Team A`
[1] "TV/24-25/001" "TV/24-25/003" "TV/24-25/005" "TV/24-25/007" "TV/24-25/009"

$`Team B`
[1] "TV/24-25/002" "TV/24-25/004" "TV/24-25/006" "TV/24-25/008" "TV/24-25/010"


The total expenditure of each office,

split(vouchers$amount, vouchers$office) |> lapply(sum)

$Kolhapur
[1] 5752500

$Nagpur
[1] 7421100

$Nashik
[1] 3816100

$Pune
[1] 3035400


And the largest voucher of each office,

split(vouchers$amount, vouchers$office) |> sapply(max)

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
  196100   610000   199500   194800 



7.4.3 tapply()

tapply() combines split() and sapply() for vectors, exactly as in the last example. It applies a function to each group of a vector. The basic syntax is
tapply(X, INDEX, FUN = NULL, ..., default = NA, simplify = TRUE)
where


X is a vector

INDEX is a factor, or a list of factors, giving the groups

FUN is the function to apply

... are any further arguments for FUN


simplify, if TRUE, simplifies the result.

The largest voucher of each office again, in one step.

tapply(vouchers$amount, vouchers$office, max)

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
  196100   610000   199500   194800 


If simplify is FALSE, the results are not simplified. See this example, the average voucher of each office.

tapply(vouchers$amount, vouchers$office, mean, simplify = FALSE)

$Kolhapur
[1] 112794.1

$Nagpur
[1] 172583.7

$Nashik
[1] 90859.52

$Pune
[1] 97916.13


With a list of two factors as INDEX, tapply() gives a cross-table. This is how the matrix qexp was made from the vouchers, with the office and the quarter as the two factors.

7.4.4 by() function
by() works like tapply(), but on a whole data frame, passing each group’s rows to the function. Let us see the voucher with the largest amount in each office. which.max() gives the position of the largest value.

by(vouchers, vouchers$office, \(d) d[which.max(d$amount), ])

vouchers$office: Kolhapur
      voucher_no   office voucher_date amount   gst
154 TV/24-25/154 Kolhapur   2025-03-17 196100 29914
------------------------------------------------------------ 
vouchers$office: Nagpur
      voucher_no office voucher_date amount   gst
161 TV/24-25/161 Nagpur   2025-03-25 610000 93051
------------------------------------------------------------ 
vouchers$office: Nashik
     voucher_no office voucher_date amount   gst
36 TV/24-25/036 Nashik   2024-07-05 199500 30432
------------------------------------------------------------ 
vouchers$office: Pune
     voucher_no office voucher_date amount   gst
32 TV/24-25/032   Pune   2024-06-30 194800 29715



7.4.5 Specifying the output type with vapply()

vapply() works like sapply(), except that we must state the type and length of each result, in the argument FUN.VALUE. If a result does not match, it stops with an error, instead of returning something unexpected. Its syntax is
vapply(X, FUN, FUN.VALUE, ..., USE.NAMES = TRUE)

In the argument FUN.VALUE we give a template of each result. See this example, the largest amount and the largest GST.


vapply(vouchers[c("amount", "gst")], max, FUN.VALUE = double(1))

amount    gst 
610000  93051 


With FUN.VALUE = double(1) we have said that each result should be a single double. To find the range of each column, which has two values,

vapply(vouchers[c("amount", "gst")], range, FUN.VALUE = double(2))

     amount   gst
[1,]  20300  3097
[2,] 610000 93051


If we try this on the whole register, which has text columns like the voucher number and the office, vapply() stops with an error, as we want it to.

vapply(vouchers, range, FUN.VALUE = double(2))

Error in `vapply()`:
! values must be type 'double',
 but FUN(X[[1]]) result is type 'character'

title: 7  Functional Programming
text:
7.5 Functional Programming in purrr

The package purrr2, part of the core tidyverse, gives a complete and consistent set of tools for functional programming. Its functions do the job of the apply family, with consistent names and arguments, and a guaranteed type of output.

library(purrr)


7.5.1 Iterate over single list/vector with map_*() family of functions
The most important family of functions in purrr is map. The map_*() functions work much like vapply(), with control over the type of output. They all take a list or vector as the argument .x and a function as .f, and return an output of the stated type.
Let us total each quarter of qexp_df once more.

map(qexp_df, .f = sum)

$Q1
[1] 31.8

$Q2
[1] 48.36

$Q3
[1] 48.91

$Q4
[1] 71.16


Note that the output is a list, just as with lapply(). If each result is a single value, we use one of these functions, depending on its type, to get a vector.


map_lgl for logical format

map_int for integer format

map_dbl for double format

map_chr for character format. Since purrr version 1.2, map_chr() no longer converts numbers or logical values into text automatically. If the function returns numbers, use map_dbl(), or convert the result explicitly with as.character().

map() always returns a list. See these further examples.
The largest amount and the largest GST, as a vector of doubles.

map_dbl(vouchers[c("amount", "gst")], max)

amount    gst 
610000  93051 


An anonymous function, written with \(x). (Older code often uses a formula instead, like ~ mean(.x). It still works, but \(x) is now recommended.) The first line gives the average bill of each office. The second turns month numbers into names.

map_dbl(office_bills, \(x) mean(x))

    Pune   Nashik   Nagpur 
37250.00 99133.33 74460.00 

map_chr(c(2, 7, 12), \(m) month.name[m])

[1] "February" "July"     "December"



7.5.2 Iterate over two or more lists/vectors using map2_*()/ pmap_*() family
So far, map_*() has iterated over the elements of one list. Any extra arguments are passed unchanged, the same in every iteration, as in the first illustration in Figure 7.23.


















Figure 7.2: Working of map vs map2 family of functions Source Advanced R by Hadley Wickham


To iterate over two vectors or lists together, taking their elements in pairs, we need the map2_*() family of functions (see the second illustration in Figure 7.2).
See the following example. Each office has its own limit for a single bill, and map2() takes the bills of each office together with its own limit.

office_limits <- c(Pune = 50000, Nashik = 100000, Nagpur = 100000)
map2(office_bills, office_limits, \(x, lim) x[x > lim])

$Pune
[1] 61000

$Nashik
numeric(0)

$Nagpur
[1] 230000


Pune has one bill above its limit, and Nagpur has one above its own. Nashik has none. Its three bills are all a little below ₹1 lakh, which is itself worth a second look (Section 15.17).
Here is another audit use. Claims under three schemes are to be checked against each scheme’s own limit. map2() takes each scheme’s claims together with its limit.

claims <- list(Health    = c(12000, 155000, 8000, 140000),
               Education = c(30000, 9000, 61000),
               Housing   = c(150000, 260000, 90000))
limits <- c(Health = 100000, Education = 50000, Housing = 250000)

map2(claims, limits, \(x, lim) x[x > lim])      # the claims above the limit

$Health
[1] 155000 140000

$Education
[1] 61000

$Housing
[1] 260000

map2_int(claims, limits, \(x, lim) sum(x > lim)) # how many

   Health Education   Housing 
        2         1         1 


Another use is a completeness check. From the first and last numbers of each cheque book issued, map2() builds the full list of cheque leaves, which can then be compared with the cheques accounted for.

cheque_books <- data.frame(first = c(500101, 500126), last = c(500125, 500150))
all_leaves <- map2(cheque_books$first, cheque_books$last, seq) |> unlist()
length(all_leaves)

[1] 50

accounted <- c(500101:500118, 500120:500150)   # say, from the cheque register
setdiff(all_leaves, accounted)                  # leaves not accounted for

[1] 500119


Similarly, to iterate over three or more lists, we use pmap_*(). The only difference is that all the lists are passed to pmap together, in one list. This can be better understood with the illustration used by Hadley Wickham in his book. See Figure 7.3.


















Figure 7.3: Working of pmap family of functions Source Advanced R by Hadley Wickham


For example, a data frame is a list of columns, so pmap() over a data frame takes one row at a time, with the column names matching the names of the function’s arguments.

bills <- data.frame(qty = c(10, 25, 40), rate = c(150, 80, 12.5), gst = c(18, 5, 18))
pmap_dbl(bills, \(qty, rate, gst) qty * rate * (1 + gst / 100))

[1] 1770 2100  590


Here, plain vector arithmetic, qty * rate * (1 + gst / 100), would have done the same. pmap() is needed when the function works on only one value at a time, like seq() above, or a function of our own with if.

7.5.3 Other useful purrr functions


walk(), walk2() and iwalk() work like map(), but for functions called for their side effects, like saving files or drawing plots, rather than for a result. We use iwalk() to save one file per district in Chapter 14.

list_rbind() binds a list of data frames into one, as when reading many files with map(). Its argument names_to adds a column with the names of the list elements, like the file each row came from. We use it in the audit use case below.

keep() and discard() keep or drop the elements of a list which meet a condition, like keep(claims, \(x) any(x > 100000)).

imap() passes each element along with its name, or position, as a second argument.







TipAudit tip



Whenever you find yourself running the same analysis on several files, districts, years or schemes, put them in a list and map() over it. One function, tested once, then runs on all of them alike. That is both quicker and more reliable than copying and editing code for each, where one small slip can go unnoticed.

title: 7  Functional Programming
section: 7.6 Audit use case, the March rush in each office
text:
7.6 Audit use case, the March rush in each office
A rush of expenditure in the last month of the year is a classic audit concern. Money spent in a hurry, to avoid its lapse, is often spent badly. The General Financial Rules, 2017 (Rule 62) treat such a rush as a breach of financial propriety. Government instructions also ask departments to keep spending in March within 15% of the budget, and in the last quarter within 33%. We have no budget figures here. So we use each office’s actual spending for the year as a rough yardstick instead.
Let us check every office in the same way. We split the vouchers into a list, one data frame per office. We write one function which checks one office. We test it on one office, and then map() it over all four.

office_list <- split(vouchers, vouchers$office)

march_check <- function(d) {
  in_march <- format(d$voucher_date, "%Y-%m") == "2025-03"
  in_q4    <- d$voucher_date >= as.Date("2025-01-01")
  data.frame(vouchers   = nrow(d),
             total_lakh = round(sum(d$amount) / 1e5, 2),
             q4_pct     = round(100 * sum(d$amount[in_q4]) / sum(d$amount), 1),
             march_pct  = round(100 * sum(d$amount[in_march]) / sum(d$amount), 1))
}

# Test on one office first
march_check(office_list$Pune)

  vouchers total_lakh q4_pct march_pct
1       31      30.35   27.6        16


The function works on one office. Now let us run it on all of them, and bind the results into one table with list_rbind(). Its argument names_to adds the name of each office as a column.

march_result <- office_list |>
  map(march_check) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "office")
march_result

    office vouchers total_lakh q4_pct march_pct
1 Kolhapur       51      57.52   24.4      13.6
2   Nagpur       43      74.21   54.6      52.2
3   Nashik       42      38.16   21.6       3.7
4     Pune       31      30.35   27.6      16.0


Let us keep the offices which cross either yardstick.

subset(march_result, q4_pct > 33 | march_pct > 15)

  office vouchers total_lakh q4_pct march_pct
2 Nagpur       43      74.21   54.6      52.2
4   Pune       31      30.35   27.6      16.0


Nagpur stands out. It spent 52.2% of its year’s money in March, and 54.6% in the last quarter. Pune is also above the March yardstick, but only just, at 16%. That may be no more than the normal ups and downs of payments.
The auditor would next look at the Nagpur vouchers of March. Were the goods received, and the works done, before payment? Were any payments made in advance, only to avoid the lapse of funds? The March vouchers, with these questions, go into the working papers.
Note that the same function ran on every office alike. Had there been forty offices, the code would not have changed at all.

title: 7  Functional Programming
text:
7.7 A suggested workflow


Spot the repetition. Notice when the same work is done on several files, districts, years or schemes.

Put the pieces in a list. Keep one data frame, or one vector, for each item. Use split() to break one table into groups if needed.

Write and test one function. Make it work correctly on a single item first. A short anonymous function written with \(x) is enough for simple jobs.

Map it over the list. Use map(), or lapply(), to run the same function on every item alike.

Ask for the type of output you expect. Use map_dbl(), map_int() or vapply(), so that a surprise result stops with an error. Be careful with apply() on data frames that have text columns.

Pair items with their own limits. Use map2() or pmap() when each item has its own limit or rate, like scheme-wise claim limits.

Combine or save the results. Bind a list of data frames with list_rbind(), and use walk() or iwalk() to save one file for each item.







ImportantRemember



Test the function on one item before mapping it over all. Ask for the output type you expect, so that an odd result stops the code instead of passing silently. One tested function is safer than many copies of edited code.

title: 7  Functional Programming
text:
7.8 Try it yourself
These exercises use the objects of this chapter, the voucher register vouchers, the matrix qexp, the list office_bills and the list office_list. Try each before opening the solution.


The heaviest quarter. With apply(), find the largest quarterly expenditure of each office in qexp. Then find which quarter it was.






TipSolution






apply(qexp, 1, max)

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
   19.80    40.51    12.62     8.86 

apply(qexp, 1, \(x) colnames(qexp)[which.max(x)])

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
    "Q2"     "Q4"     "Q3"     "Q3" 


Nagpur spent the most in Q4, which holds its March rush. No other office peaked in Q4. A peak in the last quarter is a hint, not proof. The use case of this chapter looks at it more closely.





Vouchers above ₹1 lakh. Count the vouchers of more than ₹1 lakh in each office. Use split() and vapply(), and say that each result is a single integer.






TipSolution






split(vouchers$amount, vouchers$office) |>
  vapply(\(a) sum(a > 100000), FUN.VALUE = integer(1))

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
      30       26       17       13 


sum() of a logical vector counts the TRUE values, and gives an integer. So integer(1) is the right template. If the function ever returned something else, vapply() would stop with an error instead of giving a wrong table.





A lower limit for Nashik. Suppose the limit of a single bill at Nashik is cut to ₹99,000. Copy office_limits to a new name, change the limit of Nashik, and find the bills of each office above its limit with map2(). Then count them with map2_int().






TipSolution






new_limits <- office_limits
new_limits["Nashik"] <- 99000
map2(office_bills, new_limits, \(x, lim) x[x > lim])

$Pune
[1] 61000

$Nashik
[1] 99500 99900

$Nagpur
[1] 230000

map2_int(office_bills, new_limits, \(x, lim) sum(x > lim))

  Pune Nashik Nagpur 
     1      2      1 


Nashik now has 2 bills above its limit, of ₹99,500 and ₹99,900. A limit moved by only ₹1,000 changes the result. So always take the limit from the delegation order in force on the date of the bill. We worked on a copy, so office_limits is unchanged.





Large payments in March. For each office in office_list, count the vouchers of more than ₹4 lakh paid in March 2025. Write the check as an anonymous function and use map_int().






TipSolution






office_list |>
  map_int(\(d) sum(d$amount > 400000 &
                   format(d$voucher_date, "%Y-%m") == "2025-03"))

Kolhapur   Nagpur   Nashik     Pune 
       0        6        0        0 


Only Nagpur has such vouchers, 6 of them. The other three offices have none. This confirms the use case. The March rush at Nagpur is a rush of large bills, so these vouchers are the first to call for.

title: Part II: Getting Data Ready
text:
Before any analysis, the data has to be read, cleaned and put into shape. In audit this is often most of the work. Auditees rarely send data in a form ready for analysis.
This part covers every step. You will organise files and fix the data received with a hash. You will read CSV and Excel files, and the awkward ones too, like PDFs and sheets laid out for printing. Then you will clean the data, combine many files into one, and transform, join and reshape tables. The part ends with dates, financial years and ageing, and with data too large for Excel.
The tidyverse packages, dplyr and tidyr above all, are the tools of this part and of the rest of the book. Read the dplyr and joins chapters with care. Almost every later chapter uses them.


8  Working with Files and Folders
Projects, paths and folders, and fixing the data received with a hash.


9  Protecting Personal Data
Masking, keyed hashing, k-anonymity, and encryption with a passphrase or a pair of keys.


10  Importing and Exporting Data
Reading and writing CSV and Excel files.


11  Cleaning Data
Cleaning names, blanks, types and inconsistent entries.


12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
Bank statements and orders in PDF, and workbooks made for printing.


13  Data from Web Pages
Tenders, awards and debarred lists read from web pages, kept as dated evidence.


14  Combining Many Similar Files
Stacking the files of many offices or months into one table.


15  Transforming Data with dplyr
Filtering, sorting, summarising and adding columns.


16  Joining Tables
Bringing tables together, and the audit tests built on joins.


17  Reshaping Data with tidyr
Moving data between wide and long forms.


18  Dates and Times
Dates, financial years, ageing and off-hours analysis.


19  Large Data with DuckDB and data.table
Data larger than Excel, tested in full rather than in samples.

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
text:
8.1 Handling files
In Chapter 10 we learn to read data from files and write data to them. In this chapter, we will learn some other functions which are useful while working with files and folders. We can create, rename, copy and delete files, check whether a file exists, list the files in a folder, and create and remove folders, all from R. This is handy when an audit involves many files, like one file for each district or each month.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
text:
8.1.1 Creating a file within R, using file.create()

Using file.create(), we can create a new, empty file. If a file of that name already exists, it is emptied. The function returns TRUE if the file is created, and FALSE otherwise.
For example, the following command creates a blank text file in the current working directory.

file.create("my_new_text_file.txt")

[1] TRUE



8.1.2 Checking whether a file exists, using file.exists()

Similarly, we can check whether a file of a given name exists, using file.exists(). Example-

file.exists("my_new_text_file.txt")

[1] TRUE



8.1.3 Renaming file with file.rename()

A file can be renamed using file.rename(). The basic syntax is file.rename(from = "old_name", to = "new_name"). It returns TRUE or FALSE, depending on whether the renaming succeeded. See this example.

file.rename(from = "my_new_text_file.txt", to = "my_renamed_file.csv")

[1] TRUE

# Check whether old file exists
file.exists("my_new_text_file.txt")

[1] FALSE



8.1.4 Copying file with file.copy() function
Files can be copied from one folder to another using the syntax file.copy(from = "old_path", to = "new_path").

8.1.5 Deleting file with file.remove()

The function file.remove() deletes a file of a given name. Example-

file.remove("my_renamed_file.csv")

[1] TRUE


Let us check whether the file has really been deleted.

file.exists("my_renamed_file.csv")

[1] FALSE








WarningCaution



Files deleted with file.remove() do not go to the Recycle Bin. They are gone. Never run delete commands on the folder holding the original data received from the auditee. Keep the originals in a separate, read-only folder, and work on copies.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
text:
8.2 Handling directories

8.2.1 Get/Set path of current working directory using getwd()/ setwd()

The working directory is the folder in which R looks for files, and saves them, unless told otherwise. We can see its path with getwd().

getwd()

[1] "D:/OneDrive - A c GeM CAG of INDIA/new book - quarto"


Similarly, using setwd("given/path/here") we can change the working directory.






Note



The path must be given using forward slashes /. If backslashes \ are used, as in Windows paths, each must be escaped with another backslash, like "D:\\audit\\data", because \ is itself an escape character in R.


As we will see at the end of this chapter, working in projects removes the need for setwd() altogether.

8.2.2 Create new directory using dir.create() and other operations
A new directory (folder) can be created using dir.create(). For example, the command below creates a new directory named ‘new_dir’ in the current working directory. If TRUE is returned, the directory has been created.

dir.create("new_dir")

We can check whether a directory exists using dir.exists(), which returns either TRUE or FALSE.

dir.exists("new_dir")

[1] TRUE


list.files() lists the files and folders in the current working directory, or in any other directory.

any(list.files() == 'new_dir')

[1] TRUE


list.files() has some very useful arguments. pattern keeps only the names matching a regular expression, full.names = TRUE gives the full paths, and recursive = TRUE also looks inside sub-folders. For example, list.files("data", pattern = "\\.xlsx$", full.names = TRUE, recursive = TRUE) lists every Excel file anywhere in the folder data. We will use this to read many files at once in Chapter 14.
A directory can be removed using unlink(), by setting its argument recursive to TRUE. Example

unlink("new_dir", recursive = TRUE)
dir.exists("new_dir")

[1] FALSE

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
section: 8.3 Dialog boxes for selecting files and folders
text:
8.3 Dialog boxes for selecting files and folders
We may use file.choose() to let the user select a file in a dialog box, and, on Windows, choose.dir() to select a folder.
Try these in your console.
list.files(choose.dir())
file.copy(from = file.choose(), to = "new_name")
These are convenient for one-off work. For analysis that has to be repeated, write the paths in the code instead, so that anyone can see which file was used.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
section: 8.4 Other useful functions for listing/removing variables
text:
8.4 Other useful functions for listing/removing variables
The function ls() lists all the variables in the current environment. The function rm() removes the given variables.






WarningCaution



The command rm(list = ls()) removes all variables from the environment. Use it with caution, as it erases all data held in memory.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
section: 8.5 Using save() to save objects/collection of objects
text:
8.5 Using save() to save objects/collection of objects
The function save() saves R objects to a file on disk, for later use. The saved objects can be brought back with load(). See this example.

h <- hist(Nile)
save(h, file="nile_hist")
rm(h)
any(ls() == 'h')

[1] FALSE

load("nile_hist")
any(ls() == 'h')

[1] TRUE


For a single object, saveRDS() and readRDS() are often more convenient. readRDS() returns the object, so we can give it any name we like, like results <- readRDS("results.rds").
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
section: 8.6 Recording what data was received, file hashes
text:
8.6 Recording what data was received, file hashes
An audit conclusion is only as good as the data behind it. Months later, someone may ask whether the file we analysed is the same file the auditee gave us. A hash answers this. It is a short code calculated from the full content of a file. If even one character of the file changes, the hash changes completely. The function tools::md5sum() calculates one kind of hash, called MD5.

writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-01,1250", "PV-02,45600"), "received_data.csv")
tools::md5sum("received_data.csv")

                 received_data.csv 
"1c8dff05a4b3c0d24ff45398a81d0308" 


Now suppose someone changes one amount in the file.

writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-01,1250", "PV-02,45601"), "received_data.csv")
tools::md5sum("received_data.csv")

                 received_data.csv 
"36bdd89fc49c10e66e6ec7bd505a3d01" 

file.remove("received_data.csv")

[1] TRUE


A change of one rupee has produced a completely different hash.






TipAudit tip



When data is received, record in the working papers the name, size and hash of every file, along with the date and the officer who gave it. Calculate the hashes of all files in a folder at once with tools::md5sum(list.files("received", full.names = TRUE)). The same idea is used for digital evidence in investigations. It proves that the data analysed is exactly the data received.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
text:
8.7 Working with Projects in RStudio

While working on a project, we usually want to keep all scripts, data, results, charts and figures in one place. RStudio has the concept of projects for this. A project is linked with a folder, and RStudio creates a file with the extension .Rproj in it. Opening this file reopens the project, with its scripts and settings.
To start a new project in RStudio, click the File menu, and then New Project. See the screenshots in Figure 8.1.


















Figure 8.1: Creating Projects in RStudio


After creating the project, you will notice that a file with the extension .Rproj has been created by RStudio in the chosen folder.
To resume working on the project, either double click this file, or open the project from the menu, File \(->\) Open Project.
In RStudio, we can create a project

In a new directory (first option in Figure 8.1)
In an existing directory (second option in Figure 8.1)
By cloning a version control repository (like Git), as shown in the third option in Figure 8.1.

Working in projects, one for each audit or analysis, has many benefits over working with loose R scripts.

We never have to set or find the working directory. It is always the project folder.
All paths are relative to the project folder, like "data/payments.csv". The whole folder can be copied to another computer, or shared with a colleague, and the code still works.
Results can be reproduced more easily.
Each project can have its own settings, and, with packages like renv, its own versions of packages.

A simple folder structure for an audit project could be data/original (the files received, never edited), data/working (cleaned data), scripts, and outputs.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
text:
8.8 A suggested workflow


Start a project for each audit. Create an RStudio project, so that the working directory is always the project folder and setwd() is not needed.

Set up the folders. Use dir.create() to make data/original, data/working, scripts and outputs.

Store the received files untouched. Copy the auditee’s files into data/original and never edit or delete them there.

Record the hashes. Calculate tools::md5sum() for every received file. Note the name, size, hash, date and the officer who gave it in the working papers.

List files in code. Use list.files() with pattern and full.names = TRUE instead of dialog boxes, so that anyone can see which files were used.

Save results for later. Keep intermediate objects with saveRDS() and read them back with readRDS().

Check before deleting. Use file.exists() before file.remove() or unlink(), and run such commands only on working copies.







ImportantRemember



Files deleted from R do not go to the Recycle Bin. Keep the original data in a separate folder and work only on copies. A recorded hash proves that the data analysed is exactly the data received.
crumbs: 8  Working with Files and Folders

title: 8  Working with Files and Folders
text:
8.9 Try it yourself
These exercises build a small audit folder inside the temporary folder given by tempdir(), so nothing is left in your project. Each exercise uses the folder made in the one before it. Try each one before opening the solution.


Set up the audit folders. Inside tempdir(), make a folder pension_audit with the four sub-folders of the suggested workflow, data/original, data/working, scripts and outputs. Check that all four exist.






TipSolution






audit_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "pension_audit")
dir.create(file.path(audit_dir, "data/original"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(file.path(audit_dir, "data/working"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(file.path(audit_dir, "scripts"), showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(file.path(audit_dir, "outputs"), showWarnings = FALSE)

dir.exists(file.path(audit_dir, c("data/original", "data/working", "scripts", "outputs")))

[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE


recursive = TRUE makes the folder data and the folder inside it in one step. dir.exists() takes several paths at once, and all four answers are TRUE.





Receive the district files. The Sonpur office sends three files, sonpur_apr2024.csv, sonpur_may2024.csv and covering_note.txt. Write them into data/original with writeLines(), using a few lines of made-up vouchers. Then list only the csv files.






TipSolution






original <- file.path(audit_dir, "data/original")
writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-01,1250", "PV-02,45600"),
           file.path(original, "sonpur_apr2024.csv"))
writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-03,9800"),
           file.path(original, "sonpur_may2024.csv"))
writeLines("Two files of vouchers are enclosed.",
           file.path(original, "covering_note.txt"))

list.files(original, pattern = "\\.csv$")

[1] "sonpur_apr2024.csv" "sonpur_may2024.csv"


The pattern \\.csv$ keeps only the names ending in .csv, so the covering note is left out. With many districts and months, the same line picks out every data file in the folder.





Make a register of received files. For every file in data/original, record the file name, its size in bytes and its MD5 hash in one data frame. basename() gives the file name without the folder, and file.size() gives the size.






TipSolution






received_files <- list.files(original, full.names = TRUE)
register <- data.frame(file  = basename(received_files),
                       bytes = file.size(received_files),
                       md5   = unname(tools::md5sum(received_files)))
register

                file bytes                              md5
1  covering_note.txt    37 8e6cc5c28329143cdcf061fef6bba9e8
2 sonpur_apr2024.csv    41 1c8dff05a4b3c0d24ff45398a81d0308
3 sonpur_may2024.csv    28 a2707775430f96f782dae623699bb621


This is the register the audit tip asks for. Add the date of receipt and the name of the officer who gave the files, and it can go into the working papers.





Save the register. Save register in the outputs folder with saveRDS(), read it back under the name register_back, and check that nothing was lost.






TipSolution






register_file <- file.path(audit_dir, "outputs", "register.rds")
saveRDS(register, register_file)
register_back <- readRDS(register_file)
identical(register, register_back)

[1] TRUE


identical() returns TRUE, so the saved register is exactly the register we made.





Has anything changed? Suppose someone changes the May amount from 9800 to 98000. Calculate the hashes again and find, from register_back, which file has changed. Then remove the whole pension_audit folder, checking before and after that it exists.






TipSolution






writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-03,98000"),
           file.path(original, "sonpur_may2024.csv"))

hash_now <- unname(tools::md5sum(received_files))
register_back$file[register_back$md5 != hash_now]

[1] "sonpur_may2024.csv"

dir.exists(audit_dir)

[1] TRUE

unlink(audit_dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.exists(audit_dir)

[1] FALSE


Only sonpur_may2024.csv has a new hash. The other two files are exactly as received. We deleted the folder only because it was a practice copy in tempdir(). Never delete a folder of original data in this way.
