title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.1 Why it matters
An audit party examining an old age pension scheme asks the district office for its list of beneficiaries. The file arrives on a pen drive. It has the name, date of birth, Aadhaar number, mobile number, bank account, caste category and disability status of every pensioner in the district. Within a week, copies of it sit on two laptops, in an email account and in a folder shared with the whole team. Nobody meant any harm. But if any one of those copies leaks, thousands of old people can be cheated, harassed or embarrassed, and the audit office will be the source of the leak.
Auditors receive such data all the time. Pay bills carry PAN and bank accounts. Scholarship lists carry caste. Health schemes carry diagnoses. We need this data to do our work. We also have a duty to protect it while we hold it, and to let go of it when the work is done.
In this chapter we learn practical ways to do this in R. We first sort the fields of a list by how much harm they can do. We then learn to mask numbers for display, to replace identifiers with hashes and tokens, and to see why a plain hash is not enough. We check a table for small groups of people who could be recognised before it goes into a report. Finally, we encrypt a file before it leaves our computer, first with a passphrase and then with a pair of keys. Three audit use cases show the methods at work. In the first, two departments find the persons common to their lists without sending each other a single Aadhaar number. In the second, a district table is made safe for publication. In the third, a department sends Aadhaar numbers that only the auditor can read.
Section 8.6 used a hash to prove that a file has not changed. Here we use the same tool for a different purpose, to hide a value while keeping it usable.
Prerequisites
Three reasons make the protection of personal data a part of the auditor’s job.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
Duty of care. The people in our data did not choose to give it to us. They gave it to a government office to get a pension, a scholarship or a ration card. The audit office receives it only because the law allows audit to see the records. That trust passes to us with the data.

The law. India has a law on this subject, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It covers personal data in digital form, that is, data about a person who can be identified from it. It places duties on whoever decides why and how such data is processed. In broad terms, data must be used only for a lawful purpose, kept safe with reasonable security safeguards, and not kept once the purpose is served unless another law requires it. A breach must be reported, and the penalties for failing to protect data can be heavy. The Act and the rules made under it are being brought into force in stages. The Aadhaar law separately restricts the display and publication of Aadhaar numbers. How these laws apply to audit work is a matter for the instructions of your own organisation. The duty of care does not depend on that answer.

Data minimisation. The safest data is data we never took. Ask only for the fields the audit needs. Drop the rest as soon as the data arrives. Delete the working copies when the retention period ends.







TipAudit tip



When writing the requisition for data, list the fields the audit needs and the reason for each. If the test is whether pensioners are alive and below an income limit, we may need the Aadhaar number for matching but not the caste or the mobile number. A short requisition protects the people in the data and also reduces the work of the auditee.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
section: 9.2 Our data, an old age pension list
text:
9.2 Our data, an old age pension list
The Social Welfare Department of an imaginary state pays an old age pension of ₹1,000 a month, and ₹1,500 to a person with a disability. Under the scheme rules of our example, a person who already draws a government service pension is not eligible. We have two lists.


oap, the old age pension list of five districts. For each beneficiary it has an ID, name, gender, date of birth, Aadhaar number, mobile number, bank account, IFSC, PIN code, district, social category, disability status and monthly pension.

svc, the list of service pensioners kept by the Treasury. It has the pension payment order (PPO) number, name, date of birth, Aadhaar number, PAN and monthly pension.

The code below creates both lists and plants the cases we will find.

Seven persons are on both lists. In the Treasury list their Aadhaar numbers are written with spaces or hyphens, and one has two digits swapped by a typing error.
Hillpur is a small hill district with few beneficiaries, most of them from the Scheduled Tribes. A few beneficiaries are more than 90 years old.
All mobile numbers come from one series, so that we can show how a plain hash is broken.







Note



Everything in this chapter is simulated. The names are made up. The Aadhaar numbers are random 12 digit strings and the PAN are random strings in the PAN pattern. Mobile numbers, bank accounts, IFSC and PIN codes are invented too. Because the data is simulated, we print it in full in this section so that the reader can see what we are protecting. With real data, we would not print identifiers on screen or in a report at all.



Code to create the pension listsset.seed(2026)

districts <- tibble(
  district = c("Sonpur", "Rajgarh", "Nandgaon", "Bhimnagar", "Hillpur"),
  size     = c(170, 150, 130, 110, 40),
  pin_base = c(841100, 842200, 843300, 844400, 845500)
)

            "Radha", "Sushila", "Kaushalya", "Pushpa", "Bimla", "Sarla", "Usha")

            "Bhola", "Kishan", "Jagdish", "Mahesh", "Prakash", "Dinesh", "Ramlal")

             "Munda", "Paswan", "Sharma", "Gupta", "Verma", "Mandal", "Sahu")

random_digits <- function(n, width) {
  map_chr(seq_len(n), \(i) paste(sample(0:9, width, replace = TRUE), collapse = ""))
}
random_pan <- function(n) {
  paste0(map_chr(seq_len(n), \(i) paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = "")),
         "P", sample(LETTERS, n, TRUE), random_digits(n, 4), sample(LETTERS, n, TRUE))
}

n <- sum(districts$size)
oap <- districts |>
  uncount(size) |>
  mutate(
    ben_id   = sprintf("OAP%05d", row_number()),
    gender   = sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.45)),
    name     = paste(if_else(gender == "F", sample(female, n, TRUE), sample(male, n, TRUE)),
                     sample(surname, n, TRUE)),
    age      = pmin(60 + floor(rexp(n, 1 / 9)), 99),
    dob      = as.Date("2025-03-31") - round((age + runif(n, 0.01, 0.99)) * 365.25),
    aadhaar  = paste0(sample(2:9, n, TRUE), random_digits(n, 11)),
    mobile   = paste0("70000", sprintf("%05d", sample(0:99999, n))),
    bank_account = paste0(sample(1:9, n, TRUE), random_digits(n, 10)),
    ifsc     = paste0("XBNK0", sprintf("%06d", sample(1:400, n, TRUE))),
    pin_code = as.character(pin_base + sample(1:6, n, TRUE)),
    category = if_else(
      district == "Hillpur",
      sample(c("SC", "ST", "OBC", "General"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.06, 0.8, 0.08, 0.06)),
      sample(c("SC", "ST", "OBC", "General"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.05, 0.45, 0.3))),
    disability = sample(c("Yes", "No"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.08, 0.92)),
    monthly_pension = if_else(disability == "Yes", 1500, 1000)
  ) |>
  select(ben_id, name, gender, dob, aadhaar, mobile, bank_account, ifsc,
         pin_code, district, category, disability, monthly_pension)

# Treasury list of service pensioners
m <- 250
svc <- tibble(
  ppo_no  = sprintf("PPO/%d/%04d", sample(1995:2024, m, TRUE), sample(1:9999, m)),
  name    = paste(sample(c(female, male), m, TRUE), sample(surname, m, TRUE)),
  dob     = as.Date("1940-01-01") + sample(0:9000, m, TRUE),
  aadhaar = paste0(sample(2:9, m, TRUE), random_digits(m, 11)),
  pan     = random_pan(m),
  monthly_pension = round(runif(m, 15000, 60000), -2)

# Planted. Seven old age pensioners who also draw a service pension
common <- oap |> slice(c(12, 95, 160, 233, 301, 402, 515))

  common[, c("name", "dob", "aadhaar")]

  mutate(aadhaar = paste(str_sub(aadhaar, 1, 4), str_sub(aadhaar, 5, 8),
                         str_sub(aadhaar, 9, 12)))
# Planted. One number with hyphens, and one with two digits swapped
svc$aadhaar[55]  <- str_replace_all(svc$aadhaar[55], " ", "-")
a <- svc$aadhaar[200]

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.3 Sorting the fields
Not every column carries the same risk. Before deciding how to protect a list, we sort its columns into three kinds.


Direct identifiers point to one person by themselves. Aadhaar number, PAN, mobile number, bank account and, in practice, the full name are of this kind.

Quasi-identifiers do not identify anyone alone. Combined, they often do. Date of birth, gender and PIN code are the classic three. A person may be the only woman born on a given date in a given PIN code.

Sensitive attributes are the facts that harm or embarrass a person if they become known. Caste category, disability, health condition, religion and income are of this kind.

Table 9.1 sorts the columns of our two lists.


Table 9.1: Columns of the pension lists, by kind








Column
Kind
Why




aadhaar, pan, mobile, bank_account

Direct identifier
Each points to exactly one person


name
Direct identifier
Together with the district, usually enough to find the person



ben_id, ppo_no

Direct identifier, within the department
The department can look up the person from it



dob, gender, pin_code

Quasi-identifier
Together they single out most people



district, ifsc

Quasi-identifier, weaker
Narrow the search to a place or a bank branch



category, disability

Sensitive attribute
Disclosure can lead to discrimination


monthly_pension
Sensitive attribute, mild
Reveals disability, since it is higher for disabled persons






It helps to write this sorting into the code. Then every later step can use it, and a reviewer can see what was decided.

direct_ids <- c("name", "aadhaar", "pan", "mobile", "bank_account")
quasi_ids  <- c("dob", "gender", "pin_code", "district", "ifsc")
sensitive  <- c("category", "disability", "monthly_pension")

Data minimisation now takes one line. Suppose a test needs only the district, gender, date of birth, category, disability and pension. We keep those, with the beneficiary ID to trace records back, and drop everything else.

oap_min <- oap |>
  select(ben_id, district, gender, dob, category, disability, monthly_pension)

ncol(oap)

[1] 13

ncol(oap_min)

[1] 7


The working copy now has 7 columns instead of 13. Aadhaar, mobile and bank account are no longer in it. If this copy leaks, far less harm is done.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.4 Masking numbers for display
Often we must show which record we mean, in a working paper or an audit memo, without showing the whole number. Masking replaces most of the characters with X and keeps a few, usually the last four. The masked Aadhaar issued by UIDAI follows the same idea and shows only the last four digits.
The stringr functions we learnt in Chapter 20 do this. str_sub(x, -4) takes the last four characters of a string.

x <- "987654321098"
str_sub(x, -4)

[1] "1098"

paste0("XXXX-XXXX-", str_sub(x, -4))

[1] "XXXX-XXXX-1098"


Let us write small functions for the identifiers in our data. Bank account numbers have different lengths, so we make as many X as needed with str_dup(). For PAN, str_replace() replaces the first five letters, and the regular expression ^[A-Z]{5} matches exactly those (Chapter 21).

mask_aadhaar <- function(x) paste0("XXXX-XXXX-", str_sub(x, -4))
mask_mobile  <- function(x) paste0("XXXXXX", str_sub(x, -4))
mask_account <- function(x) paste0(str_dup("X", str_length(x) - 4), str_sub(x, -4))
mask_pan     <- function(x) str_replace(x, "^[A-Z]{5}", "XXXXX")

oap |>
  transmute(ben_id, name,
            aadhaar      = mask_aadhaar(aadhaar),
            mobile       = mask_mobile(mobile),
            bank_account = mask_account(bank_account)) |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  ben_id   name         aadhaar        mobile     bank_account
  <chr>    <chr>        <chr>          <chr>      <chr>       
1 OAP00001 Mohan Mahto  XXXX-XXXX-3259 XXXXXX1035 XXXXXXX5443 
2 OAP00002 Kishan Verma XXXX-XXXX-1417 XXXXXX2720 XXXXXXX4309 
3 OAP00003 Sita Munda   XXXX-XXXX-1550 XXXXXX1947 XXXXXXX8980 
4 OAP00004 Sita Devi    XXXX-XXXX-2969 XXXXXX5314 XXXXXXX4918 

mask_pan(head(svc$pan, 3))

[1] "XXXXX6557E" "XXXXX8516V" "XXXXX8888W"


This is the form in which identifiers should appear in a working paper, an audit memo or a draft paragraph sent to the department.
Masking is meant for human eyes. It is not a way to hide a list from a determined person, and it destroys information. Many people share the same last four digits. Let us count how often that happens in our small list.

oap |>
  count(last4 = str_sub(aadhaar, -4)) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()

[1] 20


Even among 600 persons, 20 endings of four digits are shared by two or more people. So masked numbers cannot be used to match two lists. For matching, we need hashing.






WarningCaution



A masked number is still part of a record. “XXXX-XXXX-1234, Kamla Devi, Hillpur” may be enough to find the person. Mask the identifier, and also ask whether the name and place need to appear at all.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.5 Hashing for pseudonymisation
A hash turns any text into a fixed length code. The same input always gives the same code, and the code gives no visible clue about the input. Section 8.6 used the MD5 hash of a whole file. For identifiers we use a stronger hash called SHA-256. Replacing an identifier by such a code is called pseudonymisation. The records stay linked to each other, but the identifier itself is hidden.
The digest package hashes one value at a time.

digest("987654321098", algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE)

[1] "f1baafb72e1cc8b1f857f9ed9f448249a7c5ee5116fe4dbbe69823744e3dc940"








WarningCaution



Always write serialize = FALSE when hashing a value with digest(). Without it, digest() first converts the value into R’s own internal format and hashes that. The result is a valid hash, but it will not agree with the hash of the same number made by any other tool, or by another department.


For a whole column, the sha256() function of openssl is more convenient, because it hashes every element of a vector at once. It gives the same result as digest() above.

as.character(sha256("987654321098"))

[1] "f1baafb72e1cc8b1f857f9ed9f448249a7c5ee5116fe4dbbe69823744e3dc940"


Two small numbers that differ in one digit get codes that have nothing in common.

as.character(sha256(c("987654321098", "987654321099")))

[1] "f1baafb72e1cc8b1f857f9ed9f448249a7c5ee5116fe4dbbe69823744e3dc940"
[2] "6f42d301bbabdd248689eb74b9719481c70fbe52853cef63b305cdf9e5f044df"



9.5.1 Normalise before hashing
To a hash function, "9876 5432 1098" and "987654321098" are two different texts, and their hashes differ completely. So before hashing we must write every identifier in one standard form. For Aadhaar, we keep only the digits with str_remove_all() and the pattern \\D, which means any character that is not a digit.

normalise_id <- function(x) str_remove_all(x, "\\D")

normalise_id(c("9876 5432 1098", "9876-5432-1098", "987654321098"))

[1] "987654321098" "987654321098" "987654321098"


All three are now the same text, and will get the same hash. For PAN, we would also convert to upper case with str_to_upper().

9.5.2 Why a plain hash is not enough
A hash cannot be run backwards. But it does not need to be. If an outsider knows what kind of value was hashed, the outsider can hash every possible value and look up the answers. This is called a dictionary attack. It works whenever the number of possible values is small enough for a computer to try them all.
Let us see it happen. Suppose the department shares a list in which the mobile numbers have been replaced by their plain SHA-256 hashes. It looks safe.

shared <- oap |>
  transmute(ben_id, mobile_hash = as.character(sha256(mobile)))

head(shared, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  ben_id   mobile_hash                                                     
  <chr>    <chr>                                                           
1 OAP00001 516711e68278cd3befaa34d99df50753308687efb33ae4a424f2b3654d772853
2 OAP00002 f99f5c16eaa209817362ccf6d0fa21d74769866135fecbf282bcd3cac3d0c18c
3 OAP00003 92f01112ef0b5bb0f302568338a46d6ff1772134eff1aa4ecc8fa9d4e660b06e


Now suppose someone who receives this list knows, or guesses, that the numbers come from the series 70000 00000 to 70000 99999. That is only one lakh numbers. The receiver hashes all of them and keeps a table of number and hash.

attack_time <- system.time({
  all_numbers <- paste0("70000", sprintf("%05d", 0:99999))
  dictionary  <- tibble(mobile      = all_numbers,
                        mobile_hash = as.character(sha256(all_numbers)))
})

recovered <- shared |>
  inner_join(dictionary, by = "mobile_hash")

nrow(recovered)

[1] 600


Every one of the 600 mobile numbers has been recovered. On this computer, building the dictionary took about 0.2 seconds.
Real identifiers come from larger sets. There are 1010 possible ten digit numbers, and about 1012 possible Aadhaar numbers. But that is not much protection either. At the speed we just saw, R alone would try all 1010 numbers in about 6 hours. Specialised hardware is very much faster. So a plain hash of a phone number, Aadhaar number, PAN or bank account must be treated as if it were the number itself.

9.5.3 The fix, a keyed hash
The attack worked because anyone can compute SHA-256. The fix is to mix a secret key into the hash, so that only a holder of the key can compute it. This is called a keyed hash, or HMAC (hash-based message authentication code). In openssl, we just add the argument key to sha256().
A good key is long and random. rand_bytes() gives random bytes, and paste() turns them into a text of hexadecimal characters.

secret_key <- paste(rand_bytes(32), collapse = "")
nchar(secret_key)

[1] 64


The key is printed here only to show its length. In real work, the key is never printed, never stored next to the data, and never written in the script itself. We return to this below.
Now we hash the mobile numbers with the key, and try the same attack.

shared_keyed <- oap |>
  transmute(ben_id, mobile_hash = as.character(sha256(mobile, key = secret_key)))

shared_keyed |>
  inner_join(dictionary, by = "mobile_hash") |>
  nrow()

[1] 0


Nothing is recovered. The outsider can still hash every number in the series, but without the key those hashes never agree with ours. Only someone who has the key can repeat the attack. So the protection lies entirely in keeping the key secret and apart from the data.
digest has a function for the same purpose, hmac(). It takes the key first, and gives the same code as openssl.

hmac(secret_key, "7000012345", algo = "sha256") ==
  as.character(sha256("7000012345", key = secret_key))

[1] TRUE



9.5.4 Salt and key, in simple words
Two words come up whenever hashing is discussed.

A salt is a random value made separately for each record and stored next to the hash. Two persons with the same number get different hashes, because their salts differ. Salts are used for stored passwords.
A key, sometimes called a pepper, is one secret value used for every record and kept away from the data.

For audit work, the key is usually what we want. A salt has two drawbacks for us. First, because it is stored with the data, anyone who gets the data also gets the salt, and can still try every possible number for any one record. Second, because the same number gets a different hash in each record, two lists hashed with salts can no longer be matched. A small example shows this.

salted_hash <- function(x) {
  salt <- map_chr(seq_along(x), \(i) paste(rand_bytes(8), collapse = ""))
  tibble(salt = salt, hash = as.character(sha256(paste0(salt, x))))
}

salted_hash(c("987654321098", "987654321098"))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  salt             hash                                                         
  <chr>            <chr>                                                        
1 eb7a7f75c5637a90 17a5511a6bd0f6cdf62de78ccf90b9e010be6dd858e190e7bba0a7494cd8…
2 dcd4ac370ba6d717 d5dc7b8f845111ff912a95cfa94ed321cae2fbd427fb7ba93c7df5b98f68…


The same Aadhaar number has two different hashes. The keyed hash, by contrast, gives the same code for the same number every time, so long as the key is the same. That is exactly what matching needs.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
section: 9.6 Audit use case, matching two lists without sharing Aadhaar
text:
9.6 Audit use case, matching two lists without sharing Aadhaar
The audit wants to know which old age pensioners also draw a service pension, since such persons are not eligible under our scheme rules. The usual way would be to collect both lists, with Aadhaar numbers, on the auditor’s laptop. A safer way keeps every Aadhaar number inside the department that already holds it.

The audit office makes one secret key and gives it, in a sealed form or by a secure channel, to one officer in each department.
Each department normalises its Aadhaar numbers and hashes them with the key.
Each department sends only its own record ID and the hash. No names, no numbers.
The auditor joins the two hashed lists. A match means the same Aadhaar number.
The auditor sends back only the matched record IDs, and asks each department for the full records of those persons alone.

We write one function for step 2, so that both departments do exactly the same thing.

keyed_hash <- function(x, key) {
  as.character(sha256(normalise_id(x), key = key))
}

Each department now prepares its file. Note that the Treasury’s numbers have spaces and hyphens in them. normalise_id() takes care of that.

from_welfare <- oap |>
  transmute(ben_id, aadhaar_hash = keyed_hash(aadhaar, secret_key))

from_treasury <- svc |>
  transmute(ppo_no, aadhaar_hash = keyed_hash(aadhaar, secret_key))

head(from_treasury, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  ppo_no        aadhaar_hash                                                    
  <chr>         <chr>                                                           
1 PPO/2010/6219 1273cf720cca27e9bbf74b20c587f18d0535b0ed62466c9726e5d655e5d101fe
2 PPO/2005/1517 1b9e9542a844b1cecd1c7fddde44ed354b42f623fd27851c4db801e4a6094e4d
3 PPO/2009/3506 9d1b3f0d4a2c388fd049b87c23f5ac057d8fe2f6f757efc5234b78fc6e1142f4


These two files are all that the auditor receives. They can travel by email without revealing any Aadhaar number. The auditor now matches them with inner_join().

matches <- from_welfare |>
  inner_join(from_treasury, by = "aadhaar_hash") |>
  select(ben_id, ppo_no)

matches

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  ben_id   ppo_no       
  <chr>    <chr>        
1 OAP00012 PPO/1997/7784
2 OAP00095 PPO/2017/7075
3 OAP00160 PPO/2020/3608
4 OAP00233 PPO/2008/4942
5 OAP00301 PPO/2022/9220
6 OAP00515 PPO/2001/2292


The hashes have found 6 persons who are on both lists. The auditor sends these record IDs back. The Social Welfare Department confirms the details of these old age pensioners.

found <- oap |>
  semi_join(matches, by = "ben_id")

found |>
  transmute(ben_id, name, aadhaar = mask_aadhaar(aadhaar), district, monthly_pension)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  ben_id   name          aadhaar        district  monthly_pension
  <chr>    <chr>         <chr>          <chr>               <dbl>
1 OAP00012 Ramesh Sahu   XXXX-XXXX-8530 Sonpur               1000
2 OAP00095 Geeta Mahto   XXXX-XXXX-0424 Sonpur               1000
3 OAP00160 Geeta Sharma  XXXX-XXXX-5754 Sonpur               1000
4 OAP00233 Bimla Oraon   XXXX-XXXX-2613 Rajgarh              1000
5 OAP00301 Shanti Prasad XXXX-XXXX-2974 Rajgarh              1000
6 OAP00515 Shyam Prasad  XXXX-XXXX-2925 Bhimnagar            1000


If these persons were indeed ineligible, the old age pension paid to them comes to ₹72,000 a year.
We planted seven common persons, and the hashes found 6. The missing one has two digits swapped in the Treasury list. A hash matches only identical values. One wrong digit gives a completely different hash, and the match is lost. If the departments suspect typing errors, they can also hash a second identifier, such as the name and date of birth written in a standard form, and the auditor can match on either. Fuzzy matching of names, as in Chapter 36, cannot be done on hashes. It needs the actual names, inside a secure environment.
Finally, let us confirm that the hashes reveal nothing to someone without the key. An outsider who knows one Aadhaar number in the list can compute its plain hash, or a keyed hash with some other key. Neither appears in the file.

known <- oap$aadhaar[12]

as.character(sha256(known)) %in% from_welfare$aadhaar_hash

[1] FALSE

keyed_hash(known, "some other key") %in% from_welfare$aadhaar_hash

[1] FALSE

keyed_hash(known, secret_key) %in% from_welfare$aadhaar_hash

[1] TRUE


Only the right key finds the person. When the exercise is over, the key is destroyed. The hashes then cannot be linked to anything, by anyone.






TipAudit tip



Use a fresh key for each matching exercise. Hashes made with different keys cannot be joined with each other. So a list hashed for one audit cannot later be quietly linked with a list hashed for another.


What the auditor does next is the usual audit work. Ask the Treasury and the Social Welfare Department to verify the 6 persons from their records, and examine why the eligibility check at sanction did not catch them. Keep in the working papers the masked identifiers, the record IDs and the replies of the departments, not the hashed lists.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.7 Tokens
A hash is calculated from the identifier. A token is not. It is a random code given to each person, and the only link between the token and the person is a lookup table. Without the table, the token reveals nothing at all, even to someone who tries every possible number.
Tokens suit data that stays with the audit team for a long analysis. We replace the identifiers by tokens in the working copy, and keep the lookup table separately, under lock.

lookup <- oap |>
  distinct(ben_id, aadhaar) |>
  mutate(token = map_chr(ben_id, \(i) toupper(paste(rand_bytes(5), collapse = ""))))

n_distinct(lookup$token) == nrow(lookup)

[1] TRUE


Each token is ten random characters, and every token is different. The working copy keeps only the token, with no direct identifiers.

oap_work <- oap |>
  left_join(lookup |> select(ben_id, token), by = "ben_id") |>
  select(token, district, gender, dob, category, disability, monthly_pension)

head(oap_work, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  token      district gender dob        category disability monthly_pension
  <chr>      <chr>    <chr>  <date>     <chr>    <chr>                <dbl>
1 667C40A123 Sonpur   M      1958-11-09 SC       No                    1000
2 2740C07477 Sonpur   M      1955-05-28 General  No                    1000
3 338D9D3D0A Sonpur   F      1960-01-24 General  No                    1000


When a case needs to be traced back to the person, the officer who holds lookup finds the record. Nobody else needs it. Tokens made with rand_bytes() are truly random. Do not make tokens with sample() after set.seed(), because anyone who knows the seed and the order of the records can make the same tokens again.






Note



A hash is the right tool when two parties must match their lists without meeting, because both can compute the same code from the same number. A token is the right tool inside one team, because it cannot be computed by anyone, and can be undone only with the lookup table.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.8 Generalisation and k-anonymity
Removing names and numbers is not enough. Quasi-identifiers can single out a person by themselves. Let us count how many people in our list share each combination of gender, date of birth and PIN code.

oap |>
  count(gender, dob, pin_code) |>
  count(n, name = "groups")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
      n groups
  <int>  <int>
1     1    596
2     2      2


Of the 598 combinations, 596 belong to exactly one person. So anyone who knows a neighbour’s date of birth and PIN code can find her in the list, and read her caste and disability status. Removing the Aadhaar number did not help her at all.
A list is called k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifiers is shared by at least k persons. Then no record can be narrowed down to fewer than k people. A common choice is k = 5.
We reach k-anonymity by generalisation, that is, by making the quasi-identifiers coarser. Instead of the date of birth, we give the age band. Instead of the PIN code, we give the district.

oap_gen <- oap |>
  mutate(
    age = floor(as.numeric(as.Date("2025-03-31") - dob) / 365.25),
    age_band = cut(age, breaks = c(60, 70, 80, 90, Inf), right = FALSE,
                   labels = c("60-69", "70-79", "80-89", "90+"))
  ) |>
  select(district, gender, age_band, category, disability)

Now we check whether any combination has fewer than k persons. count() gives the size of each group, and filter() keeps the small ones.

k <- 5

small_groups <- oap_gen |>
  count(district, gender, age_band) |>
  filter(n < k)

small_groups

# A tibble: 13 × 4
   district  gender age_band     n
   <chr>     <chr>  <fct>    <int>
 1 Bhimnagar F      90+          2
 2 Bhimnagar M      90+          2
 3 Hillpur   F      80-89        1
 4 Hillpur   F      90+          1
 5 Hillpur   M      80-89        1
 6 Hillpur   M      90+          1
 7 Nandgaon  F      90+          4
 8 Nandgaon  M      90+          1
 9 Rajgarh   F      90+          3
10 Rajgarh   M      80-89        4
11 Rajgarh   M      90+          1
12 Sonpur    F      90+          3
13 Sonpur    M      90+          1


There are still 13 small groups, holding 25 persons. Most are the oldest pensioners, and the people of Hillpur. A woman aged over 90 in Hillpur is easy to recognise in her village. We generalise further, and join the two oldest bands into one band of 80 and above.

oap_gen <- oap_gen |>
  mutate(age_band = fct_collapse(age_band, "80+" = c("80-89", "90+")))

small_groups <- oap_gen |>
  count(district, gender, age_band) |>
  filter(n < k)

small_groups

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  district gender age_band     n
  <chr>    <chr>  <fct>    <int>
1 Hillpur  F      80+          2
2 Hillpur  M      80+          2


Now 2 small groups remain, with 4 persons, all in Hillpur. We have two choices. We may make the data coarser still, for example by dropping gender for Hillpur, or we may leave out these few records from the shared copy and say so. Which is better depends on what the receiver of the data needs.






WarningCaution



k-anonymity protects against being found in the data. It does not stop a sensitive fact from leaking if everyone in a group has it. If all five women aged 80 and above in some district are from the same category, then knowing that a woman of that age lives there tells us her category. Look also at the sensitive columns within each small group before sharing.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
section: 9.9 Audit use case, publishing a district table safely
text:
9.9 Audit use case, publishing a district table safely
The draft audit report is to include a table of old age pensioners by district and social category. The table has no names. Can it still harm anyone? It can, through small numbers. If a cell says that one person in Hillpur is from the General category, everyone in Hillpur may know who that is, and the next table may then reveal her disability or pension.
The usual rule is small-cell suppression. Any count below a threshold, often 5, is shown as “less than 5” instead of the number. Let us make the table first.

tab <- oap |>
  count(district, category) |>
  complete(district, category, fill = list(n = 0))

tab |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  district  General   OBC    SC    ST
  <chr>       <int> <int> <int> <int>
1 Bhimnagar      34    53    18     5
2 Hillpur         1     0     4    35
3 Nandgaon       49    55    22     4
4 Rajgarh        43    66    33     8
5 Sonpur         52    82    31     5


In all, 4 cells are below 5, and 3 of them are in Hillpur. One cell is zero. A zero is also below 5, so we hide it too. First we mark the cells to hide.

threshold <- 5

tab_safe <- tab |>
  mutate(suppress = n < threshold)

There is one more trap. If the table shows a row total, a single hidden cell can be worked out by subtraction. So, in every row with exactly one hidden cell, we hide the next smallest cell too. This is called secondary suppression.

tab_safe <- tab_safe |>
  mutate(
    hidden_in_row = sum(suppress),
    order_in_row  = rank(n, ties.method = "first"),
    suppress      = suppress | (hidden_in_row == 1 & order_in_row == 2),
    .by = district
  )

tab_safe |>
  mutate(shown = case_when(n < threshold ~ "less than 5",
                           suppress      ~ "not shown",
                           .default      = as.character(n))) |>
  select(district, category, shown) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, values_from = shown) |>
  left_join(count(oap, district, name = "Total"), by = "district")

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  district  General     OBC         SC          ST          Total
  <chr>     <chr>       <chr>       <chr>       <chr>       <int>
1 Bhimnagar 34          53          18          5             110
2 Hillpur   less than 5 less than 5 less than 5 35             40
3 Nandgaon  49          55          not shown   less than 5   130
4 Rajgarh   43          66          33          8             150
5 Sonpur    52          82          31          5             170


The table now hides 5 cells. The SC cell of Nandgaon, with 22 persons, is hidden only to protect the ST cell beside it. We show it as “not shown” and not as “less than 5”, so that the table never says anything untrue. A footnote in the report should explain both labels.
Column totals need the same check. A simpler way out, often good enough in an audit report, is to merge small categories into “Others”, or small districts with a neighbour, before making the table.
What the auditor does next is to read the safe table once more as an outsider would. Could anyone in the district guess who is behind any number? If yes, coarsen it further. Then put the code and the threshold used in the working papers, so that the reviewer can see how the table was made safe.






TipAudit tip



Apply the same check to charts. A bar for a group of one or two persons in a chart discloses as much as a cell in a table.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.10 Encrypting files before sharing
Sometimes the full data must travel, by email or on a pen drive. Then the file should be encrypted. An encrypted file looks like random bytes. Only someone with the right key can turn it back into the original.
We will use AES, the standard method used by governments and banks around the world, through the openssl package. AES needs a key of exactly 32 random bytes, which no person can remember. So we let the person remember a passphrase, and turn the passphrase into a key with bcrypt_pbkdf(). This function is deliberately slow. That costs us a fraction of a second, but makes it very slow for an outsider to try millions of guesses at the passphrase. It also takes a salt, a few random bytes, so that the same passphrase gives a different key for every file. The salt is not secret, and we store it at the start of the encrypted file.
Two small functions do the work. readBin() and writeBin() read and write a file as raw bytes.

encrypt_file <- function(infile, outfile, passphrase) {
  salt   <- rand_bytes(16)
  key    <- bcrypt_pbkdf(passphrase, salt, rounds = 64L, size = 32L)
  plain  <- readBin(infile, "raw", file.size(infile))
  locked <- aes_cbc_encrypt(plain, key = key)
  writeBin(c(salt, attr(locked, "iv"), locked), outfile)
}

decrypt_file <- function(infile, outfile, passphrase) {
  bytes  <- readBin(infile, "raw", file.size(infile))
  salt   <- bytes[1:16]
  iv     <- bytes[17:32]
  key    <- bcrypt_pbkdf(passphrase, salt, rounds = 64L, size = 32L)
  plain  <- aes_cbc_decrypt(bytes[-(1:32)], key = key, iv = iv)
  writeBin(plain, outfile)
}

The iv is another set of random bytes that AES needs. Like the salt, it is not secret, so we store it in the file too.
Let us save the list of matched persons to a CSV file in a temporary folder, and encrypt it. We also record its hash, as in Section 8.6, using digest() with file = TRUE.

csv_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "matched_pensioners.csv")
enc_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "matched_pensioners.csv.enc")

write_csv(found, csv_file)
hash_sent <- digest(csv_file, algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)

passphrase <- "copper monsoon ladder 47 orchid"
encrypt_file(csv_file, enc_file, passphrase)

readBin(enc_file, "raw", 24)

 [1] 0d 34 1a 54 d1 06 8d 11 4c 69 29 ee ff 1b 2f 2b 66 e8 d2 bd 8c be 22 19


The encrypted file is meaningless bytes. It is now this file, not the CSV, that goes on the pen drive or in the email. The receiver decrypts it with the same passphrase, and checks the hash.

out_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "received.csv")
decrypt_file(enc_file, out_file, passphrase)

digest(out_file, algo = "sha256", file = TRUE) == hash_sent

[1] TRUE

read_csv(out_file, show_col_types = FALSE) |> nrow()

[1] 6


The hash agrees, so the file received is exactly the file sent. With a wrong passphrase, the decryption fails.

result <- tryCatch(
  decrypt_file(enc_file, out_file, "copper monsoon ladder 48 orchid"),
  error = function(e) "Decryption failed"
)
result

[1] "Decryption failed"


Very rarely, a wrong passphrase gives no error and produces a file of garbage instead. The hash check above catches that case too, which is one more reason to record the hash before sending.
Once the work is done, we delete the plain copies.

file.remove(c(csv_file, enc_file, out_file))


9.10.1 Keys and passphrases
The encryption is only as strong as the care taken with the passphrase.


Make it long. Four or five unrelated words with a number are easier to remember and much harder to guess than a short word with symbols.

Never write it in the script. We wrote it in the code above only to show how it works. In real work, type it when needed. askpass() from openssl opens a box in which the passphrase is typed without being shown, as in passphrase <- askpass("Passphrase for the file").

Send it by a different channel. If the file goes by email, give the passphrase by a phone call or a text message, never in the same email or a second email. Anyone who can read the mailbox would otherwise have both.

Keep the secret keys of hashing the same way. The key used for matching in Section 9.6 must never travel with the hashed lists.

Do not lose it. There is no way to recover an encrypted file without its passphrase. Keep it as your organisation’s instructions say.







Note



The receiver may not use R. In that case, use an archive tool that supports AES-256 encryption, such as 7-Zip, and choose AES-256 in its settings. The older “ZIP password” method is weak and should not be used. The rules about the passphrase are the same.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
section: 9.11 Encrypting with a pair of keys
text:
9.11 Encrypting with a pair of keys
The method of the last section has one weakness. The same passphrase locks the file and unlocks it. So the sender and the receiver must both know it, and it has to travel from one to the other. This is called symmetric encryption, because both sides hold the same secret.
There is a second kind, called public key encryption. Here each person makes a pair of keys that belong together.

The public key can only lock. It cannot unlock anything, not even what it locked itself. So it is safe to give to anyone, by email or on a website.
The private key is the only key that unlocks what its public key locked. It stays with the auditor and is never sent to anyone. It is itself protected by a password, so a stolen copy of the file is of no use without the password.

Think of a box of open padlocks. The audit office hands out open padlocks to every department. Anyone can snap one shut on a box. Only the audit office has the key that opens them. No secret ever has to travel.
The encryptr package makes this easy for data frames. It is built on openssl and uses the RSA method of public key encryption.

9.11.1 Making the key pair
genkeys() makes a key pair. It writes two files, the private key id_rsa and the public key id_rsa.pub, in the working folder, and asks us to choose a password for the private key.

genkeys()

The password is typed in a box and is not shown. Like the passphrase of a file, it cannot be recovered if it is lost.
A book is built without anyone at the keyboard to type a password. encryptr asks for the password through askpass() of openssl, and that function first looks for an R option called askpass. So, for this book only, we set that option to a function that supplies the password. In real work we leave the option alone and type the password when asked. We also write the keys to a temporary folder, and never to a project folder that others can see.

key_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "audit_keys")
dir.create(key_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
private_key <- file.path(key_dir, "audit_key")
public_key  <- file.path(key_dir, "audit_key.pub")
unlink(c(private_key, public_key))

# For the book only. In real work, type the password when R asks for it.
options(askpass = function(prompt) "teak harbour violet 82 lantern")

genkeys(private_key)

Private key written with name 'C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\RtmpGKrokh/audit_keys/audit_key'
Public key written with name 'C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\RtmpGKrokh/audit_keys/audit_key.pub'
It is strongly suggested that you add the private key to your .gitignore file if you backup your project with git


Both keys are plain text files. Their first lines show what they are.

readLines(public_key, n = 1)

[1] "-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----"

readLines(private_key, n = 1)

[1] "-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY-----"


The word ENCRYPTED tells us that the private key file is itself locked with the password.

9.11.2 Locking and unlocking a column
encrypt() takes a data frame, the columns to lock and the path of the public key. Let us lock the Aadhaar numbers of the first three pensioners.

three <- oap |>
  select(ben_id, aadhaar) |>
  head(3)

three_locked <- three |>
  encrypt(aadhaar, public_key_path = public_key)

three_locked |>
  mutate(aadhaar = str_trunc(aadhaar, 40))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  ben_id   aadhaar                                 
  <chr>    <chr>                                   
1 OAP00001 6378933266c6a7663bf26acc2cadea01677d1...
2 OAP00002 63e392ff54e6f253804aeb856e5735eaad0bf...
3 OAP00003 6486df31534b63a88e48f5ecb8fcd62490325...


Each Aadhaar number has become a long string of 512 hexadecimal characters. We have shortened them with str_trunc() only to fit the page. The other columns are untouched.
decrypt() does the reverse. It needs the private key, and so it asks for the password.

three_locked |>
  decrypt(aadhaar, private_key_path = private_key) |>
  mutate(aadhaar = mask_aadhaar(aadhaar))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  ben_id   aadhaar       
  <chr>    <chr>         
1 OAP00001 XXXX-XXXX-3259
2 OAP00002 XXXX-XXXX-1417
3 OAP00003 XXXX-XXXX-1550


The numbers are back. We mask them before printing, as we would with real data.

9.11.3 Locking a whole file
RSA can lock only short values, such as an identifier. For a whole file, encrypt_file() makes a fresh random key, locks the file with it by AES, and locks that random key with the public key. The result is saved in a file whose name ends in .encryptr.bin. decrypt_file() reverses both steps with the private key.
Our chapter already has its own functions called encrypt_file() and decrypt_file(), from Section 9.10. So we write encryptr:: before the names, which tells R to use the functions of the package.

csv_file <- file.path(key_dir, "matched_pensioners.csv")
write_csv(found, csv_file)

encryptr::encrypt_file(csv_file, public_key_path = public_key)

Encrypted file written with name 'C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\RtmpGKrokh/audit_keys/matched_pensioners.csv.encryptr.bin'

file.remove(csv_file)

[1] TRUE


Only the locked file is left. The receiver, who holds the private key, opens it.

encryptr::decrypt_file(paste0(csv_file, ".encryptr.bin"),
                       private_key_path = private_key)

Decrypted file written with name 'C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\RtmpGKrokh/audit_keys/matched_pensioners.csv'

read_csv(csv_file, show_col_types = FALSE) |> nrow()

[1] 6


All 6 records have come back. Note the direction. The department that holds only the public key can lock files for the auditor, but cannot open them. Even the department cannot open a file once it has locked it.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
section: 9.12 Audit use case, a department sends Aadhaar numbers only the auditor can read
text:
9.12 Audit use case, a department sends Aadhaar numbers only the auditor can read
In Section 9.6 the auditor matched the two lists on keyed hashes, and found 6 of the seven planted persons. The seventh was lost because of two swapped digits in the Treasury list. To find such cases, the auditor must be able to see the actual numbers of a few persons. With a pair of keys, the department can send its whole list and still keep every Aadhaar number unreadable to all but the auditor.

The audit office makes a key pair. It sends the public key to the Social Welfare Department by ordinary email. The private key stays on the auditor’s machine.
The department locks the Aadhaar column with the public key, and sends the list.
The auditor analyses and matches the list on the other columns.
The auditor unlocks the Aadhaar numbers of only those few rows that a finding needs.

The department does step 2 with one call to encrypt(). It also leaves out the fields the audit has not asked for.

oap_sent <- oap |>
  select(ben_id, name, gender, dob, district, aadhaar, monthly_pension) |>
  encrypt(aadhaar, public_key_path = public_key)

oap_sent |>
  mutate(aadhaar = str_trunc(aadhaar, 30)) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  ben_id   name         gender dob        district aadhaar       monthly_pension
  <chr>    <chr>        <chr>  <date>     <chr>    <chr>                   <dbl>
1 OAP00001 Mohan Mahto  M      1958-11-09 Sonpur   2260ed161d76…            1000
2 OAP00002 Kishan Verma M      1955-05-28 Sonpur   69a38d15b79c…            1000
3 OAP00003 Sita Munda   F      1960-01-24 Sonpur   0b0e5e069505…            1000


Anyone who intercepts this file sees only long codes in place of the Aadhaar numbers. Without the private key and its password, they cannot be turned back. Unlike a plain hash, they cannot be broken by trying every possible number either, because RSA mixes fresh random bytes into every value it locks. We can see this by locking the same number twice.

twice <- encrypt(tibble(aadhaar = rep(oap$aadhaar[1], 2)), aadhaar,
                 public_key_path = public_key)
twice$aadhaar[1] == twice$aadhaar[2]

[1] FALSE


The same number gives two different codes. This protects the numbers, but it also means that the locked column cannot be used for matching. So in step 3 the auditor matches on name and date of birth, which the Treasury list also has.

candidates <- oap_sent |>
  inner_join(svc |> select(ppo_no, name, dob, aadhaar_treasury = aadhaar),
             by = c("name", "dob"))

nrow(candidates)

[1] 7


The match on name and date of birth gives 7 persons. All 7 are the persons we planted, including the one the hashes missed. These are the only rows whose Aadhaar numbers the auditor needs. Step 4 unlocks them, and compares each number with the Treasury’s number after normalise_id().

checked <- candidates |>
  decrypt(aadhaar, private_key_path = private_key) |>
  mutate(same_aadhaar = normalise_id(aadhaar) == normalise_id(aadhaar_treasury))

checked |>
  transmute(ben_id, ppo_no,
            welfare  = mask_aadhaar(aadhaar),
            treasury = mask_aadhaar(normalise_id(aadhaar_treasury)),
            same_aadhaar)

# A tibble: 7 × 5
  ben_id   ppo_no        welfare        treasury       same_aadhaar
  <chr>    <chr>         <chr>          <chr>          <lgl>       
1 OAP00012 PPO/1997/7784 XXXX-XXXX-8530 XXXX-XXXX-8530 TRUE        
2 OAP00095 PPO/2017/7075 XXXX-XXXX-0424 XXXX-XXXX-0424 TRUE        
3 OAP00160 PPO/2020/3608 XXXX-XXXX-5754 XXXX-XXXX-5754 TRUE        
4 OAP00233 PPO/2008/4942 XXXX-XXXX-2613 XXXX-XXXX-2613 TRUE        
5 OAP00301 PPO/2022/9220 XXXX-XXXX-2974 XXXX-XXXX-2974 TRUE        
6 OAP00402 PPO/2001/9648 XXXX-XXXX-6416 XXXX-XXXX-4616 FALSE       
7 OAP00515 PPO/2001/2292 XXXX-XXXX-2925 XXXX-XXXX-2925 TRUE        


For 6 persons the two numbers agree exactly. These are the persons the keyed hashes found. For Kaushalya Gupta (OAP00402) the last four digits differ, so the masked forms differ too. Placed side by side, the two full numbers differ only in two neighbouring digits that have changed places. That is a typing error, and not a different person. The auditor can now ask the Treasury to verify this person with the other 6. The Aadhaar numbers of the other 593 pensioners were never unlocked.
When the exercise is over, the auditor deletes the decrypted rows and keeps in the working papers only the record IDs, the masked numbers and the replies of the departments.

file.remove(c(csv_file, paste0(csv_file, ".encryptr.bin")))
rm(checked)
options(askpass = NULL)


9.12.1 Keyed hash or encryption
Both the keyed hash of Section 9.5.3 and the key pair hide Aadhaar numbers. They differ in one important way.


A keyed hash cannot be reversed by anyone, not even the person who holds the key. The key only lets its holder compute the same code again from a number. Use it when two parties must match their lists and nobody needs the numbers themselves.

Encryption can be reversed by the holder of the private key. Use it when the auditor must later see the actual number of a few persons, for example to settle a near match, or to name the persons behind a confirmed finding.

The two can be used together. A department may send a keyed hash for matching and an encrypted copy of the same number for later checking.






WarningCaution



If the private key file is lost, or its password is forgotten, nothing locked with the public key can ever be opened again. Nobody can recover it, not the package and not the department. Keep a backup of the private key as your organisation’s instructions say, with the password stored separately. Never put the private key on a shared drive, in a cloud folder or in an email. If a private key may have been seen by someone else, make a new pair and stop using the old public key.








TipAudit tip



Give each audit its own key pair. When the audit is over, delete the private key along with the data. Any copy of the locked file that remains anywhere then becomes useless to everyone.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.13 What never to do
Most leaks do not come from clever attacks. They come from ordinary habits. With audit data, never do any of the following.


Upload it to online tools. This includes websites that convert PDFs or merge spreadsheets, online chart makers and AI chatbots. Once uploaded, the data is on someone else’s computer, under someone else’s terms, and cannot be called back. If you need help with code, describe the columns or share a few made-up rows, never the real data.

Send it from a personal email account, or through a personal messaging app. Use the official email, and encrypt the file.

Leave copies about. This means copies on a personal laptop or phone, a shared computer, a pen drive left in a drawer, or the Downloads folder. Keep one working copy in the audit project folder, on an official machine.

Keep it after the retention period. When the period laid down by your organisation ends, delete the data and its copies, including the encrypted ones and the backups.

Print identifiers when a masked form will do. A working paper rarely needs the full Aadhaar number.







WarningCaution



Hashed, tokenised and generalised data is still personal data. Whoever holds the key or the lookup table can link it back to the person, and the law covers data about anyone who can be identified. These methods reduce the risk, and the harm if a leak happens. They do not remove the duty of care. Pseudonymised data must still be kept securely, used only for the audit, and deleted on time.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.14 A suggested workflow


Ask for less. List in the requisition only the fields the audit needs, with the reason for each.

Sort the fields. Mark each column as a direct identifier, a quasi-identifier or a sensitive attribute, and write this in the code.

Minimise on arrival. Record the file hash as in Section 8.6, then make a working copy without the fields the analysis does not need.

Pseudonymise. Replace identifiers with tokens for work inside the team, or with keyed hashes when two parties must match lists. Never use a plain hash.

Keep secrets apart. Store the key, the lookup table and the passphrases away from the data, and destroy matching keys after use.

Mask for display. Show only the last four digits of identifiers in working papers and memos.

Check before publishing. Generalise quasi-identifiers, check k-anonymity with count(), and suppress small cells, with secondary suppression where totals are shown.

Encrypt before sending. Encrypt any file that leaves the official machine, and send the passphrase by a different channel.

Receive with a key pair. Give departments the audit’s public key, ask them to encrypt identifier columns with it, and unlock only the rows a finding needs.

Delete on time. Remove all copies when the retention period ends.







ImportantRemember




Take and keep only the data the audit needs.
A plain hash of a number from a small set can be reversed by trying every value. Use a keyed hash, and keep the key apart from the data.
Masking is for display, hashing is for matching, tokens are for working, encryption is for travelling.
A keyed hash cannot be reversed by anyone. Encryption can be reversed by whoever holds the key. A lost private key or password cannot be recovered.
A table with no names can still identify people through small cells.
Pseudonymised data is still personal data. The duty of care stays with the auditor.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.15 Where next
Chapter 10 covers reading and writing the files that we encrypt here, and Section 21.10 shows how to check that Aadhaar, PAN and IFSC values are in the right format before hashing them. Chapter 34 and Chapter 36 find the same person in two lists when the identifiers do not agree exactly, which hashes cannot do. Chapter 65 builds the tables of an audit report, where the checks of Section 9.9 belong.

title: 9  Protecting Personal Data
text:
9.16 Try it yourself
These exercises use the pension lists and the functions made in this chapter. None of them prints a full identifier or writes a key to disk. Try each one before opening the solution. Some solutions use dplyr verbs such as count(), filter() and inner_join(), which Chapter 15 and Chapter 16 explain in full.


A masked list for a working paper. List the beneficiaries of Hillpur who have a disability. Show the beneficiary ID, the masked Aadhaar number, the masked bank account and the monthly pension, and leave out the name.






TipSolution






hillpur_disabled <- oap |>
  filter(district == "Hillpur", disability == "Yes") |>
  transmute(ben_id,
            aadhaar      = mask_aadhaar(aadhaar),
            bank_account = mask_account(bank_account),
            monthly_pension)
hillpur_disabled

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  ben_id   aadhaar        bank_account monthly_pension
  <chr>    <chr>          <chr>                  <dbl>
1 OAP00571 XXXX-XXXX-2624 XXXXXXX7239             1500
2 OAP00590 XXXX-XXXX-4648 XXXXXXX8843             1500


Only 2 persons in Hillpur have a disability. In so small a group, even a masked list may point to the person, so it belongs in the working papers and not in the report.





Forgetting to normalise. Hash the Treasury’s Aadhaar numbers with secret_key, but skip normalise_id(). Join the result with from_welfare. How many persons match now?






TipSolution






treasury_raw <- svc |>
  transmute(ppo_no, aadhaar_hash = as.character(sha256(aadhaar, key = secret_key)))

from_welfare |>
  inner_join(treasury_raw, by = "aadhaar_hash") |>
  nrow()

[1] 0


Not one person matches, against 6 with normalised numbers. Every Treasury number has spaces or hyphens, so its hash differs from the hash of the same digits without them. If two departments hash their lists, both must agree on the standard form first.





Drop gender instead. The chapter suggested making the data coarser by dropping gender. Using oap_gen, with the bands already joined into 80 and above, count the persons in each combination of district and age band. Are any groups still smaller than k?






TipSolution






oap_gen |>
  count(district, age_band) |>
  filter(n < k)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  district age_band     n
  <chr>    <fct>    <int>
1 Hillpur  80+          4


One group is still too small. Hillpur has only 4 pensioners aged 80 and above. Dropping gender is not enough here, so these few records must be coarsened further, or left out of the shared copy with a note saying so.





Small cells in a disability table. The report is also to show the number of pensioners with and without a disability in each district. Make this table with count() and complete(), and find the cells below the threshold of 5.






TipSolution






tab_dis <- oap |>
  count(district, disability) |>
  complete(district, disability, fill = list(n = 0))

tab_dis |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = disability, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  district     No   Yes
  <chr>     <int> <int>
1 Bhimnagar   101     9
2 Hillpur      38     2
3 Nandgaon    115    15
4 Rajgarh     132    18
5 Sonpur      156    14

tab_dis |>
  filter(n < threshold)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  district disability     n
  <chr>    <chr>      <int>
1 Hillpur  Yes            2


Only one cell is below 5, the 2 persons of Hillpur with a disability. If the table shows the district total, the other Hillpur cell must be hidden too, or the hidden number can be found by subtraction. This is the secondary suppression of Section 9.9.





A fresh key for the next audit. Make a new key with rand_bytes(), without printing it. Hash the Treasury list with the new key and join it with from_welfare, which was hashed with the old key. Then hash the welfare list with the new key too, and join again.






TipSolution






new_key <- paste(rand_bytes(32), collapse = "")

treasury_new <- svc |>
  transmute(ppo_no, aadhaar_hash = keyed_hash(aadhaar, new_key))
welfare_new <- oap |>
  transmute(ben_id, aadhaar_hash = keyed_hash(aadhaar, new_key))

nrow(inner_join(from_welfare, treasury_new, by = "aadhaar_hash"))

[1] 0

nrow(inner_join(welfare_new, treasury_new, by = "aadhaar_hash"))

[1] 6

rm(new_key)

Lists hashed with different keys find nobody in common. With the same new key on both sides, the same 6 persons are found again. This is why a fresh key for each exercise stops old hashed lists from being linked with new ones. The last line removes the key from memory once the work is done.
