title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.1 Our data, files received from a treasury
Audit data comes from outside. A district treasury sends a file of every voucher it passed in a month. A works division sends its register as an Excel workbook, with a sheet for each sub-division. A scheme’s portal gives a download of its beneficiaries. Before we can check anything, this data has to come into R, whole and correct.
This step is not as simple as it looks. A file read carelessly can lose payments without any error. An amount written as “1,25,000” can quietly become a missing value, and drop out of every total. A DDO code like 0204015 can lose its leading zero and stop matching the master. So reading a file is itself an audit step. The auditor must be able to show that the data analysed is the data received, row for row and rupee for rupee.
After the analysis, the results travel the other way. Exception lists, summaries and charts are exported, for the working papers, for the audit report, and for the auditee’s reply. In this chapter we learn both directions. We first see the base R functions for reading and writing files, and then the tidyverse packages which do these jobs faster and more safely. We end with the most important point for an auditor, checking that nothing went wrong while reading, and reconciling a treasury file with its covering letter.
Prerequisites
To practise, we need some files. So let us create them, in a temporary folder given by tempdir(), so that nothing is left behind in our project. There are four files.
Code to create the files used in this chapterfolder <- file.path(tempdir(), "audit_files")
dir.create(folder, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(2024)
n <- 120
ddo_codes <- c("0204015", "0204022", "0204031", "0204047", "0204058")
heads <- c("2054-00-095-01", "2202-01-101-02", "2210-03-103-01", "4059-01-051-03")
payees <- c("Sharma Traders", "Kaveri Infra", "Om Sai Suppliers", "Laxmi Electricals",
            "Patel Hardware", "Salaries, establishment", "Gupta Enterprises")

amarpur <- tibble(
  voucher_no = sprintf("TV/AMR/%04d", 1:n),
  ddo_code   = sample(ddo_codes, n, replace = TRUE),
  bill_date  = format(sort(as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:29, n, replace = TRUE)),
                      "%d/%m/%Y"),
  head       = sample(heads, n, replace = TRUE),
  payee      = sample(payees, n, replace = TRUE),
  mode       = sample(c("e-payment", "Cheque"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.85, 0.15)),
  amount     = round(rlnorm(n, log(80000), 1), -1)
)
# Planted. Three large payments of works contracts
amarpur$amount[c(17, 58, 93)] <- c(1245000, 1870500, 2310000)
amarpur$payee[c(17, 58, 93)] <- "Kaveri Infra"
amarpur_file <- file.path(folder, "amarpur_vouchers_apr2024.csv")
write.csv(amarpur, amarpur_file, row.names = FALSE)

cheque_file <- file.path(folder, "cancelled_cheques.txt")
writeLines(c("504117", "504123", "504188", "504190", "504201", "504236"), cheque_file)

letter_file <- file.path(folder, "covering_letter.txt")
writeLines(c("Office of the Treasury Officer, District Treasury, Amarpur",
             "To the Senior Audit Officer",
             "Data of vouchers passed in April 2024",
             "Number of vouchers passed, 120",
             "Total amount in rupees, see the enclosed file"),
           letter_file)

xl_file <- file.path(folder, "works_register.xlsx")
write_xlsx(list(
  "Amarpur North" = tibble(work_id = c("W-101", "W-102", "W-103"),
                           work = c("Road repair, Km 4 to 9", "School boundary wall",
                                    "Culvert at Sonpur"),
                           estimate_lakh = c(42.5, 18.0, 9.6)),
  "Amarpur South" = tibble(work_id = c("W-201", "W-202"),
                           work = c("Panchayat bhawan", "Drain, ward 7"),
                           estimate_lakh = c(25.0, 12.4))),
  xl_file)
file.path() joins the parts of a path with /, the separator which works on every computer. The four paths are now saved in amarpur_file, cheque_file, letter_file and xl_file, and we use these names below. With your own data, you would instead give the path of the file on your computer, like "Data/vouchers.csv".

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
amarpur_vouchers_apr2024.csv, the vouchers passed by the District Treasury, Amarpur, in April 2024. Each row has the voucher number, the code of the drawing and disbursing officer (DDO), the date of the bill, the head of account, the payee, the mode of payment and the amount in rupees.

cancelled_cheques.txt, the numbers of cheques reported as cancelled, one on each line.

covering_letter.txt, the letter sent by the treasury with the file.

works_register.xlsx, an Excel workbook from a works division, with one sheet for each of two sub-divisions.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.2 Importing data with base R
Base R has functions to import nearly any kind of external data. There are also packages which make certain tasks easier, and we will learn some of them later in this chapter. Let us first see the base R functions which are used most often.
Reading tables with read.table() and read.csv()

These two are the most common functions for reading tabular data from plain text files. read.table() reads data whose columns are separated by spaces or another separator. read.csv() reads comma separated values (.csv) files. They have three more cousins.


read.csv2() reads csv files where ; is the separator and , the decimal mark, as used in many European countries.

read.delim() reads files where a tab character separates the columns and . is the decimal mark.

read.delim2() reads tab separated files where , is the decimal mark.

The most important arguments of these functions are these.


file, the name of the file, with its path, as a string1.

header, a logical value, telling whether the first line of the file holds the column names.

sep, the character which separates the columns.

colClasses, a character vector giving the type of each column, if the columns must be read in these types only.

skip, the number of lines to skip at the beginning of the file.

Readers may see ?read.table() for the complete list of arguments. Let us read the voucher file of the Amarpur treasury.

vouchers <- read.csv(amarpur_file)
# Check dimensions
dim(vouchers)

[1] 120   7

# Check column names
colnames(vouchers)

[1] "voucher_no" "ddo_code"   "bill_date"  "head"       "payee"     
[6] "mode"       "amount"    

head(vouchers)

   voucher_no ddo_code  bill_date           head             payee      mode
1 TV/AMR/0001   204022 01/04/2024 2202-01-101-02    Patel Hardware e-payment
2 TV/AMR/0002   204058 01/04/2024 2210-03-103-01    Patel Hardware e-payment
3 TV/AMR/0003   204058 01/04/2024 2210-03-103-01  Om Sai Suppliers e-payment
4 TV/AMR/0004   204047 01/04/2024 2054-00-095-01 Laxmi Electricals e-payment
5 TV/AMR/0005   204015 01/04/2024 2202-01-101-02 Laxmi Electricals e-payment
6 TV/AMR/0006   204058 01/04/2024 4059-01-051-03      Kaveri Infra e-payment
  amount
1  10040
2  80700
3 124580
4  41620
5  16300
6 110990


The data has 120 rows and 7 columns. But look at ddo_code. The first code in the file is 0204022, but R shows 204022. read.csv() has seen digits, and read the column as numbers, so the leading zero is gone. These codes will no longer match the DDO master. The argument colClasses tells R the type of the columns we name.

vouchers <- read.csv(amarpur_file, colClasses = c(ddo_code = "character"))
head(vouchers$ddo_code)

[1] "0204022" "0204058" "0204058" "0204047" "0204015" "0204058"


A file can also be read directly from a web address, without downloading it first, by giving the address in place of the file name.






Note



Use "clipboard" as the file name to paste copied data into R. For example, copy a few rows and columns from an Excel sheet, and run read.delim("clipboard", header = FALSE). This works on Windows.


Reading data into a vector with scan() and readline()

read.table() and its cousins read data into tables. Sometimes we need to read data into a simple vector instead. The two functions scan() and readline() are used for this.
The basic syntax of scan() is as follows.
scan(file = "",
     what = double(),
     nmax = -1,
     ...
)
The arguments mean this.


file is the name of the file, or a link.

what is the type of data to be read. The default is double.

nmax is the maximum number of values to be read. The default, -1, means all.

There are many other useful arguments, which can be seen with ?scan. Let us read the numbers of the cancelled cheques.

cancelled <- scan(cheque_file)
cancelled

[1] 504117 504123 504188 504190 504201 504236


In the console, scan() also says how many items it read. The result is a plain vector, ready to be checked against the cheque issue register with %in% (Chapter 2).
scan() can also read data typed on the keyboard into a vector. Just give a blank string "" as the file name. See this example.

The function readline() does a similar job, but shows a prompt. See this example.

Reading text files with readLines()

The function readLines() reads the lines of a text file (or connection), giving one element for each line. Let us read the covering letter of the treasury.

letter <- readLines(letter_file)
letter

[1] "Office of the Treasury Officer, District Treasury, Amarpur"
[2] "To the Senior Audit Officer"                               
[3] "Data of vouchers passed in April 2024"                     
[4] "Number of vouchers passed, 120"                            
[5] "Total amount in rupees, see the enclosed file"             


Each line is now one element of a character vector, which we can search and subset like any other. We use readLines() again to read the Budget speech in Chapter 53.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.3 Exporting data with base R
In most analysis, we read external data, and then clean, transform and analyse it, all in R. So we export less often than we import. Still, cleaned data, summaries and exception lists often need to be exported. The following functions meet nearly all such needs.
Writing tables with write.table() and write.csv()

Data frames can be exported with these functions. The latter writes csv files specifically. The syntax is as follows.
write.table(x, file = "", sep = " ", ...)
write.csv(x, file = "", ...)
write.csv2(x, file = "", ...)
The arguments mean this.


x is the data frame to be exported.

file is the file name, with its path.

sep is the separator.

... are many more arguments for customised exports. See ?write.table() for full details.

For example, let us export the vouchers of ₹10 lakh or more as a csv file, for the working papers. We pick them out exactly as in Chapter 2.

big_vouchers <- vouchers[which(vouchers$amount >= 1e6), c("voucher_no", "payee", "amount")]
write.csv(big_vouchers, file.path(folder, "big_vouchers.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
big_vouchers

    voucher_no        payee  amount
17 TV/AMR/0017 Kaveri Infra 1245000
58 TV/AMR/0058 Kaveri Infra 1870500
93 TV/AMR/0093 Kaveri Infra 2310000


There are 3 such vouchers, for a total of ₹54.26 lakh. By default, write.csv() also writes the row numbers as a first, unnamed column. row.names = FALSE stops this, which is nearly always what we want.
Writing text line by line with writeLines()

Like readLines(), the function writeLines() writes text into a file of the given name, one element on each line. It is handy for a short note to go with an exported file.

writeLines(c("Vouchers of Rs 10 lakh or more, District Treasury Amarpur, April 2024",
             paste("Number of vouchers,", nrow(big_vouchers))),
           file.path(folder, "big_vouchers_note.txt"))
readLines(file.path(folder, "big_vouchers_note.txt"))

[1] "Vouchers of Rs 10 lakh or more, District Treasury Amarpur, April 2024"
[2] "Number of vouchers, 3"                                                


Getting the code for an object with dput()

This function prints the code which would recreate a given R object. It is particularly useful when asking for help online. For example, on Stack Overflow, a question should include reproducible data. Please also refer to Section 10.6. Let us make up three rows of voucher data and see.

my_data <- data.frame(voucher_no = c("TV-0001", "TV-0002", "TV-0003"),
                      amount = c(18500, 125000, 9800))
dput(my_data)

structure(list(voucher_no = c("TV-0001", "TV-0002", "TV-0003"
), amount = c(18500, 125000, 9800)), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, 
-3L))


And to recreate someone else’s data from their dput() output, we simply run it.

now_mydata <- structure(list(voucher_no = c("TV-0001", "TV-0002", "TV-0003"
), amount = c(18500, 125000, 9800)), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-3L))

now_mydata

  voucher_no amount
1    TV-0001  18500
2    TV-0002 125000
3    TV-0003   9800








WarningCaution



Never share real audit data this way. Make up a few rows of similar data instead, as we did here. Audit data often holds names, account numbers and other personal details, which must not be posted on a public forum.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.4 Reading and writing with packages

10.4.1 Package readr

The readr package2 is part of the core tidyverse, and is loaded with library(tidyverse). It has a counterpart for each of the reading and writing functions of base R.


Table 10.1: Base R and readr functions



Base R
readr
Uses



read.table
read_table
Reading tables separated by white space


read.csv
read_csv
Reading CSV file with comma as sep


read.csv2
read_csv2
Reading CSV file with semi-colon as sep


read.delim
read_tsv
Reading tab delimited file


--
read_delim
Reading files with any delimiter


read.fwf
read_fwf
Reading fixed width files


--
write_delim
Writing files with any delimiter


write.csv
write_csv
Writing files with comma delimiter


write.csv2
write_csv2
Writing files with semi-colon delimiter


--
write_tsv
Writing a tab delimited file






What is the difference between the two sets? Firstly, the readr functions are much faster, which matters for large files. Secondly, they report the problems they meet while reading, as we will see shortly. And thirdly, they never turn text into factors, or change column names, behind our back. Let us read the same voucher file with read_csv().

read_csv(amarpur_file)

Rows: 120 Columns: 7
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (6): voucher_no, ddo_code, bill_date, head, payee, mode
dbl (1): amount

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


# A tibble: 120 × 7
   voucher_no  ddo_code bill_date  head           payee             mode  amount
   <chr>       <chr>    <chr>      <chr>          <chr>             <chr>  <dbl>
 1 TV/AMR/0001 0204022  01/04/2024 2202-01-101-02 Patel Hardware    e-pa…  10040
 2 TV/AMR/0002 0204058  01/04/2024 2210-03-103-01 Patel Hardware    e-pa…  80700
 3 TV/AMR/0003 0204058  01/04/2024 2210-03-103-01 Om Sai Suppliers  e-pa… 124580
 4 TV/AMR/0004 0204047  01/04/2024 2054-00-095-01 Laxmi Electricals e-pa…  41620
 5 TV/AMR/0005 0204015  01/04/2024 2202-01-101-02 Laxmi Electricals e-pa…  16300
 6 TV/AMR/0006 0204058  01/04/2024 4059-01-051-03 Kaveri Infra      e-pa… 110990
 7 TV/AMR/0007 0204015  01/04/2024 2202-01-101-02 Salaries, establ… e-pa…  82870
 8 TV/AMR/0008 0204022  01/04/2024 4059-01-051-03 Laxmi Electricals e-pa… 165110
 9 TV/AMR/0009 0204022  02/04/2024 2054-00-095-01 Salaries, establ… e-pa… 363250
10 TV/AMR/0010 0204058  02/04/2024 2210-03-103-01 Om Sai Suppliers  e-pa…  25320
# ℹ 110 more rows


Notice that the type of each column has been printed. readr guesses the types from the first 1,000 rows. Here it has kept ddo_code as text (chr), because the values begin with a zero. But it has also read bill_date as text, since it does not recognise dates written day first. If the guesses are not what we want, we use the argument col_types. We can see the guessed types with spec(), and modify them for use in col_types. See this example.

spec(read_csv(amarpur_file))

Rows: 120 Columns: 7
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (6): voucher_no, ddo_code, bill_date, head, payee, mode
dbl (1): amount

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


cols(
  voucher_no = col_character(),
  ddo_code = col_character(),
  bill_date = col_character(),
  head = col_character(),
  payee = col_character(),
  mode = col_character(),
  amount = col_double()
)

vouchers <- read_csv(amarpur_file,
                     col_types = cols(
                       voucher_no = col_character(),
                       ddo_code   = col_character(),
                       bill_date  = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%Y"),
                       head       = col_character(),
                       payee      = col_character(),
                       mode       = col_factor(levels = c("e-payment", "Cheque")),
                       amount     = col_double()
                     ))
vouchers |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  voucher_no  ddo_code bill_date  head           payee            mode    amount
  <chr>       <chr>    <date>     <chr>          <chr>            <fct>    <dbl>
1 TV/AMR/0001 0204022  2024-04-01 2202-01-101-02 Patel Hardware   e-paym…  10040
2 TV/AMR/0002 0204058  2024-04-01 2210-03-103-01 Patel Hardware   e-paym…  80700
3 TV/AMR/0003 0204058  2024-04-01 2210-03-103-01 Om Sai Suppliers e-paym… 124580


Now bill_date is a true date, and mode a factor with the two modes of payment. The format "%d/%m/%Y" says that the day comes first, then the month, then the year in four digits, separated by /. We will learn more about such formats in Chapter 18.
Two other arguments are often useful. col_select reads only the columns we need, which saves time and memory with wide files.

read_csv(amarpur_file, col_select = c(voucher_no, amount), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  voucher_no  amount
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 TV/AMR/0001  10040
2 TV/AMR/0002  80700
3 TV/AMR/0003 124580


locale handles files with other encodings or number formats. For example, files with Hindi or other Indian scripts, saved from older software, may need locale = locale(encoding = "UTF-16LE") or another encoding, to be read correctly.

10.4.2 Package readxl

This package is also part of tidyverse, but has to be loaded separately with library(readxl). It reads Excel files. An Excel file (with extension .xls or .xlsx) can hold several sheets. The functions read_excel(), read_xlsx() and read_xls() read a sheet. The syntax is as follows.
read_excel(path, sheet = NULL, range = NULL, skip = 0, col_types = NULL)
The arguments mean this.


sheet is the name or number of the sheet. The default is the first sheet.

range reads only a block of cells, like "B3:H120".

skip skips rows at the top, like a title.

col_types = "text" reads every column as text, which is the safest way to begin with a messy file.

To get the names of all the sheets in an Excel file, we use excel_sheets(). Let us look at the works register.

excel_sheets(xl_file)

[1] "Amarpur North" "Amarpur South"

read_excel(xl_file, sheet = "Amarpur South")

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  work_id work             estimate_lakh
  <chr>   <chr>                    <dbl>
1 W-201   Panchayat bhawan          25  
2 W-202   Drain, ward 7             12.4

read_excel(xl_file, sheet = 1, range = "A1:B3")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  work_id work                  
  <chr>   <chr>                 
1 W-101   Road repair, Km 4 to 9
2 W-102   School boundary wall  


The first call read the whole of the second sheet, by its name. The second read only the cells A1:B3 of the first sheet, that is the headings and two rows of the first two columns. We read all the sheets of a file together in Chapter 14.

10.4.3 Writing Excel files
readxl cannot write Excel files. For that, the package writexl has a simple function, write_xlsx(). A named list of data frames is written as one sheet each, which is a convenient way to give the auditee all the exception lists in one file.

exceptions_file <- file.path(folder, "exceptions.xlsx")
write_xlsx(list(big_vouchers   = vouchers |> filter(amount >= 1e6),
                cheque_payments = vouchers |> filter(mode == "Cheque")),
           exceptions_file)
excel_sheets(exceptions_file)

[1] "big_vouchers"    "cheque_payments"


filter() keeps the rows meeting a condition. We will learn it properly in Chapter 15. For formatted Excel output, with colours, column widths and formulas, the package openxlsx2 can be used.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
section: 10.5 Checking that the data was read correctly
text:
10.5 Checking that the data was read correctly
This is the most important step for an auditor, and the one most often skipped. When readr cannot read a value as the type expected, it puts NA in its place and moves on. Only a short message is printed. Let us see this with a small file of payments, written in the way real files often are.

csv_text <- "voucher_no,emp_code,amount,date
PV-01,00123,1250,15/04/2024
PV-02,00456,\"1,25,000\",16/04/2024
PV-03,01789,-,2024-04-17
PV-04,12001,3400.50,NA"

payments <- read_csv(I(csv_text), col_types = cols(amount = col_double()))

Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details,
e.g.:
  dat <- vroom(...)
  problems(dat)

payments

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  voucher_no emp_code amount date      
  <chr>      <chr>     <dbl> <chr>     
1 PV-01      00123     1250  15/04/2024
2 PV-02      00456       NA  16/04/2024
3 PV-03      01789       NA  2024-04-17
4 PV-04      12001     3400. <NA>      


Here, I() tells read_csv() that the text itself is the data, not a file name. Look at the amount column. The amount of ₹1,25,000, written with Indian commas, has become NA, and so has the -. Both payments have silently disappeared from any total we calculate. problems() lists every value that could not be read.

problems(payments)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
    row   col expected actual   file                                            
  <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>    <chr>                                           
1     3     3 a double 1,25,000 C:/Users/User/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpgrqnP9/vro…
2     4     3 a double -        C:/Users/User/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpgrqnP9/vro…


The safest approach is to read such columns as text first, and convert them ourselves, with a function that understands the format. parse_number() removes the commas and any other non-numeric characters around the number. The argument na lists the values to be treated as missing.

payments <- read_csv(I(csv_text), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

payments |>
  mutate(amount_num = parse_number(amount, na = c("-", "NA")))

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  voucher_no emp_code amount   date       amount_num
  <chr>      <chr>    <chr>    <chr>           <dbl>
1 PV-01      00123    1250     15/04/2024      1250 
2 PV-02      00456    1,25,000 16/04/2024    125000 
3 PV-03      01789    -        2024-04-17        NA 
4 PV-04      12001    3400.50  <NA>            3400.


Now ₹1,25,000 has been read correctly. Notice also that emp_code keeps its leading zeros, because we read it as text. Read as a number, 00123 would have become 123, and joins with other tables would fail, as we saw in Section 20.19.






TipAudit tip



After reading any file, always check three things before analysis. (1) The number of rows matches the number in the source, or the count given by the auditee. (2) The totals of amount columns match the totals in the source. (3) problems() is empty, or every problem is understood. Read code columns, like employee numbers, PIN codes and account numbers, as text.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.6 Asking for help with reprex

The package reprex is part of tidyverse too, but has to be loaded with library(reprex). Its name is short for reproducible example. It is useful when we are stuck with a problem and seek help on a forum, such as Stack Overflow or Posit Community.
As an example, do this in your console. It uses iris, a small dataset that comes with R, since a helper on a forum will have it too.
library(reprex)

x <- dput(head(iris))
x
Thereafter, copy the code and run reprex(). A small window opens in the Viewer tab, like this, showing the code with its output. The formatted result is also copied to the clipboard, ready to paste into a question.

For more reading please refer to this page.3

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
section: 10.7 Audit use case, reconciling a treasury file with its covering letter
text:
10.7 Audit use case, reconciling a treasury file with its covering letter
The District Treasury, Belapur, has sent its vouchers for April 2024 as a csv file. Its covering letter states the number of vouchers and their total amount. Before any analysis, we must show that the file we analyse agrees with the letter. The code below creates the file and the letter. Like many real extracts, the file writes some amounts with Indian commas and some as -, and it may not be complete.

Code to create the Belapur file and covering letterset.seed(77)
m <- 85
belapur <- tibble(
  voucher_no = sprintf("TV/BLP/%04d", 1:m),
  ddo_code   = sample(c("0311004", "0311012", "0311019", "0311026"), m, replace = TRUE),
  bill_date  = format(sort(as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:29, m, replace = TRUE)),
                      "%d/%m/%Y"),
  payee      = sample(payees, m, replace = TRUE),
  amount     = round(rlnorm(m, log(90000), 0.9), -1)
)
letter_total <- sum(belapur$amount)

# Write a whole number with Indian commas, like 1,25,000
indian <- function(x) {
  s <- format(x, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  ifelse(nchar(s) <= 3, s,
         paste0(gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(s, 1, nchar(s) - 3), perl = TRUE),
                ",", substr(s, nchar(s) - 2, nchar(s))))
}

belapur_out <- belapur |>
  mutate(amount = format(amount, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))
# Planted. Amounts of a lakh or more written with Indian commas
big <- which(belapur$amount >= 1e5)
belapur_out$amount[big] <- indian(belapur$amount[big])
# Planted. Two amounts left as "-" in the extract
belapur_out$amount[c(23, 61)] <- "-"
# Planted. One voucher missing from the extract
belapur_out <- belapur_out[-47, ]

belapur_file <- file.path(folder, "belapur_vouchers_apr2024.csv")
write_csv(belapur_out, belapur_file)

belapur_letter <- file.path(folder, "belapur_letter.txt")
writeLines(c("Office of the Treasury Officer, District Treasury, Belapur",
             "Data of vouchers passed in April 2024",
             paste0("Number of vouchers passed, ", m),
             paste0("Total amount in rupees, ", indian(letter_total))),
           belapur_letter)


Step 1, take the control totals from the letter. The letter is a text file, so we read it with readLines(). parse_number() takes out the number from each line.

letter <- readLines(belapur_letter)
letter

[1] "Office of the Treasury Officer, District Treasury, Belapur"
[2] "Data of vouchers passed in April 2024"                     
[3] "Number of vouchers passed, 85"                             
[4] "Total amount in rupees, 1,06,73,100"                       

control <- parse_number(letter[3:4])
control

[1]       85 10673100


The treasury says it passed 85 vouchers, for a total of ₹106.73 lakh.
Step 2, read the file the quick way, and see what goes wrong. Suppose we tell read_csv() that the amount is a number.

quick <- read_csv(belapur_file, col_types = cols(amount = col_double()))

Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details,
e.g.:
  dat <- vroom(...)
  problems(dat)

nrow(quick)

[1] 84

sum(quick$amount, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 2464290

nrow(problems(quick))

[1] 39


The total is only ₹24.64 lakh, against ₹106.73 lakh in the letter. 39 amounts could not be read, and have become NA. Had we not compared with the letter, we would have analysed a file short of ₹82.09 lakh, without knowing it.
Step 3, read everything as text, and convert the amounts ourselves.

received <- read_csv(belapur_file, col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |>
  mutate(amount_num = parse_number(amount, na = "-"))

received |> filter(is.na(amount_num))

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  voucher_no  ddo_code bill_date  payee             amount amount_num
  <chr>       <chr>    <chr>      <chr>             <chr>       <dbl>
1 TV/BLP/0023 0311004  10/04/2024 Gupta Enterprises -              NA
2 TV/BLP/0061 0311019  20/04/2024 Patel Hardware    -              NA


Only the two vouchers written as - are now without an amount. The commas have been read correctly.
Step 4, reconcile the rows and the total.

tibble(item     = c("Vouchers", "Amount (Rs)"),
       letter   = control,
       file     = c(nrow(received), read_total),
       shortfall = letter - file)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  item          letter     file shortfall
  <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Vouchers          85       84         1
2 Amount (Rs) 10673100 10361810    311290


The file has 84 vouchers, one fewer than the letter. Since voucher numbers run in a series, the missing one is easy to find, by the method of Chapter 37.

serials <- parse_number(str_extract(received$voucher_no, "\\d+$"))
missing_voucher <- setdiff(1:max(serials), serials)
missing_voucher

[1] 47


Voucher TV/BLP/0047 is not in the file. The total is still short by ₹3,11,290. This is the amount of the missing voucher and of the two vouchers, TV/BLP/0023 and TV/BLP/0061, shown as -.
What next? The auditor writes to the treasury, asking for voucher TV/BLP/0047 and for the amounts of the two vouchers shown as -. When the corrected file arrives, the same code is run again, and the reconciliation table goes into the working papers. Only then does the analysis begin. If the treasury cannot explain the gap, the incomplete extract is itself a point to report, about the reliability of the treasury’s data.






WarningCaution



A file that reconciles in count but not in total, or the other way round, is not ready for analysis. Never “adjust” the data in R to make it agree with the letter. Find the reason, record it, and get the corrected data from the source.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.8 A suggested workflow
For any file received from the auditee, an auditor may follow these steps.


Look at the file first. Note its format, its sheets with excel_sheets(), and any title rows to skip.

Note the control totals. Take the number of records and the total amount from the covering letter, with readLines() and parse_number() if the letter is a text file.

Read everything as text to begin with. Use col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) in read_csv(), or col_types = "text" in read_excel(). This keeps leading zeros in codes and stops values from turning into NA silently.

Check for problems. Run problems() and make sure every problem is understood.

Convert amounts and dates yourself. Use parse_number() with a suitable na argument, so that amounts written with Indian commas are read correctly. Give the date format with col_date().

Keep code columns as text. DDO codes, employee numbers, PIN codes and account numbers should stay as text.

Reconcile with the source. Match the number of rows and the totals of amount columns with the covering letter. Look for missing serial numbers with setdiff().

Export the results. Write exception lists with write_csv() or write.csv(), or with write_xlsx() to put each list on its own sheet in one file.







ImportantRemember



A value that cannot be read becomes NA with only a short message. Such a payment silently drops out of every total. Always check problems(), the row count and the totals against the covering letter before starting the analysis.

title: 10  Importing and Exporting Data
text:
10.9 Try it yourself
These exercises use the files created at the start of this chapter, in the temporary folder folder. Try each one before opening the solution. Some solutions use dplyr verbs such as filter() and summarise(), which Chapter 15 explains in full.


Cheque payments only. Read the Amarpur voucher file with read_csv(), keeping only the columns voucher_no, mode and amount. How many vouchers were paid by cheque, and for what total?






TipSolution






cheques <- read_csv(amarpur_file, col_select = c(voucher_no, mode, amount),
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(mode == "Cheque")
nrow(cheques)

[1] 20

sum(cheques$amount)

[1] 3290210


There are 20 cheque payments, for ₹32.9 lakh. Cheque payments deserve a look, since most payments are now made electronically.





Large works. Read both sheets of the works register, and find the works with an estimate of ₹20 lakh or more in each.






TipSolution






read_excel(xl_file, sheet = "Amarpur North") |>
  filter(estimate_lakh >= 20)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  work_id work                   estimate_lakh
  <chr>   <chr>                          <dbl>
1 W-101   Road repair, Km 4 to 9          42.5

read_excel(xl_file, sheet = "Amarpur South") |>
  filter(estimate_lakh >= 20)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  work_id work             estimate_lakh
  <chr>   <chr>                    <dbl>
1 W-201   Panchayat bhawan            25


One work in each sub-division is estimated at ₹20 lakh or more. These would be the first works to select for a check of the sanction and the tender.





Reconcile the Amarpur file. Read the covering letter of the Amarpur treasury from letter_file. Take the number of vouchers from it, and compare it with the number of rows in vouchers.






TipSolution






amarpur_letter <- readLines(letter_file)
amarpur_letter[4]

[1] "Number of vouchers passed, 120"

parse_number(amarpur_letter[4]) == nrow(vouchers)

[1] TRUE


The count in the letter agrees with the file. But the letter gives no total amount. So the auditor should ask the treasury for the total, before the file can be fully reconciled.





Export a DDO summary and check it. For the Amarpur vouchers of ₹1 lakh or more, make a summary with the number of vouchers and their total for each DDO. Write it to folder as a csv file, read it back, and check that the DDO codes and the total survived the round trip.






TipSolution






ddo_summary <- vouchers |>
  filter(amount >= 1e5) |>
  summarise(vouchers = n(), amount = sum(amount), .by = ddo_code)

summary_file <- file.path(folder, "ddo_summary.csv")
write_csv(ddo_summary, summary_file)

ddo_back <- read_csv(summary_file, col_types = cols(ddo_code = col_character()))
ddo_back

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  ddo_code vouchers  amount
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 0204058         8 1454900
2 0204022        10 5034830
3 0204031        14 5903080
4 0204047        11 2441810
5 0204015        10 2247810

sum(ddo_back$amount) == sum(ddo_summary$amount)

[1] TRUE


The 53 vouchers of ₹1 lakh or more come to ₹170.82 lakh, and the file read back gives the same total. Reading ddo_code as text keeps its leading zero, so the codes still match the DDO master.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
11.1 Cleaning column names
An auditor asks a works division for its statement of payments, and receives a spreadsheet. It is meant for printing, not for analysis. The column names have spaces and symbols. There are title rows at the top, blank rows in between, and a total row at the bottom. Amounts are written as “1,25,000/-”. Dates are typed in four different ways. A missing amount is written as “-”, “N/A” or “Nil”. The same firm appears as “Sharma Traders” and ” sharma traders “. If we analyse such a file as it is, totals will be wrong, the same firm will be counted twice, and some payments will drop out without any warning.
So before any audit check, the data must be cleaned. This is often the longest step of the whole analysis. It is also an audit step in its own right. A missing amount, or a firm entered under two names, is a fact about the quality of the auditee’s records, and may be a finding by itself.
Several packages in R help with this. In this chapter we will use janitor, along with readr, stringr and lubridate. We first learn each tool on a small piece of office data. We then put them together to clean a messy statement of payments received from a division, and record what the cleaning revealed.
Prerequisites
Names of objects in R follow certain rules. For example, a name with a space or a special character must be wrapped in backticks `. Files from Excel often have such “dirty” column names, which we should clean before going further. The function clean_names() does this. Let us take the headings of a statement of works, as an office might type them.
# Create a data.frame with dirty names
test_df <- as.data.frame(matrix(ncol = 7))

names(test_df) <- c("Work ID", "Name of Work", "Estimate (Rs. lakh)", "% Completion",
                    "REMARKS", "REMARKS", "")
# View this data
test_df

  Work ID Name of Work Estimate (Rs. lakh) % Completion REMARKS REMARKS   
1      NA           NA                  NA           NA      NA      NA NA
Using clean_names(), which works well in a pipe, we can clean all the names in one step. The results are in snake case, with lower case words joined by underscores.
test_df |>
  clean_names()

  work_id name_of_work estimate_rs_lakh percent_completion remarks remarks_2  x
1      NA           NA               NA                 NA      NA        NA NA
clean_names() does the following.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
Brings letter case and separators to one consistent format.
Uses snake_case by default, but other cases like camelCase are available.
Handles special characters and spaces, including transliterating characters like œ to oe.
Adds numbers to duplicated names, as it did for the two REMARKS columns.
Converts "%" to “percent” and "#" to “number”, to keep their meaning.
Gives a name to a blank column, like x.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
11.2 Handling duplicate records
janitor has a ready function, get_dupes(), which finds records that are duplicates on the columns we name. It also works well in a pipe. Let us take a few bills of a division, and look for bills with the same firm and the same bill number.

bills <- tibble(
  voucher_no = c("PV/24/011", "PV/24/012", "PV/24/013", "PV/24/014", "PV/24/015", "PV/24/016"),
  firm       = c("Sharma Traders", "Kaveri Infra", "Sharma Traders", "Patel Hardware",
                 "Kaveri Infra", "Om Sai Suppliers"),
  bill_no    = c("ST/118", "KI/2024/07", "ST/121", "PH-33", "KI/2024/07", "OS/09"),
  amount     = c(48500, 312000, 26750, 9800, 312000, 61200)
)

bills |>
  get_dupes(firm, bill_no)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  firm         bill_no    dupe_count voucher_no amount
  <chr>        <chr>           <int> <chr>       <dbl>
1 Kaveri Infra KI/2024/07          2 PV/24/012  312000
2 Kaveri Infra KI/2024/07          2 PV/24/015  312000


It returns all copies of the duplicate records, with an extra column dupe_count, so that they can be examined together. Here bill KI/2024/07 of Kaveri Infra has been paid under two vouchers. Duplicate detection is covered in detail in Chapter 34.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
11.3 Removing empty rows and columns
Files exported from Excel often have empty rows, used as spacers, and empty columns. remove_empty() removes rows and columns which are entirely empty.

with_blanks <- tibble(voucher = c("PV/24/001", NA, "PV/24/002"),
                      blank   = c(NA, NA, NA),
                      amount  = c(18500, NA, 42300))
with_blanks

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  voucher   blank amount
  <chr>     <lgl>  <dbl>
1 PV/24/001 NA     18500
2 <NA>      NA        NA
3 PV/24/002 NA     42300

with_blanks |> remove_empty(c("rows", "cols"))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  voucher   amount
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 PV/24/001  18500
2 PV/24/002  42300

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
11.4 Removing constant columns
remove_constant() drops columns which have the same value in every row. Such columns, like a column holding the name of the office in every row, carry no information for analysis.

tibble(voucher = 1:3, office = "Amarpur", amount = c(500, 800, 1200)) |>
  remove_constant()

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  voucher amount
    <int>  <dbl>
1       1    500
2       2    800
3       3   1200

title: 11  Cleaning Data
section: 11.5 Fixing Excel dates stored as serial numbers
text:
11.5 Fixing Excel dates stored as serial numbers
When an Excel file is read into R, a date sometimes appears as a number like 45383 instead. Excel stores dates as the number of days since its starting date, and the format is sometimes lost. excel_numeric_to_date() converts such numbers to dates. Let us see this.

excel_numeric_to_date(45383)

[1] "2024-04-01"


The number 45383 was the first day of the financial year 2024-25.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
section: 11.6 Converting a mix of date formats
text:
11.6 Converting a mix of date formats
Similarly, a column with a mix of Excel serial numbers and dates can be converted with convert_to_date() or convert_to_datetime(). See this example.

unsorted_dates <- c('2024-05-31', '45383', 45383)
convert_to_date(unsorted_dates)

[1] "2024-05-31" "2024-04-01" "2024-04-01"








Note



The vector above mixes text and a number, but R’s coercion rules have already turned all of them into text.


When data is entered on many computers, or comes from many offices, a date column may mix several formats. The function parse_date_time() from lubridate can read such a column. The argument orders lists the possible orders of day, month and year, and the function tries each of them. Let us take the dates of payment reported by six offices.

mixed_dates <- c("13-11-2024", "13-Sep-24",
                 "20 August 2024", "15 August 24",
                 "03/31/25", "12-31-2024")

lubridate::parse_date_time(mixed_dates,
                           orders = c("d m y", "d B Y", "m/d/y", "d B y"),
                           locale = "eng")

[1] "2024-11-13 UTC" "2024-09-13 UTC" "2024-08-20 UTC" "2024-08-15 UTC"
[5] "2025-03-31 UTC" "2024-12-31 UTC"








WarningCaution, ambiguous dates



A date like 03/04/2024 can be the 3rd of April (Indian style, day first) or the 4th of March (American style, month first). No function can tell which was meant. If both orders are allowed, parse_date_time() simply takes whichever of them it tries first. Before converting, find out how each source writes dates. Where possible, check a few dates in the converted data against the documents. A day of 13 or more is never a month, which helps to identify the style of a source.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
section: 11.7 Missing values written in many ways
text:
11.7 Missing values written in many ways
Missing values are written in many ways, like an empty cell, NA, -, N/A, Nil or 0. R treats only a true NA as missing. The others are text, or worse, a real zero. Two tools help.

While reading a file, the argument na of read_csv() lists the values to be read as missing, like na = c("", "NA", "-", "N/A", "Nil").
After reading, na_if() from dplyr turns a given value into NA, like mutate(remarks = na_if(remarks, "Nil")).


tibble(status = c("Paid", "-", "Nil", "Paid")) |>
  mutate(status = na_if(status, "-"),
         status = na_if(status, "Nil"))

# A tibble: 4 × 1
  status
  <chr> 
1 Paid  
2 <NA>  
3 <NA>  
4 Paid  








WarningCaution



Be careful with zero. A zero in an amount column may be a real zero, or a missing value entered as zero. Find out which, from the source, before treating zeros as missing.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
section: 11.8 Audit use case, cleaning a file received from an office
text:
11.8 Audit use case, cleaning a file received from an office
Let us put everything together. An office has sent its statement of payments for April 2024, prepared in a spreadsheet and saved as csv. Here is how it looks, line by line. We write it to a temporary file, as if it had come by email.

messy <- 'Office of the Executive Engineer, PWD Division Amarpur
Statement of payments for April 2024

S.No.,Voucher No.,Name of Vendor,Amount (Rs.),Date of Payment,Remarks,Remarks
1,PV/24/001, Sharma Traders ,"1,25,000/-",01/04/2024,,
2,PV/24/002,GUPTA & SONS,"45,600",02-04-2024,,
,,,,,,
3,PV/24/003,Kaveri Infra,N/A,05 Apr 2024,Cancelled,
4,PV/24/004,sharma traders,"98,000/-",2024-04-08,,
5,PV/24/005,Om Sai Suppliers,-,10/04/2024,,
Total,,,,,,'

messy_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "april_payments.csv")
writeLines(messy, messy_file)

It has every problem we have discussed. There are two title lines and a blank line above the column names. The column names have spaces and symbols, and two columns have the same name. There is a blank row, and a total row at the bottom. Vendor names are in different cases and have extra spaces. Amounts have commas and “/-”, missing amounts are written as “N/A” and “-”, and dates are in four formats.
Step 1, read everything as text, skipping the title lines. Reading as text ensures that nothing is lost or wrongly converted at this stage.

raw <- read_csv(messy_file, skip = 3,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

New names:
• `Remarks` -> `Remarks...6`
• `Remarks` -> `Remarks...7`

raw

# A tibble: 7 × 7
  S.No. `Voucher No.` `Name of Vendor` `Amount (Rs.)` `Date of Payment`
  <chr> <chr>         <chr>            <chr>          <chr>            
1 1     PV/24/001     Sharma Traders   1,25,000/-     01/04/2024       
2 2     PV/24/002     GUPTA & SONS     45,600         02-04-2024       
3 <NA>  <NA>          <NA>             <NA>           <NA>             
4 3     PV/24/003     Kaveri Infra     N/A            05 Apr 2024      
5 4     PV/24/004     sharma traders   98,000/-       2024-04-08       
6 5     PV/24/005     Om Sai Suppliers -              10/04/2024       
7 Total <NA>          <NA>             <NA>           <NA>             
# ℹ 2 more variables: Remarks...6 <chr>, Remarks...7 <chr>


read_csv() has renamed the two Remarks columns to keep them apart, and told us so.
Step 2, clean the structure. Clean the names, remove empty rows and columns, and drop the total row.

step2 <- raw |>
  clean_names() |>
  remove_empty(c("rows", "cols")) |>
  filter_out(s_no == "Total")
step2

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  s_no  voucher_no name_of_vendor   amount_rs  date_of_payment remarks_6
  <chr> <chr>      <chr>            <chr>      <chr>           <chr>    
1 1     PV/24/001  Sharma Traders   1,25,000/- 01/04/2024      <NA>     
2 2     PV/24/002  GUPTA & SONS     45,600     02-04-2024      <NA>     
3 3     PV/24/003  Kaveri Infra     N/A        05 Apr 2024     Cancelled
4 4     PV/24/004  sharma traders   98,000/-   2024-04-08      <NA>     
5 5     PV/24/005  Om Sai Suppliers -          10/04/2024      <NA>     


Notice that we used filter_out(), which we learn in Chapter 15. It drops only the rows which are certainly the total row.
Step 3, clean the values.

payments <- step2 |>
  mutate(vendor = str_squish(str_to_upper(name_of_vendor)),
         amount = parse_number(amount_rs, na = c("-", "N/A")),
         date   = as.Date(parse_date_time(date_of_payment,
                                          orders = c("dmy", "ymd", "d b Y")))) |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor, amount, date, remarks = remarks_6)
payments

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  voucher_no vendor           amount date       remarks  
  <chr>      <chr>             <dbl> <date>     <chr>    
1 PV/24/001  SHARMA TRADERS   125000 2024-04-01 <NA>     
2 PV/24/002  GUPTA & SONS      45600 2024-04-02 <NA>     
3 PV/24/003  KAVERI INFRA         NA 2024-04-05 Cancelled
4 PV/24/004  SHARMA TRADERS    98000 2024-04-08 <NA>     
5 PV/24/005  OM SAI SUPPLIERS     NA 2024-04-10 <NA>     


All dates are now real dates, all amounts real numbers, and the two forms of Sharma Traders have become the same.
Step 4, record what was found. The cleaning itself has revealed facts which belong in the working papers.

found <- payments |>
  summarise(payments          = n(),
            amount_missing    = sum(is.na(amount)),
            total_amount      = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE),
            cancelled         = sum(remarks %in% "Cancelled"))
found

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  payments amount_missing total_amount cancelled
     <int>          <int>        <dbl>     <int>
1        5              2       268600         1


The statement has 5 payments. The amount of 2 of them is not given. One of these is marked cancelled, but the other, voucher PV/24/005, is not. That payment needs an explanation. And the statement’s own total row was empty, so the total of ₹2.69 lakh must be reconciled with the cash book.
What would the auditor do next? Ask the division for voucher PV/24/005 and its amount. See the cancelled voucher, to confirm that no payment was made against it. Check in the cash book that the payments to Sharma Traders, written in two ways, are to one and the same firm. Then note all of this in the working papers, along with the code that cleaned the file.






TipAudit tip



Never clean the original file. Keep it unchanged, and do all cleaning in code, as we did here. The code is then a complete record of every change made to the data, which another auditor can read and repeat. Record in the working papers the problems found while cleaning, like missing amounts and inconsistent names. They are often findings in themselves, about the quality of the auditee’s records.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
11.9 A suggested workflow
For any file received from an office, an auditor may follow these steps.


Keep the original unchanged. Do all cleaning in code, so that every change is on record and can be repeated.

Read everything as text. Skip the title lines with skip, and read all columns as text so that nothing is lost at this stage.

Clean the structure. Use clean_names(), remove_empty() and remove_constant(), and drop the total row with filter_out().

Clean the values. Standardise names with str_to_upper() and str_squish(), and convert amounts with parse_number().

Fix the dates. Use parse_date_time() with the right orders, or excel_numeric_to_date() for Excel serial numbers. Find out first whether each source writes the day or the month first.

Treat missing values properly. Turn placeholders like “-”, “N/A” and “Nil” into NA. Find out from the source whether a zero is a real zero.

Look for duplicates. Use get_dupes() on the columns that should identify a record.

Record what you found. Note missing amounts, inconsistent names and other problems in the working papers.







ImportantRemember



Never clean the original file by hand. Clean it in code, so that the code itself is the record of every change. Problems found while cleaning are often findings in themselves, about the quality of the auditee’s records.

title: 11  Cleaning Data
text:
11.10 Try it yourself
These exercises use the bills and the April statement of payments from this chapter. Try each one before opening the solution. Some solutions use the dplyr verb summarise(), which Chapter 15 explains in full.


The same amount twice. A bill may be paid twice under a new bill number. Use get_dupes() on bills to find the bills with the same amount, whatever their bill number.






TipSolution






bills |>
  get_dupes(amount)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  amount dupe_count voucher_no firm         bill_no   
   <dbl>      <int> <chr>      <chr>        <chr>     
1 312000          2 PV/24/012  Kaveri Infra KI/2024/07
2 312000          2 PV/24/015  Kaveri Infra KI/2024/07


Only the two payments of ₹3,12,000 to Kaveri Infra share an amount. Here they also share the bill number. With a different bill number, this check would still have caught them.





Bills outside the year. A statement for the year 2024-25 has bill dates stored as Excel serial numbers, 45390, 45612, 45747, 45748 and 45760. Convert them to dates, and find any that fall after 31 March 2025.






TipSolution






bill_dates <- excel_numeric_to_date(c(45390, 45612, 45747, 45748, 45760))
bill_dates

[1] "2024-04-08" "2024-11-16" "2025-03-31" "2025-04-01" "2025-04-13"

bill_dates[bill_dates > as.Date("2025-03-31")]

[1] "2025-04-01" "2025-04-13"


Of these, 2 bills are dated after the year ended. They may have been booked in the wrong year, and the auditor should see the vouchers.





Day first or month first. An office writes the dates 03/04/2024 and 13/04/2024. Read them once with orders = "dmy" and once with orders = "mdy". Which reading can be right?






TipSolution






office_dates <- c("03/04/2024", "13/04/2024")
parse_date_time(office_dates, orders = "dmy")

[1] "2024-04-03 UTC" "2024-04-13 UTC"

parse_date_time(office_dates, orders = "mdy")

Warning: 1 failed to parse.


[1] "2024-03-04 UTC" NA              


Read month first, the second date fails, since there is no 13th month. So this office writes the day first, and the first date is 3 April 2024, not 4 March.





Placeholders while reading. Read messy_file again, but this time give "-" and "N/A" in the argument na of read_csv(). Clean the structure as in Step 2, and count the missing values in the amount column.






TipSolution






raw_na <- read_csv(messy_file, skip = 3, na = c("", "NA", "-", "N/A"),
                   col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |>
  clean_names() |>
  remove_empty(c("rows", "cols")) |>
  filter_out(s_no == "Total")

New names:
• `Remarks` -> `Remarks...6`
• `Remarks` -> `Remarks...7`

sum(is.na(raw_na$amount_rs))

[1] 2


The 2 placeholders are now true NA values from the start. This agrees with the count of missing amounts found in Step 4.





One firm, one total. Count the different vendor names in step2, before cleaning, and in payments, after cleaning. Then total the amount paid to each vendor.






TipSolution






n_distinct(step2$name_of_vendor)

[1] 5

n_distinct(payments$vendor)

[1] 4

vendor_totals <- payments |>
  summarise(payments = n(), amount = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE), .by = vendor)
vendor_totals

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  vendor           payments amount
  <chr>               <int>  <dbl>
1 SHARMA TRADERS          2 223000
2 GUPTA & SONS            1  45600
3 KAVERI INFRA            1      0
4 OM SAI SUPPLIERS        1      0


Cleaning has brought 5 names down to 4 firms. Sharma Traders now shows its true total of ₹2.23 lakh in one row. Without cleaning, its payments would have been split across two names. Kaveri Infra and Om Sai Suppliers show 0 only because their one amount is missing. sum() with na.rm = TRUE gives 0 when every value is missing, so do not read this as a payment of nothing.

title: 12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
text:
12.1 Two kinds of PDF
Audit data does not always arrive as a clean CSV file. Very often it comes as a PDF: a bank statement, a set of sanction orders, work orders, invoices, or a report from a computerised system that can only “print” to PDF. And when it comes as an Excel workbook, it is usually laid out for the eye, not for analysis: a title on top, headers spread over two rows with merged cells, subtotals in between, notes at the bottom, and some cells coloured yellow to mark something the department wanted to draw attention to (or did not).
read_csv() and read_excel() (Chapter 10) expect neat rectangles of data. In this chapter we learn to get data out of the other kind of file.
Prerequisites
Install them once with install.packages(c("pdftools", "tidyxl", "unpivotr")).
Before starting, look at what kind of PDF you have. Open it and try to select a word with the mouse.
This chapter deals with text PDFs, which are by far the commoner kind in audit: bank statements downloaded from net banking, reports from IFMS or ERP systems, and orders typed on a computer.

title: 12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
text:
If the text can be selected and copied, it is a text PDF, produced by a computer program. The text is stored inside the file, and pdftools can read it exactly.
If the whole page selects as one picture, it is a scanned PDF, a photograph of paper. There is no text inside, only an image. To read it, the image must first be converted to text by optical character recognition (OCR), for example with the package tesseract. OCR makes mistakes, especially with numbers, poor scans and Indian-language text, so every figure read by OCR must be checked.

title: 12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
text:
12.2 A bank statement in PDF
A district health society has given us its bank statement for the first quarter of 2024-25, as a three-page PDF downloaded from the bank’s website. The code below creates such a file. It also plants one alteration, of the kind that is made to a statement to hide a misappropriation.

Code to create the bank statement PDFpdf_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "audit_pdfs")
dir.create(pdf_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
n <- 80
dates  <- sort(as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:90, n, TRUE))
debit  <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.65, round(rlnorm(n, log(20000), 1), 2), NA)
credit <- ifelse(is.na(debit), round(rlnorm(n, log(70000), 0.8), 2), NA)
narration <- ifelse(is.na(debit),
  sample(c("NEFT CR TREASURY", "RTGS CR GRANT", "INT CR"), n, TRUE),
  sample(c("CHQ PAID SHARMA TRADERS", "NEFT DR GUPTA AND SONS", "CHQ PAID KAVERI INFRA",
           "ATM WDL"), n, TRUE))
opening <- 500000
balance <- opening + cumsum(coalesce(credit, 0) - coalesce(debit, 0))
# Planted. The balance on one line has been altered by Rs 25,000
balance[37] <- balance[37] + 25000

fmt <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ","))
row_text <- function(d, nar, dr, cr, bal) sprintf("%-10s  %-26s  %14s  %14s  %16s", d, nar, dr, cr, bal)
lines <- row_text(format(dates, "%d-%m-%Y"), narration, fmt(debit), fmt(credit), fmt(balance))

pdf(file.path(pdf_dir, "bank_statement.pdf"), width = 8.27, height = 11.69, family = "Courier")
pages <- split(lines, ceiling(seq_along(lines) / 30))
for (p in seq_along(pages)) {
  plot.new(); par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)); plot.window(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
  header <- c("STATE BANK OF EXAMPLE - ACCOUNT STATEMENT",
              "Account: 12345678901   District Health Society, Amarpur",
              sprintf("Page %d of %d", p, length(pages)), "",
              row_text("Date", "Narration", "Debit", "Credit", "Balance"))
  if (p == 1) header <- c(header, row_text("", "OPENING BALANCE", "", "", fmt(opening)))
  y <- 0.97
  for (l in c(header, pages[[p]])) { text(0.03, y, l, adj = 0, cex = 0.62); y <- y - 0.025 }
}
invisible(dev.off())


pdf_info() tells us about the file, and pdf_text() reads its text, giving one long string for each page.

statement_file <- file.path(pdf_dir, "bank_statement.pdf")
pdf_info(statement_file)$pages

[1] 3

pages_text <- pdf_text(statement_file)
length(pages_text)

[1] 3

cat(substr(pages_text[1], 1, 700))

STATE BANK OF EXAMPLE − ACCOUNT STATEMENT

Account: 12345678901      District Health Society, Amarpur

Page 1 of 3




Date          Narration                             Debit        Credit      Balance

              OPENING BALANCE                                             500,000.00

01−04−2024    ATM WDL                           85,774.41                 414,225.59

02−04−2024    CHQ PAID KAVERI INFRA             25,147.33                 389,078.26

06−04−2024    CHQ PAID SHARMA TRADERS           54,178.07                 334,900.19

07−04−2024    RTGS CR GRANT                                   66,165.64   401,065.83

13−04−2024    CHQ PAID KAVERI INFRA              9,197.72        


The text keeps the layout of the page, with columns lined up by spaces. That is what makes it usable. Let us turn it into a table, in four steps.
Step 1. Split into lines, and clean. Each page string is split at the line breaks ("\n"). We then drop the empty lines. One more thing needs care. Look closely at the dates above. The hyphens are not ordinary hyphens but the minus sign character − (Unicode −), which looks the same but is a different character, so dmy() would not recognise the dates. Such look-alike characters are common in text taken from PDFs. We replace them with the ordinary hyphen.

all_lines <- pages_text |>
  str_split("\n") |>
  unlist() |>
  str_replace_all("−", "-")
all_lines <- all_lines[str_trim(all_lines) != ""]
head(all_lines, 8)

[1] "STATE BANK OF EXAMPLE - ACCOUNT STATEMENT"                                           
[2] "Account: 12345678901      District Health Society, Amarpur"                          
[3] "Page 1 of 3"                                                                         
[4] "Date          Narration                             Debit        Credit      Balance"
[5] "              OPENING BALANCE                                             500,000.00"
[6] "01-04-2024    ATM WDL                           85,774.41                 414,225.59"
[7] "02-04-2024    CHQ PAID KAVERI INFRA             25,147.33                 389,078.26"
[8] "06-04-2024    CHQ PAID SHARMA TRADERS           54,178.07                 334,900.19"


Step 2. Keep only the transaction lines. Bank names, page numbers and column headings are repeated on every page. The transaction lines are easy to recognise: they start with a date in the form dd-mm-yyyy. A regular expression (Chapter 21) picks them out.

txn_lines <- all_lines[str_detect(all_lines, "^\\d{2}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}")]
length(txn_lines)

[1] 80


Step 3. Find where the columns are. The amounts are right-aligned under their headings, so each amount ends where its heading ends. str_locate() finds the end of each heading in the header line.

header_line <- all_lines[str_detect(all_lines, "^Date\\s+Narration")][1]
header_line

[1] "Date          Narration                             Debit        Credit      Balance"

debit_end   <- str_locate(header_line, "Debit")[, "end"]
credit_end  <- str_locate(header_line, "Credit")[, "end"]
c(debit_end = debit_end, credit_end = credit_end)

 debit_end.end credit_end.end 
            57             71 


Step 4. Cut each line at those positions. str_sub() takes the characters between two positions. The debit column is the 15 or so characters ending at the end of “Debit”, the credit column those after it up to the end of “Credit”, and the balance everything after that. parse_number() (Section 10.5) turns "85,774.41" into a number, and an empty cut into NA.

statement <- tibble(line = txn_lines) |>
  mutate(date      = dmy(str_sub(line, 1, 10)),
         narration = str_trim(str_sub(line, 11, debit_end - 15)),
         debit     = parse_number(str_sub(line, debit_end - 14, debit_end + 1)),
         credit    = parse_number(str_sub(line, debit_end + 2, credit_end + 1)),
         balance   = parse_number(str_sub(line, credit_end + 2, -1))) |>
  select(-line)
statement

# A tibble: 80 × 5
   date       narration                debit  credit balance
   <date>     <chr>                    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 2024-04-01 ATM WDL                 85774.     NA  414226.
 2 2024-04-02 CHQ PAID KAVERI INFRA   25147.     NA  389078.
 3 2024-04-06 CHQ PAID SHARMA TRADERS 54178.     NA  334900.
 4 2024-04-07 RTGS CR GRANT              NA   66166. 401066.
 5 2024-04-13 CHQ PAID KAVERI INFRA    9198.     NA  391868.
 6 2024-04-13 CHQ PAID SHARMA TRADERS 10802.     NA  381066.
 7 2024-04-14 ATM WDL                 20954.     NA  360112.
 8 2024-04-14 RTGS CR GRANT              NA  107171. 467283.
 9 2024-04-17 CHQ PAID SHARMA TRADERS 35604.     NA  431679.
10 2024-04-18 NEFT DR GUPTA AND SONS   5557.     NA  426123.
# ℹ 70 more rows


Always check that the cutting worked, for example that every row has a balance and exactly one of debit or credit.

statement |>
  summarise(rows = n(), missing_balance = sum(is.na(balance)),
            both_or_neither = sum(is.na(debit) == is.na(credit)))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
   rows missing_balance both_or_neither
  <int>           <int>           <int>
1    80               0               0



12.2.1 An audit check: does the balance run correctly?
A bank statement has a built-in check. Each balance must equal the previous balance, plus the credit, minus the debit. Recomputing the running balance from the opening balance, and comparing it with the printed one, tests every line of the statement.

statement |>
  mutate(expected = 500000 + cumsum(coalesce(credit, 0) - coalesce(debit, 0)),
         difference = round(balance - expected, 2)) |>
  filter(difference != 0)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  date       narration        debit credit balance expected difference
  <date>     <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
1 2024-05-12 NEFT CR TREASURY    NA 57843. 274174.  249174.      25000


One line does not agree. The printed balance is ₹25,000 more than the transactions justify, and the next line is correct again. A statement downloaded from the bank should never show this. Such a line indicates that the document has been altered, and the auditor should obtain the statement directly from the bank.






TipAudit tip



Re-performing the running balance takes a minute in R and checks every line of a statement of any length. Do it for every statement obtained from an auditee. When possible, compare the PDF with a statement obtained independently, and check the PDF’s properties too: pdf_info() shows the program that created the file and the dates it was created and modified. A “bank statement” created by a word processor, or modified after its date, deserves questions.

title: 12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
text:
12.3 Facts from many PDF documents
The second common task is to read particular facts from a set of similar documents, and assemble them into a register. Say we have the PDFs of all the sanction orders issued by a directorate during the year. Each states an order number, a date, an amount and a firm, in a fixed sentence. We want them as a table, to check for duplicate order numbers, sanctions beyond delegated powers, or splitting of works.

Code to create 12 sanction order PDFsset.seed(3)
firms <- c("Sharma Traders", "Gupta and Sons", "Kaveri Infra Projects",
           "Shri Ganesh Enterprises", "Medicare Supplies")
orders <- tibble(
  no      = sprintf("HFW/2024/%03d", sample(100:400, 12)),
  date    = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sort(sample(0:300, 12)),
  amount  = round(runif(12, 50000, 480000), -3),
  firm    = sample(firms, 12, TRUE),
  purpose = sample(c("supply of medicines", "repair of hospital building",
                     "purchase of beds", "supply of lab reagents"), 12, TRUE)
)
# Planted. An order number used twice, and a sanction above the Director's power of Rs 5 lakh
orders$no[9] <- orders$no[4]
orders$amount[7] <- 735000

indian_format <- function(x) {       # 295000 -> "2,95,000"
  s <- formatC(x, format = "d"); n <- nchar(s)
  if (n <= 3) return(s)
  rest <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(s, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
  paste0(rest, ",", substr(s, n - 2, n))
}
for (i in 1:12) {
  pdf(file.path(pdf_dir, sprintf("sanction_%02d.pdf", i)), width = 8.27, height = 11.69)
  plot.new(); par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)); plot.window(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
  order_text <- c(
    "GOVERNMENT OF EXAMPLE STATE", "DIRECTORATE OF HEALTH SERVICES", "",
    sprintf("Order No. %s                    Dated: %s", orders$no[i], format(orders$date[i], "%d.%m.%Y")),
    "", "SANCTION ORDER", "",
    sprintf("Sanction of the Director is hereby accorded for an expenditure of Rs. %s/-",
            indian_format(orders$amount[i])),
    sprintf("in favour of M/s %s for %s.", orders$firm[i], orders$purpose[i]),
    "The expenditure is debitable to Head of Account 2210-01-110-01.", "",
    "Director of Health Services")
  y <- 0.95
  for (l in order_text) { text(0.06, y, l, adj = 0, cex = 0.8); y <- y - 0.03 }
  invisible(dev.off())
}


Here is one of them, as pdf_text() reads it.

order_files <- list.files(pdf_dir, pattern = "^sanction_.*\\.pdf$", full.names = TRUE)
cat(pdf_text(order_files[1]))

GOVERNMENT OF EXAMPLE STATE

DIRECTORATE OF HEALTH SERVICES



Order No. HFW/2024/360                  Dated: 12.04.2024



SANCTION ORDER



Sanction of the Director is hereby accorded for an expenditure of Rs. 2,95,000/−

in favour of M/s Kaveri Infra Projects for supply of lab reagents.

The expenditure is debitable to Head of Account 2210−01−110−01.



Director of Health Services


We read every file with map_chr() (Section 7.5), join each file’s pages into one string, and squeeze the spaces with str_squish(). Then each fact is pulled out with str_extract() and a regular expression with a lookbehind, (?<=...), which matches what comes after a fixed phrase, like “Order No. ”, without including the phrase itself.

sanctions <- tibble(file = basename(order_files),
                    text = map_chr(order_files, \(f) paste(pdf_text(f), collapse = " "))) |>
  mutate(text     = str_squish(str_replace_all(text, "−", "-")),
         order_no = str_extract(text, "(?<=Order No\\. )\\S+"),
         date     = dmy(str_extract(text, "(?<=Dated: )[0-9.]+")),
         amount   = parse_number(str_extract(text, "(?<=Rs\\. )[0-9,]+")),
         firm_purpose = str_extract(text, "(?<=M/s ).+?(?=\\.)"),
         firm     = str_extract(firm_purpose, ".+?(?= for )"),
         purpose  = str_remove(firm_purpose, ".+? for ")) |>
  select(-text, -firm_purpose)
sanctions

# A tibble: 12 × 6
   file            order_no     date       amount firm                   purpose
   <chr>           <chr>        <date>      <dbl> <chr>                  <chr>  
 1 sanction_01.pdf HFW/2024/360 2024-04-12 295000 Kaveri Infra Projects  supply…
 2 sanction_02.pdf HFW/2024/285 2024-04-15 230000 Shri Ganesh Enterpris… repair…
 3 sanction_03.pdf HFW/2024/239 2024-04-22 165000 Sharma Traders         supply…
 4 sanction_04.pdf HFW/2024/135 2024-05-10  71000 Gupta and Sons         purcha…
 5 sanction_05.pdf HFW/2024/399 2024-06-09  95000 Medicare Supplies      supply…
 6 sanction_06.pdf HFW/2024/375 2024-06-14 185000 Gupta and Sons         purcha…
 7 sanction_07.pdf HFW/2024/282 2024-07-17 735000 Sharma Traders         repair…
 8 sanction_08.pdf HFW/2024/267 2024-08-15 149000 Sharma Traders         supply…
 9 sanction_09.pdf HFW/2024/135 2024-09-12 142000 Sharma Traders         repair…
10 sanction_10.pdf HFW/2024/203 2024-12-12 427000 Sharma Traders         supply…
11 sanction_11.pdf HFW/2024/235 2024-12-17 477000 Medicare Supplies      purcha…
12 sanction_12.pdf HFW/2024/136 2024-12-30 413000 Gupta and Sons         supply…


.+? means “as few characters as possible”. The phrase after “M/s” up to the next full stop holds the firm and the purpose, which we then split at ” for “. (Extracting the purpose directly with a lookbehind for” for ” would not work, since the first ” for ” in each order is in “accorded for an expenditure”.) Now the register can be tested like any other table.

# order numbers used more than once
sanctions |> filter(n() > 1, .by = order_no)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  file            order_no     date       amount firm           purpose         
  <chr>           <chr>        <date>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
1 sanction_04.pdf HFW/2024/135 2024-05-10  71000 Gupta and Sons purchase of beds
2 sanction_09.pdf HFW/2024/135 2024-09-12 142000 Sharma Traders repair of hospi…

# sanctions beyond the Director's delegated power of Rs 5 lakh
sanctions |> filter(amount > 500000)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  file            order_no     date       amount firm           purpose         
  <chr>           <chr>        <date>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
1 sanction_07.pdf HFW/2024/282 2024-07-17 735000 Sharma Traders repair of hospi…


The same order number appears on two different sanctions, and one sanction of ₹7,35,000 exceeds the Director’s power. Both need explanation.






Caution



Before trusting a register built this way, check it. Count the NAs in each extracted column, since a document worded differently will not match the pattern and gives NA silently. And open a few documents at random to compare with the table, as we would check any extraction.

sanctions |> summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x))))

# A tibble: 1 × 6
   file order_no  date amount  firm purpose
  <int>    <int> <int>  <int> <int>   <int>
1     0        0     0      0     0       0
