title: 12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
text:
12.4 Messy Excel files
Now the second kind of awkward file. A department has sent its district-wise budget and expenditure for two years, as an Excel workbook prepared for printing.

Code to create the messy workbooklibrary(openxlsx)
wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "Statement")
writeData(wb, 1, "Department of Health - District-wise Budget and Expenditure (Rs. lakh)", startRow = 1)
writeData(wb, 1, "Prepared by: Accounts Section, as on 31.03.2025", startRow = 2)
districts <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur", "Rampur")
writeData(wb, 1, t(c("District", "2023-24", NA, "2024-25", NA)), startRow = 4, colNames = FALSE)
writeData(wb, 1, t(c(NA, "Budget", "Expenditure", "Budget", "Expenditure")), startRow = 5, colNames = FALSE)
mergeCells(wb, 1, cols = 2:3, rows = 4)
mergeCells(wb, 1, cols = 4:5, rows = 4)
mergeCells(wb, 1, cols = 1, rows = 4:5)
set.seed(9)
vals <- matrix(round(runif(24, 200, 900), 1), ncol = 4)
vals[, 2] <- round(vals[, 1] * runif(6, 0.8, 1.02), 1)
vals[, 4] <- round(vals[, 3] * runif(6, 0.8, 1.02), 1)
vals[4, 4] <- round(vals[4, 3] * 1.35, 1)      # Planted. Devgarh spends 35% above its budget
writeData(wb, 1, data.frame(districts, vals), startRow = 6, colNames = FALSE)
writeData(wb, 1, "Total", startRow = 12, startCol = 1)
for (j in 2:5) {
  writeFormula(wb, 1, sprintf("SUM(%s6:%s11)", LETTERS[j], LETTERS[j]), startCol = j, startRow = 12)
}
# Planted. The last total typed in by hand, Rs 150 lakh short of the column's sum
writeData(wb, 1, round(sum(vals[, 4]) - 150, 1), startCol = 5, startRow = 12)
writeData(wb, 1, "Note: Figures for Devgarh are provisional.", startRow = 14)
# Planted. Two cells highlighted in yellow
addStyle(wb, 1, createStyle(fgFill = "#FFFF00"), rows = 9, cols = 5)
addStyle(wb, 1, createStyle(fgFill = "#FFFF00"), rows = 7, cols = 3)
xl_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "district_statement.xlsx")
saveWorkbook(wb, xl_file, overwrite = TRUE)


Here is what read_excel() makes of it.

readxl::read_excel(xl_file)

# A tibble: 13 × 5
   Department of Health - District-wise Budget and Exp…¹ ...2  ...3  ...4  ...5 
   <chr>                                                 <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
 1 Prepared by: Accounts Section, as on 31.03.2025       <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
 2 <NA>                                                  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
 3 District                                              2023… <NA>  2024… <NA> 
 4 <NA>                                                  Budg… Expe… Budg… Expe…
 5 Amarpur                                               355.1 325.4 818.4 690.8
 6 Belapur                                               217   217.2 410.7 416.5
 7 Chandpur                                              345   306   544.9 492.2
 8 Devgarh                                               351   310.3 550.4 743  
 9 Fatehpur                                              510.6 517.2 481.4 385.6
10 Rampur                                                293.9 290   884   878  
11 Total                                                 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  3456…
12 <NA>                                                  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
13 Note: Figures for Devgarh are provisional.            <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
# ℹ abbreviated name:
#   ¹​`Department of Health - District-wise Budget and Expenditure (Rs. lakh)`


Everything is in the wrong place. The title has become a column name, the real headers are rows 3 and 4 of the data, the years are in merged cells, all the columns are text, and the total and the note have come in as data. For a one-off file, the quickest fix is to skip the title rows and supply the names ourselves.

readxl::read_excel(xl_file, skip = 5, n_max = 6,
                   col_names = c("district", "budget_2023_24", "exp_2023_24",
                                 "budget_2024_25", "exp_2024_25"))

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  district budget_2023_24 exp_2023_24 budget_2024_25 exp_2024_25
  <chr>             <dbl>       <dbl>          <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Amarpur            355.        325.           818.        691.
2 Belapur            217         217.           411.        416.
3 Chandpur           345         306            545.        492.
4 Devgarh            351         310.           550.        743 
5 Fatehpur           511.        517.           481.        386.
6 Rampur             294.        290            884         878 


That works, but it depends on our counting the rows correctly, and it loses information that the workbook holds: which cells were highlighted, and which totals are formulas. For that, we read the workbook cell by cell.

12.4.1 Reading cell by cell with tidyxl

xlsx_cells() returns one row for every cell of the workbook, with its address, its row and column numbers, its type, its value, and its formula, if any.

cells <- xlsx_cells(xl_file)
cells |>
  select(address, row, col, data_type, numeric, character, formula, local_format_id) |>
  head(12)

# A tibble: 12 × 8
   address   row   col data_type numeric character       formula local_format_id
   <chr>   <int> <int> <chr>       <dbl> <chr>           <chr>             <int>
 1 A1          1     1 character      NA Department of … <NA>                  1
 2 A2          2     1 character      NA Prepared by: A… <NA>                  1
 3 A4          4     1 character      NA District        <NA>                  1
 4 B4          4     2 character      NA 2023-24         <NA>                  1
 5 C4          4     3 blank          NA <NA>            <NA>                  1
 6 D4          4     4 character      NA 2024-25         <NA>                  1
 7 E4          4     5 blank          NA <NA>            <NA>                  1
 8 A5          5     1 blank          NA <NA>            <NA>                  1
 9 B5          5     2 character      NA Budget          <NA>                  1
10 C5          5     3 character      NA Expenditure     <NA>                  1
11 D5          5     4 character      NA Budget          <NA>                  1
12 E5          5     5 character      NA Expenditure     <NA>                  1


The value of a cell is in numeric, character, logical or date, according to its data_type. local_format_id points to the cell’s formatting, which xlsx_formats() reads. The fill colour of each format is deep inside it, at local$fill$patternFill$fgColor$rgb. Colours are written in hexadecimal with an extra “alpha” pair in front, so yellow is "FFFFFF00".

formats   <- xlsx_formats(xl_file)
fill_rgb  <- formats$local$fill$patternFill$fgColor$rgb

cells |>
  mutate(fill = fill_rgb[local_format_id]) |>
  filter(fill == "FFFFFF00") |>
  select(address, row, col, numeric)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  address   row   col numeric
  <chr>   <int> <int>   <dbl>
1 C7          7     3    217.
2 E9          9     5    743 


The two highlighted cells are C7 (Belapur, expenditure 2023-24) and E9 (Devgarh, expenditure 2024-25). Someone marked them. Why? A highlighted cell in a departmental statement is often the department’s own doubt, an unverified figure, or a correction, and it is always worth asking about.

12.4.2 Formulas and typed-over totals
The formula column shows which cells hold a formula. Let us look at the total row.

cells |>
  filter(row == 12, col > 1) |>
  select(address, numeric, formula)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  address numeric formula    
  <chr>     <dbl> <chr>      
1 B12         NA  SUM(B6:B11)
2 C12         NA  SUM(C6:C11)
3 D12         NA  SUM(D6:D11)
4 E12       3456. <NA>       


Three totals are formulas, SUM() of the column above. The fourth, E12, has no formula. Its value was typed in. (The formula cells show no value because our file was written by R and never opened in Excel. In a workbook saved by Excel, numeric holds the result of each formula as well.) A typed-in total is a classic way for a statement to say something its own figures do not. Let us compare it with the sum of the figures above it.

typed_total <- cells |> filter(address == "E12") |> pull(numeric)
column_sum  <- cells |> filter(col == 5, row %in% 6:11) |> summarise(sum(numeric)) |> pull()
c(typed_total = typed_total, sum_of_column = column_sum, difference = column_sum - typed_total)

  typed_total sum_of_column    difference 
       3456.1        3606.1         150.0 


The typed total is ₹150 lakh less than the districts’ figures add up to.






TipAudit tip



In any workbook received from an auditee, list the cells in total rows and columns that have no formula, and check them against the figures they claim to total. Look also for formulas that cover the wrong range, such as SUM(E6:E10) in a table that goes down to row 11. tidyxl makes both checks easy, because the formula text is right there in the formula column.



12.4.3 Untangling the headers with unpivotr

Finally, let us turn the table itself into tidy data, with the year and the measure taken from the two header rows. The package unpivotr does this with behead(). It strips one header at a time from the cells, and attaches it as a column to the data cells it belongs to. The direction says where the header lies relative to the data: "up" means directly above, and "up-left" means above and to the left, which is how a merged cell spanning several columns looks once read cell by cell (its value sits only in the first column).
First we keep only the table area, rows 4 to 11, and drop empty cells.

tidy_statement <- cells |>
  filter(row >= 4, row <= 11, !is_blank) |>
  behead("up-left", year) |>         # 2023-24 / 2024-25, from the merged cells
  behead("up", measure) |>           # Budget / Expenditure
  behead("left", district) |>        # district names, to the left
  select(district, year, measure, value = numeric)
tidy_statement

# A tibble: 24 × 4
   district year    measure     value
   <chr>    <chr>   <chr>       <dbl>
 1 Amarpur  2023-24 Budget       355.
 2 Amarpur  2023-24 Expenditure  325.
 3 Belapur  2023-24 Budget       217 
 4 Belapur  2023-24 Expenditure  217.
 5 Chandpur 2023-24 Budget       345 
 6 Chandpur 2023-24 Expenditure  306 
 7 Devgarh  2023-24 Budget       351 
 8 Devgarh  2023-24 Expenditure  310.
 9 Fatehpur 2023-24 Budget       511.
10 Fatehpur 2023-24 Expenditure  517.
# ℹ 14 more rows


Each number now carries its district, year and measure. From here, it is ordinary tidyr and dplyr (Chapter 17). For example, the utilisation of the budget in each year:

tidy_statement |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(utilisation_pct = round(100 * Expenditure / Budget, 1)) |>
  filter(utilisation_pct > 100) |>
  arrange(desc(utilisation_pct))

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  district year    Budget Expenditure utilisation_pct
  <chr>    <chr>    <dbl>       <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Devgarh  2024-25   550.        743             135 
2 Belapur  2024-25   411.        416.            101.
3 Fatehpur 2023-24   511.        517.            101.
4 Belapur  2023-24   217         217.            100.


Devgarh spent 35% more than its budget in 2024-25, the highlighted cell E9 (the other excesses are of about 1% or less), which the note at the foot of the sheet called “provisional”. The three clues, a highlight, a note and an excess, point to the same figure.






Note



behead() handles headers in any direction: "left", "right", "up", "down", and combinations like "up-left" for merged cells. For workbooks where blocks of data repeat across a sheet, with a heading for each block, see also partition() in unpivotr. The book Spreadsheet Munging Strategies by Duncan Garmonsway, the author of both packages, works through many real examples.

title: 12  Data from PDFs and Messy Excel Files
text:
12.5 A suggested workflow


Look at the file first. For a PDF, check whether the text can be selected. For Excel, open it and note the title rows, merged headers, totals, notes and colours.

Read the raw content: pdf_text() for PDFs, xlsx_cells() for Excel.

Clean the text: split lines, drop blanks, and replace look-alike characters.

Pick out the data: lines matching a pattern, or the cells of the table area.

Structure it: cut columns at fixed positions, extract facts with regular expressions, or behead() headers.

Check the extraction: counts of rows and NAs, totals, and a few records compared by eye.

Use what the file itself reveals: running balances, typed-over totals, highlighted cells and notes.







ImportantRemember




Text PDFs can be read exactly with pdftools; scanned PDFs need OCR, and every figure must then be checked.
PDF text keeps its layout. Cut columns at the positions of the headings, and watch for look-alike characters like −.

str_extract() with lookbehinds pulls facts out of many similar documents into one register.

tidyxl reads Excel cell by cell, with values, formulas and colours; unpivotr::behead() untangles headers.
Formatting and formulas are evidence. A highlighted cell or a typed-over total is a question to ask.

text:
12.6 Try it yourself
These exercises use the tables we built in this chapter, the bank statement statement, the register of sanctions sanctions and the tidy budget statement tidy_statement. Try each one before you open the solution. Some solutions use dplyr verbs such as arrange(), filter() and mutate(), which Chapter 15 explains in full.


A lower power of sanction. Suppose the Director’s power were only ₹3 lakh. Which sanctions would exceed it? List them, largest first.






TipSolution






ex_above_3l <- sanctions |>
  filter(amount > 300000) |>
  arrange(desc(amount)) |>
  select(order_no, date, firm, amount)
ex_above_3l

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  order_no     date       firm              amount
  <chr>        <date>     <chr>              <dbl>
1 HFW/2024/282 2024-07-17 Sharma Traders    735000
2 HFW/2024/235 2024-12-17 Medicare Supplies 477000
3 HFW/2024/203 2024-12-12 Sharma Traders    427000
4 HFW/2024/136 2024-12-30 Gupta and Sons    413000


With the lower limit, 4 sanctions are beyond the Director’s power, against only one at ₹5 lakh. The register built from the PDFs is tested like any other table.





Cash drawn from the account. How many times was cash withdrawn through an ATM during the quarter, and how much in all?






TipSolution






ex_atm <- statement |>
  filter(str_detect(narration, "ATM")) |>
  summarise(withdrawals = n(), total = sum(debit))
ex_atm

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  withdrawals   total
        <int>   <dbl>
1          18 899433.


Cash was withdrawn 18 times, for ₹8,99,433 in all. A health society should make most payments by cheque or transfer. The auditor would ask what the cash was used for, and check it with the cash book.





Is the closing balance enough? Compare the last printed balance with the opening balance plus all the credits, less all the debits. Does this simpler check find the altered line?






TipSolution






ex_closing <- statement |>
  summarise(printed  = last(balance),
            expected = round(500000 + sum(credit, na.rm = TRUE) - sum(debit, na.rm = TRUE), 2))
ex_closing

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  printed expected
    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 591602.  591602.


The two agree, with a difference of ₹0. The altered line changed only one balance, and the next line was correct again. So a check of the closing balance alone misses it. Only re-performing the balance line by line finds it.





Sanctions to each firm. Find the number of sanctions and the total amount sanctioned to each firm, largest total first.






TipSolution






ex_firms <- sanctions |>
  summarise(orders = n(), total = sum(amount), .by = firm) |>
  arrange(desc(total))
ex_firms

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  firm                    orders   total
  <chr>                    <int>   <dbl>
1 Sharma Traders               5 1618000
2 Gupta and Sons               3  669000
3 Medicare Supplies            2  572000
4 Kaveri Infra Projects        1  295000
5 Shri Ganesh Enterprises      1  230000


Sharma Traders received the largest total, ₹16.18 lakh in 5 orders. Several orders to one firm in a year are worth a look, to see whether one purchase was split to stay within the Director’s power.





Utilisation in the earlier year. From tidy_statement, work out the utilisation of the budget of each district in 2023-24. Which district used the smallest share of its budget?






TipSolution






ex_util <- tidy_statement |>
  filter(year == "2023-24") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(utilisation_pct = round(100 * Expenditure / Budget, 1)) |>
  arrange(utilisation_pct)
ex_util

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  district year    Budget Expenditure utilisation_pct
  <chr>    <chr>    <dbl>       <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Devgarh  2023-24   351         310.            88.4
2 Chandpur 2023-24   345         306             88.7
3 Amarpur  2023-24   355.        325.            91.6
4 Rampur   2023-24   294.        290             98.7
5 Belapur  2023-24   217         217.           100. 
6 Fatehpur 2023-24   511.        517.           101. 


Devgarh used the smallest share, 88.4% of its budget. Low utilisation may mean that funds were surrendered late, or that works were held up. The highlighted cell C7 was Belapur’s expenditure for this year, and Belapur used 100.1%.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.1 Our data, a mock e-procurement portal and two registers
Much of the information an auditor needs is published on the internet, and only there. A state e-procurement portal lists every tender, with the date it was published and the date it closed. It also shows who won each contract, and at what value. A department publishes the list of firms it has debarred. A price portal shows the rates notified for cement or medicines. None of this comes to us as a file. It is spread over web pages, ten or twenty rows to a page.
Yet these pages answer real audit questions. Was a tender really published for the required number of days, or only for a week? Is the contract value in the division’s register the same as the value the portal shows? Has the division paid a firm that the State had already debarred? To answer them, we must compare the auditee’s records with what was published. Copying a few hundred rows from a website by hand is slow, and it brings typing errors. R can read the pages for us. This is called web scraping.
In this chapter we learn to do it with the package rvest.
The book does not depend on any live website. Websites change, they may block programs, and copying a real portal’s pages raises questions of permission. So we use a small mock website made for this book, saved as plain HTML files in the folder Data/web. It imitates the e-procurement portal of an imaginary “Example State”. Every name on it is made up. The methods are exactly those we would use on a real site.
Prerequisites
rvest is installed with install.packages("rvest"). It also installs xml2, which does the actual reading of HTML.
We are auditing the Public Works Department (PWD), Amarpur Division, of Example State. The audit covers the tenders the division invited and the payments it made from April to November 2024. The State’s e-procurement portal is our independent source. Its pages, as they stood on 2 December 2024, are saved in Data/web.
list.files("Data/web")

[1] "award-2024_PWD_108.html" "award-2024_PWD_111.html"
[3] "award-2024_PWD_114.html" "debarred-firms.html"    
[5] "robots.txt"              "tenders-page1.html"     
[7] "tenders-page2.html"      "tenders-page3.html"
Open Data/web/tenders-page1.html in a browser (double-click it in the file explorer). It looks like a simple government portal, with a blue header, a menu and a table.
From the division we have two registers. The tender register lists the tenders the division says it invited, with the date of the notice inviting tender (NIT), the closing date and, for awarded works, the contract value. The payment register lists the payments made to contractors and suppliers. The code below creates both, with a few problems planted in them. It also defines inr(), a small helper that writes an amount with Indian commas, for use in the text.
Code to create the tender register and the payment register# Write an amount with Indian commas, like 12,45,000
inr <- function(x) {
  s <- format(round(x), scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  n <- nchar(s)
  if (n <= 3) return(s)
  head <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(s, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
  paste0(head, ",", substr(s, n - 2, n))
}

tender_register <- tribble(
  ~tender_id,     ~work,                                      ~nit_date,    ~closing_date, ~contract_value,
  "2024_PWD_131", "CC road, Ward 7, Amarpur",                 "2024-11-18", "2024-12-09",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_129", "Repair of Tehsil office, Amarpur",         "2024-10-25", "2024-11-20",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_126", "Boundary wall, Girls School, Rampur",      "2024-11-04", "2024-11-25",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_124", "Approach road to Mandi, Belapur",          "2024-10-29", "2024-11-19",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_122", "Widening of Amarpur Belapur road",         "2024-10-25", "2024-11-15",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_119", "Community hall, Fatehpur",                 "2024-10-17", "2024-10-29",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_117", "Drain along Station Road, Amarpur",        "2024-10-09", "2024-10-30",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_114", "Resurfacing of Civil Lines roads",         "2024-09-26", "2024-10-16",  6185000,
  "2024_PWD_111", "Culvert at km 12, Belapur road",           "2024-09-11", "2024-10-02",  1972400,
  "2024_PWD_108", "Rain shelter at bus stand, Rampur",        "2024-09-02", "2024-09-23",  812600
) |>
  mutate(across(c(nit_date, closing_date), ymd))
# Planted. 2024_PWD_129 shows an NIT date two weeks earlier than the portal does
# Planted. 2024_PWD_124 is in the register but was never published on the portal
# Planted. The contract value of 2024_PWD_111 is Rs 1 lakh more than the portal shows

set.seed(2024)
regular_firms <- c("Sharma Traders", "Gupta and Sons", "Kaveri Infra Projects",
                   "Bharat Stationers", "Laxmi Electricals", "Patel Hardware")

  payment_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:243, 40, replace = TRUE),

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
tenders-page1.html, tenders-page2.html and tenders-page3.html list the active tenders of all departments, six to a page, with a “Next” link at the foot of each page.
The three award-...html pages give the award details of the tenders marked “Awarded”. They are reached by a link in the tender list.

debarred-firms.html is the State’s list of debarred firms, with the period of debarment.

robots.txt is the file in which a website states which parts programs may visit. We meet it in Section 13.11.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
13  Data from Web Pages
section: 13.3 Looking inside a page with Inspect
text:
13.3 Looking inside a page with Inspect
To select elements, we must know how the page is built. Every modern browser can show this. Open tenders-page1.html in Chrome, Edge or Firefox, right-click on a tender amount and choose Inspect. A panel opens beside the page, showing the HTML, with the element we clicked highlighted.
<tr><td>1</td><td class="tender-id">2024_PWD_131</td>
    <td class="title">Construction of CC road, Ward 7, Amarpur</td>
    ...
    <td class="amount">₹ 48,60,000.00</td>
    <td class="status">Open</td></tr>
Move the mouse over the lines in the panel. The browser shades the part of the page each line draws. In a few minutes we can learn the plan of the page. Here, each tender is a row <tr> of the table with id="tender-list". Each cell has a class that names its content, such as tender-id, published, closing or amount. The “Next” link has class="next". (₹ is the code for the rupee sign ₹.)
We then write CSS selectors, short patterns that pick elements. They are the same patterns web designers use to style pages. These few cover most needs.






Selector
Picks



td
Every element with the tag td



.amount
Every element with class="amount"



#tender-list
The element with id="tender-list"



td.amount
Every td with class="amount"



#tender-list tbody tr
Every tr inside a tbody inside the element #tender-list (a space means “somewhere inside”)


a[href]
Every link that has an href attribute


a.next
The link with class="next"




In the Inspect panel, right-click an element and choose Copy, then Copy selector, to get a selector the browser writes for us. It is often long and fragile, like body > main > table > tbody > tr:nth-child(3) > td:nth-child(7). A short selector built on a meaningful id or class, like td.amount, is better, because it still works when a row is added or the layout changes a little.






TipAudit tip



Before writing any code, spend five minutes with Inspect on two or three pages of the site. Note the id of the table, the classes of the cells, how the “Next” link is marked, and whether detail pages have the same plan. Write these down in the working papers, with the date. If the site changes later, this note explains why the old code no longer works.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.4 Reading a page with rvest
read_html() reads a page. It takes a file path or a web address. Here it is a file on our disk.

page1 <- read_html("Data/web/tenders-page1.html")
page1

{html_document}
<html lang="en">
[1] <head>\n<meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=UTF-8 ...
[2] <body>\n<header><h1>Example State e-Procurement Portal</h1>\n<p>Governmen ...


html_element() (singular) gives the first matching element. html_elements() (plural) gives all of them. html_text2() gives the text as a browser would show it, with extra spaces and line breaks tidied.

page1 |> html_element("h2") |> html_text2()

[1] "Active Tenders"

page1 |> html_element("p.generated") |> html_text2()

[1] "Page generated on 02-Dec-2024 11:45"

page1 |> html_elements("td.tender-id") |> html_text2()

[1] "2024_PWD_131" "2024_HFW_077" "2024_PWD_129" "2024_WRD_064" "2024_PWD_126"
[6] "2024_HFW_074"


html_attr() gives the value of an attribute. The links of the menu, for example.

menu <- page1 |> html_elements("nav a")
tibble(text = html_text2(menu), link = html_attr(menu, "href"))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  text           link               
  <chr>          <chr>              
1 Active Tenders tenders-page1.html 
2 Debarred Firms debarred-firms.html
3 Bidder Login   bidder/login.html  



13.4.1 A whole table with html_table()

When the data sits in a proper <table>, html_table() reads it in one step.

page1 |> html_element("#tender-list") |> html_table()

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  S.No. `Tender ID`  `Title of Work`    Organisation `Published On` `Closing On`
  <int> <chr>        <chr>              <chr>        <chr>          <chr>       
1     1 2024_PWD_131 Construction of C… PWD, Amarpu… 18-Nov-2024 1… 09-Dec-2024…
2     2 2024_HFW_077 Supply of hospita… Health Depa… 15-Nov-2024 1… 06-Dec-2024…
3     3 2024_PWD_129 Repair of Tehsil … PWD, Amarpu… 11-Nov-2024 1… 20-Nov-2024…
4     4 2024_WRD_064 Desilting of mino… Water Resou… 08-Nov-2024 1… 29-Nov-2024…
5     5 2024_PWD_126 Boundary wall of … PWD, Amarpu… 04-Nov-2024 1… 25-Nov-2024…
6     6 2024_HFW_074 Supply of laborat… Health Depa… 30-Oct-2024 1… 20-Nov-2024…
# ℹ 2 more variables: `Estimated Value` <chr>, Status <chr>


That is quick, and it is enough for many pages. But note what it lost. The status “Awarded” in the table is a link to the award details, and html_table() keeps only the text, not the address. When we need links, we read the table row by row.

13.4.2 Row by row, keeping the links
We select the rows, and then, from each row, the cell we want. Here the difference between html_element() and html_elements() matters. Applied to a set of rows, html_element() returns exactly one result for each row, and NA where the row has no such element. So the columns of our table always line up, even though only some rows have an award link.

rows <- page1 |> html_elements("#tender-list tbody tr")
length(rows)

[1] 6

tibble(
  tender_id  = rows |> html_element("td.tender-id") |> html_text2(),
  status     = rows |> html_element("td.status") |> html_text2(),
  award_link = rows |> html_element("a.award-link") |> html_attr("href")
)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  tender_id    status           award_link
  <chr>        <chr>            <chr>     
1 2024_PWD_131 Open             <NA>      
2 2024_HFW_077 Open             <NA>      
3 2024_PWD_129 Under evaluation <NA>      
4 2024_WRD_064 Under evaluation <NA>      
5 2024_PWD_126 Under evaluation <NA>

Had we used html_elements() for the links, we would have got only the links that exist, with no way to tell which row each came from.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.5 Cleaning scraped text
Everything taken from a web page is text. Dates come as “18-Nov-2024 10:00” and amounts as “₹ 48,60,000.00”. Before any analysis we turn them into proper types. Let us write one function that reads a tender page into a clean table. We will reuse it for every page.

read_tender_page <- function(file) {
  rows <- read_html(file) |> html_elements("#tender-list tbody tr")
  tibble(
    tender_id   = rows |> html_element("td.tender-id") |> html_text2(),
    title       = rows |> html_element("td.title") |> html_text2(),
    org         = rows |> html_element("td.org") |> html_text2(),
    published   = rows |> html_element("td.published") |> html_text2(),
    closing     = rows |> html_element("td.closing") |> html_text2(),
    value       = rows |> html_element("td.amount") |> html_text2(),
    status      = rows |> html_element("td.status") |> html_text2(),
    award_link  = rows |> html_element("a.award-link") |> html_attr("href"),
    source_file = basename(file)
  ) |>
    mutate(published = dmy_hm(published, tz = "Asia/Kolkata"),
           closing   = dmy_hm(closing, tz = "Asia/Kolkata"),
           value     = parse_number(value))
}

read_tender_page("Data/web/tenders-page1.html") |>
  select(tender_id, published, closing, value)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  tender_id    published           closing               value
  <chr>        <dttm>              <dttm>                <dbl>
1 2024_PWD_131 2024-11-18 10:00:00 2024-12-09 15:00:00 4860000
2 2024_HFW_077 2024-11-15 11:30:00 2024-12-06 15:00:00 2240000
3 2024_PWD_129 2024-11-11 17:45:00 2024-11-20 15:00:00 1875500
4 2024_WRD_064 2024-11-08 10:15:00 2024-11-29 15:00:00 3690000
5 2024_PWD_126 2024-11-04 12:00:00 2024-11-25 15:00:00 2730000
6 2024_HFW_074 2024-10-30 16:20:00 2024-11-20 15:00:00  980000


Two functions did the cleaning.


dmy_hm() from lubridate (Chapter 18) reads a date written day first, with the month as a word, followed by hours and minutes. We give the time zone "Asia/Kolkata", since the portal shows Indian time.

parse_number() from readr (Section 10.5) drops the rupee sign and the commas and keeps the number. It does not care where the commas are, so Indian grouping like “1,24,50,000” is read correctly as 12450000.

We also kept source_file, so that every row can be traced back to the page it came from.






WarningCaution



parse_number() reads the first number it finds in the text. A cell like “₹ 12.5 lakh” becomes 12.5, not 12,50,000. A cell like “Rs. 5,00,000” gives NA with a warning, because the full stop after “Rs” confuses it. Remove such prefixes first, for example with str_remove(x, "Rs\\.?"). Look at a sample of the raw text before trusting the conversion, and check how many values came out as NA. Dates need the same care. A page may show “02/12/2024” on one screen and “2-Dec-24” on another.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.6 Many pages, one after another
A portal rarely shows everything on one page. Ours shows six tenders to a page, with a “Next” link. There are two ways to read all the pages.
When the addresses follow a pattern. Our pages are tenders-page1.html to tenders-page3.html. On real portals the pattern is often in the address itself, like .../tenders?page=2. We build the addresses with paste0(), read each with map() (Section 7.5), and stack the results with list_rbind().

page_files <- paste0("Data/web/tenders-page", 1:3, ".html")
tenders <- page_files |>
  map(read_tender_page) |>
  list_rbind()
tenders |> count(source_file)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  source_file            n
  <chr>              <int>
1 tenders-page1.html     6
2 tenders-page2.html     6
3 tenders-page3.html     6


When we only know the first page. Then we follow the “Next” link until there is none. url_absolute() turns a link like "tenders-page2.html" into a full address, by joining it to the address of the page it was found on.

current <- "Data/web/tenders-page1.html"
visited <- character()
while (!is.na(current)) {
  visited <- c(visited, current)
  next_link <- read_html(current) |> html_element("a.next") |> html_attr("href")
  current <- if (is.na(next_link)) NA else url_absolute(next_link, current)
}
visited

[1] "Data/web/tenders-page1.html" "Data/web/tenders-page2.html"
[3] "Data/web/tenders-page3.html"


The loop stops on the last page, which has no “Next” link. On a real website, add a pause with Sys.sleep() inside the loop and a limit on the number of pages, so that a fault in the site can never send the program round and round (Section 13.11).

13.6.1 Did we get everything?
A scrape that silently misses a page is worse than no scrape. Each page of our portal states the total number of tenders found. Let us compare it with what we read, and check for repeated rows and missing values.

total_on_site <- page1 |> html_element("p.total") |> html_text2() |> parse_number()

tenders |>
  summarise(rows_read = n(),
            total_on_site = total_on_site,
            distinct_ids = n_distinct(tender_id),
            missing_dates = sum(is.na(published) | is.na(closing)),
            missing_values = sum(is.na(value)))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  rows_read total_on_site distinct_ids missing_dates missing_values
      <int>         <dbl>        <int>         <int>          <int>
1        18            18           18             0              0


We read 18 tenders, the site says 18, every tender ID is distinct, and nothing is missing. The scrape is complete.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.7 Following links to detail pages
Of the 18 tenders, 3 are marked “Awarded”, and each has a link to a page of award details. Let us open one.

award_page <- read_html("Data/web/award-2024_PWD_111.html")
award_page |> html_element("table") |> html_table()

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  X1                      X2                            
  <chr>                   <chr>                         
1 Tender ID               2024_PWD_111                  
2 Title of Work           Culvert at km 12, Belapur road
3 Organisation            PWD, Amarpur Division         
4 Number of Bids Received 4                             
5 Awarded To              Gupta and Sons                
6 Contract Value          ₹ 18,72,400.00                
7 Date of Award           25-Oct-2024                   


This table is laid out with labels in the first column and values in the second. We read each award page into one row with a small function. It uses pivot_wider() (Chapter 17) to turn the labels into column names.

read_award_page <- function(file) {
  read_html(file) |>
    html_element("table.award-details") |>
    html_table(header = FALSE) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = X1, values_from = X2)
}

award_files <- tenders |>
  filter(!is.na(award_link)) |>
  mutate(file = url_absolute(award_link, "Data/web/tenders-page1.html")) |>
  pull(file)
award_files

[1] "Data/web/award-2024_PWD_114.html" "Data/web/award-2024_PWD_111.html"
[3] "Data/web/award-2024_PWD_108.html"

awards <- award_files |>
  map(read_award_page) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  transmute(tender_id      = `Tender ID`,
            bids           = as.integer(`Number of Bids Received`),
            awarded_to     = `Awarded To`,
            portal_value   = parse_number(`Contract Value`),
            award_date     = dmy(`Date of Award`))
awards

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  tender_id     bids awarded_to            portal_value award_date
  <chr>        <int> <chr>                        <dbl> <date>    
1 2024_PWD_114     3 Kaveri Infra Projects      6185000 2024-11-08
2 2024_PWD_111     4 Gupta and Sons             1872400 2024-10-25
3 2024_PWD_108     2 Sharma Traders              812600 2024-10-14


Now the portal can be compared with the division’s tender register, with a join (Chapter 16).

value_check <- tender_register |>
  inner_join(awards, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(difference = contract_value - portal_value) |>
  select(tender_id, awarded_to, contract_value, portal_value, difference)
value_check

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  tender_id    awarded_to            contract_value portal_value difference
  <chr>        <chr>                          <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
1 2024_PWD_114 Kaveri Infra Projects        6185000      6185000          0

For 2024_PWD_111, awarded to Gupta and Sons, the register shows a contract value of ₹19,72,400. The portal shows ₹18,72,400, which is ₹1,00,000 less. The auditor should see the agreement and the letter of award. If the agreement was signed for more than the awarded value, the division must explain why, and whether it was approved.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
section: 13.8 Audit use case, were tenders open long enough?
text:
13.8 Audit use case, were tenders open long enough?
A tender must stay open long enough for every interested firm to see it and prepare a bid. A short window favours a firm that knew about the work in advance, and reduces competition. In our example, suppose the procurement rules of Example State require at least 21 days from publication on the portal to the closing date. (This is an example norm for our imaginary state. The auditor must apply the norm that actually governs the auditee, which may differ with the type and value of the tender.)
We compute the days each tender was open, from the date of publication to the date of closing, and flag those below the norm.

min_days <- 21
short_window <- tenders |>
  mutate(days_open = as.numeric(as_date(closing) - as_date(published))) |>
  filter(days_open < min_days) |>
  select(tender_id, org, published, closing, days_open, value)
short_window

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  tender_id    org      published           closing             days_open  value
  <chr>        <chr>    <dttm>              <dttm>                  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 2024_PWD_129 PWD, Am… 2024-11-11 17:45:00 2024-11-20 15:00:00         9 1.88e6
2 2024_PWD_119 PWD, Am… 2024-10-17 18:10:00 2024-10-29 15:00:00        12 4.22e6
3 2024_PWD_114 PWD, Am… 2024-09-26 16:40:00 2024-10-16 15:00:00        20 6.40e6


In all, 3 tenders were open for fewer than 21 days, all of them of the PWD, Amarpur Division. 2024_PWD_129 was open for only 9 days. 2024_PWD_114 was open for 20 days, just one day short. A shortfall of one day is easy to miss by eye, and that is exactly why a computed check is useful.
Now let us bring in the division’s own tender register. Two more questions arise. Is every tender in the register on the portal at all? And do the dates in the register agree with the portal?

# tenders in the register that the portal does not show
not_on_portal <- tender_register |> anti_join(tenders, by = "tender_id")
not_on_portal

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  tender_id    work                       nit_date   closing_date contract_value
  <chr>        <chr>                      <date>     <date>                <dbl>
1 2024_PWD_124 Approach road to Mandi, B… 2024-10-29 2024-11-19               NA

# NIT dates in the register that differ from the date of publication on the portal
date_check <- tender_register |>
  inner_join(tenders |> select(tender_id, published), by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(portal_date = as_date(published),
         days_apart  = as.numeric(nit_date - portal_date)) |>
  filter(days_apart != 0) |>
  select(tender_id, nit_date, portal_date, days_apart, closing_date)
date_check

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  tender_id    nit_date   portal_date days_apart closing_date
  <chr>        <date>     <date>           <dbl> <date>      
1 2024_PWD_129 2024-10-25 2024-11-11         -17 2024-11-20  


The results tell a clear story.

2024_PWD_124, “Approach road to Mandi, Belapur”, is in the register but was never published on the portal. A tender that was not published was not open to competition at all.
For 2024_PWD_129, the register gives the NIT date as 25 October 2024. The portal shows it was published only on 11 November 2024. By the register, the tender was open for 26 days and met the norm. By the portal, it was open for 9 days. The register appears to have been written to hide the short window.

What the auditor does next. Call for the tender files of the 4 tenders. See whether a shorter period was approved, by whom and for what reason, as many rules allow in a real emergency. Count the bids received in each, since a short window often goes with a single bid. Ask how the unpublished tender was awarded. And ask the division to explain the NIT date in its register.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
section: 13.10 Keeping evidence of what was collected
text:
13.10 Keeping evidence of what was collected






WarningCaution



Scraped data is only as good as the page it came from, and web pages change. A tender may be corrected, a firm removed from the debarred list, or the whole portal redesigned. If the auditee later disputes a finding, “the website showed it” is not evidence unless we can show what it showed and when. So, for every scrape, record the address of each page and the date and time of collection, and save a copy of each page exactly as received, in the working papers.


The best copy is the file exactly as the server sent it. For our mock site we simply copy the files into a folder named with the date. On a real site, req_perform(path = ...) of httr2 saves the page straight to a file (Section 13.11). We also record a checksum of each file with tools::md5sum(). If even one character of a saved page is changed later, its checksum changes, so the log proves the copy is the one we collected.

evidence_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), paste0("web-evidence-", format(Sys.Date(), "%Y-%m-%d")))
dir.create(evidence_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

sources <- c(page_files, award_files, "Data/web/debarred-firms.html")
copies  <- file.path(evidence_dir, basename(sources))
file.copy(sources, copies, overwrite = TRUE) |> all()

[1] TRUE

evidence_log <- tibble(
  source       = sources,
  saved_as     = basename(copies),
  collected_at = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"),
  md5          = unname(tools::md5sum(copies))
)
evidence_log |> select(saved_as, md5)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  saved_as                md5                             
  <chr>                   <chr>                           
1 tenders-page1.html      f319adf6d42416c976c73db0c16c37cd
2 tenders-page2.html      37e4e50ea5fddb4e3f26f71b26cdd5bb
3 tenders-page3.html      7d3c58f7bf6176d767e260076fd16d0e
4 award-2024_PWD_114.html e2945f4f78ffc76955b25f305cbacd2b
5 award-2024_PWD_111.html 5cb3bb6dc052d1ef2f66627fdc67dc39
6 award-2024_PWD_108.html db5ae78957711bcd523c10a9bbfbcc21
7 debarred-firms.html     55b21b6d0f3308248be849204db12d82


When we have only the parsed page in R, write_html() from xml2 writes it back to a file. This keeps the content, though not always the exact bytes of the original.

xml2::write_html(page1, file.path(evidence_dir, "tenders-page1-parsed.html"))

Save the evidence log as a CSV beside the copies, and run the analysis on the saved copies, not on the live site. Then the analysis can be run again at any time, by anyone, and gives the same result. Chapter 65 shows how to organise such files in an audit project.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.11 Scraping a real website responsibly
Everything above works on a real website by giving read_html() a web address instead of a file. But a real website belongs to someone, and runs on a server that others need too. A scraper sends requests much faster than a person clicking. Careless scraping can slow a site down for everyone, break its terms of use, or be blocked as an attack. An auditor must be beyond reproach here. Follow these rules.


Look for an official source first. Many portals offer a download in Excel or CSV, an open data page, or an API (a service that gives data to programs). Ask the department or the portal’s owner for the data. Scrape only if there is no better way.

Read the site’s terms of use and its robots.txt. The file robots.txt, at the root of a site, says which parts programs may not visit, and sometimes how long to wait between requests. Respect both.

Identify yourself. Send a “user agent” that names your office and gives a contact address, so the site’s owner knows who is visiting and why.

Go slowly. Wait a few seconds between requests, and never send requests in parallel. Scrape outside office hours, when fewer people need the site.

Never log in or break any barrier. Do not use anyone’s password, do not try to get round a CAPTCHA, a login page or a block, and do not visit pages that are not open to the public. If the data is behind a login, ask for it officially.

Take only what you need, once. Save the pages (Section 13.10) and work on the copies, rather than reading the site again and again.

Here is the robots.txt of our mock portal.

readLines("Data/web/robots.txt")

[1] "# robots.txt of the mock portal (made up for this book)"
[2] "User-agent: *"                                          
[3] "Disallow: /bidder/"                                     
[4] "Disallow: /admin/"                                      
[5] "Crawl-delay: 10"                                        


It asks programs not to visit the bidder and admin sections, and to wait 10 seconds between requests. The “Bidder Login” link in the portal’s menu leads into the bidder section, so our scraper must never follow it.
The code below shows how a polite scraper of a real portal may look. It is not run in this book, and the address https://eprocure.example.gov.in is a placeholder, not a real portal. It uses httr2, which gives more control than read_html() alone. req_user_agent() identifies us, req_throttle() limits the rate of requests, req_retry() tries again a few times if the server is busy, and req_perform(path = ...) saves each page to a file. The pause with Sys.sleep() keeps us well within the 10 seconds the site asked for.

library(httr2)

base_url <- "https://eprocure.example.gov.in"   # placeholder, not a real portal

# 1. Read the site's rules first
request(base_url) |>
  req_url_path("robots.txt") |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_string() |>
  cat()

# 2. A polite request, that names us and goes slowly
polite_request <- function(url) {
  request(url) |>
    req_user_agent("Audit team, Office of the Accountant General, Example State (audit.team@example.gov.in)") |>
    req_throttle(rate = 5 / 60) |>        # at most 5 requests a minute
    req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    req_timeout(60)
}

# 3. Save each page, as received, in a dated folder
evidence_dir <- file.path("evidence", paste0("eprocure-", format(Sys.Date(), "%Y-%m-%d")))
dir.create(evidence_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

urls  <- paste0(base_url, "/tenders?page=", 1:3)
files <- file.path(evidence_dir, paste0("tenders-page", 1:3, ".html"))
for (i in seq_along(urls)) {
  polite_request(urls[i]) |> req_perform(path = files[i])
  Sys.sleep(15)                           # a pause between pages
}

# 4. Analyse the saved copies, exactly as in this chapter
tenders <- files |> map(read_tender_page) |> list_rbind()







Note



Some websites build their pages with JavaScript after they load. read_html() then gets only an empty frame, without the table we see in the browser. Open Inspect, go to the Network tab and reload the page. Often the data arrives from an API as JSON, which httr2 can read with resp_body_json(), after checking that the site allows it. rvest also has read_html_live(), which runs a real browser in the background. Use these only on public pages, and with the same care.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.12 A suggested workflow


Look for a better source. An official download, an API, or a request to the department.

Read the rules of the site. Its terms of use and robots.txt. Note them in the working papers.

Study the page with Inspect. Find the id of the table, the classes of the cells and the “Next” link, and choose short, meaningful CSS selectors.

Save the pages first. Politely, with a user agent and pauses, into a dated folder, with an evidence log of addresses, times and checksums.

Read the saved copies. Write one function for one page, using html_elements() for rows and html_element() for the cells in each row, then map() it over all the pages.

Clean the text. Dates with dmy_hm() or dmy(), amounts with parse_number(), and names with a cleaning function.

Check completeness. Compare the rows read with the total the site shows, and look for repeats and NAs.

Compare with the auditee’s records. Join on IDs and cleaned names, test dates against the norm, and confirm every hit from the documents before reporting it.







ImportantRemember




A web page is HTML. Tags make elements, and the class and id attributes help us select them with CSS selectors.

read_html() reads a page, html_elements() and html_element() select, and html_text2(), html_attr() and html_table() extract.
Select the rows first, then one cell from each row with html_element(), so that the columns line up.
Read many pages with map(), or by following the “Next” link, and check that the count matches the site.
Scraped data is evidence only if we record where and when it was collected, and keep a copy.
On real sites, prefer an official source, respect the rules, identify yourself, go slowly, and never log in or get round a barrier.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.13 Where next
The checks in this chapter rest on joins, covered in Chapter 16, and on dates, covered in Chapter 18. For cleaning names and matching them when they are spelt differently, see Chapter 20, Chapter 35 and Chapter 36. For data that arrives as PDF or awkward Excel files, see Chapter 12. Chapter 65 shows how to keep the saved pages, the evidence log and the analysis together as working papers.

title: 13  Data from Web Pages
text:
13.14 Try it yourself
These exercises use the pages of the mock portal in Data/web, and the tables we built from them in this chapter, tenders, awards, tender_register and payments. No real website is needed. Try each one before you open the solution. Some solutions use dplyr verbs such as anti_join(), arrange() and filter(), which Chapter 15 and Chapter 16 explain in full.


A shorter norm. Suppose the rules allowed only 14 days for urgent works. Which tenders would fall short even of this?






TipSolution






ex_short_14 <- tenders |>
  mutate(days_open = as.numeric(as_date(closing) - as_date(published))) |>
  filter(days_open < 14) |>
  select(tender_id, org, days_open)
ex_short_14

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  tender_id    org                   days_open
  <chr>        <chr>                     <dbl>
1 2024_PWD_129 PWD, Amarpur Division         9
2 2024_PWD_119 PWD, Amarpur Division        12


Even with the shorter norm, 2 tenders fall short, both of the PWD, Amarpur Division. 2024_PWD_129 was open for 9 days and 2024_PWD_119 for 12 days. Windows this short need a recorded reason, such as a real emergency.





Tenders of each department. From tenders, count the tenders of each organisation on the portal, and find their total value in ₹ lakh.






TipSolution






ex_by_org <- tenders |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), value_lakh = round(sum(value) / 1e5, 2), .by = org) |>
  arrange(desc(tenders))
ex_by_org

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  org                              tenders value_lakh
  <chr>                              <int>      <dbl>
1 PWD, Amarpur Division                  9      385. 
2 Health Department, Belapur             5       86.4
3 Water Resources, Chandpur Circle       4      196. 


The portal lists tenders of 3 organisations. PWD, Amarpur Division has the most, 9. A count like this, compared with the department’s own figures, is a quick test that the scrape covered what we expected.





The other direction. In the chapter we looked for tenders in the register that the portal does not show. Now look the other way. Does the portal show any tender of the PWD, Amarpur Division that is missing from the division’s register?






TipSolution






ex_not_in_register <- tenders |>
  filter(org == "PWD, Amarpur Division") |>
  anti_join(tender_register, by = "tender_id")
ex_not_in_register

# A tibble: 0 × 9
# ℹ 9 variables: tender_id <chr>, title <chr>, org <chr>, published <dttm>,
#   closing <dttm>, value <dbl>, status <chr>, award_link <chr>,
#   source_file <chr>


The result has 0 rows. Every tender of the division on the portal is in its register. A tender published but left out of the register would have been a finding too, so the check is worth making both ways.





Competition for the awarded works. From awards, find the awards that received fewer than three bids, with the firm and the value.






TipSolution






ex_few_bids <- awards |>
  filter(bids < 3) |>
  select(tender_id, bids, awarded_to, portal_value)
ex_few_bids

# A tibble: 1 × 4

2024_PWD_108 received only 2 bids, and was awarded to Sharma Traders for ₹8,12,600. Few bids suggest weak competition. The auditor would see how long the tender was open, and how widely it was advertised.





Payments after debarment ended. Using the cleaned names, list any payment made to a firm after its debarment had ended. These are not findings, but the auditor should note them.

ex_after <- payments |>
  inner_join(debarred, by = "name_key") |>

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
text:
14.1 Merging the sheets of one Excel file
Audit data often comes in pieces. A State directorate sends one Excel workbook with a sheet for each district. A district sends the returns of its blocks, one file for each block and each quarter. A department sends twelve monthly files of its pay bills. Before any analysis, the pieces must be put together into one table. Done by hand, by copying and pasting sheets, this is slow, and it is easy to miss a sheet, paste one twice, or shift a column. And nobody can check afterwards what was done.
There is also an audit question hidden in the pieces themselves. Has every office sent its return? Has any file been sent twice? Does each file agree with the total the office reported? These checks are part of the audit trail, and R can do them as it combines the files.
In this chapter we will see how to combine such pieces into one data frame with a few lines of code, keeping a record of where each row came from. We will also see the reverse, how to split one data frame into many files, for example to send each district its own list of exceptions. We end with a complete example, combining the returns of the blocks of a district and reconciling them with the district’s statement.
Prerequisites
readxl reads Excel files. It is installed along with tidyverse, but is not part of the core tidyverse, so it has to be loaded separately. writexl writes Excel files, and janitor cleans column names (Chapter 11).
The Directorate of Social Welfare of a State has sent the payments of social security pension for 2024-25. It is one Excel workbook, with a sheet for each of four districts. Each sheet has a row for each month and each scheme, with the number of beneficiaries paid and the amount paid in rupees. The code below creates the workbook in a temporary folder.
Code to create the pension workbookset.seed(15)
districts <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devipur")
fy_months <- month.abb[c(4:12, 1:3)]
rates <- c("Old age" = 1200, "Widow" = 1000)

make_sheet <- function(district) {
  expand_grid(month = fy_months, scheme = names(rates)) |>
    mutate(beneficiaries = round(runif(n(), 3500, 9000)),
           amount_paid   = beneficiaries * rates[scheme])
}
pension_sheets <- map(set_names(districts), make_sheet)
# Planted. Chandpur has not reported January
pension_sheets$Chandpur <- pension_sheets$Chandpur |> filter(month != "Jan")

pension_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "pension_2024-25.xlsx")
write_xlsx(pension_sheets, pension_file)
The following steps are used.
# Step 1
path <- pension_file
# Step 2 and Step 3
pension_data <- excel_sheets(path) |>
  set_names() |>
# Step 4
  map(\(sheet) read_excel(path, sheet = sheet)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "district")
# print the data
pension_data

# A tibble: 94 × 5
   district month scheme  beneficiaries amount_paid
   <chr>    <chr> <chr>           <dbl>       <dbl>
 1 Amarpur  Apr   Old age          6812     8174400
 2 Amarpur  Apr   Widow            4573     4573000
 3 Amarpur  May   Old age          8816    10579200
 4 Amarpur  May   Widow            7080     7080000
 5 Amarpur  Jun   Old age          5519     6622800
 6 Amarpur  Jun   Widow            8939     8939000
 7 Amarpur  Jul   Old age          7984     9580800
 8 Amarpur  Jul   Widow            4897     4897000
 9 Amarpur  Aug   Old age          7280     8736000
10 Amarpur  Aug   Widow            8073     8073000
# ℹ 84 more rows
The data of all the sheets have been merged into one table, and one extra column has been created from the sheet names. The name of that column has been given through the names_to argument of list_rbind(). If the new column is not required, simply leave out this argument. set_names() with a single vector names each element by its own value, so the sheet names become the names of the list.
Now that the sheets are one table, a quick count shows whether every district has reported every month.
pension_data |>
  summarise(months = n_distinct(month), rows = n(),
            amount_crore = round(sum(amount_paid) / 1e7, 2), .by = district)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  district months  rows amount_crore
  <chr>     <int> <int>        <dbl>
1 Amarpur      12    24         17.9
2 Belapur      12    24         16.2
3 Chandpur     11    22         17.6
4 Devipur      12    24         17.3
Chandpur has only 11 months. The month missing is January. Either no pension was paid in Chandpur that month, or the payments have been left out of the return. The auditor asks the directorate which, before using these figures.

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
text:
Store the path of the file.
Collect the names of all sheets with excel_sheets().
Name the elements of this vector with the sheet names themselves, using set_names(). The names will travel with the data, and later become a column.
Read all the sheets with purrr::map(), and combine them into one table with purrr::list_rbind().












Note



Older code often uses purrr::map_dfr(), which reads and binds in one step. It still works, but purrr now recommends map() followed by list_rbind(), which is clearer about what happens.

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
section: 14.2 Merging many files into one data frame
text:
14.2 Merging many files into one data frame
Often the source data is split into many files, which we have to combine into one data frame. For example, each district treasury sends its monthly salary expenditure in a separate file. We collect all such files in one folder and follow these steps.

Get the names of all the files with list.files().
Read all the files into a list with purrr::map().
Bind them into one data frame with list_rbind().

Let us first create a few such files in a temporary folder, to try this out.

Code to create the district filesfolder <- file.path(tempdir(), "district_files")
dir.create(folder, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(15)
for (d in c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur")) {
  tibble(month  = month.abb[4:9],
         head   = "Salaries",
         amount = round(runif(6, 20, 60), 2)) |>
    write_csv(file.path(folder, paste0(d, "_2024.csv")))
}


Each file has the salary expenditure of one district for the six months from April to September 2024, in ₹ lakh.

files <- list.files(folder, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
basename(files)

[1] "Amarpur_2024.csv"  "Belapur_2024.csv"  "Chandpur_2024.csv"

district_data <- files |>
  set_names(basename(files)) |>
  map(\(f) read_csv(f, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "source_file") |>
  mutate(amount = parse_number(amount))

district_data

# A tibble: 18 × 4
   source_file       month head     amount

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
section: 14.3 Splitting one data frame into many files
text:
14.3 Splitting one data frame into many files
Sometimes we need the reverse, for example to send each district or each office its own data, or its own list of exceptions. Let us use pension_data created above, and save the data of each district in a separate csv file. We use the following steps.

Split the data frame into a list, with a separate data frame for each district, using base R’s split(). The elements of the list are named by the district.
Write each element to a file named after its district, using purrr::iwalk(). iwalk() passes each element and its name to the function. It is used when we want the side effect, here writing a file, rather than a result.


out_folder <- file.path(tempdir(), "by_district")
dir.create(out_folder, showWarnings = FALSE)

pension_data |>
  split(pension_data$district) |>
  iwalk(\(df, district) write_csv(df, file.path(out_folder, paste0(district, ".csv"))))

We can check that four new files, named after the districts, have been created in the folder.

list.files(out_folder)

[1] "Amarpur.csv"  "Belapur.csv"  "Chandpur.csv" "Devipur.csv" 








WarningCaution



Keep each piece of data together with its name, as split() and iwalk() do. A common mistake is to make a vector of file names with unique(), and split the data with group_split(). unique() keeps the order in which the names first appear, while group_split() sorts the groups alphabetically. If the two orders differ, each file gets another district’s data, without any error.

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
section: 14.5 Audit use case, combining the returns of many blocks
text:
14.5 Audit use case, combining the returns of many blocks
A district runs a rural employment scheme in six blocks. Each block sends a quarterly return of the wages paid, one row for each muster roll, as a csv file. The district’s own statement lists, for each block, the number of muster rolls and the wages paid in the first quarter of 2024-25. We have received a folder of block files, and the district statement. Our task is to combine the files and check them against the statement.

Code to create the block returns and the district statementset.seed(31)
blocks <- c("Lalganj", "Madhopur", "Nayagaon", "Rampur", "Kherwa", "Sonpur")

make_return <- function(block) {
  k <- sample(18:30, 1)
  tibble(muster_roll_no = sprintf("MR/%s/%03d", toupper(substr(block, 1, 3)), 1:k),
         work_id        = sample(sprintf("W-%02d", 1:8), k, replace = TRUE),
         workers        = sample(8:25, k, replace = TRUE),
         days           = sample(6:14, k, replace = TRUE),
         wage_rate      = 255) |>
    mutate(amount = workers * days * wage_rate)
}
returns <- map(set_names(blocks), make_return)

# The district statement, made from the complete returns
statement <- tibble(block  = blocks,
                    rolls  = map_int(returns, nrow),
                    amount = map_dbl(returns, \(d) sum(d$amount)))

# Planted. Madhopur's file has left out its last muster roll
returns$Madhopur <- head(returns$Madhopur, -1)
# Planted. Rampur's file uses its own column headings
names(returns$Rampur) <- c("Muster Roll No.", "Work ID", "Workers", "Days",
                           "Wage Rate", "Amount")

block_folder <- file.path(tempdir(), "block_returns")
dir.create(block_folder, showWarnings = FALSE)
# Planted. Kherwa's file has not been received
for (b in setdiff(blocks, "Kherwa")) {
  write_csv(returns[[b]], file.path(block_folder, paste0(b, "_Q1_2024-25.csv")))
}
# Planted. Sonpur's file has been saved twice, under two names
invisible(file.copy(file.path(block_folder, "Sonpur_Q1_2024-25.csv"),
          file.path(block_folder, "Sonpur_Q1_2024-25 (2).csv")))



statement

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  block    rolls  amount
  <chr>    <int>   <dbl>
1 Lalganj     30 1110015
2 Madhopur    30 1225275
3 Nayagaon    26 1051875
4 Rampur      21  733125
5 Kherwa      18  869040
6 Sonpur      18  728790


Step 1, check which files have come. We list the files, and take the block name from the start of each file name.

files <- list.files(block_folder, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
basename(files)

[1] "Lalganj_Q1_2024-25.csv"    "Madhopur_Q1_2024-25.csv"  
[3] "Nayagaon_Q1_2024-25.csv"   "Rampur_Q1_2024-25.csv"    
[5] "Sonpur_Q1_2024-25 (2).csv" "Sonpur_Q1_2024-25.csv"    

received <- str_remove(basename(files), "_Q1.*$")
setdiff(statement$block, received)   # blocks with no file

[1] "Kherwa"

received[duplicated(received)]       # blocks with more than one file

[1] "Sonpur"


There are 6 files for 6 blocks. Kherwa has sent no file, and Sonpur has two.
Step 2, are the two files the same? Two files with the same name may hold different data, like a first and a corrected return. We compare their contents with a hash, a short code computed from every byte of a file (Chapter 8). Files with the same hash are identical.

hashes <- tools::md5sum(files)
tibble(file = basename(files), hash = unname(hashes)) |>
  filter(hash %in% hash[duplicated(hash)])

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  file                      hash                            
  <chr>                     <chr>                           
1 Sonpur_Q1_2024-25 (2).csv e2867fb451b5c0495ce321ae670ba9a9
2 Sonpur_Q1_2024-25.csv     e2867fb451b5c0495ce321ae670ba9a9


The two Sonpur files are identical, so we keep only one of them. Had they differed, we would have had to ask the district which one is final.

files <- files[!duplicated(hashes)]

Step 3, read and bind, cleaning the names. Let us first see what happens if we bind the files as they are.

files |>
  set_names(str_remove(basename(files), "_Q1.*$")) |>
  map(\(f) read_csv(f, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "block") |>
  names()

 [1] "block"           "muster_roll_no"  "work_id"         "workers"        
 [5] "days"            "wage_rate"       "amount"          "Muster Roll No."
 [9] "Work ID"         "Workers"         "Days"            "Wage Rate"      
[13] "Amount"         


There are now twelve columns of data, besides block, instead of six. Rampur’s file has its own headings, like Muster Roll No. and Amount, so list_rbind() has kept them as separate columns, with NA for every other block. The amounts of Rampur would be lost from any total of amount. Cleaning the names of each file inside map() fixes this.

block_data <- files |>
  set_names(str_remove(basename(files), "_Q1.*$")) |>
  map(\(f) read_csv(f, col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |> clean_names()) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "block") |>
  mutate(amount = parse_number(amount))

glimpse(block_data)

Rows: 124
Columns: 7
$ block          <chr> "Lalganj", "Lalganj", "Lalganj", "Lalganj", "Lalganj", …
$ muster_roll_no <chr> "MR/LAL/001", "MR/LAL/002", "MR/LAL/003", "MR/LAL/004",…
$ work_id        <chr> "W-01", "W-03", "W-08", "W-02", "W-08", "W-03", "W-07",…
$ workers        <chr> "9", "14", "11", "13", "12", "21", "10", "17", "12", "2…
$ days           <chr> "6", "10", "7", "8", "9", "13", "6", "7", "10", "10", "…
$ wage_rate      <chr> "255", "255", "255", "255", "255", "255", "255", "255",…
$ amount         <dbl> 13770, 35700, 19635, 26520, 27540, 69615, 15300, 30345,…


Step 4, reconcile each block with the statement. We count the muster rolls and add the wages of each block, and set them beside the statement. left_join() matches the rows of the two tables by block. We learn it properly in Chapter 16.

reconciliation <- statement |>
  left_join(block_data |> summarise(file_rolls = n(), file_amount = sum(amount), .by = block),
            by = "block") |>
  mutate(difference = amount - file_amount)
reconciliation

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  block    rolls  amount file_rolls file_amount difference
  <chr>    <int>   <dbl>      <int>       <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Lalganj     30 1110015         30     1110015          0
2 Madhopur    30 1225275         29     1164585      60690
3 Nayagaon    26 1051875         26     1051875          0
4 Rampur      21  733125         21      733125          0
5 Kherwa      18  869040         NA          NA         NA
6 Sonpur      18  728790         18      728790          0


Four blocks agree exactly. Madhopur’s file has 29 muster rolls against 30 in the statement, and is short by ₹60,690. Kherwa has no file at all, so wages of ₹8.69 lakh in the statement have no supporting return.
What would the auditor do next? Ask the district for Kherwa’s return, and for the muster roll missing from Madhopur’s file. Note that Sonpur’s return was received twice, and that the copies were identical. Keep the reconciliation table in the working papers. Only when every block agrees should the combined data be used for the analysis of wages.

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
text:
14.6 A suggested workflow
When data arrives in pieces, like one sheet for each district or one file for each block, an auditor may follow these steps.


Collect the pieces in one place. Keep all the files in one folder, and list them with list.files() using pattern and full.names = TRUE. For one Excel file, list its sheets with excel_sheets().

Check that nothing is missing or repeated. Compare the list of files or sheets with the covering letter, using setdiff() and duplicated(). Compare repeated files with tools::md5sum() to see whether they are identical.

Name each piece. Use set_names() so that the file or sheet name travels with the data.

Read every piece the same way. Use map() and read all columns as text, so that small differences in type do not stop the binding. Clean the names with clean_names() if the files use different headings.

Bind with a source column. Use list_rbind(names_to = ) so that each row records the file or sheet it came from.

Reconcile each piece. Convert the amounts, then compare the rows and totals of each file with the statement sent by the office.

Split the results back when needed. Use split() and iwalk() to write one file for each district or office, or write_xlsx() for one sheet each.







ImportantRemember



Always keep a column showing which file each row came from. Reconcile the rows and totals of each file before the analysis. When splitting, keep each piece together with its name, as split() and iwalk() do, so that no office gets another office’s data.

title: 14  Combining Many Similar Files
text:
14.7 Try it yourself
These exercises use the tables we combined in this chapter, the pension data pension_data and the block returns block_data. Any file an exercise writes goes into the temporary folder given by tempdir(). Try each one before you open the solution. Some solutions use dplyr verbs such as count(), filter() and mutate(), which Chapter 15 explains in full.


Totals by scheme. Find the number of beneficiaries paid and the amount paid in ₹ crore under each scheme, for all four districts together.






TipSolution






ex_scheme <- pension_data |>
  summarise(beneficiaries = sum(beneficiaries),
            amount_crore  = round(sum(amount_paid) / 1e7, 2), .by = scheme)
ex_scheme

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  scheme  beneficiaries amount_crore
  <chr>           <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Old age        309929         37.2
2 Widow          318080         31.8


Old age pension cost ₹37.19 crore and widow pension ₹31.81 crore. These totals can be compared with the expenditure booked under each scheme in the accounts.





Months reported by fewer districts. Without looking at each district, find the months that fewer than four districts have reported.






TipSolution






ex_months <- pension_data |>
  distinct(district, month) |>
  count(month, name = "districts") |>
  filter(districts < 4)
ex_months

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  month districts
  <chr>     <int>
1 Jan           3


Only January has fewer than four districts, 3 of them. This finds the same gap as in the chapter, Chandpur’s January, but from the side of the months. With many districts, such a count shows the gaps at a glance.





Check the rate of pension. Old age pension is ₹1,200 a month and widow pension ₹1,000. Divide the amount paid by the beneficiaries in each row. Are there rows where the result is not the rate of the scheme?






TipSolution






ex_rate <- pension_data |>
  mutate(rate_paid = amount_paid / beneficiaries,
         rate_due  = if_else(scheme == "Old age", 1200, 1000)) |>
  filter(rate_paid != rate_due)
ex_rate

# A tibble: 0 × 7
# ℹ 7 variables: district <chr>, month <chr>, scheme <chr>,
#   beneficiaries <dbl>, amount_paid <dbl>, rate_paid <dbl>, rate_due <dbl>


The result has 0 rows. In every row the amount agrees with the number of beneficiaries at the scheme’s rate. A clean result is still worth recording in the working papers, since it shows the test was done.





Recompute the wages. In block_data, every column except amount is still text. Convert workers, days and wage_rate to numbers, recompute the wages of each muster roll, and list any roll where the amount differs.






TipSolution






ex_wages <- block_data |>
  mutate(across(c(workers, days, wage_rate), parse_number),
         wages_due = workers * days * wage_rate) |>
  filter(wages_due != amount)
nrow(ex_wages)

[1] 0


The count is 0. No muster roll differs, so the amounts in the returns are arithmetically correct, including Rampur’s after its names were cleaned. The shortfall of Madhopur found in the chapter is a missing roll, not a wrong amount.





Exceptions for each block. List the muster rolls with more than 20 workers, and write one csv file for each block into a new folder inside tempdir(). Check which files were written.






TipSolution






ex_folder <- file.path(tempdir(), "large_rolls")
dir.create(ex_folder, showWarnings = FALSE)

ex_large <- block_data |>
  filter(parse_number(workers) > 20)

ex_large |>
  split(ex_large$block) |>
  iwalk(\(df, block) write_csv(df, file.path(ex_folder, paste0(block, "_large_rolls.csv"))))

list.files(ex_folder)

[1] "Lalganj_large_rolls.csv"  "Madhopur_large_rolls.csv"
[3] "Nayagaon_large_rolls.csv" "Rampur_large_rolls.csv"  
[5] "Sonpur_large_rolls.csv"  


There are 29 such rolls, in 5 blocks, and one file has been written for each of these blocks. Each block can now be asked to show the attendance of these large gangs on the muster rolls.

title: 15  Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
15.1 Our data, a payment register
Suppose we receive the payment register of a Public Works division for 2024-25. It has a few hundred vouchers, or a few lakh, with a dozen columns each. Our questions are simple. Which vouchers were paid by the Nashik office? What did each office spend? Which bills were just below the sanction limit? Was GST charged at the right rate? Which were the ten largest payments?
To answer any of these, we must first transform the data. We select the columns we need, keep the rows that matter, create new columns, sort, and summarise by groups. Most of the work in any audit analysis is of this kind. The package dplyr,1 part of the core tidyverse, does all this with a small set of functions. They are easy to read, even for someone who does not know R.
In this chapter we learn these functions one by one, on a small payment register with a few irregularities planted in it. We find a voucher with the wrong GST rate, a vendor paid in several bills just below ₹1 lakh, and works paid beyond their sanctioned amount. By the end, we can write each audit test as one readable chain of steps.
Prerequisites
We load dplyr through tidyverse. In this book we join steps with the native pipe |>, which comes with R itself, from version 4.1 (Chapter 5). You will also see the older pipe %>% in many books and websites. For everyday use the two work alike.
The functions of dplyr are called verbs, because each of them does something to the data. The verbs can be divided into three kinds, depending on what they work on (Figure 15.1).
Our register belongs to an imaginary Public Works division with four sub-division offices, at Pune, Nashik, Nagpur and Kolhapur. Each row is one payment voucher of the financial year 2024-25. All names are made up. Two kinds of irregularity are planted in the data, and we find them in this chapter. The code that creates the data is folded. New readers need not worry about it now. You may come back to it at the end of the chapter, when every verb in it will be familiar.
Code to create the payment registerset.seed(2025)
offices <- c("Pune", "Nashik", "Nagpur", "Kolhapur")
vendor_master <- tibble(
  vendor_id   = sprintf("V%02d", 1:10),
  vendor_name = c("Shree Ganesh Builders", "Patil Constructions", "Deshmukh Traders",
                  "Sai Krupa Enterprises", "Jadhav Electricals", "Kulkarni & Sons",
                  "Mahalaxmi Suppliers", "Gawande Infra", "Shinde Transport",
                  "Om Stationers")
)

# Ordinary vouchers
n <- 110
vouchers <- tibble(
  office      = sample(offices, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.25, 0.25, 0.2)),
  vendor_id   = sample(vendor_master$vendor_id, n, replace = TRUE),
  object_head = sample(c("Works", "Maintenance", "Supplies", "Office expenses"), n,
                       replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.35, 0.3, 0.2, 0.15)),
  bill_date   = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:340, n, replace = TRUE),
  taxable     = round(exp(runif(n, log(8000), log(1500000))), -2),
  gst_pct     = 18
)

# Planted 1. Five supply bills of one vendor at Nashik, each just below Rs 1 lakh
split_bills <- tibble(
  office = "Nashik", vendor_id = "V04", object_head = "Supplies",
  bill_date = as.Date("2025-01-06") + c(0, 3, 6, 9, 13),
  taxable = c(84300, 83900, 84700, 82600, 84500), gst_pct = 18
)
vouchers <- bind_rows(vouchers, split_bills)

# Planted 2. GST charged at 28% instead of 18% on three bills
wrong_gst <- sample(which(vouchers$vendor_id != "V04"), 3)
vouchers$gst_pct[wrong_gst] <- 28

vouchers <- vouchers |>
  mutate(voucher_date = bill_date + sample(5:30, n(), replace = TRUE),
         amt_gst   = round(taxable * gst_pct / 100),
         amt_gross = taxable + amt_gst,
         amt_tds   = round(taxable * 0.02),
         amt_net   = amt_gross - amt_tds,
         mode      = if_else(amt_gross > 200000, "RTGS",
                             sample(c("NEFT", "Cheque"), n(), replace = TRUE,
                                    prob = c(0.7, 0.3)))) |>
  arrange(voucher_date) |>
  mutate(voucher_no = sprintf("PV/24-25/%03d", row_number())) |>
  left_join(vendor_master, by = "vendor_id") |>
  select(voucher_no, voucher_date, office, vendor_id, vendor_name, object_head,
         bill_date, amt_gross, amt_gst, amt_tds, amt_net, mode)
Let us have a look at it with glimpse(), which shows every column on its own line, with its type and its first few values.
glimpse(vouchers)

Rows: 115
Columns: 12
