title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.1 The idea of a test
An auditor finds that one office approves 91 out of every 100 medical claims, while the rest of the department approves 84. Is that office lax in its checks, or is the difference just the kind of variation we should expect between any two offices? One dealing officer’s claims are larger on average than everyone else’s. Is that a pattern worth an inquiry, or a coincidence?
These are the questions a statistical test answers. It tells us whether a difference we see is larger than chance alone would usually produce. A test does not prove an irregularity. But it helps us decide where to spend our limited audit time, and it protects us from two embarrassments: chasing differences that mean nothing, and missing ones that matter.
In this chapter we learn the idea of a test in plain words, and then the tests an auditor needs most often. Each answers a question that comes up in real audits.
Prerequisites
All the tests themselves come with base R, in the package stats, which is always loaded.
Every test follows the same reasoning, which is very close to how an auditor already thinks.
A test can go wrong in two ways, and both have an audit meaning.
The 5% limit is the chance of a false alarm we are willing to accept. A smaller limit means fewer false alarms but more misses. With a small sample, a test may miss even a large difference, as we will see.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
Start by assuming nothing is unusual. This assumption is called the null hypothesis. For example, “this office approves claims at the same rate as the others”. It is like presuming an auditee innocent until the evidence says otherwise.

Ask how surprising the data would be, if nothing were unusual. The answer is the p-value, a probability between 0 and 1. A p-value of 0.30 means that, if nothing were unusual, a difference at least this large would turn up 30% of the time by chance alone. Not surprising at all. A p-value of 0.001 means it would turn up only once in a thousand times. Very surprising.

Decide. If the p-value is small, below a limit we fix in advance, we conclude that chance is an unlikely explanation, and call the difference statistically significant. The usual limit is 0.05, or 5%.




Table 30.1: The two errors of a test, in audit terms









Nothing is actually unusual
Something is actually unusual



Test says significant

Type I error, a false alarm. Time wasted on an inquiry, and an auditee questioned unfairly.
Correct. A real issue found.


Test says not significant
Correct. No time wasted.

Type II error, a miss. A real issue goes unreported. This is audit risk.













NoteWhat if we have the whole population?



Auditors often analyse 100% of the data, not a sample. If one office approved 94% of its claims and another 86%, that difference is a fact. Why test it? Because claims are approved or rejected for many reasons, and even two identical offices would not show identical rates in a year. The test asks whether the difference is larger than this ordinary variation in the process. So tests are useful on full data too, as long as we read “significant” as “unlikely to be ordinary variation”, and not as a finding in itself.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.2 Our data
We use one dataset through most of the chapter. It is a year’s register of medical reimbursement claims of a department with six offices, each office with two dealing officers. For each claim we have the amount, whether it was approved, and the days taken to settle it.

Code to create the claims registerset.seed(6)
n <- 3000
offices <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur", "Rampur")
claims <- tibble(
  claim_id = sprintf("MR-%04d", 1:n),
  office   = sample(offices, n, TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.18, 0.17, 0.16, 0.15, 0.14)),
  desk     = sample(1:2, n, TRUE),
  amount   = round(rlnorm(n, log(18000), 0.8), -1)
) |>
  mutate(officer = paste0(toupper(substr(office, 1, 3)), "-", desk),
         # Planted. Officer RAM-2 approves almost everything
         approved = runif(n) < if_else(officer == "RAM-2", 0.97, 0.86),
         # Planted. Chandpur is slow to settle claims
         days_to_settle = round(rgamma(n, shape = 4,
                                       rate = 4 / if_else(office == "Chandpur", 27, 21))),
         # Planted. Claims handled by DEV-2 are inflated
         amount = if_else(officer == "DEV-2", round(amount * 1.4, -1), amount)) |>
  select(claim_id, office, officer, amount, approved, days_to_settle)



claims

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
section: 30.3 Is the error rate above the tolerable rate?
text:
30.3 Is the error rate above the tolerable rate?
Let us start with a question from a test of controls. The auditor checks a random sample of 60 claims, and finds 6 settled without the required verification. The tolerable deviation rate is 5%. The sample’s rate is 10%, twice the tolerable rate. Can we conclude that the control is failing?
binom.test() compares a count of “successes” (here, deviations) in a number of trials with an expected proportion. Since we only care whether the rate is above 5%, we use alternative = "greater".

dev_test <- binom.test(x = 6, n = 60, p = 0.05, alternative = "greater")
dev_test


    Exact binomial test

data:  6 and 60
number of successes = 6, number of trials = 60, p-value = 0.07872
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is greater than 0.05
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.04445297 1.00000000
sample estimates:
probability of success 
                   0.1 


The p-value is 0.079, above 0.05. Surprisingly, a sample of 60 with 6 deviations is not enough to conclude that the true rate exceeds 5%. With 60 claims, a true rate of 5% would give 6 or more deviations about 8% of the time. The confidence interval says the same: the true rate could be as low as 4.4%.
What if the auditor had found 9 deviations instead?

binom.test(x = 9, n = 60, p = 0.05, alternative = "greater")$p.value

[1] 0.002848606


Now the conclusion is clear. This is the reason why sample sizes for tests of controls are planned in advance, as we did in Section 29.7. A test on a sample too small to detect the difference we care about can only end in “not proven”.






Caution



“Not significant” does not mean “no problem”. It means the data is not strong enough to rule out chance. Never report a control as effective only because a test was not significant, least of all on a small sample. Report what was found, 6 deviations in 60, and the limit of what the sample can tell.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.4 Comparing two rates
Back to the full register. Rampur approves more claims than the rest of the department. Is the difference more than chance?

claims |>
  summarise(claims = n(), n_approved = sum(approved),
            approval_rate = round(mean(approved), 3),
            .by = office) |>
  arrange(desc(approval_rate))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  office   claims n_approved approval_rate
  <chr>     <int>      <int>         <dbl>
1 Rampur      433        395         0.912
2 Fatehpur    445        381         0.856
3 Belapur     527        445         0.844
4 Amarpur     587        495         0.843
5 Chandpur    523        440         0.841
6 Devgarh     485        405         0.835


prop.test() compares two (or more) proportions. We give it the number approved and the number of claims in each group.

rampur <- claims$office == "Rampur"
rampur_test <- prop.test(x = c(sum(claims$approved[rampur]), sum(claims$approved[!rampur])),
                         n = c(sum(rampur), sum(!rampur)))
rampur_test


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(sum(claims$approved[rampur]), sum(claims$approved[!rampur])) out of c(sum(rampur), sum(!rampur))
X-squared = 13.355, df = 1, p-value = 0.0002577
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.03697932 0.09992800
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.9122402 0.8437865 


Rampur approved 91.2% of its claims, against 84.4% elsewhere. The p-value is 0.00026, far below 0.05. A difference this large would almost never arise by chance. The confidence interval says that Rampur’s rate is higher by somewhere between 3.7 and 10 percentage points.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.5 Comparing many groups at once
Rampur caught our eye because we looked at the table first. A fairer way is to test all six offices together, without picking one in advance. The chi-square test of independence checks whether two categorical variables, here office and approval, are related. If approval did not depend on the office, every office would approve about the same share.

approval_table <- table(claims$office, claims$approved)
approval_table

          
           FALSE TRUE
  Amarpur     92  495
  Belapur     82  445
  Chandpur    83  440
  Devgarh     80  405
  Fatehpur    64  381
  Rampur      38  395

office_test <- chisq.test(approval_table)
office_test


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  approval_table
X-squared = 14.77, df = 5, p-value = 0.01139


The p-value of 0.011 is below 0.05, so approval rates do differ between offices. But the test does not say which office is different. For that, look at the standardised residuals. Each says how far an office’s count is from what we would expect if all offices were alike, in units of standard deviation. Values beyond about 2 (or below -2) deserve attention.

round(office_test$stdres, 2)

          
           FALSE  TRUE
  Amarpur   0.79 -0.79
  Belapur   0.66 -0.66
  Chandpur  0.88 -0.88
  Devgarh   1.27 -1.27
  Fatehpur -0.16  0.16
  Rampur   -3.73  3.73


Only Rampur stands out, with 3.7 standard deviations more approvals than expected. Every other office is within 2.






TipAudit tip



The chi-square test with its residuals is one of the most useful tests in audit. It works on any cross-table of counts: rejections by inspector, tenders won by bidder and department, cases disposed of by officer and type, or exceptions by branch. The residuals point straight at the cells which are out of line.


The chi-square test needs enough data in every cell. If any expected count, office_test$expected, is below 5, R gives a warning that the result may be inaccurate. Then use fisher.test(), which is exact, or combine small groups.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
section: 30.6 Drilling down, and the problem of many tests
text:
30.6 Drilling down, and the problem of many tests
Rampur has two dealing officers. Is the high approval rate the office’s, or one officer’s? A natural step is to test every officer against the rest. But with many tests, a new problem appears.
Many tests mean some false alarms. Each test at the 5% level has a 5% chance of a false alarm. Run 20 tests where nothing is unusual, and on average one will come out “significant” anyway. Let us see this with 40 imaginary offices which all approve at exactly the same true rate of 86%.

set.seed(1)
p_values <- map_dbl(1:40, \(i) {
  approved_here <- rbinom(1, size = 300, prob = 0.86)    # this office, 300 claims
  approved_rest <- rbinom(1, size = 12000, prob = 0.86)  # all the others
  prop.test(c(approved_here, approved_rest), c(300, 12000))$p.value
})
sum(p_values < 0.05)

[1] 2


2 of the 40 identical offices look “significantly” different, purely by chance. Reporting them would be unfair to their staff. The remedy is to adjust the p-values for the number of tests. p.adjust() does this. The Holm method is a safe general choice.

sum(p.adjust(p_values, method = "holm") < 0.05)

[1] 0


After adjustment, no false alarms remain. Now the real drill-down. We test each of the 12 officers against all the others, collect the results with broom::tidy(), and adjust.

officer_tests <- map(sort(unique(claims$officer)), \(o) {
  mine <- claims$officer == o
  prop.test(x = c(sum(claims$approved[mine]), sum(claims$approved[!mine])),
            n = c(sum(mine), sum(!mine))) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(officer = o, claims = sum(mine), .before = 1)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(p_adjusted = p.adjust(p.value, method = "holm")) |>
  select(officer, claims, own_rate = estimate1, rest_rate = estimate2, p.value, p_adjusted) |>
  arrange(p.value)

officer_tests |> mutate(across(c(own_rate, rest_rate), \(x) round(x, 3)),
                        across(c(p.value, p_adjusted), \(x) signif(x, 2)))

# A tibble: 12 × 6
   officer claims own_rate rest_rate   p.value p_adjusted

 2 DEV-1      243    0.819     0.857 0.13        1       
 3 AMA-2      277    0.83      0.856 0.29        1       
 4 BEL-2      281    0.833     0.856 0.34        1       
 5 FAT-1      240    0.871     0.852 0.49        1       
 6 CHA-1      261    0.839     0.855 0.54        1       
 7 FAT-2      205    0.839     0.855 0.61        1       
 8 CHA-2      262    0.844     0.855 0.69        1

10 BEL-1      246    0.858     0.853 0.93        1       
11 DEV-2      242    0.851     0.854 0.99        1

The picture is clear. Officer RAM-2 approved 96.3% of claims, and stays significant even after adjustment (adjusted p-value less than 0.0001). The other Rampur officer, RAM-1, approved 86.2%, in line with the department. So the office’s high rate comes from one desk. That is where the audit should look, at a sample of the claims RAM-2 approved, to see whether the checks were actually done.






TipAudit tip



broom::tidy() turns the output of almost any test into a one-row table. Together with map() and list_rbind(), it lets us run the same test over every officer, vendor or district, and get one table to sort, filter and attach to working papers. Always add a column of adjusted p-values when you do this.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.7 Comparing averages
Rates are about counts. Many audit questions are about amounts and times instead. Is Chandpur slower to settle claims than the other offices? The t-test compares the means of two groups.

claims |>
  summarise(mean_days = round(mean(days_to_settle), 1),
            median_days = median(days_to_settle), .by = office)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  office   mean_days median_days
  <chr>        <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Devgarh       21.8          20
2 Rampur        21.4          20
3 Belapur       20.3          19
4 Chandpur      27            25
5 Fatehpur      21.3          19
6 Amarpur       21.4          20



chandpur_test <- t.test(days_to_settle ~ (office == "Chandpur"), data = claims)
chandpur_test


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  days_to_settle by office == "Chandpur"
t = -9.1182, df = 652.93, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group FALSE and group TRUE is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -7.057826 -4.556638
sample estimates:
mean in group FALSE  mean in group TRUE 
           21.22527            27.03250 


Chandpur takes 27 days on average, against 21.2 days elsewhere, and the p-value is extremely small. The difference is real, not chance. R uses Welch’s t-test by default, which does not assume that the two groups vary equally. Keep this default.
The formula days_to_settle ~ (office == "Chandpur") reads “days to settle, by whether the office is Chandpur”. The group FALSE (the other offices) comes first in the output.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.8 When amounts are skewed
The t-test compares means. Money amounts are usually skewed, with many small values and a few very large ones, as we saw in Chapter 27. A handful of large claims can pull a mean up or down, and make the t-test unreliable. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test (also called the Mann-Whitney test) avoids this. It ranks all the values together, and asks whether one group’s values tend to rank higher than the other’s. A single huge claim is then just “the highest rank”, whatever its size.
Are the claims handled by officer DEV-2 larger than everyone else’s?

claims |>
  mutate(group = if_else(officer == "DEV-2", "DEV-2", "Others")) |>
  summarise(claims = n(), mean_amount = round(mean(amount)),
            median_amount = median(amount), .by = group)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  group  claims mean_amount median_amount
  <chr>   <int>       <dbl>         <dbl>
1 DEV-2     242       36081         26020
2 Others   2758       24549         17980

dev2_test <- wilcox.test(amount ~ (officer == "DEV-2"), data = claims)
dev2_test


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  amount by officer == "DEV-2"
W = 234586, p-value = 1.68e-14
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


The p-value is less than 0.0001, so DEV-2’s claims are systematically larger. The median tells the same story more plainly than the mean. A follow-up might compare the hospitals, bills and rates in DEV-2’s claims with the others.






Note



Tests like Wilcoxon’s, which work on ranks, are called non-parametric, because they do not assume the data follows a normal distribution. For audit data, which is rarely normal, they are often the safer choice. When both tests are run and they agree, as they usually do on large data, we can be confident. When they disagree, trust the rank test and look for extreme values.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.9 More than two groups
To compare settlement times across all six offices at once, rather than one office against the rest, use the Kruskal-Wallis test, the rank-based version for several groups.

kruskal.test(days_to_settle ~ office, data = claims)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  days_to_settle by office
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 86.219, df = 5, p-value < 2.2e-16


It says the offices differ, but not which ones. To find out, compare every pair with pairwise.wilcox.test(), which adjusts the p-values for the many comparisons, just as we learnt above.

pairwise.wilcox.test(claims$days_to_settle, claims$office, p.adjust.method = "holm")


    Pairwise comparisons using Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction 

data:  claims$days_to_settle and claims$office 

         Amarpur Belapur Chandpur Devgarh Fatehpur
Belapur  1.00    -       -        -       -       
Chandpur 4.4e-11 3.0e-15 -        -       -       
Devgarh  1.00    0.26    1.2e-08  -       -       
Fatehpur 1.00    1.00    1.4e-10  1.00    -       
Rampur   1.00    0.76    4.3e-09  1.00    1.00    

P value adjustment method: holm 


Every pair involving Chandpur has a tiny p-value, while the other pairs do not differ. (The classic test for comparing the means of several groups is analysis of variance, aov(). It is closely related to linear regression, which we meet in Chapter 39.)

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
section: 30.10 Does the data follow an expected pattern?
text:
30.10 Does the data follow an expected pattern?
Sometimes we know what pattern the data should follow, and want to test whether it does. This is the chi-square goodness-of-fit test. The number of claims from each office should be roughly in proportion to its staff strength.

staff <- c(Amarpur = 400, Belapur = 360, Chandpur = 340,
           Devgarh = 320, Fatehpur = 300, Rampur = 280)
observed <- table(claims$office)[names(staff)]
rbind(observed = observed, expected = round(sum(observed) * staff / sum(staff)))

         Amarpur Belapur Chandpur Devgarh Fatehpur Rampur
observed     587     527      523     485      445    433
expected     600     540      510     480      450    420

fit_test <- chisq.test(observed, p = staff / sum(staff))
fit_test


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  observed
X-squared = 1.436, df = 5, p-value = 0.9203


The p-value of 0.92 is large. The claims follow the staff strength well, and there is nothing to report. This, too, is a useful audit result. Not every test should find something, and a clean result lets us move on with confidence.
We have already used goodness-of-fit tests in this book without calling them that. The Benford chi-square in Section 32.5.1 and the digit tests in Chapter 33 compare observed counts of digits with the counts expected under a known pattern.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.11 Are two things related?
Do larger claims take longer to settle? cor.test() tests whether a correlation is different from zero. For skewed amounts, use Spearman’s rank correlation, method = "spearman".

cor_test <- cor.test(claims$amount, claims$days_to_settle, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
cor_test


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  claims$amount and claims$days_to_settle
S = 4.469e+09, p-value = 0.7061
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
        rho 
0.006888644 


The correlation is 0.007, practically zero, and not significant (p = 0.71). Settlement time does not depend on the claim amount here. If it did, say if large claims were settled much faster than small ones, it would be worth asking why.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
section: 30.12 Significant is not the same as important
text:
30.12 Significant is not the same as important
A p-value measures how sure we are that a difference is not chance. It does not measure how large or how important the difference is. Two points follow, and both matter in audit.
With very large data, tiny differences become significant. Two districts, each with two lakh claims, approve 85.0% and 85.4% of them.

prop.test(x = c(170000, 170800), n = c(200000, 200000))$p.value

[1] 0.0003741535


The difference is highly significant, but 0.4 percentage points is unlikely to matter to anyone. Always look at the size of the difference, the effect size, alongside the p-value. For rates, that is the difference in percentage points, and for amounts, the difference in rupees.
With small data, even large differences may not be significant. Two small offices, each with 12 claims, approve 10 and 7 of them, 83% against 58%. With counts this small, prop.test() warns that its approximation may be inaccurate, so we use the exact fisher.test() on the cross-table of approved and rejected claims.

small_offices <- matrix(c(10, 2,    # office 1: approved, rejected
                          7, 5),    # office 2: approved, rejected
                        nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
small_test <- fisher.test(small_offices)
small_test$p.value

[1] 0.3707094


A large difference, but far from significant (p = 0.37), because 12 claims are too few to tell. As in Section 30.3, the honest conclusion is “not proven”, not “no difference”.
How much data is enough? The function power.prop.test() answers this before the analysis. How many claims per office do we need to detect a difference between an approval rate of 86% and one of 95%, with an 80% chance of catching it (the power)?

power.prop.test(p1 = 0.86, p2 = 0.95, power = 0.80)


     Two-sample comparison of proportions power calculation 

              n = 165.4353
             p1 = 0.86
             p2 = 0.95
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


About 166 claims in each group. For smaller differences, many more are needed. power.t.test() does the same for comparing means.

TipAudit tip



Decide the test, and the limit for significance, before looking at the results. If we try test after test until one gives a small p-value, the result means nothing, because with enough attempts chance alone will oblige. Write down the question, the test and the limit in the audit plan, just as we fix the sample size in advance.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.14 A suggested workflow


State the question in plain words, such as “does this officer approve more claims than the others?”, and the null hypothesis it implies.

Look at the data first. Summarise by group and plot. A test should confirm what you see, not replace looking.

Choose the test from Table 30.2. Prefer rank tests for money amounts, and check that the chi-square test has enough data in each cell.

Fix the significance limit in advance, usually 5%.

When testing many groups, adjust the p-values with p.adjust().

Report the size of the difference with the p-value, in percentage points or rupees.

Treat a significant result as a lead, not a finding. Follow it up by examining the actual records, as with RAM-2’s approved claims.

Treat a non-significant result as “not proven”, especially on small samples, and say what the data could and could not show.







ImportantRemember




A test asks one question: is this difference larger than chance would usually produce?
The p-value is the chance of seeing a difference at least this large if nothing were unusual. Small means surprising.
A false alarm wastes effort and is unfair to the auditee; a miss is audit risk. The significance limit balances the two.
Many tests produce false alarms by chance. Adjust the p-values with p.adjust().
For skewed amounts, prefer rank-based tests like wilcox.test() and kruskal.test().
Significant does not mean important, and not significant does not mean no problem.

title: 30  Statistical Tests for Auditors
text:
30.15 Try it yourself
These exercises use the claims register claims of this chapter. Try each one in your console before you open the solution. Read each p-value as the chance of a difference at least this large if nothing were unusual.


A bigger sample with the same rate. In Section 30.3, 6 deviations in 60 claims were not enough to conclude that the rate was above 5%. Suppose the auditor had tested 100 claims and found 10 deviations, the same rate of 10%. Run the test again.






TipSolution






ex_binom <- binom.test(x = 10, n = 100, p = 0.05, alternative = "greater")
ex_binom$p.value

[1] 0.02818829


The p-value is now 0.028. If the true rate were 5%, a sample of 100 would show 10 or more deviations only about 2.8% of the time. This is below 0.05, so now we can conclude that the true rate is above 5%. The rate found is the same. Only the amount of evidence has changed.





Does Chandpur approve differently? Chandpur is slow to settle claims. Test whether its approval rate differs from the rest of the department, and give the size of the difference.






TipSolution






ex_chand <- claims$office == "Chandpur"
ex_chand_test <- prop.test(x = c(sum(claims$approved[ex_chand]), sum(claims$approved[!ex_chand])),
                           n = c(sum(ex_chand), sum(!ex_chand)))
round(100 * ex_chand_test$estimate, 1)

prop 1 prop 2 
  84.1   85.6 

ex_chand_test$p.value

[1] 0.4164917


Chandpur approved 84.1% of its claims, against 85.6% elsewhere, a difference of 1.5 percentage points. The p-value of 0.42 means that a difference at least this large would turn up about 42% of the time by chance alone. It is not significant, and the difference is small anyway. Nothing here points to a problem with Chandpur’s approvals. Its problem is speed.





The office or the desk? DEV-2’s claims are larger than everyone else’s. Is this true of Devgarh as a whole? Compare the two Devgarh officers directly, and give the difference in their median claims.






TipSolution






ex_dev <- claims |> filter(office == "Devgarh")
ex_dev |>
  summarise(claims = n(), median_amount = median(amount), .by = officer)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  officer claims median_amount
  <chr>    <int>         <dbl>
1 DEV-2      242         26020
2 DEV-1      243         17140

ex_dev_test <- wilcox.test(amount ~ officer, data = ex_dev)
ex_dev_test$p.value

[1] 2.613951e-08


DEV-2’s median claim is ₹26,020, against ₹17,140 for DEV-1. That is ₹8,880 more on a typical claim, a large effect. The p-value is less than 0.0001, so chance is a most unlikely explanation. Both desks work in the same office, so the difference lies with the desk, not the office. DEV-2’s claims are the ones to examine.





Is approval related to claim size? Put the claims into three bands, up to ₹10,000, above ₹10,000 and up to ₹30,000, and above ₹30,000. Test whether the approval rate depends on the band.






TipSolution






ex_band <- cut(claims$amount, c(0, 10000, 30000, Inf),
               labels = c("Up to 10,000", "10,000 to 30,000", "Above 30,000"))
ex_band_table <- table(ex_band, claims$approved)
round(prop.table(ex_band_table, 1), 3)


ex_band            FALSE  TRUE
  Up to 10,000     0.170 0.830
  10,000 to 30,000 0.140 0.860
  Above 30,000     0.138 0.862

ex_band_test <- chisq.test(ex_band_table)
ex_band_test


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  ex_band_table
X-squared = 3.9312, df = 2, p-value = 0.1401


Small claims are approved a little less often, 83% against about 86% for the larger bands. The p-value is 0.14. A pattern at least this strong would arise about 14% of the time even if the band made no difference, so it is not significant. With 3,000 claims and a difference of only a few percentage points, there is nothing here to pursue.





Which office is slow? Test each office’s settlement times against all the other offices with wilcox.test(). Collect the results with tidy(), add the difference in median days, and adjust the p-values with the Holm method.






TipSolution






ex_slow <- map(sort(unique(claims$office)), \(o) {
  mine <- claims$office == o
  wilcox.test(claims$days_to_settle[mine], claims$days_to_settle[!mine]) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(office = o,
           median_days = median(claims$days_to_settle[mine]),
           median_others = median(claims$days_to_settle[!mine]),
           .before = 1)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(p_adjusted = p.adjust(p.value, method = "holm")) |>
  select(office, median_days, median_others, p.value, p_adjusted) |>
  arrange(p.value)

ex_slow |> mutate(across(c(p.value, p_adjusted), \(x) signif(x, 2)))

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  office   median_days median_others  p.value p_adjusted
  <chr>          <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Chandpur          25            20 2.5 e-19    1.5e-18
2 Belapur           19            21 9.60e- 5    4.8e- 4
3 Fatehpur          19            20 4.2 e- 2    1.7e- 1
4 Amarpur           20            20 8.4 e- 2    2.5e- 1
5 Rampur            20            20 3.2 e- 1    6.3e- 1
6 Devgarh           20            20 6.6 e- 1    6.6e- 1


Chandpur heads the list. Its median is 25 days against 20 elsewhere, with an adjusted p-value of less than 0.0001. Belapur is also significant after adjustment, but it is faster, by 2 days. Part of this is because the “others” include slow Chandpur, which raises their median. Such a small gain in speed is not a concern in itself. Fatehpur has a raw p-value of 0.042, below 0.05, but after adjustment it is 0.17. Without the adjustment we would have raised a false alarm about Fatehpur.

title: Part V: Forensic Tests
text:
This part brings together the tests that auditors run again and again on transaction data. Check the records against the rules. Look for amounts that have been made up. Find duplicates, exact and fuzzy, and link records of the same person across lists. Find gaps in numbered sequences. Rebuild a process from a system’s audit trail and see whether its steps were followed.
Each test produces a list of exceptions. An exception is a lead, to be verified against the records. It is not yet a finding.
The chapters can be read in any order, once Parts I and II are done.


31  Rule-Based Validation
Checking data against a rule book of rates, limits and conditions.


32  Benford Analysis
Benford’s Law for first and second digits.


33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
Largest subsets, round numbers, and amounts just below limits.


34  Duplicate Detection
Payments and bills entered twice, exactly or nearly.


35  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
Matching names by spelling and by sound.


36  Record Linkage
Finding the same person in two lists with no common ID.


37  Gaps in Sequences
Missing cheque, receipt and voucher numbers, and missing dates.


38  Process Mining
Checking from the audit trail whether a process was followed.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
text:
31.1 Our data, a month’s pay bill
Much of audit is checking whether things were done by the rules. Pay must be within the scale of the post. Dearness allowance must be at the rate in force. Nobody may be paid after retirement. A bill must add up. Every one of these is a rule that can be written down precisely, and every rule that can be written down precisely can be checked by R, on every record, in seconds.
We have already checked many such rules in this book, one at a time, with filter(). That works, but as the number of rules grows, a pile of separate filter() statements becomes hard to keep track of. Which rules were checked? On which data? How many records failed each? Was anything missed?
In this chapter we learn to keep the rules together as a rule book, apply the whole rule book to the data in one step, and get a summary of every rule with the failing records listed. The package validate does this. The rule book can be kept in a spreadsheet, maintained by the audit team, with the source of each rule recorded against it. At the end we also meet pointblank, which produces a ready report of the results.
Prerequisites
Both packages are on CRAN, and are installed with install.packages(c("validate", "pointblank")).
We audit the pay bill of a department for March 2025. There are two tables.
The rules of the game, simplified from the 7th Central Pay Commission rules, are these.
The code creates the two tables, and plants errors of each kind.
Code to create the employee master and the pay billset.seed(2025)
pay_matrix <- tibble(
  level   = 1:14,
  min_pay = c(18000, 19900, 21700, 25500, 29200, 35400, 44900, 47600, 53100, 56100,
              67700, 78800, 123100, 144200),
  max_pay = c(56900, 63200, 69100, 81100, 92300, 112400, 142400, 151100, 167800, 177500,
              208700, 209200, 215900, 218200)
)
n <- 1200
make_pan <- function(k) {
  paste0(map_chr(1:k, \(i) paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = "")), "P",
         sample(LETTERS, k, TRUE), sprintf("%04d", sample(1:9999, k, TRUE)), sample(LETTERS, k, TRUE))
}
master <- tibble(
  emp_id = sprintf("E%05d", 1:n),
  dob    = as.Date("1966-01-01") + sample(0:(365 * 37), n, TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(doj = pmin(dob + round(365.25 * runif(n, 21, 35)), as.Date("2024-12-01")),
         level = sample(1:14, n, TRUE, prob = c(8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 9, 10, 8, 7, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3)),
         city_class = sample(c("X", "Y", "Z"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3)),
         pension_scheme = if_else(doj >= as.Date("2004-01-01"), "NPS", "GPF"),
         pan = make_pan(n),
         ifsc = paste0(sample(c("SBIN", "PUNB", "CNRB", "UBIN", "BARB"), n, TRUE), "0",
                       sprintf("%06d", sample(1:999999, n, TRUE))),
         account_no = sprintf("%011.0f", runif(n, 1e10, 9.99e10)))

# Planted. Four employees who retired in 2024 are still in the master
retired <- sample(n, 4)
master$dob[retired] <- as.Date(c("1964-03-15", "1964-07-01", "1964-09-20", "1964-11-05"))

bill <- master |>
  left_join(pay_matrix, by = "level") |>
  mutate(basic_pay = round(min_pay + (max_pay - min_pay) * runif(n()) ^ 1.5, -2))

pick <- function(k, from = seq_len(nrow(bill))) sample(from, k)
# Planted. Basic pay above the maximum, or below the minimum, of the level
r_hi <- pick(3); bill$basic_pay[r_hi] <- bill$max_pay[r_hi] + c(5000, 12000, 30000)
r_lo <- pick(1); bill$basic_pay[r_lo] <- bill$min_pay[r_lo] - 2000

bill <- bill |>
  mutate(da  = round(0.53 * basic_pay),
         hra = round(c(X = 0.30, Y = 0.20, Z = 0.10)[city_class] * basic_pay),
         ta  = case_when(level >= 9 ~ 7200, level >= 3 ~ 3600, TRUE ~ 1800))

# Planted. DA paid at 55% instead of 53%
r_da <- pick(6); bill$da[r_da] <- round(0.55 * bill$basic_pay[r_da])
# Planted. HRA at the X-class rate for employees posted in Z-class cities
r_hra <- pick(8, which(bill$city_class == "Z")); bill$hra[r_hra] <- round(0.30 * bill$basic_pay[r_hra])

bill <- bill |>
  mutate(gross = basic_pay + da + hra + ta,
         pension_contrib = if_else(pension_scheme == "NPS", round(0.10 * (basic_pay + da)),
                                   round(0.08 * basic_pay)),
         income_tax = round(pmax(0, gross - 60000) * 0.12),
         net_pay = gross - pension_contrib - income_tax)

# Planted. Gross pay with TA added twice
r_gross <- pick(2); bill$gross[r_gross] <- bill$gross[r_gross] + bill$ta[r_gross]
bill$net_pay[r_gross] <- bill$net_pay[r_gross] + bill$ta[r_gross]
# Planted. Post-2004 entrants shown under GPF in the master
r_gpf <- pick(3, which(master$pension_scheme == "NPS")); master$pension_scheme[r_gpf] <- "GPF"
# Planted. PAN in an invalid format, and IFSC missing
r_pan <- pick(5); master$pan[r_pan] <- c("ABCDE1234", "AAAPX1234", "ABCP12345K", "abcpk1234q", "AB CPK1234Q")
r_ifsc <- pick(2); master$ifsc[r_ifsc] <- NA
# Planted. Two pairs of employees paid into the same account
r_acc <- pick(4); master$account_no[r_acc[3:4]] <- master$account_no[r_acc[1:2]]

bill <- bill |>
  select(emp_id, level, city_class, basic_pay, da, hra, ta, gross,
         pension_contrib, income_tax, net_pay)

# Planted. Three employees in the bill who are not in the master
strangers <- bill |> slice_sample(n = 3) |> mutate(emp_id = sprintf("E9%04d", 1:3))
bill <- bind_rows(bill, strangers)

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
text:
master, the employee master: date of birth, date of joining, pay level, city class of the place of posting, pension scheme, PAN, bank IFSC and account number.

bill, the pay bill: for each employee paid, the basic pay, dearness allowance (DA), house rent allowance (HRA), transport allowance (TA), gross pay, deductions and net pay.



Basic pay must lie within the range of the employee’s level in the pay matrix.
DA is 53% of basic pay, the rate in force for our example.
HRA is 30%, 20% or 10% of basic pay, for cities of class X, Y and Z.
Gross pay is basic pay plus DA, HRA and TA, and net pay is gross pay less deductions.
An employee retires on the last day of the month in which he or she attains 60 years. (A person attains an age on the day before the birthday, so someone born on the 1st of a month retires at the end of the previous month.)
Employees who joined on or after 1 January 2004 are in the National Pension System (NPS); earlier entrants are in the General Provident Fund (GPF) scheme.
PAN must be in the valid format (Section 21.10), and IFSC must be present and valid.
No two employees may be paid into the same bank account.
Everyone in the bill must be in the employee master.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
section: 31.2 The rules, one filter() at a time
text:
31.2 The rules, one filter() at a time
Before using a package, let us see the plain way, which we already know. To find employees whose DA is not at 53%, allowing a rupee for rounding:

bill |> filter(abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) > 1) |> select(emp_id, basic_pay, da)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  emp_id basic_pay    da
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1 E00295     43800 24090
2 E00408     20300 11165
3 E00755     27600 15180
4 E00936     38400 21120
5 E01025    141100 77605
6 E01171     52400 28820


This works perfectly for one rule. But we have more than a dozen rules, on two tables. Writing and re-running a dozen such statements, and keeping a record of which passed and which failed, quickly gets untidy. And a rule that silently returns no rows looks the same as a rule that was never run, or one that failed because a column name was mistyped. What we want is to treat the rules as data, kept together, applied together, and reported together.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
text:
31.3 A rule book with validator()

First, we bring together the columns the rules need. The bill has the pay figures, the master has the dates and identifiers, and the pay matrix has the limits of each level. We also work out each employee’s date of retirement, as described above, with lubridate (Chapter 18).

pay_check <- bill |>
  left_join(master |> select(-level, -city_class), by = "emp_id") |>
  left_join(pay_matrix, by = "level") |>
  mutate(retirement_date = rollforward(dob %m+% years(60) - days(1)))

rollforward() moves a date to the last day of its month. So the date of retirement is the last day of the month in which the employee attains 60, that is, the day before the 60th birthday.
Now the rule book. validator() takes the rules, each written as an R expression that is TRUE when the rule is met. Each rule gets a short name.

pay_rules <- validator(
  # identity and completeness
  id_unique      = is_unique(emp_id),
  in_master      = !is.na(dob),
  ifsc_present   = !is.na(ifsc),
  # pay within the level, and the allowances at the right rates
  pay_in_range   = basic_pay >= min_pay & basic_pay <= max_pay,
  da_rate        = abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) <= 1,
  hra_rate       = abs(hra - ifelse(city_class == "X", 0.30,
                                    ifelse(city_class == "Y", 0.20, 0.10)) * basic_pay) <= 1,
  # the bill adds up
  gross_total    = gross == basic_pay + da + hra + ta,
  net_total      = net_pay == gross - pension_contrib - income_tax,
  # service conditions
  not_retired    = retirement_date >= as.Date("2025-03-31"),
  pension_scheme = (doj >= as.Date("2004-01-01") & pension_scheme == "NPS") |
                   (doj <  as.Date("2004-01-01") & pension_scheme == "GPF"),
  # identifiers
  pan_format     = grepl("^[A-Z]{3}[PCHFATBLJG][A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$", pan),
  account_unique = is_unique(account_no)
)
pay_rules

Object of class 'validator' with 12 elements:
 id_unique     : is_unique(emp_id)
 in_master     : !is.na(dob)
 ifsc_present  : !is.na(ifsc)
 pay_in_range  : basic_pay >= min_pay & basic_pay <= max_pay
 da_rate       : abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) <= 1
 hra_rate      : abs(hra - ifelse(city_class == "X", 0.3, ifelse(city_class == "Y", 0.2, 0.1)) * basic_pay) <= 1
 gross_total   : gross == basic_pay + da + hra + ta
 net_total     : net_pay == gross - pension_contrib - income_tax
 not_retired   : retirement_date >= as.Date("2025-03-31")
 pension_scheme: (doj >= as.Date("2004-01-01") & pension_scheme == "NPS") | (doj < as.Date("2004-01-01") & pension_scheme == "GPF")
 pan_format    : grepl("^[A-Z]{3}[PCHFATBLJG][A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$", pan)
 account_unique: is_unique(account_no)


A few points about the rules.


is_unique() comes from validate. It checks that each value occurs only once in the column.
Employees not in the master get NA for every master column after the left join, so !is.na(dob) is TRUE only for those found in the master.
Amounts computed with percentages can differ by a rupee because of rounding, so the rate rules allow a difference of up to ₹1 (Chapter 1 warned against comparing computed decimals with ==).
The PAN pattern requires the fourth character to be one of the holder types (P for an individual, C for a company, and so on), as in Section 21.10.
validate accepts only certain kinds of expressions as rules: comparisons, logical operators like & and |, and functions returning TRUE or FALSE. A rule written with ifelse() is ignored with a warning, so the pension scheme rule is written with & and |: “joined on or after 2004 and in NPS, or joined before 2004 and in GPF”.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
section: 31.4 Confronting the data with the rules
text:
31.4 Confronting the data with the rules
confront() applies every rule to the data, and summary() reports the result of each.

1                                                                                                   is_unique(emp_id)

3                                                                                                        !is.na(ifsc)
4                                                        basic_pay - min_pay >= -1e-08 & basic_pay - max_pay <= 1e-08
5                                                                                     abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) <= 1
6                     abs(hra - ifelse(city_class == "X", 0.3, ifelse(city_class == "Y", 0.2, 0.1)) * basic_pay) <= 1
7                                                                   abs(gross - (basic_pay + da + hra + ta)) <= 1e-08

12                                                                                              is_unique(account_no)


Each row is one rule. items is the number of records checked, passes and fails the number that met or broke the rule, and nNA the number where the rule could not be decided because a value was missing. error and warning say whether R could evaluate the rule at all, which catches mistyped column names. expression shows the rule as validate understood it. Notice that validate has rewritten gross == ... with a tiny tolerance, since exact equality of decimals is unsafe.
This one table is the backbone of the audit working paper. Every rule is listed, run or not, passed or not. Let us read it.


in_master fails for 3 records, the employees paid but not in the master.

pay_in_range fails for 4, and da_rate and hra_rate for 6 and 8.

not_retired fails for 4, employees paid after their retirement, and pension_scheme for 3.

not_retired and pension_scheme also show nNA of 3. These are the employees missing from the master, for whom the dates are empty, so the rules could not be decided.

ifsc_present and pan_format fail for 5 and 8 records, including those same missing employees. !is.na() and grepl() return FALSE, not NA, for a missing value, so these rules count a missing value as a failure. How a rule treats missing values depends on how it is written, so read the counts with that in mind.

plot() shows the same as a chart, which is useful for a quick view of many rules.

plot(results)



Results of each rule









Caution



A rule with nNA greater than zero has not been passed by those records, only left undecided. Never count them as passes. Find out why the values are missing, and decide whether that is a finding in itself, as it is here.

31.5 The failing records
To examine the failures, violating() returns the rows of the data that break any of the given rules. Let us take the DA and HRA rules.

violating(pay_check, results[c("da_rate", "hra_rate")]) |>
  select(emp_id, city_class, basic_pay, da, hra) |>
  mutate(da_pct = round(100 * da / basic_pay, 1), hra_pct = round(100 * hra / basic_pay, 1))

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
text:
31.6 Valuing the findings
Each failure is checked against the records before it becomes an observation. For the money involved, we compute the excess paid under each rule.

excess <- pay_check |>
  mutate(
    hra_due = round(c(X = 0.30, Y = 0.20, Z = 0.10)[city_class] * basic_pay),
    excess_da  = pmax(0, da - round(0.53 * basic_pay)),
    excess_hra = pmax(0, hra - hra_due),
    paid_after_retirement = if_else(!is.na(retirement_date) & retirement_date < as.Date("2025-03-31"),
                                    net_pay, 0),
    paid_not_in_master = if_else(is.na(dob), net_pay, 0)
  ) |>
  summarise(across(c(excess_da, excess_hra, paid_after_retirement, paid_not_in_master), sum))
excess

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  excess_da excess_hra paid_after_retirement paid_not_in_master
      <dbl>      <dbl>                 <dbl>              <dbl>
1      6472     173260                579338             366757


In one month’s pay bill, about ₹11.3 lakh is at stake, before counting the pay above the scale, the doubtful accounts and the PAN errors. Since pay bills repeat every month, the annual effect of the same errors would be about twelve times as much, which is why such checks are worth running every month and not once a year.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
section: 31.7 Keeping the rule book in a spreadsheet
text:
31.7 Keeping the rule book in a spreadsheet
Rules written in R code are fine for the analyst who wrote them. An audit team, however, needs rules that anyone can read, review and keep up to date, along with the source of each rule, so that each failure can be traced to the order it breaks. validate can read the rules from a data frame, with columns rule, name, label and description. Such a table can be kept in Excel and read with readxl::read_excel() (Chapter 10).

rule_book <- tribble(
  ~name,          ~label,                              ~rule,                                                  ~description,
  "da_rate",      "DA at the rate in force",           "abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) <= 1",                       "DA order in force for March 2025: 53% of basic pay",
  "pay_in_range", "Basic pay within the level",        "basic_pay >= min_pay & basic_pay <= max_pay",           "Pay matrix, 7th CPC",
  "not_retired",  "Not paid after superannuation",     "retirement_date >= as.Date('2025-03-31')",              "Superannuation at the end of the month of attaining 60",
  "in_master",    "Paid employee exists in master",    "!is.na(dob)",                                           "Internal control: payment only to verified employees",
  "pan_format",   "PAN in valid format",               "grepl('^[A-Z]{3}[PCHFATBLJG][A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$', pan)", "Income Tax Act; needed for TDS"
)

book_rules <- validator(.data = rule_book)
book_rules

Object of class 'validator' with 5 elements:
 da_rate [DA at the rate in force]          : abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) <= 1
 pay_in_range [Basic pay within the level]  : basic_pay >= min_pay & basic_pay <= max_pay
 not_retired [Not paid after superannuation]: retirement_date >= as.Date("2025-03-31")
 in_master [Paid employee exists in master] : !is.na(dob)
 pan_format [PAN in valid format]           : grepl("^[A-Z]{3}[PCHFATBLJG][A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$", pan)


The labels and descriptions travel with the rules, so the summary can be joined back to the rule book to produce a readable table for the working papers.

summary(confront(pay_check, book_rules)) |>
  left_join(rule_book |> select(name, label, description), by = "name") |>
  select(label, items, passes, fails, nNA, description)

TipAudit tip



Build one rule book for each recurring audit area, such as pay bills, pension, contracts or a scheme, and keep it with the audit programme. Each year, update the rates and limits, add the rules suggested by last year’s findings, and re-run the whole book on the new data. Over time, the rule book becomes the team’s institutional memory, and new members can see at once what is checked and why.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
text:
31.8 A ready report with pointblank
The package pointblank does a similar job with a different style. Instead of a rule book, we build an agent, give it a series of validation steps, and let it interrogate the data. Its strength is the report it produces, a formatted table of every step with the share of records that passed, which can be shared directly.

library(pointblank)

agent <- create_agent(tbl = pay_check, tbl_name = "Pay bill, March 2025",
                      label = "Pay bill checks") |>
  rows_distinct(columns = vars(emp_id)) |>
  col_vals_not_null(columns = vars(ifsc)) |>
  col_vals_between(columns = vars(basic_pay), left = vars(min_pay), right = vars(max_pay)) |>
  col_vals_expr(expr = expr(abs(da - 0.53 * basic_pay) <= 1)) |>
  col_vals_regex(columns = vars(pan), regex = "^[A-Z]{3}[PCHFATBLJG][A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$") |>
  col_vals_gte(columns = vars(retirement_date), value = as.Date("2025-03-31")) |>
  interrogate()

Each row is a step, with the number of records tested, and the number and share that passed and failed. Missing values count as failures in pointblank by default (the argument na_pass changes this), which is why the steps involving master columns show a few more failures than validate did. get_sundered_data() splits the data into the rows that passed every step and those that failed at least one.

failed_rows <- get_sundered_data(agent, type = "fail")
nrow(failed_rows)

[1] 24


pointblank can also set action levels, such as a warning if more than 1% of records fail a step, and stopping a process if more than 5% do. This is useful when the same checks are run every month on data received from a department, as an early warning that something has gone wrong with the data itself.






Note



Which package to use? validate suits audit work where the rule book itself is the main product: rules kept as data, with labels and sources, applied to many datasets. pointblank suits repeated checks on incoming data with a polished report. Both are good, and they can be used together, as here.

title: 31  Rule-Based Validation
text:
31.9 A suggested workflow


Collect the rules from the acts, rules, orders and manuals governing the area, and note the source of each.

Write them as a rule book, in a spreadsheet, with a name, label, rule and description for each.

Prepare the data: join the tables the rules need, and compute derived values like the date of retirement.

Confront the data with the rule book, and read the summary, rule by rule. Check rules with errors, warnings or missing values first.

List the failing records with violating(), and examine them against the documents.

Value the findings, and project the effect over the year where the data repeats.

Report the summary table with the rule sources, or a pointblank report.

Maintain the rule book: update rates, and add rules from new findings.







ImportantRemember




Many audit checks are rules that can be written exactly. Keep them together as a rule book, not as scattered filters.

validator() holds the rules, confront() applies them, summary() reports every rule, and violating() lists the failing records.
Records with missing values are undecided, not passed.
Keep the rule book in a spreadsheet, with the source of each rule, so that the team can review and update it.
A rule failure is a lead to be verified against documents, like every other analytic finding.

31.10 Try it yourself
These exercises use the pay bill data of this chapter, mainly pay_check, pay_rules, results and rule_book. Try each one in your console before you open the solution.


Pay outside the scale. Use plain filter() to list the employees whose basic pay is above the maximum or below the minimum of their level. Show the level, the basic pay and both limits.

  filter(basic_pay > max_pay | basic_pay < min_pay) |>
  select(emp_id, level, basic_pay, min_pay, max_pay)

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.1 A short history
A public works division passes thousands of bills in a year. Most of the amounts are genuine. But some may be made up. A contractor may inflate a bill. An official may split one large purchase into many small bills, each just below the limit that needs a higher sanction. A clerk may invent a few claims for medical reimbursement. How can an auditor find such amounts among thousands of vouchers, without reading every one?
Benford’s Law gives a quick first answer. It tells us how often each digit (1, 2, 3 and so on) should appear as the first digit of numbers in many real-life datasets. Surprisingly, the digits do not appear equally often. Numbers starting with 1 are far more common than numbers starting with 9, as shown in Figure 32.4. People who make up numbers do not know this. So invented amounts usually leave a mark on the digit pattern, and the analysis can point to it.
The same idea works wherever figures may be adjusted to meet a rule. For instance, eligibility for government assistance often depends on an income below a certain level. Declared incomes may be pushed just below that level. Such figures do not follow the pattern of Benford’s Law, and this is exactly what the analysis can detect.
In this chapter we will first learn the law, where it came from, and the tests built on it. Then we will run the tests in R with the package benford.analysis. We will use it on the payment vouchers of an imaginary works division, where two kinds of unusual amounts are planted. We will then compare ten district offices, one of which has made-up bills. Finally, we will see data on which the law should not be used at all.
The Law is named after physicist Frank Benford, who studied it in 1938, in a paper titled The Law of Anomalous Numbers.1 However, it had been noticed more than five decades earlier by the astronomer Simon Newcomb. Newcomb observed that the first pages of books of logarithm tables were more worn out than the later pages. He published a two-page note titled Note on the Frequency of Use of the Different Digits in Natural Numbers in 1881.2
Many researchers continued to work on the law and its extensions. But it took several decades to find a truly practical use for it. In the 1990s, Dr. Mark J. Nigrini, a professor of accounting, applied the law to fraud detection. He studied many data sources, like sales figures, insurance claims and expense reimbursements. He showed how the law could detect overstatement and understatement of financial figures. His work established the law as a practical tool for fraud examiners and auditors.
His reasoning, in simple words, is this. If somebody tries to falsify, say, their tax return, they will have to invent some numbers. When people invent numbers, they tend to use too many numbers starting with middle digits like 5, 6 and 7. They use too few starting with 1.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
section: 32.2 Where can Benford analysis help an auditor?
text:
32.2 Where can Benford analysis help an auditor?


Expense and reimbursement claims, such as travel, medical or contingent bills, where claimants may invent amounts.

Vendor payments and invoices, to find made-up invoices or unusual groups of amounts, such as bills split to stay below a limit.

Revenue and tax data, such as declared incomes or turnover, where figures may be understated.

Comparing units. Running the test separately for each office, vendor or employee, and looking for the ones that stand out.

Checking data quality. Unexpected digit patterns can also reveal data entry errors and duplicated records. They can also show data that has been rounded, or generated by a system rather than recorded from real transactions.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.3 Benford’s Law, properties and extensions

32.3.1 Law of first digit
When thinking about the chance of each digit appearing in the first position, our first guess may be one in nine for each digit. That is, a uniform distribution. This idea was challenged by the Canadian-American astronomer Simon Newcomb in 1881. While turning the pages of a book of logarithm tables, he noticed a curious pattern. The first pages were much more worn out than the later ones.
Later, Frank Benford analysed 20 very different datasets. They included the areas of rivers, the weights of chemical compounds, population figures and more. He found that the chance of a digit appearing first falls steadily from 1 to 9. The digit 1 appears first most often, and the digit 9 least often.
Mathematically, Benford’s Law, or the Law of first digits, states that the probability of a digit \(d\) being the first digit is given by Equation 32.1.
\[
P(d) = \log_{10}\left(1 + \frac{1}{d}\right), \qquad d = 1, 2, \ldots, 9
\tag{32.1}\]
These probabilities are plotted in Figure 32.4. About 30% of numbers should start with 1, and less than 5% with 9.







Figure 32.4: Diminishing probabilities of first digits under Benford’s Law




To test the proposed law, Benford analysed 20 different datasets. He observed that nearly all of them follow the distribution in Equation 32.1.
Let us also check whether the law holds on six different datasets, which come with the R package benford.analysis. We will discuss the package in detail in Section 32.6. The six datasets are listed in Table 32.1.

32.3.2 Scale invariance
In 1961, Roger Pinkham showed that the law is scale invariant.3 This means that the law does not depend on the unit of measurement. If it holds for amounts in rupees, it also holds when the same amounts are converted to dollars. If it holds for lengths in kilometres, it also holds for the same lengths in miles.
Let us check this on one of the six datasets, census.2009. It contains the population of towns and cities of the United States, as of July 2009. The left plot of Figure 32.6 shows the first digits of the original data. For the right plot, we multiply every figure by the same random positive number, and test again.


















Figure 32.6: First Digit Analysis on US Census 2009 data (Left) and Scaled Data (Right)


The law holds in both cases. Scale invariance is an important practical property. It means that the test can be applied to amounts in any currency, without adjustment.

32.3.3 First two digits
Nigrini’s work led many scholars and practitioners to use Benford’s Law as a forensic accounting and auditing tool. In 1995, Theodore P. Hill gave a rigorous mathematical explanation of why the law holds.4 His work also covers the significant-digit law. It describes the expected frequencies not only of the first digit, but also of the second and later digits, and of combinations of digits.
The probability of a digit \(d\) appearing in the second position is given by Equation 32.2.
\[
P(d) = \sum_{k = 1}^{9}\log_{10}\left(1 + \frac{1}{10k + d}\right), \qquad d = 0, 1, \ldots, 9
\tag{32.2}\]
Here, \(k\) runs over all possible first digits. The second digits are much closer to uniform than the first digits. The digit 0 appears second about 12% of the time, and 9 about 8.5% of the time.
For the first two digits together, such as 10, 11, …, 99, the probability is simply \(\log_{10}(1 + 1/n)\), where \(n\) is the two-digit number. These probabilities are shown in Table 32.3. Each cell gives the probability of a number starting with a particular pair of digits. The first digit is in the rows and the second digit in the columns. The row totals give back the probabilities of the first digit alone. For example, the probability of a number starting with 10 is the highest, at 4.14%.

The first-two digits test is the one most used by auditors. It is much more focused than the first digit test. A spike at a particular pair, say 49, can point directly to a group of suspicious amounts, such as amounts kept just below ₹50,000. We can verify that the law of first two digits holds for the census.2009 data in Figure 32.7.







Figure 32.7: Law holds for first two digits as well





32.3.4 Second order test
Nigrini and Miller, in 2009,5 introduced another test based on Benford’s Law. The test states the following.

Let \(x_1\), …, \(x_N\) be a data set comprising \(N\) observations, and let \(y_1\), …, \(y_N\) be the observations \(x_i\)’s in ascending order. Then, for many natural data sets, and for large \(N\), the digits of the differences between adjacent observations \(y_{i+1} - y_i\) is close to Benford’s Law. Large deviations from Benford’s Law indicate an anomaly that should be investigated.

So the steps are these.

Sort the data from smallest to largest.
Calculate the \(N-1\) differences between consecutive numbers.
Apply Benford’s Law to these differences.

Nigrini showed that the first digits of these differences are expected to follow Benford’s Law closely. He used four different datasets. He showed that this test can detect three things. These are (i) anomalies in the data, (ii) rounding of the data, and (iii) fake or statistically generated data used in place of actual transactions. A big advantage of this test is that it works even on data which does not itself follow Benford’s Law.

32.3.5 Summation test
The summation test looks for excessively large numbers in a dataset. It was also proposed by Nigrini.6 It rests on a simple fact. In data following Benford’s Law, the sum of all numbers starting with each pair of first two digits (10, 11, 12, … 99) should be about the same. So each of the 90 groups should account for about 1/90, or 1.1%, of the total. A spike in one group shows that it contains some very large single numbers, or many numbers of the same large size.
The last-two digits test and the number duplication test, which also come from Nigrini’s work, are covered in Chapter 33.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.4 When does Benford’s Law apply?
Benford’s Law does not apply to every set of numbers. Before running the test, check that the data is of the right kind. The law may not hold in the following circumstances.


Assigned numbers. Cheque numbers, invoice numbers, telephone numbers, pin codes and account numbers are labels, not measurements.

Numbers influenced by human choice or rules. ATM withdrawals in multiples of ₹500, prices like ₹99, or fixed rates of a scheme.

Numbers with a minimum or maximum. Passengers in a bus, hourly wage rates, or amounts within a narrow fixed range.

Too few records. With only a few hundred numbers, chance variations are large. The more data, the better. For the first-two digits test, a thousand or more records are preferable.

In general, the law fits best when the data describes the sizes of similar things, like amounts of payments or populations of towns. It should also span several orders of magnitude (from hundreds to lakhs, say), and have more small values than large ones. We will see data that fails these conditions in Section 32.9.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.5 Goodness of fit metrics
In Table 32.2 we saw that digit frequencies largely followed Benford’s Law in five of the six datasets. But how close is close enough? To judge how well the actual distribution fits the expected one, we use some measures. Three are commonly used.

32.5.1 Chi-square statistic
The first measure is the chi-square statistic. It tests the whole distribution of first digits (or first two digits) at once, against the frequencies expected under Benford’s Law. The null hypothesis is that the digits follow Benford’s Law. The formula is given in Equation 32.3.
\[
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
\tag{32.3}\]
where


\(O_i\) is the observed count of the i-th digit, or pair of digits,

\(E_i\) is the count expected under Benford’s Law, and

\(K\) is 9 for the first digit test and 90 for the first-two digits test.

The calculated statistic is compared with a critical value from the chi-square distribution7. The degrees of freedom are one less than the number of digit groups. That is, 8 for the first digit test and 89 for the first-two digits test. The critical values are given in Table 32.4.



Table 32.4: Critical values for Chi-Square Test












First Digit Test


First-Two Digits Test



Significance level
8 degrees of freedom

If the calculated statistic is above the critical value, we reject the null hypothesis. We then conclude that the data does not conform to Benford’s Law.
For example, the chi-square statistic for the first digits of the census.2009 data is 17.524. This is above the 5% critical value of 15.507, but just below the 2.5% critical value of 17.535. So, at the usual 5% level of significance, the test says that the data does not conform. At the 2.5% level, it does.






WarningCaution



The chi-square test becomes more and more sensitive as the number of records grows. With tens of thousands of records, even a tiny, unimportant deviation becomes “statistically significant”. The census data has 19,509 records, and its digits follow Benford’s Law very closely, as Figure 32.6 shows. Yet the chi-square test rejects it at the 5% level. For this reason, Nigrini recommends relying mainly on the MAD for large datasets. Treat the chi-square only as a supporting measure.



32.5.2 Z-statistic
The Z-statistic checks each digit separately. It tells whether the share of one particular digit differs significantly from what Benford’s Law expects. It takes into account the size of the difference, the number of records and the expected share. The formula is given in Equation 32.4.
\[
Z = \frac{\lvert p - p_0\rvert - \frac{1}{2n}}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}
\tag{32.4}\]
where


\(p\) is the observed proportion of the digit in the data,

\(p_0\) is the proportion expected under Benford’s Law, and

\(n\) is the number of records.

The term \(\frac{1}{2n}\) in the numerator is a continuity correction. It is used only when it is smaller than \(\lvert p - p_0\rvert\). If the value of Z exceeds 1.96, the share of that digit differs significantly from Benford’s Law at the 5% level. For the 1% and 10% levels, the critical values are 2.576 and 1.645 respectively. Like the chi-square, the Z-statistic also becomes very sensitive with large data.

32.5.3 Mean absolute deviation
The Mean Absolute Deviation, or MAD, is the average of the absolute differences between the actual and expected proportions of the digits. Its formula is given in Equation 32.5.
\[
MAD = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{i=1}^{K} \lvert AP_i - EP_i \rvert
\tag{32.5}\]
Here \(AP_i\) and \(EP_i\) are the actual and expected proportions of the i-th digit group. \(K\) is the number of groups (9 for the first digit, 90 for the first two digits).
The MAD does not depend on the number of records, which is why it is preferred for large data. There is no statistical table of critical values for it. Instead, Mark Nigrini has proposed the ranges in Table 32.5, based on his study of many real datasets. These are also the ranges used by the benford.analysis package.

Notice that the ranges for the first-two digits are much smaller. With 90 groups instead of 9, each expected proportion is small, and so are the differences.

32.5.4 The mantissa
There is one more way to check conformity. The mantissa of a number is the fractional part of its logarithm (base 10). For example, \(\log_{10}(250) = 2.398\), so its mantissa is \(0.398\). If the data follows Benford’s Law, the mantissas are spread evenly between 0 and 1. Their summary statistics should then be close to those shown in Table 32.6, as suggested by Mark Nigrini.


Table 32.6: Ideal statistics of mantissas, for data that follows Benford’s Law

The benford.analysis package reports these mantissa statistics as part of its results.






ImportantBenford’s Law is a signal, not a proof



Benford analysis is a powerful way to uncover possible irregularities in a dataset. But a deviation from the law does not always mean fraud. Deviations can also come from data entry errors. They can come from the way a process works, such as fixed fees or rates, or from mixing data from different sources. A deviation is a signal to investigate further, not a finding.
Conversely, data that follows Benford’s Law is not proof of honesty. A small fraud hidden in a large dataset will hardly change the overall digit frequencies. And a fraudster who knows about the law could fabricate numbers that follow it.
So when the analysis points to an unusual digit pattern, dig deeper. Look at the records behind it, cross-check them with other data, verify the documents, and speak with the people responsible. Only this further work can separate a harmless quirk from a serious problem.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.6 Practical approach in R
As already stated, we will use the package benford.analysis for Benford analysis in R. Let us load it.

library(benford.analysis)

This package provides tools that make it easier to validate data using Benford’s Law. It has been developed by Carlos Cinelli. As the package author himself states, the main purpose of the package is to identify suspicious data that needs further verification. So we should always keep in mind that this analysis only gives us red-flagged transactions. They must be verified further.

32.6.1 A first run, the census data
Apart from useful functions, the package also includes some datasets, including some of those used by Frank Benford. To see how the functions work, let us first use the census 2009 data. It contains the population of towns and cities of the United States as of July 2009. Let us view its top 6 rows.

data("census.2009")
head(census.2009)

    state             town pop.2009
1 Alabama   Abbeville city     2930
2 Alabama  Adamsville city     4782
3 Alabama     Addison town      709
4 Alabama       Akron town      433
5 Alabama   Alabaster city    29861
6 Alabama Albertville city    20115


In all, it contains 19,509 records.
The main function benford() takes a vector of numbers to be tested, and creates an object of a special class benford. Its syntax is
benford(data, number.of.digits = 2, sign = "positive")
where


data is the numeric vector to be tested,

number.of.digits is the number of leading digits to be tested. The default value is 2, that is, the first-two digits test.

sign says which values to analyse. The default "positive" keeps only the positive values. We may also give "negative" or "both".

Let us test the first digits of the 2009 population.

census_first_digit <- benford(census.2009$pop.2009, number.of.digits = 1)

title: 32  Benford Analysis
section: 32.7 Audit use case, payments of a works division
text:
32.7 Audit use case, payments of a works division
Let us now look for red flags in the payment vouchers of an imaginary public works division for 2024-25. The division pays contractors and suppliers for works, materials and services. In this division, any bill above ₹50,000 needs the sanction of the Superintending Engineer. Bills up to ₹50,000 can be passed by the Executive Engineer alone.
The code to create the data is folded below. Two things have been planted in it.

Three vendors have been paid many bills between ₹48,000 and ₹49,999. These look like purchases split to stay below the limit of ₹50,000.
A vehicle hiring firm is paid exactly ₹18,500 every time, under a rate contract. This is genuine, but it too will disturb the digit pattern.


Code to create the payment vouchers of the works divisionset.seed(2025)

vendors <- c("Shree Ganesh Constructions", "Maa Durga Enterprises", "Narmada Builders",
             "Vindhya Road Works", "Satpura Traders", "Kshipra Electricals",
             "Malwa Cement Agency", "Chambal Stone Suppliers", "Betwa Engineering Works",
             "Tapti Infra Projects", "Omkar Hardware", "Sai Krupa Contractors")

# Genuine bills, from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1 crore
genuine <- tibble(vendor = sample(vendors, 7500, replace = TRUE),
                  amount = round(exp(runif(7500, log(1000), log(1e7)))))

# Planted case 1. Bills kept just below the limit of Rs 50,000
split_bills <- tibble(vendor = sample(c("Satpura Traders", "Omkar Hardware",
                                        "Sai Krupa Contractors"), 210, replace = TRUE),
                      amount = round(runif(210, 48000, 49999)))

# Planted case 2. A rate contract for hiring vehicles, Rs 18,500 per bill
vehicle_hire <- tibble(vendor = "Rewa Tours and Travels", amount = rep(18500, 144))

works <- bind_rows(genuine, split_bills, vehicle_hire) |>
  mutate(voucher_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:364, n(), replace = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(voucher_date) |>
  mutate(voucher_no = sprintf("PV/2024-25/%05d", row_number()), .before = 1) |>
  select(voucher_no, voucher_date, vendor, amount)

There are 7,854 vouchers, worth ₹844.2 crore in all. The amounts run from ₹1,001 to nearly ₹1 crore. So they span several orders of magnitude, and they measure the size of payments. This is the kind of data for which Benford’s Law should hold.






TipAudit tip



Before a Benford test, check that the amount column is numeric. Amounts exported with commas or the ₹ sign are often read as text, and must be converted first. Also decide what to do with negative amounts, such as recoveries and credit notes. By default, benford() analyses only the positive values, since its argument sign is "positive". Negative amounts can be tested separately with sign = "negative".



32.7.2 Step 2. Create the benford object
This time we will use the first-two digits test.

works_bfd <- benford(works$amount, number.of.digits = 2)


32.7.3 Step 3. Look at the plots first
This time we use another argument of plot(), called except. plot() can draw seven different charts, and by default draws five of them. Writing except = "none" draws all seven. Otherwise, we list the charts to leave out, from c("digits", "second order", "summation", "mantissa", "chi squared", "abs diff", "ex summation"). Another argument, multiple, is TRUE by default, and draws the charts together in one window.
So let us draw just (i) the digit distribution and (ii) the second order test.

plot(
  works_bfd,
  except = c(
    "summation",
    "mantissa",
    "chi squared",
    "abs diff",
    "ex summation",
    "chisq diff",
    "legend"
  ),
  multiple = TRUE
)

The MAD of 0.0015 falls in the range of acceptable conformity. So the data as a whole looks acceptable. Yet the plot showed three sharp spikes. This is an important lesson. A few hundred unusual bills among thousands of genuine ones hardly move a single overall measure. The spikes in the plot are what the auditor must follow.






WarningCaution



Do not stop at the conformity verdict. An “acceptable” MAD does not mean that every group of amounts is clean. Always look at the plot and at the largest deviations, whatever the MAD says.



32.7.6 Step 6. Look for repeated amounts
A spike at one pair of digits is often caused by one amount repeated many times. duplicatesTable() shows the amounts that are repeated most often. For brevity, we print the top 5.
