32.7.9 What the auditor does next
The analysis has done its job. It has pointed to two small groups of vouchers in a large register. Now the auditor takes over.

For the ₹18,500 payments, ask for the rate contract with Rewa Tours and Travels. If the payments match the contract and the log books, this spike is explained. It goes into the working papers as a genuine cause.
For the bills just below ₹50,000, list them by vendor and by date. Look for bills from the same vendor, for the same kind of material, on the same day or in the same week. Such bills suggest a purchase split to avoid the sanction of the Superintending Engineer. Check the indents, the stock entries and the quotations. Ask the division to explain.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.8 Audit use case, comparing offices
In audit, we are rarely interested in whether a whole dataset follows Benford’s Law. A more useful question is, which unit stands out? If an organisation has many offices, we can run the test for each office separately, and compare them.
Let us create payment data for ten district offices of a department. All offices make genuine payments, with amounts spread over a wide range. In one office, about a third of the bills have been made up. The person who made them up chose amounts between ₹5,000 and ₹9,999, which looked reasonable to them. The code is folded below.

Code to create payments of ten district officesset.seed(2025)

offices <- c("Ajmer", "Alwar", "Barmer", "Bhilwara", "Bikaner",
             "Churu", "Dausa", "Jhunjhunu", "Kota", "Sikar")

payments <- map(offices, function(o) {
  n <- sample(600:1200, 1)
  amount <- round(rlnorm(n, log(12000), 1.1))
  if (o == "Dausa") {
    k <- round(0.35 * n)
    amount[1:k] <- round(runif(k, 5000, 9999))   # made-up bills
  }
  tibble(office = o, amount = amount)
}) |>
  list_rbind()



glimpse(payments)

Rows: 8,904
Columns: 2
$ office <chr> "Ajmer", "Ajmer", "Ajmer", "Ajmer", "Ajmer", "Ajmer", "Ajmer", …
$ amount <dbl> 12480, 28089, 48650, 18047, 10032, 18573, 10989, 8211, 25979, 7…


Now we calculate the first digit MAD for each office. Since MAD() needs a benford object, we create one for each office inside summarise().

office_mad <- payments |>
  summarise(payments = n(),
            mad = MAD(benford(amount, number.of.digits = 1)),
            .by = office) |>
  arrange(desc(mad))

office_mad |>
  mutate(mad = round(mad, 4))

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   office    payments    mad
   <chr>        <int>  <dbl>
 1 Dausa          666 0.0539
 2 Bikaner        678 0.0125
 3 Barmer         825 0.011 
 4 Kota           631 0.0098
 5 Sikar         1093 0.0098
 6 Alwar          929 0.0071
 7 Churu          932 0.0067
 8 Ajmer         1059 0.0063
 9 Bhilwara      1176 0.0062
10 Jhunjhunu      915 0.005 


One office stands far apart. The MAD of Dausa is 0.054. That is several times that of any other office. Let us look at its first digits.

payments |>
  filter(office == office_mad$office[1]) |>
  mutate(first_digit = as.integer(str_sub(as.character(amount), 1, 1))) |>
  count(first_digit) |>
  mutate(actual = n / sum(n),
         benford = log10(1 + 1 / first_digit)) |>
  ggplot(aes(first_digit)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = actual), fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = benford), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  labs(x = "First digit", y = "Share of payments") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 32.11: First digits of payments in the office that stands out, against Benford’s Law




In Figure 32.11, the digits 5 to 9 appear far more often than Benford’s Law expects, and the digits 1 to 4 less often. This is exactly the pattern Nigrini described for invented numbers.
The next step is to pull out the payments of this office that start with 5 to 9, and see where they lie.

odd_office <- payments |>
  filter(office == office_mad$office[1]) |>
  mutate(first_digit = as.integer(str_sub(as.character(amount), 1, 1)))

odd_office |>
  filter(first_digit >= 5) |>
  mutate(band = if_else(amount >= 5000 & amount <= 9999,
                        "5,000 to 9,999", "Other amounts")) |>
  summarise(payments = n(), total = sum(amount), .by = band)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  band           payments   total
  <chr>             <int>   <dbl>
1 5,000 to 9,999      331 2452097
2 Other amounts        31 2054337


Most of them lie in one narrow band. There are 331 payments between ₹5,000 and ₹9,999 in Dausa, worth ₹24.5 lakh. These are the vouchers the auditor should examine first, with their bills, sanctions and receipts.






NoteSmall offices and the MAD



Notice that most of the genuine offices have MAD values above the “close conformity” limit of 0.006. One is even in the “marginally acceptable” range. This is because each office has only about a thousand payments, and smaller datasets naturally deviate more by chance. So, when comparing units of modest size, do not judge each unit against Nigrini’s fixed ranges. Instead, compare the units with each other, and look for the ones that stand far apart.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
section: 32.9 When not to use Benford’s Law
text:
32.9 When not to use Benford’s Law
Let us also see what happens when the test is applied to the wrong kind of data. We will take two examples.

32.9.1 Measuring the wrong thing, lake perimeters
The lakes.perimeter8 data also comes with the package. Let us run the first-two digits test on it.

data(lakes.perimeter)
nrow(lakes.perimeter)

[1] 248607

head(lakes.perimeter)

  perimeter.km
1          1.0
2          1.0
3          1.1
4          1.1
5          1.1
6          1.1

lake_ben <- benford(lakes.perimeter$perimeter.km, number.of.digits = 2)

Let us see the plots and the measures.

plot(lake_ben)



Benford analysis of lake perimeter data




chisq(lake_ben)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  lakes.perimeter$perimeter.km
X-squared = 88111, df = 89, p-value < 2.2e-16

MAD(lake_ben)

[1] 0.006012766

lake_ben$MAD.conformity

[1] "Nonconformity"


The data does not conform to Benford’s Law, as is clear from the plot as well as the MAD value. The chi-square value of 88,111 also exceeds the critical value by a very wide margin. Nigrini and Miller have given some plausible explanations for this in their research paper.9 One of them is that the perimeter is not a correct measure of the size of a lake. This is a useful reminder. Benford’s Law applies to measures of size. A non-conformity may come from what is being measured, not from any wrongdoing.

32.9.2 Amounts set by a rule, insurance claims
In the imaginary health insurance scheme of Chapter 46, hospitals are paid fixed rates for each treatment package. Let us run the first-two digits test on the claim amounts.

ssy_claims <- read_csv("Data/ssy_claims.csv")

ssy_bfd <- benford(ssy_claims$claim_amount, number.of.digits = 2)

ssy_bfd$MAD.conformity

[1] "Nonconformity"

duplicatesTable(ssy_bfd) |>
  head(5)

   number duplicates
    <num>      <int>
1:  12000       4152
2:   9000       3397
3:   6000       3203
4:   8000       2561
5:  30000       2429


The data does not conform at all. But this is not a sign of fraud. The claim amounts are made up of a small number of fixed package rates, like ₹12,000, ₹9,000 and ₹6,000, repeated thousands of times. Such numbers are set by a rule, and fall in category 2 of our list of limitations above. Benford’s Law simply does not apply here. For such data, the tests of Chapter 33 and the methods of Chapter 48 are more suitable.

title: 32  Benford Analysis
text:
32.10 A suggested workflow


Check that the data is suitable. It should measure the size of things, span a wide range, not be assigned or set by rules, and have enough records.

Check the amount column. Make sure it is numeric, and decide how to treat negative amounts.

Start with the first-two digits test, using benford(x, number.of.digits = 2).

Look at the plot first. Spikes and patterns tell more than any single number.

Judge conformity mainly by the MAD, especially for large data. Use the chi-square and Z-statistics as supporting measures. Do not let an acceptable MAD hide a spike.

Find the cause of each spike, with suspectsTable(), duplicatesTable() and getSuspects(). Then look inside each group by amount range and by vendor.

Compare units, such as offices or vendors, and look for the ones that stand out.

Examine the records behind every suspicious digit group, before drawing any conclusion. Record genuine causes, like a rate contract, in the working papers.







ImportantRemember



Benford’s Law tells us what honest, natural data usually looks like. It cannot tell us whether a particular number is honest. Its strength lies in pointing, quickly and cheaply, to the corner of a large dataset where something unusual is going on.

text:

Chapter 33 covers the other tests of Nigrini, such as the last-two digits test, the number duplication test and the relative size factor.

32.12 Try it yourself
These exercises use the payment vouchers works of the works division, created earlier in this chapter. Try each one in your console before you open the solution.


The first digit test. Run the first digit test, instead of the first-two digits test, on the amounts in works. What are the MAD and its conformity level? Which first digit deviates most?






TipSolution






ex_first <- benford(works$amount, number.of.digits = 1)
MAD(ex_first)

[1] 0.006647354

ex_first$MAD.conformity

[1] "Acceptable conformity"

suspectsTable(ex_first) |> head(3)

   digits absolute.diff
    <int>         <num>
1:      4     204.86876
2:      2     128.02075
3:      3      56.26884


The MAD is 0.0066, which is acceptable conformity. The digit that deviates most is 4. That is a hint, but a blunt one. The first digit test cannot tell ₹48,000 from ₹40,000 or ₹4 lakh. The first-two digits test narrows the problem to the groups 48 and 49, just below the limit of ₹50,000.





Set aside the rate contract. The payments of exactly ₹18,500 to Rewa Tours and Travels have a genuine cause. Leave them out, run the first-two digits test again, and list the three digit groups that deviate most.

suspectsTable(ex_no_hire_bfd) |> head(3)

The spike at 18 is gone, and the groups 49 and 48 now lead the list. Once a spike is explained, removing its records lets the remaining ones show more clearly.

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.1 Prerequisites
In Chapter 32 we met Mark Nigrini, the accounting professor who turned Benford’s Law into a practical tool for fraud detection. Benford analysis is only one part of his work. Nigrini also put together a full set of simple tests, which forensic auditors now use all over the world. Each test looks at the amounts in a dataset from a different angle. Each one is good at catching a different kind of problem.
The good thing about these tests is that none of them needs advanced statistics. They mostly count, sort and compare. Yet together they can point an auditor to a handful of suspicious records out of lakhs.
Some of these tests are already covered in this book. The rest are covered in this chapter. Table 33.1 gives the complete picture.
Gaps in sequence numbers, which is another standard check, are covered in Chapter 37.
We will need only tidyverse in this chapter.
library(tidyverse)

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.2 Our sample data
Let us imagine a government department with five district offices in Uttar Pradesh. Each office makes small payments for day-to-day needs, like stationery, printing, catering, taxis, repairs and security. Such payments are often called contingent expenditure. Our data has all such bills paid during the financial year 2024-25.
One rule is important for this data. The head of a district office can sanction a bill only up to ₹50,000. A bill above this limit needs sanction from a higher authority. Such limits exist in almost every organisation. They are known as delegation of financial powers.
As in the other chapters of this part, we have planted a few problems in the data. We will find them one by one, using a different test each time. The code to create the data is folded below.

Code to create the sample data of contingent billsset.seed(1947)

offices <- c("Agra", "Bareilly", "Gorakhpur", "Jhansi", "Varanasi")

# Each vendor has a typical bill amount and a number of bills in the year
vendors <- tibble(
  vendor = c("Annapurna Caterers", "Bharat Stationers", "City Cab Services",
             "Deep Electricals", "Ganga Printers", "Gupta Computers",
             "Himalaya Furnishers", "Kaveri Suppliers", "Laxmi Hardware",
             "National Xerox Centre", "New India Tent House", "Om Sai Caterers",
             "Prakash Medical Store", "Rajdhani Travels", "Sai Ram Plumbing Works",
             "Shree Ganesh Transport", "Sharma Office Solutions",
             "Surya Security Services", "Verma & Sons", "Yamuna Cleaning Services"),
  typical = c(18000, 6000, 9000, 22000, 14000, 45000, 60000, 15000, 7000, 3500,
              25000, 20000, 4000, 30000, 8000, 50000, 12000, 70000, 16000, 28000),
  n_bills = c(60, 110, 90, 45, 70, 30, 20, 80, 75, 140,
              35, 50, 95, 40, 55, 45, 65, 24, 60, 36)
)

# Genuine bills. Amounts vary around each vendor's typical amount.
bills <- vendors |>
  rowwise() |>
  reframe(vendor = vendor,
          amount = round(rlnorm(n_bills, log(typical), 0.45))) |>
  mutate(office = sample(offices, n(), replace = TRUE),
         bill_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:364, n(), replace = TRUE))

# A vendor with only two bills in the year
mehta <- tibble(vendor = "Mehta Interiors", amount = c(42000, 168000),
                office = "Agra", bill_date = as.Date(c("2024-06-12", "2024-12-03")))

# Planted case 1. A bill of 21,450 keyed in as 2,14,500
slip <- tibble(vendor = "Kaveri Suppliers", amount = 214500,
               office = "Jhansi", bill_date = as.Date("2024-11-18"))

# Planted case 2. One hugely inflated transport bill
inflated <- tibble(vendor = "Shree Ganesh Transport", amount = 392800,
                   office = "Gorakhpur", bill_date = as.Date("2025-01-22"))

# Planted case 3. Bills kept just below the limit of 50,000
below_limit <- tibble(vendor = "Om Sai Caterers", office = "Varanasi",
                      amount = c(rep(49500, 7), 49800, 49900, 49999, 48750, 49200),
                      bill_date = as.Date("2024-08-01") + sort(sample(0:150, 12)))

# Planted case 4. Made-up round amounts
round_bills <- tibble(vendor = "Verma & Sons", office = "Bareilly",
                      amount = c(15000, 18000, 20000, 12000, 25000, 16000,
                                 14000, 20000, 18000, 22000, 15000, 17500),
                      bill_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sort(sample(0:364, 12)))

bills <- bind_rows(bills, mehta, slip, inflated, below_limit, round_bills) |>
  arrange(bill_date) |>
  mutate(voucher_no = sprintf("CV-%04d", row_number())) |>
  select(voucher_no, bill_date, office, vendor, amount)


Let us have a quick look.

glimpse(bills)

Rows: 1,253
Columns: 5
$ voucher_no <chr> "CV-0001", "CV-0002", "CV-0003", "CV-0004", "CV-0005", "CV-…
$ bill_date  <date> 2024-04-01, 2024-04-01, 2024-04-01, 2024-04-01, 2024-04-02…
$ office     <chr> "Agra", "Jhansi", "Gorakhpur", "Jhansi", "Varanasi", "Agra"…
$ vendor     <chr> "City Cab Services", "Deep Electricals", "Shree Ganesh Tran…
$ amount     <dbl> 13785, 17848, 87368, 86991, 5523, 10355, 1829, 26908, 4331,…


We have 1253 bills from 21 vendors. The columns are simple. voucher_no is the contingent voucher number. bill_date is the date of the bill. office is the district office which paid it. vendor is the vendor who was paid, and amount is the amount paid in rupees.

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.3 Largest subsets test
Before looking for anything unusual, an auditor should first know where the money goes. In Nigrini’s language, a subset is a group of records which share something in common. Here, all bills of one vendor form a subset. All bills of one office form another kind of subset.
The largest subsets test simply ranks the subsets by their total amount. It needs only summarise() and arrange(), which we learnt in Chapter 15.

bills |>
  summarise(bills = n(),
            total = sum(amount),
            .by = vendor) |>
  arrange(desc(total)) |>
  head(6)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  vendor                  bills   total
  <chr>                   <int>   <dbl>
1 Shree Ganesh Transport     46 2881647
2 Surya Security Services    24 1938008
3 Om Sai Caterers            62 1804706
4 Himalaya Furnishers        20 1596145
5 Gupta Computers            30 1539797
6 Kaveri Suppliers           81 1468401


Six vendors account for a large part of the money. Shree Ganesh Transport is at the top. Om Sai Caterers is third, though the typical bill of a caterer is not large. That itself is a small hint, and we will come back to it.






TipAudit tip



The largest subsets test does not find fraud by itself. It tells you where to look first. A vendor, an employee or a scheme which receives a big share of money deserves more attention, simply because more money is at risk there. Run the same test by office, by head of account and by month as well.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.4 Relative Size Factor (RSF) test
The purpose of the RSF test is to identify anomalies where the largest amount for subsets in a given key is outside the norm for those subsets. This test compares the top two amounts for each subset and calculates the RSF for each.
\[
RSF = \frac{Largest\:Record\:in\:a\:Subset}{Second\:Largest\:Record\:in\:a\:Subset}
\tag{33.1}\]
Let us understand the idea with a simple example. Suppose a vendor usually sends bills of ₹10,000 to ₹20,000. One day a bill of ₹1,80,000 is paid to the same vendor. Compared with the whole data, ₹1,80,000 may not look large at all, because other vendors are paid much more. So a simple sort on amount will not show it. But compared with this vendor’s own bills, it is nine times the next largest. RSF catches exactly this.
A large RSF usually means one of these.


A keying error. For example, ₹21,450 entered as ₹2,14,500, because of an extra zero or a missed decimal point.

An inflated bill. The vendor, possibly with someone inside, has claimed far more than the actual supply.

A genuine but unusual purchase. For example, the annual purchase of furniture in one go. This must be confirmed from documents.


33.4.1 Calculating RSF in R
For each vendor, we need the largest amount and the second largest amount. max() gives the largest. For the second largest, we sort the amounts in decreasing order and pick the second one with [2].

rsf <- bills |>
  summarise(bills = n(),
            largest = max(amount),
            second_largest = sort(amount, decreasing = TRUE)[2],
            .by = vendor) |>
  mutate(rsf = round(largest / second_largest, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(rsf))

rsf

# A tibble: 21 × 5
   vendor                   bills largest second_largest   rsf
   <chr>                    <int>   <dbl>          <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Kaveri Suppliers            81  214500          48822  4.39
 2 Mehta Interiors              2  168000          42000  4   
 3 Shree Ganesh Transport      46  392800         127604  3.08
 4 Gupta Computers             30  181403         104889  1.73
 5 Prakash Medical Store       95   18183          11391  1.6 
 6 Ganga Printers              70   56501          39998  1.41
 7 Annapurna Caterers          60   93906          67254  1.4 
 8 Bharat Stationers          110   23434          17435  1.34
 9 Verma & Sons                72   58331          43532  1.34
10 Yamuna Cleaning Services    36  108126          85885  1.26
# ℹ 11 more rows


For most vendors, RSF is between 1 and 2. That is normal. The largest bill of a vendor is usually not very far from its second largest. But three vendors stand out at the top, with RSF of 3 or more.

33.4.2 Subsets with very few records
Look at Mehta Interiors. Its RSF is 4. But it has only two bills in the whole year. With just two bills, one of them is bound to be the largest, and the ratio can easily be large. So the RSF of a small subset tells us very little.
That is why we normally apply RSF only to subsets with some minimum number of records. Let us keep only vendors with at least five bills.

rsf |>
  filter(bills >= 5, rsf >= 2.5)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  vendor                 bills largest second_largest   rsf
  <chr>                  <int>   <dbl>          <dbl> <dbl>
1 Kaveri Suppliers          81  214500          48822  4.39
2 Shree Ganesh Transport    46  392800         127604  3.08


Now two vendors remain. Let us look at their three largest bills each. slice_max() picks the rows with the largest values in each group.

bills |>
  filter(vendor %in% c("Kaveri Suppliers", "Shree Ganesh Transport")) |>
  slice_max(amount, n = 3, by = vendor)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  voucher_no bill_date  office    vendor                 amount
  <chr>      <date>     <chr>     <chr>                   <dbl>
1 CV-1009    2025-01-22 Gorakhpur Shree Ganesh Transport 392800
2 CV-0285    2024-06-23 Agra      Shree Ganesh Transport 127604
3 CV-1064    2025-02-06 Bareilly  Shree Ganesh Transport 118242
4 CV-0783    2024-11-18 Jhansi    Kaveri Suppliers       214500
5 CV-1057    2025-02-05 Bareilly  Kaveri Suppliers        48822
6 CV-0950    2025-01-07 Gorakhpur Kaveri Suppliers        43107


It also helps to compare the largest bill with the usual bill of the vendor. The median is a good measure of the usual bill.

bills |>
  filter(vendor %in% c("Kaveri Suppliers", "Shree Ganesh Transport")) |>
  summarise(median_bill = median(amount),
            largest = max(amount),
            times_median = round(max(amount) / median(amount), 1),
            .by = vendor)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  vendor                 median_bill largest times_median
  <chr>                        <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Shree Ganesh Transport      51190.  392800          7.7
2 Kaveri Suppliers            13513   214500         15.9


The bill of ₹2,14,500 of Kaveri Suppliers is many times its usual bill. Its digits “2145” also look like a typical bill of this vendor with an extra zero, which points towards a keying error. The bill of ₹3,92,800 of Shree Ganesh Transport is also several times its usual bill.
Notice one more thing. Both these bills are far above ₹50,000, the limit of the office head. So the auditor should also check whether sanction of the higher authority was taken for them.






NoteChoosing the cut-offs



The minimum of five bills and the RSF cut-off of 2.5 are not fixed rules. Sort the table by RSF and read from the top. Look at the bills behind each high RSF until the cases stop being interesting. In large data, it also helps to add a materiality condition, for example, consider only those subsets where the largest amount is above a certain value.



33.4.3 Variations of RSF
The classic RSF compares the largest amount (often written as L1) with the second largest (L2). It is simple and works well when a subset has one odd amount. But it has a blind spot. Suppose a vendor has managed to get two inflated bills paid. Then the largest and second largest are both inflated, and their ratio is close to 1. Both bills hide behind each other.
Let us see this with a small example. Sunrise Electricals usually sends bills of about ₹15,000. But two bills of about ₹1.6 lakh each have also been paid.

sunrise <- c(14200, 16850, 12900, 15400, 13750, 168500, 154200)

largest <- max(sunrise)
second  <- sort(sunrise, decreasing = TRUE)[2]
others  <- sort(sunrise, decreasing = TRUE)[-1]   # all except the largest

c(L1_by_L2          = largest / second,
  L1_by_mean_others = largest / mean(others),
  L1_by_median      = largest / median(sunrise))

         L1_by_L2 L1_by_mean_others      L1_by_median 
         1.092737          4.447866         10.941558 


The classic RSF is only about 1.1, and the vendor looks perfectly normal. So auditors also use other measures in the denominator.


L1 / average of the other records. The largest amount is compared with the mean of all the remaining amounts. We leave out the largest one itself, otherwise it would pull the mean up. This measure catches our vendor better, at about 4.4. But the second inflated bill is still inside the mean, and still pulls it up.

L1 / median. The median is the middle value of the subset. It hardly moves even when a few amounts are very large. So it represents the usual amount well. Here, the largest bill is about 11 times the usual bill, and the problem is obvious.

Let us calculate all three on our bills data.

bills |>
  summarise(bills     = n(),
            l1_l2     = round(max(amount) / sort(amount, decreasing = TRUE)[2], 2),
            l1_mean   = round(max(amount) / mean(sort(amount, decreasing = TRUE)[-1]), 2),
            l1_median = round(max(amount) / median(amount), 2),
            .by = vendor) |>
  filter(bills >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(l1_median)) |>
  head(6)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  vendor                   bills l1_l2 l1_mean l1_median
  <chr>                    <int> <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Kaveri Suppliers            81  4.39   13.7      15.9 
2 Shree Ganesh Transport      46  3.08    7.1       7.67
3 Annapurna Caterers          60  1.4     4.28      4.57
4 Gupta Computers             30  1.73    3.87      4.22
5 Prakash Medical Store       95  1.6     3.8       4.2 
6 Yamuna Cleaning Services    36  1.26    3.65      4.02


All three measures put Kaveri Suppliers and Shree Ganesh Transport at the top. In our data, each of them has only one odd bill, so the classic RSF was enough. But notice that the values of the three measures are on different scales. Even for an ordinary vendor in our data, the largest bill is about four times the median bill. So a cut-off that suits one measure does not suit another. Choose the cut-off separately for each measure, by reading down the sorted list as before.
Table 33.2 sums up the three measures.


Table 33.2: Variations of the Relative Size Factor









Measure
Compares the largest amount with
Strength
Weakness



L1 / L2
The second largest amount
Simple, and standard in forensic literature
Misses a subset with two or more odd amounts


L1 / average of others
The mean of all other amounts
Uses all records of the subset
Mean is still pulled up by other large amounts


L1 / median
The middle amount of the subset
Not disturbed by a few odd amounts
Needs a different, higher cut-off












TipAudit tip



Run more than one variation. A subset flagged by L1/median but not by L1/L2 is a sign that it may have more than one odd amount. In that case, look at all its large amounts, and not just the largest one. A still more robust option is to measure how far the largest amount is from the median in units of the median absolute deviation, which R calculates with mad(). This is often called a robust z-score.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.5 Number duplication test
In real life, amounts of bills vary a lot. A stationery bill may be ₹5,523 one day and ₹6,218 the next. So if we count how many times each exact amount appears in the data, most amounts should appear only once, or perhaps twice by coincidence.
The number duplication test counts each exact amount and looks at the ones which repeat the most. count() with sort = TRUE does exactly this.

bills |>
  count(amount, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  amount     n
   <dbl> <int>
1  49500     7
2   4501     3
3   2491     2
4   2599     2
5   2647     2
6   2924     2
7   3202     2
8   3410     2


The amount of ₹49,500 has been paid seven times. No other amount appears more than three times. Let us see who received these payments.

bills |>
  filter(amount == 49500)

# A tibble: 7 × 5
  voucher_no bill_date  office   vendor          amount
  <chr>      <date>     <chr>    <chr>            <dbl>
1 CV-0456    2024-08-11 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500
2 CV-0482    2024-08-18 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500
3 CV-0531    2024-09-04 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500
4 CV-0555    2024-09-09 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500
5 CV-0595    2024-09-22 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500
6 CV-0601    2024-09-24 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500
7 CV-0681    2024-10-20 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500


All seven bills are of the same vendor, and from the same office.






NoteNumber duplication and Same-Same-Same



How is this different from the duplicate tests of Chapter 34? There we looked for the same bill paid twice. Here, the bills are different, with different voucher numbers and dates. What repeats is only the amount. Repeated amounts are a sign that the amounts may not come from real supplies. Of course, there can be genuine reasons, like a fixed monthly rent or a fixed rate contract. Those can be quickly ruled out.



33.5.1 Amounts just below a limit
The amount of ₹49,500 is suspicious for one more reason. It is just below ₹50,000, the limit up to which the office head can sanction a bill. If bills are deliberately kept below this limit, the purchase escapes the scrutiny of the higher authority. A large purchase may also be split into several smaller bills for the same reason. This is commonly called splitting of bills or threshold avoidance.
So let us count, for each vendor, how many bills fall in a narrow band just below the limit, say between ₹45,000 and ₹50,000.

bills |>
  summarise(bills = n(),
            near_limit = sum(amount >= 45000 & amount < 50000),
            .by = vendor) |>
  filter(near_limit > 0) |>
  mutate(pct_near_limit = round(100 * near_limit / bills, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(near_limit))

# A tibble: 11 × 4
   vendor                   bills near_limit pct_near_limit
   <chr>                    <int>      <int>          <dbl>
 1 Om Sai Caterers             62         14           22.6
 2 Shree Ganesh Transport      46          6           13  
 3 Surya Security Services     24          3           12.5
 4 Himalaya Furnishers         20          3           15  
 5 Gupta Computers             30          2            6.7
 6 Yamuna Cleaning Services    36          2            5.6
 7 Deep Electricals            45          1            2.2
 8 Kaveri Suppliers            81          1            1.2
 9 Rajdhani Travels            40          1            2.5
10 Annapurna Caterers          60          1            1.7
11 New India Tent House        35          1            2.9


Om Sai Caterers has the most bills in this band. Let us read this along with what we already know. A caterer’s typical bill is not near ₹50,000. Yet this vendor’s bills crowd just below the limit, seven of them for the very same amount, all from one office. This is a strong lead.
Shree Ganesh Transport also has several bills in the band. But this vendor’s usual bill is itself around ₹50,000, as we saw in the RSF section. So for this vendor, bills near ₹50,000 are expected. This is a good example of why the output of every test must be read with business sense.






TipAudit tip



Also look at the dates of bills near the limit. Several bills of the same vendor, from the same office, within a few days of each other, strongly suggest that one purchase has been split. In our data, try filter(vendor == "Om Sai Caterers", amount >= 45000) and look at the bill_date column.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.6 Round number test
When a person makes up an amount, they tend to choose a round figure. ₹15,000 or ₹20,000 comes to mind more easily than ₹15,437. Real bills, on the other hand, are made of quantities multiplied by rates, plus taxes. So they rarely come out as exact thousands.
In R, the operator %% gives the remainder of a division. If amount %% 1000 is zero, the amount is an exact multiple of ₹1,000. Let us find the share of such round amounts for each vendor.

bills |>
  mutate(is_round = amount %% 1000 == 0) |>
  summarise(bills = n(),
            round_bills = sum(is_round),
            pct_round = round(100 * mean(is_round), 1),
            .by = vendor) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_round)) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  vendor                bills round_bills pct_round
  <chr>                 <int>       <int>     <dbl>
1 Mehta Interiors           2           2     100  
2 Verma & Sons             72          12      16.7
3 Laxmi Hardware           75           1       1.3
4 National Xerox Centre   140           1       0.7
5 City Cab Services        90           0       0  


Taking the mean of a logical (TRUE/FALSE) column gives the proportion of TRUE values. We learnt this trick in Chapter 4.
Again, Mehta Interiors is at the top only because it has two bills, both round. We can ignore it, for the same reason as in the RSF test. The real outlier is Verma & Sons, with a much higher share of round amounts than any other vendor. For genuine bills, this share is close to zero.






WarningCaution



Some payments are genuinely round. Fixed monthly charges, advances, honorarium and lump-sum contracts are good examples. Before treating round amounts as suspicious, check whether the nature of payment allows round figures.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.7 Last-two digits test
The round number test looks at amounts ending in 000. The last-two digits test looks at the endings more broadly. Take the last two digits of every amount. For example, ₹15,437 ends in 37, and ₹49,500 ends in 00. In genuine data, every ending from 00 to 99 should be about equally common. So each ending should appear in about 1% of the amounts.
Made-up amounts break this pattern. They end in 00 or 50 too often, because people like such numbers.
We can get the last two digits with amount %% 100. We consider amounts of ₹100 or more only, because smaller amounts do not have two meaningful last digits.

last_two <- bills |>
  filter(amount >= 100) |>
  mutate(last_two = amount %% 100) |>
  count(last_two)

expected <- sum(last_two$n) / 100
expected

[1] 12.53


On average, each ending should appear about 13 times. Let us see the actual counts in a bar chart, with the expected count as a dashed line (Figure 33.1).

ggplot(last_two, aes(last_two, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = expected, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 90, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Last two digits of amount", y = "Number of bills") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 33.1: Last-two digits test on contingent bills




Most bars are close to the dashed line, rising and falling by chance. But the bar at 00 stands far above all others.
Is this difference large enough, or could it be just chance? The chi-square test, which we discussed in Section 32.5.1, answers this. We compare the observed counts with equal expected counts for all 100 endings.

endings <- bills |>
  filter(amount >= 100) |>
  pull(amount) %% 100

observed <- tabulate(endings + 1, nbins = 100)
chisq.test(observed)


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  observed
X-squared = 175.33, df = 99, p-value = 3.583e-06


The p-value is far below 0.05. So the endings are not evenly spread, and this is unlikely to be due to chance. Now let us find who contributes to the extra 00 endings.

bills |>
  filter(amount %% 100 == 0) |>
  count(vendor, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  vendor                n
  <chr>             <int>
1 Verma & Sons         13
2 Om Sai Caterers      11
3 City Cab Services     2
4 Mehta Interiors       2
5 Bharat Stationers     1


The same names appear again. Verma & Sons with its round amounts and Om Sai Caterers with its ₹49,500 bills together explain most of the spike.






NoteAbout tabulate()



tabulate() counts how many times each whole number from 1 to nbins appears. Endings run from 0 to 99, so we add 1 to make them run from 1 to 100. This also makes sure that endings which never appear are counted as zero, instead of being left out.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.8 Putting the tests together
Each test looked at the data from a different angle. A vendor which shows up in more than one test is a stronger lead than one which shows up only once. So let us build one table, with one row per vendor, and a flag for each test.

vendor_flags <- bills |>
  summarise(
    bills      = n(),
    rsf        = max(amount) / sort(amount, decreasing = TRUE)[2],
    repeats    = max(table(amount)),
    near_limit = sum(amount >= 45000 & amount < 50000),
    pct_round  = 100 * mean(amount %% 1000 == 0),
    .by = vendor
  ) |>
  filter(bills >= 5) |>
  mutate(
    flag_rsf    = rsf >= 2.5,
    flag_repeat = repeats >= 4,
    flag_limit  = near_limit >= 5,
    flag_round  = pct_round >= 10,
    total_flags = flag_rsf + flag_repeat + flag_limit + flag_round
  ) |>
  filter(total_flags > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(total_flags))

vendor_flags |>
  select(vendor, bills, starts_with("flag"), total_flags)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  vendor            bills flag_rsf flag_repeat flag_limit flag_round total_flags
  <chr>             <int> <lgl>    <lgl>       <lgl>      <lgl>            <int>
1 Shree Ganesh Tra…    46 TRUE     FALSE       TRUE       FALSE                2
2 Om Sai Caterers      62 FALSE    TRUE        TRUE       FALSE                2
3 Verma & Sons         72 FALSE    FALSE       FALSE      TRUE                 1
4 Kaveri Suppliers     81 TRUE     FALSE       FALSE      FALSE                1


max(table(amount)) gives the number of times the most repeated amount of a vendor appears. Adding logical columns counts the TRUE values, so total_flags is the number of tests in which a vendor was flagged.
This short table is what an auditor carries forward. Each vendor in it has a clear reason for being there. But the flags must still be read, not just counted. Shree Ganesh Transport has two flags. Yet we already know that bills near ₹50,000 are normal for this vendor. Its real issue is the single inflated bill. On the other hand, Om Sai Caterers also has two flags, and both point to the same story of bills kept just below the limit. The next step is to call for the original bills, sanctions and payment records of these vendors.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.9 A suggested workflow


Know the data and the rules. Find the financial limits, rate contracts and fixed payments which apply. Without these, the output of the tests cannot be judged.

Run the largest subsets test to know where the money goes.

Run the RSF test on subsets with a reasonable number of records. Compare the largest amount with the usual amount of the subset.

Run the number duplication test, and look especially at amounts just below any financial limit.

Run the round number and last-two digits tests to look for made-up amounts.

Combine the results in one table, and examine first the subsets flagged by more than one test.

Verify with documents. Every flag is a question, not an answer.







ImportantRemember



These tests are filters. They reduce lakhs of records to a few dozen worth examining. A flag does not prove any wrongdoing. Genuine reasons, such as a fixed rate contract or a one-time bulk purchase, must be ruled out from records before any audit observation is made.
crumbs: 33  Nigrini's Tests for Unusual Amounts

title: 33  Nigrini’s Tests for Unusual Amounts
text:
33.10 Try it yourself
These exercises use the contingent bills bills of this chapter. Try each one in your console before you open the solution.


Largest subsets by office. Run the largest subsets test with the office as the subset. Which office paid the most, and what share of the total did it pay?






TipSolution






ex_office <- bills |>
  summarise(bills = n(), total = sum(amount), .by = office) |>
  mutate(pct_total = round(100 * total / sum(total), 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(total))
ex_office

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  office    bills   total pct_total
  <chr>     <int>   <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Varanasi    282 5796121      23.7
2 Gorakhpur   244 5118112      20.9
3 Agra        252 4559148      18.7
4 Jhansi      244 4484245      18.4
5 Bareilly    231 4474895      18.3


Varanasi paid the most, ₹58 lakh, or 23.7% of all bills. The shares are close, so size alone is no finding. But note that Varanasi is also the office that paid the seven bills of ₹49,500 to Om Sai Caterers.





How close together? List the bills of Om Sai Caterers paid by the Varanasi office for ₹45,000 or more, in order of date. Add a column with the number of days since the previous such bill.






TipSolution






ex_omsai <- bills |>
  filter(vendor == "Om Sai Caterers", office == "Varanasi", amount >= 45000) |>
  arrange(bill_date) |>
  mutate(days_since_last = as.numeric(bill_date - lag(bill_date)))
ex_omsai

 2 CV-0482    2024-08-18 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500               7
 3 CV-0531    2024-09-04 Varanasi Om Sai Caterers  49500              17

There are 13 such bills, from August 2024 to January 2025. Of these, 9 came within 15 days of the previous one. A caterer sending a bill just under ₹50,000 every few weeks looks like one large order split to stay within the powers of the office head.





Round to ₹500. Change the round number test to count amounts that are exact multiples of ₹500. Keep vendors with at least five bills. Which vendors now lead?






TipSolution






ex_round500 <- bills |>
  summarise(bills = n(),
            pct_round_500 = round(100 * mean(amount %% 500 == 0), 1),
            .by = vendor) |>
  filter(bills >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_round_500)) |>
  head(4)
ex_round500

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  vendor           bills pct_round_500
  <chr>            <int>         <dbl>
1 Verma & Sons        72          18.1
2 Om Sai Caterers     62          12.9
3 Deep Electricals    45           2.2
4 Laxmi Hardware      75           1.3


Verma & Sons and Om Sai Caterers lead, at 18.1% and 12.9%. Om Sai Caterers now joins Verma & Sons, because ₹49,500 is a multiple of ₹500 but not of ₹1,000. The choice of the round unit decides what the test can see.





A robust z-score. For vendors with at least five bills, measure how far the largest bill is from the median bill, in units of mad(). List the top five.






TipSolution






ex_robust <- bills |>
  summarise(bills = n(),
            largest = max(amount),
            median_bill = median(amount),
            robust_z = round((max(amount) - median(amount)) / mad(amount), 1),
            .by = vendor) |>
  filter(bills >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(robust_z)) |>
  head(5)
ex_robust

  vendor                   bills largest median_bill robust_z

1 Kaveri Suppliers            81  214500      13513      41.1
2 Shree Ganesh Transport      46  392800      51190.     15  
3 Yamuna Cleaning Services    36  108126      26909       9.5
4 Verma & Sons                72   58331      15662.      8.7
5 Ganga Printers              70   56501      15107       8.1


Kaveri Suppliers and Shree Ganesh Transport are again at the top, with scores of 41.1 and 15. The rest are well below. The same two bills that RSF found stand out on this measure too, which makes them stronger leads.

title: 34  Duplicate Detection
text:
34.1 Prerequisites
Duplicate detection is one of the oldest and most useful checks in audit. It is simple to understand. It is also simple to run. Yet it often gives the quickest results in a fraud or forensic audit.
A duplicate payment means money has gone out twice for the same thing. Sometimes it is an honest mistake. Sometimes it is not. In either case, it is a loss to the organisation, and the auditor must find it.
Duplicates may point to many kinds of problems. A few common ones are:
In this chapter we will learn how to find such duplicates in R. We will start with the simplest case, where two records are exactly the same. We will then move to cases where records are almost the same. These are harder to find, and they are usually the more interesting ones for an auditor.
We will use three packages in this chapter. tidyverse gives us dplyr and stringr. janitor gives us a very handy function get_dupes(). stringdist will help us find names which are similar but not identical. Later in the chapter, we will also use fullmetaphone to find names which sound alike. Its installation is explained in Chapter 35.
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(stringdist)

title: 34  Duplicate Detection
text:
34.2 Our sample data
To learn the tests, we need some data where we already know the answers. So let us create a small payment register of an imaginary office for the financial year 2024-25. It has about 170 payments made to 14 vendors. We have deliberately planted a few duplicates in it. Our job in this chapter is to find all of them using R.
The code to create the data is given below. New readers need not worry about this code right now. You may expand it later, once you are comfortable with dplyr.

Code to create the sample payment registerset.seed(2025)

# Vendor master
vendors <- tibble(
  vendor_id   = sprintf("V%03d", 1:14),
  vendor_name = c("Sharma Traders", "Gupta Enterprises", "Bharat Stationers",
                  "Kaveri Suppliers", "Laxmi Electricals", "National Printers",
                  "Om Sai Caterers", "Patel Hardware", "Rajdhani Computers",
                  "Shree Ganesh Transport", "Ashok Estates", "Verma & Sons",
                  "Sharma Trader's", "Guptha Enterprises")
)

# 150 ordinary payments
n <- 150
payments <- tibble(
  vendor_id    = sample(vendors$vendor_id[c(1:10, 12)], n, replace = TRUE),
  invoice_no   = paste0("INV-", sample(1000:9999, n)),
  invoice_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:330, n, replace = TRUE),
  amount       = round(runif(n, 2000, 200000))
)

# Monthly office rent. Same amount every month, but genuine.
rent <- tibble(
  vendor_id    = "V011",
  invoice_no   = paste0("AE/RENT/", 1:12),
  invoice_date = seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), by = "month", length.out = 12),
  amount       = 45000
)

# Planted case 1. Invoices paid twice (one of them thrice).
paid_again <- payments[c(12, 47, 47, 101), ]

# Planted case 2. Same invoice keyed in again with a slightly different number.
retyped <- payments[c(23, 88), ] |>
  mutate(invoice_no = c(str_remove(invoice_no[1], "-"),
                        str_to_lower(invoice_no[2])))

# Planted case 3. Same bill raised again with a suffix "A", two days later.
suffixed <- payments[64, ] |>
  mutate(invoice_no   = paste0(invoice_no, "A"),
         invoice_date = invoice_date + 2)

# Planted case 4. Same invoice paid to a look-alike vendor.
lookalike <- payments |>
  filter(vendor_id %in% c("V001", "V002")) |>
  slice(c(2, 5)) |>
  mutate(vendor_id = if_else(vendor_id == "V001", "V013", "V014"))

payments <- bind_rows(payments, rent, paid_again, retyped, suffixed, lookalike) |>
  mutate(payment_date = invoice_date + sample(7:45, n(), replace = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(payment_date) |>
  mutate(voucher_no = sprintf("PV-%04d", row_number())) |>
  left_join(vendors, by = "vendor_id") |>
  select(voucher_no, payment_date, vendor_id, vendor_name,
         invoice_no, invoice_date, amount)

# Planted case 5. Two rows repeated in the data extract itself.
payments <- bind_rows(payments, payments[c(30, 90), ]) |>
  arrange(voucher_no)


Let us have a look at the first few rows.

head(payments)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  voucher_no payment_date vendor_id vendor_name   invoice_no invoice_date amount
  <chr>      <date>       <chr>     <chr>         <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
1 PV-0001    2024-04-18   V011      Ashok Estates AE/RENT/1  2024-04-01    45000
2 PV-0002    2024-04-21   V005      Laxmi Electr… INV-6900   2024-04-01   169386
3 PV-0003    2024-05-02   V009      Rajdhani Com… INV-5628   2024-04-20   171411
4 PV-0004    2024-05-07   V008      Patel Hardwa… INV-4836   2024-04-27    43171
5 PV-0005    2024-05-11   V009      Rajdhani Com… INV-2321   2024-04-19    97584
6 PV-0006    2024-05-13   V004      Kaveri Suppl… INV-9114   2024-04-27     2354


Each row is one payment. The columns are:


voucher_no is the payment voucher number, given by the office.

payment_date is the date on which payment was made.

vendor_id and vendor_name tell us who was paid.

invoice_no and invoice_date come from the bill submitted by the vendor.

amount is the amount paid, in rupees.

title: 34  Duplicate Detection
section: 34.3 What do we mean by a duplicate?
text:
34.3 What do we mean by a duplicate?
This question looks simple. But it is the most important step of the whole exercise. Two records are “duplicates” only with respect to some columns, which we choose. These chosen columns are called the key.
Consider two payments to Sharma Traders. Both are for ₹25,000. Are they duplicates? We cannot say yet. If they also have the same invoice number, they almost certainly are. If the invoice numbers differ and the payments are a month apart, they are probably two genuine supplies.
So, before running any test, the auditor must decide the key. Forensic auditors commonly use the kinds of tests summarised in Table 34.1.


Table 34.1: Types of duplicate tests









Test
What matches
What differs
Typical finding



Exact duplicate
Every column
Nothing
Same row repeated in data, or keyed in twice


Same-Same-Same
All key columns, say vendor, invoice number and amount
Other columns like voucher number and date
Same invoice paid twice


Same-Same-Different
Two key columns, say vendor and amount
The third key column, say invoice number
Same bill re-submitted with a new or altered number


Fuzzy duplicate
Values are similar, not equal
Spelling, case, punctuation
Look-alike vendors, retyped invoice numbers






The names Same-Same-Same and Same-Same-Different are commonly used in forensic analytics literature. They are easy to remember. Three key columns are compared. The name tells us which of the three should match and which should not.

title: 34  Duplicate Detection
text:
34.4 Exact duplicates
Let us begin with the easiest case. Are there rows which are the same in every column?
Base R has a function duplicated(), which we met in Chapter 4. It returns TRUE for every row which has already appeared earlier in the data. So summing it up gives the number of extra copies.

sum(duplicated(payments))

[1] 2


There are two such rows. But duplicated() marks only the second copy as TRUE. The first copy is marked FALSE. An auditor usually wants to see both copies side by side. For this, get_dupes() from janitor is much more convenient. If we do not give it any column names, it uses all columns.

payments |>
  get_dupes()

# A tibble: 4 × 8
  voucher_no payment_date vendor_id vendor_name   invoice_no invoice_date amount
  <chr>      <date>       <chr>     <chr>         <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
1 PV-0030    2024-07-08   V007      Om Sai Cater… INV-2410   2024-06-07    41810
2 PV-0030    2024-07-08   V007      Om Sai Cater… INV-2410   2024-06-07    41810
3 PV-0090    2024-10-20   V001      Sharma Trade… INV-7755   2024-09-29   103923
4 PV-0090    2024-10-20   V001      Sharma Trade… INV-7755   2024-09-29   103923
# ℹ 1 more variable: dupe_count <int>


The output shows each duplicate row along with a new column dupe_count. This column tells us how many times that row appears.
Note that even the voucher numbers are the same here. A real office would never issue the same voucher number twice. So these are not two payments. These are the same payment appearing twice in our data. This usually happens when data is exported from a system, or when two files are merged carelessly.






TipAudit tip



Always check exact duplicates first, and before any other analysis. If the data itself has repeated rows, every total, average and count you calculate will be wrong. Ask the data owner why the rows are repeated. Do not just delete them silently. The answer may itself be an audit finding about the quality of the IT system.


Once we are satisfied with the reason, we may remove the repeated rows using dplyr::distinct(). It keeps only the first copy of each row.

payments <- payments |>
  distinct()

nrow(payments)

[1] 171

title: 34  Duplicate Detection
text:
34.5 Same-Same-Same test
Now let us look for the real problem. Has any invoice been paid more than once?
For this, our key will be three columns. These are vendor_id, invoice_no and amount. If all three match, the same bill has been paid again. Voucher numbers and payment dates will be different, of course, because these are two separate payments.
We just have to pass the key columns to get_dupes().

sss <- payments |>
  get_dupes(vendor_id, invoice_no, amount)

sss

# A tibble: 7 × 8
  vendor_id invoice_no amount dupe_count voucher_no payment_date vendor_name    
  <chr>     <chr>       <dbl>      <int> <chr>      <date>       <chr>          
1 V006      INV-3315    50572          3 PV-0069    2024-09-03   National Print…
2 V006      INV-3315    50572          3 PV-0071    2024-09-05   National Print…
3 V006      INV-3315    50572          3 PV-0079    2024-09-22   National Print…
4 V005      INV-2863   135555          2 PV-0087    2024-10-16   Laxmi Electric…
5 V005      INV-2863   135555          2 PV-0088    2024-10-19   Laxmi Electric…
6 V005      INV-4296   172125          2 PV-0032    2024-07-10   Laxmi Electric…
7 V005      INV-4296   172125          2 PV-0035    2024-07-15   Laxmi Electric…
# ℹ 1 more variable: invoice_date <date>


We see three invoices here. One invoice of National Printers has been paid three times. Two invoices of Laxmi Electricals have been paid twice each. Look at the payment_date column. In one case the second payment was made only two days after the first. In real life, such cases need a closer look at the approval process.

34.5.1 How much money is involved?
An audit observation is incomplete without the money value. In each group, one payment was correct and the rest were extra. So the excess payment is the amount multiplied by one less than the number of times it was paid.

sss |>
  summarise(
    times_paid = n(),
    amount = first(amount),
    excess_paid = (n() - 1) * first(amount),
    .by = c(vendor_id, invoice_no)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  vendor_id invoice_no times_paid amount excess_paid
  <chr>     <chr>           <int>  <dbl>       <dbl>
1 V006      INV-3315            3  50572      101144
2 V005      INV-2863            2 135555      135555
3 V005      INV-4296            2 172125      172125


We may add a further summarise() to get the grand total. That total is the figure which goes into the audit observation.

sss |>
  summarise(excess_paid = (n() - 1) * first(amount), .by = c(vendor_id, invoice_no)) |>
  summarise(total_excess = sum(excess_paid))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  total_excess
         <dbl>
1       408824


So, in our small data, ₹4,08,824 has been paid in excess on just three invoices.






NoteChoosing the key wisely



Why did we not use invoice_date in the key? We could have. But dates are often entered differently by different clerks, so adding more columns to the key can make us miss duplicates. On the other hand, too few columns produce too many false alarms. Start with a small key. Then add columns if the output is too long to examine.

title: 34  Duplicate Detection
text:
34.6 Same-Same-Different test
A clever fraudster knows that most accounting software rejects an invoice number already entered for a vendor. So they change the invoice number a little. They may add a suffix, or change one digit. The Same-Same-Same test above will not catch this.
This is where the Same-Same-Different test helps. Here we look for records where the vendor and the amount are the same, but the invoice number is different.
In dplyr, we can do this with filter() and its .by argument, which we learnt in Chapter 15. Inside each group of vendor and amount, we keep the group only if it has more than one distinct invoice number. The function n_distinct() counts the distinct values.

ssd <- payments |>
  filter(n_distinct(invoice_no) > 1, .by = c(vendor_id, amount)) |>
  arrange(vendor_id, amount, invoice_date)

ssd |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, amount)

# A tibble: 18 × 5
   voucher_no vendor_name        invoice_no invoice_date amount
   <chr>      <chr>              <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
 1 PV-0139    Gupta Enterprises  INV-9665   2025-01-10    29117
 2 PV-0155    Gupta Enterprises  INV9665    2025-01-10    29117
 3 PV-0160    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850   2025-02-15    93149
 4 PV-0171    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850A  2025-02-17    93149
 5 PV-0066    Rajdhani Computers inv-3601   2024-08-14   127872
 6 PV-0077    Rajdhani Computers INV-3601   2024-08-14   127872
 7 PV-0001    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/1  2024-04-01    45000
 8 PV-0008    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/2  2024-05-01    45000
 9 PV-0034    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/3  2024-06-01    45000
10 PV-0047    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/4  2024-07-01    45000
11 PV-0058    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/5  2024-08-01    45000
12 PV-0078    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/6  2024-09-01    45000
13 PV-0099    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/7  2024-10-01    45000
14 PV-0116    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/8  2024-11-01    45000
15 PV-0133    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/9  2024-12-01    45000
16 PV-0152    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/10 2025-01-01    45000
17 PV-0149    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/11 2025-02-01    45000
18 PV-0169    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/12 2025-03-01    45000


Let us read this output carefully, group by group.


Gupta Enterprises, ₹29,117. Invoice numbers are INV-9665 and INV9665. Only the hyphen is missing. This is clearly the same invoice entered again.

Rajdhani Computers, ₹93,149. Invoice numbers are INV-8850 and INV-8850A, dated two days apart. Adding a suffix like “A” is a classic way to get a bill paid twice. This needs to be examined with the original documents.

Rajdhani Computers, ₹1,27,872. Invoice numbers are inv-3601 and INV-3601. Only the case differs. Again the same invoice.

Ashok Estates, ₹45,000. Twelve invoices, one for each month. This is the monthly rent of the office building. It is not a duplicate. The same amount is genuinely paid every month.

So the test has found the real problems. But it has also raised one false alarm. This is normal. Every duplicate test produces some false alarms. The auditor’s job is to reduce them sensibly and then examine the rest.

34.6.1 Reducing false alarms with a date window
Rent, salary, annual maintenance charges and similar payments repeat by their very nature. But they repeat after a gap, usually a month or more. A bill re-submitted for double payment usually comes within a few days or weeks of the original.
So let us also calculate how many days have passed since the previous invoice of the same vendor and amount. The function lag() gives us the previous value within each group.

ssd <- ssd |>
  mutate(days_since_previous = as.numeric(invoice_date - lag(invoice_date)),
         .by = c(vendor_id, amount))

ssd |>
  select(vendor_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, amount, days_since_previous)

# A tibble: 18 × 5
   vendor_name        invoice_no invoice_date amount days_since_previous
   <chr>              <chr>      <date>        <dbl>               <dbl>
 1 Gupta Enterprises  INV-9665   2025-01-10    29117                  NA
 2 Gupta Enterprises  INV9665    2025-01-10    29117                   0
 3 Rajdhani Computers INV-8850   2025-02-15    93149                  NA
 4 Rajdhani Computers INV-8850A  2025-02-17    93149                   2
 5 Rajdhani Computers inv-3601   2024-08-14   127872                  NA
 6 Rajdhani Computers INV-3601   2024-08-14   127872                   0
 7 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/1  2024-04-01    45000                  NA
 8 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/2  2024-05-01    45000                  30
 9 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/3  2024-06-01    45000                  31
10 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/4  2024-07-01    45000                  30
11 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/5  2024-08-01    45000                  31
12 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/6  2024-09-01    45000                  31
13 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/7  2024-10-01    45000                  30
14 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/8  2024-11-01    45000                  31
15 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/9  2024-12-01    45000                  30
16 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/10 2025-01-01    45000                  31
17 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/11 2025-02-01    45000                  31
18 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/12 2025-03-01    45000                  28


For rent, the gap is around 30 days each time. For the suspicious groups, the gap is zero or two days. Now we keep only those groups where some invoice came within, say, 15 days of the previous one.

ssd |>
  filter(any(days_since_previous <= 15, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(vendor_id, amount)) |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, amount)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  voucher_no vendor_name        invoice_no invoice_date amount
  <chr>      <chr>              <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
1 PV-0139    Gupta Enterprises  INV-9665   2025-01-10    29117
2 PV-0155    Gupta Enterprises  INV9665    2025-01-10    29117
3 PV-0160    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850   2025-02-15    93149
4 PV-0171    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850A  2025-02-17    93149
5 PV-0066    Rajdhani Computers inv-3601   2024-08-14   127872
6 PV-0077    Rajdhani Computers INV-3601   2024-08-14   127872


The rent payments are gone. Only the three suspicious groups remain.






WarningCaution



The window of 15 days is only an example. Choose it according to the business. A fortnightly payment would need a shorter window. A fraudster who knows about this test may also wait for a few weeks before re-submitting the bill. So treat the date window as a way to rank cases for examination, not as a final rule.



34.6.2 Other combinations
The Same-Same-Different idea works with any combination of columns. We only have to decide which two should match and which one should differ. For example, let us look for the same invoice number and amount, but paid to different vendors.

payments |>
  filter(n_distinct(vendor_id) > 1, .by = c(invoice_no, amount)) |>
  arrange(invoice_no) |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor_id, vendor_name, invoice_no, amount)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  voucher_no vendor_id vendor_name        invoice_no amount
  <chr>      <chr>     <chr>              <chr>       <dbl>
1 PV-0111    V002      Gupta Enterprises  INV-8297    29819

4 PV-0100    V001      Sharma Traders     INV-8564    93897


This is an interesting result. An invoice of Sharma Traders has also been paid to Sharma Trader’s. An invoice of Gupta Enterprises has also been paid to Guptha Enterprises. These look-alike names have different vendor codes. This is a serious red flag. We will come back to it in Section 34.8.
A few other useful combinations are given in Table 34.2.
