title: 41  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
41.7 How good is the model?

41.7.1 The accuracy trap
The obvious way to use a probability is to call a claim “irregular” if its score is above 0.5. Let us count how that works on the test set, in a confusion matrix.

table(predicted_irregular = test$score > 0.5, actually_irregular = test$irregular)

                   actually_irregular
predicted_irregular FALSE TRUE
              FALSE   486   87
              TRUE      9   18


The model is right for 84% of the claims. That sounds good, until we notice that calling every claim regular would be right for 82.5%, since most claims are regular. Worse, it catches only 18 of the 105 irregular claims, 17%. When “yes” cases are rare, as irregularities usually are, accuracy is a misleading measure. Two other measures matter to an auditor.


Recall (or sensitivity), the share of irregular claims that the selection catches. Low recall means irregularities slip through.

Precision, the share of selected claims that turn out irregular. Low precision means examining many clean claims.

A lower cut-off catches more irregular claims, at the cost of examining more clean ones.

evaluate_cutoff <- function(cutoff) {
  picked <- test$score > cutoff
  tibble(cutoff,
         selected  = sum(picked),
         caught    = sum(picked & test$irregular),
         recall    = round(mean(picked[test$irregular]), 2),
         precision = round(mean(test$irregular[picked]), 2))
}
map(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1), evaluate_cutoff) |> list_rbind()

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  cutoff selected caught recall precision
   <dbl>    <int>  <int>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1    0.5       27     18   0.17      0.67
2    0.3       77     38   0.36      0.49
3    0.2      149     62   0.59      0.42
4    0.1      290     86   0.82      0.3 


There is no single right cut-off. It depends on how many claims the audit party can examine, and on the cost of missing an irregular claim compared with examining a clean one.

41.7.2 Ranking: the ROC curve and AUC
In audit we rarely need a yes/no prediction at all. We need a good ranking, so that we can examine claims from the top down as far as our resources allow. The standard measure of ranking quality is the AUC, the area under the ROC curve. It has a simple meaning. Pick one irregular claim and one regular claim at random. The AUC is the probability that the model gives the irregular one the higher score. An AUC of 0.5 is no better than tossing a coin, and 1 is a perfect ranking. In practice, 0.7 to 0.8 is useful, and above 0.8 is good.
The AUC can be calculated from ranks, in the same way as the Wilcoxon test of Section 30.8.

auc <- function(score, actual) {
  r  <- rank(score)
  n1 <- sum(actual)
  n0 <- sum(!actual)
  (sum(r[actual]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
auc1 <- auc(test$score, test$irregular)
auc1

[1] 0.7983261


The AUC on the test set is 0.80. The ROC curve itself shows, for every possible cut-off, the share of irregular claims caught against the share of regular claims wrongly selected.

roc_points <- function(score, actual) {
  ord <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(false_alarm_rate = c(0, cumsum(!actual[ord]) / sum(!actual)),
         catch_rate       = c(0, cumsum(actual[ord]) / sum(actual)))
}
roc_points(test$score, test$irregular) |>
  ggplot(aes(false_alarm_rate, catch_rate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Share of regular claims selected (false alarms)",
       y = "Share of irregular claims caught",
       subtitle = paste("AUC =", sprintf("%.2f", auc1), "; the dashed line is random selection")) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()



ROC curve of the refund risk model on the test set



The further the curve bows towards the top-left corner, the better. The dashed diagonal is what random selection would achieve.

41.7.3 The gains table, in audit language
The most useful view for planning is the gains table. Sort the claims by score, divide them into ten equal groups (deciles), and count how many irregular claims each group holds.

gains <- test |>
  mutate(decile = ntile(desc(score), 10)) |>
  summarise(claims = n(), irregular = sum(irregular), .by = decile) |>
  arrange(decile) |>
  mutate(cum_claims_pct = round(100 * cumsum(claims) / sum(claims)),
         cum_caught_pct = round(100 * cumsum(irregular) / sum(irregular)))
gains

# A tibble: 10 × 5
   decile claims irregular cum_claims_pct cum_caught_pct
    <int>  <int>     <int>          <dbl>          <dbl>

 2      2     60        23             20             50
 3      3     60        21             30             70
 4      4     60         8             40             78

10     10     60         1            100            100


Examining the top 20% of claims by score would have caught 50% of the irregular ones, and the top 30%, 70%. Random selection of 20% of claims would catch only about 20%. That is the value of the model, stated in terms any audit manager understands.

title: 41  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
41.8 Making better features
Remember the registration table. The risk was high for claimants registered for less than a year, and much lower after that. But model1 uses reg_months as a straight-line effect, a small change in risk for every month. It cannot capture a jump at one year. A simple feature that says whether the claimant is a new registrant matches the pattern better.

train <- train |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
test  <- test  |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)

model2 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
              family = binomial, data = train)
or2 <- tidy(model2, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
or2 |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term                  estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)              0.012     0.295    -15.0    0        0.007     0.021
2 exporter_typeMerchant    3.74      0.182      7.26   0        2.63      5.38 
3 new_registrantTRUE       5.49      0.184      9.26   0        3.84      7.91 
4 log(amount_lakh)         1.22      0.091      2.14   0.032    1.02      1.46 
5 nonfiler_pct             1.09      0.008     11.9    0        1.08      1.11 

test <- test |> mutate(score2 = predict(model2, newdata = test, type = "response"))
auc2 <- auc(test$score2, test$irregular)
c(model1 = round(auc1, 3), model2 = round(auc2, 3))

model1 model2 
 0.798  0.825 


New registrants have 5.5 times the odds of an irregular claim, and the AUC on the test set improves from 0.798 to 0.825.
With only about 100 irregular claims in the test set, a small difference in AUC could be the luck of one particular split. A simple check is to repeat the split many times, and see how often the new model wins. (Repeating the split in a systematic way is called cross-validation.)

auc_gain <- map_dbl(1:40, \(i) {
  set.seed(i)
  rows <- sample(nrow(past), size = 0.7 * nrow(past))
  tr <- past[rows, ] |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
  te <- past[-rows, ] |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
  m1 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + reg_months + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
            family = binomial, data = tr)
  m2 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
            family = binomial, data = tr)
  auc(predict(m2, te), te$irregular) - auc(predict(m1, te), te$irregular)
})
c(splits = length(auc_gain), new_model_better = sum(auc_gain > 0),
  average_gain = round(mean(auc_gain), 3))

          splits new_model_better     average_gain 
          40.000           38.000            0.028 


The new feature improves the ranking in 38 of 40 random splits, so the gain is real. Features built from audit knowledge, like “registered less than a year ago”, “supplier and claimant share an address” or “claim filed in the last week of the quarter”, often add more than any statistical refinement. Looking at the data first, as we did, is how such features are found.






TipAudit tip



Compare models on the test set, never on the training set. Adding features always improves the fit on the training data, even useless ones. Only the test set tells whether a change really helps on new cases.

title: 41  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
section: 41.9 Using the model on new claims
text:
41.9 Using the model on new claims
This year, 1,500 refund claims are pending, and the audit party can examine 150 of them. Their outcomes are, of course, not known yet. We first refit the model on all of last year’s claims, since the test set has done its job, and then score the new claims.

past <- past |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
final_model <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
                   family = binomial, data = past)

set.seed(2029)
pending <- make_claims(1500, "RF24") |>
  select(-irregular) |>                         # outcomes not known yet
  mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)

pending <- pending |>
  mutate(risk_score = predict(final_model, newdata = pending, type = "response"),
         risk_rank  = min_rank(desc(risk_score)))

pending |> arrange(risk_rank) |>
  select(claim_id, exporter_type, reg_months, amount_lakh, nonfiler_pct, risk_score) |>
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 6
   claim_id  exporter_type reg_months amount_lakh nonfiler_pct risk_score
   <chr>     <chr>              <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
 1 RF24-1343 Merchant              53       14.1          67.5      0.974
 2 RF24-0411 Merchant               5        3.69         47.6      0.964
 3 RF24-1298 Manufacturer           1        7.25         57.4      0.956
 4 RF24-0360 Merchant               3       10.6          41        0.946
 5 RF24-0685 Merchant              11        7.94         39.9      0.938
 6 RF24-1477 Merchant              10       62.7          34.1      0.928
 7 RF24-1157 Manufacturer           1        8.17         48.3      0.905
 8 RF24-0892 Manufacturer           1       17.2          46.8      0.905
 9 RF24-0535 Merchant               8       17.2          32.8      0.901
10 RF24-0110 Manufacturer           4       27.6          45.3      0.900


How should the 150 claims be chosen? Not only from the top of the list.

set.seed(11)
top_risk    <- pending |> slice_max(risk_score, n = 120)
random_part <- pending |> anti_join(top_risk, by = "claim_id") |> slice_sample(n = 30)

selection <- bind_rows(top_risk |> mutate(basis = "Risk score"),
                       random_part |> mutate(basis = "Random")) |>
  arrange(desc(risk_score))
count(selection, basis)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  basis          n
  <chr>      <int>
1 Random        30
2 Risk score   120


We take the 120 highest-risk claims, and 30 more chosen at random from the rest, using anti_join() from Chapter 16 so that no claim is picked twice. The random part is not a waste. It keeps the selection unpredictable, so claimants cannot learn to stay just below the model’s radar. It catches kinds of irregularity the model has never seen. And it gives unbiased data for training next year’s model, which brings us to the cautions.






CautionCautions in using risk models





The model learns only from what was examined. If last year’s audit examined mostly large claims, the model knows little about small ones. Outcomes from a partly random selection, as above, correct this over time.

The past is not the future. Once a risk becomes known, the fraud moves elsewhere. Refit the model every year, and check its AUC on the new year’s results.

Do not use features that should not decide treatment, such as the religion, caste or gender of a proprietor, even if they appear predictive. Such a selection cannot be defended, and usually reflects bias in past selections rather than real risk.

A score is not evidence. A high score is a reason to examine a claim, never a finding in itself. The finding comes from the examination.

Watch for perfect separation. If some feature predicts the outcome perfectly in the training data, say every claim from one district was irregular, glm() warns that “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”, and the coefficients become unreliable. Merge such small groups, or drop the feature.

title: 41  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
section: 41.10 More than two outcomes, multinomial regression
text:
41.10 More than two outcomes, multinomial regression
So far each claim was either regular or irregular. Real audit results are often richer. Suppose last year’s audit party had recorded three outcomes for each claim examined.


Clean, nothing wrong.

Procedural lapse, such as a missing document or a wrongly filled form. The refund is due, but the claim needs correcting.

Fraudulent, a refund claimed on fake input tax credit.

These call for very different responses. A procedural lapse calls for a letter, a fraud for an investigation. And they may have quite different causes. Lumping them together as “irregular” throws this information away. Multinomial logistic regression extends logistic regression to an outcome with three or more categories.
The idea is a small step from what we know. One category is chosen as the baseline, here Clean. The model then fits one logistic regression for each other category against the baseline: lapse against clean, and fraud against clean, at the same time. Each feature gets one coefficient for each comparison. So a feature can raise the risk of fraud while having no effect on lapses, or the other way round.
Let us give last year’s claims such three-way outcomes. Unknown to the auditor, procedural lapses are commoner among new registrants and among small claims, while fraud goes with merchant exporters, large claims and credit from non-filers, as before.

Code to create the three-way outcomesset.seed(2030)
outcomes <- past |>
  mutate(lp_lapse = -1.6 + 1.3 * new_registrant - 0.35 * log(amount_lakh),
         lp_fraud = -4.6 + 1.2 * (exporter_type == "Merchant") + 0.3 * log(amount_lakh) +
                    0.09 * nonfiler_pct,
         # probabilities of the three outcomes, from the two log-odds
         p_lapse = exp(lp_lapse) / (1 + exp(lp_lapse) + exp(lp_fraud)),
         p_fraud = exp(lp_fraud) / (1 + exp(lp_lapse) + exp(lp_fraud)),
         u = runif(n()),
         outcome = case_when(u < p_fraud ~ "Fraudulent",
                             u < p_fraud + p_lapse ~ "Procedural lapse",
                             .default = "Clean"),
         outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("Clean", "Procedural lapse", "Fraudulent"))) |>
  select(claim_id, exporter_type, new_registrant, amount_lakh, nonfiler_pct, outcome)



count(outcomes, outcome) |> mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  outcome              n   pct
  <fct>            <int> <dbl>
1 Clean             1561  78  
2 Procedural lapse   266  13.3
3 Fraudulent         173   8.7


The first level of the factor, Clean, is the baseline. Multinomial regression is fitted with multinom() from the package nnet, which comes with every installation of R. The formula is written as before. (trace = FALSE stops it printing the progress of its calculations.)

library(nnet)
multi_model <- multinom(outcome ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
                        data = outcomes, trace = FALSE)

broom::tidy() works here too, with one row for each feature and each comparison. With exponentiate = TRUE, the estimates are again odds ratios, now the odds of that outcome rather than a clean claim. We show them side by side.

multi_or <- tidy(multi_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

multi_or |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(result = paste0(round(estimate, 2), " (", round(p.value, 3), ")")) |>
  select(term, y.level, result) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = y.level, values_from = result)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  term                  `Procedural lapse` Fraudulent  
  <chr>                 <chr>              <chr>       
1 exporter_typeMerchant 1.61 (0.001)       3.78 (0)    
2 new_registrantTRUE    4.22 (0)           0.71 (0.146)
3 log(amount_lakh)      0.65 (0)           1.42 (0)    
4 nonfiler_pct          1.01 (0.376)       1.09 (0)    


Each cell shows the odds ratio, with its p-value in brackets. Reading across a row tells a clear story.


New registrants have 4.2 times the odds of a procedural lapse, but their odds of fraud (0.71) are not clearly different from others’. Newcomers make mistakes; they are not, on this evidence, more dishonest.

Merchant exporters have 3.8 times the odds of fraud, and a smaller rise, 1.6 times, in the odds of a lapse. (We did not plant this second effect. Even in simulated data, chance produces patterns, which is one more reason to confirm a model’s findings on fresh data.)

Credit from non-filers raises the odds of fraud by a factor of 1.094 for each percentage point, and has little to do with lapses.

Larger claims are more likely to be fraudulent, and less likely to have lapses, perhaps because large claimants employ professionals to file their claims.

A two-way logistic regression on “irregular” would have mixed these opposite patterns together, and blurred both.
Predictions. predict() with type = "probs" gives the probability of each outcome for each claim, and the three add up to 1.

multi_probs <- predict(multi_model, newdata = outcomes, type = "probs")
head(round(multi_probs, 3))

  Clean Procedural lapse Fraudulent
1 0.849            0.123      0.028
2 0.803            0.135      0.062
3 0.876            0.091      0.033
4 0.766            0.199      0.035
5 0.875            0.087      0.038
6 0.668            0.325      0.007


These support two separate selections from the same list of claims: the highest probabilities of fraud for the investigation wing, and the highest probabilities of a procedural lapse for a compliance drive by letter. Each can be judged with the AUC and gains table, exactly as before, using its own column.

c(fraud_auc = round(auc(multi_probs[, "Fraudulent"], outcomes$outcome == "Fraudulent"), 3),
  lapse_auc = round(auc(multi_probs[, "Procedural lapse"], outcomes$outcome == "Procedural lapse"), 3))

fraud_auc lapse_auc 
    0.813     0.722 


(These are measured on the same claims the model learnt from, to keep the example short. In practice, use a training and test split, as earlier in the chapter.)






Note



If the categories have a natural order, such as nil, minor and major irregularity, an ordinal logistic regression uses that order and needs fewer coefficients. It is fitted with polr() from the package MASS. When the categories are simply different kinds, as here, multinomial regression is the right choice.

title: 41  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
41.11 A suggested workflow


Define the outcome clearly, such as “irregularity of more than ₹1 lakh found on examination”, and collect past cases with known outcomes.

List candidate features from audit knowledge, and look at the outcome rate by each feature, banding numeric ones with cut().

Split the data into training and test sets.

Fit with glm(..., family = binomial), and read the odds ratios with tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE).

Evaluate on the test set with the AUC and a gains table. Do not rely on accuracy.

Improve the features, comparing models only on the test set.
Refit on all the data, and score the new cases.

Select mostly by risk score, with a random part, within the capacity available.

Record the model, its features and its test results in the working papers, and refit when new outcomes arrive.







ImportantRemember




Logistic regression predicts the probability of a yes/no outcome, and its scores rank cases by risk.

exp() of a coefficient is an odds ratio, the factor by which the odds change for one unit of the feature.
Judge a model on data it has not seen. Use the AUC and a gains table, not accuracy, when “yes” is rare.
Good features come from audit knowledge and from looking at the data.
Select mostly by risk, partly at random, and treat a score as a lead, never as evidence.
For three or more kinds of outcome, multinomial regression fits one comparison per outcome against a baseline, and shows how the drivers differ.

41.12 Try it yourself
These exercises use the refund claims of this chapter, with the training and test sets, the pending claims and the models already fitted. Try each one before you open the solution.


Two more cut-offs. Use evaluate_cutoff() to see what happens at cut-offs of 0.15 and 0.25. How many claims would be selected, and what share of the irregular ones would be caught?






TipSolution






ex_cuts <- map(c(0.15, 0.25), evaluate_cutoff) |> list_rbind()
ex_cuts

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  cutoff selected caught recall precision
   <dbl>    <int>  <int>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1   0.15      208     79   0.75      0.38
2   0.25      102     46   0.44      0.45


At 0.25, 102 claims are selected and 44% of the irregular ones are caught. At 0.15 the selection grows to 208 claims, and recall rises to 75%. Precision falls from 45% to 38%, so more of the extra work goes into clean claims. The audit party chooses the cut-off from the number of claims it can examine.





Score two claims. Use final_model to find the risk score of two claims of ₹10 lakh each. One is from a merchant exporter registered last month, with 25% of its credit from non-filers. The other is from a manufacturer registered five years ago, with 2% from non-filers. Convert each score into odds too.






TipSolution






ex_two_claims <- tibble(exporter_type  = c("Merchant", "Manufacturer"),
                        new_registrant = c(TRUE, FALSE),
                        amount_lakh    = 10,
                        nonfiler_pct   = c(25, 2))
ex_two_claims <- ex_two_claims |>
  mutate(score = predict(final_model, newdata = ex_two_claims, type = "response"),
         odds  = score / (1 - score))
ex_two_claims

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  exporter_type new_registrant amount_lakh nonfiler_pct  score   odds
  <chr>         <lgl>                <dbl>        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Merchant      TRUE                    10           25 0.800  4.00  
2 Manufacturer  FALSE                   10            2 0.0240 0.0246


The first claim scores 0.80, odds of about 4.0 to 1. The second scores only 0.024. The model estimates that about 8 in 10 past claims like the first were irregular, so it belongs near the top of the list. The score is a reason to examine the claim, not a finding against the claimant.





Does the amount help? Fit model2 again without log(amount_lakh), on the training set. Compare its AUC on the test set with that of model2.






TipSolution






ex_model3 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + nonfiler_pct,
                 family = binomial, data = train)
ex_auc3 <- auc(predict(ex_model3, newdata = test), test$irregular)
c(model2 = round(auc2, 3), without_amount = round(ex_auc3, 3))

        model2 without_amount 
         0.825          0.821 


The AUC is 0.821 without the amount and 0.825 with it. The amount adds very little to the ranking. A difference this small could be the luck of one split, so we would repeat the split, as we did for new_registrant, before deciding to drop it.





Describe the selection. Compare the 120 highest-risk pending claims with the other pending claims. What share are merchant exporters and new registrants, and what is the median share of credit from non-filers in each group?






TipSolution






ex_profile <- pending |>
  mutate(group = if_else(risk_rank <= 120, "Top 120", "Other claims")) |>
  summarise(claims       = n(),
            merchant_pct = round(100 * mean(exporter_type == "Merchant")),
            new_reg_pct  = round(100 * mean(new_registrant)),
            median_nonfiler_pct = median(nonfiler_pct),
            .by = group)
ex_profile

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  group        claims merchant_pct new_reg_pct median_nonfiler_pct
  <chr>         <int>        <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
1 Other claims   1380           31          23                 4.4
2 Top 120         120           64          71                27.0


In the top 120, 64% are merchant exporters and 71% are new registrants, against 31% and 23% among the others. Their median credit from non-filers is about 27%, against about 4%. A table like this goes into the working papers. It explains in plain words why these claims were chosen.





Top fraud scores. Using multi_probs, take the 50 claims with the highest probability of fraud. How many of them were actually fraudulent, clean or procedural lapses?






TipSolution






ex_fraud50 <- outcomes |>
  mutate(p_fraud = multi_probs[, "Fraudulent"]) |>
  slice_max(p_fraud, n = 50) |>
  count(outcome)
ex_fraud50

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  outcome              n
  <fct>            <int>
1 Clean               15
2 Procedural lapse     1
3 Fraudulent          34


Of the 50 claims, 34 were fraudulent, against about 4 we would expect in 50 claims picked at random. But the model learnt from these same claims, so this result flatters it. On new claims it would probably do worse. The investigation wing would still have to examine each claim, since 16 of the 50 were not fraudulent.

41  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring

title: 42  Decision Trees
text:
42.1 Our data, audited works contracts
A decision tree is a chain of yes/no questions, the kind an experienced auditor asks without thinking. Was the tender open for less than three weeks? If yes, did it get fewer than three bids? If yes, this contract needs a close look. A tree learns such questions from data. It finds which feature to ask about first, where to draw the line (why three weeks, and not two?), and what to ask next, separately for each answer.
Trees have two great strengths for audit work.
In this chapter we use trees for two audit tasks: learning risk rules from past audit results, and finding out what rule a department actually follows in its decisions, as against the rule it is supposed to follow.
Prerequisites
rpart comes with every installation of R. rpart.plot is installed from CRAN with install.packages("rpart.plot").
Last year’s audit examined 3,000 works contracts of a State’s public works, irrigation and water supply departments, and recorded whether each was found irregular (excess payment, splitting of works, inflated quantities, and so on). For each contract we know
Code to create the contracts dataset.seed(33)
n <- 3000
works <- tibble(
  work_id     = sprintf("WK-%04d", 1:n),
  department  = sample(c("Roads", "Buildings", "Irrigation", "Water Supply"), n, TRUE),
  tender_mode = sample(c("Open", "Limited", "Nomination"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1)),
  value_lakh  = round(rlnorm(n, log(60), 0.9), 1),
  window_days = pmax(3, round(rnorm(n, 26, 7))),
  bidders     = pmax(1, rpois(n, 4.5))
) |>
  mutate(bidders = if_else(tender_mode == "Nomination", 1, bidders),
         # The true risk, unknown to the auditor. Planted:
         # - short tender windows with at most two bidders are very risky
         # - large contracts awarded on nomination are very risky
         risk = case_when(
           tender_mode == "Nomination" & value_lakh > 100 ~ 0.60,
           window_days < 21 & bidders <= 2               ~ 0.65,
           window_days < 21                              ~ 0.15,
           TRUE                                          ~ 0.04),
         irregular = as.numeric(runif(n) < risk)) |>
  select(-risk)
works

# A tibble: 3,000 × 7

 9 WK-0009 Roads        Open              92.6          40       6         0
10 WK-0010 Roads        Open              46.7          28       3         0

mean(works$irregular)

irregular is 1 for an irregular contract and 0 otherwise, so its mean, 0.112, is the share of irregular contracts, about 11%. As in Section 41.4, we keep 30% of the contracts aside as a test set.
set.seed(1)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(works), size = 0.7 * nrow(works))
train <- works[train_rows, ]
test  <- works[-train_rows, ]

department,

tender_mode, whether the contract was awarded through an open tender, a limited tender, or on nomination to a single contractor,

title: 42  Decision Trees
text:
42.2 Growing a tree
rpart() takes a formula, like lm() and glm(). Since irregular is coded 0 and 1, we use method = "anova". The tree then predicts the share of irregular contracts in each group, which is exactly the risk score we want. (For a yes/no label instead of a score, method = "class" is used, as we will see in Section 42.7.)

set.seed(1)   # rpart uses random numbers for cross-validation, explained later
tree1 <- rpart(irregular ~ department + tender_mode + value_lakh + window_days + bidders,
               data = train, method = "anova")


rpart.plot(tree1, roundint = FALSE, digits = 2)



Decision tree for irregularity in works contracts



How to read the tree. Start at the top, the root, which holds all the training contracts. Each box shows two numbers. The upper one is the share of irregular contracts in that group, and the lower one is the percentage of all contracts which fall in it. The root shows the overall share, 0.11, for 100% of contracts. Below each box is a question. Contracts for which the answer is yes go to the left, and the others to the right. The boxes at the bottom, the leaves, are the final groups.
The first question is whether the tender was open for 21 days or more. For the contracts where it was not, on the right, the tree next asks about bidders. Short-window contracts with fewer than 2.5 (that is, at most two) bidders end in a leaf where about three in five were irregular. On the left, among contracts with a proper window, the tree separates those awarded on nomination, and among them those worth more than about ₹1 crore, another high-risk leaf. Every other group has a low share. The tree has found both the planted patterns, and even the 21-day line of the rules, without being told any of them.
crumbs: Part VI: Modelling and Risk Scoring

title: 42  Decision Trees
section: 42.3 How a tree chooses its questions
text:
42.3 How a tree chooses its questions
At each step, the tree tries every feature and every possible dividing line. For window_days it tries “less than 4”, “less than 5”, and so on. It picks the question which splits the contracts into two groups that are each as pure as possible, one group with mostly irregular contracts and the other with mostly clean ones. Then it repeats the search inside each group separately. That is why the second question can be different on each side. The tree asks about bidders only for contracts with short windows, because that is where bidders matter.
Left alone, this splitting would go on until every leaf held a single contract. rpart() stops earlier, by default, when a split would improve the fit by less than 1%. This limit is the complexity parameter, cp, which we will meet again in Section 42.6.
crumbs: Part VI: Modelling and Risk Scoring

title: 42  Decision Trees
section: 42.4 From a tree to audit rules
text:
42.4 From a tree to audit rules
rpart.rules() writes out the path to each leaf as a rule, sorted by risk.

rpart.rules(tree1, roundint = FALSE)

 irregular                                                                                             
     0.024 when window_days >= 21 & tender_mode is      Nomination                  & value_lakh <  109
     0.043 when window_days >= 21 & tender_mode is Limited or Open                                     
     0.180 when window_days <  21                                  & bidders >= 2.5                    
     0.590 when window_days >= 21 & tender_mode is      Nomination                  & value_lakh >= 109
     0.612 when window_days <  21                                  & bidders <  2.5                    


These read almost like paragraphs of an audit programme. The rules can be turned into dplyr code to flag contracts in any new dataset. For example, the two high-risk rules become the following. (The tree’s line for nomination was ₹109 lakh, which we have rounded to ₹1 crore, for the reason explained below.)

works |>
  mutate(risk_rule = case_when(
    window_days < 21 & bidders <= 2                     ~ "Short window, few bidders",
    tender_mode == "Nomination" & value_lakh >= 100     ~ "Large nomination",
    .default = "Other")) |>
  summarise(contracts = n(), irregular_pct = round(100 * mean(irregular), 1), .by = risk_rule)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  risk_rule                 contracts irregular_pct
  <chr>                         <int>         <dbl>
1 Other                          2760           6.9
2 Short window, few bidders       176          62.5
3 Large nomination                 64          54.7


The thresholds from a tree, like ₹109 lakh here, come from the data and can wobble a little from sample to sample. Before writing them into an audit programme, round them to the nearest limit with a meaning, such as the ₹1 crore beyond which a higher authority must approve, or the 21 days required by the rules.






TipAudit tip



Show the tree itself to the audit team and to the department. Unlike most models, a tree can be checked against experience. If a rule makes no sense, say a high risk for contracts awarded on a Tuesday, it is probably chance, and the tree should be pruned or the feature dropped. If a rule makes sense but was not known, it is a finding worth sharing.

title: 42  Decision Trees
text:
42.5 How good is the tree?
We judge the tree on the test set, using the AUC from Section 41.7. predict() on a tree gives the share of irregular contracts in the leaf each contract falls into.

auc <- function(score, actual) {
  r  <- rank(score)
  n1 <- sum(actual)
  n0 <- sum(!actual)
  (sum(r[actual]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
test <- test |> mutate(tree_score = predict(tree1, newdata = test))
auc_tree <- auc(test$tree_score, test$irregular == 1)
auc_tree

[1] 0.7749985


How does a logistic regression with the same features do?

logit1 <- glm(irregular ~ department + tender_mode + value_lakh + window_days + bidders,
              family = binomial, data = train)
auc_logit <- auc(predict(logit1, newdata = test), test$irregular == 1)
auc_logit

[1] 0.6897514


The tree ranks the contracts better, with an AUC of 0.775 against 0.69. The reason is the combinations. In this data, a short window is risky mainly when there are few bidders, and nomination mainly when the contract is large. Logistic regression adds up the effect of each feature separately, so it cannot see this unless we build such combinations ourselves, and to do that we would have to know them already.
This does not make trees always better. When risk rises smoothly with a feature, like the share of credit from non-filers in Chapter 41, logistic regression captures it in one number, while a tree can only approximate it with steps. In practice, fit both and compare them on the test set.
Which features matter? The tree also reports how much each feature contributed to its splits.

round(tree1$variable.importance / sum(tree1$variable.importance) * 100)

window_days     bidders  value_lakh tender_mode 
         37          32          17          14 


The department does not appear at all. Irregularity here does not depend on the department, which is itself useful to know.

title: 42  Decision Trees
text:
42.6 Trees that grow too far
A tree can always be grown until it fits the training data almost perfectly. Let us lower cp and the smallest group allowed to split, minsplit, and see what happens.

set.seed(1)
deep_tree <- rpart(irregular ~ department + tender_mode + value_lakh + window_days + bidders,
                   data = train, method = "anova",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0.0005, minsplit = 10))

c(leaves    = sum(deep_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>"),
  auc_train = round(auc(predict(deep_tree, train), train$irregular == 1), 3),
  auc_test  = round(auc(predict(deep_tree, test), test$irregular == 1), 3))

   leaves auc_train  auc_test 
  147.000     0.967     0.653 


The deep tree has 147 leaves. On the training data its AUC is a splendid 0.967, but on the test data it falls to 0.653, worse than the small tree. It has memorised the training contracts, chance coincidences included, instead of learning the general pattern. This is called overfitting, and it is the main danger with trees.
The cure is pruning, cutting the tree back to the size that works best on new data. rpart() helps by cross-validation. While growing the tree, it splits the training data into 10 parts, grows the tree on 9 and checks it on the tenth, ten times over. The results are in the complexity table.

round(deep_tree$cptable, 4) |> head(8)   # the first 8 rows of the complexity table

      CP nsplit rel error xerror   xstd
1 0.1052      0    1.0000 1.0006 0.0544
2 0.0859      1    0.8948 0.8970 0.0467
3 0.0279      2    0.8088 0.8120 0.0476
4 0.0070      4    0.7530 0.7635 0.0449
5 0.0051      7    0.7319 0.8022 0.0475
6 0.0048     10    0.7165 0.8257 0.0489
7 0.0047     12    0.7068 0.8248 0.0492
8 0.0041     13    0.7021 0.8362 0.0503


Each row is a tree of a different size (nsplit is the number of splits, one less than the number of leaves). rel error is the error on the training data, which keeps falling as the tree grows. xerror is the cross-validated error, an estimate of the error on new data. It falls at first, and then rises again as the tree starts memorising. The lowest xerror here is at 4 splits. plotcp() shows the same thing as a chart.

plotcp(deep_tree)



Cross-validated error by tree size



We prune the deep tree at the cp with the lowest cross-validated error.

best_cp <- cpt[which.min(cpt[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
pruned_tree <- prune(deep_tree, cp = best_cp)

c(leaves   = sum(pruned_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>"),
  auc_test = round(auc(predict(pruned_tree, test), test$irregular == 1), 3))

  leaves auc_test 
   5.000    0.775 

rpart.rules(pruned_tree, roundint = FALSE)

 irregular                                                                                             
     0.024 when window_days >= 21 & tender_mode is      Nomination                  & value_lakh <  109
     0.043 when window_days >= 21 & tender_mode is Limited or Open                                     
     0.180 when window_days <  21                                  & bidders >= 2.5                    
     0.590 when window_days >= 21 & tender_mode is      Nomination                  & value_lakh >= 109
     0.612 when window_days <  21                                  & bidders <  2.5                    


Pruning brings the tree back to 5 leaves, with the same rules and the same test AUC as our first tree, far better than the deep tree. A common, more cautious alternative is the one standard error rule: choose the smallest tree whose xerror is within one xstd of the lowest. It gives simpler trees, which are easier to explain.






Caution



Trees are unstable. A small change in the data can change the first question, and with it the whole tree below. Do not read too much into the exact thresholds or the lower branches of a single tree. Check that the main rules hold on the test set, and, where possible, on a second year’s data. Methods which average many trees, such as random forests (the package ranger), are much more stable and usually rank better, but give up the readable rules which are a tree’s main attraction for audit.

title: 42  Decision Trees
section: 42.7 What rule is actually being applied?
text:
42.7 What rule is actually being applied?
Trees have a second, quite different use in audit. Instead of predicting irregularity, we can fit a tree to the decisions an office has made, and read off the rule it actually follows. Then we compare it with the rule it is supposed to follow.
A State scholarship scheme is open to students whose family income is up to ₹2.5 lakh a year and who scored at least 60% in their last examination. Here are 2,000 applications from five districts, with the decision taken on each.

Code to create the scholarship applicationsset.seed(5)
m <- 2000
applications <- tibble(
  app_id      = sprintf("SCH-%04d", 1:m),
  district    = sample(c("Anandpur", "Bhimnagar", "Keshavpur", "Lalganj", "Motipur"), m, TRUE),
  applicant   = sample(c("Fresh", "Renewal"), m, TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)),
  income_lakh = round(runif(m, 0.5, 6), 2),
  marks_pct   = round(pmin(99, rnorm(m, 66, 12)), 1)
) |>
  mutate(decision = case_when(
    # Planted. Keshavpur quietly applies an income limit of 4 lakh
    district == "Keshavpur" & income_lakh <= 4 & marks_pct >= 60 ~ "Approved",
    income_lakh <= 2.5 & marks_pct >= 60                         ~ "Approved",
    .default = "Rejected"))
# A few decisions which follow no rule at all
odd <- sample(m, 30)
applications$decision[odd] <- if_else(applications$decision[odd] == "Approved",
                                      "Rejected", "Approved")
applications <- applications |>
  mutate(decision = factor(decision, levels = c("Rejected", "Approved")))


This time the outcome is a category, so we use method = "class".

decision_tree <- rpart(decision ~ district + applicant + income_lakh + marks_pct,
                       data = applications, method = "class")
rpart.plot(decision_tree, roundint = FALSE, extra = 104)



The rule actually followed in scholarship decisions



In a class tree, each box shows the predicted decision, the share of each decision in the group, and the percentage of applications in it (extra = 104 asks for these). The rules make it plain.

rpart.rules(decision_tree, roundint = FALSE)

 decision                                                                                                           
     0.00 when income_lakh is 2.5 to 4.0 & marks_pct <  61 & district is                                   Keshavpur
     0.00 when income_lakh <  2.5        & marks_pct <  60                                                          
     0.01 when income_lakh >=        4.0                   & district is                                   Keshavpur
     0.02 when income_lakh >=        2.5                   & district is Anandpur or Bhimnagar or Lalganj or Motipur
     0.97 when income_lakh is 2.5 to 4.0 & marks_pct >= 61 & district is                                   Keshavpur
     0.99 when income_lakh <  2.5        & marks_pct >= 60                                                          


The numbers are the share approved. Across the State, the tree recovers the scheme’s rule: income below ₹2.5 lakh and marks of about 60% or more. But in Keshavpur alone there is one more approving rule, for incomes between ₹2.5 lakh and ₹4 lakh. The district has been applying an income limit of ₹4 lakh. No one told the tree to look at districts. It found the deviation because the decisions themselves could not be explained without it.
The finding is then confirmed and quantified directly.

applications |>
  filter(decision == "Approved", income_lakh > 2.5 | marks_pct < 60) |>
  count(district, name = "approved_outside_rule")

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  district  approved_outside_rule
  <chr>                     <int>
1 Anandpur                      7
2 Bhimnagar                     4
3 Keshavpur                    67
4 Lalganj                       3
5 Motipur                       7


The handful of such cases in the other districts are the scattered odd decisions, each worth checking, but the pattern is in Keshavpur. The next step in audit would be to examine the Keshavpur files, and to see whether any order authorised the higher limit.






TipAudit tip



This “what rule is really applied” analysis works for any decision taken against stated criteria: admissions, recruitment, pension and subsidy sanctions, grant of licences, or selection of beneficiaries. If the tree’s rule matches the stated one, the process is consistent. If it splits on something that should not matter, such as a district, an officer or a time period, there is a deviation to investigate.

title: 42  Decision Trees
text:
42.8 A suggested workflow


Define the outcome: a past audit result coded 0/1 for risk rules, or the decision taken for rule discovery.

Split the data into training and test sets (for rule discovery on the full data, this can be skipped).

Grow a tree with rpart(), method = "anova" for a 0/1 risk score, or method = "class" for a category.

Draw it with rpart.plot(), and write out the rules with rpart.rules().

Check for overfitting: grow a deeper tree, look at printcp() and plotcp(), and prune() at the lowest cross-validated error.

Evaluate on the test set with the AUC, and compare with logistic regression.

Sense-check the rules with experienced auditors, and round thresholds to meaningful limits.

Turn the rules into dplyr filters, and apply them to new data.







ImportantRemember




A decision tree is a chain of yes/no questions learnt from data, and its result is a set of readable rules.
Trees find combinations of features, like “short window and few bidders”, by themselves.
Deep trees memorise their training data. Prune them using the cross-validated error.
Trees are unstable. Trust the main rules that hold on test data, not every branch.
A tree fitted to an office’s decisions shows the rule it actually applies.

title: 42  Decision Trees
text:
42.9 Try it yourself
These exercises use the works contracts works, the training and test sets train and test, the first tree tree1 and the scholarship applications of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.


A lower limit for nominations. Suppose contracts on nomination above ₹50 lakh, not ₹1 crore, needed a higher approval. Flag the contracts again with this limit, and see what share of the large nominations was irregular.






TipSolution






ex_rules <- works |>
  mutate(risk_rule = case_when(
    window_days < 21 & bidders <= 2                ~ "Short window, few bidders",
    tender_mode == "Nomination" & value_lakh >= 50 ~ "Nomination of 50 lakh or more",
    .default = "Other")) |>
  summarise(contracts = n(), irregular_pct = round(100 * mean(irregular), 1), .by = risk_rule)
ex_rules

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  risk_rule                     contracts irregular_pct
  <chr>                             <int>         <dbl>
1 Other                              2694           7.1
2 Short window, few bidders           176          62.5
3 Nomination of 50 lakh or more       130          27.7


With the lower limit, 130 contracts are flagged as large nominations, but only 27.7% of them were irregular. Nominations between ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore were mostly clean, so they dilute the flag. The ₹1 crore limit, close to the tree’s own line, picks out the risky group far better.





Eligible but rejected. The chapter looked at approvals outside the rule. Now look the other way. Count, district by district, the applicants who met the stated rule (income up to ₹2.5 lakh and marks of 60% or more) but were rejected.






TipSolution






ex_rejected <- applications |>
  filter(decision == "Rejected", income_lakh <= 2.5, marks_pct >= 60) |>
  count(district, name = "eligible_but_rejected")
ex_rejected

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  district  eligible_but_rejected
  <chr>                     <int>
1 Anandpur                      3
2 Bhimnagar                     1
3 Lalganj                       1


Only 5 eligible applicants were rejected, spread over a few districts. These are the scattered odd decisions, not a pattern. Keshavpur does not appear, because its error lies the other way, in approving too many. Even so, each such case is a deserving student denied a scholarship, and the file is worth a look.





A shallower tree. Grow the tree of Section 42.2 again, but allow it only two levels of questions with rpart.control(maxdepth = 2). Write out its rules, and compare its test AUC with that of tree1.






TipSolution






set.seed(1)
ex_tree2 <- rpart(irregular ~ department + tender_mode + value_lakh + window_days + bidders,
                  data = train, method = "anova",
                  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 2))
rpart.rules(ex_tree2, roundint = FALSE)

 irregular                                        
     0.054 when window_days >= 21                 
     0.180 when window_days <  21 & bidders >= 2.5
     0.612 when window_days <  21 & bidders <  2.5

ex_auc2 <- auc(predict(ex_tree2, test), test$irregular == 1)
round(c(two_levels = ex_auc2, first_tree = auc_tree), 3)

two_levels first_tree 
     0.705      0.775 


With only two levels, the tree finds the short window and few bidders rule, but has no room left for large nominations. Its test AUC falls to 0.705, against 0.775 for tree1. A tree that is too small misses real patterns, just as one that is too large learns false ones.





Keshavpur’s own rule. Fit a class tree to the applications of Keshavpur alone, using income and marks. What income limit does the district actually apply?






TipSolution






ex_kesh <- applications |> filter(district == "Keshavpur")
ex_kesh_tree <- rpart(decision ~ income_lakh + marks_pct, data = ex_kesh, method = "class")
rpart.rules(ex_kesh_tree, roundint = FALSE)

 decision                                        
     0.00 when income_lakh <  4 & marks_pct <  60
     0.01 when income_lakh >= 4                  
     0.99 when income_lakh <  4 & marks_pct >= 60


Within Keshavpur the tree splits on an income of ₹4 lakh, not ₹2.5 lakh, along with marks of 60%. Applicants below ₹4 lakh with good marks were almost all approved. This confirms the finding of the chapter, and gives the exact limit to put to the district in the audit.

title: 43  Random Forests
text:
43.1 Our data, refund claims with many red flags
A single decision tree (Chapter 42) is easy to read, but it has a weakness we noted there. It is unstable. Grow it on a slightly different sample, and the questions, the thresholds and the predictions can all change. A random forest turns this weakness into a strength. It grows hundreds of trees, each on a slightly different sample of the data, and lets them vote. Individual trees make different mistakes, and in the average, many of the mistakes cancel out.
It is the same reason why an audit committee is wiser than any one of its members, or why the average of many independent estimates is usually closer to the truth than most of the estimates themselves. Random forests are among the most reliable methods for scoring risk, and they need very little tuning. The price is that a forest of 500 trees cannot be read like a single tree. We will see how to look inside it all the same.
Prerequisites
ranger is installed from CRAN with install.packages("ranger"). We also need the AUC function of Section 41.7.
We return to GST refund claims, as in Chapter 41, but this time the audit party recorded many more features for each of the 5,000 claims examined last year.
Some of these matter and some do not, and the ones that matter do so in different ways: some gradually, some beyond a threshold, some only in combination with another feature. This is the kind of data where forests do well. The code is folded, and its comments say what was planted.
Code to create the refund claimsset.seed(46)
n <- 5000
claims <- tibble(
  exporter_type    = sample(c("Manufacturer", "Merchant"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.65, 0.35)),
  sector           = sample(c("Textiles", "Engineering", "Chemicals", "Agro",
                              "Electronics", "Gems"), n, TRUE),
  reg_months       = pmax(1, round(rexp(n, 1 / 40))),
  amount_lakh      = round(rlnorm(n, log(8), 1), 2),
  nonfiler_pct     = round(100 * rbeta(n, 0.6, 6), 1),
  refund_ratio     = round(rbeta(n, 2, 5), 3),
  n_suppliers      = rpois(n, 8) + 1,
  top_supplier_pct = round(100 * rbeta(n, 2, 2.5), 1),
  shared_address   = runif(n) < 0.06,
  quarter_end      = runif(n) < 0.3,
  prior_claims     = rpois(n, 3)
) |>
  mutate(
    # The true risk, unknown to the auditor:
    true_logodds = -3.2 +
      0.03 * nonfiler_pct +                                   # gradual effect
      0.07 * nonfiler_pct * (exporter_type == "Merchant") +   # stronger for merchants
      2.2 * (refund_ratio > 0.45) +                           # a threshold
      1.8 * (n_suppliers <= 5 & top_supplier_pct > 60) +      # a combination
      1.6 * shared_address +
      1.2 * (reg_months < 12) +
      0.6 * sin(amount_lakh / 6),                             # a weak, wavy effect
    # sector, quarter_end and prior_claims have no effect at all
    irregular = runif(n) < plogis(true_logodds)) |>
  select(-true_logodds)

set.seed(1)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(claims), size = 0.7 * nrow(claims))
train <- claims[train_rows, ]
test  <- claims[-train_rows, ]
claims

title: 43  Random Forests
text:
43.2 From one tree to many
Before using a ready-made forest, let us build a small one by hand, to see why it works. First, a single tree, judged on the test set.

set.seed(1)
one_tree <- rpart(irregular ~ ., data = train, method = "anova")
auc(predict(one_tree, test), test$irregular)

[1] 0.7450786


Now we grow 50 trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training data: a sample of the same size, drawn with replacement, so that some claims appear twice and others not at all. Each tree sees a slightly different picture of the data.

set.seed(2)
many_trees <- map(1:50, \(i) {
  boot <- train[sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE), ]
  rpart(irregular ~ ., data = boot, method = "anova")
})

# each tree's own AUC on the test set
tree_aucs <- map_dbl(many_trees, \(t) auc(predict(t, test), test$irregular))
summary(tree_aucs)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.7148  0.7423  0.7497  0.7485  0.7618  0.7748 

# the AUC of their average prediction
avg_score <- map(many_trees, \(t) predict(t, test)) |> reduce(`+`) / 50
auc(avg_score, test$irregular)

[1] 0.7838601


The 50 trees vary, with AUCs from 0.715 to 0.775. But their average scores 0.784, better than even the best single tree among them. This is called bagging (from bootstrap aggregating), and it is the heart of a random forest.
A random forest adds one more twist. At every split, each tree may choose only from a random subset of the features, not from all of them. This stops all the trees from asking the same strong question first, and makes them more different from one another. Usually that improves the average further, though, as we will see, not always by much.

title: 43  Random Forests
section: 43.3 Growing a random forest with ranger()
text:
43.3 Growing a random forest with ranger()

ranger() does all this, quickly. The formula is as before; irregular ~ . means “irregular, explained by all the other columns”. We turn the outcome into a factor and ask for probability = TRUE, so that the forest gives the share of trees voting irregular, a risk score, rather than just a yes or no.

set.seed(1)
forest <- ranger(irregular ~ ., data = train |> mutate(irregular = factor(irregular)),
                 num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE, importance = "permutation")
forest

Ranger result

Call:
 ranger(irregular ~ ., data = mutate(train, irregular = factor(irregular)),      num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE, importance = "permutation") 

Type:                             Probability estimation 
Number of trees:                  500 
Sample size:                      3500 
Number of independent variables:  11 
Mtry:                             3 
Target node size:                 10 
Variable importance mode:         permutation 
Splitrule:                        gini 
OOB prediction error (Brier s.):  0.1369406 


The printout gives the settings. Mtry is the number of features each split may choose from (by default, about the square root of the number of features), and Target node size the smallest group a tree will split further. These defaults work well most of the time.
The OOB prediction error deserves a word. Each tree was grown on a bootstrap sample, which leaves out about a third of the claims. For each claim, the trees that did not see it can predict it, like a test set built into the method. This out-of-bag (OOB) error is an honest estimate of how the forest will do on new data, available without setting aside a test set. For a probability forest, it is the Brier score, the average squared difference between the predicted probability and the actual outcome (0 or 1). Smaller is better.
Predictions on new data come from predict(). The result holds a matrix of probabilities, one column per outcome.

forest_score <- predict(forest, data = test)$predictions[, "TRUE"]
head(round(forest_score, 3))

[1] 0.097 0.053 0.363 0.263 0.726 0.278

title: 43  Random Forests
section: 43.4 Forest, tree and logistic regression compared
text:
43.4 Forest, tree and logistic regression compared
Let us fit a logistic regression with all the features too, and compare the three on the test set.

logit <- glm(irregular ~ ., family = binomial, data = train)

model_aucs <- c(logistic    = auc(predict(logit, test), test$irregular),
                single_tree = auc(predict(one_tree, test), test$irregular),
                forest      = auc(forest_score, test$irregular))
round(model_aucs, 3)

   logistic single_tree      forest 
      0.753       0.745       0.769 


The forest ranks the claims better than the other two. Logistic regression assumes each feature acts separately and in a straight line, so it misses the threshold, the combination and the stronger effect for merchants. The single tree can capture these, but crudely and unstably. The forest captures them more smoothly.
Notice, though, that our hand-made bag of 50 pruned trees did a little better still (0.784). The reason is in the settings. By default, ranger() grows each tree very deep, until groups of about 10 claims remain. Whether a claim turned out irregular is partly chance, and such deep trees learn some of that chance. Our pruned trees were shallower. We come back to this in Section 43.6.
In audit terms, the gains table of Section 41.7 shows what this means for a team that can examine one claim in five.

top_fifth_capture <- function(score) {
  picked <- rank(-score) <= 0.2 * length(score)
  round(100 * sum(test$irregular[picked]) / sum(test$irregular))
}
map_dbl(list(logistic = predict(logit, test), single_tree = predict(one_tree, test),
             forest = forest_score), top_fifth_capture)

   logistic single_tree      forest 
         49          41          52 


The figures are the percentage of all the irregular claims that fall in the top 20% of each model’s scores.
crumbs: Part VI: Modelling and Risk Scoring

title: 43  Random Forests
text:
43.5 Looking inside the forest
A forest cannot be drawn like a tree, but two tools tell us what it has learnt.

43.5.1 Which features matter? Variable importance
We asked for importance = "permutation". For each feature, the forest shuffles that column, so that its link with the outcome is broken, and measures how much worse the out-of-bag predictions become. A feature the forest relies on causes a big loss when shuffled. A useless one causes none.

importance_df <- tibble(feature = names(forest$variable.importance),
                        importance = forest$variable.importance) |>
  arrange(importance)

importance_df |>
  ggplot(aes(importance, fct_inorder(feature))) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(x = "Loss in accuracy when the feature is shuffled", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()



Permutation importance of each feature



The refund-to-turnover ratio and the credit from non-filers matter most, followed by exporter type, new registration and a shared address. sector, quarter_end and prior_claims, which we planted with no effect, are at or near zero, and slightly negative values simply mean “no use at all”. Note also top_supplier_pct. It does matter, but only together with a small number of suppliers, a combination that affects few claims, so its importance is low. Importance measures a feature’s overall contribution, and a real but rare pattern can score low. So read a low importance as “rarely useful”, not as “never matters”. This alone is valuable to an audit team. It tells them which red flags have actually gone with irregularity in the past, and which are folklore.

43.5.2 How does risk change with a feature? Partial dependence
Importance says how much a feature matters, not how. A partial dependence plot shows how the average predicted risk changes as one feature changes, with everything else as it was. We compute it ourselves: set the feature to each value in turn for every claim in the test set, predict, and average.

partial_dependence <- function(model, data, feature, values) {
  map_dbl(values, \(v) {
    data[[feature]] <- v
    mean(predict(model, data = data)$predictions[, "TRUE"])
  })
}

ratio_grid <- seq(0.05, 0.80, by = 0.05)
pd_ratio <- tibble(refund_ratio = ratio_grid,
                   avg_risk = partial_dependence(forest, test, "refund_ratio", ratio_grid))


pd_ratio |>
  ggplot(aes(refund_ratio, avg_risk)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Refund claimed as a share of turnover", y = "Average predicted risk") +
  theme_minimal()



Partial dependence of risk on the refund-to-turnover ratio



The risk is flat up to a ratio of about 0.45, then jumps, and is flat again. The forest has found the threshold we planted, without being told, and shows it in a form an audit team can turn into a rule of thumb: refund claims above about 45% of turnover deserve a closer look. A logistic regression would have drawn a smooth slope instead, too high below the threshold and too low above it.
The same function, applied separately to merchants and manufacturers, shows the combined effect of exporter type and credit from non-filers.

nonfiler_grid <- seq(0, 60, by = 5)
pd_nonfiler <- map(c("Manufacturer", "Merchant"), \(type) {
  subset <- test |> filter(exporter_type == type)
  tibble(exporter_type = type, nonfiler_pct = nonfiler_grid,
         avg_risk = partial_dependence(forest, subset, "nonfiler_pct", nonfiler_grid))
}) |> list_rbind()

pd_nonfiler |>
  ggplot(aes(nonfiler_pct, avg_risk, colour = exporter_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Input credit from non-filing suppliers (%)", y = "Average predicted risk",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()



Risk rises faster with credit from non-filers for merchant exporters



For merchants the risk climbs much more steeply.

title: 43  Random Forests
text:
43.6 Tuning, briefly
Forests need little tuning, but three settings are worth knowing.


num.trees, the number of trees. More is never worse, only slower. 500 is usually plenty.

mtry, the number of features each split may choose from. Smaller values make the trees more different.

min.node.size, the smallest group a tree may split. Larger values make simpler trees.

The out-of-bag error lets us compare settings without touching the test set.

tuning <- expand_grid(mtry = c(2, 3, 5), min.node.size = c(10, 50, 200)) |>
  mutate(oob_error = map2_dbl(mtry, min.node.size, \(m, s) {
    set.seed(1)
    ranger(irregular ~ ., data = train |> mutate(irregular = factor(irregular)),
           num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE, mtry = m, min.node.size = s)$prediction.error
  }))
tuning |> arrange(oob_error)

# A tibble: 9 × 3
   mtry min.node.size oob_error
  <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>
1     3            50     0.136
2     2            50     0.136
3     5            50     0.136
4     5           200     0.137
5     2            10     0.137
6     3            10     0.137
7     3           200     0.137
8     5            10     0.138
9     2           200     0.139


The lowest out-of-bag error is at mtry = 3 and min.node.size = 50. Larger leaves, as we suspected, suit this noisy outcome better than the default of 10. Let us refit with the chosen settings, and only now check the test set.

set.seed(1)
forest_tuned <- ranger(irregular ~ ., data = train |> mutate(irregular = factor(irregular)),
                       num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE,
                       mtry = best$mtry, min.node.size = best$min.node.size)
tuned_auc <- auc(predict(forest_tuned, data = test)$predictions[, "TRUE"], test$irregular)
round(c(default_forest = model_aucs[["forest"]], tuned_forest = tuned_auc), 3)

default_forest   tuned_forest 
         0.769          0.780 


The tuned forest’s AUC rises to 0.78, level with our hand-made bag of pruned trees. The differences between settings are small, as they usually are. Do not expect tuning to transform a forest. Better features (Section 41.8) usually help far more. One more point: the out-of-bag error measures how close the predicted probabilities are to the outcomes, while the AUC measures the ranking. The two usually agree on what is better, but not always exactly.

title: 43  Random Forests
section: 43.7 When a forest does not help
text:
43.7 When a forest does not help
Forests are not always better. In Chapter 42, irregularity in works contracts followed two simple rules, “short window and few bidders” and “large nomination”. A single pruned tree is exactly the right shape for such data. Let us grow a forest on the same data.

Code to recreate the works contracts of the decision trees chapterset.seed(33)
n_w <- 3000
works <- tibble(
  department  = sample(c("Roads", "Buildings", "Irrigation", "Water Supply"), n_w, TRUE),
  tender_mode = sample(c("Open", "Limited", "Nomination"), n_w, TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1)),
  value_lakh  = round(rlnorm(n_w, log(60), 0.9), 1),
  window_days = pmax(3, round(rnorm(n_w, 26, 7))),
  bidders     = pmax(1, rpois(n_w, 4.5))
) |>
  mutate(bidders = if_else(tender_mode == "Nomination", 1, bidders),
         risk = case_when(
           tender_mode == "Nomination" & value_lakh > 100 ~ 0.60,
           window_days < 21 & bidders <= 2               ~ 0.65,
           window_days < 21                              ~ 0.15,
           TRUE                                          ~ 0.04),
         irregular = runif(n_w) < risk) |>
  select(-risk)
set.seed(1)
w_rows  <- sample(nrow(works), size = 0.7 * nrow(works))
w_train <- works[w_rows, ]
w_test  <- works[-w_rows, ]



set.seed(1)
w_tree <- rpart(irregular ~ ., data = w_train, method = "anova")
set.seed(1)
w_forest <- ranger(irregular ~ ., data = w_train |> mutate(irregular = factor(irregular)),
                   num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)

round(c(single_tree = auc(predict(w_tree, w_test), w_test$irregular),
        forest = auc(predict(w_forest, data = w_test)$predictions[, "TRUE"], w_test$irregular)), 3)

single_tree      forest 
      0.775       0.736 


Here the single tree does as well as, or better than, the forest. The forest’s many deep trees also pick up chance patterns in the noise, while the pruned tree keeps only the two real rules, and gives them to us in readable form. So, as always, compare the methods on test data, and prefer the simpler one when it does as well.


Table 43.2: Choosing between the three methods










Logistic regression
Single tree
Random forest



Ranking accuracy
Good when effects are gradual and separate
Good when risk follows a few simple rules
Usually the best, especially with many features and mixed effects


Explaining the result
Odds ratios, one per feature
Readable rules
Importance and partial dependence plots only


Stability
Stable
Unstable
Very stable


Effort
Needs features shaped by hand
Needs pruning
Works well with defaults












TipAudit tip



Use a forest to rank cases and to learn which red flags matter, and a logistic regression or a tree to explain the selection. A common pattern is to select cases by forest score, and then show, in the audit plan, the importance chart and partial dependence plots, along with a simple tree fitted to the forest’s scores, as a readable summary of what drove the selection.








Note



The isolation forest of Section 50.9 is a cousin of the random forest. It too grows many random trees, but uses them to find unusual records, without needing any past audit outcomes.








Caution



A forest is harder to explain to an auditee, or to a court, than a rule. Never present a forest’s score as the reason for an observation. The observation must rest on what the examination of the case found. The score only explains why the case was examined.

title: 43  Random Forests
text:
43.8 A suggested workflow


Prepare past cases with known outcomes, and split them into training and test sets.

Fit a baseline: a logistic regression and a pruned tree.

Grow a forest with ranger(..., probability = TRUE, importance = "permutation"), with default settings.

Compare all three on the test set, with the AUC and the share caught in the top-ranked cases.

Look inside the forest with variable importance and partial dependence plots, and check them against audit experience.

Tune lightly with the out-of-bag error. For noisy audit outcomes, try larger values of min.node.size.

Score new cases, select mostly by score with a random part, and explain the selection with the plots and a simple summary model.







ImportantRemember




A random forest averages hundreds of trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample with random subsets of features.
Averaging cancels out the mistakes of individual trees, so forests are stable and usually rank well.
The out-of-bag error is a free, honest estimate of performance on new data.
Permutation importance shows which features matter; partial dependence shows how.
A forest is not always better. Compare it with simpler models, and prefer them when they do as well.
crumbs: Part VI: Modelling and Risk Scoring

title: 43  Random Forests
text:
43.9 Try it yourself
These exercises use the refund claims claims, the sets train and test, the forest forest, its test scores forest_score and the function partial_dependence() of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.


A smaller team. Suppose the team can examine only one claim in ten. What percentage of all the irregular claims in the test set falls in the top 10% of the forest’s scores?






TipSolution






ex_capture <- function(score, share) {
  picked <- rank(-score) <= share * length(score)
  round(100 * sum(test$irregular[picked]) / sum(test$irregular))
}
ex_cap10 <- ex_capture(forest_score, 0.1)
ex_cap10

[1] 32


The top 10% of the scores hold 32% of all the irregular claims, against 52% for the top 20%. A random tenth would hold only about 10%. So even a small team, guided by the forest, finds about three times as many irregular claims as chance would give it.





The ten riskiest claims. List the ten test claims with the highest forest scores, with their refund ratio, credit from non-filers and exporter type. How many of them were actually irregular?






TipSolution






ex_top10 <- test |>
  mutate(score = round(forest_score, 3)) |>
  slice_max(score, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(score, refund_ratio, nonfiler_pct, exporter_type, irregular)
ex_top10

# A tibble: 10 × 5
   score refund_ratio nonfiler_pct exporter_type irregular
   <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl> <chr>         <lgl>    
 1 0.842        0.625          7   Manufacturer  FALSE    
 2 0.837        0.494         36.3 Merchant      TRUE     
 3 0.837        0.824         17.6 Manufacturer  FALSE    
 4 0.822        0.512         21.9 Merchant      TRUE     
 5 0.815        0.756         28.1 Merchant      TRUE     
 6 0.811        0.516         11.4 Manufacturer  FALSE    
 7 0.791        0.629         26.5 Manufacturer  TRUE     
 8 0.783        0.127         29.2 Merchant      TRUE     
 9 0.781        0.61          36.2 Manufacturer  TRUE     
10 0.779        0.79          27.8 Merchant      TRUE     

sum(ex_top10$irregular)

[1] 7


7 of the ten were irregular. Most have a high refund ratio, a large share of credit from non-filers, or both. The others were clean, which is a reminder that a score is a chance of irregularity, not a verdict. Each case must still be examined.





Newly registered exporters. Draw the partial dependence of risk on reg_months, the months since GST registration, from 2 to 48 months. Where does the risk change?






TipSolution






ex_months <- seq(2, 48, by = 2)
ex_pd_reg <- tibble(reg_months = ex_months,
                    avg_risk = partial_dependence(forest, test, "reg_months", ex_months))
ex_pd_reg |>
  ggplot(aes(reg_months, avg_risk)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Months since GST registration", y = "Average predicted risk") +
  theme_minimal()







The average risk is about 0.37 for exporters registered two months earlier. It falls steeply until about 12 months, and is flat after that, at about 0.2. This is the planted rule, that registrations under a year old are riskier. Refund claims from newly registered exporters deserve a closer look.





Drop the folklore. Grow the forest again without sector, quarter_end and prior_claims, the three features with no effect. Compare its out-of-bag error and test AUC with those of forest.






TipSolution






set.seed(1)
ex_forest <- ranger(irregular ~ .,
                    data = train |>
                      select(-sector, -quarter_end, -prior_claims) |>
                      mutate(irregular = factor(irregular)),
                    num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)
ex_score <- predict(ex_forest, data = test)$predictions[, "TRUE"]
ex_compare <- tibble(model     = c("All features", "Without the three"),
                     oob_error = c(forest$prediction.error, ex_forest$prediction.error),
                     test_auc  = c(auc(forest_score, test$irregular),
                                   auc(ex_score, test$irregular)))
ex_compare |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4)))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  model             oob_error test_auc
  <chr>                 <dbl>    <dbl>
1 All features          0.137    0.769
2 Without the three     0.137    0.776


The out-of-bag error is about 0.137 with or without them, and the test AUC moves from 0.769 to 0.775. Useless features do the forest little harm, because its trees rarely choose them. Dropping them still makes the model simpler to explain.

44.1 A little history
A district has 30 Community Health Centres. Each has some doctors, nurses and beds. Each treats patients and conducts deliveries. Some centres do much more with what they have. Some do much less. A performance audit wants to know which centres lag behind, by how much, and which records to examine first.
A simple ratio, like patients per doctor, answers part of this question. But a health centre has several inputs and several outputs. A centre may look good on patients per doctor and poor on deliveries per nurse. Which ratio should the auditor trust? And how do we add up patients and deliveries, which have no common price?
Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) solves this problem. It measures the relative efficiency of a set of similar units, like bank branches, schools, hospitals, bus depots or offices. In DEA, these units are called decision-making units (DMUs). DEA finds the best performers in the group. It then compares every other unit with them, using all the inputs and outputs together. It does not need any prices or weights to be decided in advance.
For an auditor, DEA gives three things. It shows which units lag behind, and by how much. It shows which of the best units each weak unit should be compared with. And it gives targets, which turn the shortfall into numbers. These may be patients not treated, or diesel not needed, which can then be valued in rupees.
In this chapter we will first see the idea with a simple picture. We will then learn the functions of the deaR package on a small set of schools of a district. Two audit use cases follow. In the first, DEA finds weak health centres, and also a centre whose figures look too good to be true. In the second, it finds the excess diesel and staff of bus depots, and values them in rupees.
The idea goes back to M. J. Farrell, who in 1957 measured efficiency by comparing each unit with the best performers. Abraham Charnes, William Cooper and Edwardo Rhodes turned it into a practical method in 1978. Rhodes was then studying a large programme for disadvantaged school children in the United States. He had to compare schools which used several inputs, like teachers and funds, to produce several outputs, like test scores. There were no common prices to add them up. DEA was the answer. Since then, it has been used for banks, hospitals, police stations, ports, power plants and many other sectors.

title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
text:
44.2 How DEA works
Let us start with the simplest case, one input and one output. Suppose six offices, A to F, process files (output) with some staff (input). The office with the highest output per staff is the most efficient. Every other office can be compared with it. See the dashed line in Figure 44.1. It passes through the best office and the origin. This line is the efficient frontier, and the efficiency of every other office is how close it comes to this line.







Figure 44.1: Efficient frontiers with one input and one output. The dashed line is the frontier under constant returns to scale. The solid line is the frontier under variable returns to scale.




Office B processes 5 files with 4 staff, which is the best rate, 1.25 files per staff. If we assume constant returns to scale (CRS), that is, doubling the staff should double the output, then every office should achieve this rate. Office D processes 3 files with 5 staff, a rate of 0.6. So its efficiency is \(0.6 / 1.25 = 0.48\), or 48%.
But bigger offices may not be able to keep the same rate as small ones, and very small ones may lack the staff to work efficiently. If we allow for this, we assume variable returns to scale (VRS). The frontier is then the solid line in Figure 44.1, which joins the best offices of each size, A, B, C and E. Each office is compared only with offices of a similar size. Under VRS, more offices are efficient, and the scores of the others are higher, or the same.
With many inputs and outputs, we cannot draw the frontier, but the idea is the same. DEA works out the efficiency of each DMU as
\[
\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{weighted sum of outputs}}{\text{weighted sum of inputs}}
\tag{44.1}\]
The clever part is the choice of weights. DEA lets each DMU choose the weights which make it look as good as possible, with one condition. With these same weights, no DMU may have an efficiency above 1. If a DMU cannot reach 1 even with the weights most favourable to it, it is clearly inefficient. Finding these weights is a linear programming problem, solved separately for each DMU. R does all this for us.
Some terms we will meet are


Efficient frontier. The best performing DMUs, which no other DMU or combination of DMUs beats. Their efficiency score is 1.

Peers (or reference set). For an inefficient DMU, the efficient DMUs which it is compared with. A combination of the peers produces at least the same outputs with fewer inputs.

Lambdas. The weights of the peers in this combination.

Targets. The input and output levels at which the inefficient DMU would become efficient.

Slacks. Extra reduction in a particular input (or increase in an output) needed even after the proportional reduction, to reach the target.

Orientation. An input oriented model asks how much the inputs could be reduced while producing the same outputs. An output oriented model asks how much the outputs could be increased with the same inputs.

Returns to scale. Constant (CRS) or variable (VRS), as explained above.
