title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
text:
44.3 Where DEA helps in audit
DEA is a natural tool for performance audit, which asks whether resources are used economically, efficiently and effectively. It suits any set of units doing the same kind of work, like schools, health centres, anganwadi centres, bank branches, police stations, treasuries or depots. Some uses are


Benchmarking units. Compare districts, offices, hospitals, schools or depots doing the same work. DEA shows which units lag behind, which of the best units they should learn from (their peers), and the targets they could reach.

Selecting units for detailed audit. Units with low efficiency scores, and the ones at the frontier, can be chosen for field visits, instead of a purely random selection.

Quantifying the shortfall. Targets tell us how much more output (patients treated, files cleared, revenue collected) was possible with the same resources, or how many resources were in excess. The excess can be valued in rupees. We will do this for bus depots in Section 44.7.

Testing the reported data. DEA compares each unit with the best reported performance. If a unit reports outputs which are far too good to be true, DEA will put it on the frontier, and it will become the yardstick for others. Such a unit deserves a check of its records. We will see this with health centres in Section 44.6.

44.4 Prerequisites
We will use the package deaR to calculate DEA efficiency, and tidyverse to arrange the results.

library(deaR)
library(tidyverse)

section: 44.5 A first model, schools of a district
text:
44.5 A first model, schools of a district
Let us learn the functions of deaR on a small example from a school education audit.

44.5.1 Our sample data, twelve schools
An imaginary district has 12 Government Senior Secondary Schools (GSSS). For the year 2024-25, we have two inputs and two outputs for each school.


teachers is the number of teachers in position.

grant is the composite school grant released to the school, in ₹ lakh.

pass_10 and pass_12 are the numbers of students who passed the Class 10 and Class 12 board examinations.

We have planted two cases in this data. One school gets poor results for the teachers it has. Another receives far more grant than schools of its size. Let us see whether DEA finds them.

Code to create the school dataschools <- data.frame(
  school   = c("GSSS Amarpur", "GSSS Bhagwanpur", "GSSS Chandpur", "GSSS Dharampur",
               "GSSS Fatehgarh", "GSSS Ganeshpura", "GSSS Hariharpur", "GSSS Jagatpur",
               "GSSS Kherwa", "GSSS Lalganj", "GSSS Madhopur", "GSSS Nayagaon"),
  teachers = c(24L, 31L, 18L, 27L, 22L, 35L, 20L, 29L, 30L, 25L, 19L, 33L),
  grant    = c(12.5, 15.0, 9.0, 13.5, 11.0, 17.5, 10.5, 14.0, 15.5, 19.0, 9.5, 16.0),

44.5.2 Performing DEA in R
Our objective is to find out which schools use their teachers and grants efficiently. We first assume constant returns to scale, that is, results should double if teachers and grants are doubled. We also take an input oriented view, asking how much the inputs could be reduced for the same results.
DEA in deaR is a two step process.


Step 1. We put the data in the form the package needs, using the function make_deadata(). The arguments inputs, outputs and dmus take the column numbers (or names) in the data.

Step 2. We run the actual analysis using model_basic(), which takes the data created in step 1 and two other essential arguments.


orientation is a string, "io" (input oriented), "oo" (output oriented), or "dir" (directional).

rts is a string giving the type of returns to scale, "crs" (constant), "vrs" (variable), "nirs" (non-increasing), "ndrs" (non-decreasing) or "grs" (generalized).
Other arguments may be passed as needed. See ?model_basic for more help.




school_dea <- make_deadata(schools, inputs = 2:3, outputs = 4:5, dmus = 1)
model <- model_basic(school_dea, orientation = 'io', rts = 'crs')

The DEA model is now stored in model. We can use the functions efficiencies(), targets(), lambdas(), references() and slacks() to see its results.

round(efficiencies(model), 3)

   GSSS Amarpur GSSS Bhagwanpur   GSSS Chandpur  GSSS Dharampur  GSSS Fatehgarh 
          0.973           1.000           1.000           0.964           0.988 
GSSS Ganeshpura GSSS Hariharpur   GSSS Jagatpur     GSSS Kherwa    GSSS Lalganj 
          0.989           0.988           0.984           0.622           0.990 
  GSSS Madhopur   GSSS Nayagaon 
          0.962           0.979 


Only 2 schools, Bhagwanpur and Chandpur, are on the frontier, with a score of 1. Most of the others are close behind, above 0.95. One school stands apart. GSSS Kherwa has a score of 0.622. In an input oriented model, this means Kherwa could produce its present results using only about 62% of its present teachers and grant, if it worked as well as the best schools. This is the first school we planted.
Which schools is Kherwa compared with? references() gives the peers of each inefficient school, with their lambdas. Let us look at Kherwa’s.

references(model)[["GSSS Kherwa"]]

GSSS Bhagwanpur   GSSS Chandpur 
        0.33415         0.46192 


Kherwa’s peers are Bhagwanpur and Chandpur. Take 0.33 times Bhagwanpur’s inputs and outputs, and add 0.46 times Chandpur’s. This combination, a virtual school, produces at least Kherwa’s results, with fewer teachers and less grant. The full table of lambdas, for every school, is given by lambdas(model).
targets() gives the levels of inputs and outputs at which each school would be efficient.

school_targets <- targets(model)$target_input
round(school_targets, 1)

GSSS Kherwa         18.7   9.2

Kherwa should be able to produce its results with about 19 teachers instead of 30, and a grant of ₹9.2 lakh instead of ₹15.5 lakh. The efficient schools’ targets are the same as their actual values.
The targets include the slacks. After reducing both inputs of a school in the same proportion, one input can sometimes be reduced still further. slacks() shows this extra reduction.

round(slacks(model)$slack_input, 2)

                teachers grant
GSSS Amarpur        0.00  0.70
GSSS Bhagwanpur     0.00  0.00

GSSS Fatehgarh      0.00  0.17

Look at GSSS Lalganj. Its efficiency score is 0.99, which looks almost perfect. Yet even after the proportional reduction, its grant can come down by a further ₹6.7 lakh. No other school has a slack anywhere near this. Lalganj received ₹19 lakh, more than any other school, although it has only 25 teachers. This is the second school we planted. A high score did not hide it, because we looked at the slacks.
Finally, the plot() function gives three plots, in Figure 44.2. The first shows how many DMUs fall in each range of efficiency. The second shows how many times each efficient DMU is a peer for others. The third draws the network of inefficient DMUs and their peers.
plot(model)









(a) Efficiencies









(b) Times each DMU is a peer









(c) Peers of inefficient DMUs






Figure 44.2: Data Envelopment Analysis Plots



44.5.3 Constant or variable returns to scale?
Let us run the same model with variable returns to scale, and compare.

model_vrs <- model_basic(school_dea, orientation = 'io', rts = 'vrs')

data.frame(crs = efficiencies(model),
           vrs = efficiencies(model_vrs)) |>
  mutate(scale_efficiency = crs / vrs) |>
  round(3)

                  crs   vrs scale_efficiency
GSSS Amarpur    0.973 0.973            1.000
GSSS Bhagwanpur 1.000 1.000            1.000
GSSS Chandpur   1.000 1.000            1.000
GSSS Dharampur  0.964 0.976            0.988
GSSS Fatehgarh  0.988 0.991            0.997
GSSS Ganeshpura 0.989 1.000            0.989
GSSS Hariharpur 0.988 0.994            0.994
GSSS Jagatpur   0.984 0.984            1.000
GSSS Kherwa     0.622 0.636            0.979
GSSS Lalganj    0.990 0.994            0.996
GSSS Madhopur   0.962 1.000            0.962
GSSS Nayagaon   0.979 0.986            0.993


Under VRS, the scores are the same or higher, since each school is compared only with schools of a similar size. Ganeshpura, the largest school, and Madhopur, one of the smallest, now join the frontier. The ratio of the CRS score to the VRS score is called scale efficiency. It tells us how much of the inefficiency is due to the size of the unit rather than how well it is managed. Kherwa’s VRS score is still only 0.636. So its problem is about management, not size.






NoteChoosing between CRS and VRS



Use CRS when units can freely change their size and output should grow in proportion to inputs, as with depots running similar buses. Use VRS when units differ a lot in size and cannot easily change it, as with schools, hospitals or offices whose staff is fixed by sanction. When in doubt, run both and compare.


In a real audit, these two schools would be the leads. For Kherwa, the auditor would look at the posting of teachers, the subjects they teach, attendance, and the results of earlier years. For Lalganj, the auditor would ask why it got the largest grant, and check the utilisation certificates and the purchases made from it.

title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
section: 44.6 Audit use case, efficiency of community health centres
text:
44.6 Audit use case, efficiency of community health centres
Let us now apply DEA in a performance audit of health services. A district has 30 Community Health Centres (CHCs). The audit wants to know which CHCs are making poor use of their doctors, nurses and beds, and by how much.

44.6.1 Our sample data, thirty CHCs
For each CHC we have three inputs, the number of doctors, nurses and beds, and three outputs for the year. These are the number of OPD patients (in thousands), in-patient admissions (IPD), and institutional deliveries. Staff and beds are fixed by sanction, and a CHC cannot easily reduce them. So the relevant question is how much more each CHC could deliver with what it has. We will therefore use an output oriented model with variable returns to scale.
We have planted two kinds of cases.

Three CHCs, CHC-07, CHC-18 and CHC-26, deliver about 40% less than they should, given their staff.

CHC-12 has reported inflated figures of OPD patients and deliveries, more than double its actual work. Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), an incentive is paid for every institutional delivery, so there is a motive to inflate the deliveries.


Code to create the CHC dataset.seed(2025)
n <- 30
chc <- tibble(chc     = sprintf("CHC-%02d", 1:n),
              doctors = sample(4:10, n, TRUE),
              nurses  = round(doctors * runif(n, 1.8, 2.6)),
              beds    = sample(c(30, 30, 30, 50), n, TRUE))

# How well each CHC is managed, between 80% and 100% of the best
managed <- runif(n, 0.80, 1.00)

chc <- chc |>
  mutate(opd        = round(managed * (2.2 * doctors + 0.5 * nurses) * runif(n, 0.92, 1.08), 1),
         ipd        = round(managed * (40 * beds / 30 + 3 * nurses) * runif(n, 0.9, 1.1)),
         deliveries = round(managed * 12 * nurses * runif(n, 0.85, 1.15)))

# Planted. Three poorly performing CHCs
weak <- c(7, 18, 26)
chc[weak, c("opd", "ipd", "deliveries")] <- round(chc[weak, c("opd", "ipd", "deliveries")] * 0.6)

# Planted. Inflated OPD and deliveries reported by CHC-12
chc[12, c("opd", "deliveries")] <- round(chc[12, c("opd", "deliveries")] * 2.2)

chc <- as.data.frame(chc)



head(chc)

     chc doctors nurses beds  opd ipd deliveries
1 CHC-01       8     17   30 23.5  76        160
2 CHC-02       7     16   30 23.2  92        211
3 CHC-03       7     16   30 21.9  87        199
4 CHC-04       5      9   50 15.0  86        108
5 CHC-05       4      8   30 13.1  58         93
6 CHC-06      10     19   50 32.1 107        248








TipAudit tip



Keep the number of inputs and outputs small compared with the number of units. A common rule of thumb is that the number of DMUs should be at least three times the number of inputs plus outputs. With too many variables, almost every unit finds some weights which make it efficient, and DEA can no longer tell them apart. Here we have 30 CHCs and 6 variables, which just meets the rule. Also pass a plain data.frame to make_deadata(), as we did with as.data.frame() above.



44.6.2 Running the model

chc_dea <- make_deadata(chc, inputs = 2:4, outputs = 5:7, dmus = 1)
chc_model <- model_basic(chc_dea, orientation = "oo", rts = "vrs")

In an output oriented model, deaR reports a score \(\phi\) of 1 or more. It is the factor by which all outputs could be increased. A score of 1.25 means the CHC could deliver 25% more of everything. It is easier to read the reciprocal, \(1/\phi\), as the efficiency. A CHC with \(\phi = 1.25\) delivers \(1/1.25 = 80\%\) of what it could. Let us calculate both and look at the weakest CHCs.

chc_eff <- tibble(chc        = names(efficiencies(chc_model)),
                  phi        = efficiencies(chc_model),
                  efficiency = round(100 / phi, 1)) |>
  arrange(efficiency)

head(chc_eff, 6)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  chc      phi efficiency
  <chr>  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 CHC-07  1.64       60.8
2 CHC-18  1.54       64.8
3 CHC-26  1.54       64.9
4 CHC-25  1.30       77.1
5 CHC-23  1.25       79.8
6 CHC-01  1.22       82  


The three weakest CHCs are exactly the ones we planted. They deliver only 60.8% to 64.9% of what CHCs with similar staff and beds deliver. 12 of the 30 CHCs are on the frontier, with an efficiency of 100%.
targets() tells us what the weak CHCs could deliver. Let us compare the actual outputs of CHC-18 with its targets.

rbind(actual = chc[chc$chc == "CHC-18", c("opd", "ipd", "deliveries")],
      target = round(targets(chc_model)$target_output["CHC-18", ], 1))

        opd  ipd deliveries
actual 20.0 63.0      142.0
target 30.9 97.2      234.7



44.6.3 Who sets the standard?
Every inefficient CHC is compared with its peers. Let us count how many times each efficient CHC appears as a peer.

chc_peers <- references(chc_model) |>
  map(names) |>
  unlist() |>
  table() |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)

head(chc_peers)


CHC-12 CHC-02 CHC-21 CHC-10 CHC-14 CHC-29 
    11      9      6      4      4      4 


CHC-12 is a peer for 11 CHCs. It is one of the main yardsticks against which the whole district is judged. Is it really that good? Let us look at its figures next to the average of the other CHCs, per doctor.

chc |>
  mutate(group = if_else(chc == "CHC-12", "CHC-12", "Other CHCs (average)")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(opd_per_doctor        = mean(opd / doctors),
            ipd_per_doctor        = mean(ipd / doctors),
            deliveries_per_doctor = mean(deliveries / doctors)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  group                opd_per_doctor ipd_per_doctor deliveries_per_doctor
  <chr>                         <dbl>          <dbl>                 <dbl>
1 CHC-12                          7.1           11.9                  63.1
2 Other CHCs (average)            2.9           12.1                  23  


Its OPD and deliveries per doctor are about double those of other CHCs, while its in-patient admissions are ordinary. That is strange. More deliveries should mean more admissions.

44.6.4 Super-efficiency
Ordinary DEA gives every efficient unit the same score of 1, so it cannot tell us how far ahead of the others a unit is. Super-efficiency models answer this. They measure each efficient unit against all the other units, leaving itself out. In an output oriented model, a super-efficiency score below 1 means that the unit could reduce its outputs and still be on the frontier. The lower the score, the further it is ahead of everyone else.

chc_super <- model_supereff(chc_dea, orientation = "oo", rts = "vrs")

tibble(chc = names(efficiencies(chc_super)),
       super_efficiency = round(efficiencies(chc_super), 3)) |>
  arrange(super_efficiency) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  chc    super_efficiency
  <chr>             <dbl>
1 CHC-12            0.464
2 CHC-04            0.767
3 CHC-10            0.903
4 CHC-15            0.914
5 CHC-21            0.929


CHC-12 stands far apart. Its score of 0.46 means that it could deliver only 46% of what it reports and still be on the frontier. No other CHC comes close. In real life, such performance is rarely genuine.

44.6.5 Without the doubtful CHC
If CHC-12’s figures are inflated, it has also made the other CHCs look worse than they are. Let us run the model again without it and compare.

chc_model2 <- model_basic(make_deadata(chc[chc$chc != "CHC-12", ], inputs = 2:4,
                                       outputs = 5:7, dmus = 1),
                          orientation = "oo", rts = "vrs")

chc_compare <- tibble(chc   = names(efficiencies(chc_model2)),
                      with_chc12    = round(100 / efficiencies(chc_model)[chc], 1),
                      without_chc12 = round(100 / efficiencies(chc_model2), 1)) |>
  mutate(change = without_chc12 - with_chc12) |>
  arrange(desc(change))

head(chc_compare)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  chc    with_chc12 without_chc12 change
  <chr>       <dbl>         <dbl>  <dbl>
1 CHC-23       79.8          95.3  15.5 
2 CHC-07       60.8          70.3   9.5 
3 CHC-01       82            89.7   7.7 
4 CHC-25       77.1          84.5   7.40
5 CHC-20       83.2          89     5.8 
6 CHC-06       94.8         100     5.2 


The efficiency of 11 CHCs goes up when the doubtful CHC is removed, some of them by several percentage points. CHC-23, which looked like the fifth weakest CHC of the district, goes up from 79.8% to 95.3%. If the audit had reported the first results, these CHCs would have been unfairly criticised.






WarningCaution



DEA compares each unit with the best reported performance, and it has no way to tell an error or an inflated figure from a genuinely good performance. One wrong figure can shift the whole frontier. So always check the units on the frontier, especially those which are peers for many others or have very high super-efficiency, before reporting the results for the rest.








NoteWhat DEA does not see



DEA only knows the inputs and outputs we give it. A CHC in a remote hilly block may treat fewer patients because fewer people live near it, not because it is poorly run. Quality is also missing. Treating more patients is not better if the care is worse. Discuss the results with the department, and add such factors to the analysis where data is available.



44.6.6 What the auditor does next
The analysis gives two kinds of leads, and each needs a different follow-up.


The doubtful CHC first. For CHC-12, examine the OPD registers, the labour room register, the bed head tickets and the JSY payment records. Match a sample of deliveries with the mothers’ addresses and bank accounts. If the figures are inflated, the JSY payments on false deliveries are a recoverable loss.

Then the weak CHCs. Once CHC-12 is verified or removed, take the efficiency scores from the corrected model. For CHC-07, CHC-18 and CHC-26, ask the department why output is low. Check staff attendance, vacant posts, equipment lying idle and the population each CHC serves.

Record the work. Put the model, the inputs and outputs used, the peers and targets of each weak CHC, and the replies of the department in the working papers. Report the shortfall against the targets only where the reasons do not explain it.

title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
section: 44.7 Audit use case, excess diesel and staff in bus depots
text:
44.7 Audit use case, excess diesel and staff in bus depots
In the health centres, the question was about outputs. Now let us take a case where the question is about inputs, and the answer is in rupees. Audits of State Road Transport Undertakings regularly examine the consumption of diesel and the deployment of staff in bus depots. Both are big items of cost. A depot that uses more diesel than others for the same kilometres may have poor maintenance, or pilferage. A depot with more staff than others for the same work is overstaffed.

44.7.1 Our sample data, twenty-five depots
An imaginary State transport undertaking has 25 depots. For each depot we have two inputs for the year, the number of staff and the diesel consumed (in kilolitres), and one output, the effective kilometres operated (in lakh km). We have planted two problems.


Depot-05 and Depot-22 consumed 20% more diesel than they should have, as if fuel was being pilfered.

Depot-02 had 30% more staff than it needed.


Code to create the depot dataset.seed(404)
n <- 25
depots <- tibble(depot   = sprintf("Depot-%02d", 1:n),
                 km_lakh = round(runif(n, 45, 115), 1)) |>
  mutate(staff   = round(km_lakh * 5.9 * runif(n, 0.94, 1.06)),        # about 5.9 staff per lakh km
         fuel_kl = round(km_lakh * 100 / 4.8 * runif(n, 0.97, 1.05)))  # about 4.8 km per litre

# Planted. Excess diesel in two depots
depots$fuel_kl[c(5, 22)] <- round(depots$fuel_kl[c(5, 22)] * 1.20)

# Planted. Excess staff in one depot
depots$staff[2] <- round(depots$staff[2] * 1.30)

# Inputs first, then the output
depots <- depots |>
  select(depot, staff, fuel_kl, km_lakh) |>
  as.data.frame()



head(depots)

     depot staff fuel_kl km_lakh
1 Depot-01   554    2034    99.6
2 Depot-02   642    1717    83.8
3 Depot-03   456    1727    81.7
4 Depot-04   519    1920    92.6
5 Depot-05   425    1801    71.3
6 Depot-06   391    1507    69.0


Here the outputs are given by the routes and schedules, and the question is how much of the inputs was really needed. So we use an input oriented model. All depots do the same kind of work, and more kilometres need proportionally more staff and diesel, so we assume constant returns to scale.

depot_dea <- make_deadata(depots, inputs = 2:3, outputs = 4, dmus = 1)
depot_model <- model_basic(depot_dea, orientation = "io", rts = "crs")


44.7.2 Seeing the frontier
With two inputs and one output, we can actually see the frontier. Let us plot the staff and the diesel used by each depot per lakh km. A depot closer to the bottom left uses less of both for the same work. The efficient depots form the frontier, the blue line in Figure 44.3. Every other depot is compared with the point where the line from the origin to it crosses the frontier.

depot_ratio <- depots |>
  mutate(staff_per_km = staff / km_lakh,
         fuel_per_km  = fuel_kl / km_lakh,
         efficient    = efficiencies(depot_model) > 0.9999)

front <- depot_ratio |> filter(efficient) |> arrange(staff_per_km)

ggplot(depot_ratio, aes(staff_per_km, fuel_per_km)) +
  # the frontier, extended vertically and horizontally from its ends
  annotate("segment", x = min(front$staff_per_km), xend = min(front$staff_per_km),
           y = max(front$fuel_per_km), yend = 26, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = front, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = max(front$staff_per_km), xend = 8,
           y = min(front$fuel_per_km), yend = min(front$fuel_per_km),
           colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = depot %in% c("Depot-02", "Depot-05", "Depot-22")),
             size = 2.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = \(d) filter(d, efficient | depot %in% c("Depot-02", "Depot-05", "Depot-22")),
            aes(label = depot), size = 3, vjust = -0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "red")) +
  labs(x = "Staff per lakh km", y = "Diesel (kl) per lakh km") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 44.3: Staff and diesel per lakh km. The blue line is the efficient frontier.





44.7.3 Excess diesel and staff
Now let us look at the efficiency scores, and the excess staff and diesel, which is the actual minus the target.

depot_targets <- targets(depot_model)$target_input

depot_excess <- tibble(depot          = depots$depot,
                       efficiency     = round(efficiencies(depot_model), 3),
                       excess_staff   = round(depots$staff - depot_targets[, "staff"]),
                       excess_fuel_kl = round(depots$fuel_kl - depot_targets[, "fuel_kl"]))

depot_excess |> arrange(desc(excess_fuel_kl)) |> head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  depot    efficiency excess_staff excess_fuel_kl
  <chr>         <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Depot-22      0.915           52            493
2 Depot-05      0.933           28            345
3 Depot-11      0.939           38            140
4 Depot-15      0.937           36            130
5 Depot-19      0.99             6            100


Depot-22 and Depot-05 have the lowest efficiency, and by far the largest excess diesel, 838 kilolitres between them. At ₹90 a litre, that is about ₹7.5 crore in a year. Now let us sort the depots by excess staff.

depot_excess |> arrange(desc(excess_staff)) |> head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  depot    efficiency excess_staff excess_fuel_kl
  <chr>         <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Depot-02      0.989          156             19
2 Depot-22      0.915           52            493
3 Depot-16      0.969           42             67
4 Depot-11      0.939           38            140
5 Depot-15      0.937           36            130


Depot-02 has 156 more staff than its target. Yet its efficiency score is 0.989, which looks almost perfect! How is that possible? In Figure 44.3, Depot-02 uses very little diesel per km, so it lies close to the flat part of the frontier. Reducing both its inputs in the same proportion takes it to the frontier quickly, and gives a high score. But even there, it still has far more staff than the efficient depot next to it. This extra reduction in one input, beyond the proportional reduction, is the slack.

round(slacks(depot_model)$slack_input[c("Depot-02", "Depot-05", "Depot-22"), ], 1)

         staff fuel_kl
Depot-02 148.7     0.0
Depot-05   0.0   224.5
Depot-22   0.0   277.9


Nearly all of Depot-02’s excess staff is slack. At an average cost of, say, ₹6 lakh per employee per year, its 156 excess staff cost about ₹9.4 crore a year.






TipAudit tip



Never judge a unit by its efficiency score alone. The score measures only the proportional reduction of all inputs. A unit can score close to 1 and still waste a lot of one particular input. Always look at the targets and slacks, input by input, and convert the excess into rupees.








WarningCaution



The targets of almost every depot show some excess, because the frontier is made of the best depots, and normal variation puts everyone else a little behind them. Report only the large and clear gaps, as with Depot-02, Depot-05 and Depot-22 here. Confirm them with the records, like the fuel issue registers, log books, kilometre-per-litre statements and sanctioned staff strength, before calling them excess.



44.7.4 What the auditor does next
Let us put the three depots in one table, valued in rupees, as a draft for the working papers. We use the same assumptions as above, ₹90 a litre of diesel and ₹6 lakh a year per employee. Both should be replaced by the actual rates from the undertaking’s accounts.

depot_finding <- depot_excess |>
  filter(depot %in% c("Depot-02", "Depot-05", "Depot-22")) |>
  transmute(depot, excess_staff, excess_fuel_kl,
            staff_rs_lakh  = round(excess_staff * 6, 1),
            diesel_rs_lakh = round(excess_fuel_kl * 1000 * 90 / 1e5, 1))

depot_finding

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  depot    excess_staff excess_fuel_kl staff_rs_lakh diesel_rs_lakh
  <chr>           <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Depot-02          156             19           936           17.1
2 Depot-05           28            345           168          310. 
3 Depot-22           52            493           312          444. 


The clear gaps are the staff of Depot-02 and the diesel of Depot-05 and Depot-22. Together they come to about ₹16.9 crore in one year. The smaller figures in the other cells come from the proportional reduction of both inputs. Report them only if the records confirm them. Even the clear gaps are a lead, not yet a finding. The next steps are these.


For the diesel. Obtain the fuel issue registers and log books of Depot-05 and Depot-22. Compare the kilometres per litre of each bus with its type and age. Check the stock of diesel at the depot pump with the purchases.

For the staff. Compare the men-in-position of Depot-02 with its sanctioned strength and with the schedules it operates. Ask why staff were not redeployed to depots in need.

Ask the undertaking. Send the targets and the excess to the management, and record their reply. Some excess may have reasons, like hilly routes or old buses. Report what remains unexplained, valued at the actual rates.

title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
text:
44.8 A suggested workflow


Choose comparable units. The DMUs must do the same kind of work, like CHCs of a district or depots of a transport undertaking.

Choose a few inputs and outputs which capture the work. Keep their number small, at most a third of the number of DMUs. Check that more input should mean more output.

Check the data. Look for zero, missing and extreme values before running DEA, as DEA is very sensitive to them.

Choose the orientation and returns to scale. Output oriented when inputs are fixed, input oriented when outputs are fixed. VRS when units differ a lot in size.

Run the model with make_deadata() and model_basic(), and read the efficiencies().

Check the frontier. Count how often each efficient unit is a peer, and run model_supereff(). Verify the figures of units which stand far ahead.

Quantify the gaps with targets() and slacks(), and identify the peers each weak unit can learn from with references(). Value the excess inputs in rupees.

Verify and discuss the findings with the department, keeping in mind factors which DEA does not see.







ImportantRemember



DEA measures relative efficiency. A unit with a score of 100% is only as good as the best of the group, not necessarily good in any absolute sense. And a low score is a lead, not a finding. The reasons for it must be examined before any conclusion is drawn.

title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
text:
44.9 Where next
DEA ranks units on a few chosen inputs and outputs. When units have many measures, Chapter 46 shows how to reduce them to a few. To group similar units before comparing them, see Chapter 47. DEA tells us how efficiently units work. Whether a scheme made a difference to its outcomes is a different question, taken up in Chapter 45.

title: 44  Data Envelopment Analysis
text:
44.10 Try it yourself
These exercises use the school, CHC and depot data of this chapter, and the models built from them. Try each one before you open the solution.


The schools, output oriented. Run the school model again with orientation = "oo", keeping constant returns to scale. Turn each score \(\phi\) into an efficiency, \(1/\phi\), and put it beside the input oriented score of model.






TipSolution






ex_model_oo <- model_basic(school_dea, orientation = "oo", rts = "crs")
data.frame(input_oriented  = efficiencies(model),
           output_oriented = 1 / efficiencies(ex_model_oo)) |>
  round(3)

                input_oriented output_oriented
GSSS Amarpur             0.973           0.973
GSSS Bhagwanpur          1.000           1.000
GSSS Chandpur            1.000           1.000
GSSS Dharampur           0.964           0.964
GSSS Fatehgarh           0.988           0.988
GSSS Ganeshpura          0.989           0.989
GSSS Hariharpur          0.988           0.988
GSSS Jagatpur            0.984           0.984
GSSS Kherwa              0.622           0.622
GSSS Lalganj             0.990           0.990
GSSS Madhopur            0.962           0.962
GSSS Nayagaon            0.979           0.979


The two columns are the same. Under constant returns to scale, the input oriented score and the reciprocal of the output oriented score are always equal. Kherwa, at 0.622, could either use fewer inputs or get more results. Under variable returns to scale, the two orientations can give different scores.





Targets for another weak CHC. Compare the actual outputs of CHC-07 with its targets from chc_model, as the chapter did for CHC-18. How many more deliveries could it have conducted?






TipSolution






ex_chc07 <- rbind(actual = chc[chc$chc == "CHC-07", c("opd", "ipd", "deliveries")],
                  target = round(targets(chc_model)$target_output["CHC-07", ], 1))
ex_chc07

        opd  ipd deliveries
actual 17.0 58.0      148.0
target 30.6 95.4      243.3


CHC-07 conducted 148 deliveries, against a target of 243.3. It could have conducted about 95 more with its staff and beds. Before reporting this, remember that CHC-12 is on the frontier, and its inflated figures may have raised the targets of others.





A simple ratio first. Before DEA, an auditor might simply rank the depots by diesel used per lakh km, and by staff per lakh km. Show the top three depots on each ratio. Do the ratios find the three planted depots?






TipSolution






ex_ratios <- depots |>
  mutate(fuel_per_km  = round(fuel_kl / km_lakh, 1),
         staff_per_km = round(staff / km_lakh, 2))
ex_ratios |> arrange(desc(fuel_per_km)) |> head(3)

     depot staff fuel_kl km_lakh fuel_per_km staff_per_km
1 Depot-22   605    2525    99.5        25.4         6.08
2 Depot-05   425    1801    71.3        25.3         5.96
3 Depot-06   391    1507    69.0        21.8         5.67

ex_ratios |> arrange(desc(staff_per_km)) |> head(3)

     depot staff fuel_kl km_lakh fuel_per_km staff_per_km
1 Depot-02   642    1717    83.8        20.5         7.66
2 Depot-25   404    1399    64.8        21.6         6.23
3 Depot-13   377    1228    60.6        20.3         6.22


Yes. Depot-22 and Depot-05 top the diesel ratio, and Depot-02 tops the staff ratio. With one output and constant returns to scale, simple ratios work well. DEA adds what ratios cannot give, a single score over all inputs and outputs, targets for each input, and peers. With several outputs, ratios would no longer agree with one another.





The actual rates. The undertaking’s accounts show that diesel cost ₹94 a litre and an employee cost ₹7.2 lakh a year. Value the clear gaps again, the staff of Depot-02 and the diesel of Depot-05 and Depot-22, and give the total in crore.






TipSolution






ex_staff_lakh  <- depot_excess$excess_staff[depot_excess$depot == "Depot-02"] * 7.2
ex_diesel_lakh <- sum(depot_excess$excess_fuel_kl[depot_excess$depot %in%
                                                    c("Depot-05", "Depot-22")]) * 1000 * 94 / 1e5
ex_staff_lakh <- unname(ex_staff_lakh)
round(c(staff_lakh = ex_staff_lakh, diesel_lakh = ex_diesel_lakh,
        total_crore = (ex_staff_lakh + ex_diesel_lakh) / 100), 1)

 staff_lakh diesel_lakh total_crore 
     1123.2       787.7        19.1 


At the actual rates, the clear gaps come to about ₹19.1 crore a year, against ₹16.9 crore at the assumed rates. The excess quantities do not change. Only the rates do. This is why the working papers should keep the quantities and the rates separately.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.1 A little history
In 2022-23 a State gave smart classrooms to about 300 of its 1,500 government high schools. Each school got a projector, a digital board and a library of lessons. Two years later the department reports a success. Pass rates in smart-classroom schools are far higher than in other schools. A performance audit must ask whether the scheme really caused this.
This is one of the most common questions in performance audit. Did the scheme achieve its outcomes? The natural way to answer it is to compare the beneficiaries with everyone else. But this comparison is often misleading. Beneficiaries are rarely chosen at random. The schools that got smart classrooms may have been larger, urban and better run even before the scheme. They would have done better anyway. This is called selection bias, and it can make a weak scheme look strong.
Matching makes the comparison fair. It pairs each beneficiary with a non-beneficiary that looked the same before the scheme. If the two still differ after the scheme, the scheme is the most likely reason.
In this chapter we will first make the naive comparison and see why it misleads. We will then try regression adjustment, from Chapter 40, as one remedy. Next we learn the idea of matching with three schools, and then apply it to all 1,500 with the MatchIt package. Our data has a true effect planted in it, so we can see how close each method comes. The first audit use case turns the result into a finding for the audit report. In the second, matching shows that a skill training scheme made no difference at all.
The problem is old. Every comparison of people who chose a treatment with people who did not faces it. In 1983 Paul Rosenbaum and Donald Rubin showed that we need not match on every characteristic separately. It is enough to match on one number, the chance of getting the treatment given those characteristics. They called it the propensity score. Since then, matching on the propensity score has been used to evaluate job training, health insurance, school programmes and many other public schemes.

section: 45.3 Our data, smart classrooms in 1,500 schools
text:
45.3 Our data, smart classrooms in 1,500 schools
An imaginary State has 1,500 government high schools. For each school we know four things from 2021-22, the year before the scheme.


urban is 1 for a school in a town and 0 for a village school.

enrolment is the number of students in Class 10.

vacancy_pct is the percentage of sanctioned teacher posts lying vacant.

pass_2122 is the Class 10 pass percentage in 2021-22.

smart is 1 if the school got a smart classroom in 2022-23. pass_2425 is the Class 10 pass percentage in 2024-25, the outcome the scheme was meant to improve.
We have planted two things. First, schools were not chosen at random. Urban schools, larger schools, schools with better results and schools with fewer vacancies were more likely to be chosen. Second, the smart classroom really does help, but only a little. It raises the pass percentage by exactly 3 percentage points. Our job is to find this 3 in the data.

Code to create the school dataset.seed(123)
n <- 1500
schools <- tibble(
  school_id   = sprintf("SCH-%04d", 1:n),
  urban       = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3),
  enrolment   = round(rlnorm(n, log(60) + 0.3 * urban, 0.45)),
  vacancy_pct = round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 18 - 6 * urban, 10), 0), 50)),
  pass_2122   = round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 68 + 5 * urban - 0.2 * vacancy_pct, 10), 25), 99), 1)
)

# Planted. Selection. Urban, larger, better and better-staffed schools were more likely to be chosen
chance <- with(schools, plogis(-2.15 + 1.0 * urban + 1.2 * log(enrolment / 60) +
                                 0.11 * (pass_2122 - 68) - 0.05 * (vacancy_pct - 15)))
schools$smart <- rbinom(n, 1, chance)

# Planted. The true effect of a smart classroom is +3 percentage points
true_effect <- 3
schools <- schools |>
  mutate(pass_2425 = round(pmin(pmax(
    20 + 0.75 * pass_2122 + 2 * urban - 0.12 * vacancy_pct + log(enrolment / 60) +
      true_effect * smart + rnorm(n, 0, 5), 20), 100), 1))

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.4 The naive comparison
The department compares the pass percentage of smart-classroom schools with that of other schools. Let us do the same.

schools |>
  summarise(schools = n(), mean_pass_2425 = round(mean(pass_2425), 1), .by = smart)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  smart schools mean_pass_2425
  <int>   <int>          <dbl>
1     0    1202           66.4
2     1     298           78.7


The difference looks large. Is it more than chance? The t-test from Section 30.7 answers this.

naive_test <- t.test(pass_2425 ~ smart, data = schools)
naive_test


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  pass_2425 by smart
t = -20.6, df = 438.47, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 0 and group 1 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -13.50236 -11.15035
sample estimates:
mean in group 0 mean in group 1 
       66.39143        78.71779 


Smart-classroom schools passed 12.3 percentage points more students, and the p-value is tiny. The difference is certainly not chance. This is the department’s claim, that pass rates in smart-classroom schools are 12 points higher. Yet we know the true effect is only 3 points. Where do the other 9.3 points come from?
The t-test only tells us that the two groups differ. It does not tell us why. Let us compare the two groups before the scheme, in 2021-22.

schools |>
  summarise(schools        = n(),
            urban_share    = round(mean(urban), 2),
            mean_enrolment = round(mean(enrolment)),
            mean_vacancy   = round(mean(vacancy_pct), 1),
            mean_pass_2122 = round(mean(pass_2122), 1),
            .by = smart)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  smart schools urban_share mean_enrolment mean_vacancy mean_pass_2122
  <int>   <int>       <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1     0    1202        0.22             69         17.7           64  
2     1     298        0.62             92         11             74.2


The chosen schools were already ahead. Their pass percentage in 2021-22 was 10.2 points higher, before any smart classroom was installed. They were also more often urban, larger, and had fewer vacant posts. Figure 45.1 shows the same picture. Most of the “effect” of the scheme was there before the scheme began.

schools |>
  mutate(group = if_else(smart == 1, "Chosen for smart classroom", "Not chosen")) |>
  ggplot(aes(pass_2122, fill = group)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Class 10 pass percentage, 2021-22", y = "Density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")






Figure 45.1: Pass percentage in 2021-22, before the scheme. The schools that were later chosen were already ahead.










WarningCaution



A difference between beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries is a fact. It is not, by itself, the effect of the scheme. Before accepting any such claim, always ask how the beneficiaries were chosen, and compare the two groups on what was known before the scheme.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.5 Adjusting with regression
One remedy is the multiple regression of Chapter 40. We put the scheme and the earlier characteristics in one model. The coefficient of smart is then the difference between schools that are alike on the other variables.

reg_model <- lm(pass_2425 ~ smart + urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122, data = schools)
round(coef(summary(reg_model)), 3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   20.093      0.972  20.677        0
smart          3.102      0.370   8.378        0
urban          1.562      0.309   5.063        0
enrolment      0.014      0.004   3.846        0
vacancy_pct   -0.116      0.014  -8.356        0
pass_2122      0.735      0.014  54.205        0


The estimate falls from 12.3 to 3.1 points, close to the true 3. Regression works well here. It works because we built the data with straight-line relationships, and the model has the right shape.
Real data is rarely so kind. Regression has two weaknesses for impact evaluation. First, it assumes a shape for the relationship, and a wrong shape gives a wrong answer. Second, it happily compares a large urban school with a tiny village school, filling the gap with the straight line. It never warns us that some chosen schools have no real counterpart among the others. Matching avoids both problems, and lets us see whether the comparison is fair. It is also easier to explain to a department. “We compared each smart-classroom school with a similar school without one” is a sentence anyone can follow. This is the reason we treat matching as the main method, and regression as a check.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.6 The idea of matching
Let us start with just three schools.

three <- tibble(
  school    = c("GHS Amarpur", "GHS Bhimpur", "GHS Chandganj"),
  smart     = c(1, 0, 0),
  urban     = c(1, 1, 0),
  enrolment = c(95, 90, 30),
  pass_2122 = c(80, 79, 55),
  pass_2425 = c(85, 82, 58)
)
three

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  school        smart urban enrolment pass_2122 pass_2425
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 GHS Amarpur       1     1        95        80        85
2 GHS Bhimpur       0     1        90        79        82
3 GHS Chandganj     0     0        30        55        58


Amarpur got a smart classroom. Its pass percentage rose to 85. To measure the effect, we need to know what Amarpur would have scored without the smart classroom. We cannot see that. So we look for a school that was like Amarpur before the scheme, but did not get one.
Chandganj is a small village school with a pass percentage of 55. Comparing Amarpur with it would give an “effect” of 27 points, most of which is just the gap between a strong urban school and a weak village school. Bhimpur is urban, of similar size, and passed 79% in 2021-22, almost the same as Amarpur. Bhimpur is Amarpur’s match. The difference between them in 2024-25, 85 minus 82, or 3 points, is a fair estimate of the effect.
Matching does exactly this for every beneficiary. With four characteristics and 1,500 schools, finding a close match is harder. Here the propensity score helps. It is the chance of getting the scheme, given what we knew before the scheme. Two schools with the same score were equally likely to be chosen. One was chosen and one was not, almost as if by a toss of a coin. So comparing them is fair, at least on what we measured. We estimate the score with a logistic regression of smart on the earlier characteristics, just like the risk scores of Chapter 41.
The steps are always the same.


Check balance before matching. How different are the two groups on the earlier characteristics?

Match. Pair each beneficiary with the non-beneficiary closest to it on the propensity score.

Check balance after matching. The matched groups should now look alike. If not, change the matching.

Estimate the effect on the matched data.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.7 Matching in R

45.7.1 Step 1. Balance before matching
bal.tab() from cobalt compares the two groups on each characteristic. We give it a formula with the scheme on the left and the earlier characteristics on the right.

bal.tab(smart ~ urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122, data = schools,
        s.d.denom = "treated", binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

Balance Measures
               Type Diff.Un     M.Threshold.Un
urban        Binary  0.8286 Not Balanced, >0.1
enrolment   Contin.  0.4960 Not Balanced, >0.1
vacancy_pct Contin. -0.8045 Not Balanced, >0.1
pass_2122   Contin.  1.0500 Not Balanced, >0.1

Balance tally for mean differences
                   count
Balanced, <0.1         0
Not Balanced, >0.1     4

Variable with the greatest mean difference
  Variable Diff.Un     M.Threshold.Un
 pass_2122    1.05 Not Balanced, >0.1

Sample sizes
    Control Treated
All    1202     298


The column Diff.Un is the standardised mean difference. It is the difference between the two group means, divided by the standard deviation of the beneficiaries. That is what s.d.denom = "treated" asks for, and it is also what matchit() uses later. This puts all characteristics on one scale, whether they are percentages, counts or yes or no. A common rule of thumb is that a difference below 0.1 is small enough to ignore. Here every characteristic fails the rule, and pass_2122 most of all, at more than one standard deviation. The two groups are not comparable.

45.7.2 Step 2. Matching with matchit()

matchit() estimates the propensity score and finds the matches in one step.

match_out <- matchit(smart ~ urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122, data = schools,
                     method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.2)
match_out

A `matchit` object
 - method: 1:1 nearest neighbor matching without replacement
 - distance: Propensity score [matching, caliper]
             - estimated with logistic regression
 - caliper: <distance> (0.044)
 - number of obs.: 1500 (original), 478 (matched)
 - target estimand: ATT
 - covariates: urban, enrolment, vacancy_pct, pass_2122


The arguments are these.

The formula lists the scheme and the characteristics known before the scheme. Never put anything measured after the scheme here.

method = "nearest" is nearest-neighbour matching. Each smart-classroom school is paired with the one other school whose propensity score is closest. Each school is used at most once.

distance = "glm" estimates the propensity score with a logistic regression.

caliper = 0.2 refuses a partner that is too far away. If no school without a smart classroom has a score within 0.2 standard deviations (of the logit of the score), the smart-classroom school is left unmatched. We come back to these schools below.

45.7.3 Step 3. Balance after matching
Now we give bal.tab() the matching result, and ask it to show the balance both before and after.

bal.tab(match_out, un = TRUE, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

Balance Measures
                Type Diff.Un Diff.Adj    M.Threshold
distance    Distance  1.1768   0.0576 Balanced, <0.1
urban         Binary  0.8286  -0.0086 Balanced, <0.1
enrolment    Contin.  0.4960  -0.0103 Balanced, <0.1
vacancy_pct  Contin. -0.8045  -0.0030 Balanced, <0.1
pass_2122    Contin.  1.0500   0.0814 Balanced, <0.1

Balance tally for mean differences
                   count
Balanced, <0.1         5
Not Balanced, >0.1     0

Variable with the greatest mean difference
  Variable Diff.Adj    M.Threshold
 pass_2122   0.0814 Balanced, <0.1

Sample sizes
          Control Treated
All          1202     298
Matched       239     239
Unmatched     963      59


The first row, distance, is the propensity score itself, which MatchIt calls the distance. The column Diff.Adj shows the differences after matching. All of them are now below 0.1, the largest being 0.081. On what we measured, the matched groups look alike. The table also shows the sample sizes. We come back to the unmatched schools in a moment.
A love plot shows the same thing in one picture, in Figure 45.2. Each characteristic has two dots, one before and one after matching. The dashed line is the limit of 0.1.

love.plot(match_out, binary = "std", abs = TRUE, thresholds = c(m = 0.1),
          var.order = "unadjusted", colors = c("grey50", "steelblue"))






Figure 45.2: Standardised differences between the two groups, before and after matching.




Let us also look at the matched groups in plain units, which is easier to explain than standardised differences. match_data() returns only the matched schools, with two new columns. weights is 1 for every matched school here. subclass numbers the pairs, so each pair shares one number.

matched <- match_data(match_out)

matched |>
  summarise(schools        = n(),
            urban_share    = round(mean(urban), 2),
            mean_enrolment = round(mean(enrolment)),
            mean_vacancy   = round(mean(vacancy_pct), 1),
            mean_pass_2122 = round(mean(pass_2122), 1),
            .by = smart)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  smart schools urban_share mean_enrolment mean_vacancy mean_pass_2122
  <int>   <int>       <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1     1     239        0.55             86         12             72  
2     0     239        0.55             87         12.1           71.2


Now the outcome, in 2024-25, for the same matched schools.

matched |>
  summarise(schools = n(), mean_pass_2425 = round(mean(pass_2425), 1), .by = smart)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  smart schools mean_pass_2425
  <int>   <int>          <dbl>
1     1     239           76.7
2     0     239           72.9


Before the scheme, the matched groups had almost the same pass percentage. After the scheme, the smart-classroom schools are ahead by a few points. This gap is our first rough estimate of the effect.

45.7.4 Schools with no comparable partner
59 smart-classroom schools found no partner within the caliper. Who are they? Let us compare them with the smart-classroom schools that were matched.

schools |>
  filter(smart == 1) |>
  mutate(status = if_else(school_id %in% matched$school_id, "Matched", "No partner")) |>
  summarise(schools        = n(),
            urban_share    = round(mean(urban), 2),
            mean_enrolment = round(mean(enrolment)),
            mean_pass_2122 = round(mean(pass_2122), 1),
            .by = status)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  status     schools urban_share mean_enrolment mean_pass_2122
  <chr>        <int>       <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>
1 No partner      59        0.92            113           83.3
2 Matched        239        0.55             86           72  


They are the strongest schools of the State, mostly large urban schools with very good results. Almost every school like them got a smart classroom. So there is no similar school without one to compare them with. This is called a lack of common support. Figure 45.3 shows it. Above the line are the propensity scores of schools without a smart classroom (0), and below it those of the smart-classroom schools (1). The left panel is before matching. At the high end of the scale there are many smart-classroom schools, and hardly any others. The right panel is after matching. The two halves now mirror each other closely.

bal.plot(match_out, var.name = "distance", which = "both",
         type = "histogram", mirror = TRUE)






Figure 45.3: Propensity scores of the two groups, before and after matching. Above the line, schools without a smart classroom. Below it, smart-classroom schools.




Dropping these schools is honest. Any estimate for them would rest on guesswork, the straight line of a regression, not on real comparable schools. But we must report it. Our estimate applies to the 239 matched smart-classroom schools, not to all 298.






TipAudit tip



The unmatched beneficiaries are a finding in themselves. If almost every strong urban school got the scheme, and almost no weak village school did, the scheme may have gone where it was least needed. Compare the list of beneficiaries with the selection criteria in the scheme guidelines.



45.7.5 Step 4. Estimating the effect
The simplest estimate uses the pairs directly. In each pair, we subtract the control school’s pass percentage from the smart-classroom school’s. The average of these differences is the effect, and a one-sample t-test, as in Section 30.7, gives its confidence interval.

pair_diff <- matched |>
  arrange(subclass, smart) |>
  summarise(difference = pass_2425[smart == 1] - pass_2425[smart == 0], .by = subclass)

pair_test <- t.test(pair_diff$difference)
pair_test


    One Sample t-test

data:  pair_diff$difference
t = 6.7147, df = 238, p-value = 1.371e-10
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.753737 5.040405
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 3.897071 


The average difference within pairs is 3.9 points, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.75 to 5.04.
The matches are close, but not perfect. The vignettes of MatchIt recommend one more step to remove what remains of the differences. We fit a regression on the matched data, with the scheme and the characteristics. Then avg_comparisons() from marginaleffects asks the model a plain question. For each smart-classroom school, how much higher is its predicted pass percentage with the scheme than without? It averages the answers.

effect_model <- lm(pass_2425 ~ smart * (urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122),
                   data = matched, weights = weights)

smart_effect <- avg_comparisons(effect_model, variables = "smart",
                                vcov = ~subclass,
                                newdata = subset(matched, smart == 1))
smart_effect


 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
     3.35      0.469 7.13   <0.001 39.8  2.43   4.27

Term: smart
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - 0


Three arguments matter.


variables = "smart" names the scheme whose effect we want.

vcov = ~subclass calculates cluster-robust standard errors by pair. The two schools of a pair were chosen together, so they are not independent observations. This makes the confidence interval honest.

newdata = subset(matched, smart == 1) averages over the smart-classroom schools only. So the answer is the effect of the scheme on the schools that got it. This is what an audit of the scheme wants to know.

The * in the formula lets the effect differ between kinds of schools, for example between urban and village schools. avg_comparisons() then averages it over the smart-classroom schools, so we need not read the many coefficients ourselves.

45.7.6 How close did we come?
Let us put all the estimates side by side with the truth.

tibble(method   = c("Naive comparison", "Regression adjustment",
                    "Matching, pair differences", "Matching with regression"),
       estimate = round(c(naive_diff, reg_est, pair_est, m_est), 2),
       lower_95 = round(c(naive_test$conf.int[2] * -1, reg_ci[1], pair_ci[1], m_lo), 2),
       upper_95 = round(c(naive_test$conf.int[1] * -1, reg_ci[2], pair_ci[2], m_hi), 2))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  method                     estimate lower_95 upper_95
  <chr>                         <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Naive comparison              12.3     11.2     13.5 
2 Regression adjustment          3.1      2.38     3.83
3 Matching, pair differences     3.9      2.75     5.04
4 Matching with regression       3.35     2.43     4.27


The naive comparison says 12.3 points, more than four times the truth. Matching gives 3.35 points, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.43 to 4.27. The true value of 3 lies inside it. The estimate is not exactly 3, and it should not be. The schools vary from year to year for many reasons, and any estimate from data carries this noise. That is why we report a range, not a single number. (The t-test puts the group without smart classrooms first, so we turned its interval around to show smart minus others.)






WarningCaution



Matching makes the groups alike only on what we measured. Suppose the chosen schools also had more dynamic headmasters, who pushed for the smart classroom and would have improved results anyway. No column records this, so matching cannot balance it, and the estimate will still be too high. Always ask the department how beneficiaries were chosen, and whether anything that is not in the data played a part.
Matching also needs data from before the scheme. Characteristics measured afterwards may themselves have been changed by the scheme. Matching on them would hide part of the effect. If the department kept no records from before the scheme, say so, and be careful with any conclusion.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
section: 45.8 Audit use case, what did the smart classrooms achieve?
text:
45.8 Audit use case, what did the smart classrooms achieve?
We now have all we need for the audit finding. The department claimed a large effect. The evidence shows a much smaller one. A good finding states both, explains the difference in plain words, and gives the effect as a range.

45.8.1 Is a small effect worth its cost?
Suppose each smart classroom cost ₹7.5 lakh. How many more students passed because of the scheme? We multiply the estimated effect, and its two limits, by the Class 10 students of the matched smart-classroom schools.

cost_per_school <- 7.5e5
students <- sum(matched$enrolment[matched$smart == 1])

tibble(estimate      = c("Lower limit", "Central", "Upper limit"),
       effect_points = round(c(m_lo, m_est, m_hi), 2),
       extra_passes  = round(students * c(m_lo, m_est, m_hi) / 100),
       cost_per_pass_rs = round(n_matched_t * cost_per_school /
                               (students * c(m_lo, m_est, m_hi) / 100)))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  estimate    effect_points extra_passes cost_per_pass_rs
  <chr>               <dbl>        <dbl>            <dbl>
1 Lower limit          2.43          500           358262
2 Central              3.35          690           259728
3 Upper limit          4.27          880           203703


The 239 matched schools had 20,629 students in Class 10. The scheme helped about 690 more of them pass in 2024-25. The range is from 500 to 880. These schools cost ₹17.9 crore. That is roughly ₹2.6 lakh for each extra student who passed, in the first year.
Is that good value? Statistics cannot answer this alone. The classrooms will serve later batches too, which lowers the cost per pass. On the other hand, the same money might have filled vacant teacher posts, which also raise results. This is a value-for-money question for the audit to put to the department, with the numbers above as its basis.

45.8.2 Phrasing the finding
A finding based on this analysis might read as follows.

The Department reported that Class 10 pass rates in schools with smart classrooms were 12 percentage points higher than in other schools. Audit observed that schools were not chosen at random. Schools selected for smart classrooms already had pass rates 10.2 points higher in 2021-22, before the scheme. When each smart-classroom school was compared with a similar school without one, the scheme was found to have raised pass rates by about 3.3 percentage points (95% confidence interval 2.4 to 4.3 points). Most of the difference reported by the Department therefore existed before the scheme began. A further 59 beneficiary schools, mostly large urban schools with high pass rates, had no comparable school without a smart classroom, and their results could not be evaluated.

Notice what the finding does. It does not say the scheme failed. The scheme had a real, positive effect. It says the Department’s claim was about 3.7 times the effect, and why. It gives a range, not a single number. And it is open about the schools that could not be evaluated.






TipAudit tip



Keep the matching code, the balance table and the love plot in the working papers. When the department disputes the finding, the balance table is the strongest answer. It shows, characteristic by characteristic, that the comparison was between like and like.



45.8.3 What the auditor does next


Check the selection. Obtain the selection orders and criteria for smart classrooms. Find out whether anything not in our data, like a headmaster’s request or a local representative’s recommendation, played a part.

Check the robustness. Run the matching again with a different caliper, or with two controls for each school (ratio = 2), and with regression adjustment. If all give a similar range, the finding is solid.

Verify use. A small effect may also mean the classrooms are not used. Visit a sample of schools, and check the usage logs, power supply and teacher training.

Raise the value-for-money question with the department, using the cost per extra pass.

section: 45.9 Audit use case, a skill training scheme that made no difference
text:
45.9 Audit use case, a skill training scheme that made no difference
Matching does not only shrink effects. It can also show that a scheme made no difference at all. Let us see this with a skill training scheme.
An imaginary State runs a free three-month skill training course for unemployed youth. In 2023-24, 4,000 young people registered with the State’s employment portal, and some of them joined the course. A year later, a tracer survey recorded whether each of them was employed. The department reports that trained youth were far more likely to find work.
We have planted two things again. Better-educated youth were much more likely to join the course, and they are also more likely to find work anyway. And the course itself has no effect at all on employment.

Code to create the skill training dataset.seed(9)
n <- 4000
youth <- tibble(
  youth_id      = sprintf("YT-%05d", 1:n),
  age           = sample(18:30, n, TRUE),
  female        = rbinom(n, 1, 0.45),
  rural         = rbinom(n, 1, 0.6),
  schooling     = sample(c(8, 10, 12, 15), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.35, 0.3, 0.15)),
  worked_before = rbinom(n, 1, 0.35)
)

# Planted. Better-educated and urban youth were more likely to join the course
youth$trained <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(with(youth, -1.6 + 0.35 * (schooling - 10) - 0.4 * rural +
                                              0.2 * worked_before - 0.03 * (age - 24))))

# Planted. Employment depends on schooling and experience, NOT on the course
youth$employed <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(with(youth, -0.9 + 0.3 * (schooling - 10) - 0.5 * female -
                                               0.3 * rural + 0.8 * worked_before +
                                               0.03 * (age - 24))))



youth

# A tibble: 4,000 × 8
   youth_id   age female rural schooling worked_before trained employed
   <chr>    <int>  <int> <int>     <dbl>         <int>   <int>    <int>
 1 YT-00001    28      0     1        15             1       1        1
 2 YT-00002    22      0     1        10             0       0        0
 3 YT-00003    23      1     1        10             1       0        0
 4 YT-00004    28      1     1        10             0       1        0
 5 YT-00005    25      0     1         8             1       0        0
 6 YT-00006    20      0     1        10             0       0        0
 7 YT-00007    20      0     0        15             0       1        1
 8 YT-00008    29      0     1        10             0       0        0
 9 YT-00009    28      1     1        15             0       0        0
10 YT-00010    29      0     0        12             0       1        0
# ℹ 3,990 more rows


schooling is the years of schooling, where 15 means a graduate. worked_before is 1 for youth who had worked before registering. All these were recorded at registration, before the course.

45.9.1 The naive comparison
Employment is a yes or no outcome, so we compare two rates with prop.test(), from Section 30.4.

youth |>
  summarise(youth = n(), n_employed = sum(employed),
            employment_rate = round(mean(employed), 3), .by = trained)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  trained youth n_employed employment_rate
    <int> <int>      <int>           <dbl>
1       1   847        353           0.417
2       0  3153        991           0.314

naive_youth <- prop.test(x = c(sum(youth$employed[youth$trained == 1]),
                               sum(youth$employed[youth$trained == 0])),
                         n = c(sum(youth$trained == 1), sum(youth$trained == 0)))

41.7% of trained youth found work, against 31.4% of the others, a difference of 10.2 percentage points. The p-value is less than 0.0001. On its face, the course works.

45.9.2 Matching
We follow the same four steps. First the balance before matching.

bal.tab(trained ~ age + female + rural + schooling + worked_before, data = youth,
        s.d.denom = "treated", binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

Balance Measures
                 Type Diff.Un     M.Threshold.Un
age           Contin. -0.0955     Balanced, <0.1
female         Binary  0.0259     Balanced, <0.1
rural          Binary -0.1741 Not Balanced, >0.1
schooling     Contin.  0.7384 Not Balanced, >0.1
worked_before  Binary  0.0555     Balanced, <0.1

Balance tally for mean differences
                   count
Balanced, <0.1         3
Not Balanced, >0.1     2

Variable with the greatest mean difference

 schooling  0.7384 Not Balanced, >0.1

Sample sizes
    Control Treated
All    3153     847


Schooling is badly out of balance, and rural youth are fewer among the trained. Now we match and check the balance again.

match_youth <- matchit(trained ~ age + female + rural + schooling + worked_before,
                       data = youth, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.2)
bal.tab(match_youth, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

Balance Measures
                  Type Diff.Adj    M.Threshold
distance      Distance   0.0212 Balanced, <0.1
age            Contin.   0.0252 Balanced, <0.1
female          Binary  -0.0118 Balanced, <0.1
rural           Binary  -0.0875 Balanced, <0.1

Not Balanced, >0.1     0

    rural  -0.0875 Balanced, <0.1

Sample sizes

All          3153     847
Matched       847     847
Unmatched    2306       0


Every characteristic is now balanced, and every trained youth found a partner. Since the outcome is yes or no, we use a logistic regression, as in Chapter 41, in place of lm(). avg_comparisons() then reports the effect as a difference in the chance of employment.

youth_model <- glm(employed ~ trained * (age + female + rural + schooling + worked_before),
                   data = matched_youth, weights = weights, family = binomial)

training_effect <- avg_comparisons(youth_model, variables = "trained",
                                   vcov = ~subclass,
                                   newdata = subset(matched_youth, trained == 1))
training_effect


 Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)   S   2.5 % 97.5 %
  0.00339     0.0221 0.153    0.878 0.2 -0.0399 0.0467

Term: trained
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - 0


The estimated effect is 0.3 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from -4 to 4.7. The interval includes zero. The 10.2 points of the naive comparison came from who joined the course, not from the course itself. Trained youth found work more often because they were better educated to begin with.

45.9.3 Reading a zero honestly
“No evidence of an effect” is not quite the same as “proof of no effect”. The interval tells us how large an effect could still be hiding. Here the course might at most raise employment by about 4.7 points, and it might even lower it slightly. It certainly does not raise it by anything like the 10 points the naive figures suggest. If the course costs ₹32,000 a trainee, the State spent about ₹2.71 crore on 847 trainees, for no measurable gain in employment.
A finding might read as follows.

The Department reported that 42% of youth trained under the scheme were employed, against 31% of untrained youth. Audit observed that trained youth were better educated than untrained youth even before training. When each trained youth was compared with an untrained youth of the same age, sex, area, schooling and work experience, no difference in employment was found (estimated effect 0.3 percentage points, 95% confidence interval -4 to 4.7 points).


45.9.4 What the auditor does next


Look inside the course. A course with no effect may be poorly taught, in trades with no local demand, or not completed. Check attendance, the trades offered, and assessment and certification records.

Check the placement claims. If training partners are paid for placements, verify a sample of reported placements with employers and with provident fund records.

Report the range. Do not write that the course “failed completely”. Write that it showed no measurable effect, and give the interval.







NoteOther designs auditors may meet



Matching is one of several ways to measure impact. Two others appear often in evaluation reports that auditors read.


Difference in differences. When we have the outcome both before and after the scheme, for both beneficiaries and others, we can compare how much each group changed. The change in the comparison group stands in for what would have happened without the scheme. It also removes differences that stay fixed over time, even unmeasured ones, like a good headmaster who was there throughout.

Randomised pilots. When a department tries a scheme first in randomly chosen villages or schools, the two groups are alike on everything, measured or not. A simple comparison of means is then fair. This is the strongest evidence of all, and auditors may recommend it before a scheme is scaled up.

Both need planning before the scheme starts. An audit can ask whether the department built such an evaluation into the scheme at all.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.10 A suggested workflow


Write down the claim. What outcome did the scheme promise, and what does the department say it achieved?

Find out how beneficiaries were chosen. Read the guidelines and selection orders. This tells you what to match on, and what may be missing.

Collect data from before the scheme for beneficiaries and others, along with the outcome after it.

Make the naive comparison, and compare the groups before the scheme. A large gap before the scheme is a warning of selection bias.

Check balance with bal.tab().

Match with matchit(), using only characteristics measured before the scheme.

Check balance again, with bal.tab() and love.plot(). If any difference stays above 0.1, change the matching, for example with a tighter caliper.

Look at the unmatched beneficiaries. Report how many there are and who they are.

Estimate the effect with lm() or glm() and avg_comparisons(), with cluster-robust standard errors by pair. Check it against the simple pair differences and against regression.

Report the effect as a range, with the claim beside it, and raise the question of value for money.







ImportantRemember




A gap between beneficiaries and others is not the effect of a scheme. Beneficiaries are usually different to begin with.
Matching compares each beneficiary with a similar non-beneficiary, on what was known before the scheme.
The propensity score is the chance of getting the scheme, given what we knew before. Matching on it balances many characteristics at once.
Always check balance before and after matching. Matching that does not balance the groups has not done its job.
Matching cannot fix differences that were never measured.
Report the effect with its range, and say for which beneficiaries it holds.

text:
45.11 Where next
Matching estimates the effect of a scheme. The size of that effect then feeds the value-for-money questions of performance audit, alongside the efficiency comparisons of Chapter 44. For the tests used on the naive comparisons, see Chapter 30. For regression as a check, see Chapter 40, whose section on Simpson’s paradox shows another way a hidden variable can mislead. To present the finding in a reproducible report, see Chapter 65.

title: 45  Measuring the Impact of a Scheme
text:
45.12 Try it yourself
These exercises use the school data schools, the matching result match_out, the matched schools matched and the matched youth matched_youth of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.


A check before the scheme. In Section 45.7.5 we took pair differences in the 2024-25 pass percentage. Take the same pair differences in the 2021-22 pass percentage, before the scheme, and test them with t.test(). What should we expect?






TipSolution






ex_before <- matched |>
  arrange(subclass, smart) |>
  summarise(difference = pass_2122[smart == 1] - pass_2122[smart == 0], .by = subclass)
ex_before_test <- t.test(ex_before$difference)
ex_before_test


    One Sample t-test

data:  ex_before$difference
t = 1.3579, df = 238, p-value = 0.1758
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.3566235  1.9390502
sample estimates:
mean of x 
0.7912134 


We should expect a difference close to zero, because the pairs were chosen to be alike before the scheme. The average difference is 0.79 points, and the 95% confidence interval, from -0.36 to 1.94, includes zero. A large gap here would mean the matching had failed, and any effect found later could not be trusted.





A tighter caliper. Match the schools again with caliper = 0.1. How many smart-classroom schools are left without a partner now, and what is the average pair difference in 2024-25?






TipSolution






set.seed(1)
ex_match <- matchit(smart ~ urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122, data = schools,
                    method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.1)
ex_matched <- match_data(ex_match)
ex_unmatched <- sum(schools$smart) - sum(ex_matched$smart)
ex_pairs <- ex_matched |>
  arrange(subclass, smart) |>
  summarise(difference = pass_2425[smart == 1] - pass_2425[smart == 0], .by = subclass)
ex_pair_test <- t.test(ex_pairs$difference)
c(unmatched = ex_unmatched, estimate = round(unname(ex_pair_test$estimate), 2),
  lower_95 = round(ex_pair_test$conf.int[1], 2), upper_95 = round(ex_pair_test$conf.int[2], 2))

unmatched  estimate  lower_95  upper_95 
    70.00      3.89      2.71      5.07 


With the tighter caliper, 70 smart-classroom schools have no partner, against 59 with a caliper of 0.2. The pair difference is 3.89 points, from 2.71 to 5.07, close to the 3.9 of the chapter. Closer matches cost us some schools, but the answer hardly moves, which makes the finding more solid.





Urban and village schools. Does the smart classroom help urban and village schools alike? Use effect_model with avg_comparisons() as in the chapter, and add by = "urban".






TipSolution






ex_by_area <- avg_comparisons(effect_model, variables = "smart",
                              vcov = ~subclass,
                              newdata = subset(matched, smart == 1),
                              by = "urban")
ex_by_area


 urban Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
     0     4.27      0.709 6.02   <0.001 29.1  2.88   5.66
     1     2.58      0.599 4.31   <0.001 15.9  1.41   3.76

Term: smart
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - 0


The estimate is 4.27 points for village schools and 2.58 for urban ones. But the two intervals overlap, and both include the true 3. So the data does not show that the scheme works better in one kind of school. A difference between two estimates must be judged by their ranges, not by the estimates alone.





Two controls for each school. The chapter suggested matching each smart-classroom school with two schools without one (ratio = 2). Do this, check the balance, and estimate the effect with a regression and avg_comparisons(), as in Section 45.7.5.






TipSolution






set.seed(1)
ex_match2 <- matchit(smart ~ urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122, data = schools,
                     method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.2, ratio = 2)
bal.tab(ex_match2, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

ex_matched2 <- match_data(ex_match2)
ex_model2 <- lm(pass_2425 ~ smart * (urban + enrolment + vacancy_pct + pass_2122),
                data = ex_matched2, weights = weights)
ex_effect2 <- avg_comparisons(ex_model2, variables = "smart",
                              vcov = ~subclass,
                              newdata = subset(ex_matched2, smart == 1))
ex_effect2


 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %

Term: smart
Type: response

Every characteristic is still balanced. The effect is 3.14 points, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.29 to 3.98. This is close to the one-to-one estimate of 3.35, and the interval is a little narrower, because more control schools are used. Two methods agreeing is exactly the robustness check the auditor wants.





The trainees, after matching. For the skill training scheme, compare the employment rates of trained and untrained youth among the matched youth only, with prop.test(). How does the gap compare with the naive one?






TipSolution






ex_rates <- matched_youth |>
  summarise(youth = n(), n_employed = sum(employed),
            employment_rate = round(mean(employed), 3), .by = trained)
ex_rates

  trained youth n_employed employment_rate
    <int> <int>      <int>           <dbl>
1       1   847        353           0.417
2       0   847        346           0.409

ex_employed <- c(sum(matched_youth$employed[matched_youth$trained == 1]),
                 sum(matched_youth$employed[matched_youth$trained == 0]))
ex_youth_n <- c(sum(matched_youth$trained == 1), sum(matched_youth$trained == 0))
ex_youth_test <- prop.test(ex_employed, ex_youth_n)
ex_youth_test
