alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.03980213  0.05633106
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.4167651 0.4085006 


Among the matched youth, 41.7% of the trained and 40.9% of the untrained found work. The gap of 0.8 points is far from the naive 10.2 points, and the p-value of 0.77 shows it could easily be chance. The simple comparison of matched groups tells the same story as the model.

title: Part VII: Finding Hidden Patterns
text:
Often there are no past findings to learn from. The question is simply what in the data does not fit. This part covers methods that find structure, and the cases that break it.
Principal components reduce many indicators to a few. Clustering groups units by behaviour. Association rules find items, or bidders, that go together. Time series show trend and season, and test whether this year’s figures are believable. Anomaly detection, from box plots to isolation forests, ranks the records that stand apart.


46  Principal Component Analysis
Many indicators reduced to a few, to see which units stand apart.


47  Clustering with k-Means
Grouping units by behaviour, and finding those that fit no group.


48  Association Rules (Apriori)
Things that occur together, including collusion in tenders.


49  Time Series Analysis
Trend, seasons and forecasts, and whether this year’s revenue is believable.


50  Anomaly Detection
From robust z-scores to isolation forests and change points.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.1 Where can PCA help an auditor?
Auditors today rarely look at just one number. To judge a hospital, a school, a fair price shop or a taxpayer, we often build ten or twenty indicators. Claims per bed, average bill, length of stay, share of surgeries, and so on. Each indicator tells a part of the story. But reading twenty indicators for hundreds of units, and keeping all of them in mind at once, is very difficult.
Principal Component Analysis, or PCA, helps with exactly this problem. It takes many indicators and combines them into a few new indicators, called principal components. These few components keep most of the information of the original indicators. With just two of them, we can draw every unit as a point on a simple chart, and see at a glance which units behave alike and which ones stand apart.
A simple way to understand PCA is to think of a photograph. A building has length, breadth and height. A photograph is flat, with only two dimensions. Yet a photograph taken from the right angle shows the building quite well. PCA finds the “best angle” from which to look at our many-dimensional data, so that a flat, two-dimensional picture shows as much as possible.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
Profiling units on many indicators. Hospitals under a health insurance scheme, schools on UDISE indicators, fair price shops under PDS, GST taxpayers, or bank branches. PCA gives one map of all units.

Spotting unusual units. Units which lie far from the rest on this map deserve attention. This is a natural extension of the anomaly detection methods of Chapter 50.

Risk-based selection of units for audit. A score built from the components can rank units, instead of looking at twenty separate rankings.

Removing duplication among indicators. Many indicators measure nearly the same thing. PCA combines them, so that the same information is not counted twice. This is useful before clustering (next chapter) and before regression, where highly correlated variables cause problems, as we saw while discussing multi-collinearity in Chapter 40.

Understanding what drives the differences. The components show which indicators move together. This often gives useful insight into how the units actually operate.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
section: 46.2 Our data, an imaginary health insurance scheme
text:
46.2 Our data, an imaginary health insurance scheme
In this chapter and the next two, we will use one common dataset. It belongs to an imaginary State health insurance scheme, which we will call the Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY). Under the scheme, poor families get free treatment at empanelled hospitals. Hospitals treat the patients and then raise claims on the scheme for fixed package rates. For example, an appendectomy is paid at ₹25,000, and an ICU stay can be added on for ₹15,000.
Schemes like this are audited regularly. Typical audit concerns include hospitals admitting patients who do not need admission, discharging them too early, readmitting the same patients to claim again, billing for procedures not done, and adding costly items like ICU stays without need.
The data has three files, all made up for this book. You can download them from the Data folder of the book’s GitHub repository. The code that creates them is in tools/make_health_scheme_data.R.


ssy_hospitals.csv has one row per empanelled hospital.

ssy_packages.csv has the list of treatment packages and their rates.

ssy_claims.csv has one row per claim paid during 2024-25.


library(tidyverse)

hospitals <- read_csv("Data/ssy_hospitals.csv")
packages  <- read_csv("Data/ssy_packages.csv")
claims    <- read_csv("Data/ssy_claims.csv")

Let us have a look at each.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.3 Building indicators for each hospital
PCA works on a table with one row per unit and one column per indicator. So we first build such a table from the claims. Let us think like an auditor and choose indicators that may reveal problems.


Table 46.1: Indicators built for each hospital








Indicator
What it measures
Why it matters in audit



claims_per_bed
Claims in the year per bed
Too many claims for the size of the hospital


avg_claim
Average claim, ₹ thousand
Costly treatment, or inflated bills


avg_los
Average length of stay, days
Very short stays may mean unneeded admission


pct_surgical
Share of claims for surgery
Unneeded surgeries


pct_icu
Share of claims with ICU add-on
ICU billed without need


pct_short_stay
Share of non-day-care claims discharged within a day
Admission only to make a claim


pct_weekend
Share of admissions on Saturday or Sunday
Patients brought in through weekend “camps”


pct_readmit
Share of claims where the same patient was discharged by the same hospital within the previous 30 days
Discharging and readmitting to claim twice


pct_female
Share of female patients
Patient mix


pct_senior
Share of patients aged 60 or above
Patient mix


addons_per_claim
Average number of add-ons per claim
Unbundling, that is, billing separately what is included in a package






First, we add a few helper columns to the claims.

claims_plus <- claims |>
  mutate(main_package = str_extract(packages, "^[A-Z][0-9]+"),
         los = as.numeric(discharge_date - admission_date),
         n_addons = str_count(packages, ";")) |>
  left_join(packages |> select(main_package = package_code, surgical, day_care),
            by = "main_package") |>
  arrange(hospital_id, patient_id, admission_date) |>
  mutate(readmit = !is.na(lag(discharge_date)) &
                   admission_date - lag(discharge_date) <= 30,
         .by = c(hospital_id, patient_id))

A few points about this code.


str_extract(packages, "^[A-Z][0-9]+") takes out the first package code, which is the main package.

str_count(packages, ";") counts the semicolons. A claim with two add-ons has two semicolons.
For readmissions, we sort the claims of each patient at each hospital by date. Then lag() gives the discharge date of the previous claim of the same patient at the same hospital. If the new admission is within 30 days of that discharge, it is a readmission.







TipAudit tip



After a join, always check the number of rows. Here nrow(claims_plus) should be the same as nrow(claims). If a package code appeared twice in the package list, some claims would be counted twice, and every indicator would be wrong.


Now we summarise the claims for each hospital.

indicators <- claims_plus |>
  summarise(n_claims         = n(),
            avg_claim        = mean(claim_amount) / 1000,
            avg_los          = mean(los),
            pct_surgical     = 100 * mean(surgical),
            pct_icu          = 100 * mean(str_detect(packages, "A01")),
            pct_short_stay   = 100 * mean(los <= 1 & !day_care),
            pct_weekend      = 100 * mean(wday(admission_date, week_start = 1) >= 6),
            pct_readmit      = 100 * mean(readmit),
            pct_female       = 100 * mean(gender == "F"),
            pct_senior       = 100 * mean(age >= 60),
            addons_per_claim = mean(n_addons),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  left_join(hospitals, by = "hospital_id") |>
  mutate(claims_per_bed = n_claims / beds)

indicators |>
  select(hospital_name, type, claims_per_bed, avg_claim, avg_los, pct_icu, pct_readmit) |>
  head()

  select(claims_per_bed, avg_claim, avg_los, pct_surgical, pct_icu,

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
section: 46.4 Many indicators say the same thing
text:
46.4 Many indicators say the same thing
Before running PCA, let us see how the indicators relate to each other. The correlation matrix shows this. A correlation close to 1 means two indicators rise together. Close to -1 means one rises when the other falls. Close to 0 means no relation.

cor(X) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("ind_1") |>
  pivot_longer(-ind_1, names_to = "ind_2", values_to = "r") |>
  ggplot(aes(ind_1, ind_2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 1)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))






Figure 46.1: Correlation between hospital indicators




Look at Figure 46.1. Many cells are dark. For example, hospitals with more claims per bed also have more short stays, more weekend admissions and more readmissions. And they have shorter average stays. These indicators are, to a large extent, telling the same story. This is exactly the situation where PCA is useful.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
section: 46.5 The idea of PCA, with two indicators
text:
46.5 The idea of PCA, with two indicators
Let us first understand PCA with just two indicators, which we can draw. Take avg_los and pct_short_stay. They are strongly related, with a correlation of -0.84.
Before anything else, we standardise both indicators. That is, we subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, using scale(). After this, both have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This is important, because PCA looks at variation. An indicator measured in larger units would otherwise dominate merely because of its units.

two <- X |>
  select(avg_los, pct_short_stay) |>
  scale() |>
  as.data.frame()

pca_two <- prcomp(two)

slope <- pca_two$rotation[2, 1] / pca_two$rotation[1, 1]

ggplot(two, aes(avg_los, pct_short_stay)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = 0, colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(slope = -1 / slope, intercept = 0, colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Average length of stay (standardised)",
       y = "Short stays, % (standardised)") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 46.2: Two related indicators, and the direction of the first principal component




The points in Figure 46.2 run broadly from the top left to the bottom right. Hospitals with longer stays have fewer short stays, as we would expect. (The few points at the far top left are hospitals with very short stays. We will meet them again soon.) The red line runs along this general direction. This is the direction in which the hospitals differ the most. It is the first principal component (PC1). The blue dashed line is at right angles to it, across the cloud. This is the second principal component (PC2). Hospitals differ only a little in this direction.
So instead of two indicators, we can describe each hospital by its position along the red line, and lose very little. Let us check how much of the total variation each component captures.

summary(pca_two)

Importance of components:
                          PC1     PC2
Standard deviation     1.3562 0.40077
Proportion of Variance 0.9197 0.08031
Cumulative Proportion  0.9197 1.00000


The first component alone captures 92% of the variation in the two indicators. That is the essence of PCA. When indicators move together, a few components can carry most of their information.
With eleven indicators, we cannot draw the picture. But PCA does exactly the same thing in eleven dimensions. It finds the direction of largest variation (PC1). Then, at right angles to it, the next largest (PC2), and so on.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.6 Running PCA on all indicators
In R, PCA is done with the function prcomp() from base R. The argument scale. = TRUE standardises every indicator before the analysis.

hosp_pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)







WarningAlways scale



Our indicators are on very different scales. avg_claim is in thousands of rupees, addons_per_claim is a small fraction, and percentages run from 0 to 100. Without scale. = TRUE, the indicator with the largest numbers would dominate the result, simply because of its units. Unless all indicators are in the same unit and you have a good reason, always scale.


The result has three parts that we need.


sdev gives the standard deviation of each component. Its square tells how much variation the component carries.

rotation gives the loadings. These are the weights of each indicator in each component.

x gives the scores. These are the values of each component for each hospital.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.7 How many components to keep?
There are as many components as indicators, eleven here. But the first few carry most of the information. summary() shows how much.

summary(hosp_pca)

Importance of components:
                          PC1    PC2    PC3     PC4     PC5     PC6     PC7
Standard deviation     2.4534 1.5424 0.9221 0.67578 0.61716 0.55340 0.52871
Proportion of Variance 0.5472 0.2163 0.0773 0.04152 0.03463 0.02784 0.02541
Cumulative Proportion  0.5472 0.7635 0.8408 0.88228 0.91690 0.94474 0.97016
                           PC8     PC9    PC10    PC11
Standard deviation     0.39076 0.32963 0.21515 0.14368
Proportion of Variance 0.01388 0.00988 0.00421 0.00188
Cumulative Proportion  0.98404 0.99392 0.99812 1.00000


The row Proportion of Variance shows the share of each component. The row Cumulative Proportion adds them up. The first two components together carry 76% of all the variation in eleven indicators. The first three carry 84%.
A scree plot shows the same thing as a chart (Figure 46.3). The function fviz_eig() from the package factoextra draws it.

library(factoextra)
fviz_eig(hosp_pca, addlabels = TRUE)






Figure 46.3: Scree plot, share of variation carried by each component




There are three common ways to decide how many components to keep.


The elbow. Look for the point where the scree plot bends and flattens out. Components after the bend add little.

Cumulative share. Keep enough components to cover around 70% to 80% of the variation.

Eigenvalue above 1. The eigenvalue of a component is the square of its standard deviation. Keep components with eigenvalue above 1, because such a component carries more information than a single original indicator.

Let us check the eigenvalues.

round(hosp_pca$sdev^2, 2)

 [1] 6.02 2.38 0.85 0.46 0.38 0.31 0.28 0.15 0.11 0.05 0.02


In our data, all three rules point in the same direction. Two components carry most of the information, and only the first two have eigenvalues above 1. We will work mainly with the first two.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.8 What do the components mean?
A component is a weighted combination of the original indicators. The weights are the loadings. To understand what a component stands for, we look at which indicators have large loadings, positive or negative.

round(hosp_pca$rotation[, 1:3], 2)

                   PC1   PC2   PC3
claims_per_bed    0.32  0.21 -0.04
avg_claim         0.27 -0.46 -0.06
avg_los          -0.39 -0.08  0.00
pct_surgical      0.37 -0.17 -0.01
pct_icu           0.10 -0.49 -0.50
pct_short_stay    0.32  0.30 -0.08
pct_weekend       0.27  0.33  0.04
pct_readmit       0.27  0.36  0.00
pct_female       -0.17  0.26 -0.80
pct_senior        0.32 -0.27  0.18
addons_per_claim  0.37 -0.04 -0.25


It is easier to see this in a chart (Figure 46.4).

hosp_pca$rotation[, 1:2] |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("indicator") |>
  pivot_longer(-indicator, names_to = "component", values_to = "loading") |>
  ggplot(aes(loading, fct_reorder(indicator, loading), fill = loading > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~component) +
  labs(x = "Loading", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()






Figure 46.4: Loadings of indicators on the first two components




Let us read the two components.


PC1, the “throughput” component. It is high for hospitals with many claims per bed, more surgeries, more short stays, more add-ons, more weekend admissions and more readmissions. It is low for hospitals with long average stays. So a high PC1 means a hospital that pushes a lot of patients through quickly, mostly for surgery.

PC2, “costly care” versus “quick churn”. Its large negative loadings are for ICU share, average claim and senior patients. Its positive loadings are for readmissions, weekend admissions, short stays and female patients. So a low PC2 means expensive care, with many ICU stays. A high PC2 means quick, repeated, low-cost turnover.







NoteThe sign of a component is arbitrary



PCA decides the direction of a component, but not which end is “positive”. Another software, or even another version of R, may give the same component with all signs reversed. The meaning does not change. Only the reading flips. So always interpret a component from its loadings, and never assume that a high score is “good” or “bad” without checking.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.9 The map of hospitals
Now comes the most useful part. The scores give the position of every hospital on each component. Plotting PC1 against PC2 draws a map of all 120 hospitals, built from all eleven indicators.

scores <- indicators |>
  select(hospital_id, hospital_name, type) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(hosp_pca$x[, 1:3]))

ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(colour = "Hospital type") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 46.5: Hospitals on the first two principal components




Several things are visible at once in Figure 46.5.

Public hospitals sit mostly on the left, with lower throughput and longer stays. Private hospitals spread to the right. This is the normal, expected difference between the two.
A small group of private hospitals sits far to the right and up. Very high throughput, with quick churn. These are worth a close look.
Two private hospitals sit at the very bottom of the private group. Costly care, with many ICU stays. They are less dramatic than the group on the right, but still unusual.

Without PCA, we would have had to look at eleven separate rankings to see this.

46.9.1 A biplot
A biplot shows the hospitals and the indicators on the same chart. Each indicator is drawn as an arrow. The arrow points in the direction in which that indicator increases. Hospitals lying in the direction of an arrow have high values of that indicator. fviz_pca_biplot() from factoextra draws it (Figure 46.6).

fviz_pca_biplot(hosp_pca,
                geom.ind = "point",
                habillage = factor(indicators$type),
                col.var = "black",
                repel = TRUE,
                title = "Hospitals and indicators")






Figure 46.6: Biplot of hospitals and indicators




Now we can see why the unusual hospitals are unusual. The group on the right lies in the direction of the arrows for claims per bed, short stays, weekend admissions and readmissions. The pair at the bottom lies in the direction of ICU share and average claim.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
section: 46.10 Audit use case 1, ranking hospitals for audit
text:
46.10 Audit use case 1, ranking hospitals for audit
The map shows the unusual hospitals visually. For an audit plan, we need a ranked list. A simple measure is the distance of each hospital from the centre of the map. The centre represents an average hospital. A hospital far from it is unusual in some combination of indicators.
We use the first three components, which together carry 84% of the variation. The distance is the square root of the sum of squared scores, the usual straight-line distance.

scores <- scores |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2 + PC3^2))

scores |>
  arrange(desc(distance)) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

Now each hospital can be described in plain words in an audit plan. Six hospitals have more than twice the usual claims per bed, less than half the usual length of stay, about four times the usual share of short stays, many more weekend admissions, about three times the usual readmissions, and twice the add-ons per claim. These are exactly the kind of leads an auditor would want to examine first.






TipAudit tip



This ranking is a good basis for risk-based selection of units for audit. Instead of selecting hospitals at random or by size alone, select the top few by distance, along with a random sample of the rest. The random sample protects against the risk of missing problems that the indicators do not capture.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
section: 46.11 Audit use case 2, a composite index
text:
46.11 Audit use case 2, a composite index
Sometimes management or audit wants a single index to rank units, for example a “throughput risk index”. Since PC1 combines many indicators with weights decided by the data, it can serve as such an index.

scores |>
  select(hospital_name, type, PC1) |>
  arrange(desc(PC1)) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  hospital_name                   type      PC1
  <chr>                           <chr>   <dbl>
1 Arpan Hospital                  Private  8.29
2 Prerna Hospital                 Private  8.03
3 Suraksha Nursing Home           Private  7.93
4 Ganga Nursing Home              Private  7.90
5 Madhuban Medical Centre         Private  7.83
6 Kamdhenu Nursing Home           Private  7.71
7 Om Sai Multispeciality Hospital Private  2.40
8 Pragati Nursing Home            Private  2.27


But use such an index with care. Remember that the sign of a component is arbitrary. Also, PC1 is the direction of largest variation, which is not always the direction of highest risk. In our data, PC1 also separates public from private hospitals, a difference which is perfectly normal. An index for risk should be checked against the loadings, and against audit judgement.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
section: 46.12 Audit use case 3, preparing for clustering and regression
text:
46.12 Audit use case 3, preparing for clustering and regression
When indicators are highly correlated, methods like clustering and regression can be misled. In clustering, a group of correlated indicators gets counted several times over. In regression, correlated predictors make the estimates unstable, as we saw with multi-collinearity in Chapter 40.
The principal components are, by design, not correlated with each other. Let us verify this.

round(cor(hosp_pca$x[, 1:4]), 2)

    PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4
PC1   1   0   0   0
PC2   0   1   0   0
PC3   0   0   1   0
PC4   0   0   0   1


All the off-diagonal correlations are zero. So using the first few components, instead of the original indicators, removes the duplication. We will use this idea in the next chapter, where we will group the hospitals into clusters.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.13 Things to keep in mind






WarningLimitations of PCA





PCA works only on numeric data. Categorical columns, like the type of hospital, cannot go in directly. We used the type only to colour the chart.

Extreme units pull the components towards themselves. In our data, a few unusual hospitals strongly shape PC1. This is useful for spotting them. But if your aim is to understand the normal structure, run PCA once more after setting aside the extreme units.

PCA finds variation, not wrongdoing. A unit far from the centre is different. Whether it is wrong can only be decided from records.

Components can be hard to name. Not every component has a neat meaning. Do not force one. Use the loadings and the biplot to describe what you see.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.14 A suggested workflow


Decide the unit and the indicators. Choose indicators that relate to the audit questions. Build them carefully from transaction data.

Look at the correlations. If indicators are not correlated at all, PCA will not reduce much.
Run prcomp() with scale. = TRUE.

Decide how many components to keep, using the scree plot, cumulative share and eigenvalues.

Interpret the components from their loadings. Give them simple names if they have a clear meaning.

Draw the map and the biplot. Look for groups and for units standing apart.

Rank units by distance from the centre, and go back to the original indicators to describe each in plain words.

Verify with records before drawing any conclusion.







ImportantRemember



PCA is a way of looking at data. It turns many numbers into a picture that the human eye can read. It does not, by itself, prove anything. Its value in audit is in pointing to the units, and the indicators, that deserve a closer look.

title: 46  Principal Component Analysis
text:
46.15 Try it yourself
These exercises use the objects of this chapter, the indicators table indicators, the indicator columns X, the PCA result hosp_pca and the scores table. Try each before opening the solution.


Weekend admissions and readmissions. Repeat the two-indicator PCA of Figure 46.2 with pct_weekend and pct_readmit in place of the two length-of-stay indicators. How much of the variation does the first component carry?






TipSolution






pca_wr <- prcomp(X[, c("pct_weekend", "pct_readmit")], scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca_wr)

Importance of components:
                          PC1    PC2
Standard deviation     1.2980 0.5615
Proportion of Variance 0.8424 0.1576
Cumulative Proportion  0.8424 1.0000


The first component carries 84% of the variation. So hospitals with many weekend admissions also tend to have many readmissions. For an auditor, this is one pattern seen twice. It is consistent with patients brought in through weekend camps and then admitted again.





Forgetting to scale. Run prcomp() on X without scale. = TRUE. Which indicator has the largest loading on the first component? Compare it with the variance of each indicator.






TipSolution






pca_raw <- prcomp(X)
round(pca_raw$rotation[, 1], 2)

  claims_per_bed        avg_claim          avg_los     pct_surgical 
            0.04             0.33            -0.03             0.87 
         pct_icu   pct_short_stay      pct_weekend      pct_readmit 
            0.09             0.14             0.10             0.05 
      pct_female       pct_senior addons_per_claim 
           -0.15             0.27             0.00 

round(sapply(X, var), 1)

  claims_per_bed        avg_claim          avg_los     pct_surgical 
             1.5             44.3              0.4            235.4 
         pct_icu   pct_short_stay      pct_weekend      pct_readmit 
            16.4             18.5             16.5              4.1 
      pct_female       pct_senior addons_per_claim 
            27.2             29.9              0.0 


Without scaling, pct_surgical has by far the largest loading on PC1. The second output shows that it also has by far the largest variance. So the first component now mostly repeats one indicator, simply because its numbers are spread widely. This is why we always scale.





Two components or three? Rank the hospitals by their distance from the centre using only PC1 and PC2. Compare the top eight with the top eight by the three-component distance of Section 46.10.






TipSolution






scores_2 <- scores |>
  mutate(distance_2 = sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2))

top_3pc <- scores_2 |> slice_max(distance, n = 8) |> pull(hospital_name)
top_2pc <- scores_2 |> slice_max(distance_2, n = 8) |> pull(hospital_name)

setdiff(top_3pc, top_2pc)

[1] "Navjeevan Hospital"

setdiff(top_2pc, top_3pc)

[1] "CHC Gopalganj-5"

round(hosp_pca$rotation[, 3], 2)

  claims_per_bed        avg_claim          avg_los     pct_surgical 
           -0.04            -0.06             0.00            -0.01 
         pct_icu   pct_short_stay      pct_weekend      pct_readmit 
           -0.50            -0.08             0.04             0.00 
      pct_female       pct_senior addons_per_claim 
           -0.80             0.18            -0.25 


Seven of the eight hospitals are the same. Navjeevan Hospital drops out, and CHC Gopalganj-5 comes in. The loadings of PC3 show that it is mainly about the share of women patients and the share of ICU stays. Navjeevan Hospital bills an ICU stay in 28% of its claims, against a median of 10%. So a ranking on two components alone would have missed a hospital worth checking for ICU billing.





Public hospitals alone. Run PCA on the public hospitals only. How much of the variation do the first two components carry now? What does this tell an auditor?






TipSolution






X_public <- indicators |>
  filter(type == "Public") |>
  select(all_of(names(X)))

pca_public <- prcomp(X_public, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca_public)

Importance of components:
                          PC1    PC2    PC3    PC4     PC5     PC6     PC7
Standard deviation     1.4921 1.4498 1.3074 1.0472 0.98325 0.86188 0.83769
Proportion of Variance 0.2024 0.1911 0.1554 0.0997 0.08789 0.06753 0.06379
Cumulative Proportion  0.2024 0.3935 0.5489 0.6486 0.73649 0.80402 0.86781
                          PC8     PC9    PC10    PC11
Standard deviation     0.7918 0.61004 0.53693 0.40822
Proportion of Variance 0.0570 0.03383 0.02621 0.01515
Cumulative Proportion  0.9248 0.95864 0.98485 1.00000


Among the 48 public hospitals, the first two components carry only 39% of the variation, against 76% for all hospitals. The indicators of public hospitals hardly move together. So there is no strong common pattern among them, and no group that stands apart. This is step 2 of the workflow above. When indicators are not correlated, PCA cannot reduce much.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.1 Where can clustering help an auditor?
In the previous chapter, PCA helped us look at many indicators at once. On the map of hospitals, we could see that hospitals were not spread evenly. They sat in groups. Public hospitals in one area, most private hospitals in another, and a small set far away from both.
Clustering is the task of finding such groups automatically. A cluster is a group of units which are similar to each other, and different from units in other groups. No one tells the method what the groups are. It finds them from the data itself. In machine learning, such methods are called unsupervised, because there is no “correct answer” given to learn from.
The difference from PCA is simple. PCA reduces the columns, eleven indicators into two or three components. Clustering groups the rows, a hundred and twenty hospitals into a few groups.
The most widely used clustering method is k-means. It is simple, fast and easy to explain, which is important when the results go into an audit report.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
Peer groups. A small rural CHC and a large private multispeciality hospital should not be judged against each other. Clustering creates groups of similar units, so that each unit can be compared with its real peers.

Spotting an odd group. Sometimes a whole group of units behaves differently from the rest. For example, a set of hospitals all following the same unusual billing pattern, perhaps run by the same people. Clustering can bring such a group out.

Spotting the odd one out within a group. A unit far from the centre of its own cluster is unusual even among its peers.

Planning audit coverage. Clusters can serve as strata for sampling, so that every kind of unit is covered in the audit.

Segmenting vendors, beneficiaries or taxpayers by their behaviour, to design different checks for different segments.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.2 How does k-means work?
Suppose we want to divide the hospitals into k groups. k-means works in a few simple steps.


Start. Pick k points at random as the starting centres of the groups.

Assign. Put every hospital into the group whose centre is nearest to it.

Update. Move each centre to the average position of the hospitals now in its group.

Repeat steps 2 and 3, until hospitals stop changing groups.

That is all. The final centres are called centroids. Each centroid is like an “average hospital” of its group.
The method tries to make each group as tight as possible. It measures tightness by the within-cluster sum of squares, that is, the sum of squared distances of hospitals from their own centroid. The smaller this number, the tighter the groups.
Since k-means works with distances, the scale of the columns matters a lot. We will meet distances again, in anomaly detection, in Chapter 50. Most importantly, all columns must be on the same scale.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.3 Our data
We will continue with the hospitals of the imaginary Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY), described in Chapter 46 and in Section B.2. We build the same eleven indicators for each hospital. The code is the same as in the PCA chapter, and is folded below.

Code to build hospital indicators (same as in the PCA chapter)library(tidyverse)

hospitals <- read_csv("Data/ssy_hospitals.csv")
packages  <- read_csv("Data/ssy_packages.csv")
claims    <- read_csv("Data/ssy_claims.csv")

claims_plus <- claims |>
  mutate(main_package = str_extract(packages, "^[A-Z][0-9]+"),
         los = as.numeric(discharge_date - admission_date),
         n_addons = str_count(packages, ";")) |>
  left_join(packages |> select(main_package = package_code, surgical, day_care),
            by = "main_package") |>
  arrange(hospital_id, patient_id, admission_date) |>
  mutate(readmit = !is.na(lag(discharge_date)) &
                   admission_date - lag(discharge_date) <= 30,
         .by = c(hospital_id, patient_id))

indicators <- claims_plus |>
  summarise(n_claims         = n(),
            avg_claim        = mean(claim_amount) / 1000,
            avg_los          = mean(los),
            pct_surgical     = 100 * mean(surgical),
            pct_icu          = 100 * mean(str_detect(packages, "A01")),
            pct_short_stay   = 100 * mean(los <= 1 & !day_care),
            pct_weekend      = 100 * mean(wday(admission_date, week_start = 1) >= 6),
            pct_readmit      = 100 * mean(readmit),
            pct_female       = 100 * mean(gender == "F"),
            pct_senior       = 100 * mean(age >= 60),
            addons_per_claim = mean(n_addons),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  left_join(hospitals, by = "hospital_id") |>
  mutate(claims_per_bed = n_claims / beds)

X <- indicators |>
  select(claims_per_bed, avg_claim, avg_los, pct_surgical, pct_icu,
         pct_short_stay, pct_weekend, pct_readmit, pct_female,
         pct_senior, addons_per_claim)


We have 120 hospitals and 11 indicators. As discussed, we first scale the indicators, so that each has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

X_scaled <- scale(X)

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
section: 47.4 A first look, with two indicators
text:
47.4 A first look, with two indicators
To see k-means in action, let us start with just two indicators, which we can draw. We take claims per bed and average length of stay, and ask for 3 clusters.
kmeans() is a base R function. Its first argument is the data, and centers is the number of clusters. Since the starting centres are chosen at random, we fix the random seed with set.seed(), so that the result can be reproduced.

two <- X_scaled[, c("claims_per_bed", "avg_los")]

set.seed(123)
km_two <- kmeans(two, centers = 3, nstart = 25)

as_tibble(two) |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(km_two$cluster)) |>
  ggplot(aes(claims_per_bed, avg_los, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = as_tibble(km_two$centers), colour = "black",
             shape = 4, size = 6, stroke = 2) +
  labs(x = "Claims per bed (standardised)", y = "Average length of stay (standardised)") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 47.1: k-means with 3 clusters on two indicators. Crosses show the centroids.




In Figure 47.1, the method has found three groups, and each cross marks the centroid of a group. One small group sits at the bottom right. These hospitals have many claims per bed and very short stays. The other two groups differ mainly in their length of stay.
Now let us use all eleven indicators.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.5 The nstart argument
Before that, one practical point. Because k-means starts from random centres, a poor start can lead to a poor final result. The argument nstart = 25 asks R to run the whole method 25 times, each time from a different random start, and to keep the best result, the one with the smallest within-cluster sum of squares. Always use a value of nstart of 20 or more.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.6 How many clusters?
k-means needs us to tell it k, the number of clusters. But usually we do not know it in advance. Two common methods help us choose.

47.6.1 The elbow method
We run k-means for k = 1, 2, 3, ... and note the total within-cluster sum of squares each time. It always falls as k rises, because more groups means tighter groups. But after a point, adding one more group helps very little. That point, where the curve bends like an elbow, is a good choice for k.
The function fviz_nbclust() from factoextra does all this and draws the chart (Figure 47.2).

library(factoextra)

set.seed(123)
fviz_nbclust(X_scaled, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8, nstart = 25)






Figure 47.2: Elbow method




The total sum of squares falls sharply up to k = 3, and only slowly after that. So the elbow is at 3.

47.6.2 The silhouette method
The silhouette measures how well each unit fits in its own cluster, compared with the nearest other cluster. It ranges from -1 to 1.

Close to 1 means the unit sits well inside its own cluster, far from others.
Close to 0 means it lies on the border between two clusters.

Negative means it is probably in the wrong cluster.

We calculate the average silhouette of all units for each k, and choose the k with the highest average (Figure 47.3).

set.seed(123)
fviz_nbclust(X_scaled, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8, nstart = 25)






Figure 47.3: Average silhouette for different numbers of clusters




The average silhouette is highest at k = 3. Both methods agree, so we will use 3 clusters.






NoteBusiness sense comes first



These methods are guides, not rules. If an elbow is unclear, or the two methods disagree, try two or three values of k and look at the clusters each gives. Choose the one whose groups make the most sense for the audit. A clustering that you cannot explain is of little use in an audit report.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.7 Running k-means

set.seed(123)
km <- kmeans(X_scaled, centers = 3, nstart = 25)

The result has several parts. The ones we need most are these.


cluster gives the cluster number of each hospital.

size gives the number of hospitals in each cluster.

centers gives the centroids, in the scaled units.


km$size

[1] 48  6 66


The three clusters have 48, 6, 66 hospitals. One cluster is very small. Let us attach the cluster numbers to our indicators table.

indicators <- indicators |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(km$cluster))







NoteCluster numbers are only labels



The numbers 1, 2 and 3 have no meaning by themselves. With a different seed, the same groups may come out with different numbers. Always describe a cluster by what is in it, not by its number.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.8 What are the clusters?
The centroids are in scaled units, which are hard to read. It is easier to look at the average of the original indicators in each cluster. This is called profiling the clusters.

cluster_profile <- indicators |>
  summarise(hospitals = n(),
            public    = sum(type == "Public"),
            across(c(claims_per_bed, avg_los, pct_short_stay, pct_weekend, pct_readmit,
                     pct_surgical, pct_icu, avg_claim, addons_per_claim), mean),
            .by = cluster)

cluster_profile |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)

Now each cluster can be given a plain name.


Cluster 1, public hospitals. All 48 hospitals in it are public. They have longer stays, fewer surgeries, and lower average claims.

Cluster 3, regular private hospitals. 66 private hospitals, with more surgery and higher claims, as one would expect of private hospitals.

Cluster 2, a small and very different group. Only 6 private hospitals. They have more than twice the claims per bed of other hospitals, very short stays, many weekend admissions, about three times the usual readmissions, and nearly nine out of ten of their claims are for surgery.

It is worth noticing that we never told k-means which hospitals are public and which are private. It found this difference by itself, from the indicators alone.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.9 Seeing the clusters
fviz_cluster() from factoextra draws the clusters on the first two principal components, the same kind of map we drew in the PCA chapter (Figure 47.4).

fviz_cluster(km, data = X_scaled,
             geom = "point", ellipse.type = "convex",
             main = "Three clusters of hospitals") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 47.4: Clusters of hospitals, drawn on the first two principal components




The small cluster sits far away from the other two, exactly where PCA showed us the unusual hospitals.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
section: 47.10 Audit use case 1, an unusual group
text:
47.10 Audit use case 1, an unusual group
The small cluster is the most obvious lead. Let us list its members.

indicators |>
  filter(cluster == small) |>
  select(hospital_name, district, beds, claims_per_bed, avg_los, pct_weekend, pct_readmit)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  hospital_name    district  beds claims_per_bed avg_los pct_weekend pct_readmit
  <chr>            <chr>    <dbl>          <dbl>   <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Kamdhenu Nursin… Kishanp…    68           8.19    1.44        34.8        9.34
2 Suraksha Nursin… Devgarh     73           7.88    1.52        35.7       11.7 
3 Prerna Hospital  Devgarh     96           7.85    1.51        36.6       10.6 
4 Ganga Nursing H… Belapur     18           7.39    1.50        36.1       10.5 
5 Madhuban Medica… Haripur     31           8.55    1.54        28.7        9.81
6 Arpan Hospital   Gopalga…    22           7.91    1.44        36.2       11.5 


These hospitals are in different districts, yet they behave in the same unusual way. In a real audit, this would raise some natural questions. Are they owned or managed by the same people? Do they share doctors? Do their patients come through the same agents or camps? The cluster does not answer these questions, but it tells the auditor exactly where to ask them.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
section: 47.11 Audit use case 2, the odd one out among peers
text:
47.11 Audit use case 2, the odd one out among peers
The cluster of regular private hospitals looks normal as a whole. But are all its members normal? A hospital can be very different from its peers, yet not different enough to form a cluster of its own. k-means will simply put it in the nearest cluster.
So we measure, for each hospital, the distance from the centroid of its own cluster. A hospital far from its own centroid is unusual even among its peers. We will meet a similar idea, the kNN distance, in Section 50.7. Here the distance is measured from the group’s centre.

centre_of_own <- km$centers[km$cluster, ]

indicators <- indicators |>
  mutate(dist_own = sqrt(rowSums((X_scaled - centre_of_own)^2)))

indicators |>
  arrange(desc(dist_own)) |>
  select(hospital_id, hospital_name, type, cluster, dist_own) |>
  head(6)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  hospital_id hospital_name                     type    cluster dist_own
  <chr>       <chr>                             <chr>   <fct>      <dbl>
1 H085        Pragati Nursing Home              Private 3           4.48
2 H087        Dhanvantari Medical Centre        Private 3           4.41
3 H104        Navjeevan Hospital                Private 3           4.27
4 H109        Disha Nursing Home                Private 3           3.32
5 H084        Samarpan Multispeciality Hospital Private 3           3.12
6 H097        Prakash Medical Centre            Private 3           2.84


The rows of X_scaled and of centre_of_own match hospital by hospital. So X_scaled - centre_of_own gives the difference of each hospital from its own centroid, for every indicator. Squaring, adding across indicators with rowSums(), and taking the square root gives the distance.
Three private hospitals stand at the top. But why is each of them different? We can find this by looking at which indicators are farthest from the centroid. Since the data is scaled, the differences are in units of standard deviation, and can be compared across indicators.

top3 <- indicators |> slice_max(dist_own, n = 3) |> pull(hospital_id)

(X_scaled - centre_of_own) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(hospital_name = indicators$hospital_name,
         hospital_id   = indicators$hospital_id) |>
  filter(hospital_id %in% top3) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(hospital_name, hospital_id),
               names_to = "indicator", values_to = "difference") |>
  slice_max(abs(difference), n = 2, by = hospital_name) |>
  mutate(difference = round(difference, 1))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  hospital_name              hospital_id indicator        difference
  <chr>                      <chr>       <chr>                 <dbl>
1 Pragati Nursing Home       H085        pct_icu                 4  
2 Pragati Nursing Home       H085        addons_per_claim        1.6
3 Dhanvantari Medical Centre H087        pct_female             -3  
4 Dhanvantari Medical Centre H087        pct_icu                -1.8
5 Navjeevan Hospital         H104        pct_icu                 3.7
6 Navjeevan Hospital         H104        addons_per_claim        1.6


For each hospital, we kept the two indicators with the largest difference from the centroid. A positive difference means the hospital is higher than its peers, and a negative difference means it is lower.
Two of these hospitals, Pragati Nursing Home and Navjeevan Hospital, are far above their peers on the share of claims with an ICU stay. That is a clear lead for an audit of medical records, to check whether ICU care was really needed. The third, Dhanvantari Medical Centre, is different for another reason. It has far fewer women patients than its peers. This may have an innocent reason, for example a hospital that does not offer gynaecology or obstetrics. But under a scheme meant for all poor families, it may also be worth checking whether women beneficiaries are being turned away. Not every outlier points to fraud. But each one deserves a reason.






TipAudit tip



Always ask why a unit is flagged, and write the answer in simple words, as we did above. “Far from its cluster centre” means nothing to an auditee. “ICU billed in nearly three times the usual share of claims” is an observation that can be examined and answered.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
section: 47.12 Audit use case 3, clusters as strata for sampling
text:
47.12 Audit use case 3, clusters as strata for sampling
When we cannot examine every unit, we select a sample. In Section 29.5 we learnt about stratified sampling, where the population is divided into groups (strata) and a sample is drawn from each. Clusters make natural strata, because units within a cluster are alike.
A sensible plan for our hospitals could be this.

Take all hospitals of the small unusual cluster, since the risk there is high.
Take a random 20% of each of the other two clusters.


set.seed(2025)

audit_sample <- bind_rows(
  indicators |> filter(cluster == small),
  indicators |> filter(cluster != small) |> slice_sample(prop = 0.2, by = cluster)
)

audit_sample |>
  count(cluster, type)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  cluster type        n
  <fct>   <chr>   <int>
1 1       Public      9
2 2       Private     6
3 3       Private    13


The sample covers every kind of hospital, while giving full attention to the high-risk group. We may further add the hospitals that stood out as odd ones within their peer groups.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.13 Clustering on principal components
In the PCA chapter we saw that many of our indicators are strongly correlated. When this happens, a group of correlated indicators gets more say in the distances than it deserves. One way to avoid this is to run k-means on the first few principal components instead of the original indicators. The components are uncorrelated, and carry most of the information.

pcs <- prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)$x[, 1:3]

set.seed(123)
km_pc <- kmeans(pcs, centers = 3, nstart = 25)

table(original = km$cluster, on_pcs = km_pc$cluster)

        on_pcs
original  1  2  3
       1 48  0  0
       2  0  6  0
       3  0  0 66


This table compares the two clusterings. Each row is a cluster from the original indicators, each column a cluster from the components. If every row has all its hospitals in a single column, the two clusterings found the same groups, only perhaps with different numbers. In our data, the result is the same either way. With other data, it may not be, and the clustering on components is usually the more reliable one.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.14 Things to keep in mind






WarningLimitations of k-means





You must choose k. The elbow and silhouette methods help, but the final choice needs judgement.

Scale first. Without scaling, the indicator with the largest numbers decides the clusters.

Extreme units pull centroids. A few extreme units can drag a centroid towards themselves, or form a cluster of their own. Here that helped us. In other data, you may want to set aside obvious outliers first.

k-means likes round, similar-sized groups. It may not find groups of odd shapes, or very small groups, like our two ICU hospitals.

Numeric data only. For data with categorical columns, use a method that works with Gower distance, such as pam() from the cluster package, together with daisy(), which we will meet in Section 50.10.

Results can change with the seed. Use set.seed() and a large nstart.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.15 A suggested workflow


Choose the unit and the indicators, guided by the audit questions.

Scale the indicators. If they are strongly correlated, consider using principal components instead.

Choose k with the elbow and silhouette methods, and with business sense.

Run kmeans() with set.seed() and nstart = 25 or more.

Profile the clusters using the original indicators, and give each a plain name.

Look for unusual clusters and for units far from their own centroid.

Explain each flagged unit in simple words, from the indicators that differ most.

Use the clusters for peer comparison and for planning the audit sample, and verify with records.







ImportantRemember



Clustering always produces clusters, even from data which has no natural groups. So a cluster is not a finding by itself. It becomes useful only when it makes sense, and when its members, on examination, really share something.

title: 47  Clustering with k-Means
text:
47.16 Try it yourself
These exercises use the objects of this chapter, the indicators table (which now holds cluster and dist_own), the scaled indicators X_scaled and the k-means result km. Try each before opening the solution.


Clusters on ICU billing. Repeat the two-indicator k-means of Figure 47.1 with pct_icu and avg_claim in place of claims per bed and length of stay. Use 3 clusters and set.seed(123). Which cluster has the highest ICU share, and does it hold the two ICU hospitals of Section 47.11?






TipSolution






two_icu <- X_scaled[, c("pct_icu", "avg_claim")]

set.seed(123)
km_icu <- kmeans(two_icu, centers = 3, nstart = 25)

icu_profile <- indicators |>
  mutate(icu_cluster = km_icu$cluster) |>
  summarise(hospitals = n(),
            public    = sum(type == "Public"),
            pct_icu   = mean(pct_icu),
            avg_claim = mean(avg_claim),
            .by = icu_cluster)
icu_profile

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  icu_cluster hospitals public pct_icu avg_claim
        <int>     <int>  <int>   <dbl>     <dbl>
1           1        56     48    7.62      18.5
2           2        45      0   11.1       30.0
3           3        19      0   17.2       32.6

icu_top <- icu_profile$icu_cluster[which.max(icu_profile$pct_icu)]
indicators$hospital_name[km_icu$cluster == icu_top & indicators$hospital_name %in% icu_two]

[1] "Pragati Nursing Home" "Navjeevan Hospital"  


The cluster with the highest ICU share has 19 hospitals, with an average ICU share of 17.2%. Both ICU hospitals are in it. But they are not alone. They share the cluster with 17 other private hospitals. k-means does not give two hospitals a cluster of their own. To find them, the distance from the centroid is still needed.





Four clusters instead of three. Run k-means on all indicators with centers = 4 and set.seed(123). Compare the result with km using table(). Which cluster was split?






TipSolution






set.seed(123)
km4 <- kmeans(X_scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25)

table(three = km$cluster, four = km4$cluster)

     four
three  1  2  3  4
    1  0  0 48  0
    2  6  0  0  0
    3  0 31  0 35

The public cluster and the small unusual cluster stay exactly as they were. Only cluster 3, the regular private hospitals, is split in two. The profile shows that the two halves differ mainly in their share of ICU stays. Both are large groups. So a fourth cluster adds some detail for peer comparison, but no new lead.





The odd one out in every cluster. Find the hospital farthest from its own centroid in each of the three clusters.






TipSolution






odd_each <- indicators |>
  slice_max(dist_own, n = 1, by = cluster) |>
  select(cluster, hospital_name, type, dist_own)
odd_each

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  cluster hospital_name           type    dist_own
  <fct>   <chr>                   <chr>      <dbl>
1 1       CHC Devgarh-3           Public      2.64
2 3       Pragati Nursing Home    Private     4.48
3 2       Madhuban Medical Centre Private     1.89


The list includes a public hospital, CHC Devgarh-3. The top of the overall list in Section 47.11 had only private hospitals, because the public cluster is tight and its members stay close to the centre. Looking within each cluster makes sure that every peer group gets its own odd one out.





A larger sample, with the odd ones added. Draw the audit sample again with set.seed(2025), but take 30% of each of the two large clusters instead of 20%. Then add the three hospitals in top3, if they are not already in it. How many hospitals are in the final sample?






TipSolution






set.seed(2025)

sample_30 <- bind_rows(
  indicators |> filter(cluster == small),
  indicators |> filter(cluster != small) |> slice_sample(prop = 0.3, by = cluster),
  indicators |> filter(hospital_id %in% top3)
) |>
  distinct(hospital_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

sample_30 |>
  count(cluster, type)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  cluster type        n
  <fct>   <chr>   <int>
1 1       Public     14
2 2       Private     6
3 3       Private    20


The final sample has 40 hospitals. distinct() removes any hospital that was picked twice, once at random and once as an odd one. Every high-risk hospital is in, every cluster is covered, and the hospitals that stood out among their peers are not left to chance.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
text:
48.1 Prerequisites
Some things tend to happen together. A customer who buys bread often buys butter too. A patient who undergoes a heart angioplasty usually needs a stay in the ICU. A firm that bids in a tender may always seem to bid alongside the same two or three other firms.
Association rule mining finds such patterns automatically. It looks at a large number of baskets, and finds which items appear together more often than chance would explain. It then states these patterns as simple rules, like
The method was first made popular for analysing shopping baskets in supermarkets, so it is also called market basket analysis. The most widely used algorithm for it is called Apriori.
The ideas of basket and item are very general. A basket can be anything that groups items together, as these examples show.
In this chapter, we will work through two examples in detail. First, the health insurance claims of the imaginary Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana, which we used in the last two chapters. Second, bids received in tenders, to look for collusion among bidders.
We will use the package arules, along with tidyverse.
library(tidyverse)
library(arules)

text:
NoteA name clash



arules has some functions with the same names as functions in base R or tidyverse. If you load it after tidyverse and later get a strange error from a familiar function, call the function with its package name, like dplyr::recode(). We discussed such conflicts in the section on packages and libraries in the first chapter.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
section: 48.2 Example 1, packages billed together in health claims
text:
48.2 Example 1, packages billed together in health claims

48.2.1 The data as baskets
Let us read the claims of the SSY scheme. The data is described in Chapter 46 and Section B.2.

claims   <- read_csv("Data/ssy_claims.csv")
packages <- read_csv("Data/ssy_packages.csv")

claims |>
  select(claim_id, hospital_id, packages) |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  claim_id hospital_id packages
  <chr>    <chr>       <chr>   
1 CL000001 H001        M04     
2 CL000002 H001        G02     
3 CL000003 H001        S01;A04 
4 CL000004 H001        M04     
5 CL000005 H001        M01;A01 
6 CL000006 H001        M02;A02 


Each claim is a basket. Its items are the packages in the packages column, separated by ;. The first package is the main treatment, and the rest are add-ons. Let us recall the codes.

packages |>
  select(package_code, package_name) |>
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 21 × 2
   package_code package_name                   
   <chr>        <chr>                          
 1 M01          Acute febrile illness          
 2 M02          Acute gastroenteritis          
 3 M03          Pneumonia                      
 4 M04          Dengue fever                   
 5 M05          Diabetic ketoacidosis          
 6 S01          Appendectomy                   
 7 S02          Inguinal hernia repair         
 8 S03          Laparoscopic cholecystectomy   
 9 G01          Hysterectomy                   
10 G02          Caesarean delivery             
11 G03          Normal delivery                
12 O01          Cataract surgery with lens     
13 R01          Total knee replacement         
14 R02          Fracture fixation              
15 C01          Coronary angioplasty           
16 A01          ICU stay (add-on)              
17 A02          Blood transfusion (add-on)     
18 A03          CT scan (add-on)               
19 A04          Ultrasound abdomen (add-on)    
20 A05          Diagnostic laparoscopy (add-on)
21 A06          Intraocular lens (add-on)      


arules needs the data in a special format, called transactions. The simplest way to create it is from a list, where each element of the list is the vector of items of one basket. str_split() from stringr gives us exactly that.

baskets <- str_split(claims$packages, ";")
names(baskets) <- claims$claim_id

baskets[1:3]

$CL000001
[1] "M04"

$CL000002
[1] "G02"

$CL000003
[1] "S01" "A04"


Now we convert the list into transactions with the function transactions().

trans <- transactions(baskets)
trans

transactions in sparse format with
 33476 transactions (rows) and
 21 items (columns)


So we have 33,476 transactions (claims) and 21 distinct items (packages). summary() gives more details.

summary(trans)

most frequent items:

element (itemset/transaction) length distribution:

23450  9046   951    29

1      CL000001
2      CL000002

The part element (itemset/transaction) length distribution shows how many claims have 1, 2, 3 or 4 packages. Most claims have just one package, the main treatment. The rest have one or more add-ons.
We can see how often each item appears with itemFrequencyPlot() (Figure 48.1).

itemFrequencyPlot(trans, topN = 21, col = "steelblue",
                  main = "Packages in claims", ylab = "Share of claims")






Figure 48.1: Share of claims containing each package





48.2.2 Three measures, support, confidence and lift
Before running Apriori, we must understand three simple measures. Let us take one rule as an example.

{C01} => {A01}, that is, if a claim has a coronary angioplasty (C01), then it also has an ICU stay (A01).

The left side, {C01}, is called the antecedent or lhs (left-hand side). The right side, {A01}, is the consequent or rhs (right-hand side). Let us count the claims we need.

has_C01 <- str_detect(claims$packages, "C01")
has_A01 <- str_detect(claims$packages, "A01")

n_total <- nrow(claims)
n_C01   <- sum(has_C01)
n_A01   <- sum(has_A01)
n_both  <- sum(has_C01 & has_A01)

c(total = n_total, C01 = n_C01, A01 = n_A01, both = n_both)

total   C01   A01  both 
33476  1010  3303   897 


Support is the share of all baskets that contain both sides of the rule. It tells how common the pattern is.

support <- n_both / n_total
support

[1] 0.02679532


About 2.7% of all claims have both an angioplasty and an ICU stay.
Confidence is the share of baskets with the left side that also have the right side. It tells how reliable the rule is.

confidence <- n_both / n_C01
confidence

[1] 0.8881188


Of all claims with an angioplasty, 89% also have an ICU stay.
Lift compares the confidence with how common the right side is anyway. It tells whether the two items are really linked, or just both common.

lift <- confidence / (n_A01 / n_total)
lift

[1] 9.00111


Only 10% of all claims have an ICU stay. But among angioplasty claims, 89% do. That is 9 times more than usual. So the lift is 9.


Table 48.2: How to read lift







Lift
Meaning



Close to 1
The items appear together about as often as chance would give. No real link.


Well above 1
The items appear together much more often than chance. A real link.


Below 1
The items tend to avoid each other.












TipWhich measure matters most in audit?



Support tells how big a pattern is. Confidence tells how dependable it is. Lift tells how surprising it is. For finding irregularities, lift and confidence are usually more useful than support. A fraud often involves a small number of records, so its support is low. What gives it away is that, within those records, the pattern is very strong and very unusual.



48.2.3 Running Apriori
Finding all rules by counting, as we did above, would take very long. There are a huge number of possible combinations of items. The Apriori algorithm speeds this up with one clever idea. If a combination of items is rare, then any bigger combination that includes it must be rarer still. So it never needs to look at those bigger combinations at all.
We call the function apriori(), and give it three limits through the parameter argument.


supp is the minimum support. Rules rarer than this are ignored.

conf is the minimum confidence.

minlen = 2 asks for rules with at least two items in all, so that rules have something on both sides.


claim_rules <- apriori(trans,
                       parameter = list(supp = 0.002, conf = 0.2, minlen = 2),
                       control = list(verbose = FALSE))
claim_rules

set of 25 rules 


The argument control = list(verbose = FALSE) only stops the function from printing its progress. A minimum support of 0.002 means a pattern must appear in at least 0.2% of claims, that is, in about 67 claims.

48.2.4 Reading the rules
inspect() prints the rules. Let us sort them by lift and look at the top ones.

inspect(head(sort(claim_rules, by = "lift"), 12))

rules_df <- DATAFRAME(claim_rules) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

rules_df |>
  arrange(desc(lift)) |>
  select(LHS, RHS, support, confidence, lift, count) |>
  head(12)

# A tibble: 12 × 6
   LHS       RHS   support confidence  lift count
   <fct>     <fct>   <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1 {A05}     {S01}   0.007      1     14.8    229
 2 {A04,A05} {S01}   0.002      1     14.8     68
 3 {A01,A02} {R01}   0.002      0.471 14.4     82
 4 {A06}     {O01}   0.017      1     11.6    562
 5 {C01}     {A01}   0.027      0.888  9.00   897
 6 {A01}     {C01}   0.027      0.272  9.00   897
 7 {S03}     {A04}   0.037      0.687  8.27  1223
 8 {A04}     {S03}   0.037      0.44   8.27  1223

10 {A01,R01} {A02}   0.002      0.412  7.55    82
11 {R01}     {A02}   0.013      0.391  7.16   430
12 {A02}     {R01}   0.013      0.235  7.16   430


Most of these rules make medical sense. They tell us what normal billing looks like in this scheme.


{C01} => {A01}. An angioplasty is usually followed by an ICU stay.

{S03} => {A04}. A gall bladder surgery usually comes with an ultrasound of the abdomen.

{R01} => {A02}. Knee replacements often need a blood transfusion.

{A01, A03} => {M03}. Claims with both an ICU stay and a CT scan are often for pneumonia.

This is useful in itself. An auditor new to a sector can quickly learn its normal patterns from the data.
But two rules near the top of the list are of a different kind.


{A06} => {O01}. The intraocular lens add-on is always billed with cataract surgery. Confidence 1.

{A05} => {S01}. The diagnostic laparoscopy add-on is always billed with an appendectomy. Confidence 1.

Why are these suspicious? Look at the name of package O01. It is Cataract surgery with lens. The lens is already included in the package rate. Billing it again as a separate add-on is unbundling, that is, charging separately for something already paid for in the package. Similarly, a diagnostic laparoscopy before an appendectomy is rarely needed, because the diagnosis is usually clear by then.






ImportantThe algorithm finds the pattern, the auditor judges it



Apriori did not know that the lens was included in the cataract package. It only found that A06 never appears without O01. The auditor, who reads the package definitions, recognises that this is double billing. Association rules are a search tool. The audit judgement comes from knowledge of the rules of the scheme.



48.2.5 Where does the pattern come from?
A pattern in the whole data may come from all hospitals, or only from a few. Let us look at the confidence of {O01} => {A06} separately for each hospital. That is, the share of each hospital’s cataract claims which also bill the separate lens.

claims |>
  filter(str_detect(packages, "O01")) |>
  summarise(cataract_claims = n(),
            with_lens_addon = sum(str_detect(packages, "A06")),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  mutate(confidence = round(with_lens_addon / cataract_claims, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(confidence)) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  hospital_id cataract_claims with_lens_addon confidence
  <chr>                 <int>           <int>      <dbl>
1 H098                     74              65       0.88
2 H070                    206             176       0.85
3 H066                    166             132       0.8 
4 H063                    161             127       0.79
5 H116                     47              34       0.72
6 H071                     39              28       0.72
7 H012                     24               0       0   
8 H056                     18               0       0   


The picture is now very clear. In 6 hospitals, most cataract claims also bill the lens separately. In every other hospital, not a single one does. Let us check the laparoscopy add-on in the same way.

claims |>
  filter(str_detect(packages, "A05|A06")) |>
  count(hospital_id,
        addon = if_else(str_detect(packages, "A06"), "A06 lens", "A05 laparoscopy")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = addon, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  hospital_id `A05 laparoscopy` `A06 lens`
  <chr>                   <int>      <int>
1 H063                       55        127
2 H066                       44        132
3 H070                       62        176
4 H071                       14         28
5 H098                       31         65
6 H116                       23         34


The same hospitals bill both of these add-ons. These are the high-volume “camp” hospitals that PCA and k-means picked out in the previous two chapters. Now we also know one specific way in which they inflate their claims, and we can work out the money involved.

rate <- setNames(packages$rate, packages$package_code)

claims |>
  summarise(lens_addons = sum(str_detect(packages, "A06")),
            laparoscopy_addons = sum(str_detect(packages, "A05"))) |>
  mutate(amount_lens = lens_addons * rate["A06"],
         amount_laparoscopy = laparoscopy_addons * rate["A05"],
         total_amount = amount_lens + amount_laparoscopy)

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  lens_addons laparoscopy_addons amount_lens amount_laparoscopy total_amount
        <int>              <int>       <dbl>              <dbl>        <dbl>
1         562                229     2248000            2748000      4996000


The separate lens alone accounts for ₹22.48 lakh, which is wholly inadmissible. The laparoscopy add-ons need examination of case records, claim by claim.






TipAudit tip



Once association rules reveal a pattern, turn it into a simple, permanent check. For example, “flag every claim which has both O01 and A06”. Such checks can be run on the whole data every month, by the scheme authorities themselves, without any machine learning. This is how analytics in audit leads to better internal controls.



48.2.6 Looking at a specific item
Sometimes we want rules about one particular item only. subset() filters rules, and the operator %in% checks whether a rule’s side contains a given item. Let us find all rules that lead to an ICU stay.

icu_rules <- subset(claim_rules, rhs %in% "A01")
inspect(sort(icu_rules, by = "lift"))

    lhs           rhs   support     confidence coverage   lift     count
[1] {C01}      => {A01} 0.026795316 0.8881188  0.03017087 9.001110 897  
[2] {M05}      => {A01} 0.017385590 0.4084211  0.04256781 4.139359 582  
[3] {A03, M03} => {A01} 0.004301589 0.2051282  0.02097025 2.078980 144  
[4] {M03}      => {A01} 0.013950293 0.2050944  0.06801888 2.078638 467  


These are the treatments after which an ICU stay is common, like angioplasty and diabetic ketoacidosis. An auditor can compare each hospital against these normal patterns. For example, ICU stays billed after a simple fever or gastroenteritis would stand out. This is how the two ICU “upcoders” of the earlier chapters could be examined claim by claim.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
section: 48.3 Audit use case, collusion among bidders in tenders
text:
48.3 Audit use case, collusion among bidders in tenders
Bid rigging is one of the most damaging frauds in public procurement. A group of firms, called a cartel, agree among themselves who will win a tender. The others put in higher bids, just to make the tender look competitive. These are called cover bids. Next time, another member of the group wins. This is called bid rotation. The government ends up paying more than it would in a truly competitive tender.
Cartels leave traces in the data. The most basic trace is that the same firms keep turning up together in the same tenders. This is exactly the kind of pattern association rules can find. Here, each tender is a basket, and the firms that bid in it are the items.

48.3.1 The data
Let us create bid data for 400 tenders of an imaginary works department. There are 40 firms. A cartel of a few firms has been planted, and the code is folded below.

Code to create the tender and bid dataset.seed(77)

firms  <- sprintf("F%02d", 1:40)
cartel <- c("F07", "F12", "F19", "F23")

make_tender <- function(t) {
  est <- round(runif(1, 10, 200), 1)            # estimated cost, Rs lakh
  if (t %% 8 == 0) {
    # A cartel tender. Members bid together, take turns to win,
    # and quote close to the estimate. The others give cover bids.
    winner <- cartel[((t %/% 8) - 1) %% 4 + 1]
    win_bid <- est * runif(1, 0.97, 1.03)
    bidders <- c(winner, setdiff(cartel, winner))
    bids <- c(win_bid, win_bid * runif(3, 1.02, 1.06))
    if (runif(1) < 0.4) {                        # sometimes an outsider also bids
      bidders <- c(bidders, sample(setdiff(firms, cartel), 1))
      bids <- c(bids, est * runif(1, 1.05, 1.15))
    }
  } else {
    # A normal, competitive tender
    k <- sample(3:7, 1)
    bidders <- sample(firms, k)
    bids <- est * runif(k, 0.80, 1.05)
  }
  tibble(tender_id = sprintf("T%03d", t), estimate = est,
         firm = bidders, bid = round(bids, 2))
}

bids <- map(1:400, make_tender) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(rank = rank(bid), .by = tender_id) |>
  arrange(tender_id, rank)



head(bids, 10)

48.3.2 Firms as baskets
As before, we make a list of the firms in each tender, and convert it to transactions.

tender_trans <- transactions(split(bids$firm, bids$tender_id))
summary(tender_trans)

split(x, f) divides the vector x into groups defined by f. So split(bids$firm, bids$tender_id) gives a list with one element per tender, holding the firms that bid in it. This is another easy way of making baskets.

48.3.3 Frequent itemsets
Before rules, it is often useful to look at frequent itemsets. These are groups of items that appear together in many baskets. We get them from the same apriori() function, by setting target = "frequent itemsets". Let us ask for groups of at least two firms which appear together in at least 3% of tenders, that is, in 12 or more of them.

firm_sets <- apriori(tender_trans,
                     parameter = list(supp = 0.03, minlen = 2,
                                      target = "frequent itemsets"),
                     control = list(verbose = FALSE))

inspect(head(sort(firm_sets, by = "support"), 10))

     items           support count
[1]  {F07, F19}      0.1325  53   
[2]  {F12, F23}      0.1325  53   
[3]  {F07, F23}      0.1300  52   
[4]  {F19, F23}      0.1300  52   
[5]  {F12, F19}      0.1275  51   
[6]  {F07, F12}      0.1250  50   
[7]  {F07, F12, F19} 0.1250  50   
[8]  {F07, F12, F23} 0.1250  50   
[9]  {F07, F19, F23} 0.1250  50   
[10] {F12, F19, F23} 0.1250  50   


The same four firms, F07, F12, F19, F23, appear in every one of the top groups, in pairs, threes and all four together. No other combination of firms comes close.
Is this just because these firms bid more often than others? Lift answers that. Let us look at the rules, sorted by lift.

firm_rules <- apriori(tender_trans,
                      parameter = list(supp = 0.03, conf = 0.6, minlen = 2),
                      control = list(verbose = FALSE))

DATAFRAME(firm_rules) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  arrange(desc(lift)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 7
  LHS           RHS   support confidence coverage  lift count
  <fct>         <fct>   <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 {F12,F19,F23} {F07}    0.12       1        0.12  4.94    50
2 {F12,F19}     {F07}    0.12       0.98     0.13  4.84    50
3 {F19,F23}     {F07}    0.12       0.96     0.13  4.75    50
4 {F12,F23}     {F07}    0.12       0.94     0.13  4.66    50
5 {F07,F12}     {F19}    0.12       1        0.12  4.55    50
6 {F07,F12,F23} {F19}    0.12       1        0.12  4.55    50

8 {F07,F23}     {F12}    0.12       0.96     0.13  4.37    50


The confidence is close to 1. Whenever three of these firms bid, the fourth almost always bids too. And the lift is far above 1. They bid together many times more often than they would if each decided independently. Also notice that no rule involving any other firm passed our limits. In an honest market, firms decide on their own whether to bid, and such tight groups do not form.

48.3.4 Counts or lift?
In Section 62.5 we found rings by simply counting how often each pair of firms bid in the same tender. Let us do the same count here, and set lift beside it. For a pair of firms, lift is the share of tenders in which both bid, divided by the product of each firm’s own share. An easier way to see it is through an expected count. If two firms chose their tenders independently, they would meet in about (bids of the first firm × bids of the second firm ÷ number of tenders) tenders by chance alone. Lift is the actual count divided by this expected count.

n_tenders  <- n_distinct(bids$tender_id)
firm_count <- count(bids, firm, name = "bids_made")

firm_pairs <- bids |>
  select(tender_id, firm) |>
  inner_join(bids |> select(tender_id, firm), by = "tender_id",
             suffix = c("_a", "_b"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  filter(firm_a < firm_b) |>
  count(firm_a, firm_b, name = "together") |>
  left_join(rename(firm_count, firm_a = firm, bids_a = bids_made), by = "firm_a") |>
  left_join(rename(firm_count, firm_b = firm, bids_b = bids_made), by = "firm_b") |>
  mutate(expected = round(bids_a * bids_b / n_tenders, 1),
         lift = round((together / n_tenders) /
                        ((bids_a / n_tenders) * (bids_b / n_tenders)), 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(together))
