 4 F19    F23          52     88     94     20.7  2.51
 5 F12    F19          51     88     88     19.4  2.63
 6 F07    F12          50     81     88     17.8  2.81
 7 F05    F33          12     44     51      5.6  2.14
 8 F18    F38          12     41     49      5    2.39
 9 F21    F27          12     57     35      5    2.41
10 F23    F32          11     94     47     11    1   
11 F24    F29          11     53     49      6.5  1.69
12 F31    F38          11     45     49      5.5  2   


There are 770 pairs of firms that met at least once. By count, the six pairs of the cartel lead easily. Each met in 50 to 53 tenders. No other pair met in more than 12.
We must be honest about one thing. In this data, the four busiest firms are F07, F12, F19, F23, the cartel itself, with 81 to 94 bids each. They bid in their own tenders and in open tenders too. So here the busy firms are the guilty ones, and a plain count does not hide them. But the count still flatters busy firms in a quieter way. Look at pair F23 and F32, at number 10 in the list. It met in 11 tenders, more than 614 of the 620 pairs of ordinary firms. Is it a second ring? No. Chance alone would bring these two together in about 11 tenders, because one of them is a very busy firm. Its lift is 1, which means no link at all. Here are the top pairs made of one cartel firm and one outsider.

firm_pairs |>
  filter(xor(firm_a %in% cartel, firm_b %in% cartel)) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  firm_a firm_b together bids_a bids_b expected  lift
  <chr>  <chr>     <int>  <int>  <int>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 F23    F32          11     94     47     11    1   
2 F10    F19          10     56     88     12.3  0.81
3 F11    F23          10     44     94     10.3  0.97
4 F13    F23          10     53     94     12.5  0.8 
5 F02    F19           9     40     88      8.8  1.02


All of them have a lift close to 1, from 0.8 to 1.02. Their high counts come only from the busy cartel firm in each pair. The cartel pairs are different. They met in about 52 tenders where chance would give about 19. Their lift is 2.51 to 2.97.
Now let us sort the same pairs by lift.

firm_pairs |>
  arrange(desc(lift)) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 7
  firm_a firm_b together bids_a bids_b expected  lift
  <chr>  <chr>     <int>  <int>  <int>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 F07    F19          53     81     88     17.8  2.97
2 F07    F12          50     81     88     17.8  2.81
3 F07    F23          52     81     94     19    2.73
4 F20    F27          10     42     35      3.7  2.72
5 F12    F19          51     88     88     19.4  2.63
6 F12    F23          53     88     94     20.7  2.56
7 F19    F23          52     88     94     20.7  2.51
8 F21    F27          12     57     35      5    2.41


The cartel pairs are near the top again. But lift on its own has a weakness too. Pair F20 and F27 comes in at number 4, with a lift of 2.72. Yet it met in only 10 tenders, where chance would give about 3.7. With so many pairs, a few small pairs will look unusual by luck. So we read count and lift together. A real ring meets often and far more often than chance. In this data, only the six pairs of the cartel do both. This is just what apriori() did for us above. The minimum support kept out the small, lucky pairs, and lift then showed that the four firms are truly linked. With two or three firms on the left side, the rules had a lift of up to about 5, much higher than any pair.
Why does this matter? A firm that bids in many tenders will meet many other firms often, by chance alone. A plain count rewards such busy firms. Lift asks a fairer question. Do these firms meet more often than their own busyness would explain?






NoteOther screens for bid rigging



Part IX applies these ideas to tenders in full. The counting approach and the other screens for bid rigging, such as rotation of wins, cover margins, links between bidders and firms that always lose, are in Chapter 62. The red flags in the tender process are in Chapter 61, and the shapes of bids in Chapter 63.



48.3.5 Confirming the suspicion
Association rules have shown who bids together. A careful auditor now looks for the other signs of a cartel in the tenders where these four bid together. First, let us pick out those tenders, and compare them with the rest.

cartel_tenders <- bids |>
  summarise(all_four = all(cartel %in% firm), .by = tender_id) |>
  filter(all_four) |>
  pull(tender_id)

length(cartel_tenders)

[1] 50


Sign 1, do they take turns to win?

bids |>
  filter(tender_id %in% cartel_tenders, rank == 1) |>
  count(firm, name = "tenders_won")

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  firm  tenders_won
  <chr>       <int>
1 F07            13
2 F12            13
3 F19            12
4 F23            12


Each of the four has won almost the same number of these tenders. In an honest market, the firm with the lowest cost would win more often. An even share among a fixed group is the classic sign of bid rotation.
Signs 2 and 3, how close are the bids, and how close is the winning bid to the estimate? Let us compare these tenders with all other tenders.

bids |>
  mutate(cartel_tender = tender_id %in% cartel_tenders) |>
  summarise(win_bid  = bid[rank == 1],
            second   = bid[rank == 2],
            estimate = first(estimate),
            .by = c(tender_id, cartel_tender)) |>
  mutate(win_vs_estimate_pct = 100 * win_bid / estimate,
         gap_to_second_pct   = 100 * (second - win_bid) / win_bid) |>
  summarise(tenders = n(),
            avg_win_vs_estimate_pct = mean(win_vs_estimate_pct),
            avg_gap_to_second_pct   = mean(gap_to_second_pct),
            .by = cartel_tender) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 1)))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  cartel_tender tenders avg_win_vs_estimate_pct avg_gap_to_second_pct
  <lgl>           <int>                   <dbl>                 <dbl>
1 FALSE             350                    84.3                   5.4
2 TRUE               50                    99.8                   3  


In the tenders where the four bid together, the winning bid is close to the full estimate. In other tenders, competition brings the winning bid well below the estimate. The losing bids of the group are only a little above the winning bid, as cover bids tend to be.
We can even put a rough figure on the loss. If the cartel tenders had seen the same discount from the estimate as the competitive ones, the government would have paid less.

win <- bids |>
  filter(rank == 1) |>
  mutate(cartel_tender = tender_id %in% cartel_tenders,
         ratio = bid / estimate)

normal_ratio <- mean(win$ratio[!win$cartel_tender])

win |>
  filter(cartel_tender) |>
  summarise(paid = sum(bid),
            competitive_price = sum(estimate * normal_ratio)) |>
  mutate(possible_excess = paid - competitive_price) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 1)))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
   paid competitive_price possible_excess
  <dbl>             <dbl>           <dbl>
1 4718.             3989.            729.


This is in ₹ lakh. It is only an indicative figure, but it shows the scale of what is at stake.






WarningCaution



Firms bidding together is a red flag, not proof of collusion. Firms in the same town, or specialising in the same kind of work, may genuinely bid in the same tenders. Collusion becomes likely when several signs appear together. These signs are a fixed group bidding together, rotation of wins, cover bids just above the winner, and winning bids close to the estimate. Further evidence may come from common addresses, common directors, bank guarantees from the same branch, bids uploaded from the same computer (IP address), or identical errors in the bid documents. The network analysis of Section 55.2 is useful for finding such common links.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
text:
48.4 Choosing the limits
The results of Apriori depend heavily on the limits we set.


Minimum support too high hides rare patterns, which are often the interesting ones in audit. Too low produces thousands of rules and takes longer.

Minimum confidence removes weak rules. A value between 0.2 and 0.6 is a common starting point.
Start with moderate limits, look at the number of rules, and adjust. Aim for a number of rules that you can actually read, say 20 to 200.
Use subset() to focus on the items you care about, rather than reading every rule.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
text:
48.5 Things to keep in mind






WarningLimitations of association rules





Rules show co-occurrence, not cause. {C01} => {A01} does not say that angioplasty causes ICU stays, only that they appear together.

A rule’s direction can mislead. {A01} => {C01} has the same support as {C01} => {A01}, but a very different confidence. Read both sides carefully.

Common items create many dull rules. If an item is in most baskets, it will appear in many rules. Lift helps filter these out.

Only presence or absence matters. Apriori does not look at amounts, quantities or dates. Use it to find patterns, and then examine amounts and dates with dplyr, as we did for the tenders.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
text:
48.6 A suggested workflow


Decide what a basket is, and what the items are, keeping the audit question in mind.

Build the transactions from a list of baskets, using transactions().

Look at the item frequencies, to understand the data.

Run apriori() with moderate limits. Adjust until the number of rules is manageable.

Sort by lift and confidence. First understand the normal patterns. Then look for the ones that do not make sense.

Drill down. Find which units (hospitals, firms, offices) produce the unusual pattern.

Look for supporting signs, using amounts, dates and other records.

Turn confirmed patterns into routine checks, and quantify the money involved.







ImportantRemember



Association rules are excellent at showing what goes with what. In audit, the most valuable rules are often the ones that should not exist. A lens billed apart from a cataract package. Four firms always bidding together. Finding them needs the algorithm. Understanding them needs the auditor.

title: 48  Association Rules (Apriori)
text:
48.7 Try it yourself
These exercises use the objects of this chapter, the claims data, the transactions trans and tender_trans, the rules claim_rules, and the bids data with its cartel. Try each before opening the solution.


A higher confidence limit. Run apriori() on the claims again with the same support, but a minimum confidence of 0.5. How many rules are left? Do the two unbundling rules survive?






TipSolution






strict_rules <- apriori(trans,
                        parameter = list(supp = 0.002, conf = 0.5, minlen = 2),
                        control = list(verbose = FALSE))
length(strict_rules)

[1] 6

inspect(sort(strict_rules, by = "lift"))

    lhs           rhs   support     confidence coverage    lift      count
[1] {A05}      => {S01} 0.006840722 1.0000000  0.006840722 14.773169  229 
[2] {A04, A05} => {S01} 0.002031306 1.0000000  0.002031306 14.773169   68 
[3] {A06}      => {O01} 0.016788147 1.0000000  0.016788147 11.583391  562 
[4] {C01}      => {A01} 0.026795316 0.8881188  0.030170869  9.001110  897 
[5] {S03}      => {A04} 0.036533636 0.6870787  0.053172422  8.270638 1223 
[6] {A01, A03} => {M03} 0.004301589 0.5538462  0.007766758  8.142536  144 


The rules fall from 25 to 6. Both unbundling rules, {A05} => {S01} and {A06} => {O01}, are still there, because their confidence is 1. A higher limit gives a shorter list to read. The strongest patterns stay.





What goes with a blood transfusion? Find all rules in claim_rules whose right side is the blood transfusion add-on A02.






TipSolution






blood_rules <- subset(claim_rules, rhs %in% "A02")
inspect(sort(blood_rules, by = "lift"))

    lhs           rhs   support     confidence coverage    lift     count
[1] {A01, R01} => {A02} 0.002449516 0.4120603  0.005944557 7.546023  82  
[2] {R01}      => {A02} 0.012845023 0.3912648  0.032829490 7.165197 430  


There are 2 rules, and both have a knee replacement (R01) on the left. So in normal billing, a transfusion goes with a knee replacement. An auditor can now look for transfusions billed with treatments that rarely need one.





Turning a rule around. Work out the confidence of {A01} => {C01} by counting, as we did in the chapter for {C01} => {A01}. Compare the two.






TipSolution






conf_C01_A01 <- n_both / n_C01
conf_A01_C01 <- n_both / n_A01
round(c(C01_to_A01 = conf_C01_A01, A01_to_C01 = conf_A01_C01), 3)

C01_to_A01 A01_to_C01 
     0.888      0.272 


The support is the same both ways, since it counts the same 897 claims. But 89% of angioplasty claims have an ICU stay, while only 27% of ICU claims have an angioplasty. Most ICU stays come with other treatments. So always read a rule in the direction it is written.





ICU stays after fever or gastroenteritis. The chapter said that an ICU stay billed after a simple fever (M01) or gastroenteritis (M02) would stand out. For each hospital, find the share of such claims that also bill an ICU stay. Which hospitals stand out?






TipSolution






simple_cases <- claims |>
  filter(str_detect(packages, "^M01|^M02"))

icu_simple <- simple_cases |>
  summarise(claims   = n(),
            with_icu = sum(str_detect(packages, "A01")),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  mutate(share = round(with_icu / claims, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(share))

head(icu_simple, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  hospital_id claims with_icu share
  <chr>        <int>    <int> <dbl>
1 H085            64       40  0.62
2 H104            28       16  0.57
3 H071             7        1  0.14
4 H041            42        5  0.12
5 H089            17        2  0.12


Across all hospitals, only 4.5% of these claims bill an ICU stay. But H085 bills one in 62% of them, and H104 in 57%. These are Pragati Nursing Home and Navjeevan Hospital, the two ICU hospitals that k-means flagged in Section 47.11. Their fever and gastroenteritis claims with an ICU stay are the case records to call for first.





Any other group of bidders? Run apriori() on tender_trans with lower limits, a support of 0.02 and a confidence of 0.3. Keep only the rules that include at least one firm outside the cartel. Is there another suspicious group?






TipSolution






loose_rules <- apriori(tender_trans,
                       parameter = list(supp = 0.02, conf = 0.3, minlen = 2),
                       control = list(verbose = FALSE))
length(loose_rules)

[1] 29

loose_df <- DATAFRAME(loose_rules) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

cartel_pattern <- paste(cartel, collapse = "|")
outside <- loose_df |>
  filter(!str_detect(LHS, cartel_pattern) | !str_detect(RHS, cartel_pattern))
outside

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  LHS   RHS   support confidence coverage  lift count
  <fct> <fct>   <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 {F27} {F21}    0.03       0.34     0.09  2.41    12


Of 29 rules, only one involves a firm outside the cartel. It is {F27} => {F21}, seen in 12 tenders, with a lift of 2.41 and a confidence of 0.34. Compare that with the cartel rules, which have a confidence close to 1 and a lift of about 5. This pair is a weak link. It is worth a look only if other signs, such as rotation of wins, appear too.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.1 Our data
Every office keeps figures month by month. A treasury records the expenditure of each department every month. A sub-registrar office records the stamp duty it collects. A commercial tax circle records its tax collections every quarter. An auditor who looks at only one month, or only one year, sees a single number. An auditor who looks at the whole run of months sees a pattern. And a pattern tells us what to expect.
That is the idea behind this chapter. If receipts have grown by about 8% every year, and always peak in March, then we know roughly what this year’s receipts should be. If the actual receipts fall well short, we have a lead. Perhaps some revenue has leaked. In the same way, if a department always spends much more in March, we can measure that March rush, and spot a March which is unusual even for March.
A sequence of values recorded over time, in order, is called a time series. Monthly expenditure, daily cash balance, quarterly GST collections and yearly excise revenue are all time series. Time series analysis means studying such data to understand its patterns, and to predict its future values. So it serves for description as well as prediction.
A few uses in audit are these.
In this chapter we will learn how to turn monthly figures into a time series in R, and how to plot it. We will separate a series into its trend and its seasonal pattern. We will forecast it with simple and advanced methods, and test which method forecasts best. Finally, we will use a forecast to judge whether a year’s stamp duty receipts are believable.
All the series in this chapter are made up. They are realistic, but no real office or State is meant. We use five of them.
New readers may skip the code which creates the data.
Code to create the five seriesset.seed(2025)

# Monthly expenditure of the rural development department, Rs crore
# April 2014 to March 2024. Growth of 7% a year and a March rush.
n <- 120
spend_season <- c(0.55, 0.70, 0.80, 0.75, 0.80, 0.90,   # April to September
                  0.95, 1.00, 1.05, 1.10, 1.25, 2.15)   # October to March
x <- 40 * 1.07^((0:(n - 1)) / 12) * rep(spend_season, 10) * exp(rnorm(n, 0, 0.06))
# Planted case. March 2021 (month 84) is 45% above its usual March rush
x[84] <- x[84] * 1.45
spend <- ts(round(x, 1), start = c(2014, 4), frequency = 12)

# Yearly penalties of a district transport office, Rs lakh, 1985 to 2024
fines <- ts(round(120 + 6 * arima.sim(list(ar = 0.5), 40), 1), start = 1985)

# Yearly mineral royalty of a district mining office, Rs lakh, 1975 to 2024
# Booms and slumps of uneven length, 6 to 10 years each
phase   <- cumsum(2 * pi / runif(50, 6, 10))
royalty <- ts(round(200 + 60 * sin(phase) + rnorm(50, 0, 12), 1), start = 1975)

# Quarterly commercial tax of a state, Rs crore, April-June 2005 to Jan-March 2024
ctax_season <- c(0.92, 0.95, 1.00, 1.13)   # Q1 (Apr-Jun) to Q4 (Jan-Mar)
ctax <- ts(round(1500 * 1.09^((0:75) / 4) * rep(ctax_season, 19) * exp(rnorm(76, 0, 0.03))),
           start = c(2005, 2), frequency = 4)

# Yearly state excise revenue, Rs crore, 1995 to 2023
excise <- ts(round(800 * 1.10^(0:28) * exp(rnorm(29, 0, 0.04))), start = 1995)
Let us look at the first of them. The monthly expenditure is printed in a calendar layout, one row for each calendar year.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
spend, the monthly expenditure of a State’s rural development department, in ₹ crore, from April 2014 to March 2024. It grows by about 7% a year, and has a strong March rush. We have planted one irregularity in it. In March 2021 the department spent far more than even its usual March rush. This is the kind of year-end spending that an auditor would want to examine, to see whether funds were parked or drawn only to avoid lapse.

fines, the yearly penalties collected by a district transport office, in ₹ lakh, from 1985 to 2024. It goes up and down from year to year, around a steady level.

royalty, the yearly mineral royalty collected by a district mining office, in ₹ lakh, from 1975 to 2024. It rises and falls with booms and slumps in construction.

ctax, the quarterly commercial tax collections of a State, in ₹ crore, from the April to June quarter of 2005 to the January to March quarter of 2024.

excise, the yearly State excise revenue of a State, in ₹ crore, from 1995 to 2023.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.2 Components of a time series
A time series can be broken down into several components.


Level. The baseline value or average of the series. If a series were a straight horizontal line, it would have only a level. The transport penalties in Figure 49.1 (b) wander up and down, but always come back to about the same level. They have no lasting rise or fall.

Trend. The long-term direction of the series. It shows whether the series is rising, falling or staying about constant over time. For example, a clear rising trend can be seen in the commercial tax collections in Figure 49.1 (d).

Seasonality. A pattern which repeats at a fixed and known interval, like every year, every quarter or every week. In Figure 49.1 (d), commercial tax rises and falls in the same way every year, with the January to March quarter on top. In Figure 49.1 (a), expenditure peaks every March.

Cycle. Rises and falls which are not of a fixed length. The mineral royalty in Figure 49.1 (c) rises in construction booms and falls in slumps. Each boom and slump lasts 6 to 10 years, and the length varies from one to the next. That is why they form a cycle and not a season.

Errors (residuals). The random ups and downs that cannot be explained by the level, trend, seasonality or cycle. The year-to-year changes in the transport penalties in Figure 49.1 (b) are mostly of this kind. The error component tells us how variable the data is, and so how much we can trust a forecast.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.3 Additive or multiplicative components
The trend, seasonal and error components can combine with each other in two ways, additive or multiplicative. Which one fits depends on the data.
An additive model assumes that the components are added together. The value of the series at any time is the sum of the trend, seasonal and error components at that time.
\[
y_t = T_t + S_t + e_t
\tag{49.1}\]
where \(y_t\), \(T_t\), \(S_t\) and \(e_t\) are the values of the series, trend component, seasonal component and residuals, respectively, at time \(t\). In an additive series, the seasonal ups and downs stay about the same size, whatever the level of the series.
A multiplicative model assumes that the components are multiplied together.
\[
y_t = T_t \times S_t \times e_t
\tag{49.2}\]
where \(y_t\), \(T_t\), \(S_t\) and \(e_t\) are defined as before. In a multiplicative series, the seasonal ups and downs grow as the series grows. The seasonal component is then a percentage of the trend, like “March is 40% above an average month”. Look at the expenditure in Figure 49.1 (a). The March peaks rise higher every year, because the March rush is a share of a growing budget. So its seasonality is multiplicative.
We can convert a multiplicative series into an additive one by taking its logarithm, because \(\log(T \times S \times e) = \log T + \log S + \log e\). See Figure 49.2. On the log scale, the March peaks of spend stand about the same height above the other months every year.


















Figure 49.2: Transforming a time series


We will learn how to separate these components in later sections.
Damped trends. Gardner and McKenzie1 observed in 1985 that most forecasting methods assume a trend will continue forever, however far ahead we forecast. Based on their findings, they suggested that forecasts become more accurate if trends are damped, that is, made to flatten out gradually. We will learn about this idea as well in later sections.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
section: 49.4 Working with time series in R
text:
49.4 Working with time series in R
Let us first see how time series objects are handled in R.
Prerequisites
Most of the time we will use base R. For forecasting, we will use forecast, a fabulous package developed by Rob Hyndman. Forecasting future values also tells us how well we have captured the trends and patterns in a series. We will also use zoo for rolling averages, patchwork for combining plots, and tidyverse for the audit use case.

library(forecast)
library(zoo)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)


49.4.1 Creating a time series object in R
R provides a simple function ts() to convert a series of observations (basically a vector) into a time series object. The main arguments are
ts(data,
  start = 1,
  end = numeric(),
  frequency = 1,
  ...)
where


data is a numeric vector or matrix containing the observations.

start is the time of the first observation. It is a single number, like 1985 for yearly data, or a pair of numbers, like c(2022, 4) for April 2022 in monthly data.

end is the time of the last observation, written the same way. We usually give only start, and R works out end from the length of the data.

frequency is the number of observations per unit of time. Monthly data has a frequency of 12, quarterly data 4, and yearly data 1.

... are other, rarely needed arguments, like names for the columns of a matrix of series.

Let us create a small time series. A block office spent the following amounts, in ₹ lakh, in each month of the financial year 2022-23.

# Monthly expenditure of a block office in FY 2022-23, Rs lakh
block_exp <- c(12, 15, 18, 16, 17, 20, 22, 21, 24, 26, 30, 58)

# A monthly time series starting from April 2022
block_ts <- ts(block_exp, start = c(2022, 4), frequency = 12)

# Print the time series object
block_ts

     Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
2022              12  15  18  16  17  20  22  21  24
2023  26  30  58                                    


Notice that R has placed the 12 values from April 2022 to March 2023 in a calendar layout. The March rush is already visible. We can check the class of the object.

class(block_ts)

[1] "ts"


Let us also print fines. It is a yearly series, so it has a frequency of 1.

fines

We can take out a part of a time series with window(). For example, the penalties from 2015 onwards are

window(fines, start = 2015)

End = 2024

For a monthly series, start and end are again pairs. The expenditure of the financial year 2023-24 alone is window(spend, start = c(2023, 4), end = c(2024, 3)).

49.4.2 Plotting time series objects
To plot a ts object we can simply use plot(). Alternatively we can use autoplot(), which draws the series with ggplot2.

# Plotting in base R
plot(block_ts, main = "Block office expenditure, FY 2022-23",
     ylab = "Rs lakh")

# Plotting with ggplot2, on a log scale
autoplot(spend) +
  scale_y_log10('Rs crore, log scale') +
  ggtitle('Department expenditure on a log scale') +
  theme_bw()






Figure 49.3: Plotting a time series in base R (left) and ggplot2 (right)









Figure 49.4: Plotting a time series in base R (left) and ggplot2 (right)




autoplot() is a function of ggplot2. The package forecast teaches it how to draw time series and forecasts. The plot is a ggplot2 object, so it can be fine-tuned with the usual ggplot2 functions, as we did with scale_y_log10() above.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.5 Time series modelling and forecasting
Forecasting the future is an important part of time series analysis. For an auditor, a forecast is an expectation. It says what the figures should have been if the office behaved as it always did. To forecast, we first need to model the data, that is, describe its pattern. Forecasting techniques can be broadly divided into two groups. Data-based techniques, like averaging, smoothing and decomposition, work directly on the observed values. Model-based techniques, like ARIMA, assume a particular statistical structure for the data and estimate its parameters. In practice the line between the two is not sharp. We will start with the simplest ones.

49.5.1 Naive method
This method assumes that the future value will be the same as the last observed value. It is the simplest and most basic forecasting method, and hence named naive. The formula is
\[
\text{Naive method: }\hat{Y}_{T+1} = Y_T
\tag{49.3}\]
Here, \(\hat{Y}_{T+1}\) is the forecast for the next period and \(Y_T\) is the last observed value, in a series of \(T\) observations. So predicting with the naive method needs no special skill. Yet it is useful. Any better method should at least beat the naive forecast.
Let us forecast the transport penalties for 5 future years. The package forecast has a function naive() which does this, once we give the value of the parameter h, short for forecasting horizon. In Figure 49.5, the forecast values (the blue line) are exactly the same as the last observed value. The shaded bands show the range in which the actual values are likely to fall.

forecast::naive(fines, h = 5) %>%
  autoplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Transport penalties, forecast by the naive method",
       x = "Year", y = "Rs lakh")






Figure 49.5: Naive forecasting




By default, 80% and 95% prediction intervals are shown as bands. We can choose other levels with the parameter level, for example level = 90. If we do not want the bands at all, we can use autoplot(..., PI = FALSE).
For seasonal data, there is a variant called the seasonal naive method, snaive(). It forecasts each month as the value of the same month last year. Auditors use this idea all the time, when they compare this March with last March.






TipAudit tip



For a seasonal series, never compare a month with the month just before it. March expenditure will always look alarming next to February. Compare it with the same month of earlier years, as snaive() does, or with a forecast that allows for the season.



49.5.2 Moving averages
In this technique, the forecast is the average of the most recent \(n\) observations. As new data comes in, the window of \(n\) observations slides forward. A moving average smooths a time series by averaging neighbouring values. It reduces noise and reveals the underlying trend.
The formula for forecasting with a moving average is
\[
\hat{Y}_{t+1} = \frac{1}{n}(Y_t + Y_{t-1} + ... + Y_{t-n+1})
\tag{49.4}\]
Here, \(\hat{Y}_{t+1}\) is the forecast for the next period and \(Y_t\), \(Y_{t-1}\), …, \(Y_{t-n+1}\) are the past \(n\) observations.
A moving average can be centred or trailing.

In a centred moving average of order \(k\), each value is replaced by the mean of itself, the \((k-1)/2\) values before it and the \((k-1)/2\) values after it. So \(k\) is naturally an odd number. For an even \(k\), like 12 for monthly data, ma() from forecast takes care of centring automatically. Centred averages are used to see the trend in past data.
In a trailing moving average, each value is replaced by the mean of itself and the \(k-1\) values before it. It uses only past data, so it is the one we use for forecasting. The function rollmeanr() from zoo calculates it.

Smoothed versions of the monthly expenditure for different \(k\) can be seen in Figure 49.6. A 7-month average softens the March peaks but does not remove them. A 12-month average removes them almost fully, because each average contains exactly one March. Notice also that the trailing average lags behind the data, since it uses only the past.







Figure 49.6: Simple moving averages of monthly expenditure




Let us now forecast with a moving average. For the transport penalties, we take a trailing moving average of the last 7 years with rollmeanr(). The forecast for every future year is then simply the last value of this moving average. Applying naive() to the moving average gives exactly that, as in the left side of Figure 49.7.
In the right side of Figure 49.7, we have done the same with the monthly expenditure. This series has a strong seasonal pattern, so we have used a 12-month moving average. An average over exactly one full year contains every month once, so the seasonal ups and downs cancel out and only the trend remains. We have also drawn the original series in black, so we can see both the original and the smoothed series.



# Transport penalties, 7 year trailing moving average
fines_ma <- rollmeanr(fines, k = 7)
naive(fines_ma, h = 10) |>
  plot(ylim = range(fines), col = "red",
       main = "Forecasting\ntransport penalties")
lines(fines)

# Monthly expenditure, 12 month trailing moving average
naive(rollmeanr(spend, k = 12), h = 12) |>
  plot(ylim = range(spend),
       xlim = c(2014, 2025.5),
       col = "red",
       main = "Forecasting\nmonthly expenditure")
lines(spend)















Figure 49.7: Forecasting with simple moving averages








WarningCaution



A moving average forecast is flat. It cannot follow a trend or a seasonal pattern into the future. Look at the expenditure forecast in Figure 49.7. It gives the average month, not the March rush that we can clearly expect. An auditor who used it would find every March “unusual”. For such data we need the methods discussed next.



49.5.3 Exponential smoothing
Exponential smoothing methods forecast with weighted averages of past observations, giving more weight to recent observations. Examples are simple exponential smoothing, Holt’s method and the Holt-Winters method.
Simple exponential smoothing (SES) is the simplest of these. It is a weighted moving average in which the weights fall exponentially as the observations get older. This method is suitable for data with no clear trend or seasonal pattern.
\[
\hat{y}_{T+1} = \alpha{y_T} + \alpha(1- \alpha){y_{T-1}} + \alpha(1 - \alpha)^2{y_{T-2}} + ...
\tag{49.5}\]
The smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) lies between \(0\) and \(1\). A value close to 1 gives almost all the weight to the latest observation, so the forecast follows the data closely. A value close to 0 spreads the weight over many past observations, so the forecast is very smooth. An example with \(\alpha = 0.1\), on the transport penalties, is shown in Figure 49.8 (left).
Holt extended SES by adding a trend component, with its own smoothing parameter \(\beta\). The method is named after him as Holt’s linear method. Mathematically, there are now three equations.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}_{t+h|t} &= l_t + hb_t \\
l_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(l_{t-1} + b_{t-1}) \\
b_t &= \beta(l_t - l_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)b_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
\tag{49.6}\]
Here \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (again \(0 \le \beta \le 1\)) are the smoothing parameters for level and trend respectively, and \(h\) is the forecast horizon. Also, \(y_t\) is the actual value, \(l_t\) is the level (or intercept) and \(b_t\) is the trend (or slope) of the series at time \(t\). The first equation says that the forecast \(h\) periods ahead is the latest level plus \(h\) times the latest slope. We apply it to the yearly excise revenue, which has a clear upward trend. See Figure 49.8 (right).
To apply SES in R, we use the function ses(), and for Holt’s method, holt(), both from forecast. If we do not give the values of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), R chooses the best values itself. Here we have fixed them, to see their effect.



fines_ses <- ses(fines, h = 10, alpha = 0.1)
holtfit <- holt(excise, h = 10, alpha = 0.3, beta = 0.1)

autoplot(fines_ses) +
  autolayer(fines_ses$fitted) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle('SES with alpha = 0.1, transport penalties') +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  ggplot2::labs(color = "", y = "Rs lakh")

autoplot(holtfit) +
  autolayer(holtfit$fitted) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Holt's linear method with beta = 0.1, excise revenue") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  ggplot2::labs(color = "", y = "Rs crore")















Figure 49.8: Simple exponential smoothing (left) and Holt’s linear method (right)


As discussed earlier, damped trends often work better. Based on the work of Gardner and McKenzie, a damping parameter \(\phi\) was added. The equations become
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}_{t+h|t} &= l_t + (\phi + \phi^2 + ... + \phi^h)b_t \\
l_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(l_{t-1} + \phi b_{t-1}) \\
b_t &= \beta(l_t - l_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\phi b_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
\tag{49.7}\]
If \(\phi = 1\), these are the same as Holt’s linear method. A value \(0 < \phi < 1\) damps the trend, so the forecast line gradually flattens, as shown in Figure 49.9 (left). The two methods are compared in Figure 49.9 (right).
To use damped trends in R, we set damped = TRUE in the holt() function. Example code is below.



holtfit <- holt(excise, h = 10, alpha = 0.3, beta = 0.1, damped = TRUE, phi = 0.8)
autoplot(holtfit) +
  autolayer(holtfit$fitted) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle('Damped trend forecast with phi = 0.8') +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  ggplot2::labs(color = "", y = "Rs crore")

holtfit <- holt(excise,
                h = 10,
                alpha = 0.3,
                beta = 0.1)

holtfit2 <- holt(
  excise,
  h = 10,
  alpha = 0.3,
  beta = 0.1,
  damped = TRUE,
  phi = 0.8
)

autoplot(excise) +
  autolayer(holtfit, series = "Holt's method", PI = FALSE) +
  autolayer(holtfit2, series = "Holt's method with damped trend", PI = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Holt's method") + xlab("Year") +
  ylab("Excise revenue (Rs crore)") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Method")) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")















Figure 49.9: Linear method and damped trend


Which one should an auditor prefer? If we expect revenue to keep growing at the same pace, the linear trend is right. If growth is likely to slow down, for example because a tax base is nearing saturation, the damped trend is safer. It is a judgement, and it should be recorded in the working papers.
To include seasonality with \(m\) periods in a year (12 for monthly data) along with trend and level, Holt and Winters added a seasonal component \(s_t\) with its own smoothing parameter \(\gamma\). The equations of the Holt-Winters additive method are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}_{t+h|t} &= l_t + hb_t + s_{t+h-m(k+1)} \\
l_t &= \alpha(y_t - s_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)(l_{t-1} + b_{t-1}) \\
b_t &= \beta(l_t - l_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)b_{t-1} \\
s_t &= \gamma(y_t - l_{t-1} - b_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma)s_{t-m}
\end{aligned}
\tag{49.8}\]
where \(k\) is the whole number part of \((h-1)/m\). The term \(s_{t+h-m(k+1)}\) looks complicated, but it only means “the seasonal value of the same month in the latest year of data”. So a forecast for next March uses the seasonal effect estimated for the latest March. In the multiplicative version, the seasonal effect multiplies the level and trend instead of being added.
To apply the Holt-Winters method in R, we use the function hw(). In the code below, we forecast the monthly expenditure with both additive and multiplicative seasonality. See Figure 49.10.



hw1 <- hw(spend, seasonal = "additive")
hw2 <- hw(spend, seasonal = "multiplicative")

autoplot(hw1) +
  ggtitle("Additive method") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rs crore") +
  theme_bw()

autoplot(hw2) +
  ggtitle("Multiplicative method") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rs crore") +
  theme_bw()















Figure 49.10: Holt-Winters method of forecasting


The multiplicative forecast (right) lets the March peaks keep growing with the budget, as in the data. The additive one (left) keeps the seasonal swings at a fixed size in rupees. As we saw, the seasonality of spend is multiplicative, so the right one is more believable.
We do not always have to choose between SES, Holt and Holt-Winters ourselves. The function ets() (short for Error, Trend, Seasonal) tries all these methods, with and without damping, additive and multiplicative. It picks the best one automatically. We will use it in the audit use case.
Seasonal decomposition methods
Seasonal decomposition separates a time series into its components, like trend, seasonality and noise. This lets us study each component and its effect on the series separately. There are several methods. We will discuss two of them.

49.5.4 Classical seasonal decomposition
The first is the classical decomposition method. It assumes that the seasonal pattern repeats identically every year. Its steps are


Trend component. The trend is estimated with a centred moving average over one full season, a 12-month average for monthly data. As we saw in the moving averages section, such an average cancels out the seasonal ups and downs.

Seasonal component. The trend is removed from the series. What is left is averaged for each month (or quarter) across all the years. This gives one seasonal value for each month.

Residual component. The trend and seasonal components are removed from the original series. What remains is the residual.

Let us decompose the monthly expenditure to see its components. In R, we use the function decompose(). Since we know the seasonality of spend is multiplicative, we set type = "multiplicative" (the default is additive).

spend_dec <- decompose(spend, type = "multiplicative")

The result is a list. Its element figure gives the seasonal value of each month. In a multiplicative decomposition, these are seasonal indices. An index of 1.10 means that the month is usually 10% above the trend. The values are in the order of the months of the series. Our series starts in April, so we name them from April to March.

spend_idx <- round(spend_dec$figure, 3) |>
  setNames(month.abb[c(4:12, 1:3)])
spend_idx

  Apr   May   Jun   Jul   Aug   Sep   Oct   Nov   Dec   Jan   Feb   Mar 
0.545 0.684 0.802 0.754 0.790 0.904 0.926 1.013 1.033 1.119 1.239 2.190 


March has an index of 2.19. So the department usually spends about 2.2 times as much in March as in an average month of the year. The lowest month is April, the first month of the financial year, at about 45% below the trend. Such an index is a good way to report the March rush. It is one number, it allows for the growth of the budget, and it can be compared across departments.






TipAudit tip



The financial rules of most governments discourage a rush of expenditure in the last months of the year. A March index above 2 means that the March of an average year carries twice the spending of an average month. Compute this index for each department, and take up the departments with the highest index for detailed checks of March vouchers.


A plot of the decomposed expenditure is shown in Figure 49.11. It has four panels, (i) the observed, that is, original values, (ii) the trend, (iii) the seasonal pattern and (iv) the random noise.

spend_dec |>
  plot()






Figure 49.11: Classical decomposition of monthly expenditure (multiplicative)




Notice that the trend is missing for the first six and last six months. A centred 12-month average needs six months on each side, which are not available at the ends of the series. Notice also the tall spike in the random panel early in 2021. We will find out which month it is in the next section.

49.5.5 Seasonal and trend decomposition using Loess2

STL (Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess) is a robust and flexible method for decomposing a time series into trend, seasonal and remainder components. Instead of simple averages, it uses Loess, a method of fitting smooth curves, to estimate both the trend and the seasonal component. It repeats the two steps a few times, each time improving both estimates. It has some advantages over classical decomposition.

It gives a trend for the whole series, including the first and last months.
The seasonal pattern may be allowed to change slowly over the years.
It is robust, meaning a few unusual values do not spoil the estimates much.

STL works only with additive components. So for a multiplicative series like spend, we first take its logarithm. In R, we use the function stl(). Setting s.window = "periodic" tells it to keep the seasonal pattern the same every year. Setting robust = TRUE asks it to resist unusual months. A plot of the STL decomposition is shown in Figure 49.12.

spend_stl <- stl(log(spend), s.window = "periodic", robust = TRUE)
spend_stl |>
  plot()






Figure 49.12: STL decomposition of log(monthly expenditure)




The element time.series of the result holds the three components. The remainder is what is left after removing the trend and the March rush. On the log scale, a remainder of 0.1 means that the month was about 10% above what its trend and season would suggest. Let us list the months with the largest remainders.

spend_rem <- tibble(month     = as.yearmon(time(spend)),
                    spend     = as.numeric(spend),
                    remainder = round(as.numeric(spend_stl$time.series[, "remainder"]), 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(remainder))
head(spend_rem, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  month     spend remainder
  <yearmon> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Mar 2021  187.      0.321
2 Feb 2016   67.2     0.193
3 Dec 2019   68.3     0.184
4 Dec 2021   78.2     0.183
5 Nov 2015   51.5     0.121


March 2021 stands out, with a remainder of 0.321. So the department spent ₹186.8 crore that month, about 38% more than even a normal March would explain. This is our planted case. An auditor would examine the vouchers of that March. Were the funds drawn and kept in bank accounts, or released to agencies only to avoid lapse of the budget? The anomaly detection chapter shows how to flag such months with a formal rule, in Section 50.11.
Model-based techniques
Model-based techniques fit a specific statistical model to the time series, and estimate its parameters from the data. They need more assumptions, but can give a more detailed understanding of the series. The most widely used are


Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) models. These explain each value from the previous values of the series (the autoregressive part, of order \(p\)) and from the previous forecast errors (the moving average part, of order \(q\)). Many series, like those with a trend, do not have a constant level. ARIMA handles them by working on the differences between consecutive values (the integrated part, of order \(d\)). An ARIMA model is written as ARIMA(\(p\),\(d\),\(q\)).

Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) models. These extend ARIMA to include seasonality, by also relating each value to the values of the same month in earlier years. They are written as ARIMA(\(p\),\(d\),\(q\))(\(P\),\(D\),\(Q\))\(_m\), where the second set of orders is for the seasonal part, and \(m\) is the number of periods in a season.

Choosing \(p\), \(d\), \(q\) and their seasonal versions by hand needs experience. Fortunately, the function auto.arima() from forecast tries many combinations and picks the best one. The argument lambda = 0 asks it to work on the logarithm of the series, as spend is multiplicative. The forecasts are converted back to the original scale automatically.

spend_arima <- auto.arima(spend, lambda = 0)
spend_arima

Series: spend 
ARIMA(0,0,0)(2,1,0)[12] with drift 
Box Cox transformation: lambda= 0 

Coefficients:
         sar1     sar2   drift
      -0.7799  -0.3633  0.0054
s.e.   0.0918   0.0932  0.0003

sigma^2 = 0.006138:  log likelihood = 119.25
AIC=-230.49   AICc=-230.1   BIC=-219.76


auto.arima() has chosen the model ARIMA(0,0,0)(2,1,0)[12] with drift. The seasonal difference (\(D = 1\)) means that the model works on the change from the same month of last year. This is the auditor’s familiar “this March compared with last March”, built into a model. Its forecast for the next two years is shown in Figure 49.13.

forecast(spend_arima, h = 24) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rs crore") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 49.13: Forecast of monthly expenditure with a seasonal ARIMA model





49.5.6 Which method to choose?
We have seen many methods. Which one forecasts best? The honest way to find out is to test them. We hide the last part of the data, forecast it with each method using only the earlier data, and compare the forecasts with what actually happened. The earlier part is called the training data, and the hidden part the test data.
Let us keep April 2014 to March 2022 of spend for training, and the last two financial years, 2022-23 and 2023-24, for testing. The function accuracy() compares a forecast with the actual values. It gives the error measures we met in the regression chapter (Chapter 39), like RMSE, MAE and MAPE.

train <- window(spend, end = c(2022, 3))
test  <- window(spend, start = c(2022, 4))

forecasts <- list(
  "Naive"                 = naive(train, h = 24),
  "Seasonal naive"        = snaive(train, h = 24),
  "Holt-Winters (mult.)"  = hw(train, h = 24, seasonal = "multiplicative"),
  "ETS (automatic)"       = forecast(ets(train), h = 24),
  "ARIMA (automatic)"     = forecast(auto.arima(train, lambda = 0), h = 24)
)

sapply(forecasts, \(f) accuracy(f, test)["Test set", c("RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE")]) |>
  t() |>
  round(1)

                     RMSE  MAE  MAPE
Naive                72.3 69.9 118.5
Seasonal naive       11.7  8.5  10.6
Holt-Winters (mult.)  5.1  3.9   5.5
ETS (automatic)       5.8  4.8   6.7
ARIMA (automatic)     5.3  4.1   5.9


The naive forecast is off by 118.5% on average. It is badly wrong because the last month of the training data is a March. It repeats that March peak for every month of the next two years. The seasonal naive forecast does far better, at 10.6%. The best here is Holt-Winters (mult.), at 5.5%. The other two methods that allow for trend and season are close, between 5.9% and 6.7%.






NoteNo method is always best



The automatic choices of ets() and auto.arima() are made on the training data. They are good starting points, but they do not always win on the test data. Here the automatic ETS model came a little behind the multiplicative Holt-Winters method. On another series, the order may change. So it is good practice to try a few methods and compare them on test data, as we did here.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
section: 49.6 Plotting different elements of time series
text:
49.6 Plotting different elements of time series
forecast has some more plots which help us see the elements of a time series.


ggseasonplot() draws each year as a separate line against the months. It shows the seasonal pattern and how it changes over the years.

ggsubseriesplot() draws a mini plot for each month across the years, with the mean of that month as a horizontal line.

gglagplot() plots the series against lagged (earlier) values of itself.

ggAcf() plots the autocorrelation function (ACF), that is, the correlation of the series with its own lagged values.

The seasonal plot and sub-series plot of the monthly expenditure are in Figure 49.14. Both show that March is far above every other month, every year. The seasonal plot also shows that each year lies above the previous one, which is the trend. In the sub-series plot, the highest point on the March line is March 2021. It is again our planted case.

g1 <- ggseasonplot(spend) +
  labs(y = "Rs crore") +
  theme_bw()
g2 <- ggsubseriesplot(spend) +
  ggtitle('Sub-series plot') +
  labs(y = "Rs crore") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
(g1 / g2)






Figure 49.14: Seasonality through seasonal and sub-series plots




Note that the seasonal plot runs from January to December, the calendar year. So each financial year is split across two lines. This does not matter for seeing the pattern.
The lag plots of the monthly expenditure can be seen in Figure 49.15. Each panel plots the series against itself a certain number of months earlier. Look at the panel for lag 12. The points lie close to the diagonal line, and the March points sit together at the top right. So each month is very similar to the same month a year earlier. This tells us that the series has a seasonality of 12 periods.

gglagplot(spend) +
  ggtitle('Lag plots') +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(color = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1))






Figure 49.15: Seasonality through lag plots




The same information appears as numbers in the ACF plot of Figure 49.16. Each bar is the correlation of the series with itself at that lag. The bars peak at lags 12, 24 and 36, because of the March rush every twelve months. Bars crossing the blue dashed lines are significantly different from zero.

ggAcf(spend, lag.max = 36) +
  ggtitle('Autocorrelation function') +
  theme_bw()






Figure 49.16: Autocorrelation of monthly expenditure

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
section: 49.7 Audit use case, is this year’s revenue believable?
text:
49.7 Audit use case, is this year’s revenue believable?
Let us now use forecasting the way an auditor would. Revenue collected by a government office usually follows a steady pattern of growth and seasonality. If we forecast this year’s revenue from the past years, and the actual revenue falls well below the forecast, we have a lead. There may be leakage of revenue, like undervaluation, short levy, or receipts not accounted for.

49.7.1 Our sample data
We create monthly stamp duty receipts of an imaginary sub-registrar office, in ₹ lakh, from April 2017 to March 2024. Receipts grow by about 8% every year. They dip in the monsoon months, rise in the festive months of October and November, and peak in March. We have built two events into the data.

In April and May 2020, receipts nearly stopped because of the COVID-19 lockdown. This is a genuine, known event.
From September 2023, receipts are about 22% lower than they should be. This is our planted case of leakage.

As usual, new readers may skip the code which creates the data.

Code to create the stamp duty receiptsset.seed(2024)
n <- 84  # April 2017 to March 2024

# Seasonal pattern from April to March
season <- c(0.95, 0.95, 0.85, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 1.10, 1.15, 1.00, 1.00, 1.05, 1.40)

receipts <- 250 * 1.08^((0:(n - 1)) / 12) * rep(season, 7) * exp(rnorm(n, 0, 0.05))

# Lockdown in April and May 2020
receipts[37:38] <- receipts[37:38] * c(0.08, 0.35)

# Planted case. Receipts about 22% lower from September 2023
receipts[78:84] <- receipts[78:84] * 0.78

stamp <- ts(round(receipts, 1), start = c(2017, 4), frequency = 12)



stamp

       Jan   Feb   Mar   Apr   May   Jun   Jul   Aug   Sep   Oct   Nov   Dec
2017                   249.5 244.7 214.1 201.7 231.0 247.8 293.5 298.8 247.5
2018 250.4 257.4 384.5 267.4 262.0 197.4 218.6 224.8 256.7 284.8 293.7 300.9
2019 290.6 318.5 401.3 282.6 258.1 249.6 246.1 229.5 269.5 310.2 345.1 299.3
2020 328.1 318.4 446.7  24.3 102.8 263.5 262.4 262.9 292.6 369.0 418.1 312.3
2021 335.8 358.4 489.2 333.6 358.3 284.8 267.0 287.2 300.3 375.8 380.8 374.4
2022 356.1 400.3 510.1 377.9 366.6 324.9 302.2 347.8 339.2 380.0 457.9 396.3
2023 350.0 435.2 519.5 382.5 380.7 344.9 318.5 371.5 297.6 335.8 372.5 306.1
2024 344.5 361.7 425.8                                                      


Let us plot the data in Figure 49.17. The lockdown dip in 2020 is obvious. The fall after September 2023 is harder to see by eye.

autoplot(stamp) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Receipts (₹ lakh)") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 49.17: Monthly stamp duty receipts of the sub-registrar office





49.7.2 Forecasting the year under audit
The year under audit is 2023-24. So we take the data up to March 2023 as training data, and keep 2023-24 aside to compare with the forecast.

train_stamp  <- window(stamp, end = c(2023, 3))
actual_stamp <- window(stamp, start = c(2023, 4))

We fit a model with ets() on the training data and forecast the 12 months of 2023-24, with a 95% prediction interval. Let us also write a small function to put the forecast and actual values side by side.

compare_with_actual <- function(fc, actual) {
  tibble(month    = as.yearmon(time(actual)),
         actual   = as.numeric(actual),
         forecast = as.numeric(fc$mean),
         lower    = as.numeric(fc$lower),
         upper    = as.numeric(fc$upper)) |>
    mutate(gap   = actual - forecast,
           below = actual < lower)
}

fc1 <- forecast(ets(train_stamp), h = 12, level = 95)
compare_with_actual(fc1, actual_stamp)

# A tibble: 12 × 7
   month     actual forecast lower upper    gap below
   <yearmon>  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <lgl>
 1 Apr 2023    382.     331.  239.  424.  51.1  FALSE
 2 May 2023    381.     344.  245.  443.  36.8  FALSE
 3 Jun 2023    345.     334.  229.  438.  11.3  FALSE
 4 Jul 2023    318.     327.  216.  437.  -8.11 FALSE
 5 Aug 2023    372.     337.  222.  453.  34.1  FALSE
 6 Sep 2023    298.     357.  237.  478. -59.9  FALSE
 7 Oct 2023    336.     412.  287.  538. -76.5  FALSE
 8 Nov 2023    372.     433.  303.  563. -60.6  FALSE

10 Jan 2024    344.     392.  254.  531. -47.8  FALSE
11 Feb 2024    362.     410.  268.  553. -48.6  FALSE
12 Mar 2024    426.     520.  373.  667. -93.8  FALSE


Not a single month is below the lower limit. The intervals are very wide. On average, the range from the lower to the upper limit is about ₹243 lakh, almost as large as a month’s receipts. With such wide limits, almost nothing can look unusual. Why?
The reason is the lockdown. The model has seen receipts fall to nearly zero in April 2020, and so it believes that such falls can happen any time. A single extraordinary event in the past has made the model very unsure about the future.

49.7.3 Cleaning a known event
The lockdown was a known, one-time event. It is not part of the normal behaviour of this office. So it is fair to replace those two months with values the series would normally have had. The function tsclean() from forecast finds such outliers and replaces them with values estimated from the rest of the series.

train_clean <- tsclean(train_stamp)

# Compare the original and cleaned values for March to June 2020
cbind(original = train_stamp, cleaned = train_clean) |>
  window(start = c(2020, 3), end = c(2020, 6))

         original  cleaned
Mar 2020    446.7 446.7000
Apr 2020     24.3 316.7061
May 2020    102.8 305.6639
Jun 2020    263.5 263.5000


Only April and May 2020 have changed. Now let us forecast again from the cleaned data.

fc2 <- forecast(ets(train_clean), h = 12, level = 95)
cmp2 <- compare_with_actual(fc2, actual_stamp)
cmp2

# A tibble: 12 × 7
   month     actual forecast lower upper      gap below

10 Jan 2024    344.     405.  359.  451.  -60.5   TRUE 
11 Feb 2024    362.     440.  390.  491.  -78.5   TRUE 
12 Mar 2024    426.     580.  513.  647. -154.    TRUE 


The intervals are now much narrower, about ₹91 lakh on average. And the picture is clear. From April to August 2023, the actual receipts are close to the forecast. From September 2023 onwards, every month is below the lower limit. Together, the receipts in these 7 months are ₹639 lakh, or about ₹6.4 crore, less than forecast. Figure 49.18 shows this.

autoplot(fc2) +
  autolayer(actual_stamp, series = "Actual", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Actual = "red")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2021, 2024.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Receipts (₹ lakh)", title = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")






Figure 49.18: Forecast (blue, with 95% interval) and actual receipts (red) for 2023-24




What would the auditor do next? The shortfall is a lead, so it goes into the working papers with the forecast, the interval and the gap in rupees. The next step is to ask the sub-registrar office what changed from September 2023, and to test-check the documents registered after that point.






TipAudit tip



A sustained shortfall, month after month from a clear starting point, is a much stronger lead than a single bad month. Find out what changed at that point. It could be a new officer, a change in the guideline values of property, new software, or a change in the procedure of registration. Then examine the documents registered after that point, for example for undervaluation of property.








WarningCaution



Clean only those past events which are known, genuine and one-time, like a lockdown, a strike or a system failure. Record what was cleaned and why. Never clean the period under audit itself. That would hide the very problem we are looking for.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.8 A suggested workflow
For any time series analysis in audit, we may follow these steps.


Create the time series. Arrange the data by month or quarter, without gaps, and convert it with ts(), giving the correct start and frequency. A financial year series starts at c(year, 4).

Plot it. Look at the trend, the seasonality and any unusual events with autoplot(), ggseasonplot() and ggsubseriesplot().

Decide additive or multiplicative. If the seasonal swings grow with the level of the series, take the logarithm, or use multiplicative methods.

Decompose the series with decompose() or stl(), to measure the seasonal pattern (like the March index) and see the trend clearly. Look at the largest remainders for unusual months.

Clean known one-time events in the past with tsclean(), and record what was cleaned.

Forecast the period under audit from the earlier data, with ets(), hw() or auto.arima(). Where possible, compare methods on test data with accuracy().

Compare the actual values with the forecast and its prediction interval. Quantify the gap in rupees.

Verify with records. Find out what changed, and examine the documents of the period.







ImportantRemember



A forecast is the auditor’s expectation, not the truth. A gap between the actual and the forecast is a lead, not a finding. There may be a genuine reason, like a change in tax rates, a court order or a slowdown in the market. Always find out the reason and examine the records before reporting.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.9 Where next
This chapter looked at the pattern of a series as a whole. The anomaly detection chapter picks out single months which are unusual after allowing for trend and season (Section 50.11). It also finds the point at which a series shifted to a new level and stayed there (Section 50.13), as the stamp duty receipts did in September 2023.

title: 49  Time Series Analysis
text:
49.10 Try it yourself
These exercises use the series of this chapter, spend, ctax and stamp, and the objects built from them. Try each one before you open the solution.


The March share of one year. Take out the financial year 2020-21 of spend with window(). What percentage of that year’s expenditure was spent in March 2021?






TipSolution






fy_2021 <- window(spend, start = c(2020, 4), end = c(2021, 3))
march_share_2021 <- round(100 * fy_2021[12] / sum(fy_2021), 1)
march_share_2021

[1] 23.5


March 2021 alone carried 23.5% of the year’s expenditure. The last value of the window is March, because the financial year runs from April to March. Against a norm of 15% for March, this is a clear point for the audit report.





The busiest quarter for commercial tax. Decompose ctax with decompose(), using a multiplicative model, and print the seasonal index of each quarter. Which quarter collects the most tax, compared with its trend?






TipSolution






ctax_idx <- round(decompose(ctax, type = "multiplicative")$figure, 3) |>
  setNames(c("Apr-Jun", "Jul-Sep", "Oct-Dec", "Jan-Mar"))
ctax_idx

Apr-Jun Jul-Sep Oct-Dec Jan-Mar 
  0.932   0.946   0.996   1.126 


The series starts in the April to June quarter, so the indices are in that order. The Jan-Mar quarter is the highest, at about 13% above the trend. A quarterly return checked against this index will show whether a circle’s collections follow the State pattern.





The weakest month. The table spend_rem lists the STL remainders of spend, largest first. Which month was furthest below what its trend and season would suggest?






TipSolution






weak_month <- spend_rem |> arrange(remainder) |> head(3)
weak_month

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  month     spend remainder
  <yearmon> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Sep 2019   44.8    -0.178
2 Sep 2023   60.7    -0.144
3 Jul 2018   37.2    -0.113


September 2019 has the most negative remainder, -0.178. On the log scale, this means the department spent about 16% less than expected that month. September is a quiet month, and a single dip with no other sign is a weak lead. It is worth a question to the department. The March 2021 spike, about 38% above normal, remains the stronger lead.





A second opinion on the stamp duty. Forecast 2023-24 from the cleaned training data train_clean with auto.arima(train_clean, lambda = 0) instead of ets(), with a 95% interval. Use compare_with_actual() to list the months below the lower limit. Does ARIMA tell the same story?






TipSolution






fc3  <- forecast(auto.arima(train_clean, lambda = 0), h = 12, level = 95)
cmp3 <- compare_with_actual(fc3, actual_stamp)
cmp3 |> filter(below) |> select(month, actual, forecast, lower)

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  month     actual forecast lower
  <yearmon>  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 Sep 2023    298.     369.  328.
2 Oct 2023    336.     443.  394.
3 Nov 2023    372.     510.  453.
4 Dec 2023    306.     414.  368.
5 Jan 2024    344.     406.  361.
6 Feb 2024    362.     464.  413.
7 Mar 2024    426.     596.  530.


ARIMA puts 7 months below the lower limit, from September 2023 onwards. The shortfall against the ARIMA forecast in these months is about ₹757 lakh. When two different methods point to the same months, the lead is much stronger.
