title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.1 Definition and types of anomalies
Anomalies play a significant role in the field of audit. An anomaly is something that does not fit. It may be a payment far larger than usual, a claim that breaks a pattern, or a month when expenditure suddenly jumps. As auditors examine data, whether financial statements, transactions or other records, such anomalies give valuable leads.
Anomalies often point to problems like these.
Detecting and investigating anomalies is therefore a core skill for an auditor. In this chapter, we will learn several methods to detect them, from simple box plots to machine learning methods. Table 50.1 gives a road map.
Anomalies are patterns or data points that deviate significantly from the expected or normal behaviour within a dataset. They are also known as outliers, novelties or deviations. There are three types of anomalies.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
Point anomalies. A single record which is unusual when compared with the rest of the data. For example, a stationery bill of ₹2,00,000 in an office where such bills are usually below ₹10,000.

Contextual anomalies. A record which is unusual only in a particular context. For example, an electricity bill of ₹3 lakh may be normal for an office in May, when air conditioners run all day, but unusual for the same office in December. The amount is not odd by itself. The month makes it odd.

Collective anomalies. A group of records which is unusual when seen together, though each record may look normal by itself. For example, twenty cash withdrawals of ₹49,000 each from one account within a week. No single withdrawal is unusual. Together, they suggest that someone is avoiding a reporting limit of ₹50,000.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.2 Anomaly detection by inspection
Many times, anomalies or outliers can be spotted just by looking at the data. The summary() function prints the minimum, maximum, lower and upper quartiles, the mean and the median. It gives a sense of how far an extreme point lies from the rest of the data.
As an example, let us take the mean annual temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit in New Haven, Connecticut, from 1912 to 1971. This data is available in base R as nhtemp.

summary(nhtemp)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  47.90   50.58   51.20   51.16   51.90   54.60 


The easiest way to see how unusual a value is, is a graphical summary like a box plot. In base R, it is drawn with the boxplot() function. It shows the distribution of values as a box with whiskers, and draws extreme values as separate points. This makes them easy to spot. We can also draw box plots using ggplot2.
For an audit example, let us take the stationery and printing bills of a district office for one year. Three vendors supply the office. Shree Ram Stationers sends small bills for paper and pens. Kaveri Office Supplies sends somewhat larger bills for toner and files. Modern Printers prints forms and registers, and its bills are the largest. One bill has been planted. It is a bill of Shree Ram Stationers for ₹38,000.

Code to create the stationery billsset.seed(311)
stationery <- tibble(
  vendor = rep(c("Shree Ram Stationers", "Kaveri Office Supplies", "Modern Printers"),
               times = c(40, 30, 20)),
  amount = round(c(rnorm(40, 4500, 1200), rnorm(30, 9500, 2000), rnorm(20, 34000, 7000)), -1)
)
# Planted. A bill far above what this vendor usually charges
stationery$amount[17] <- 38000



glimpse(stationery)

Rows: 90
Columns: 2
$ vendor <chr> "Shree Ram Stationers", "Shree Ram Stationers", "Shree Ram Stat…
$ amount <dbl> 5400, 5300, 3860, 2480, 4530, 6410, 4410, 3570, 5990, 6550, 344…


Figure 50.1 shows both kinds of box plot. The left panel is the base R box plot of the nhtemp data, the mean annual temperatures of New Haven. The right panel draws the stationery bills, one box for each vendor.



boxplot(nhtemp, main = "Box plot of nhtemp data")
ggplot(stationery, aes(vendor, amount, colour = vendor)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Stationery bills by vendor", x = NULL, y = "Amount (₹)")















Figure 50.1: Outliers through box plot


The planted bill of ₹38,000 shows as a red point above the box of Shree Ram Stationers. Notice that the same amount would be quite ordinary for Modern Printers. If we had drawn one box for all the bills together, this bill would have hidden among the printing bills.
The separate points in a box plot are decided by a simple rule, often called the IQR rule. The box covers the middle 50% of the data, from the lower quartile (Q1) to the upper quartile (Q3). The difference Q3 - Q1 is called the inter-quartile range or IQR. Any value more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1, or above Q3, is drawn as a separate point.
We do not have to read these values from the plot. boxplot.stats() returns them in its out element.

boxplot.stats(nhtemp)$out

[1] 47.9 48.4 54.0 54.6


For the bills, we apply the same rule within each vendor.

stationery |>
  filter(amount %in% boxplot.stats(amount)$out, .by = vendor)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  vendor               amount
  <chr>                 <dbl>
1 Shree Ram Stationers  38000
2 Modern Printers       19870


The planted bill is listed. So is one unusually small bill of Modern Printers. A value far below the rest is also an outlier. A small printing bill is less likely to hide a loss, but it may point to an order split into parts, so it is worth a glance too.






TipAudit tip



The box plot is the quickest first check on any amount column. Draw it by group rather than for the whole data. For example, draw a box plot of bill amounts for each vendor or each head of account. A bill which is normal for the whole office may be very unusual for its own vendor. We saw this idea in the RSF test in Chapter 33.


It is important to note that a point anomaly need not always be an extreme value. A point anomaly can also arise as an unusual combination of values across several columns. We will see such an example in Section 50.10.
A collective anomaly, on the other hand, is a group of records which is unusual together. In Figure 50.2, a period of five consecutive days with high temperatures is shown by red points. These daily temperatures are unusual because they occur together, and are likely caused by the same weather event.







Figure 50.2: Collective Anomalies

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.3 Grubbs’ test
Visual inspection works well when most data points are grouped together and a few lie clearly apart. But it is a matter of judgement. Statistics offers formal tests to decide whether a value is an outlier. Grubbs’ test, named after Frank Grubbs, is one of these.
Grubbs’ test checks whether the single value lying farthest from the mean could be an outlier. This value will be either the largest or the smallest value in the data. The test assumes that the data is normally distributed. So, before using it, we must check that this assumption is reasonable. A histogram is a quick way to check this. (For other ways of checking normality, refer to the chapter on linear regression.)
Let us run the test on the nhtemp data, which we saw in Figure 50.1. First, the histogram.

hist(nhtemp, breaks = 20)






Figure 50.3: Histogram for Grubbs’ test




In Figure 50.3 we can see that the data is roughly bell shaped, so the assumption is nearly satisfied. Let us run the test, using grubbs.test() from the outliers package.

library(outliers)
grubbs.test(nhtemp)


    Grubbs test for one outlier

data:  nhtemp
G = 2.71806, U = 0.87266, p-value = 0.1539
alternative hypothesis: highest value 54.6 is an outlier


How do we read this? The null hypothesis of the test is that there is no outlier. The output shows the alternative hypothesis, that the highest value, 54.6, is an outlier. The p-value is about 0.15, which is more than the usual cut-off of 0.05. So we do not have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis. In simple words, we cannot conclude that 54.6 is an outlier, though it looked separate in the box plot.






WarningCaution



Grubbs’ test checks only one value at a time, the most extreme one. If there are several outliers, they can hide each other. For testing several suspected outliers together, a related test called Rosner’s test can be used. It is available as rosnerTest() in the EnvStats package. Also remember that most financial data, like bill amounts, is not normally distributed. It usually has a long tail of large values. For such data, Grubbs’ test is not suitable unless the data is first transformed, for example by taking logs.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.4 Robust z-scores and peer groups
The best-known way to measure how unusual a value is, is the z-score. It tells how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean. A value with a z-score beyond 3, or below -3, is commonly called an outlier. But the plain z-score has two weaknesses which matter a great deal in audit data.
It is not robust. The mean and the standard deviation are themselves pulled by extreme values. A few large outliers raise the mean and inflate the standard deviation, and so make themselves look less unusual. This is called masking. See this small example.

x <- c(10, 11, 12, 10, 11, 12, 11, 95, 98, 99)
round((x - mean(x)) / sd(x), 2)

 [1] -0.64 -0.62 -0.60 -0.64 -0.62 -0.60 -0.62  1.39  1.46  1.49


The three obviously odd values, 95, 98 and 99, have z-scores below 1.5. They have hidden one another. The remedy is to use measures which outliers cannot pull. These are the median in place of the mean, and the median absolute deviation (MAD) in place of the standard deviation. The MAD is the median of the distances of the values from their median. R’s mad() scales it so that, for normal data, it matches the standard deviation. The result is the robust z-score.

round((x - median(x)) / mad(x), 2)

 [1] -1.01 -0.34  0.34 -1.01 -0.34  0.34 -0.34 56.32 58.34 59.02


Now the three odd values stand out at once. A common rule, suggested by Iglewicz and Hoaglin, is to flag robust z-scores beyond 3.5. For money amounts, which are skewed, compute the score on the logarithm of the amount, as we did in Section 50.11.
It compares everything with everything. The second weakness matters even more. A district hospital spends far more per patient than a primary health centre. Compared with all facilities together, every district hospital looks “unusual”, and a primary health centre spending three times as much as other PHCs looks normal. The fair comparison is with the peer group. That means PHCs with PHCs, and district hospitals with district hospitals.
Let us see both points on the medicine expenditure of 300 health facilities of a State.

Code to create the facility dataset.seed(2028)
types <- c(PHC = 200, CHC = 70, DH = 30)   # primary, community health centres, district hospitals
facilities <- tibble(type = rep(names(types), types)) |>
  mutate(facility = paste0(type, "-", sprintf("%03d", row_number())), .by = type) |>
  mutate(beds = round(case_when(type == "PHC" ~ runif(n(), 6, 10),
                                type == "CHC" ~ runif(n(), 30, 50),
                                TRUE          ~ runif(n(), 100, 300))),
         patients = round(beds * rlnorm(n(), log(140), 0.25)),          # patients per month
         cost_per_patient = round(case_when(type == "PHC" ~ 120, type == "CHC" ~ 330,
                                            TRUE ~ 850) * rlnorm(n(), 0, 0.18)),
         # Planted. Medicine spending far above the facility's own peers
         cost_per_patient = case_when(facility == "PHC-037" ~ 410,
                                      facility == "CHC-012" ~ 1250,
                                      TRUE ~ cost_per_patient),
         medicine_lakh = round(patients * cost_per_patient / 1e5, 2))



facilities |>
  summarise(facilities = n(), median_cost = median(cost_per_patient), .by = type)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  type  facilities median_cost
  <chr>      <int>       <dbl>
1 PHC          200         118
2 CHC           70         329
3 DH            30         898


First, the plain z-score of the cost per patient, over all 300 facilities.

facilities |>
  mutate(z = (cost_per_patient - mean(cost_per_patient)) / sd(cost_per_patient)) |>
  filter(abs(z) > 3) |>
  count(type)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  type      n
  <chr> <int>
1 CHC       1
2 DH        7


Of the 8 facilities flagged, 7 are district hospitals, flagged simply for being district hospitals. Now the robust z-score of the log cost, computed within each type with .by.

robust_z <- function(x) (x - median(x)) / mad(x)

facilities <- facilities |>
  mutate(rz_peer = robust_z(log(cost_per_patient)), .by = type)

facilities |>
  filter(abs(rz_peer) > 3.5) |>
  select(facility, type, cost_per_patient, rz_peer) |>
  mutate(rz_peer = round(rz_peer, 1))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  facility type  cost_per_patient rz_peer
  <chr>    <chr>            <dbl>   <dbl>
1 PHC-037  PHC                410     6.2
2 CHC-012  CHC               1250     7.5


Only the two planted facilities are flagged. PHC-037 spends ₹410 per patient, ordinary for a CHC but more than three times what other PHCs spend, which the plain z-score over all facilities could not see. CHC-012 spends far more than other CHCs.






TipAudit tip



Robust z-scores within peer groups are the simplest anomaly method that an audit team can explain to anyone, and often the most useful. Choose peer groups that should behave alike. Examples are facilities of one type, schools of one level, police stations of one category, DDOs of one department, vendors of one commodity. Use a ratio that removes size, like cost per patient or expenditure per student. And make sure each group has enough members, at least 20 or 30, for the median and MAD to be reliable.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.5 Unusual combinations, robust Mahalanobis distance
Robust z-scores look at one measure at a time. Some anomalies show only in a combination. When a natural ratio exists, like cost per patient, the ratio captures the combination, and the z-score of the ratio is the best tool. But often the measures are related in a way no single ratio captures.
Take the primary health centres of a district. Larger PHCs see more patients in the outpatient department (OPD) and also conduct more deliveries, so the two numbers rise together. Each delivery in a public facility earns an incentive under the Janani Suraksha Yojana, so inflated delivery figures are a known risk. Now suppose one PHC reports a fairly low OPD but a fairly high number of deliveries. Neither number is unusual by itself. Together, they are.

Code to create the PHC dataset.seed(12)
n_phc <- 200
size  <- rlnorm(n_phc, 0, 0.35)              # some PHCs serve larger populations
phc <- tibble(phc        = sprintf("PHC-%03d", 1:n_phc),
              opd        = round(1100 * size * rlnorm(n_phc, 0, 0.12)),   # patients per month
              deliveries = round(30 * size * rlnorm(n_phc, 0, 0.15)))     # deliveries per month
# Planted. Low OPD (15th percentile) but high deliveries (88th percentile)
phc$opd[77]        <- round(quantile(phc$opd, 0.15))
phc$deliveries[77] <- round(quantile(phc$deliveries, 0.88))



phc <- phc |> mutate(z_opd = robust_z(log(opd)), z_deliveries = robust_z(log(deliveries)))
phc |> filter(phc == "PHC-077") |> mutate(across(starts_with("z_"), \(z) round(z, 2)))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  phc       opd deliveries z_opd z_deliveries
  <chr>   <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl>
1 PHC-077   745         46  -1.1         1.15


Neither robust z-score of PHC-077 comes anywhere near 3.5. A scatter plot shows the problem at once.

ggplot(phc, aes(opd, deliveries)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = filter(phc, phc == "PHC-077"), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "OPD patients per month (log scale)", y = "Deliveries per month (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal()



OPD and deliveries rise together; PHC-077 breaks the pattern



The Mahalanobis distance measures how far a point lies from the centre of the data, taking account of how the measures vary together. A point along the main band of the scatter, even far out, is not unusual. A point across the band, like PHC-077, is. It works for any number of measures, where scatter plots are no longer possible.
Like the z-score, it needs a centre and a measure of spread, and like the z-score, these are pulled by outliers. So we use robust estimates, from cov.rob() in the package MASS, which comes with R. Its “minimum covariance determinant” method finds the centre and spread of the most tightly packed half of the data, ignoring the rest. We work on the logarithms, since the counts are skewed.

X <- cbind(log(phc$opd), log(phc$deliveries))
robust_fit <- MASS::cov.rob(X, method = "mcd")
phc$mahal <- mahalanobis(X, center = robust_fit$center, cov = robust_fit$cov)

phc |>
  arrange(desc(mahal)) |>
  select(phc, opd, deliveries, mahal) |>
  mutate(mahal = round(mahal, 1)) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  phc       opd deliveries mahal
  <chr>   <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>
1 PHC-077   745         46  27.6
2 PHC-092   548         23   9.7
3 PHC-001   458         18   9.7
4 PHC-192  1357         23   9.4
5 PHC-029  1413         24   9.3


PHC-077 stands far above the rest. How large is “large”? For normal data, the squared Mahalanobis distance, which is what mahalanobis() returns, follows a chi-square distribution, with as many degrees of freedom as there are measures. So qchisq(0.999, df = 2) gives a cut-off that a normal point exceeds only once in a thousand times.

cutoff <- qchisq(0.999, df = ncol(X))
round(cutoff, 1)

[1] 13.8

phc |> filter(mahal > cutoff) |> pull(phc)

[1] "PHC-077"


Only PHC-077 crosses the cut-off. The next step would be to compare its delivery register with its OPD register, the beds used, and the incentive payments made.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.6 Seasonal Hybrid ESD algorithm
Grubbs’ test has two limitations. It needs normally distributed data, and it looks only at the extreme values of the whole data. Neither suits a time series with seasonal ups and downs, like monthly sales or quarterly revenue. A value may be normal for one season and unusual for another.
The Seasonal Hybrid ESD (S-H-ESD) algorithm was developed at Twitter for exactly this purpose. It first removes the seasonal pattern, and then looks for unusual values in what remains. It is available in the AnomalyDetection package, which can be installed from GitHub using remotes::install_github("twitter/AnomalyDetection").
Let us take the monthly receipts of stamp duty and registration fees of a sub-registrar office, from April 2018 to March 2025, in ₹ lakh. Receipts rise slowly over the years. They are higher in the winter months and highest in March, when many property deals are closed before the financial year ends. Two months have been planted. In August 2021 the receipts were far above normal. In November 2023 they were far below normal, as if part of the money collected was never brought to account.

Code to create the monthly receiptsset.seed(415)
receipt_months <- seq(as.Date("2018-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-01"), by = "month")
# Seasonal pattern from April to March. Winter months and March are busier.
receipt_season <- c(0.9, 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.85, 0.9, 1.05, 1.1, 1.0, 1.05, 1.1, 1.35)
fy_position <- ((month(receipt_months) + 8) %% 12) + 1   # April = 1, ..., March = 12

receipts <- tibble(
  month = receipt_months,
  receipts_lakh = round(60 + 0.25 * seq_along(receipt_months) +
                          40 * (receipt_season[fy_position] - 1) +
                          rnorm(length(receipt_months), 0, 2.5), 1)
)
# Planted. A spike in August 2021 and a shortfall in November 2023
spike <- receipts$month == as.Date("2021-08-01")
dip   <- receipts$month == as.Date("2023-11-01")
receipts$receipts_lakh[spike] <- round(receipts$receipts_lakh[spike] * 1.6, 1)
receipts$receipts_lakh[dip]   <- round(receipts$receipts_lakh[dip] * 0.55, 1)



head(receipts)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  month      receipts_lakh
  <date>             <dbl>
1 2018-04-01          56.4
2 2018-05-01          56.5
3 2018-06-01          65.5
4 2018-07-01          55.3
5 2018-08-01          59  
6 2018-09-01          58  


AnomalyDetectionVec() takes the values as a plain vector. Since the data is monthly, the seasonal pattern repeats every 12 records, so we use period = 12.

#remotes::install_github("twitter/AnomalyDetection")
library(AnomalyDetection)
shesd <- AnomalyDetectionVec(receipts$receipts_lakh,
                             period = 12,  # Seasonality
                             plot = TRUE,  # set FALSE when plot not needed
                             direction = 'both' # set 'pos' for higher values
                                                # or 'neg' for lower values
                             )
shesd$anoms

  index anoms
1    41 101.1
2    68  45.4

shesd$plot






Figure 50.4: Seasonal Hybrid ESD Algorithm




In Figure 50.4, the anomalies are marked with blue circles. They are also listed in the $anoms element of the output, with their positions and values. Position 41 is August 2021 and position 68 is November 2023. These are the two planted months. The March peaks are not flagged, because the algorithm has allowed for them as part of the season.
The office would now be asked to explain both months. For the spike, we may check whether some documents of other months were entered in August 2021, or whether one very large deal was registered. For the shortfall, we may compare the receipts booked with the documents registered in November 2023, and with the challans deposited in the treasury.






WarningCaution



S-H-ESD assumes that the seasonal ups and downs stay about the same size over the years. In many financial series they grow along with the level. When that happens, the later peaks look unusual compared with the earlier ones, though they follow the same pattern. This is a common trap with growing financial series. We will see how to deal with it, by working on the log scale, in Section 50.11.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.7 k-Nearest Neighbour distance score
One big limitation of the methods so far is that they work on a single column, or a single series. In real audit work, data is rarely so simple. A vendor may be described by its total payments, number of bills, average bill and share of round amounts. An anomaly may show up only when all these are seen together. The k-Nearest Neighbour (kNN) method works on many columns at once.
The idea of kNN is that records which are close to each other are similar. For each record, we find its k nearest neighbours, and calculate the average distance to them. A record lying far away from even its nearest neighbours is likely to be an anomaly.
Distance between records is usually measured as the straight-line Euclidean distance. For this to be fair, all columns must be on the same scale. Otherwise a column measured in lakhs will swamp a column measured in single digits. So we must always scale the data first.
Let us take the vendors of a Zila Parishad. For each of its 60 vendors, the accounts section has worked out four indicators for the financial year 2023-24.


bills, the number of bills paid.

avg_bill_lakh, the average bill, in ₹ lakh.

round_pct, the percentage of bills in round amounts, that is, exact multiples of ₹1,000.

days_to_pay, the median number of days between receipt of a bill and its payment.

The vendors are of three kinds. Suppliers of materials send many small bills. Service providers send fewer, larger bills. Works contractors send a few very large bills. Three vendors have been planted at the end of the data. V-058 is a supplier with unusually large bills, mostly in round amounts, paid within days. V-059 is a supplier which looks ordinary, except that it is paid much faster than other suppliers. V-060 is a service provider whose bills look like those of a works contractor. We will come back to V-060 in Section 50.10.

Code to create the vendor indicatorsset.seed(1804)
n_cat  <- c(Supplies = 25, Services = 17, Works = 15)
first  <- c("Shree Ganesh", "Om Sai", "Jai Ambe", "Maa Durga", "Balaji", "Ganga", "Laxmi",
            "Shiv Shakti", "Krishna", "Narmada", "Sri Venkateswara", "Kaveri", "Annapurna",
            "Bharat", "Gayatri", "Hanuman", "Mahalaxmi", "Saraswati", "Vishwakarma", "Umiya")
suffix <- c(Supplies = "Traders", Services = "Services", Works = "Constructions")

vendors <- tibble(category = rep(names(n_cat), n_cat)) |>
  mutate(bills = round(case_when(category == "Supplies" ~ rnorm(n(), 48, 6),
                                 category == "Services" ~ rnorm(n(), 24, 5),
                                 TRUE                   ~ rnorm(n(), 8, 2))),
         avg_bill_lakh = round(case_when(category == "Supplies" ~ rnorm(n(), 0.9, 0.12),
                                         category == "Services" ~ rnorm(n(), 2.8, 0.5),
                                         TRUE                   ~ rnorm(n(), 11, 1.6)), 2),
         round_pct   = round(runif(n(), 5, 25)),
         days_to_pay = round(rnorm(n(), 32, 6)))

# Planted. V-058 far from everyone, V-059 a local oddity, V-060 a category mismatch
planted_vendors <- tibble(category      = c("Supplies", "Supplies", "Services"),
                          bills         = c(60, 44, 9),
                          avg_bill_lakh = c(4.6, 1.05, 10.5),
                          round_pct     = c(85, 16, 15),
                          days_to_pay   = c(4, 13, 31))

vendors <- bind_rows(vendors, planted_vendors) |>
  mutate(vendor   = sprintf("V-%03d", row_number()),
         name     = paste(sample(first, n(), replace = TRUE), suffix[category]),
         category = factor(category),
         .before  = 1)



glimpse(vendors)

Columns: 7

tail(vendors, 4)

  vendor name                 category bills avg_bill_lakh round_pct days_to_pay

1 V-057  Krishna Constructio… Works        9         14.0         18          34
2 V-058  Laxmi Traders        Supplies    60          4.6         85           4
3 V-059  Krishna Traders      Supplies    44          1.05        16          13
4 V-060  Shiv Shakti Services Services     9         10.5         15          31


The indicators are on very different scales. We use the scale() function of base R to normalise them. Remember that scale() returns a matrix, so we may need to convert it into a data frame for ggplot2. We also keep the vendor codes as row names, so that we can refer to vendors later.

indicators <- c("bills", "avg_bill_lakh", "round_pct", "days_to_pay")
vend_scaled <- vendors |>
  select(all_of(indicators)) |>
  scale()
rownames(vend_scaled) <- vendors$vendor

Let us visualise the data, first in two dimensions only, the number of bills and the average bill. As the data is already scaled, we can also see all four dimensions together in a box plot. Both are shown in Figure 50.5. The points are labelled with the last two digits of the vendor code.



vend_df <- vend_scaled |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(vendor = vendors$vendor, label = str_sub(vendor, -2))

vend_df |>
  ggplot(aes(bills, avg_bill_lakh)) +
  geom_point(color = "seagreen") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  theme_bw()

# Helper Function
find_outlier <- function(x) {
  return(x < quantile(x, .25) - 1.5*IQR(x) | x > quantile(x, .75) + 1.5*IQR(x))
}

vend_df |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(indicators), names_to = "Dimension", values_to = "Values") |>
  group_by(Dimension) |>
  mutate(outlier = ifelse(find_outlier(Values), label, NA)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Dimension, Values)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red") +
  geom_text(aes(label = outlier), na.rm = TRUE, hjust = -.5) +
  theme_bw()















Figure 50.5: Number of bills and average bill of vendors (left), all four scaled indicators (right)


In the left panel, the three kinds of vendor form three groups, from many small bills to a few large ones. Vendor 58 sits apart from all three groups. In the right panel, it is the outlier on the round amounts and on the days to pay. Vendor 59 is also an outlier on the days to pay.
Now, let us find the outliers in R. We will use the get.knn() function from the FNN package. We must choose the value of k, the number of neighbours, beforehand. Let us take k = 5.

# Load the library
library(FNN)
# get kNN object, using k = 5, on first two columns only
vendor_knn <- FNN::get.knn(vend_scaled[, 1:2], 5)

The object created above has two matrices, each with k columns. nn.index holds the row numbers of the nearest neighbours of each record. nn.dist holds the distances to them. Let us view the top 6 rows of each.

head(vendor_knn$nn.index)

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
[1,]   23   22   59   16   19
[2,]   10   24    6   12   15
[3,]    5   21   18   14   17
[4,]   11   18    6   12    3
[5,]    3   21   18   14   17
[6,]   12   10   11   24    4

head(vendor_knn$nn.dist)

            [,1]       [,2]       [,3]       [,4]       [,5]
[1,] 0.059971590 0.06581837 0.22567982 0.28338626 0.28500369
[2,] 0.058758849 0.06779867 0.07826081 0.09532600 0.11292475
[3,] 0.002259956 0.03615929 0.05713677 0.05859313 0.06360851
[4,] 0.009039823 0.05682305 0.05859313 0.06825636 0.11393784
[5,] 0.002259956 0.03841925 0.05753762 0.05924328 0.06259679
[6,] 0.022599557 0.05659790 0.05682305 0.05802378 0.05859313


Using rowMeans(), we can calculate the average distance of each record from its neighbours. This is the kNN score. The bigger the score, the more likely the record is an outlier. Let us store the score and show it as the size of the points. In Figure 50.6, the points lying far away are bigger, because their chance of being outliers is higher.

score <- rowMeans(vendor_knn$nn.dist)
vend_df |>
  mutate(score = score) |>
  ggplot(aes(bills, avg_bill_lakh)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score), color = "seagreen") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "KNN method of outlier")






Figure 50.6: k-Nearest Neighbour Distance




Now, we can run the algorithm on all four columns of the data.

vendor_knn <- FNN::get.knn(vend_scaled, 5)
score <- rowMeans(vendor_knn$nn.dist)
names(score) <- vendors$vendor
# Which vendor is farthest from its neighbours
which.max(score)

V-058 
   58 

# The five highest scores
round(head(sort(score, decreasing = TRUE), 5), 2)

V-058 V-059 V-052 V-039 V-048 
 6.80  1.61  1.16  1.13  1.08 


On all four indicators, V-058 is far ahead of every other vendor, with a score of 6.8. V-059 comes next. It is a supplier which is paid much faster than its peers, a difference that did not show in the scatter plot of bills and average bill.






NoteHow to choose k?



There is no single correct value of k. A very small k, like 1 or 2, makes the score sensitive to chance. Two odd records lying close to each other will look normal, because each is the other’s nearest neighbour. A very large k blurs the picture. A value between 5 and 20 works well in most cases. It is a good practice to try two or three values and see whether the same records come out on top.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.8 Local Outlier Factor
kNN is good at finding records which are far from all others. These are sometimes called global anomalies. But it can miss records which lie close to a group, yet are not like their immediate neighbours. These are called local anomalies.
To understand the difference, see the dummy data in Figure 50.7. Think of it as sales and profit of branches of a company.







Figure 50.7: Local Outlier factor




The red points are global outliers. They are far from everything else. The blue points are not far from the tight group on the right. But that group is very tightly packed, and the blue points do not share its tightness. So they are local anomalies. kNN may miss them, because their distance from the group is small in absolute terms.
The Local Outlier Factor (LOF) solves this. Instead of distance, it looks at density, that is, how crowded the neighbourhood of a record is. It compares the density around each record with the density around its neighbours.

A score close to 1 means the record is as crowded as its neighbours. It is normal.
A score clearly above 1 means the record is in a much emptier area than its neighbours. It may be an anomaly.

We will use the lof() function from the dbscan package. Its second argument is the number of neighbours to consider, like k in kNN. Let us apply it to the same vendor data, using all four indicators.



library(dbscan)
lof_score <- lof(vend_scaled, 5)
vend_df |>
  mutate(score = lof_score) |>
  ggplot(aes(bills, avg_bill_lakh)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score), color = "seagreen") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_size_continuous(guide = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "LOF method of outlier")

vend_prcomp <- prcomp(vend_scaled, scale. = TRUE)

vend_df |>
  mutate(score = lof_score,
         PC1 = vend_prcomp$x[,1],
         PC2 = vend_prcomp$x[,2]) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score), color = "seagreen") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_size_continuous(guide = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "LOF method of outlier\nVisualised on principal components")















Figure 50.8: LOF


In Figure 50.8 (left), we have plotted the data in two dimensions only, though LOF was calculated on all four. So vendor 59, which has the second highest LOF score, sits right inside the group of suppliers in this plot. It is a local anomaly. Its bills look like those of any supplier, but it is paid much faster than the suppliers around it.
To see all four dimensions in one picture, we can use the first two principal components (Figure 50.8, right). Principal components combine many columns into a few new columns which keep most of the information. We learnt about them in Chapter 46. For now, it is enough to know that they give a fair two-dimensional picture of four-dimensional data.
Let us also compare the biggest anomalies according to each method.

# Biggest Anomaly - kNN
which.max(score)

V-058 
   58 

# Biggest Anomaly - LOF
which.max(lof_score)

[1] 58

# Top five vendors by each method
tibble(knn = names(sort(score, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5],
       lof = vendors$vendor[order(lof_score, decreasing = TRUE)][1:5])

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  knn   lof  
  <chr> <chr>
1 V-058 V-058
2 V-059 V-059
3 V-052 V-025
4 V-039 V-012
5 V-048 V-001


Both methods put V-058 first and V-059 second. Below the top two, the lists differ. This will often happen. kNN looks for records far from all others. LOF looks for records unlike their own neighbourhood. In our data the two planted vendors are both, so both methods find them. In other data the top records may differ, and each method may catch a case that the other misses. Both are useful, and they answer slightly different questions.
Histograms of both kNN and LOF scores can also be drawn, as in Figure 50.9. In both, most records have low scores, and a few stand apart on the right.



hist(score, breaks = 40,
     main = "Histogram of KNN scores of vendors")
hist(lof_score, breaks = 40,
     main = "Histogram of LOF scores of vendors")















Figure 50.9: Histograms of kNN scores (left) and LOF scores (right)








TipAudit tip



kNN and LOF give scores, not a yes or no answer. Sort the records by score and examine them from the top, until the cases stop being interesting. The histogram of scores helps decide where to stop. Look for the point where the long tail on the right begins.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.9 Isolation Forest
Isolation forest takes a completely different approach. It does not measure distance or density. Instead, it asks a simple question. How easy is it to separate this record from all the others?
Imagine we pick a column at random, and a random cut-point within its range. This splits the data into two parts. We repeat this on each part, again and again, until every record sits alone. Such a series of random splits is called an isolation tree. A normal record, sitting in a crowd, needs many splits before it is alone. An anomaly, sitting far from the crowd, gets separated in very few splits. So the number of splits (the path length in the tree) tells us how unusual a record is.
One tree is based on random choices, so its result can vary. A forest is a collection of many such trees. Averaging over many trees gives a stable score.
We will use the isotree package, which is available on CRAN. The main function is isolation.forest(). Its argument ntrees sets the number of trees. sample_size sets how many records are drawn to build each tree. We also set ndim = 1, which gives the classic isolation forest that splits on one column at a time, and a seed so that the results can be reproduced.






NoteA note on packages



An older package, isofor, is sometimes mentioned in tutorials, but it is available only on GitHub and is no longer maintained. isotree does the same job, is faster, and is regularly updated on CRAN. It can be installed with install.packages("isotree").


Let us work on the same vendor indicators as above. First, let us build a single tree.

library(isotree)
# Generate a single tree
vendor_tree_1 <- isolation.forest(vend_scaled, ntrees = 1, sample_size = 50,
                                  ndim = 1, seed = 1, nthreads = 1)

# Generate isolation score
iso_score_1 <- predict(vendor_tree_1, vend_scaled)

# View first 10 scores
iso_score_1[1:10]

    V-001     V-002     V-003     V-004     V-005     V-006     V-007     V-008 
0.5519703 0.6094383 0.5519703 0.5519703 0.5519703 0.4679782 0.6728896 0.5519703 
    V-009     V-010 
0.5519703 0.5519703 


Score interpretation. The scores lie between 0 and 1. The closer a score is to 1, the more likely the record is an anomaly. Scores below 0.5 usually mean normal records.
Let us visualise the scores on the principal component plot again (Figure 50.10).



vend_df |>
  mutate(score = iso_score_1,
         PC1 = vend_prcomp$x[,1],
         PC2 = vend_prcomp$x[,2]) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score), color = "seagreen") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_size_continuous(guide = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Isolation Tree based outlier\nVisualised on principal components")

vend_df |>
  mutate(score = iso_score_1,
         PC1 = vend_prcomp$x[,1],
         PC2 = vend_prcomp$x[,2],
         is_outlier = factor(ifelse(ntile(iso_score_1, 10) >= 10, "O", "N"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score, color = is_outlier)) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(O = "red", N = "black"), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(guide = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Isolation Tree based outlier\nTop-10%")















Figure 50.10: Isolation Tree Method


In the right panel, the top 10% of records by score are shown in red. ntile(x, 10) divides the records into ten equal groups by score, so group 10 is the top 10%.
Let us now build a forest of 100 trees (Figure 50.11). The right panel compares the scores of one tree with those of the forest. If both gave the same scores, all points would lie on the diagonal line. They do not, because a single tree depends heavily on its random splits. As the number of trees increases, the scores become stable.



iso_100 <- isolation.forest(vend_scaled, ntrees = 100, sample_size = 50,
                            ndim = 1, seed = 1, nthreads = 1)

# Generate scores
iso_score_100 <- predict(iso_100, vend_scaled)

# View Results
vend_df |>
  mutate(score = iso_score_100,
         PC1 = vend_prcomp$x[,1],
         PC2 = vend_prcomp$x[,2],
         is_outlier = factor(ifelse(ntile(iso_score_100, 10) >= 10, "O", "N"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score, color = is_outlier)) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), arrow = grid::arrow(), max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(O = "red", N = "black"), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(guide = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Isolation Tree based outlier\nNumber of Trees = 100")

plot(iso_score_1, iso_score_100, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),
     main = "Comparison of Tree Vs. Forest Method")
abline(a = 0, b = 1)















Figure 50.11: 100 Isolation Trees (Left) Comparison of 1 vs. 100 trees (Right)


Let us list the vendors with the highest forest scores.

vendors |>
  mutate(iso_score = round(iso_score_100, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(iso_score)) |>
  select(vendor, name, category, all_of(indicators), iso_score) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 8
  vendor name       category bills avg_bill_lakh round_pct days_to_pay iso_score
  <chr>  <chr>      <fct>    <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 V-058  Laxmi Tra… Supplies    60          4.6         85           4      0.76
2 V-053  Laxmi Con… Works        9         12.0          8          49      0.56
3 V-025  Shree Gan… Supplies    35          0.69         5          36      0.54
4 V-045  Sri Venka… Works        9         13.1         11          47      0.54
5 V-055  Mahalaxmi… Works        6         14.0         16          27      0.54


V-058 is at the top by a clear margin, with a score of 0.76. V-059, the supplier paid unusually fast, is at position 3. The scores after the top one are close together, so the forest separates the far-away vendor much more sharply than the local oddity. This is typical. Isolation forest is best at global anomalies.
Contour plots. We can also show the anomaly scores of a whole area as a contour plot, like the height lines of a map. We build a fine grid of points covering the first two principal components, score every grid point, and draw lines joining equal scores. See Figure 50.12. Records falling in the high-score regions are anomalies.

# Create PRCOMP data
df_grid <- data.frame(
  PC1 = vend_prcomp$x[,1],
  PC2 = vend_prcomp$x[,2]
)

# Create Sequences
pc1_seq <- seq(min(vend_prcomp$x[,1]), max(vend_prcomp$x[,1]), length.out = 25)
pc2_seq <- seq(min(vend_prcomp$x[,2]), max(vend_prcomp$x[,2]), length.out = 25)
# Create Grid
my_grid <- expand.grid(PC1 = pc1_seq, PC2 = pc2_seq)

# Create model for Pr comp
iso_model <- isolation.forest(df_grid, ntrees = 100, sample_size = 50,
                              ndim = 1, seed = 1, nthreads = 1)
# append scores
my_grid$scores <- predict(iso_model, my_grid)

# Draw Plot
library(lattice)
contourplot(scores ~ PC1 + PC2, data = my_grid, region = TRUE)






Figure 50.12: Contour Plot




Including categorical variables. One benefit of the isolation forest is that it can use categorical columns directly. The only condition is that they should be of factor type.
Let us now find anomalies in the vendor data again, this time including the category column. We keep the four indicators unscaled, since an isolation forest does not need scaling. We can check the column types before proceeding.

vendors_mixed <- vendors |> select(category, all_of(indicators))
sapply(vendors_mixed, class)

     category         bills avg_bill_lakh     round_pct   days_to_pay 
     "factor"     "numeric"     "numeric"     "numeric"     "numeric" 


Our condition is met, as category is already a factor. So we can build the forest directly. Refer Figure 50.13.

# New isolation forest model, including category
iso_model_new <- isolation.forest(vendors_mixed, ntrees = 100, ndim = 1,
                                  seed = 1, nthreads = 1)
new_scores <- predict(iso_model_new, vendors_mixed)
head(new_scores)

        1         2         3         4         5         6 
0.4453272 0.4425183 0.4268078 0.4078696 0.4073524 0.4302865 

# Principal components of the four indicators, for the picture
vend_pr <- prcomp(vendors_mixed[, indicators], scale. = TRUE)

data.frame(
  PC1 = vend_pr$x[,1],
  PC2 = vend_pr$x[,2]
) |>
  mutate(score = new_scores,
         category = vendors$category,
         label = str_sub(vendors$vendor, -2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, color = category)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score)) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = ifelse(score > quantile(score, 0.9), label, "")),
                           show.legend = FALSE) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Isolation Forest\nVisualised on Principal Components")






Figure 50.13: Including categorical variable




With the category included, V-060 moves up from position 38 to position 4. It is a service provider whose bills look like a works contractor’s. The forest can now see that its numbers do not fit its category. In Figure 50.13 the ten per cent of vendors with the highest scores are labelled.






TipAudit tip



Isolation forest is a good default for large audit data. It is fast, needs no scaling, handles many columns, and accepts categorical columns. A common practice is to run it on a table of indicators built for each vendor, employee or beneficiary. Then examine the top 1% or top 50 records by score.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.10 Including categorical variables in LOF
We can also include categorical variables in the Local Outlier Factor, using the Gower distance. Gower distance can measure the distance between records which have both numeric and categorical columns, even when the categories have no natural order. It is calculated with the function daisy() from the cluster package. Let us calculate LOF scores on the vendor data, including category. The result is shown in Figure 50.14.

library(cluster)
vendor_dist <- daisy(vendors_mixed, metric = "gower")
vendor_lof <- lof(vendor_dist, minPts = 5)

data.frame(
  PC1 = vend_pr$x[,1],
  PC2 = vend_pr$x[,2]
) |>
  mutate(score = vendor_lof,
         category = vendors$category,
         label = str_sub(vendors$vendor, -2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, color = category)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = score)) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = ifelse(score > quantile(score, 0.9), label, "")),
                           show.legend = FALSE) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "LOF Scores\nVisualised on Principal Components")






Figure 50.14: Including categorical variable





vendors |>
  mutate(lof_numeric = round(lof_score, 2),
         lof_gower   = round(vendor_lof, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(lof_gower)) |>
  select(vendor, category, bills, avg_bill_lakh, lof_numeric, lof_gower) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  vendor category bills avg_bill_lakh lof_numeric lof_gower
  <chr>  <fct>    <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 V-058  Supplies    60          4.6         8.78      6.58
2 V-060  Services     9         10.5         0.97      3.55
3 V-059  Supplies    44          1.05        1.73      2.04
4 V-025  Supplies    35          0.69        1.63      1.96
5 V-030  Services    39          3.22        1.22      1.48


On the four numbers alone, V-060 was at position 50 by LOF. With the category included through Gower distance, it rises to position 2. Its nearest neighbours are works contractors, and it is the only one among them labelled as a service provider. The auditor would now ask why a service provider is raising bills of the size of works contracts. Was the work split from a works contract to avoid a tender? Was the firm registered under the wrong category?

50.10.1 How does Gower distance work?
kNN and LOF need a distance between every pair of records. For numbers this is easy. But what is the distance between “Air” and “Sleeper”, or between “Group A” and “Group C”? Gower distance answers this in a simple way.

For a numeric column, it takes the difference between the two values and divides it by the range (maximum minus minimum) of that column. So the result is always between 0 and 1.
For a categorical column, the distance is 0 if the two values are the same, and 1 if they are different.
The final distance is the average of these column-wise distances.

So every column contributes equally, and the final distance is always between 0 and 1. This is why we did not have to scale the data before using daisy().

50.10.2 Why categories matter, an audit example
Let us see why including categorical columns can make a real difference. Consider travel allowance (TA) claims of employees. Each claim records the grade of the employee, the mode of travel, the distance travelled and the amount claimed. Suppose the entitlement rules are as below.


Table 50.2: Travel entitlement in our example



Grade
Entitled to travel by



Group A
Air or AC-2


Group B
AC-2 or AC-3


Group C
AC-3 or Sleeper






We have about 300 claims, created in the folded code below. Three problem claims have been planted. Two Group C employees have claimed air fare. Their amounts are quite normal for an air journey of that distance. The third claim is an AC-3 journey with a hugely inflated amount.

Code to create the TA claims dataset.seed(2611)

entitled <- list(`Group A` = c("Air", "AC-2"),
                 `Group B` = c("AC-2", "AC-3"),
                 `Group C` = c("AC-3", "Sleeper"))
rate_per_km <- c(Air = 6, `AC-2` = 2.6, `AC-3` = 1.8, Sleeper = 0.7)

n <- 300
claims <- tibble(grade = sample(names(entitled), n, replace = TRUE,
                                prob = c(0.25, 0.35, 0.4))) |>
  mutate(mode        = map_chr(grade, \(g) sample(entitled[[g]], 1)),
         distance_km = round(runif(n, 200, 1800)),
         amount      = round(distance_km * rate_per_km[mode] * 2 *
                               runif(n, 0.9, 1.15) + 500))

planted <- tibble(grade       = c("Group C", "Group C", "Group B"),
                  mode        = c("Air", "Air", "AC-3"),
                  distance_km = c(1150, 1420, 900),
                  amount      = c(14300, 17600, 41000))

claims <- bind_rows(claims, planted) |>
  mutate(claim_id = sprintf("TA-%03d", row_number()), .before = 1)



tail(claims, 4)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  claim_id grade   mode  distance_km amount
  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>
1 TA-300   Group B AC-3          745   3503
2 TA-301   Group C Air          1150  14300
3 TA-302   Group C Air          1420  17600
4 TA-303   Group B AC-3          900  41000


Step 1. LOF on numeric columns only. First, let us do what we did earlier in this chapter. We use only the two numeric columns, distance and amount, scale them, and calculate LOF.

claims$lof_numeric <- claims |>
  select(distance_km, amount) |>
  scale() |>
  lof(minPts = 10)

claims |>
  arrange(desc(lof_numeric)) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  claim_id grade   mode  distance_km amount lof_numeric
  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>
1 TA-303   Group B AC-3          900  41000        6.37
2 TA-042   Group A Air           255   3862        2.10
3 TA-284   Group A Air           287   4319        1.83
4 TA-072   Group A Air           304   3948        1.80
5 TA-175   Group A AC-2         1795   9694        1.76


The inflated AC-3 claim, TA-303, is at the top, with a very high score. That is good. But the two Group C air claims are nowhere near the top. This is not surprising. Looking at distance and amount alone, these claims look exactly like the many genuine air claims of Group A officers.
Step 2. LOF with categorical columns, using Gower distance. Now we include grade and mode of travel as well. daisy() needs categorical columns as factors, so we convert them first.

gower_dist <- claims |>
  select(grade, mode, distance_km, amount) |>
  mutate(across(c(grade, mode), as.factor)) |>
  daisy(metric = "gower")

claims$lof_gower <- lof(gower_dist, minPts = 10)

claims |>
  arrange(desc(lof_gower)) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  claim_id grade   mode  distance_km amount lof_numeric lof_gower
  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 TA-303   Group B AC-3          900  41000       6.37      14.1 
2 TA-301   Group C Air          1150  14300       1.06       6.10
3 TA-302   Group C Air          1420  17600       0.987      5.72
4 TA-004   Group B AC-2         1756   9706       1.50       2.43
5 TA-106   Group B AC-2         1715   8783       1.07       1.99


Now all three planted claims are at the top. A Group C employee travelling by air is a rare combination in the data, and Gower distance makes that rarity visible to LOF.
Let us compare the rank of the three claims under both methods. A rank of 1 means the most anomalous claim.

claims |>
  mutate(rank_numeric = rank(-lof_numeric),
         rank_gower   = rank(-lof_gower)) |>
  filter(claim_id %in% c("TA-301", "TA-302", "TA-303")) |>
  select(claim_id, grade, mode, amount, rank_numeric, rank_gower)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  claim_id grade   mode  amount rank_numeric rank_gower
  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>  <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
1 TA-301   Group C Air    14300           83          2
2 TA-302   Group C Air    17600          222          3
3 TA-303   Group B AC-3   41000            1          1








TipAudit tip



If the rules are known and simple, as in our entitlement table, a direct rule-based check is better. Just join the claims with the entitlement table and list every claim where the mode is not allowed for the grade. Anomaly detection is useful when the rules are not known, are too many to code, or when we want to discover patterns that nobody has thought of. In practice, use both.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.11 Time series anomalies
In time series data, an anomaly is a value which does not follow the usual trend, seasonal pattern or cycle of the series, and is clearly different from the rest of the data.
To detect such anomalies in R, we will use the package timetk. This package works on a tibble (data frame) with a date column, instead of a ts object. So we may need to prepare our data accordingly.
Let us return to the monthly receipts of the sub-registrar office, which we used for the Seasonal Hybrid ESD algorithm in Section 50.6. Our receipts tibble already has a date column, month, so it is ready for timetk. We tell it that the season repeats every 12 months, with .frequency = 12.

library(timetk)
receipts |>
  plot_anomaly_diagnostics(month, receipts_lakh, .frequency = 12,
                           .interactive = FALSE)

receipts |>
  tk_anomaly_diagnostics(month, receipts_lakh, .frequency = 12) |>
  filter(anomaly == 'Yes') |>
  select(month, observed, season, trend, remainder)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  month      observed season trend remainder
  <date>        <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 2021-08-01    101.   -5.40  71.3      35.1
2 2023-11-01     45.4   5.33  77.0     -37.0







Figure 50.15: Time Series Anomalies




We can see the anomalies highlighted in red in Figure 50.15, and listed by the code above. They are the same two planted months, August 2021 and November 2023, that S-H-ESD found. When two different methods agree, the lead is stronger.

50.11.1 How does this method work?
tk_anomaly_diagnostics() works in two steps.

It first splits the series into three parts, using a method called STL decomposition. The trend is the long-term rise or fall. The season is the pattern which repeats every year, or every week. The remainder is whatever is left after removing the trend and season.
It then looks for unusually large values in the remainder only. The usual rule of the box plot is used, so a value far outside the middle 50% of the remainders is called an anomaly.

So a value is called an anomaly only if it cannot be explained by the trend and the usual seasonal pattern. We learnt about these components of a time series in Chapter 49.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
section: 50.12 Audit use case, an odd month of expenditure
text:
50.12 Audit use case, an odd month of expenditure
Every auditor in government knows the March rush. Offices spend much more in March than in other months, to use up the budget before the financial year ends. So a high expenditure in March is expected. What an auditor wants to find is a month which is unusual even after allowing for this pattern.
Let us create six years of monthly expenditure of an office, from April 2019 to March 2025, in ₹ lakh. The expenditure grows a little every year, and March is always much higher than other months. We have planted one odd month, October 2023, when some unusual payments were made.

Code to create the monthly expenditure dataset.seed(2611)

months <- seq(as.Date("2019-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-01"), by = "month")

# Seasonal pattern from April to March. March is the rush month.
season <- c(0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.9, 0.95, 0.95, 1, 1, 1.05, 1.1, 1.3, 2.4)
position_in_fy <- ((month(months) + 8) %% 12) + 1   # April = 1, ..., March = 12

expenditure <- tibble(
  month = months,
  amount = round(40 * 1.06^(seq_along(months) / 12) * season[position_in_fy] *
                   runif(length(months), 0.92, 1.08), 2)
)

# Planted case. Unusual payments in October 2023.
odd <- expenditure$month == as.Date("2023-10-01")
expenditure$amount[odd] <- expenditure$amount[odd] * 2.3



head(expenditure)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  month      amount
  <date>      <dbl>
1 2019-04-01   34.6
2 2019-05-01   32.3
3 2019-06-01   34.6
4 2019-07-01   37.9
5 2019-08-01   41.4
6 2019-09-01   40.1


Attempt 1. A simple box plot rule. Let us first try what we learnt at the start of this chapter, using boxplot.stats().

outliers <- boxplot.stats(expenditure$amount)$out

expenditure |>
  filter(amount %in% outliers)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  month      amount
  <date>      <dbl>
1 2020-03-01  109. 
2 2021-03-01  110. 
3 2022-03-01  115. 
4 2023-03-01  128. 
5 2023-10-01  122. 
6 2024-03-01  131. 
7 2025-02-01   79.2
8 2025-03-01  145. 


Every single March has been flagged, along with October 2023. Even February 2025 is flagged, only because expenditure has grown over the years and recent months are naturally higher. This is not useful. The March peaks are the normal pattern of this office, and the one really odd month is lost in the crowd.
Attempt 2. Allowing for the season. Now let us use tk_anomaly_diagnostics(). We tell it that the season repeats every 12 months, with .frequency = 12.

expenditure |>
  tk_anomaly_diagnostics(month, amount, .frequency = 12, .message = FALSE) |>
  filter(anomaly == "Yes") |>
  select(month, observed, season, trend, remainder)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  month      observed season trend remainder
  <date>        <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 2020-03-01     109.  73.1   48.5     -13.1
2 2021-03-01     110.  73.1   49.9     -13.0
3 2022-03-01     115.  73.1   53.4     -11.9
4 2023-10-01     122.  -6.17  58.8      69.7


This is much better. October 2023 is flagged. But so are a few early Marches. Why? Look at how the March peak behaves. It is not a fixed amount above other months. It is a fixed proportion, about 2.4 times a normal month. As total expenditure grows over the years, the March peak grows in rupees too. STL expects a season of the same size every year, so it gets the early Marches slightly wrong.
Attempt 3. Working on the log scale. The fix is simple. We take the logarithm of the amounts. On the log scale, “2.4 times” becomes a fixed difference, whatever the size of the expenditure. So the seasonal pattern becomes the same size every year.

expenditure |>
  mutate(log_amount = log(amount)) |>
  tk_anomaly_diagnostics(month, log_amount, .frequency = 12, .message = FALSE) |>
  filter(anomaly == "Yes") |>
  select(month, observed, remainder)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  month      observed remainder
  <date>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 2023-10-01     4.81     0.840


Now only October 2023 is flagged. This is exactly the month we planted. The same result can be seen in Figure 50.16.

expenditure |>
  mutate(log_amount = log(amount)) |>
  plot_anomaly_diagnostics(month, log_amount, .frequency = 12,
                           .interactive = FALSE, .message = FALSE,
                           .title = "Monthly expenditure (log scale)")






Figure 50.16: Anomalies in monthly expenditure, on log scale










TipAudit tip



Use the log scale whenever the ups and downs of a series grow along with its level. This is true of most financial data, like expenditure, revenue, sales or tax collections. A quick look at a line plot of the data will tell you. If the March peaks get taller over the years, use the log.








NoteThe March rush is itself an audit issue



The seasonal method treats the March rush as normal, because it happens every year. But for an auditor, the rush itself may be a finding. The General Financial Rules, 2017 (Rule 62) treat a rush of expenditure at the end of the year as a breach of financial propriety, and government instructions ask departments to keep expenditure in March within 15% of the budget for the year. We can check this directly, by finding the share of March in each financial year’s expenditure.

expenditure |>
  mutate(fin_year = if_else(month(month) >= 4, year(month), year(month) - 1)) |>
  summarise(total = sum(amount),
            march = sum(amount[month(month) == 3]),
            .by = fin_year) |>
  mutate(march_share_pct = round(100 * march / total, 1))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  fin_year total march march_share_pct
     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>           <dbl>
1     2019  565.  109.            19.2
2     2020  562.  110.            19.6
3     2021  620.  115.            18.5
4     2022  658.  128.            19.5
5     2023  768.  131.            17.1
6     2024  750.  145.            19.3


Here fin_year 2019 means the financial year 2019-20, and so on. In every year, March accounts for more than 15% of the annual expenditure.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
section: 50.13 When did behaviour change? Change points
text:
50.13 When did behaviour change? Change points
The time series methods of Section 50.11 find single periods that are unusual. Sometimes the question is different. When did a series shift to a new level, and stay there? A vendor’s rate that steps up when a new officer takes charge, a sudden and lasting rise in a hospital’s claims after it was empanelled with a new third-party administrator, or collections that drop after a change in the inspection system. Such a lasting shift is not one odd month, so methods looking for odd months may miss it. Change point detection looks for exactly these shifts.
Let us take the rate charged per bag of cement by one supplier to a public works division, month by month for four years.

Code to create the cement ratesset.seed(7)
cement <- tibble(month = seq(as.Date("2021-04-01"), by = "month", length.out = 48),
                 # Planted. A lasting step up after the 30th month, and a one-off spike in month 12
                 rate  = round(c(rnorm(30, 365, 8), rnorm(18, 405, 8))))
cement$rate[12] <- 440


The package changepoint finds the points where the mean of a series changes, with cpt.mean(). The PELT method searches efficiently for any number of change points. One preparation is needed. The function measures changes in units of the series’ natural month-to-month noise, and assumes that noise has a standard deviation of 1. So we first divide the series by a robust estimate of its noise, the MAD of the month-to-month differences divided by \(\sqrt{2}\).

library(changepoint)
noise <- mad(diff(cement$rate)) / sqrt(2)
cp <- cpt.mean(cement$rate / noise, method = "PELT")
cpts(cp)

[1] 11 12 30


cpts() gives the positions after which the mean changes. They are 11, 12, 30. Let us read them with the dates. The changes after months 11 and 12 enclose a single month, March 2022. That is the one-off spike, a point anomaly, which the method sees as a tiny segment of its own. The change after month 30, September 2023, is the lasting shift. The average rate in each segment shows its size.

cement |>
  mutate(segment = cut(row_number(), breaks = c(0, cps, nrow(cement)))) |>
  summarise(from = min(month), to = max(month), months = n(), mean_rate = round(mean(rate)),
            .by = segment)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  segment from       to         months mean_rate
  <fct>   <date>     <date>      <int>     <dbl>
1 (0,11]  2021-04-01 2022-02-01     11       366
2 (11,12] 2022-03-01 2022-03-01      1       440
3 (12,30] 2022-04-01 2023-09-01     18       368
4 (30,48] 2023-10-01 2025-03-01     18       405



cement |>
  mutate(segment = cut(row_number(), breaks = c(0, cps, nrow(cement)))) |>
  mutate(segment_mean = mean(rate), .by = segment) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, rate)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_step(aes(y = segment_mean), colour = "red", linewidth = 1, direction = "mid") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rate per bag (₹)") +
  theme_minimal()



Cement rates with the detected segments



From October 2023, the supplier has charged about ₹37 more per bag, month after month. The audit questions follow naturally. Did the market rate rise at the same time? Did other suppliers’ rates rise too? Was the rate contract revised, and by whom? Did anything else change that month, like the officer in charge?






TipAudit tip



Run change point detection on many series at once, say the rate of every major item from every supplier, with map() (Section 7.5), and list the series with a lasting shift, the date and the size of the shift. Then compare the dates with known events, such as rate revisions, transfers of officers and new contracts. A shift with no explanation is a strong lead. cpt.meanvar() looks for changes in both the mean and the variability, which can reveal, for example, a period when rates suddenly stopped varying, as if copied.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.14 Combining several methods
Each method in this chapter sees anomalies in its own way. A robust z-score sees one extreme measure. The Mahalanobis distance sees a broken relationship. An isolation forest sees records that are easy to separate from the rest, and LOF sees records unlike their own neighbours. A record flagged by several methods is a stronger lead than one flagged by a single method, and different methods catch different kinds of irregularity. So in practice we run several, and combine their verdicts into one ranked list for examination.
The scores of different methods are on different scales. A z-score may be 4, a Mahalanobis distance 25 and an isolation score 0.6. They cannot be added directly. The simplest fair way is to convert each method’s scores into ranks, or rather percentile ranks between 0 and 1, and average them. A record which every method places near the top gets a combined score near 1.
Let us add a third measure to our PHC data, medicine expenditure, and plant two more cases of different kinds.

Code to add medicine expenditure and two more planted casesset.seed(21)
phc <- phc |>
  mutate(medicine_lakh = round(opd * 120 * rlnorm(n(), 0, 0.15) / 1e5, 2))
# Planted. PHC-140 spends far more on medicines than its OPD explains
phc$medicine_lakh[140] <- round(phc$medicine_lakh[140] * 2.6, 2)
# Planted. PHC-021 reports far less of everything than any other PHC
phc$opd[21]           <- round(min(phc$opd) * 0.45)
phc$deliveries[21]    <- max(1, round(min(phc$deliveries) * 0.45))
phc$medicine_lakh[21] <- round(min(phc$medicine_lakh) * 0.45, 2)


Now we score every PHC with four methods. All of them work on the logarithms of the three measures.

library(isotree)
library(dbscan)

logs <- phc |> transmute(l_opd = log(opd), l_del = log(deliveries), l_med = log(medicine_lakh))

scores <- phc |>
  transmute(
    phc,
    # 1. largest robust z-score among the three measures, and medicine per OPD patient
    robust_z = pmax(abs(robust_z(logs$l_opd)), abs(robust_z(logs$l_del)),
                    abs(robust_z(logs$l_med)), abs(robust_z(logs$l_med - logs$l_opd))),
    # 2. robust Mahalanobis distance
    mahal = {
      fit <- MASS::cov.rob(as.matrix(logs), method = "mcd")
      mahalanobis(as.matrix(logs), fit$center, fit$cov)
    },
    # 3. isolation forest score
    iforest = {
      set.seed(1)
      predict(isolation.forest(logs, ntrees = 200), logs)
    },
    # 4. local outlier factor, on scaled values
    lof = lof(scale(logs), minPts = 10)
  )

Each column is a score where higher means more unusual. Now we turn each into a percentile rank with percent_rank(), and average.

combined <- scores |>
  mutate(across(c(robust_z, mahal, iforest, lof), percent_rank, .names = "pr_{.col}")) |>
  mutate(combined = (pr_robust_z + pr_mahal + pr_iforest + pr_lof) / 4) |>
  arrange(desc(combined))

combined |>
  select(phc, starts_with("pr_"), combined) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 6
  phc     pr_robust_z pr_mahal pr_iforest pr_lof combined
  <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
1 PHC-021       0.995    0.995      1      1        0.997
2 PHC-140       1        1          0.98   0.995    0.994
3 PHC-102       0.99     0.985      0.899  0.985    0.965
4 PHC-001       0.98     0.96       0.975  0.94     0.964
5 PHC-147       0.975    0.955      0.995  0.92     0.961
6 PHC-193       0.97     0.93       0.985  0.955    0.96 
7 PHC-158       0.935    0.869      0.99   0.935    0.932
8 PHC-128       0.96     0.899      0.97   0.889    0.93 


PHC-021 and PHC-140 top the list. But where is PHC-077, the PHC whose deliveries were out of line with its OPD? It is at position 22. Let us see how each method ranked the three planted PHCs, out of 200.

map(c(robust_z = "robust_z", mahalanobis = "mahal", isolation_forest = "iforest", lof = "lof"),
    \(col) rank(-combined[[col]])[match(planted, combined$phc)]) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(phc = planted, .before = 1)

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  phc     robust_z mahalanobis isolation_forest   lof
  <chr>      <dbl>       <dbl>            <dbl> <dbl>
1 PHC-021       2            2                1     1
2 PHC-077     110.           3                9     3
3 PHC-140       1            1                5     2


Three methods placed PHC-077 near the top, but the robust z-score, which looks at one measure at a time, saw nothing unusual in it, exactly as we found in Section 50.5. Its low rank on that one method pulled the average down. This is the weakness of averaging. It dilutes an anomaly that only some methods can see, and different kinds of anomaly are, by their nature, seen by different methods.
A remedy that auditors find natural is a vote. Count, for each record, how many methods place it in their top 5%, and rank records first by the number of votes, then by the average.

top_share <- 0.05
voted <- combined |>
  mutate(votes = (pr_robust_z >= 1 - top_share) + (pr_mahal >= 1 - top_share) +
                 (pr_iforest >= 1 - top_share) + (pr_lof >= 1 - top_share)) |>
  arrange(desc(votes), desc(combined))

voted |>
  select(phc, votes, combined) |>
  mutate(combined = round(combined, 3)) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  phc     votes combined
  <chr>   <int>    <dbl>
1 PHC-021     4    0.997
2 PHC-140     4    0.994
3 PHC-102     3    0.965
4 PHC-001     3    0.964
5 PHC-147     3    0.961
6 PHC-193     3    0.96 
7 PHC-077     3    0.845
8 PHC-128     2    0.93 


Now the three planted PHCs are at positions 1, 2, 7. A record that most methods flag, for whatever reason each has, rises to the top, while a record that one method alone happens to place high stays lower. In all, 9 PHCs are flagged by two or more methods, a short and well-founded list for examination. Not every record on it is planted. The others with several votes are simply the smallest or largest PHCs in the data, and an examination would quickly clear them. That is normal. Anomaly methods find the unusual, and only the records can say whether it is wrong.






TipAudit tip



Keep the individual method scores alongside the combined score in your working papers. When a record is examined, they explain why it was selected. For example, “medicine spending three times what its OPD explains” (robust z of the ratio), or “deliveries out of line with OPD” (Mahalanobis). An explained selection is much easier to defend than a single number.








Note



Averaging and voting both give every method an equal say. If experience shows that one method finds more real issues in your data, give it a larger weight. And when outcomes of past examinations are available, consider the supervised methods of Chapter 41 and Chapter 43, which learn directly from what was found.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.15 Choosing a method
With so many methods, which one should an auditor use? Table 50.3 gives a simple guide.


Table 50.3: Choosing an anomaly detection method







Your data
Suggested method



One amount column, quick check
Box plot, drawn group-wise


Entities that fall into natural peer groups
Robust z-score of a size-free ratio, within each group


A few related measures for each entity
Robust Mahalanobis distance


One column, roughly bell-shaped, one suspect value
Grubbs’ test


A monthly, weekly or daily series
STL decomposition with timetk, on log scale for money


A series that may have shifted to a new level
Change point detection with changepoint



Several methods, one list to examine
Average of percentile ranks


A table of numeric indicators for each vendor, employee or beneficiary
Isolation forest first, then LOF to look for local anomalies


Numeric and categorical columns together
LOF with Gower distance, or isolation forest with factors


Known rules, like entitlements or limits
A direct rule-based check, before any of the above

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.16 A suggested workflow


Understand the data. Know what each column means, and what “normal” looks like for the business.

Apply the known rules first. Limits, entitlements and rates can be checked directly, without any algorithm.

Look at the data. Draw box plots and histograms, group-wise. Many anomalies are visible at this stage itself.

Prepare the data for the algorithm. Scale numeric columns for kNN and LOF. Use the log for money amounts. Convert categorical columns to factors.

Compare like with like. Use peer groups and size-free ratios, so that big entities are not flagged merely for being big.

Run more than one method, and combine them by rank. A record flagged by several methods is a stronger lead.

Rank, do not label. Sort records by score and examine them from the top.

Verify with documents. Explain every flagged record from the records, before treating it as a finding.







ImportantRemember



An anomaly is only unusual. It is not necessarily wrong. Many anomalies have perfectly good explanations, like a one-time bulk purchase or a new scheme. Anomaly detection tells the auditor where to look. Only the examination of records can tell what happened.

title: 50  Anomaly Detection
text:
50.17 Try it yourself
These exercises use the data of this chapter, the stationery bills, the health facilities, the TA claims, the vendor indicators and the PHC scores. Try each one before you open the solution.


One box for the whole office. Apply boxplot.stats() to all the stationery bills together, without grouping by vendor. Is the planted bill of ₹38,000 flagged?






TipSolution






office_out <- boxplot.stats(stationery$amount)$out
office_out

 [1] 38000 27340 38390 30130 36320 36800 35850 25540 25270 31600 34680 37130
[13] 39110 35730 43150 41150 30420 31120 30510 31270

38000 %in% office_out

[1] TRUE


Over the whole office, 20 bills are flagged, and the planted bill is among them. But so are 19 other bills, all of them ordinary printing bills of Modern Printers. The planted bill is lost in this crowd, and nothing marks it as the odd one. This is why the box plot should be drawn vendor by vendor.





A looser cut-off for peer groups. The chapter flagged facilities with a robust z-score beyond 3.5 within their own type. Lower the cut-off to 3, using the column rz_peer of facilities. How many facilities are flagged now?






TipSolution






flag_3 <- facilities |>
  filter(abs(rz_peer) > 3) |>
  select(facility, type, cost_per_patient, rz_peer) |>
  mutate(rz_peer = round(rz_peer, 1))
flag_3

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  facility type  cost_per_patient rz_peer
  <chr>    <chr>            <dbl>   <dbl>
1 PHC-037  PHC                410     6.2
2 PHC-044  PHC                234     3.4
3 CHC-012  CHC               1250     7.5


With a cut-off of 3, 3 facilities are flagged, against 2 at 3.5. A lower cut-off gives a longer list to examine. Choose the cut-off to suit the time available for the examination of records, and record it in the working papers.





The rule-based check first. The audit tip on TA claims says a direct check of entitlements is better when the rules are known. Use the list entitled to find every claim in claims whose mode of travel is not allowed for the grade of the employee.






TipSolution






not_entitled <- claims |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(mode, grade, \(m, g) m %in% entitled[[g]])) |>
  select(claim_id, grade, mode, distance_km, amount)
not_entitled

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  claim_id grade   mode  distance_km amount
  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>
1 TA-301   Group C Air          1150  14300
2 TA-302   Group C Air          1420  17600


The rule finds 2 claims, TA-301 and TA-302, the two Group C air journeys. It does not find TA-303, whose mode is allowed but whose amount is inflated. So the rule and the anomaly method catch different problems, and we use both.





Does the choice of k matter? Calculate the kNN score of the vendors on all four scaled indicators with k = 10 instead of 5. Do the same vendors come out on top?






TipSolution






vendor_knn10 <- FNN::get.knn(vend_scaled, 10)
score_10 <- rowMeans(vendor_knn10$nn.dist)
names(score_10) <- vendors$vendor
round(head(sort(score_10, decreasing = TRUE), 5), 2)

V-058 V-059 V-053 V-029 V-045 
 6.99  1.75  1.52  1.37  1.34 


With k = 10, V-058 is first and V-059 is second, against V-058 and V-059 with k = 5. When the top records stay the same for two values of k, we can be more confident that they are real leads.





A wider vote. In the vote on the PHC data, a method gave its vote to records in its top 5%. Widen this to the top 10%, using the percentile ranks in combined. Where do the three planted PHCs now stand, and how many PHCs get two or more votes?






TipSolution






voted_10 <- combined |>
  mutate(votes = (pr_robust_z >= 0.9) + (pr_mahal >= 0.9) +
                 (pr_iforest >= 0.9) + (pr_lof >= 0.9)) |>
  arrange(desc(votes), desc(combined))

match(planted, voted_10$phc)

[1]  1 13  2

sum(voted_10$votes >= 2)

[1] 20


The planted PHCs are now at positions 1, 2, 13, against 1, 2, 7 with the top 5%. And 20 PHCs now get two or more votes, against 9 before. The wider net gives a much longer list to clear, and it does not bring the planted cases any closer to the top. Here the narrower net of 5% is the better choice. On other data, try two or three widths and compare, as we did here.
