Two checks, one answer. In the housing data, flag every beneficiary whose completion photo was taken more than 100 metres from the sanctioned site. Compare this list with the same-spot group. Who is in the group but not flagged, and why?






TipSolution






far_photo <- photos |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(site_to_photo_km = sqrt((photo_x - site_x)^2 + (photo_y - site_y)^2)) |>
  filter(site_to_photo_km > 0.1) |>
  pull(ben_id)

group_ids <- photos |> filter(group == big$group) |> pull(ben_id)

length(far_photo)

[1] 9

all(far_photo %in% group_ids)

[1] TRUE

setdiff(group_ids, far_photo)

[1] "PH0002"


9 photos were taken more than 100 metres from their sites, and all of them belong to the same-spot group. The one member of the group who is not flagged, PH0002, is the beneficiary whose own house was photographed again and again. The distance check alone would miss that this house was used for others. The grouping check alone would not tell us whose house it is. Together they give the full picture.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.1 Where can geocoding help an auditor?
Most records give location as an address, not as coordinates. A vendor’s address, a beneficiary’s village, a hospital’s location. To put such records on a map, or to measure distances between them, we must first convert the address into latitude and longitude. This is called geocoding.
The reverse, converting latitude and longitude into an address, is called reverse geocoding. We will learn it in the next chapter.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
Checking claimed distances. Travel allowance, transport charges and freight claims depend on distance. Geocoding the places lets us compare the claimed distance with the actual one.

Shared locations. Two “different” vendors, or many beneficiaries, at the same address can point to fake entities or duplicate registration. This complements the duplicate tests of Chapter 34.

Distance between supplier and site. A supplier located far away from the delivery site may be a front for someone else, or may be charging for transport that never happened.

Mapping records which only have addresses, so that the techniques of Chapter 56 can be applied.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.2 How geocoding works
A geocoding service keeps a large database of places and addresses with their coordinates. We send it an address as text. It searches for the best match, and returns the coordinates, along with details like the full address it matched.
Several services are available.


OpenStreetMap Nominatim. Free and open, based on the OpenStreetMap community map. It is the default in R’s tidygeocoder package. Its usage policy allows only light use, about one request per second, and asks users to credit OpenStreetMap.

Commercial services, such as those offered by Google, ArcGIS and several Indian map providers. They often give better results for Indian addresses, but need an account and an API key, and usually charge beyond a free limit.







WarningNever send personal data to a public service



Geocoding sends your addresses to someone else’s server. Do not send addresses of beneficiaries, patients, employees or taxpayers to public services. Use only services approved by your organisation for such data. In this chapter, we geocode only public places, such as monuments and well-known markets.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.3 Prerequisites
We will use tidygeocoder for geocoding, and sf for distances.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidygeocoder)
library(sf)

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.4 Geocoding a few places
The function geocode() from tidygeocoder works on a data frame. We tell it which column holds the address, and which service (method) to use. Let us geocode a few well-known places.

places <- tibble(place = c("Taj Mahal, Agra",
                           "Hawa Mahal, Jaipur",
                           "Charminar, Hyderabad",
                           "Victoria Memorial, Kolkata",
                           "Gateway of India, Mumbai",
                           "Xyzabc Nagar, Nowhere"))

places_geo <- places |>
  geocode(address = place, method = "osm")

places_geo

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  place                        lat  long
  <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl>
1 Taj Mahal, Agra             27.2  78.0
2 Hawa Mahal, Jaipur          26.9  75.8
3 Charminar, Hyderabad        17.4  78.5
4 Victoria Memorial, Kolkata  22.5  88.3
5 Gateway of India, Mumbai    18.9  72.8
6 Xyzabc Nagar, Nowhere       NA    NA  


geocode() has added two columns, lat and long. The last “place” is made up, and the service could not find it. So its coordinates are NA. Always check for such failures before going ahead.

places_geo |>
  filter(is.na(lat))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  place                   lat  long
  <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl>
1 Xyzabc Nagar, Nowhere    NA    NA








TipGeocode once, save the result



Geocoding is slow, and free services limit how much you can use them. Do not geocode the same addresses again and again. Geocode once, save the result with write_csv(), and read the saved file in later work.



57.4.1 More details about each match
With full_results = TRUE, the service returns everything it knows about the match. This is useful to judge the quality of each match.

places_geo_full <- places |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  geocode(address = place, method = "osm", full_results = TRUE)

places_geo_full |>
  select(place, lat, long, display_name, class, type)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  place                  lat  long display_name                      class type 
  <chr>                <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                             <chr> <chr>
1 Taj Mahal, Agra       27.2  78.0 Taj Mahal, Taj East Gate Road, T… tour… attr…
2 Hawa Mahal, Jaipur    26.9  75.8 Hawa Mahal, Amer Road, Ramganj, … tour… attr…
3 Charminar, Hyderabad  17.4  78.5 Charminar, Charminar Circle, Laa… tour… attr…


The display_name column shows the full address that the service actually matched. The class and type columns tell what kind of place it is. Reading these is the best way to catch wrong matches.






WarningBeware of approximate matches



When a service cannot find the exact address, it often returns the centre of the town, district or pin code instead, without any warning. In Indian addresses, which are often written in very different ways, this is common. So two vendors may appear to be at “the same location” only because both were matched to the centre of the same town. Always look at what was matched, before drawing conclusions.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.5 From coordinates to map points
Latitude and longitude are in the WGS 84 coordinate system, whose code is EPSG:4326. We met coordinate systems in Chapter 56. To turn the geocoded table into map points, we use st_as_sf(). Note that the longitude comes first, because it is the x-coordinate.

places_sf <- places_geo |>
  filter(!is.na(lat)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

places_sf

Simple feature collection with 5 features and 1 field
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 72.83457 ymin: 17.3616 xmax: 88.34255 ymax: 27.17501
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  place                                 geometry
* <chr>                              <POINT [°]>
1 Taj Mahal, Agra             (78.0421 27.17501)
2 Hawa Mahal, Jaipur         (75.82687 26.92393)
3 Charminar, Hyderabad        (78.47464 17.3616)
4 Victoria Memorial, Kolkata (88.34255 22.54496)
5 Gateway of India, Mumbai   (72.83457 18.92197)



57.5.1 Measuring distances
st_distance() measures distances between points. For latitude and longitude, sf correctly measures along the curved surface of the earth, and returns the result in metres. Let us find the distances between our places, in kilometres.

dist_matrix <- st_distance(places_sf)

dist_km <- round(units::drop_units(dist_matrix) / 1000)
dimnames(dist_km) <- list(places_sf$place, places_sf$place)

dist_km

                           Taj Mahal, Agra Hawa Mahal, Jaipur
Taj Mahal, Agra                          0                221
Hawa Mahal, Jaipur                     221                  0
Charminar, Hyderabad                  1092               1098
Victoria Memorial, Kolkata            1159               1354
Gateway of India, Mumbai              1061                941
                           Charminar, Hyderabad Victoria Memorial, Kolkata
Taj Mahal, Agra                            1092                       1159
Hawa Mahal, Jaipur                         1098                       1354
Charminar, Hyderabad                          0                       1181
Victoria Memorial, Kolkata                 1181                          0
Gateway of India, Mumbai                    621                       1661
                           Gateway of India, Mumbai
Taj Mahal, Agra                                1061
Hawa Mahal, Jaipur                              941
Charminar, Hyderabad                            621
Victoria Memorial, Kolkata                     1661
Gateway of India, Mumbai                          0


st_distance() with a single set of points returns a matrix of the distance between every pair. units::drop_units() removes the unit “m”, so that we can divide by 1,000 to get kilometres.
These are straight-line distances, as a bird would fly. Roads and railway lines are always longer. This simple fact is the basis of our first audit check.

title: 57  Geocoding
section: 57.6 Audit use case 1, checking claimed travel distances
text:
57.6 Audit use case 1, checking claimed travel distances
Suppose a department pays travel allowance partly on the basis of the distance claimed by the employee. Let us check a few claims. The table below is made up. The places are well-known towns.

ta_claims <- tribble(
  ~claim_no, ~from,               ~to,                   ~claimed_km,
  "TA-01",   "Lucknow",           "Varanasi",            320,
  "TA-02",   "Bhopal",            "Indore",              195,
  "TA-03",   "Patna",             "Gaya",                115,
  "TA-04",   "Jaipur",            "Ajmer",               60,
  "TA-05",   "Dehradun",          "Haridwar",            160,
  "TA-06",   "Bhubaneswar",       "Puri",                65
)

We need the coordinates of each town. Since a town appears in more than one claim, we geocode each town only once.

towns <- tibble(town = unique(c(ta_claims$from, ta_claims$to))) |>
  mutate(address = paste0(town, ", India")) |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm")

towns

# A tibble: 12 × 4
   town        address              lat  long
   <chr>       <chr>              <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Lucknow     Lucknow, India      26.8  80.9
 2 Bhopal      Bhopal, India       23.3  77.4
 3 Patna       Patna, India        25.6  85.1
 4 Jaipur      Jaipur, India       26.9  75.8
 5 Dehradun    Dehradun, India     30.3  78.0
 6 Bhubaneswar Bhubaneswar, India  20.3  85.8
 7 Varanasi    Varanasi, India     25.3  83.0
 8 Indore      Indore, India       22.7  75.9
 9 Gaya        Gaya, India         24.8  85.0
10 Ajmer       Ajmer, India        26.5  74.6
11 Haridwar    Haridwar, India     29.9  78.1
12 Puri        Puri, India         19.8  85.8


We added “, India” to each name, so that the service does not pick a town of the same name in another country. Now we join the coordinates to both ends of each claim, and measure the straight-line distance.

from_pts <- ta_claims |>
  left_join(towns, by = c("from" = "town")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

to_pts <- ta_claims |>
  left_join(towns, by = c("to" = "town")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

ta_checked <- ta_claims |>
  mutate(straight_km = round(as.numeric(st_distance(from_pts, to_pts, by_element = TRUE)) / 1000),
         ratio = round(claimed_km / straight_km, 2))

ta_checked

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  claim_no from        to       claimed_km straight_km ratio
  <chr>    <chr>       <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 TA-01    Lucknow     Varanasi        320         266  1.2 
2 TA-02    Bhopal      Indore          195         168  1.16
3 TA-03    Patna       Gaya            115          91  1.26
4 TA-04    Jaipur      Ajmer            60         127  0.47
5 TA-05    Dehradun    Haridwar        160          44  3.64
6 TA-06    Bhubaneswar Puri             65          50  1.3 


How do we read the ratio? Road distance in India is usually around 1.2 to 1.5 times the straight-line distance. So a ratio in that range is normal.

A ratio below 1 is impossible. No road is shorter than a straight line. Such a claim is certainly wrong. Here, that means the claim from Jaipur to Ajmer.
A ratio far above 1.5 suggests an inflated claim. Here, the claim from Dehradun to Haridwar is more than three times the straight-line distance.


ta_checked |>
  filter(ratio < 1 | ratio > 1.8)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  claim_no from     to       claimed_km straight_km ratio
  <chr>    <chr>    <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 TA-04    Jaipur   Ajmer            60         127  0.47
2 TA-05    Dehradun Haridwar        160          44  3.64








NoteStraight-line or road distance?



The straight-line distance is a quick filter, not the final answer. For the flagged claims, check the actual road or rail distance from official tables, or from a routing service. Some routes are genuinely long because of hills, rivers or the lack of a direct road.

title: 57  Geocoding
section: 57.7 Audit use case 2, different vendors, same place
text:
57.7 Audit use case 2, different vendors, same place
In Chapter 34, we found look-alike vendor names. Another sign of fake or related vendors is that their addresses point to the same place, even though they are written differently. Let us look at a few vendors of a department. The addresses are of well-known commercial areas, and the vendors are made up.

vendors <- tribble(
  ~vendor,                   ~address,
  "Shubh Laxmi Traders",     "Nehru Place, New Delhi",
  "Gupta Office Supplies",   "Chandni Chowk, Delhi",
  "Shree Balaji Enterprises","Nehru Place, Delhi",
  "Raj Computers",           "Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi",
  "Om Sai Suppliers",        "Karol Bagh, New Delhi",
  "Modern Stationers",       "Nehru Place Market, New Delhi"
)


vendors_geo <- vendors |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm")

vendors_geo

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  vendor                   address                         lat  long
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl>
1 Shubh Laxmi Traders      Nehru Place, New Delhi         28.6  77.2
2 Gupta Office Supplies    Chandni Chowk, Delhi           28.7  77.2
3 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi             28.5  77.3
4 Raj Computers            Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi        28.6  77.2
5 Om Sai Suppliers         Karol Bagh, New Delhi          28.6  77.2
6 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi  28.5  77.3


Three vendors give addresses in Nehru Place, written in three different ways. To find vendors at the same place, we round the coordinates to three decimal places, which is about 100 metres, and look for vendors that share a rounded location.

vendors_geo |>
  mutate(spot = paste(round(lat, 3), round(long, 3))) |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = spot) |>
  arrange(spot)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  vendor                   address                         lat  long spot       
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      
1 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi             28.5  77.3 28.549 77.…
2 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi  28.5  77.3 28.549 77.…


Two vendors share a location. But what happened to the third Nehru Place vendor? Let us see what the service actually matched for each of the three addresses.

vendors |>
  filter(str_detect(address, "Nehru Place")) |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm", full_results = TRUE) |>
  select(vendor, address, display_name)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  vendor                   address                       display_name           
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <chr>                  
1 Shubh Laxmi Traders      Nehru Place, New Delhi        Motilal Nehru Place, C…
2 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi            Nehru Place, South, De…
3 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi Mahadev communications…


“Nehru Place, New Delhi” has been matched to Motilal Nehru Place, a road in central Delhi, several kilometres away from the Nehru Place market. A small difference in how the address was written led to a completely different place. This is exactly the problem of approximate matches that we warned about earlier. An auditor who relied on the coordinates alone would have missed that all three vendors are in the same market.
So the analysis finds two vendors at one spot, and a careful reading of the matched addresses adds the third. Three “different” vendors are located in the same market. This is not wrong by itself. A market like Nehru Place has hundreds of shops. But if these three vendors also bid in the same tenders, as in Chapter 48, or share a mobile number or bank account, the case for a closer look becomes strong.






TipAudit tip



Rounding to three decimal places groups points within about 100 metres. Rounding to four places, about 10 metres, is stricter. Choose according to the quality of your addresses. With precise addresses, use four places. With addresses that only give a locality, three or even two places may be better.

title: 57  Geocoding
section: 57.8 Audit use case 3, excess lead charges in works
text:
57.8 Audit use case 3, excess lead charges in works
In road and building works, contractors are paid for carrying materials like stone aggregate from a quarry to the work site. This carriage charge is called lead, and it is paid per cubic metre per kilometre. So the longer the claimed lead, the bigger the payment. Two common irregularities are,

claiming carriage from a distant quarry, when an approved quarry is much nearer, and
claiming a lead much longer than the actual distance to the quarry named.

Excess payment on lead is a frequent finding in audits of works. Let us check six works in Rajasthan. The work sites are real towns. The quarries, quantities and claims are made up, and the carriage rate is imaginary.

works <- tribble(
  ~work_id, ~site,       ~quantity_cum, ~claimed_quarry,  ~claimed_lead_km,
  "W-01",   "Churu",      12000,        "Bikaner",         175,
  "W-02",   "Sikar",      15000,        "Kotputli",        150,
  "W-03",   "Nagaur",      9000,        "Jodhpur",         135,
  "W-04",   "Jhunjhunu",  18000,        "Jodhpur",         410,
  "W-05",   "Tonk",       10000,        "Sawai Madhopur",   85,
  "W-06",   "Bhilwara",   14000,        "Kishangarh",      290
)

approved_quarries <- c("Kishangarh", "Bikaner", "Jodhpur", "Kotputli", "Sawai Madhopur")
rate_per_cum_km <- 4.5   # rupees, imaginary

We geocode each town once, sites and quarries together.

rj_towns <- tibble(town = unique(c(works$site, approved_quarries))) |>
  mutate(address = paste0(town, ", Rajasthan, India")) |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm")

rj_sf <- rj_towns |> st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)
quarry_sf <- rj_sf |> filter(town %in% approved_quarries)

For each work, we need two distances. First, the straight-line distance to the quarry it claims. Second, the straight-line distance to the nearest approved quarry. st_nearest_feature() gives, for each point, the row number of the nearest feature in another layer.

site_sf <- works |>
  left_join(rj_towns, by = c("site" = "town")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

claimed_sf <- quarry_sf[match(works$claimed_quarry, quarry_sf$town), ]
nearest_sf <- quarry_sf[st_nearest_feature(site_sf, quarry_sf), ]

lead_check <- works |>
  mutate(km_to_claimed  = round(as.numeric(st_distance(site_sf, claimed_sf, by_element = TRUE)) / 1000),
         nearest_quarry = nearest_sf$town,
         km_to_nearest  = round(as.numeric(st_distance(site_sf, nearest_sf, by_element = TRUE)) / 1000),
         lead_ratio     = round(claimed_lead_km / km_to_claimed, 2))

lead_check |>
  select(work_id, site, claimed_quarry, claimed_lead_km, km_to_claimed, lead_ratio,
         nearest_quarry, km_to_nearest) |>
  print(width = Inf)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  work_id site      claimed_quarry claimed_lead_km km_to_claimed lead_ratio
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>                    <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 W-01    Churu     Bikaner                    175           136       1.29
2 W-02    Sikar     Kotputli                   150           115       1.3 
3 W-03    Nagaur    Jodhpur                    135           104       1.3 
4 W-04    Jhunjhunu Jodhpur                    410           317       1.29
5 W-05    Tonk      Sawai Madhopur              85            65       1.31
6 W-06    Bhilwara  Kishangarh                 290           125       2.32
  nearest_quarry km_to_nearest
  <chr>                  <dbl>
1 Bikaner                  136
2 Kotputli                 115
3 Jodhpur                  104
4 Kotputli                  77
5 Sawai Madhopur            65
6 Kishangarh               125


Two works stand out.


W-04 at Jhunjhunu claims stone from Jodhpur, although the approved quarry at Kotputli is much nearer. Its lead ratio is normal. The distance claimed is genuine, but the quarry choice is not.

W-06 at Bhilwara names the nearest quarry, Kishangarh, but claims a lead of more than twice the straight-line distance.

To estimate the excess payment, we take a reasonable lead as 1.3 times the straight-line distance to the nearest approved quarry, as discussed in use case 1. Any lead claimed beyond this is excess.

lead_excess <- lead_check |>
  mutate(reasonable_lead_km = round(1.3 * km_to_nearest),
         excess_km          = pmax(claimed_lead_km - reasonable_lead_km, 0),
         excess_rupees      = excess_km * quantity_cum * rate_per_cum_km) |>
  filter(excess_km > 0.2 * reasonable_lead_km) |>
  select(work_id, site, claimed_lead_km, reasonable_lead_km, excess_km, quantity_cum, excess_rupees)

lead_excess |> print(width = Inf)

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  work_id site      claimed_lead_km reasonable_lead_km excess_km quantity_cum
  <chr>   <chr>               <dbl>              <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
1 W-04    Jhunjhunu             410                100       310        18000
2 W-06    Bhilwara              290                162       128        14000
  excess_rupees
          <dbl>
1      25110000
2       8064000


We keep only works whose claimed lead exceeds the reasonable lead by more than 20%, to allow for genuinely longer roads. The two works together involve an estimated excess payment of about ₹3.32 crore.

57.8.1 An interactive map
For presenting such findings, and for exploring them, an interactive map helps. The package leaflet draws maps which can be zoomed and clicked, with OpenStreetMap as the background. Unlike our imaginary State in Chapter 56, these are real places with latitude and longitude, so leaflet can place them on a real map (Figure 57.1). Click a line to see the claim.

library(leaflet)

# One straight line from each work site to its claimed quarry
route_lines <- map2(st_geometry(site_sf), st_geometry(claimed_sf),
                    \(a, b) st_linestring(rbind(st_coordinates(a), st_coordinates(b)))) |>
  st_sfc(crs = 4326) |>
  st_sf(geometry = _) |>
  mutate(work_id = works$work_id,
         flagged = work_id %in% lead_excess$work_id,
         popup   = paste0(work_id, ": ", works$site, " to ", works$claimed_quarry,
                          "<br>Claimed lead ", works$claimed_lead_km, " km"))

leaflet(width = "100%", height = 450) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolylines(data = route_lines, color = ~if_else(flagged, "red", "grey"),
               weight = 3, popup = ~popup) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = site_sf, radius = 5, color = "steelblue", label = ~site) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = quarry_sf, radius = 6, color = "darkgreen", label = ~town)






Figure 57.1: Claimed carriage routes. Red lines are works with excess lead.









TipAudit tip



When a work claims material from a distant quarry, ask why the nearer approved quarry was not used. Sometimes there is a good reason, like the quality of stone or the nearer quarry being closed. That reason must be on record, with the approval of the competent authority, before the work was done. Also compare the claimed lead with the lead chart approved for the district, if one exists.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.9 A suggested workflow


Use an approved service. Never send personal addresses to a public geocoder.

Clean the addresses first. Add the State and “India”, remove extra spaces, and expand common short forms.

Geocode each unique address once, and save the results.

Check the failures (NA coordinates) and the quality of matches, using full_results = TRUE.

Turn the results into points with st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326).

Measure distances with st_distance(), and compare with claims.

Look for shared locations, by rounding coordinates.

Verify each flagged case with records, and with official distance tables or site visits.







ImportantRemember



Geocoding gives the location of the address as written, not necessarily the location of the thing. A wrong or vague address gives a wrong or vague location. Treat geocoded locations as approximate, and always look at the matched address before drawing a conclusion.

title: 57  Geocoding
text:
57.10 Try it yourself
These exercises use the coordinates that we have already geocoded in this chapter. None of them sends anything to a geocoding service. Try each one before you open the solution.


A tighter band for travel claims. In the travel allowance check, flag every claim whose ratio is below 1.2 or above 1.5, instead of below 1 or above 1.8. Which extra claims are now flagged?






TipSolution






tight <- ta_checked |> filter(ratio < 1.2 | ratio > 1.5)
tight

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  claim_no from     to       claimed_km straight_km ratio
  <chr>    <chr>    <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 TA-02    Bhopal   Indore          195         168  1.16
2 TA-04    Jaipur   Ajmer            60         127  0.47
3 TA-05    Dehradun Haridwar        160          44  3.64

setdiff(tight$claim_no, filter(ta_checked, ratio < 1 | ratio > 1.8)$claim_no)

[1] "TA-02"


The tighter band flags 3 claims. The extra claim is TA-02. A tighter band catches more cases but also more genuine long routes, so each extra case needs a look at the actual road distance.





How many kilometres too many? For each travel claim, take a reasonable distance as 1.3 times the straight-line distance. Work out the kilometres claimed beyond this, and keep only the claims where it is more than 20 km.






TipSolution






ta_excess <- ta_checked |>
  mutate(reasonable_km = round(1.3 * straight_km),
         excess_km     = claimed_km - reasonable_km) |>
  filter(excess_km > 20)

ta_excess

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  claim_no from     to      claimed_km straight_km ratio reasonable_km excess_km
  <chr>    <chr>    <chr>        <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>
1 TA-05    Dehradun Haridw…        160          44  3.64            57       103


Only TA-05 exceeds the reasonable distance by more than 20 km. This is the same idea that we used for lead charges. A rough excess, in kilometres, tells the auditor how much is at stake before the actual road distance is obtained.





Rounding to two places. In the vendor check, round the coordinates to two decimal places, about one kilometre, instead of three. How many vendors now share a location with another vendor?






TipSolution






shared_2 <- vendors_geo |>
  mutate(spot = paste(round(lat, 2), round(long, 2))) |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = spot) |>
  arrange(spot)

shared_2

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  vendor                   address                         lat  long spot       
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      
1 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi             28.5  77.3 28.55 77.25
2 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi  28.5  77.3 28.55 77.25


With two decimal places, 2 vendors share a location with at least one other vendor, against 2 with three places. Coarser rounding can group more vendors, and the extra ones may simply be shops in the same part of the city. That is why the choice of decimal places should follow the quality of the addresses, as the audit tip says.





A different allowance for lead. In the lead check, allow a reasonable lead of 1.5 times the straight-line distance to the nearest approved quarry, instead of 1.3. What is the estimated excess payment now?






TipSolution






lead_excess_15 <- lead_check |>
  mutate(reasonable_lead_km = round(1.5 * km_to_nearest),
         excess_km          = pmax(claimed_lead_km - reasonable_lead_km, 0),
         excess_rupees      = excess_km * quantity_cum * rate_per_cum_km) |>
  filter(excess_km > 0.2 * reasonable_lead_km) |>
  select(work_id, site, claimed_lead_km, reasonable_lead_km, excess_rupees)

lead_excess_15

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  work_id site      claimed_lead_km reasonable_lead_km excess_rupees
  <chr>   <chr>               <dbl>              <dbl>         <dbl>
1 W-04    Jhunjhunu             410                116      23814000
2 W-06    Bhilwara              290                188       6426000


With the more generous allowance, 2 works remain flagged, and the estimated excess is about ₹3.02 crore, against ₹3.32 crore with 1.3. Showing the result under a generous assumption makes the observation harder to dispute, because the auditee cannot say the allowance was too strict.





Which quarry should it have been? For every work site, list the approved quarries in order of straight-line distance. Then count the works whose claimed quarry is not the nearest one.






TipSolution






site_quarry_km <- round(units::drop_units(st_distance(site_sf, quarry_sf)) / 1000)
dimnames(site_quarry_km) <- list(works$work_id, quarry_sf$town)
site_quarry_km

W-01        180     136     268      158            271
W-02        121     173     249      115            203
W-03        120     122     104      256            269
W-04        179     218     317       77            219
W-05         95     314     263      184             65
W-06        125     314     190      290            182

lead_check |>
  filter(claimed_quarry != nearest_quarry) |>
  select(work_id, site, claimed_quarry, km_to_claimed, nearest_quarry, km_to_nearest)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  work_id site      claimed_quarry km_to_claimed nearest_quarry km_to_nearest
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>                  <dbl> <chr>                  <dbl>

The matrix gives every distance at once, so the auditor can see not only the nearest quarry but also the second nearest. Only W-04 claims a quarry other than the nearest approved one. For each, ask for the recorded reason and the approval of the competent authority.

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
text:
58.1 Introduction
Geocoding, which we learnt in Chapter 57, is the process of converting a human-readable address into geographic coordinates, such as latitude and longitude. It lets us place addresses on a map.
Reverse geocoding, on the other hand, is the process of converting geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) into a human-readable address, such as a street, village or city, district, state and country. In other words, it determines the address of a place from its coordinates.
Both are important in geospatial data analysis. They allow us to link spatial information with non-spatial information, such as demographic data or land records, and to see patterns and relationships based on location.
Reverse geocoding is especially useful in forensic data analysis. Mobile phones and handheld devices now record the coordinates of almost every activity. A photo of a newly built house, an attendance marked by a field worker, a ration distributed through a point-of-sale machine, a payment made at an ATM. Each comes with a latitude and a longitude. Reverse geocoding turns these numbers into places that an auditor can read and check, such as “is this photo really from the village where the work was claimed?”.

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
text:
58.2 Widely used databases
OpenStreetMap (OSM) is one of the most popular and widely used databases for geocoding and reverse geocoding. OSM is a free and open map of the world, created and maintained by a community of volunteers. It has a rich and detailed set of spatial data, including street names, addresses and other points of interest. Its free service, called Nominatim, allows only light use, about one request per second.
Other popular services include Google Maps, ArcGIS and several Indian map providers. They provide geocoding and reverse geocoding through paid APIs, and are widely used in web and mobile applications.






WarningPrivacy



Coordinates of a beneficiary’s home are personal data, just like the address. Do not send such coordinates to public services. Use only services approved by your organisation. In this chapter, we use the coordinates of well-known monuments only.

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
text:
58.3 Example in R

58.3.1 Prerequisites

library(tidyverse)
library(tidygeocoder)


58.3.2 Function to be used
We will use the reverse_geo() function from tidygeocoder. Its main arguments are these.
reverse_geo(
  lat,
  long,
  method = "osm",
  address = "address",
  full_results = FALSE,
  ...
)


lat and long are, as the names suggest, the latitude and longitude of the place whose address is to be found.

method is the service to be used. The default is osm. Other services available include arcgis, geocodio and google.

address is the name of the output column holding the address.

full_results is FALSE by default. If set to TRUE, it returns all available details from the service, such as the city, district, state and postcode in separate columns.
For other arguments, please check the help of the function.

58.3.3 A single place
Let us find the address of the Taj Mahal, from its coordinates.

reverse_geo(lat = 27.1751, long = 78.0421, method = "osm")

# A tibble: 1 × 3
    lat  long address                                                           
  <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                                                             
1  27.2  78.0 Taj Mahal, Taj East Gate Road, Taj Ganj, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, 282…








TipCoordinates need care



Each digit of a coordinate matters. One degree of latitude is about 111 km, so the third decimal place is about 100 metres. If the longitude above is mistyped as 78.421 instead of 78.0421, the “Taj Mahal” turns out to be a village in Firozabad district, about 40 km away. When coordinates are typed by hand, always check a few of them on a map.



58.3.4 Several places at once
reverse_geo() is vectorised. We can give it vectors of latitudes and longitudes, and it returns one row for each. Let us build a sample dataset of four places of interest in India.

sample_places <- tibble(
  lat  = c(27.1751, 24.8318, 27.1795, 28.5245),
  long = c(78.0421, 79.9199, 78.0211, 77.1855)
)

results <- sample_places |>
  reverse_geocode(lat = lat, long = long, method = "osm", full_results = TRUE)

results |>
  select(lat, long, address, any_of(c("state_district", "state", "postcode"))) |>
  knitr::kable()

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
section: 58.4 Audit use case 1, checking geotagged photos
text:
58.4 Audit use case 1, checking geotagged photos
Many government schemes ask field staff to upload a geotagged photo of each completed work, such as a house, a pond or a road. The work is claimed to be at a particular place. Reverse geocoding the photo’s coordinates tells us where the photo was actually taken.
Let us use our four coordinates as the geotags of four such photos. Each comes with the place where the work was claimed to be. One of the claims is wrong.

photos <- sample_places |>
  mutate(photo_id      = c("PH-101", "PH-102", "PH-103", "PH-104"),
         claimed_place = c("Agra", "Khajuraho", "Mathura", "Delhi"),
         .before = 1)

photos

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  photo_id claimed_place   lat  long
  <chr>    <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 PH-101   Agra           27.2  78.0
2 PH-102   Khajuraho      24.8  79.9
3 PH-103   Mathura        27.2  78.0
4 PH-104   Delhi          28.5  77.2


We reverse geocode the photos, and check whether the address returned contains the claimed place.

photos_checked <- photos |>
  reverse_geocode(lat = lat, long = long, method = "osm") |>
  mutate(matches_claim = str_detect(str_to_lower(address), str_to_lower(claimed_place)))

photos_checked |>
  select(photo_id, claimed_place, address, matches_claim)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  photo_id claimed_place address                                   matches_claim
  <chr>    <chr>         <chr>                                     <lgl>        
1 PH-101   Agra          Taj Mahal, Taj East Gate Road, Taj Ganj,… TRUE         
2 PH-102   Khajuraho     Khajuraho, Jatkra, Rajnagar Tahsil, Chha… TRUE         
3 PH-103   Mathura       Agra Fort, SH62, Balkeshwar, Agra, Uttar… FALSE        
4 PH-104   Delhi         Qutb Minar, Kalka Das Marg, Mehrauli, So… TRUE         


Photo PH-103 was claimed to show a work in Mathura. But its geotag is in Agra, more than 50 km away. Such a photo needs explanation. It may be a photo of a different work, or of no work at all.






WarningCaution



Comparing text in this way is a rough first check. Place names are spelt in many ways, such as Gurgaon and Gurugram, and the address returned by the service may use a different name, or a larger or smaller unit, than the claim. Treat a mismatch as a question to be checked, not as a finding. For large data, it is better to compare codes, such as district codes, or to use the map-based checks of Chapter 56, where we measured the distance between a geotag and the site directly.

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
section: 58.5 Audit use case 2, checking geotags without sending them anywhere
text:
58.5 Audit use case 2, checking geotags without sending them anywhere
Reverse geocoding needs an online service, and we cannot send the coordinates of beneficiaries’ homes or works to a public one. But many problems in geotags can be found without any service at all, using only the numbers themselves. Let us take the geotags of 1,000 works completed under a scheme in a district of Rajasthan. We have planted five common problems.

15 geotags with latitude and longitude swapped, a frequent error when data passes between systems.
8 geotags of 0, 0, which is what some devices record when the GPS has failed.
20 geotags with only two decimal places, which suggests they were typed by hand, not captured by the phone.
3 geotags outside India altogether.
40 works in different villages, all geotagged at exactly the same spot. This is the block office, from where the photos were actually uploaded.


Code to create the geotagsset.seed(7)
n <- 1000
geotags <- tibble(work_id = sprintf("WK%04d", 1:n),
                  village = sprintf("Village-%02d", sample(1:60, n, TRUE)),
                  lat  = round(runif(n, 26.60, 27.20), 6),
                  long = round(runif(n, 75.50, 76.10), 6))

problem_rows <- sample(1:n, 86)
swapped <- problem_rows[1:15]
zeros   <- problem_rows[16:23]
typed   <- problem_rows[24:43]
office  <- problem_rows[44:83]
abroad  <- problem_rows[84:86]

geotags <- geotags |>
  mutate(
    tmp  = lat,
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% swapped, long, lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% swapped, tmp, long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% zeros, 0, lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% zeros, 0, long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% typed, round(lat, 2), lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% typed, round(long, 2), long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% office, 26.912437, lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% office, 75.787271, long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% abroad, lat - 30, lat)
  ) |>
  select(-tmp)


Let us add one column for each check. India lies roughly between latitudes 6° and 38° north, and longitudes 68° and 98° east. A swapped point has its latitude in the range of India’s longitudes, and the other way round.

count_decimals <- function(x) {
  str_length(coalesce(str_extract(as.character(x), "(?<=\\.)\\d+"), ""))
}

geotag_checks <- geotags |>
  add_count(lat, long, name = "same_spot") |>
  mutate(
    zero_point    = lat == 0 & long == 0,
    swapped       = between(lat, 68, 98) & between(long, 6, 38),
    outside_india = !zero_point & !swapped &
                    !(between(lat, 6, 38) & between(long, 68, 98)),
    low_precision = !zero_point & (count_decimals(lat) <= 2 | count_decimals(long) <= 2),
    shared_spot   = same_spot >= 5 & !zero_point
  )

geotag_checks |>
  summarise(across(zero_point:shared_spot, sum))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  zero_point swapped outside_india low_precision shared_spot
       <int>   <int>         <int>         <int>       <int>
1          8      15             3            20          40


count_decimals() uses a look-behind, (?<=\\.), which we learnt in Chapter 21, to take the digits after the decimal point and count them. A phone usually gives five or six decimals. Two decimals mean an accuracy of only about a kilometre.
Every planted problem has been found. The most serious is the shared spot. Let us look at it.

geotag_checks |>
  filter(shared_spot) |>
  summarise(works = n(), villages = n_distinct(village), .by = c(lat, long))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
    lat  long works villages
  <dbl> <dbl> <int>    <int>
1  26.9  75.8    40       29


40 works, in 29 different villages, have exactly the same geotag, to the sixth decimal place. No two houses or ponds can be at the same spot. These photos were taken, or at least uploaded, at one place. This one location, unlike a beneficiary’s home, is an office, so it can be reverse geocoded to confirm what it is.






TipAudit tip



Run these checks first, on the whole data, before any mapping or reverse geocoding. They need no internet, raise no privacy concern, and often find the most important problems. Swapped and zero coordinates are data errors to be corrected. Typed coordinates and shared spots suggest that the photo was not taken at the site, and need verification in the field.

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
text:
58.6 A suggested workflow


Use an approved service for any coordinates that relate to people.

Check the coordinates offline first, for swapped, zero, typed, outside-India and shared values, as in the second use case.

Reverse geocode each unique location once, using reverse_geocode() on a data frame, and save the results.

Compare the returned place with the claimed place, by name or preferably by code.

Measure the distance between the geotag and the claimed site, where the site’s coordinates are known.

Verify every mismatch with records or a field visit.







ImportantRemember



A geotag tells us where the phone was, not necessarily where the work is. And geotags can be faked. A correct geotag supports a claim, but does not prove it. A wrong one is a strong reason to look closer.

title: 58  Reverse Geocoding
text:
58.7 Try it yourself
These exercises use the 1,000 geotags of the second use case. They work only on the numbers, so nothing is sent to any service. Try each one before you open the solution.


A stricter shared spot. Flag a shared spot when two or more works, not five, have exactly the same geotag. Does this find anything beyond the block office?






TipSolution






spots_2 <- geotag_checks |>
  filter(same_spot >= 2, !zero_point) |>
  summarise(works = n(), villages = n_distinct(village), .by = c(lat, long))

spots_2

# A tibble: 1 × 4
    lat  long works villages
  <dbl> <dbl> <int>    <int>
1  26.9  75.8    40       29


With the lower limit, there is still only one spot. Genuine geotags with six decimals almost never repeat, so even a pair at exactly the same spot would be worth a question.





Correct the swapped geotags. Make a corrected copy of the geotags, in which the swapped latitude and longitude are put back in place. Check that every corrected point now lies within India’s range.






TipSolution






geotags_fixed <- geotag_checks |>
  mutate(new_lat  = if_else(swapped, long, lat),
         new_long = if_else(swapped, lat, long))

geotags_fixed |>
  filter(swapped) |>
  summarise(corrected = n(),
            now_in_india = sum(between(new_lat, 6, 38) & between(new_long, 68, 98)))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  corrected now_in_india
      <int>        <int>
1        15           15


All 15 swapped geotags now fall within India’s range. We wrote the corrections into new columns, new_lat and new_long, and kept the original values. A working paper should always show both, so that anyone can see what was changed and why.





Villages with the most problems. Count, for each village, the works with at least one problem of any kind. List the five villages with the most.






TipSolution






village_problems <- geotag_checks |>
  mutate(any_problem = zero_point | swapped | outside_india | low_precision | shared_spot) |>
  summarise(works = n(), problems = sum(any_problem), .by = village) |>
  mutate(pct = round(100 * problems / works, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(problems))

head(village_problems, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  village    works problems   pct
  <chr>      <int>    <int> <dbl>
1 Village-57    19        5  26.3
2 Village-40    19        4  21.1
3 Village-32    22        4  18.2
4 Village-28    28        3  10.7
5 Village-47    15        3  20  


Village-57 has the most, 5 of its 19 works. With so few works in each village, four or five problems can arise by chance, and in our data the problems were planted at random. In real data, a village or a block with a much higher share would point to one field worker or one office.





Close to the office, but not at it. One degree of latitude is about 111 km. In this area one degree of longitude is about 99 km. Using these figures, find the works, other than the 40 at the office spot, whose geotag lies within 2 km of the block office.






TipSolution






office_lat  <- 26.912437
office_long <- 75.787271

near_office <- geotag_checks |>
  filter(!shared_spot) |>
  mutate(km_from_office = sqrt(((lat - office_lat) * 111)^2 +
                               ((long - office_long) * 99)^2)) |>
  filter(km_from_office < 2) |>
  arrange(km_from_office)

near_office |> select(work_id, village, lat, long, km_from_office, low_precision)

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  work_id village      lat  long km_from_office low_precision
  <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>          <dbl> <lgl>        
1 WK0641  Village-55  26.9  75.8          0.592 FALSE        
2 WK0069  Village-46  26.9  75.8          0.851 FALSE        
3 WK0421  Village-30  26.9  75.8          0.882 TRUE         
4 WK0223  Village-15  26.9  75.8          1.22  FALSE        
5 WK0702  Village-41  26.9  75.8          1.29  TRUE         


5 other works lie within 2 km of the office. Some works are genuinely near the block headquarters, so this is not a finding by itself. But if such works are claimed in villages far from the headquarters, the photos may have been taken at or near the office too. Check the claimed village against these geotags.





One exception list. Make one exception list with a single column problem, naming the first problem found in each work, in the order zero, swapped, outside India, shared spot, typed. Count the works under each problem.






TipSolution






exceptions <- geotag_checks |>
  mutate(problem = case_when(
    zero_point    ~ "Zero point",
    swapped       ~ "Latitude and longitude swapped",
    outside_india ~ "Outside India",
    shared_spot   ~ "Shared spot",
    low_precision ~ "Typed, two decimals or fewer"
  )) |>
  filter(!is.na(problem)) |>
  select(work_id, village, lat, long, problem)

exceptions |> count(problem, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  problem                            n
  <chr>                          <int>
1 Shared spot                       40
2 Typed, two decimals or fewer      20
3 Latitude and longitude swapped    15
4 Zero point                         8
5 Outside India                      3


The list has 86 works, one row each, which matches the 86 works with at least one problem. case_when() takes the first condition that is true, so a work with two problems is counted once. This is the form a field party needs, one row per work to verify.

title: Part IX: Applying the Toolkit
text:
The earlier parts taught the techniques one by one. Real audit problems seldom fit a single technique. This part takes an audit area and brings together everything that helps with it, from simple counts to association rules, networks, record linkage and machine learning.
It begins with the accounts. Journal entries are where management can override controls, and auditing standards on fraud require them to be tested. The first chapter tests every entry in a general ledger. The second reconciles records that should agree, such as the cash book and the bank statement, and checks claims against independent records.
Public procurement follows. Tenders are where a great deal of public money is spent, and where competition can be quietly restricted or rigged. The first of these chapters checks the tendering process itself, with red flags that work for every tender. The next two look for bid rigging, where firms that should compete secretly decide who will win.
The part ends with a whole scheme audited from start to end. It gathers what earlier chapters found about one health insurance scheme, and builds a case from several independent sources.
The chapters draw on many earlier ones, so read them after Parts I to VIII, or at least after the chapters they point to.

Accounts


59  Journal Entry Testing
Every journal entry tested for the signs of management override, combined into a risk score for selecting entries.


60  Reconciliation and Cross-verification
Matching a cash book with the bank statement, and claims with independent records, step by step even when there is no common key.




Tenders and bid rigging


61  Red Flags in Tendering
Red flags in the tendering process, combined into a simple risk index that works for every tender.


62  Bid Rigging, Patterns Across Tenders
Patterns across many tenders that reveal bid rigging, even when each tender gets only two or three bids.


63  Bid Rigging, Shapes of Bids and Machine Learning
The shape of bids in larger tenders, what research shows, and a machine learning model used honestly.




Schemes


64  Auditing a Health Insurance Scheme
One health insurance scheme audited from start to end, bringing claims, grievances, feedback, maps and inspections together to build a case.

title: 59  Journal Entry Testing
text:
59.1 Why journal entries matter
A State warehousing corporation keeps its accounts on an ERP system. Every bill, receipt, salary run and depreciation charge reaches the general ledger as a journal entry. Most entries are made by the system itself, or keyed in by the accountants as part of their daily work. A few are different. A manager books a large sum as income on the last day of the year. A store keeper, who has no business in the ledger, posts bills late at night. An accountant keeps every bill just below the amount that needs the General Manager’s approval. Each of these entries looks ordinary on its own. Among twenty thousand others, nobody notices them.
Journal entries are where management can override controls. A person with enough authority can record an entry that no ordinary control will stop, because the controls are run by the same people. Standards on auditing therefore single out journal entries for testing. This chapter shows how to test every entry in a general ledger with R, rather than a handful picked by hand.
This chapter opens Part IX, which applies the techniques of earlier chapters to whole audit areas. The chapters after it do the same for tenders. We will check that the ledger received is complete. We will profile who posts, when and to which accounts. We will then run one test for each characteristic of a suspicious entry, using dates and times (Chapter 18), round numbers and approval limits (Chapter 33), duplicates (Chapter 34), narrations (Section 51.11), segregation of duties (Section 38.6) and rare combinations (Chapter 48). Finally we will combine the tests into a simple risk score, in the spirit of Section 61.8, and select entries for examination.
As with every chapter in this part, a flag is not a finding. Most flagged entries will have a good reason. The aim is to find the few that need a question, and to show in the working papers why those were chosen.
Prerequisites
The standards on auditing that deal with fraud are SA 240, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, and ISA 240, its international counterpart. Both recognise that management is in a unique position to commit fraud by overriding controls. So, whatever the auditor’s view of the risk, both require procedures to test the appropriateness of journal entries recorded in the general ledger, and of other adjustments made in preparing the financial statements. The auditor is expected to select entries made at the end of the reporting period, and to consider entries made throughout the period. The standards also ask the auditor to understand the entity’s process for making entries, and to talk to the people who make them.
Auditing guidance describes the features that fraudulent entries often have. They are general characteristics, not rules, and each of them also fits many honest entries. The table below lists them, with the test this chapter uses for each.
The same question arises in Indian government audit wherever accounts are kept on the commercial pattern. Public sector undertakings, autonomous bodies and corporations increasingly run ERP systems, whose ledgers can be extracted in full. Testing every entry is then quicker than testing a sample. It also shows patterns that a sample cannot, such as one user’s entries clustering below a limit.

title: 59  Journal Entry Testing
section: 59.2 Our data, a general ledger of a State warehousing company
text:
59.2 Our data, a general ledger of a State warehousing company
Our auditee is an imaginary State warehousing corporation. It stores foodgrains and other goods for depositors, earns storage and handling charges, and is building new godowns. We have received its general ledger for 2024-25, and for April and May 2025, the months in which the accounts were closed.
The table gl has one row for each line of a journal entry, with these columns.


je_id is the entry number, and line the line within the entry. Every entry has two or more lines.

fy and period give the financial year and the month within it. April is period 1 and March is period 12. Entries dated 31 March but recorded after the year end go to a special period 13, which the ERP keeps for year-end adjustments.

posting_date is the accounting date, and document_date the date of the bill or voucher behind it. entered_at is the date and time when the entry was actually keyed in, in Indian Standard Time.

account_code, account_name and account_type (Asset, Liability, Income or Expense) identify the account.

debit and credit are the amounts, in rupees. On each line, one of them is zero.

source is “System” for entries made by an interface, such as billing or payroll, and “Manual” for entries keyed in by a person.

user_id is the person who made the entry, and approver_id the person who approved it. System entries have no approver.

narration is the explanation typed with the entry.

There are also four smaller tables. coa is the chart of accounts. users is the user master, with each user’s department, role, and dates of joining and leaving. tb is the trial balance for 2024-25, printed from the ERP. holidays lists the gazetted holidays of the State. The company works Monday to Friday.
The company’s own rules, which we will test against, are simple. A manual entry above ₹10 lakh must be approved by the General Manager (Finance). Smaller entries are approved by one of the two Managers (Finance). Every manual entry above ₹1 lakh must be approved by someone other than the person who made it.
Most of the ledger is routine. The billing interface posts storage bills every night, and bank receipts are imported each morning. The system posts payroll and depreciation at month end. Accountants book provisions on the last working day of each month, and the system reverses them the next day. The accountants worked over the closing weekend in March. After the year end, the finance team booked genuine provisions, and late bills of March were entered in April. Eight cases have been planted.


A year-end revenue boost. A manager books six entries of storage income, dated 31 March 2025 but keyed in during April. They debit receivables and credit revenue. In May they are reversed.

A user who should not be posting. A store keeper posts bills of one vendor, often late at night or on holidays.

Self-approved entries. A manager approves their own entries above ₹1 lakh.

Entries just below the approval limit. One accountant keeps keying in bills a little under ₹10 lakh.

Round amounts to suspense and provisions. Round sums are moved to the suspense account, and round provisions for repairs are booked in March.

A rare account combination. Capital work-in-progress is paid in cash, three times.

Narrations that explain nothing. A dozen entries say only “adj”, “ok” or “as per instructions”, or nothing at all.

A duplicate. One vendor’s bill is posted twice, two days apart.

The extract also has a problem of completeness, which we must find before running any test.

Code to create the general ledgerset.seed(2425)

# Gazetted holidays of the imaginary State, and the company's working days (Monday to Friday)
holidays <- as.Date(c("2024-04-11", "2024-04-17", "2024-05-23", "2024-08-15", "2024-08-26",
                      "2024-10-02", "2024-10-31", "2024-11-15", "2024-12-25", "2025-01-26",
                      "2025-02-26", "2025-03-14", "2025-04-18", "2025-05-12"))
all_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-05-31"), by = "day")
work_days <- all_days[wday(all_days, week_start = 1) <= 5 & !all_days %in% holidays]
next_wd <- function(d) work_days[pmin(findInterval(as.numeric(d) - 1, as.numeric(work_days)) + 1,
                                      length(work_days))]
stamp <- function(d, h) force_tz(as_datetime(d), "Asia/Kolkata") + round(h * 3600)
office_h <- function(n) pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 13.8, 2), 9.7), 18.6)
fy_wd <- work_days[work_days <= as.Date("2025-03-31")]

coa <- tribble(
  ~account_code, ~account_name,                      ~account_type,
  "1101",        "Cash in hand",                     "Asset",
  "1102",        "Bank current account",             "Asset",
  "1201",        "Trade receivables",                "Asset",
  "1301",        "Advances to staff",                "Asset",
  "1401",        "Capital work-in-progress",         "Asset",
  "1501",        "Buildings and warehouses",         "Asset",
  "1502",        "Accumulated depreciation",         "Asset",
  "1601",        "Suspense account",                 "Asset",
  "1701",        "GST input credit",                 "Asset",
  "2101",        "Trade payables",                   "Liability",
  "2201",        "Salary payable",                   "Liability",
  "2301",        "TDS payable",                      "Liability",
  "2302",        "GST output payable",               "Liability",
  "2401",        "Provision for expenses",           "Liability",
  "2402",        "Provision for doubtful debts",     "Liability",
  "2403",        "Provision for gratuity",           "Liability",
  "2501",        "Security deposits from depositors", "Liability",
  "3101",        "Storage charges",                  "Income",
  "3102",        "Handling charges",                 "Income",
  "3201",        "Interest income",                  "Income",
  "3301",        "Miscellaneous income",             "Income",
  "4101",        "Salaries and wages",               "Expense",
  "4102",        "Gratuity expense",                 "Expense",
  "4201",        "Electricity",                      "Expense",
  "4202",        "Repairs and maintenance",          "Expense",
  "4203",        "Security services",                "Expense",
  "4204",        "Fumigation and chemicals",         "Expense",
  "4301",        "Depreciation",                     "Expense",
  "4401",        "Office expenses",                  "Expense",
  "4402",        "Audit fee",                        "Expense",
  "4501",        "Bad and doubtful debts",           "Expense"
)
acc_label <- c("4201" = "electricity", "4202" = "repairs of godowns", "4203" = "security services",
               "4204" = "fumigation chemicals", "4401" = "office expenses")

users <- tribble(
  ~user_id, ~department,              ~role,                       ~joined,      ~left,
  "ACC01",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2016-07-01", NA,
  "ACC02",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2018-03-12", NA,
  "ACC03",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2019-08-01", NA,
  "ACC04",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2021-01-04", NA,
  "ACC05",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2022-06-15", NA,
  "ACC06",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2025-01-01", NA,
  "ACC07",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2012-04-02", "2024-12-31",
  "ACM01",  "Accounts",               "Manager (Finance)",         "2010-09-01", NA,
  "ACM02",  "Accounts",               "Manager (Finance)",         "2014-02-17", NA,
  "FIN01",  "Finance",                "General Manager (Finance)", "2008-05-05", NA,
  "HR01",   "Human Resources",        "Payroll officer",           "2017-11-20", NA,
  "ITA02",  "Information Technology", "System administrator",      "2020-10-01", NA,
  "STR03",  "Stores",                 "Store keeper",              "2019-02-11", NA,
  "SYSTEM", "Information Technology", "Batch interface",           NA,           NA
) |>
  mutate(across(c(joined, left), as.Date))

acc_for <- function(d) {
  sixth <- if_else(d <= as.Date("2024-12-31"), "ACC07", "ACC06")
  pick <- sample(1:6, length(d), TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.18, 0.14, 0.14, 0.14))
  if_else(pick == 6, sixth, sprintf("ACC%02d", pick))
}
approver_for <- function(amount) {
  if_else(amount > 1e6, "FIN01", sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), length(amount), TRUE))
}

# Entries are collected in E and their lines in L
E <- list(); L <- list(); k <- 0
keys <- function(n) { k <<- k + n; seq_len(n) + k - n }
dr <- function(e, acc, amt) tibble(key = e$key, account_code = acc, debit = amt, credit = 0)
cr <- function(e, acc, amt) tibble(key = e$key, account_code = acc, debit = 0, credit = amt)
add <- function(e, lines, case = NA_character_) {
  E[[length(E) + 1]] <<- mutate(e, case = case)
  L[[length(L) + 1]] <<- lines
}
entry <- function(d, entered, source, user, approver, narration, doc = d) {
  tibble(key = keys(length(d)), posting_date = d, document_date = doc, entered_at = entered,
         source = source, user_id = user, approver_id = approver, narration = narration)
}

# 1. Storage bills, posted every night by the billing interface
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 16)); n <- length(d)
storage <- round(rlnorm(n, log(110000), 0.8), 2)
handling <- if_else(runif(n) < 0.3, round(rlnorm(n, log(25000), 0.6), 2), 0)
gst <- round(0.18 * (storage + handling), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 23 + runif(n, 0, 0.9)), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
           paste0("Storage bill SB/", sample(10000:99999, n, TRUE), " to depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1201", storage + handling + gst), cr(e, "3101", storage),
                 cr(e[handling > 0, ], "3102", handling[handling > 0]), cr(e, "2302", gst)))

# 2. Receipts from depositors, imported from the bank statement each morning
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 15)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(120000), 0.8), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, runif(n, 10, 10.8)), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
           paste0("Receipt from depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE), ", UTR ", sample(1e8:9e8, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "1201", amt)))

# 3. Vendor bills keyed in by the accountants
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 10)); n <- length(d)
base <- round(rlnorm(n, log(45000), 1.1), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
exp_acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.35, 0.2, 0.25))
ent_d <- next_wd(d + if_else(runif(n) < 0.3, sample(1:3, n, TRUE), 0L))
e <- entry(d, stamp(ent_d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(base + gst),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, n, TRUE), " of vendor V-",
                  sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, n, TRUE)), " for ", acc_label[exp_acc]),
           doc = d - sample(0:20, n, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, exp_acc, base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)))

# 4. Payments to vendors
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 9)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(52000), 1.1), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(amt),
           paste0("Payment to vendor V-", sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, n, TRUE)),
                  " against bill no ", sample(100:9999, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2101", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))

# 5. Petty cash. Many small round amounts, and a few entries keyed in without a narration
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 2)); n <- length(d)
amt <- if_else(runif(n) < 0.5, sample(c(500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 5000), n, TRUE),
               round(runif(n, 200, 9000)))
narr <- paste0("Petty cash, ", sample(c("tea and refreshments", "courier charges", "local conveyance",
                                         "stationery", "minor repairs to furniture"), n, TRUE))
narr[sample(n, 6)] <- ""
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE), narr)
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", amt), cr(e, "1101", amt)))

# 6. Cash drawn from the bank every Monday
d <- work_days[wday(work_days, week_start = 1) == 1]; n <- length(d)
amt <- sample(c(20000, 25000, 30000), n, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, runif(n, 10.5, 12)), "Manual", "ACC03", "ACM01",
           paste0("Cash drawn for petty expenses, cheque no ", sample(400000:499999, n)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1101", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))

# 7. Advances to staff, and their adjustment against bills a few weeks later
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 1)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(runif(n, 5000, 50000), -3)
emp <- sprintf("E-%03d", sample(1:350, n, TRUE))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE),
           paste0("Advance to employee ", emp, " for tour"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1301", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))
d2 <- next_wd(d + sample(10:40, n, TRUE)); keep <- d2 > d
adj <- round(amt * runif(n, 0.7, 1), 2)
e <- entry(d2[keep], stamp(d2[keep], office_h(sum(keep))), "Manual", acc_for(d2[keep]),
           sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), sum(keep), TRUE),
           paste0("Tour advance of ", emp[keep], " adjusted against TA bill"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", adj[keep]), cr(e, "1301", adj[keep])))

# 8. Running bills of contractors building new godowns, and capitalisation on completion
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 0.5)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(600000), 0.8), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(amt),
           paste0("Being RA bill no ", sample(1:12, n, TRUE), " of contractor V-",
                  sample(c("041", "057", "063"), n, TRUE), " for construction of godown"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1401", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))
d <- as.Date(c("2024-09-30", "2024-12-31", "2025-03-28")); amt <- c(21000000, 14000000, 33000000)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, c(15.5, 16.2, 15.1)), "Manual", "ACM01", "FIN01",
           paste("Capitalisation of godown at", c("Rampur", "Keshavnagar", "Sitapur"), "on completion"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1501", amt), cr(e, "1401", amt)))

# 9. Security deposits received from depositors
d <- rep(fy_wd, rpois(length(fy_wd), 0.7)); n <- length(d)
amt <- sample(c(25000, 50000, 75000, 100000, 150000, 200000), n, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(amt),
           paste0("Security deposit received from depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "2501", amt)))

# 10. Interest on deposits, each quarter, and small miscellaneous income
d <- as.Date(c("2024-06-28", "2024-09-30", "2024-12-31", "2025-03-28")); n <- 4
amt <- round(runif(n, 1800000, 2500000), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", "ACC02", "FIN01", "Interest on fixed deposits for the quarter")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "3201", amt)))
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 0.1)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(15000), 0.8), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE),
           sample(c("Sale of tender forms", "Sale of scrap gunny bags", "Penalty recovered from depositor"), n, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "3301", amt)))

# 11. Unidentified bank receipts parked in suspense, and cleared when the depositor is known
d <- rep(fy_wd, rpois(length(fy_wd), 0.3)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(80000), 0.7), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, runif(n, 10, 10.8)), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
           paste0("Unidentified credit in bank, UTR ", sample(1e8:9e8, n)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "1601", amt)))
d2 <- next_wd(d + sample(5:40, n, TRUE))
e <- entry(d2, stamp(d2, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d2), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE),
           paste0("Unidentified receipt cleared, depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE), " identified"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1601", amt), cr(e, "1201", amt)))

# 12. Monthly postings. Payroll, statutory dues, depreciation, rent of security, accruals
godowns <- c("Rampur", "Keshavnagar", "Sitapur", "Bhawanipur", "Chandgarh", "Dhanpur",
             "Madhopur", "Ratanpur")
months_list <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-05-01"), by = "month")
for (i in seq_along(months_list)) {
  m <- months_list[i]
  wd_m <- work_days[work_days >= m & work_days < m %m+% months(1)]
  last_day <- m %m+% months(1) - 1
  gross <- round(rnorm(1, 16200000, 300000), 2); tds <- round(0.08 * gross, 2)
  e <- entry(max(wd_m), stamp(max(wd_m), 20.5), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
             paste("Salary for", format(m, "%B %Y"), "from payroll"))
  add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4101", gross), cr(e, "2201", gross - tds), cr(e, "2301", tds)))
  e <- entry(last_day, stamp(last_day, 23.8), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
             paste("Depreciation for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
  add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4301", 1842300), cr(e, "1502", 1842300)))
  sec_d <- wd_m[4]
  e <- entry(sec_d, stamp(sec_d, office_h(1)), "Manual", "ACC02", "ACM01",
             paste("Being bill of vendor V-012 for security services,", format(m, "%B %Y")))
  add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4203", 385000), dr(e, "1701", 69300), cr(e, "2101", 454300)))
  if (i < length(months_list)) {
    wd_next <- work_days[work_days >= m %m+% months(1) & work_days < m %m+% months(2)]
    e <- entry(wd_next[1], stamp(wd_next[1], 11.5), "Manual", "ACC01", "FIN01",
               paste("Salary paid for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2201", gross - tds), cr(e, "1102", gross - tds)))
    d7 <- next_wd(m %m+% months(1) + 5)
    e <- entry(d7, stamp(d7, 12.5), "Manual", "ACC02", "FIN01", paste("TDS deposited for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2301", tds), cr(e, "1102", tds)))
    d20 <- next_wd(m %m+% months(1) + 18); gst_amt <- round(rnorm(1, 9000000, 900000), 2)
    e <- entry(d20, stamp(d20, 15), "Manual", "ACC03", "FIN01", paste("GST paid for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2302", gst_amt), cr(e, "1102", gst_amt)))
    # Month-end accruals, reversed automatically on the first day of the next month
    acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), 8, TRUE)
    amt <- round(rlnorm(8, log(150000), 0.6), -4)
    gd <- sample(godowns)
    e <- entry(rep(max(wd_m), 8), stamp(max(wd_m), runif(8, 15, 18)), "Manual",
               sample(c("ACC01", "ACC02"), 8, TRUE), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), 8, TRUE),
               paste0("Being provision for ", acc_label[acc], " at ", gd, " godown for ",
                      format(m, "%B %Y"), ", bill awaited"))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, acc, amt), cr(e, "2401", amt)))
    first_day <- m %m+% months(1)
    e <- entry(rep(first_day, 8), stamp(first_day, 0.3), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
               paste0("Auto reversal of provision for ", acc_label[acc], " at ", gd, " godown for ",
                      format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2401", amt), cr(e, acc, amt)))
  }
}

# 13. Payroll corrections by the payroll officer, and two test entries by the system administrator
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd, 12)); amt <- round(runif(12, 5000, 60000))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(12)), "Manual", "HR01", "ACM01",
           paste0("Arrears of DA to employee E-", sample(100:350, 12), ", payroll correction"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4101", amt), cr(e, "2201", amt)))
d <- as.Date("2024-08-17")
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 15.2), "Manual", "ITA02", "ITA02", "Test entry after ERP patch")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", 1), cr(e, "1101", 1)))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 15.4), "Manual", "ITA02", "ITA02", "Reversal of test entry after ERP patch")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1101", 1), cr(e, "4401", 1)))

# 14. Genuine year-end work. Bills keyed in over the closing weekend, late bills for March
#     entered in April, and year-end provisions by the finance team
d <- rep(as.Date("2025-03-28"), 20)
ent <- stamp(as.Date("2025-03-29") + rep(0:1, each = 10), runif(20, 10.5, 17.5))
base <- round(rlnorm(20, log(60000), 0.9), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), 20, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, ent, "Manual", sample(c("ACC01", "ACC02", "ACC03"), 20, TRUE), approver_for(base + gst),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 20), " of vendor V-", sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, 20)),
                  " for ", acc_label[acc]), doc = d - sample(0:10, 20, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, acc, base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)))
d <- rep(as.Date("2025-03-31"), 15)
ent_d <- sort(sample(work_days[work_days >= as.Date("2025-04-01") & work_days <= as.Date("2025-04-25")], 15, TRUE))
base <- round(rlnorm(15, log(80000), 0.9), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), 15, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, stamp(ent_d, office_h(15)), "Manual", sample(c("ACC01", "ACC02"), 15, TRUE),
           approver_for(base + gst),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 15), " of vendor V-", sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, 15)),
                  " for ", acc_label[acc], ", March 2025, received late"),
           doc = as.Date("2025-03-31") - sample(0:20, 15, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, acc, base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)))
d <- rep(as.Date("2025-03-31"), 3)
e <- entry(d, stamp(as.Date(c("2025-04-22", "2025-04-24", "2025-04-15")), c(11.5, 16.2, 12)),
           "Manual", c("FIN01", "FIN01", "ACM01"), c("FIN01", "FIN01", "FIN01"),
           c("Provision for gratuity as per actuarial valuation report dated 18.04.2025",
             "Provision for doubtful debts on receivables over three years old, as per Board note",
             "Provision for statutory audit fee for 2024-25"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, c("4102", "4501", "4402"), c(3846215, 6240000, 300000)),
                 cr(e, c("2403", "2402", "2401"), c(3846215, 6240000, 300000))))

# ---- Planted cases ----
# Planted 1. Storage income booked on 31 March 2025, entered in April, reversed in May
amt <- c(4860000, 5230000, 3975000, 6120000, 4490000, 5540000)
e <- entry(rep(as.Date("2025-03-31"), 6),
           stamp(as.Date(c("2025-04-09", "2025-04-10", "2025-04-11", "2025-04-12", "2025-04-12", "2025-04-12")),
                 c(18.8, 17.6, 19.3, 11.1, 11.7, 12.2)),
           "Manual", "ACM01", "FIN01", "Storage income for March 2025, bills under preparation")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1201", amt), cr(e, "3101", amt)), "1 Revenue boost")
d <- as.Date(c("2025-05-07", "2025-05-07", "2025-05-08", "2025-05-08", "2025-05-09", "2025-05-09"))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(6)), "Manual", "ACM01", "FIN01", "Rectification of entry dated 31.03.2025")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "3101", amt), cr(e, "1201", amt)), "1 Revenue boost reversal")

# Planted 2. A store keeper posts bills of one vendor, often at night or on holidays
ent <- ymd_hm(c("2024-07-09 22:40", "2024-08-15 12:15", "2024-08-29 23:05", "2024-09-21 16:30",

                "2025-02-20 00:20", "2025-03-08 17:45"), tz = "Asia/Kolkata")
d <- as_date(ent - hours(2)); base <- round(rlnorm(14, log(320000), 0.35), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
bill_no <- sample(2000:2999, 14)
e <- entry(d, ent, "Manual", "STR03", "ACM02",
           paste0("Being bill no ", bill_no, " of vendor V-217 for fumigation chemicals"),
           doc = d - sample(2:10, 14, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4204", base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)), "2 Store keeper")
d2 <- next_wd(d + sample(12:25, 14, TRUE))
e <- entry(d2, stamp(d2, office_h(14)), "Manual", acc_for(d2), "ACM02",
           paste0("Payment to vendor V-217 against bill no ", bill_no))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2101", base + gst), cr(e, "1102", base + gst)))

# Planted 3. A manager approves their own entries above Rs 1 lakh

gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(8)), "Manual", "ACM02", "ACM02",
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 8), " of vendor V-1", sample(10:99, 8),
                  " for repairs of godown no G-", sample(10:60, 8)), doc = d - sample(1:15, 8, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)), "3 Self-approved")

# Planted 4. Bills just below the approval limit of Rs 10 lakh, all keyed in by one accountant

base <- round(tot / 1.18, 2)

           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 22), " of vendor V-", sample(c("131", "142", "158"), 22, TRUE),
                  " for repairs of godowns"), doc = d - sample(1:15, 22, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", base), dr(e, "1701", tot - base), cr(e, "2101", tot)), "4 Below limit")

# Planted 5. Round amounts sent to suspense, and round provisions for repairs in March
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd[fy_wd >= as.Date("2024-10-01")], 6))
amt <- c(200000, 500000, 300000, 750000, 400000, 250000)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(6)), "Manual", "ACC05", "ACM02", "Amount transferred to suspense, to be adjusted")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1601", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)), "5 Round to suspense")

add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", amt), cr(e, "2401", amt)), "5 Round to provision")

# Planted 6. Capital work paid in cash
d <- as.Date(c("2024-10-22", "2025-01-09", "2025-03-19")); amt <- c(184500, 226000, 197300)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(3)), "Manual", "ACC02", "ACM01", "Payment to contractor for godown shed work")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1401", amt), cr(e, "1101", amt)), "6 Rare pair")

# Planted 7. Narrations that explain nothing
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd, 12)); amt <- round(runif(12, 40000, 400000), 2)
usr <- sample(c(rep("ACC05", 8), "ACC03", "ACC03", "ACC07", "ACC07"))
usr[usr == "ACC07" & d > as.Date("2024-12-31")] <- "ACC06"
