Figure 64.2 draws the same table as a grid.

signals |>
  mutate(hospital = fct_rev(fct_inorder(paste0(hospital_id, " (", sources, ")")))) |>
  pivot_longer(profile:inspection, names_to = "evidence", values_to = "flagged") |>
  mutate(evidence = fct_inorder(evidence)) |>
  ggplot(aes(evidence, hospital, fill = flagged)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "firebrick", `FALSE` = "grey92"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Flagged", `FALSE` = "Not flagged")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Hospital (number of sources)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))






Figure 64.2: Lines of evidence that flag each hospital. Hospitals are ordered by the number of independent sources.




The table sorts itself into four groups.


Strong cases. Six hospitals are flagged by three or more independent sources, and they are exactly the six camp hospitals. H066, Suraksha Nursing Home, is flagged by five sources, the most of any hospital. Its claims, its grievances, its patients’ feedback, its patients’ homes and its inspection photo all point the same way.

A case resting on one source. H085 and H104 are flagged by two tests each, but both tests read the same claims. No grievance, feedback or map supports them. This does not make them innocent. Overbilling of ICU stays is done on paper, so patients may never notice it, and would not complain. But the case rests on the claims alone, and needs the medical records to stand.

False alarms, most likely. H107 and H108 are just over the line of the ICU rule, and H082 and H102 are flagged on about ten comments each. Nothing else supports them. With 120 hospitals and eight tests, a few such flags are bound to appear by chance.

A monitoring failure. H010, H024, H042, H084, H109, H115 are flagged only for a desk inspection. This says nothing about these hospitals. It says the inspection system cannot be relied on.

Note one more point. The six camp hospitals and the two ICU hospitals were planted in the data by different processes, and the evidence tells them apart. That is what triangulation is for. One signal is a lead. Several independent signals make a strong case.






WarningCaution



Triangulation makes a lead stronger. It does not make it proven. Every signal in the table is a pattern in data that the hospital has not yet been asked to explain. A hospital in a remote area may genuinely draw patients from far away. A surgeon with a good name may attract patients from other districts. Grievances can be filed by rivals. The audit observation must rest on records seen, patients met and explanations received, not on the table alone.

title: 64  Auditing a Health Insurance Scheme
text:
64.12 Valuing the findings
An observation needs a money value. But we must be careful to say what kind of value it is. Some amounts are wrong on the face of the claim. Others are only at risk until the records are seen. Let us work out four amounts, one for each specific pattern.
For the ICU stays, we cannot say that every ICU stay at H085 and H104 was unneeded. Instead we work out the expected number. For each medical package, we take the share of claims with an ICU stay at all other hospitals. Applied to the two hospitals’ own claims, this gives the number of ICU stays they would bill if they behaved like the rest. The excess is the number above this.

icu_rate <- medical |>
  filter(!hospital_id %in% icu_two) |>
  summarise(expected_rate = mean(str_detect(packages, "A01")), .by = main_package)

icu_excess <- medical |>
  filter(hospital_id %in% icu_two) |>
  left_join(icu_rate, by = "main_package") |>
  summarise(claims   = n(),
            actual   = sum(str_detect(packages, "A01")),
            expected = round(sum(expected_rate), 1),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  mutate(excess = round(actual - expected))

icu_excess

  hospital_id claims actual expected excess

1 H085           120     74     13.1     61
2 H104            43     25      4.5     20


Now the four amounts together.

lens  <- claims |> filter(hospital_id %in% six, str_detect(packages, "A06"))
lapar <- claims |> filter(hospital_id %in% six, str_detect(packages, "A05"))
young <- claims |> filter(hospital_id %in% six, str_detect(packages, "^G01"), age < 40)

value <- tibble(
  item = c("Lens billed again with cataract surgery (A06)",
           "Diagnostic laparoscopy with appendectomy (A05)",
           "Hysterectomy in women under 40, whole claim",
           "ICU stays after medical packages, above the expected number"),
  hospitals = c("Six camp hospitals", "Six camp hospitals", "Six camp hospitals",
                paste(icu_two, collapse = " and ")),
  claims = c(nrow(lens), nrow(lapar), nrow(young), sum(icu_excess$excess)),
  amount = c(nrow(lens) * rate[["A06"]], nrow(lapar) * rate[["A05"]],
             sum(young$claim_amount), sum(icu_excess$excess) * rate[["A01"]]),
  status = c("Inadmissible on the face of the claim", "At risk, needs case records",
             "At risk, needs medical records", "At risk, needs medical records"))

The four items come to ₹1.65 crore. They do not overlap, because each item is a different set of claims. But they are of different strength.

The separate lens, ₹22.5 lakh on 562 claims, is inadmissible as soon as we read the package master. No medical judgement is needed. It can be recovered once the scheme confirms the package definition.
The laparoscopies, ₹27.5 lakh, and the hysterectomies in young women, ₹1.03 crore, are amounts at risk. Some of these operations may have been needed. Only the case records, and a doctor’s opinion on them, can decide.
The excess ICU stays, ₹12.2 lakh, rest on a comparison with other hospitals. They are an estimate, and should be reported as one.

Beyond these items, the whole of the claims of the flagged hospitals is exposed. The six camp hospitals were paid ₹6.41 crore in the year, 8.1% of the scheme’s claims. The two ICU hospitals were paid ₹1.77 crore. If field visits find that patients were not treated at all, much more than the four items above may be wrong. But we should not report the whole ₹6.41 crore as a loss. Most of those patients were probably treated. The audit report should give it as the value of claims under examination, not as an irregular payment.






NoteAmounts at risk, not losses



Keep three kinds of figure apart in the report. An inadmissible amount breaks a clear rule and can be recovered. An amount at risk is open to question until the records are seen. Exposure is the total value of the transactions in which the problem lies. Mixing them up overstates the finding, and the auditee will rightly dispute it.

1 H066                    2 2024-06-15      INS-05           32.2


A draft observation follows the usual order of facts, criteria, cause, effect and recommendation. Its wording must be careful. At this stage the audit has patterns in data, not proof of fraud. So the draft states what the data shows, and asks for the records. It does not say “fraud”, “fake” or “bogus”.

Unusual claims of Suraksha Nursing Home, Devgarh
Facts. Suraksha Nursing Home (H066), a private hospital with 73 beds in Devgarh district, was paid ₹1.49 crore on 575 claims in 2024-25. This is 7.9 claims per bed, against a median of 3.6 for other private hospitals. Of its admissions, 36% were on Saturdays or Sundays, and 11.7% of its claims were for a patient it had admitted in the previous 30 days. In 21 claims, the patient was admitted again before the earlier stay had ended. In 132 claims for cataract surgery with lens, a lens was billed again as a separate add-on, for ₹5.3 lakh. In 44 claims for appendectomy, a diagnostic laparoscopy was billed in addition, for ₹5.3 lakh. Of 113 hysterectomies, 73 were on women under 40 years, for ₹22.7 lakh. Of a sample of 59 patients, 59% lived more than 50 km from the hospital. The scheme received 33 grievances against the hospital, of which 16 described village camps, agents or surgery done without explanation. The photo of the inspection of 15 June 2024 was taken 32 km from the hospital.
Criteria. The package for cataract surgery includes the lens. Add-on packages are to be billed only when clinically needed and recorded. Hysterectomy is to be done only on documented medical grounds. Empanelled hospitals are to be inspected at the site twice a year.
Cause. Claims of this hospital with a separate lens were paid in 12 of the 12 months of the year. This suggests that the claim system had no check against an add-on that a package already includes. No check on the age of women for hysterectomy, or on claims per bed, was evident. The inspection report was accepted without checking the geotag of the photo.
Effect. ₹5.3 lakh was paid for lenses already covered by the package. ₹28.0 lakh on laparoscopies and hysterectomies is at risk until the case records are examined. The pattern of camps, distant patients and complaints raises doubt whether all patients needed admission.
Recommendation. The scheme may recover the separate lens charges, and have its medical auditors examine the case records of the flagged claims. It may verify a sample of patients at their homes, and refer the hospital to its anti-fraud unit for investigation. It may also add system checks on add-ons, hysterectomy in young women and claims per bed, and require geotag checks on every inspection.

format(x, "%d %B %Y") prints a date as day, month name and year. Notice what the draft does. It counts, compares with peers, and quotes rates. It names the rule broken only where a rule clearly exists. It separates the amount already inadmissible from the amount at risk. And it leaves the question of intent to the investigation that follows.

64.13.1 What the auditor does next


Ask the scheme for the records. For a sample of the flagged claims, ask for the pre-authorisation, the case sheet and the operation notes. Ask also for the discharge summary and any photos uploaded by the hospital. Select the sample with Chapter 29, all claims with the separate lens and a random sample of the rest.

Get a medical opinion. The audit team cannot judge whether a hysterectomy or an ICU stay was needed. A doctor from outside the hospital, through the scheme’s medical audit or a government hospital, must review the case records.

Meet the patients. Visit a sample of patients at home, with the scheme’s district staff. Confirm that they were admitted, for how long, for what, whether they paid anything, and how they came to the hospital. Patient confirmation is the strongest evidence of all.

Visit the hospital. Check the beds, the operation theatre register, the ICU register and the staff on duty against the claims of the same days. A joint physical verification with the scheme’s officers is best.

Look for links. Check whether the six camp hospitals share owners, doctors, agents or vehicles, with the methods of Chapter 55.

Refer, do not conclude. If the records and visits confirm the pattern, the scheme’s anti-fraud unit or the competent authority must investigate. The audit report states the facts found and the action taken.

text:
64.14 Audit use case, a lead from one source
Pragati Nursing Home and Navjeevan Hospital are flagged only by their claims. Nobody complained about them. Their patients did not travel far, and their inspections were done at the site. Should the auditor drop them?
No. Some irregularities leave traces in only one place. Billing an ICU stay that was never given happens on paper. The patient, who paid nothing, may never know. So a lack of complaints is not evidence of good practice. But a case on one source needs a different next step. Let us see when these ICU stays were billed.

medical |>
  filter(hospital_id %in% icu_two) |>
  left_join(packages |> select(main_package = package_code, package_name),
            by = "main_package") |>
  summarise(claims   = n(),
            with_icu = sum(str_detect(packages, "A01")),
            avg_los  = round(mean(los), 1),
            .by = c(hospital_id, package_name)) |>
  mutate(share_icu = round(with_icu / claims, 2)) |>
  arrange(hospital_id, desc(claims))

   hospital_id package_name          claims with_icu avg_los share_icu
   <chr>       <chr>                  <int>    <int>   <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 H085        Acute gastroenteritis     32       17     3.1      0.53
 2 H085        Acute febrile illness     32       23     4.3      0.72
 3 H085        Pneumonia                 23       12     6.2      0.52
 4 H085        Dengue fever              20       14     4.7      0.7 
 5 H085        Diabetic ketoacidosis     13        8     4.8      0.62
 6 H104        Acute febrile illness     17       10     4        0.59
 7 H104        Acute gastroenteritis     11        6     2.5      0.55
 8 H104        Diabetic ketoacidosis      6        5     4.8      0.83
 9 H104        Dengue fever               5        4     4.6      0.8 
10 H104        Pneumonia                  4        0     6.5      0   


The ICU stays are spread over every medical package, including fever and stomach infection, where an ICU stay is rarely needed. For fever and gastroenteritis together, the two hospitals bill an ICU stay in 61% of claims, against 3.7% elsewhere. The excess over the expected number is ₹12.2 lakh.

64.14.1 What the auditor does next


Ask for the ICU records. Take a random sample of medical claims with an ICU stay. Ask for the ICU admission register, the nursing charts, and the bills for oxygen and monitoring. An ICU stay leaves many traces in a hospital. A stay on paper leaves few.

Check capacity. Count ICU beds at each hospital, and the number of patients the claims place in the ICU on each day. If the claims need more ICU beds than exist, the claims cannot all be right.

Get a medical opinion on whether each sampled ICU stay was justified.

Report honestly. If the records support the stays, record that the lead was examined and cleared. If not, report the excess as at risk, with the method of estimation stated.

title: 64  Auditing a Health Insurance Scheme
section: 64.15 What this audit did not test
text:
64.15 What this audit did not test
Analytics covered a great deal, but not everything. An honest report says what was not tested.


Claims rejected or never raised. We had only paid claims. Patients refused treatment, and claims wrongly rejected, need the pre-authorisation and rejection data. Many grievances were about denial of treatment.

Who got a card. We did not test whether the beneficiaries were eligible. That needs the enrolment database, matched with other lists as in Chapter 36.

Treatment that the data cannot see. Whether an operation was done well, or at all, cannot be judged from a claim. Only records, doctors and patients can tell.

Package rates themselves. We tested whether claims followed the rates, not whether the rates were reasonable.

Payment to hospitals. We assumed that claims were paid as approved. A reconciliation of approved claims with bank payments, as in Chapter 60, would test it.

Digits of claim amounts. Benford’s Law does not apply to amounts made of fixed package rates, as Section 32.9 showed for these very claims.

Analytics also has limits of its own. Every test above used a threshold that we chose, such as twice the usual ICU share or 50 km. A different threshold gives a slightly different list. The patient homes are a sample, so the travel test can miss a hospital with few sampled patients. Feedback and grievances come from people who chose to write. And the data was what the scheme gave us. If claims were changed before they reached the database, no test on the database will show it.

title: 64  Auditing a Health Insurance Scheme
text:
64.16 A suggested workflow


Fix the objectives first. Write down the audit questions, and the evidence that would answer each.

Ask for the data in writing. Claims, masters, grievances, feedback, inspections and locations, with record counts and totals.

Test the data. Keys, codes, amounts against rates, dates, blanks, and the total against the accounts.

Profile the scheme. Hospitals, districts, packages and money, so that you know what is normal.

Gather each line of evidence separately. Fix each rule and threshold in advance, and keep each list of flagged hospitals.

Put the evidence side by side. Count independent sources, not tests. Sort the hospitals into strong cases, one-source cases, likely false alarms and system failures.

Value the findings carefully. Separate inadmissible amounts, amounts at risk and exposure.

Draft the observation in neutral words. Facts, criteria, cause, effect and recommendation, with no allegation of fraud.

Verify. Records, medical opinion, patient visits and hospital visits, and refer confirmed cases to the scheme’s anti-fraud unit.
Say what was not tested.







ImportantRemember




One audit, many techniques. Each technique gives a lead. The audit comes from putting them together.
Check the data before analysing it. A finding on incomplete data is not a finding.
Count independent sources, not tests. Two tests on the same claims are one source.
Some real problems show in only one source. Do not drop them, but verify them differently.
Expect false alarms. Many tests on many hospitals will flag a few by chance.
Keep inadmissible amounts, amounts at risk and exposure apart.
Patterns are leads. Records, doctors and patients turn them into findings.

64.17 Where next
Each line of evidence is taught in full in its own chapter. The hospital indicators and their map are in Chapter 46 and Chapter 47, and other ways to find outliers are in Chapter 50. Packages billed together are in Chapter 48. Grievances and feedback are in Chapter 51, Chapter 52 and Chapter 53. Distances and geotags are in Chapter 56. Many of the checks of this chapter, such as an add-on never billed with its package, can be written as a permanent rule book, as in Chapter 31. Links among the flagged hospitals can be traced with Chapter 55. To choose the claims for examination, see Chapter 29. To turn this chapter’s analysis into a report that can be run again next year, see Chapter 65.

64.18 Try it yourself
These exercises use the tables claims, claims_plus, hospitals, grievances, homes_sf, districts, icu_medical and overall_icu, and the lists six and icu_two, of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.


Readmissions and overlapping stays. The column readmit in claims_plus marks a claim that starts within 30 days of the same patient’s earlier discharge from the same hospital. The column overlap marks a claim that starts before that discharge. For the six camp hospitals together, and for all others together, find the share of claims that are readmissions after a discharge, and the share that overlap.






TipSolution






ex_readmit <- claims_plus |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hospital_id %in% six, "Six camp hospitals", "All others")) |>
  summarise(claims          = n(),
            pct_after_stay  = round(100 * mean(readmit & !overlap), 1),
            pct_overlap     = round(100 * mean(overlap), 1),
            amount_readmit  = sum(claim_amount[readmit]),
            .by = group)
ex_readmit

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  group              claims pct_after_stay pct_overlap amount_readmit
  <chr>               <int>          <dbl>       <dbl>          <dbl>
1 All others          31018            0.8         2.2       22678000
2 Six camp hospitals   2458            6.1         4.4        7148500


In the six hospitals, 6.1% of claims are readmissions after a discharge and 4.4% overlap an open stay. Elsewhere the shares are 0.8% and 2.2%. Both are higher in the six. All the claims marked readmit in the six cost ₹71.5 lakh. Some readmissions are genuine, so this is exposure, not loss, until the case records show why each patient came back. The overlapping stays need an explanation in every case.





Patients from other districts. Use st_join() to find the district in which each sampled patient of the six camp hospitals lives. What share of them live outside the district of their hospital?






TipSolution






ex_home_district <- homes_sf |>
  filter(hospital_id %in% six) |>
  st_join(districts |> select(home_district = district)) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(hospitals |> select(hospital_id, district), by = "hospital_id") |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            pct_other_district = round(100 * mean(home_district != district, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .by = hospital_id)
ex_home_district

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  hospital_id patients pct_other_district
  <chr>          <int>              <dbl>
1 H066              59                 68
2 H070              99                 57
3 H063              69                 55
4 H071              19                 63
5 H098              26                 73
6 H116              21                 67


Between 55% and 73% of the sampled patients of each hospital live in another district. A spatial join, from Chapter 56, turns a distance into a fact that the district staff can check on the ground.





Money demanded. Count the grievances in each hospital that mention money being demanded, with the pattern "demand|paid|pay |took money|took rs|cash|extra|receipt" of Chapter 51. Divide by the number of claims to get a rate per 1,000 claims. Which hospitals have the highest rate?






TipSolution






ex_money <- grievances |>
  filter(str_detect(clean_text, "demand|paid|pay |took money|took rs|cash|extra|receipt")) |>
  count(hospital_id, name = "money_grievances") |>
  left_join(count(claims, hospital_id, name = "claims"), by = "hospital_id") |>
  mutate(per_1000_claims = round(1000 * money_grievances / claims, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(per_1000_claims))
head(ex_money, 8)

  hospital_id money_grievances claims per_1000_claims
  <chr>                  <int>  <int>           <dbl>
1 H071                      13    133            97.7
2 H116                       9    174            51.7
3 H098                      12    265            45.3
4 H066                      14    575            24.3
5 H084                       1     45            22.2
6 H109                       1     48            20.8
7 H038                       2    106            18.9
8 H094                       1     53            18.9


Four of the top six by rate are camp hospitals. Patients should pay nothing under the scheme, so each such grievance is worth following up with the patient. A rate per 1,000 claims is fairer than a count, because large hospitals get more grievances simply by being large.





A stricter rule for ICU stays. Flag hospitals whose share of medical claims with an ICU stay is more than three times the overall share, on at least 20 claims. Which hospitals drop out compared with the rule of the chapter?






TipSolution






ex_icu3 <- icu_medical |>
  filter(claims >= 20, share > 3 * overall_icu) |>
  pull(hospital_id)
ex_icu3

[1] "H085" "H104"

setdiff(flag_icu, ex_icu3)

[1] "H107" "H108"


With the stricter rule, only H085 and H104 remain. H107 and H108 drop out. A stricter rule gives fewer false alarms, but may also miss a real case that is less extreme. Fix the rule before looking at the results, and record why it was chosen.





Was the lens billed all year? Count the claims with the separate lens (A06) in each month of 2024-25. Was it a habit throughout the year, or a short episode?






TipSolution






ex_lens_month <- claims |>
  filter(str_detect(packages, "A06")) |>
  count(month = floor_date(admission_date, "month"))
ex_lens_month

title: Part X: Reporting
text:
Analysis has to end in a report. This part shows how to produce the reports themselves from code, so that every number in them is computed and none is copied by hand.
You will build a report for every district from one template, and Excel working papers for the field party.


65  Reproducible Audit Reports
One template, a report for every district, and Excel working papers.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.1 Our audit, a scheme in five districts
Every analysis in this book ends the same way. The results have to reach someone: the audit officer, the head of the audit party, the auditee, or the report. Too often, this last step is done by hand. Figures are copied from the R console into Word, tables are pasted into Excel and formatted, and the whole process is repeated for each district, each month, each audit. Every copy is a chance for a mistake, and when the data changes, everything has to be done again.
In this chapter we learn to produce the reports themselves with code.
This book itself is written in Quarto, so everything you see here is a small version of the same idea.
Prerequisites
For rendering reports from R we also need the package quarto (install.packages("quarto")), and Quarto itself, which comes with RStudio.
A State’s Kisan Sahayata scheme pays each eligible farmer ₹2,000 in each of three instalments a year. We have the payment register and the beneficiary list for 2024-25, for five districts, and four checks to run.
The audit party wants one report for each district, to send to the District Collector, and one Excel workbook of the exceptions for each district, for verification in the field.
Code to create the data filesproject_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "kisan_audit")
dir.create(project_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(2025)
districts <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur")
n_ben <- 2500
beneficiaries <- tibble(
  ben_id   = sprintf("KS%06d", 1:n_ben),
  district = sample(districts, n_ben, TRUE),
  status   = sample(c("Active", "Deceased", "Ineligible"), n_ben, TRUE, prob = c(0.96, 0.025, 0.015)),
  account  = sprintf("%011.0f", runif(n_ben, 1e10, 9.99e10))
)
instalments <- tibble(instalment = 1:3,
                      due = as.Date(c("2024-06-15", "2024-10-15", "2025-02-15")))
payments <- beneficiaries |>
  filter(status == "Active" | runif(n()) < 0.5) |>      # some not-active beneficiaries still paid
  cross_join(instalments) |>
  mutate(paid_on = due + sample(0:20, n(), TRUE), amount = 2000) |>
  select(ben_id, district, instalment, paid_on, amount, account)
# Planted. Instalments paid twice, more often in Chandpur
dup <- payments |>
  slice_sample(n = 60, weight_by = if_else(district == "Chandpur", 5, 1)) |>
  mutate(paid_on = paid_on + sample(1:30, n(), TRUE))
payments <- bind_rows(payments, dup)
# Planted. Wrong amounts
wrong <- sample(nrow(payments), 40)
payments$amount[wrong] <- sample(c(4000, 20000, 6000), 40, TRUE)
# Planted. Six beneficiaries in Devgarh sharing one account
share <- beneficiaries |> filter(district == "Devgarh") |> slice_sample(n = 6) |> pull(ben_id)
beneficiaries$account[beneficiaries$ben_id %in% share] <- "50012345678"
payments$account[payments$ben_id %in% share] <- "50012345678"

write_csv(arrange(payments, paid_on), file.path(project_dir, "payments.csv"))
write_csv(beneficiaries, file.path(project_dir, "beneficiaries.csv"))
list.files(project_dir)

[1] "beneficiaries.csv" "payments.csv"

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
Was any instalment paid more than once to the same beneficiary?
Was any payment different from the entitlement of ₹2,000?
Was anything paid to a beneficiary marked deceased or ineligible?
Is any bank account shared by more than one beneficiary?

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
section: 65.2 Step 1. Put the checks in functions
text:
65.2 Step 1. Put the checks in functions
The first step towards any repeatable report is to write each check as a function (Chapter 3), which takes the data of one district and returns its exceptions. The functions are kept in one file, checks.R, which every report and every script then uses with source("checks.R"). A correction made once in this file applies everywhere.

check_duplicates <- function(pay) {
  pay |> filter(n() > 1, .by = c(ben_id, instalment)) |> arrange(ben_id, instalment, paid_on)
}
check_amount <- function(pay, entitlement = 2000) {
  pay |> filter(amount != entitlement)
}
check_status <- function(pay, ben) {
  pay |>
    inner_join(ben |> select(ben_id, status), by = "ben_id") |>
    filter(status != "Active")
}
check_shared_accounts <- function(ben) {
  ben |> filter(n() > 1, .by = account) |> arrange(account)
}

run_checks <- function(pay, ben) {
  list(duplicates      = check_duplicates(pay),
       wrong_amount    = check_amount(pay),
       not_active      = check_status(pay, ben),
       shared_accounts = check_shared_accounts(ben))
}

run_checks() returns a list of four data frames, one for each check. Let us try it on one district, and make the summary that the report will show.

payments_all <- read_csv(file.path(project_dir, "payments.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
benef_all    <- read_csv(file.path(project_dir, "beneficiaries.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                         col_types = cols(account = col_character()))

summarise_checks <- function(results, entitlement = 2000) {
  dup <- results$duplicates
  tibble(
    check  = c("Same instalment paid more than once",
               "Amount different from the entitlement",
               "Payment to deceased or ineligible beneficiaries",
               "Bank account shared by more than one beneficiary"),
    cases  = c(nrow(dup) - nrow(distinct(dup, ben_id, instalment)),
               nrow(results$wrong_amount),
               nrow(results$not_active),
               n_distinct(results$shared_accounts$account)),
    amount = c(sum(dup$amount) - sum(distinct(dup, ben_id, instalment, .keep_all = TRUE)$amount),
               sum(results$wrong_amount$amount - entitlement),
               sum(results$not_active$amount),
               NA)
  )
}

chandpur <- run_checks(filter(payments_all, district == "Chandpur"),
                       filter(benef_all, district == "Chandpur"))
summarise_checks(chandpur)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  check                                            cases amount
  <chr>                                            <int>  <dbl>
1 Same instalment paid more than once                 27  54000
2 Amount different from the entitlement               10  72000
3 Payment to deceased or ineligible beneficiaries     21  42000
4 Bank account shared by more than one beneficiary     0     NA


For duplicates, the cases and the amount count only the extra payments, not the first, legitimate one. The shared accounts are counted as accounts, and are not valued, since the money may have reached the right people.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.3 Step 2. Formatted tables with gt

A tibble printed in the console is fine for the analyst, but a report needs a proper table. The package gt builds one step by step, much as ggplot2 builds a chart: a title, formatted numbers, a note for missing values.

summarise_checks(chandpur) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", cases = "Cases", amount = "Amount (₹)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = amount, decimals = 0) |>
  sub_missing(columns = amount, missing_text = "Not valued") |>
  tab_header(title = "Summary of exceptions", subtitle = "Chandpur district, 2024-25") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: payment register and beneficiary list of the scheme.")

fmt_number() adds the thousands separators, and sub_missing() writes a phrase in place of NA. The same table appears correctly in HTML and in Word reports.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.4 Step 3. A parameterised Quarto report
A Quarto document is a plain text file with the extension .qmd. It has three kinds of content.

A header, between two lines of ---, written in a format called YAML. It gives the title, the output formats, and other options.

Text, written in Markdown: ## for headings, *italics*, **bold**, lists with -, and so on.

Code chunks, between ```{r} and ```, whose results (tables, charts, numbers) appear in the report. Numbers can also be placed inside sentences with inline code, written as a backtick, the letter r, the code, and a closing backtick.

The key to producing many reports from one file is a parameter. In the header, under params:, we declare a value with a default, here the district. Inside the document, the value is available as params$district. Change the parameter, and the same document becomes the report for another district.
Here is the complete template, audit_report.qmd.
---
title: "Kisan Sahayata payments: audit findings"
subtitle: "District report"
date: today
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
  docx: default
params:
  district: "Amarpur"
  payments_file: "payments.csv"
  beneficiaries_file: "beneficiaries.csv"
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
source("checks.R")

pay_all <- read_csv(params$payments_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
ben_all <- read_csv(params$beneficiaries_file, show_col_types = FALSE,
                    col_types = cols(account = col_character()))
pay <- pay_all |> filter(district == params$district)
ben <- ben_all |> filter(district == params$district)
results <- run_checks(pay, ben)
summary_tbl <- summarise_checks(results)

lakh <- function(x) paste0("₹", format(round(x / 1e5, 2), nsmall = 2), " lakh")
```

## District: `r params$district`

During 2024-25, `r format(nrow(pay), big.mark = ",")` payments totalling
`r lakh(sum(pay$amount))` were made to `r n_distinct(pay$ben_id)` beneficiaries
in `r params$district` district. The results of the checks are summarised below.

```{r}
summary_tbl |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", cases = "Cases", amount = "Amount (₹)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = amount, decimals = 0) |>
  sub_missing(columns = amount, missing_text = "Not valued")
```

In all, `r lakh(sum(summary_tbl$amount, na.rm = TRUE))` was paid irregularly
in the cases that could be valued.

## Payments by month

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
pay |>
  count(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month"), wt = amount, name = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, amount / 1e5)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "₹ lakh") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## About this report

```{r}
data_hash <- unname(tools::md5sum(c(params$payments_file, params$beneficiaries_file)))
```

Generated on `r format(Sys.time(), "%d %B %Y, %H:%M")` from `r params$payments_file`
(MD5 `r data_hash[1]`) and `r params$beneficiaries_file` (MD5 `r data_hash[2]`),
with `r R.version.string`.
A few points about the template.


execute: echo: false hides the code, so that the report shows only results. A report for the Collector should not contain R code.

embed-resources: true packs the charts and styles into the single HTML file, so that it can be sent by email.
Every number in the text is inline code. None is typed in, so none can go out of date.
The last section records when the report was made, from which data files, identified by their hashes (Section 8.6), and with which version of R. Anyone can later confirm that the report came from those files. This is the working-paper trail.

summarise_checks() is also kept in checks.R, along with the four checks.

To produce the report for one district from RStudio, open the file and click Render. The default district, Amarpur, is used.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
section: 65.5 Step 4. One report for every district
text:
65.5 Step 4. One report for every district
To render the template for every district, we call quarto_render() from the package quarto in a loop, giving a different parameter each time with execute_params. Since the subtitle is part of the header, not the code, we pass it as metadata with quarto_args. Each report gets its own file name.

library(quarto)

districts <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur")

walk(districts, \(d) {
  for (fmt in c("html", "docx")) {
    quarto_render(
      input          = "audit_report.qmd",
      output_format  = fmt,
      output_file    = paste0("audit_report_", d, ".", fmt),
      execute_params = list(district = d),
      quarto_args    = c("--metadata", paste0("subtitle:District report, ", d)),
      quiet          = TRUE
    )
  }
})

This produces ten files, an HTML and a Word report for each district, in under a minute, each with its own figures, table and chart. (We have not run the loop while building this book, since it renders separate documents, but it was tested on the files created above.) When the data is corrected, or a new month’s data arrives, running the loop again regenerates every report.






TipAudit tip



Word (docx) output is usually the most convenient for audit, since draft paras and reports go through several rounds of editing by people who do not use R. Generate the Word report from Quarto, so that the numbers are right, and let the editing happen in Word. Quarto can also use your office’s Word template for styles and letterhead, through the reference-doc option of the docx format.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.6 Step 5. Excel working papers
The field party needs the exceptions themselves, one row per case, to verify against the records. An Excel workbook is the most convenient form. With openxlsx we can build it exactly as we want: a summary sheet, a sheet for each check, a bold header, number formats, filters and frozen header rows.
We write a function that builds the workbook for one district.

write_working_paper <- function(district, pay_all, ben_all, folder) {
  pay <- filter(pay_all, district == !!district)
  ben <- filter(ben_all, district == !!district)
  results <- run_checks(pay, ben)

  wb <- createWorkbook()
  header_style <- createStyle(textDecoration = "bold", fgFill = "#DDEBF7", border = "bottom")
  money_style  <- createStyle(numFmt = "#,##0")

  # Summary sheet
  addWorksheet(wb, "Summary")
  writeData(wb, "Summary", paste("Kisan Sahayata audit, 2024-25:", district, "district"),
            startRow = 1)
  addStyle(wb, "Summary", createStyle(textDecoration = "bold", fontSize = 13), rows = 1, cols = 1)
  writeData(wb, "Summary", summarise_checks(results), startRow = 3, headerStyle = header_style)
  addStyle(wb, "Summary", money_style, rows = 4:7, cols = 3)
  setColWidths(wb, "Summary", cols = 1:3, widths = c(50, 10, 14))

  # One sheet per check
  for (check in names(results)) {
    addWorksheet(wb, check)
    writeData(wb, check, results[[check]], headerStyle = header_style, withFilter = TRUE)
    freezePane(wb, check, firstRow = TRUE)
    setColWidths(wb, check, cols = seq_along(results[[check]]), widths = "auto")
  }
  file <- file.path(folder, paste0("working_paper_", district, ".xlsx"))
  saveWorkbook(wb, file, overwrite = TRUE)
  file
}

A few details. withFilter = TRUE adds the filter buttons to the header row, freezePane() keeps the header visible while scrolling, and setColWidths(widths = "auto") fits the columns to their contents. The !!district inside filter() uses the value of the function’s argument, not a column of the same name, as in Section 19.4.
Now one workbook for each district.

wp_folder <- file.path(project_dir, "working_papers")
dir.create(wp_folder, showWarnings = FALSE)

wp_files <- map_chr(districts, \(d) write_working_paper(d, payments_all, benef_all, wp_folder))
basename(wp_files)

[1] "working_paper_Amarpur.xlsx"  "working_paper_Belapur.xlsx" 
[3] "working_paper_Chandpur.xlsx" "working_paper_Devgarh.xlsx" 
[5] "working_paper_Fatehpur.xlsx"


Let us check one of them by reading it back.

getSheetNames(wp_files[4])

Note



The newer package openxlsx2 offers the same features with a modern design, and is worth considering for new work. For simple output without formatting, writexl::write_xlsx(), which takes a named list of data frames and writes one sheet for each, is the quickest way (Chapter 10).

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.7 Organising an audit project
When reports are produced by code, the files of an audit fall naturally into a simple structure, as suggested in Chapter 8.
kisan_audit/
  data/                 the files received, never edited
  checks.R              the check functions, used by everything else
  audit_report.qmd      the report template
  run_all.R             the loop that renders every report and working paper
  reports/              the generated reports
  working_papers/       the generated workbooks
The rule is that nothing in reports/ or working_papers/ is ever edited by hand. If something is wrong, the fix goes into the data, the checks or the template, and run_all.R is run again. Then the reports, the working papers and the code always agree, and the whole audit can be reproduced from the data files by anyone, at any time.






Caution



Generated reports are only as right as the code behind them. Before sending reports to auditees, check one or two of them thoroughly by hand: recount a few cases from the raw data, and confirm the totals against the source. Once a template is verified, every report from it can be trusted to the same standard, which is far more than can be said for reports typed by hand.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.8 A suggested workflow


Write each check as a function, in one file, and test it on one unit.

Make a summary function that turns the results into a report-ready table.

Write the report template in Quarto, with a parameter for the unit, inline code for every number, and a section recording the data files, their hashes, and the date.

Render it once for the default unit, and check it thoroughly.

Render for every unit in a loop with quarto_render() and execute_params.

Generate the Excel working papers with openxlsx, one workbook per unit.

Never edit outputs by hand. Fix the inputs and re-run.







ImportantRemember




A report generated by code has no copying errors, and updates itself when the data changes.
Parameters, declared under params: and used as params$name, turn one template into many reports.

quarto_render(execute_params = ...) renders a template for each value in a loop.

gt makes formatted tables for HTML and Word; openxlsx makes formatted Excel working papers.
Record the data files, their hashes and the date in every report, so that it can be reproduced and verified.

title: 65  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
65.9 Try it yourself
These exercises use the payment register, the beneficiary list and the check functions of this chapter. Any file they write goes into the temporary folder of the R session. Try each one before you open the solution.


The Devgarh summary. Run the four checks for Devgarh, and show the summary as a gt table with the title “Summary of exceptions” and the subtitle “Devgarh district, 2024-25”.






TipSolution






devgarh <- run_checks(filter(payments_all, district == "Devgarh"),
                      filter(benef_all, district == "Devgarh"))

summarise_checks(devgarh) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", cases = "Cases", amount = "Amount (₹)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = amount, decimals = 0) |>
  sub_missing(columns = amount, missing_text = "Not valued") |>
  tab_header(title = "Summary of exceptions", subtitle = "Devgarh district, 2024-25")






Summary of exceptions


Devgarh district, 2024-25


Check
Cases
Amount (₹)




Same instalment paid more than once
6
12,000


Amount different from the entitlement
7
48,000


Payment to deceased or ineligible beneficiaries
27
56,000


Bank account shared by more than one beneficiary
1
Not valued






Only the district name changed. Devgarh shows 1 shared account, the planted one with six beneficiaries. This is the whole point of putting the checks in functions. The same code serves every district.





All districts in one table. Run the checks for every district, and make one table with a row for each district and a column for the cases of each check. Which district has the most duplicate instalments?






TipSolution






state_summary <- map(districts, \(d) {
  res <- run_checks(filter(payments_all, district == d),
                    filter(benef_all, district == d))
  summarise_checks(res) |> mutate(district = d)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

cases_wide <- state_summary |>
  mutate(check = c("duplicates", "wrong_amount", "not_active", "shared_accounts")[match(check, unique(check))]) |>
  select(district, check, cases) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = check, values_from = cases)

cases_wide |> arrange(desc(duplicates))

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  district duplicates wrong_amount not_active shared_accounts
  <chr>         <int>        <int>      <int>           <int>
1 Chandpur         27           10         21               0
2 Belapur          12           10         24               0
3 Fatehpur          8            4         30               0
4 Amarpur           7            9         42               0
5 Devgarh           6            7         27               1


Chandpur has the most duplicate instalments, 27. This agrees with what was planted, since duplicates were made more likely in Chandpur. A State-level table like this one tells the audit party where to send the field team first.





Irregular payments in lakh. From the State table of the previous exercise, work out the total irregular amount in each district, in lakh of rupees, leaving out the shared accounts which are not valued. Show it as a gt table with one decimal place.






TipSolution






irregular <- state_summary |>
  summarise(amount_lakh = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e5, .by = district) |>
  arrange(desc(amount_lakh))

irregular |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(district = "District", amount_lakh = "Irregular amount (₹ lakh)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = amount_lakh, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "Irregular payments by district", subtitle = "Kisan Sahayata, 2024-25")






Irregular payments by district


Kisan Sahayata, 2024-25


District
Irregular amount (₹ lakh)




Amarpur
1.8


Chandpur
1.7

1.6

1.5

1.2






In all, ₹7.7 lakh was paid irregularly in the cases that could be valued, the most in Amarpur. We divided by 1e5 before formatting, so the table shows lakh directly. na.rm = TRUE leaves out the NA of the shared accounts.





A State workbook. Save the table of cases by district as a one-sheet Excel workbook in the temporary folder, with a bold header row and a filter. Read it back to check it.






TipSolution






wb_state <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb_state, "Cases by district")
writeData(wb_state, "Cases by district", cases_wide, withFilter = TRUE,
          headerStyle = createStyle(textDecoration = "bold", fgFill = "#DDEBF7"))
setColWidths(wb_state, "Cases by district", cols = 1:5, widths = "auto")

state_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "cases_by_district.xlsx")
saveWorkbook(wb_state, state_file, overwrite = TRUE)

read.xlsx(state_file)

  district duplicates wrong_amount not_active shared_accounts
1  Amarpur          7            9         42               0
2  Belapur         12           10         24               0
3 Chandpur         27           10         21               0
4  Devgarh          6            7         27               1
5 Fatehpur          8            4         30               0


The workbook read back has the same 5 districts and the same counts. Reading a workbook back is a quick check that what we handed over is what we meant to hand over.





Does the hash catch a change? Make a copy of the payment register in the temporary folder, change the amount of one payment, and save it. Compare the MD5 hash of the copy with that of the original.






TipSolution






original_file <- file.path(project_dir, "payments.csv")
edited_file   <- file.path(tempdir(), "payments_edited.csv")

edited <- read_csv(original_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
edited$amount[1] <- edited$amount[1] + 1
write_csv(edited, edited_file)

hashes <- unname(tools::md5sum(c(original_file, edited_file)))
hashes

[1] "ca51f92c84c8e5de820820d114bb2031" "7aaf1b0a546953264a98a69fed3b3d09"

hashes[1] == hashes[2]

[1] FALSE


A change of just one rupee in one of 7,419 rows gives a completely different hash. So if a report records the hash of its data file, anyone can later prove whether the report was made from that exact file. This is why the template records the hashes in its last section.

title: Appendix B — Datasets Used in This Book
text:
B.1 Datasets that come with R
The book uses two kinds of data: datasets that come with R and its packages, which are convenient for showing how a function works, and data simulated for this book, which carry the audit examples.
The following datasets are available in every installation of R. Their descriptions below are taken from R’s own help pages.

title: Appendix B — Datasets Used in This Book
text:
anscombe: Four x-y datasets which have the same traditional statistical properties (mean, variance, correlation, regression line, etc.), yet are quite different.
iris: This famous (Fisher’s or Anderson’s) iris data set gives the measurements in centimeters of the variables sepal length and width and petal length and width, respectively, for 50 flowers from each of 3
nhtemp: The mean annual temperature in degrees Fahrenheit in New Haven, Connecticut, from 1912 to 1971.
Nile: Measurements of the annual flow of the river Nile at Aswan (formerly ‘Assuan’), 1871-1970, in 10^8 m^3, “with apparent changepoint near 1898” (Cobb(1978), Table 1, p.249).

title: Appendix B — Datasets Used in This Book
section: B.2 Data simulated for this book
text:
B.2 Data simulated for this book
Most audit examples use data simulated in R, because real audit data cannot be published. The data is made to look like what auditors receive, and irregularities are planted in it for the analysis to find. All names of persons, firms, offices and places are made up, and do not relate to any real entity.
In most chapters, the code that creates the data is shown, folded, at the start of the example, so that readers can see exactly what was planted, change it, and run it again. The table lists these datasets, chapter by chapter, in the order of the book. Chapters which use only a few values typed in by hand are left out.

The Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana data
Several chapters share one larger dataset, for an imaginary State health insurance scheme, Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY). They are the chapters on principal components (Chapter 46), clustering (Chapter 47), association rules (Chapter 48), text (Chapter 51, Chapter 52 and Chapter 53), maps (Chapter 56) and Benford’s Law (Chapter 32). The last chapter of Part IX, Chapter 64, brings all of them together in one audit. Its files are in the Data folder of the book’s repository. Planted in it are six hospitals behaving like “camps” (high claims per bed, short stays, weekend admissions, repeated admissions, unbundled packages) and two hospitals upcoding to intensive care, which the chapters find in different ways. The text and map files carry the same story. Grievances and feedback complain about the camp hospitals, their patients come from far away, and some inspection photos were taken far from the hospital.

title: Appendix C — R Packages Used in This Book
text:
C.1 Packages by part
R comes with a large set of functions, called base R. Most of the work in this book also uses packages, collections of functions written by others and shared freely, mostly through CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. Section 5 explains how packages are installed and loaded. This appendix lists all the packages used in the book. It gives one install command for each part, so that you can install only what you need and start learning straight away.
MASS, lattice and nnet, also used in the book, come with every installation of R and need no separate installation.

title: Appendix C — R Packages Used in This Book
text:
C.2 Installing the packages
The commands below need an internet connection, and may take a while the first time. If your office network blocks downloads, see the note on installing packages on an office network in Section 5.
There is no need to install everything at once. Start with the first command, which is enough for Gearing Up and Part I. Then install the packages of each part when you reach it.

# To begin, and for Part I
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "conflicted", "remotes"))

# Part II, Getting Data Ready
install.packages(c("digest", "openssl", "encryptr", "readxl", "writexl", "openxlsx", "janitor", "pdftools", "tidyxl",
                   "unpivotr", "rvest", "httr2", "xml2", "stringdist", "data.table", "duckdb", "dbplyr"))

# Part III, Working with Text Fields
install.packages("rebus")

# Part IV, Exploring and Sampling
install.packages(c("scales", "ggrepel", "patchwork", "RColorBrewer", "colorspace", "psych",
                   "skimr", "GGally", "PerformanceAnalytics", "broom"))

# Part V, Forensic Tests
install.packages(c("validate", "pointblank", "benford.analysis", "kableExtra", "stringdist", "phonics", "fullmetaphone",
                   "PGRdup", "bupaR", "processmapR", "edeaR", "processcheckR"))

# Part VI, Modelling and Risk Scoring
install.packages(c("broom", "performance", "car", "moderndive", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
                   "ranger", "deaR", "MatchIt", "cobalt", "marginaleffects", "sandwich"))

# Part VII, Finding Hidden Patterns
install.packages(c("cluster", "factoextra", "arules", "forecast", "timetk", "zoo",
                   "outliers", "FNN", "dbscan", "isotree", "changepoint"))

# Part VIII, Beyond Tables
install.packages(c("tidytext", "SnowballC", "wordcloud", "RColorBrewer", "igraph",
                   "igraphdata", "ggraph", "visNetwork", "sf", "leaflet", "tidygeocoder"))

# Part IX, Applying the Toolkit
install.packages("ranger")

# Part X, Reporting
install.packages(c("gt", "openxlsx", "quarto"))

If you prefer to install everything in one go, run all the commands above one after another.
One package used in Part VII is not on CRAN, and is installed from GitHub with the package remotes, which the first command above installs.

# Seasonal Hybrid ESD anomaly detection, by Twitter
remotes::install_github("twitter/AnomalyDetection")

The package fullmetaphone, installed with Part V above, is a full implementation of the Double Metaphone algorithm keeping phonetic codes of up to 32 characters. It was developed by Atharv Tyagi and the author, and is available on CRAN. It is used in Chapter 35, Chapter 34 and Chapter 36.






TipKeeping an analysis reproducible



Packages are updated from time to time, and occasionally a function changes its behaviour. For an audit that must be reproducible, record the versions used, as shown in Section 7 with sessionInfo(). For larger projects, the package renv keeps a separate, fixed set of package versions for each project, so that an analysis written today runs the same way next year.
